chapters.title: Nursing Today and the Health Care Delivery System

members.title: Nursing Today and the Health Care Delivery System
Nursing Today and the Health Care Delivery System

questions.stem: Select all of the components of evidence based practice.

options.text: The nurse's clinical expertise
options.rationale: Three legs plus context: evidence, expertise and the patient's values, which is why evidence based practice is not the same as doing whatever the literature says. Tradition is the thing evidence based practice exists to replace, and a single new study is not evidence; the level of the evidence and the quality of the design are what make it usable.

options.text: The available resources and the practice context
options.rationale: Three legs plus context: evidence, expertise and the patient's values, which is why evidence based practice is not the same as doing whatever the literature says. Tradition is the thing evidence based practice exists to replace, and a single new study is not evidence; the level of the evidence and the quality of the design are what make it usable.

options.text: The way the unit has always done it
options.rationale: Near miss concept Tradition is what evidence based practice replaces.

options.text: The best available research evidence
options.rationale: Three legs plus context: evidence, expertise and the patient's values, which is why evidence based practice is not the same as doing whatever the literature says. Tradition is the thing evidence based practice exists to replace, and a single new study is not evidence; the level of the evidence and the quality of the design are what make it usable.

options.text: The most recently published single study, regardless of its quality
options.rationale: Near miss concept Newest is not strongest; the level and quality of evidence decide.

options.text: The patient's values and preferences
options.rationale: Three legs plus context: evidence, expertise and the patient's values, which is why evidence based practice is not the same as doing whatever the literature says. Tradition is the thing evidence based practice exists to replace, and a single new study is not evidence; the level of the evidence and the quality of the design are what make it usable.

questions.takeaway: Patient values are part of the evidence, not an obstacle to it.
questions.strategy: One wrong option is tradition and the other confuses recency with quality.

questions.stem: Select all of the statements that describe the registered nurse's scope of practice.

options.text: The nurse assesses the patient and interprets the findings
options.rationale: Assessment, nursing diagnosis, planning, evaluation and delegation sit inside nursing practice and cannot be given away. The two wrong options are the two lines that never move: medical diagnosis and prescribing belong to another scope, and accountability stays with the delegating nurse no matter who performs the task.

options.text: The nurse evaluates the patient's response and modifies the plan
options.rationale: Assessment, nursing diagnosis, planning, evaluation and delegation sit inside nursing practice and cannot be given away. The two wrong options are the two lines that never move: medical diagnosis and prescribing belong to another scope, and accountability stays with the delegating nurse no matter who performs the task.

options.text: The nurse diagnoses medical conditions and prescribes treatment
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Medical diagnosis and prescribing are outside the registered nurse's scope.

options.text: The nurse delegates tasks while retaining accountability for the outcome
options.rationale: Assessment, nursing diagnosis, planning, evaluation and delegation sit inside nursing practice and cannot be given away. The two wrong options are the two lines that never move: medical diagnosis and prescribing belong to another scope, and accountability stays with the delegating nurse no matter who performs the task.

options.text: The nurse develops and revises the nursing plan of care
options.rationale: Assessment, nursing diagnosis, planning, evaluation and delegation sit inside nursing practice and cannot be given away. The two wrong options are the two lines that never move: medical diagnosis and prescribing belong to another scope, and accountability stays with the delegating nurse no matter who performs the task.

options.text: The nurse may hand off accountability along with a delegated task
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Accountability remains with the delegating nurse.

questions.takeaway: You can delegate the task. You never delegate the accountability.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options move a boundary that does not move.

questions.stem: Which nursing care delivery model assigns one nurse responsibility for a patient's care from admission through discharge, including planning when she is not on duty?

options.text: Primary nursing
options.rationale: Primary nursing gives one registered nurse round the clock accountability for a caseload, with associate nurses carrying out the plan on other shifts. Team nursing divides work among a group led by a registered nurse. Functional nursing assigns tasks rather than patients, one person doing all the medications. Case management coordinates across settings rather than within one.

options.text: Functional nursing
options.rationale: Near miss concept Assigns tasks across many patients rather than patients to a nurse.

options.text: Team nursing
options.rationale: Near miss concept A group led by a registered nurse, within one shift and unit.

options.text: Case management
options.rationale: Near miss concept Coordinates across settings and episodes, not continuous bedside accountability.

questions.takeaway: Primary is one nurse owning the plan. Case management is one nurse following the patient between buildings.
questions.strategy: Primary nursing and case management both center one nurse. The difference is whether she crosses settings.

questions.stem: Classify each activity by level of prevention.

rows.text: Cardiac rehabilitation after a myocardial infarction
Immunizing a healthy adult against influenza
Teaching a patient with a below knee amputation to use a prosthesis
Screening mammography in a woman with no symptoms

questions.takeaway: Primary stops disease before it starts. Secondary finds it early in someone without symptoms. Tertiary limits disability in someone who already has it, which is what rehabilitation is. Potter and Perry also place patients who already have a disease and are at risk of complications under secondary prevention, so a borderline case such as diabetic foot teaching can be argued either way; the clean tertiary examples are the ones where a deficit already exists. Ask first whether the patient already has the disease. That decides primary versus tertiary before you think about anything else.
questions.strategy: Smoking cessation is primary in a healthy person and tertiary in someone who already has lung disease. The same action changes level with the patient.

questions.stem: Select all of the ways health information technology supports safe practice.

options.text: Alert fatigue from a high volume of low value warnings
options.rationale: Near miss concept A real phenomenon and a hazard, not a support.

options.text: Copying forward a previous note to save charting time
options.rationale: Near miss concept Propagates outdated findings into the current record.

options.text: Clinical decision support alerting to an interaction
options.rationale: Technology helps where it removes dependence on a human remembering. It hurts where it adds noise or lets stale information propagate. Alert fatigue is a recognized safety hazard, and copying a note forward carries yesterday's assessment into today's chart, where the next clinician will believe it.

options.text: Standardized order sets reducing reliance on memory
options.rationale: Technology helps where it removes dependence on a human remembering. It hurts where it adds noise or lets stale information propagate. Alert fatigue is a recognized safety hazard, and copying a note forward carries yesterday's assessment into today's chart, where the next clinician will believe it.

options.text: A shared electronic record reducing information lost at handoff
options.rationale: Technology helps where it removes dependence on a human remembering. It hurts where it adds noise or lets stale information propagate. Alert fatigue is a recognized safety hazard, and copying a note forward carries yesterday's assessment into today's chart, where the next clinician will believe it.

options.text: Barcode medication administration verifying patient and drug
options.rationale: Technology helps where it removes dependence on a human remembering. It hurts where it adds noise or lets stale information propagate. Alert fatigue is a recognized safety hazard, and copying a note forward carries yesterday's assessment into today's chart, where the next clinician will believe it.

questions.takeaway: Copy forward charting puts a finding nobody assessed into a record people trust.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options are real consequences of the technology, and they reduce safety.

questions.stem: A patient is discharged from the hospital to a skilled nursing facility for several weeks of rehabilitation before going home. Which level of care is the facility providing?

options.text: Tertiary care
options.rationale: Near miss concept A highly specialized center such as a burn unit.

options.text: Secondary acute care
options.rationale: Near miss concept That was the hospital stay he just finished.

options.text: Continuing care
options.rationale: Near miss concept Indefinite support for chronic illness, not a several week rehabilitation stay with a discharge home at the end.

options.text: Restorative care
options.rationale: Restorative care is post acute, time limited and aimed at getting function back: rehabilitation, home health, a skilled nursing stay for recovery. Continuing care is ongoing and indefinite support for chronic illness or disability, such as long term care, assisted living, adult day care or hospice, and it is not defined by regaining function. The word for several weeks in the stem is what makes this restorative.

questions.takeaway: Restorative gets function back and ends. Continuing holds a life steady and does not.
questions.strategy: Levels of CARE are places. Levels of PREVENTION are purposes. Same adjectives, different question.

questions.stem: Select all of the actions that reflect the QSEN safety competency.

options.text: Keeping a personal log of other nurses' mistakes
options.rationale: Near miss concept Surveillance of individuals, which drives reporting underground.

options.text: Using barcode scanning rather than relying on memory
options.rationale: The safety competency is minimizing harm through system effectiveness and individual performance: use technology and standardized practice, reduce reliance on memory, communicate hazards, and take part in analyzing errors and designing improvements. Tracking colleagues' mistakes privately is the opposite of a blame free culture, and speed is a cause of error, not a defense against it.

options.text: Reporting a near miss so the system can be examined
options.rationale: The safety competency is minimizing harm through system effectiveness and individual performance: use technology and standardized practice, reduce reliance on memory, communicate hazards, and take part in analyzing errors and designing improvements. Tracking colleagues' mistakes privately is the opposite of a blame free culture, and speed is a cause of error, not a defense against it.

options.text: Working faster to stay ahead of the workload
options.rationale: Near miss concept Speed is where errors come from.

options.text: Speaking up about a hazard to the team and the patient
options.rationale: The safety competency is minimizing harm through system effectiveness and individual performance: use technology and standardized practice, reduce reliance on memory, communicate hazards, and take part in analyzing errors and designing improvements. Tracking colleagues' mistakes privately is the opposite of a blame free culture, and speed is a cause of error, not a defense against it.

options.text: Participating in an error analysis to redesign the process
options.rationale: The safety competency is minimizing harm through system effectiveness and individual performance: use technology and standardized practice, reduce reliance on memory, communicate hazards, and take part in analyzing errors and designing improvements. Tracking colleagues' mistakes privately is the opposite of a blame free culture, and speed is a cause of error, not a defense against it.

questions.takeaway: Reducing reliance on memory is the competency people forget, and it is the most useful one.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options are individual behaviors that make the system less safe, not more.

questions.stem: A patient's family is pressing for a feeding tube that the patient stated in writing he would not want. The nurse raises the advance directive at the care conference. Which nursing role is this?

options.text: Manager
options.rationale: Near miss concept Coordinating and delegating the work, not representing his wishes.

options.text: Educator
options.rationale: Near miss concept She is not teaching; she is asserting his documented wish.

options.text: Caregiver
options.rationale: Near miss concept Direct physical care, which is not what is happening here.

options.text: Advocate
options.rationale: Advocacy is speaking for a patient whose own voice is being discounted, and this is the classic case: he said what he wanted, he cannot say it now, and someone has to put it on the table. Caregiver is hands on care, educator is teaching, manager is coordinating the work. Students under recognize advocacy because it rarely looks like a task.

questions.takeaway: Advocacy is not a feeling. It is the thing you say out loud when a patient's choice is being rolled over.
questions.strategy: Ask what the nurse is doing for the patient in that sentence, not what she is generally responsible for.

questions.stem: Select all of the characteristics that make nursing a profession.

options.text: A code of ethics that governs practice
options.rationale: Knowledge, ethics, autonomy and self regulation are what separate a profession from a job, and autonomy is the one that matters at the bedside, because it is the basis for questioning an order that is unsafe. Following orders without question is the opposite of professional accountability and employment has nothing to do with professional status.

options.text: A requirement to follow every physician order without question
options.rationale: Near miss concept Contradicts autonomy and the duty to question an unsafe order.

options.text: A guarantee of employment after graduation
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Not a characteristic of a profession.

options.text: Autonomy in its own sphere of practice
options.rationale: Knowledge, ethics, autonomy and self regulation are what separate a profession from a job, and autonomy is the one that matters at the bedside, because it is the basis for questioning an order that is unsafe. Following orders without question is the opposite of professional accountability and employment has nothing to do with professional status.

options.text: Licensure and standards set by the profession and the state
options.rationale: Knowledge, ethics, autonomy and self regulation are what separate a profession from a job, and autonomy is the one that matters at the bedside, because it is the basis for questioning an order that is unsafe. Following orders without question is the opposite of professional accountability and employment has nothing to do with professional status.

options.text: A defined body of knowledge with its own research base
options.rationale: Knowledge, ethics, autonomy and self regulation are what separate a profession from a job, and autonomy is the one that matters at the bedside, because it is the basis for questioning an order that is unsafe. Following orders without question is the opposite of professional accountability and employment has nothing to do with professional status.

questions.takeaway: Autonomy is why you are obligated to question an unsafe order rather than carry it out.
questions.strategy: One wrong option is irrelevant to professional status; the other contradicts it.

questions.stem: A nurse is unsure whether a skill is within her scope. Which source defines it?

options.text: The Nurse Practice Act of the state where she is licensed
options.rationale: The Nurse Practice Act is state law and it is what defines scope. The Code of Ethics tells you how to practice, not what you are permitted to do. Policy can narrow scope within a facility but never widen it, and no policy makes something legal that the Act does not allow.

options.text: The National Council Licensure Examination test plan
options.rationale: Near miss concept Describes what is tested for entry to practice, not what you may do.

options.text: The American Nurses Association Code of Ethics for Nurses and its provisions
options.rationale: Near miss concept Professional obligations, not legal authority.

options.text: Her hospital's policy and procedure manual for the unit
options.rationale: Institution as rationale Policy restricts within the law and cannot expand it.

questions.takeaway: Law sets the ceiling. Policy can only lower it.
questions.strategy: An option naming an ethical code or an employer is answering a different question than what is legally permitted.

questions.stem: A nurse wants to know what constitutes competent performance of the nursing process. Which source answers that?

options.text: The facility's job description for a staff nurse
options.rationale: Institution as rationale One employer's expectations.

options.text: The American Nurses Association Standards of Practice
options.rationale: The ANA Standards of Practice describe competent nursing care through the nursing process: assessment, diagnosis, outcomes identification, planning, implementation and evaluation. The Standards of Professional Performance cover the other half, things like ethics, collaboration and quality. Accreditation goals and job descriptions sit on top of these.

options.text: The state Board of Nursing's disciplinary record
options.rationale: Near miss concept Shows what went wrong, not what competent practice is.

options.text: The Joint Commission National Patient Safety Goals
options.rationale: Near miss concept Accreditation requirements for organizations, not a definition of nursing competence.

questions.takeaway: Standards of Practice is the nursing process. Standards of Professional Performance is everything else about being a professional.
questions.strategy: Three options describe an employer, an accreditor or a regulator. The profession writes its own standards.

questions.stem: A nurse licensed in one state accepts a travel assignment in another. What governs her practice there?

options.text: The Nurse Practice Act of the state that issued her original license
options.rationale: Near miss concept A compact license grants the privilege to practice elsewhere, not to bring your home rules along.

options.text: The Nurse Practice Act of the state where the patient is located
options.rationale: You practice under the law of the state where the patient is, which matters for travel nursing and for telehealth across state lines. A multistate compact license grants the privilege to practice in other compact states; it does not export your home state's rules. The board in the state where the care happened is the one that investigates.

options.text: The standards of the agency employing her
options.rationale: Institution as rationale Agency policy operates within the law, never above it.

options.text: The American Nurses Association scope and standards
options.rationale: Near miss concept Professional standards, not legal authority.

questions.takeaway: The patient's location sets the law, not your license's address.
questions.strategy: Two options substitute an employer or a professional body for state law.

questions.stem: A unit notices its catheter infection rate is rising and begins testing a daily line necessity review, measuring the rate monthly. Is this quality improvement or research?

options.text: Research, because it would need institutional review board approval
options.rationale: Near miss concept Quality improvement generally does not require it, which follows from the aim.

options.text: Neither, because the project does not include a control group
options.rationale: Near miss concept A control group is not required for quality improvement.

options.text: Quality improvement, because it applies known practice locally
options.rationale: Quality improvement takes an intervention already known to work and adapts it locally, measuring whether the local process improved. Research generates new generalizable knowledge and requires institutional review board oversight and informed consent. Measuring something does not make it research, which is the distinction that confuses people most.

options.text: Research, because it collects data and then measures an outcome
options.rationale: Near miss concept Quality improvement measures too; the aim is what differs.

questions.takeaway: Research creates new knowledge. Quality improvement applies known knowledge here.
questions.strategy: Collecting data is not what defines research. Generalizable new knowledge is.

questions.stem: A patient's care involves nursing, physical therapy, nutrition, social work and pharmacy. Which action best reflects the nurse's coordinating role?

options.text: Carry out each discipline's recommendations exactly as written
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome Executes without reconciling, which is where contradictions reach the patient.

options.text: Ask the provider to decide which recommendations come first
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Coordination of care is nursing's, not something to hand upward.

options.text: Combine each discipline's input into one plan the patient can follow
options.rationale: The nurse is the one person who sees the whole patient across all of it, which is why coordination lands here. Five separate expert plans can contradict each other, and the patient goes home with instructions that do not fit together. Someone has to reconcile them into one set of things the patient will actually do.

options.text: Document each discipline's notes in the nursing record at the end of each shift
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Copies information rather than integrating it.

questions.takeaway: Five good plans that conflict is not a plan. Reconciling them is nursing work.
questions.strategy: Two options pass the synthesis to someone else or skip it entirely.

questions.stem: A hospital adds a program to reduce nurse burnout alongside its existing work on cost, population health and patient experience. Which framework does this complete?

options.text: The Quadruple Process
options.rationale: Near miss concept No such thing. The word is Aim.

options.text: The Triple Aim
options.rationale: Near miss concept The original three, without the clinician.

options.text: Magnet recognition
options.rationale: Near miss concept A nursing excellence credential, not these aims.

options.text: The Quadruple Aim
options.rationale: The Triple Aim is better patient experience, better population health and lower cost. The Quadruple Aim adds improved clinician well being, on the reasoning that the first three cannot be achieved by a workforce that is burning out. That fourth aim is why staffing and burnout are system quality issues and not personal resilience problems.

questions.takeaway: The fourth aim is the clinician. It was added because the other three depend on it.
questions.strategy: When a stem adds something to an existing set of three, it is asking what the addition is called.

questions.stem: A patient with extensive burns is transferred to a regional burn center. Which level of care is this?

options.text: Secondary or acute
options.rationale: Near miss concept The general hospital episode, which is what he is being transferred out of.

options.text: Tertiary
options.rationale: Tertiary care is the highly specialized setting that a community hospital cannot provide: burn centers, transplant programs, neonatal intensive care. Secondary acute care is the ordinary hospital episode. Restorative care picks the patient up afterward and works on function. Do not confuse these with the levels of PREVENTION, which describe intent rather than setting.

options.text: Restorative
options.rationale: Near miss concept Rehabilitation after the acute phase, which comes later for this patient.

options.text: Preventive or primary
options.rationale: Near miss concept Keeping people well, which is not what a burn center does.

questions.takeaway: Tertiary care is a place. Tertiary prevention is a purpose. Same word, different question.
questions.strategy: Read the noun. Care means setting and intensity; prevention means what you are trying to accomplish.

questions.stem: A patient is admitted at 0200 through the emergency department with a new diagnosis of heart failure. When should discharge planning begin?

options.text: When the case manager completes the initial consultation
options.rationale: Institution as rationale A process step, not the standard.

options.text: On admission
options.rationale: Discharge planning begins on admission because the home situation, support, equipment needs and teaching time all have to be identified while there is still time to arrange them. Waiting for stability or for an order compresses the work into the last hours of the stay.

options.text: When the provider writes the discharge order
options.rationale: Institution as rationale Workflow convenience offered as clinical reasoning.

options.text: After the patient demonstrates understanding of the medication regimen
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is an outcome of discharge teaching, which happens inside the plan.

options.text: Once the patient is medically stable
options.rationale: Correct but premature Stability is not the trigger; admission is.

questions.takeaway: Discharge planning starts on admission, not at discharge.
questions.strategy: A single sentence answers a surprising number of items. This is one of them.

questions.stem: A nurse reads that a long standing unit practice is not supported by current evidence. What should she do?

options.text: Change her own practice quietly and continue with her shift
options.rationale: Near miss concept Right conclusion, and an unannounced variation the next nurse will not expect.

options.text: Wait for the provider group to raise the issue with the unit
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Nursing practice is nursing's to examine.

options.text: Bring the evidence to the practice council for protocol review
options.rationale: Evidence based practice means the best available evidence, clinical expertise and patient preference together, and changing a protocol is a system action rather than a private one. Acting alone creates a practice variation nobody else knows about, which is its own safety problem. Policy being old is not a reason to keep it.

options.text: Continue the current practice, because it is still unit policy
options.rationale: Institution as rationale Policy as the reason to ignore evidence.

questions.takeaway: One nurse quietly doing it differently is a variation, not an improvement.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options defer to tradition or to another discipline. Neither is how practice changes.

questions.stem: A patient is being discharged home with a new oxygen concentrator, three new medications and a wound that needs daily dressing changes. What is the nurse's priority before discharge?

options.text: Review the discharge paperwork with him and get his signature
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome Documents the handoff rather than securing the care.

options.text: Give written instructions and verify that he is able to read and follow them
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome Reading is not doing, and literacy is only one barrier.

options.text: Schedule the follow up appointment with the provider before he leaves
options.rationale: Correct but premature Necessary, and it is days away from the dressing change due tomorrow.

options.text: Confirm he or a caregiver can do the care and services are arranged
options.rationale: Discharge planning begins at admission and ends with a teach back, not a handout. Someone has to actually do the dressing change tomorrow, and the equipment has to be at the house. Paperwork and appointments are part of it, and they do not establish that the care will happen.

questions.takeaway: Discharge teaching is finished when the patient shows you, not when you have told them.
questions.strategy: Three options complete a task. One confirms an outcome.

questions.stem: A patient refuses a scheduled bath because he is exhausted and wants to rest. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ask a family member to persuade him to have it now
options.rationale: Near miss concept Recruits pressure rather than respecting a competent decision.

options.text: Reschedule the bath and document his preference and reason
options.rationale: Patient centered care means the patient's values direct the plan where safety allows, and a bath is not time critical. Recording why matters: a patient who is too exhausted to bathe is giving you an assessment finding, not just a preference.

options.text: Document a refusal of care and move on to the next task
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Records the no and loses the why.

options.text: Explain that baths are given in the morning and proceed
options.rationale: Institution as rationale Routine as the reason, over the patient's stated need.

questions.takeaway: A refusal with a reason is data. Chart the reason, not just the refusal.
questions.strategy: The word refusal in an option often signals a chart entry that closes a problem instead of exploring it.

questions.stem: A patient with limited English has been scheduled for a procedure. The consent was obtained with his adult son interpreting. Select all of the nurse's appropriate actions.

options.text: Proceed, since a family member interpreted and the form is signed
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Treats the signature as the consent.

options.text: Notify the provider that the consent process needs to be repeated with an interpreter
options.rationale: A signature on a form is not consent; understanding is. A family interpreter filters, softens and may lack the vocabulary, and the patient may not disclose in front of a relative, so the consent is not established. The nurse witnesses understanding, which means she cannot proceed. Asking the son to vouch for his own interpretation proves nothing.

options.text: Arrange a professional interpreter and verify his understanding before the procedure
options.rationale: A signature on a form is not consent; understanding is. A family interpreter filters, softens and may lack the vocabulary, and the patient may not disclose in front of a relative, so the consent is not established. The nurse witnesses understanding, which means she cannot proceed. Asking the son to vouch for his own interpretation proves nothing.

options.text: Document what the patient can state about the procedure in his own words
options.rationale: A signature on a form is not consent; understanding is. A family interpreter filters, softens and may lack the vocabulary, and the patient may not disclose in front of a relative, so the consent is not established. The nurse witnesses understanding, which means she cannot proceed. Asking the son to vouch for his own interpretation proves nothing.

options.text: Ask the son to confirm that he explained everything accurately
options.rationale: Near miss concept Asks the untrained interpreter to validate his own interpretation.

options.text: Hold the procedure until informed consent is established
options.rationale: A signature on a form is not consent; understanding is. A family interpreter filters, softens and may lack the vocabulary, and the patient may not disclose in front of a relative, so the consent is not established. The nurse witnesses understanding, which means she cannot proceed. Asking the son to vouch for his own interpretation proves nothing.

questions.takeaway: A signed form with no verified understanding is a defective consent, and the nurse is the one who notices.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options accept the form, one by relying on the signature and one by relying on the interpreter to audit himself.

questions.stem: A patient asks the nurse whether she should take the antihypertensive the provider prescribed, given the side effects she has read about. What is the nurse's most appropriate response?

options.text: Explore her concerns, teach about the drug, and involve the provider
options.rationale: Teaching about a medication is squarely nursing. Prescribing and deprescribing are not, so you neither tell her to stop nor dismiss her question with deference. The nursing work is finding out what she actually read and fears, giving her accurate information, and getting her in front of the person who can change the prescription if it should change.

options.text: Advise her that she can stop it if the side effects begin to bother her
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Stopping an antihypertensive is a prescribing decision.

options.text: Tell her she should decide for herself, since it is her own body
options.rationale: Near miss concept True about autonomy and it withholds the teaching that makes the decision informed.

options.text: Tell her the provider knows best and to take it exactly as prescribed
options.rationale: Institution as rationale Deference instead of teaching, and it leaves her concern unanswered.

questions.takeaway: Teach the drug, do not prescribe or deprescribe it, and get her to the person who can.
questions.strategy: Two options abandon her to a decision without the information she asked for.

questions.stem: A hospital policy allows assistive personnel to administer oral medications. The state Nurse Practice Act does not. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Follow the hospital policy, since it governs practice within that particular facility
options.rationale: Institution as rationale Policy does not override state law, and it will not defend you.

options.text: Follow the Nurse Practice Act and raise the conflict up the chain
options.rationale: Law sets the ceiling and policy can only lower it, never raise it. A policy permitting something the Act prohibits does not protect you, and delegating under it leaves you accountable. The second half matters as much: a conflict like this will catch someone else, so it goes up the chain rather than being quietly worked around.

options.text: Ask the attending provider which of the two rules to follow
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Nursing scope is not a provider's to determine.

options.text: Follow whichever rule is stricter without raising the conflict
options.rationale: Near miss concept Safe for you today and leaves the conflict live for the next nurse.

questions.takeaway: Policy can narrow the law. It can never widen it.
questions.strategy: The option that merely follows the more restrictive rule is close, and it leaves a dangerous policy in place for everyone else.

questions.stem: A nurse discovers she gave a medication to the wrong patient. The patient is unharmed. What should she do first?

options.text: Complete the occurrence report
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting A quality document, and it comes after the patient is safe.

options.text: Document the error in the patient's chart
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting The chart records the clinical facts after the assessment is done.

options.text: Assess the patient and notify the provider
options.rationale: The patient comes first in every error. Assess, notify the provider so any needed monitoring or antidote starts, then tell the manager, document the clinical facts in the chart, and complete the occurrence report separately. The report is a quality document and is never referenced in the chart.

options.text: Notify her manager
options.rationale: Correct but premature Happens, and after the clinical response.

questions.takeaway: Patient, provider, manager, chart, report. In that order.
questions.strategy: Three options start the paperwork before anyone has looked at the patient.

questions.topic: the nurse as a member of a profession
questions.stem: A nurse disagrees with a new unit protocol she believes is unsafe. Which action best reflects professional accountability?
questions.objective: the nurse as a member of a profession

options.text: Follow it exactly and record her disagreement in each patient chart
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting The chart is not the venue for practice disputes.

options.text: Discuss her concerns informally with colleagues on the unit
options.rationale: Correct but premature A reasonable first conversation that changes nothing on its own.

options.text: Bring her safety concern and the evidence to the practice council
options.rationale: Professional accountability means using the mechanisms that can actually change practice, with evidence rather than preference. Charting a disagreement puts an opinion in a legal record without changing anything. Quietly practicing differently creates a variation nobody knows about, which is its own safety problem. Talking only to colleagues builds frustration and no change.

options.text: Quietly continue her previous practice, which she believes is safer
options.rationale: Near miss concept An undocumented variation the next nurse will not expect.

questions.takeaway: Shared governance exists for this. Use it rather than practicing an unannounced exception.
questions.strategy: Three options register the disagreement somewhere that cannot act on it.

questions.stem: Which question is the most appropriate opening for a sexual history?

options.text: "Is there any chance you could be pregnant right now?"
options.rationale: Correct but premature A necessary screening question in the right context, and it assumes anatomy and partners you have not asked about yet.

options.text: "Do you have a boyfriend or a husband at home?"
options.rationale: Near miss concept Assumes a male partner and makes correcting you the patient's job.

options.text: "You're not married at the moment, are you?"
options.rationale: Near miss concept A leading question that invites the answer you expect.

options.text: "Are you sexually active, and with what partners?"
options.rationale: The open version does not assume a gender, a relationship structure or a kind of sex, and it lets the patient tell you what is relevant to screening. The gendered version makes the patient decide whether to correct you, and many will not bother, which costs you the history.

questions.takeaway: An assuming question gets you an edited answer.
questions.strategy: The pregnancy question is reasonable later and assumes anatomy and behavior you have not established.

questions.stem: Select all of the factors that contribute to health disparities in LGBTQ+ patients.

options.text: Higher rates of minority stress affecting mental health
options.rationale: The disparities come from how care is delivered and from the chronic stress of stigma, not from anything inherent to the patients. Delayed care, clinician assumptions, systems with nowhere to record the right name, and minority stress are the mechanisms. Both wrong options locate the problem in the patient.

options.text: A general unwillingness to follow prescribed treatment plans
options.rationale: Near miss concept Blames the patient for a system that has often treated them badly.

options.text: A biological predisposition to most chronic diseases
options.rationale: Near miss concept No such predisposition; the excess risk is from stress and access.

options.text: Intake forms with no place for an affirmed name or pronouns
options.rationale: The disparities come from how care is delivered and from the chronic stress of stigma, not from anything inherent to the patients. Delayed care, clinician assumptions, systems with nowhere to record the right name, and minority stress are the mechanisms. Both wrong options locate the problem in the patient.

options.text: Clinicians assuming orientation or identity instead of asking
options.rationale: The disparities come from how care is delivered and from the chronic stress of stigma, not from anything inherent to the patients. Delayed care, clinician assumptions, systems with nowhere to record the right name, and minority stress are the mechanisms. Both wrong options locate the problem in the patient.

options.text: Delaying care because of earlier negative experiences
options.rationale: The disparities come from how care is delivered and from the chronic stress of stigma, not from anything inherent to the patients. Delayed care, clinician assumptions, systems with nowhere to record the right name, and minority stress are the mechanisms. Both wrong options locate the problem in the patient.

questions.takeaway: The disparity is in the system and the stress, never in the person.
questions.strategy: Any option that blames the patient's biology or cooperation is wrong on its face.

questions.stem: Select all of the practices that make a health history inclusive for a transgender patient.

options.text: Ask about surgical history only if the patient volunteers it first
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Sounds respectful and misses care the patient needs.

options.text: Ask which organs are present rather than assuming from the recorded sex
options.rationale: Screening follows anatomy, not the gender marker, which is why you ask what organs are present rather than guessing, and why a trans woman who has retained her prostate still needs that considered. Explaining the reason for a question is what makes it clinical rather than intrusive. Waiting to be volunteered means missing care, and using the legal name when the patient uses another is the single most common reason trans patients avoid health care.

options.text: Ask what words the patient uses for their own body and use those words
options.rationale: Screening follows anatomy, not the gender marker, which is why you ask what organs are present rather than guessing, and why a trans woman who has retained her prostate still needs that considered. Explaining the reason for a question is what makes it clinical rather than intrusive. Waiting to be volunteered means missing care, and using the legal name when the patient uses another is the single most common reason trans patients avoid health care.

options.text: Ask for and use the patient's name and pronouns, and document them
options.rationale: Screening follows anatomy, not the gender marker, which is why you ask what organs are present rather than guessing, and why a trans woman who has retained her prostate still needs that considered. Explaining the reason for a question is what makes it clinical rather than intrusive. Waiting to be volunteered means missing care, and using the legal name when the patient uses another is the single most common reason trans patients avoid health care.

options.text: Use the legal name throughout the encounter to keep the record consistent
options.rationale: Institution as rationale Record both; address the patient by their name.

options.text: Explain why a sensitive question is being asked before you ask it
options.rationale: Screening follows anatomy, not the gender marker, which is why you ask what organs are present rather than guessing, and why a trans woman who has retained her prostate still needs that considered. Explaining the reason for a question is what makes it clinical rather than intrusive. Waiting to be volunteered means missing care, and using the legal name when the patient uses another is the single most common reason trans patients avoid health care.

questions.takeaway: Screen the anatomy that is there. The gender marker in the chart does not tell you what to screen.
questions.strategy: One wrong option waits for the patient to raise it; the other uses a name the patient did not choose.

questions.stem: Select all of the factors that reduce health care access for LGBTQ+ patients.

options.text: An inherent unwillingness to engage with preventive care
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Avoidance is a learned response to past treatment, not a trait.

options.text: Intake forms and systems that do not record the patient's identity accurately
options.rationale: Every real barrier here sits in the system or the clinician, not in the patient, which is the whole point: disparities in this population come from how care is delivered and from avoidance earned by past experience. The two wrong options locate the problem inside the patient, one as biology and one as attitude, and both are false.

options.text: A higher baseline rate of genetic disease in this population
options.rationale: Near miss concept Not supported; the disparities are access and treatment driven.

options.text: Previous experiences of discrimination in health settings
options.rationale: Every real barrier here sits in the system or the clinician, not in the patient, which is the whole point: disparities in this population come from how care is delivered and from avoidance earned by past experience. The two wrong options locate the problem inside the patient, one as biology and one as attitude, and both are false.

options.text: Clinician assumptions that the patient is heterosexual or cisgender
options.rationale: Every real barrier here sits in the system or the clinician, not in the patient, which is the whole point: disparities in this population come from how care is delivered and from avoidance earned by past experience. The two wrong options locate the problem inside the patient, one as biology and one as attitude, and both are false.

options.text: Fear that disclosure will change the quality of care received
options.rationale: Every real barrier here sits in the system or the clinician, not in the patient, which is the whole point: disparities in this population come from how care is delivered and from avoidance earned by past experience. The two wrong options locate the problem inside the patient, one as biology and one as attitude, and both are false.

questions.takeaway: The barriers are in the system, not in the patient. That is what makes them fixable.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options blame the patient for a disparity the system produces.

questions.stem: Which nursing statement reflects the most appropriate approach to a patient whose gender presentation the nurse cannot categorize?

options.text: "I just want to make sure I put you in the right room."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Frames the person as a logistics problem.

options.text: "Are you a man or a woman?"
options.rationale: Near miss concept Forces a binary answer and reads as a demand to explain themselves.

options.text: Saying nothing and checking the chart for the legal sex
options.rationale: Near miss concept The chart may be wrong, and this avoids a question that takes four seconds.

options.text: "How would you like me to address you?"
options.rationale: One short question, asked of everyone, answers it without making the patient a puzzle you are solving. Asking someone to categorize themselves in binary terms is intrusive and often unanswerable. Checking the chart gets you the legal sex, which may be wrong, and framing the question around room assignment makes the patient a logistical problem.

questions.takeaway: Ask how to address them. Ask it of everybody and it stops being a loaded question.
questions.strategy: Two options make the patient's identity an administrative problem to be solved.

questions.stem: Select all of the measures that make a unit more welcoming to LGBTQ+ patients.

options.text: Asking about gender identity only when the patient appears to be transgender
options.rationale: Near miss concept Selective questioning based on appearance, which singles people out and misses everyone else.

options.text: Discussing a patient's identity with staff who are not involved in their care
options.rationale: Near miss concept A privacy violation under the need to know standard.

options.text: Providing staff education on inclusive communication
options.rationale: Asking everyone is what makes the question routine rather than an accusation, and it catches the patients you would not have guessed. Neutral language in every conversation costs nothing. Asking selectively based on appearance is profiling, and discussing a patient's identity with uninvolved staff is a privacy violation.

options.text: Asking all patients their pronouns as part of routine admission
options.rationale: Asking everyone is what makes the question routine rather than an accusation, and it catches the patients you would not have guessed. Neutral language in every conversation costs nothing. Asking selectively based on appearance is profiling, and discussing a patient's identity with uninvolved staff is a privacy violation.

options.text: Documenting affirmed name and pronouns where the care team will see them
options.rationale: Asking everyone is what makes the question routine rather than an accusation, and it catches the patients you would not have guessed. Neutral language in every conversation costs nothing. Asking selectively based on appearance is profiling, and discussing a patient's identity with uninvolved staff is a privacy violation.

options.text: Using partner or spouse rather than assuming husband or wife
options.rationale: Asking everyone is what makes the question routine rather than an accusation, and it catches the patients you would not have guessed. Neutral language in every conversation costs nothing. Asking selectively based on appearance is profiling, and discussing a patient's identity with uninvolved staff is a privacy violation.

questions.takeaway: Ask everyone. Selective asking is profiling and it singles people out.
questions.strategy: One wrong option profiles, the other breaches confidentiality.

questions.stem: A nurse is taking a history from a woman who mentions her wife. What is the most appropriate approach to the sexual and reproductive history?

options.text: Ask whether she has considered how her lifestyle affects her health
options.rationale: Near miss concept Framed as health teaching and heard as judgment.

options.text: Skip the sexual history unless the patient brings it up herself
options.rationale: Near miss concept Leaves out screening the patient came in for.

options.text: Ask the same screening questions as for anyone, based on anatomy
options.rationale: Screening follows anatomy, not partner or identity. A woman with a cervix needs cervical screening regardless of who she is married to, and assuming otherwise is a documented cause of missed cancers in this population. Ask what organs are present, what the patient does, and go from there.

options.text: Omit the cervical screening questions, since she is not at risk
options.rationale: Near miss concept A real and documented error. Risk follows anatomy and behavior, not orientation.

questions.takeaway: Screen the organs the patient has, not the partner you assumed.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options drop a screening or a question based on an assumption about risk.

questions.stem: Match each term to what it describes.

rows.text: How a person presents through clothing, name, voice and behavior
The designation recorded at birth based on anatomy
A person's internal sense of being male, female, both or neither
To whom a person is physically and emotionally attracted

questions.takeaway: These four are independent of each other, which is the whole point. Knowing someone's gender identity tells you nothing about their orientation, and expression is separate from both. Conflating them is the most common error and it produces assumptions that patients notice immediately. Identity is who you are. Orientation is who you are drawn to. They do not predict each other.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the sentence is about the self, the presentation, or the other person.

questions.stem: A transgender woman is admitted. Select all of the nurse's appropriate actions regarding her information.

options.text: Ask her which visitors are aware before discussing it in front of them
options.rationale: Both names belong in the record for different purposes, and the affirmed one belongs where staff will actually read it. The need to know standard limits the rest. Asking who among her visitors knows prevents an accidental outing, which can cost someone housing or family. A nursing station announcement and a door sign both disclose to people who do not need it.

options.text: Share her identity only with care team members who need to know
options.rationale: Both names belong in the record for different purposes, and the affirmed one belongs where staff will actually read it. The need to know standard limits the rest. Asking who among her visitors knows prevents an accidental outing, which can cost someone housing or family. A nursing station announcement and a door sign both disclose to people who do not need it.

options.text: Keep the legal name on the band and record for ID and billing
options.rationale: Both names belong in the record for different purposes, and the affirmed one belongs where staff will actually read it. The need to know standard limits the rest. Asking who among her visitors knows prevents an accidental outing, which can cost someone housing or family. A nursing station announcement and a door sign both disclose to people who do not need it.

options.text: Record her affirmed name and pronouns where the team will see them
options.rationale: Both names belong in the record for different purposes, and the affirmed one belongs where staff will actually read it. The need to know standard limits the rest. Asking who among her visitors knows prevents an accidental outing, which can cost someone housing or family. A nursing station announcement and a door sign both disclose to people who do not need it.

options.text: Mention her history at the nursing station so everyone is prepared
options.rationale: Near miss concept An open area and an audience wider than the care team.

options.text: Place a note on the door so all staff use the correct pronouns
options.rationale: Near miss concept Visible to everyone who walks past, including visitors.

questions.takeaway: Ask who in the room knows, before you say anything in front of them.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options come from good intentions and broadcast her information.

questions.stem: A patient on long term estrogen therapy is admitted. Which nursing consideration is most relevant?

options.text: Estrogen raises clot risk, so assess and address thromboembolism
options.rationale: Estrogen therapy increases clotting risk, and a hospitalized, immobilized patient is already at risk, so prophylaxis and mobility matter more here. Hormone therapy is not routinely stopped on admission, and stopping it abruptly causes physical and psychological harm. Any hold is a clinical decision with the patient, not an administrative default.

options.text: Hormone therapy should always be held during a hospital stay
options.rationale: Near miss concept Not routine; abrupt discontinuation causes harm.

options.text: Hormone therapy has no drug interactions worth monitoring
options.rationale: Near miss concept It has real effects on clotting, lipids and liver values.

options.text: Ask the patient to justify continuing the hormone therapy
options.rationale: Near miss concept No other long term medication is treated this way.

questions.takeaway: Think clot risk with estrogen, and do not stop the therapy by default.
questions.strategy: Two options treat gender affirming care as optional in a way no other chronic therapy would be.

questions.stem: A 68 year old transgender woman has been on estrogen for 20 years and had vaginoplasty. She asks what cancer screening she needs. What should the nurse explain?

options.text: She needs only the screening recommended for cisgender men
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would omit breast tissue developed over 20 years of estrogen.

options.text: Screening follows her organs: breast, and the prostate still present
options.rationale: Vaginoplasty does not remove the prostate, so prostate tissue remains and remains screenable. Long term estrogen develops breast tissue, so breast screening applies. Neither a male nor a female template fits, which is exactly why the rule is to inventory the organs rather than apply a category. Ask what tissue is present, then screen it.

options.text: She needs only the screening recommended for cisgender women
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would omit prostate tissue that is still present.

options.text: Twenty years of estrogen removes the need for cancer screening
options.rationale: Absolute language It changes some risks and eliminates no screening.

questions.takeaway: Take an organ inventory. Neither standard template fits, and the organs decide.
questions.strategy: Both category based options fail for the same reason: they screen a template instead of a person.

questions.stem: A transgender man is admitted for an appendectomy. He has a cervix and a uterus and takes testosterone. Which preoperative question is essential?

options.text: Whether pregnancy is possible, asked as for any patient with a uterus
options.rationale: Testosterone usually stops menstruation and does not reliably prevent pregnancy, and pregnancy status changes imaging, anesthesia and drug choices. So the question is clinically essential and it is asked of anyone with a uterus, which is what makes it neutral rather than intrusive. Surgical history matters only where it affects this operation, and the other two questions serve curiosity.

options.text: Whether he has had gender affirming surgery, for the medical record and anesthesia
options.rationale: Near miss concept Relevant only where it affects this procedure; for the record is not an indication.

options.text: How long he has identified as male, to document his history
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Serves curiosity and changes nothing clinically.

options.text: Whether his family is aware of his gender identity before surgery
options.rationale: Near miss concept His to disclose, and relevant only if he raises it around visitors.

questions.takeaway: Screen by the anatomy present. Testosterone is not contraception.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the answer would change the care in the next hour. If not, you do not need it now.

questions.stem: A nurse notices the unit's admission form offers only male and female and has no field for an affirmed name. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Ask the patient to choose whichever listed option is closest
options.rationale: Near miss concept Asks the patient to absorb the system's shortcoming.

options.text: Leave the fields blank to avoid recording anything inaccurate
options.rationale: Near miss concept Leaves the next nurse with nothing, which is how misgendering happens.

options.text: Use the legal information only, since that is all the current admission form allows you to record
options.rationale: Institution as rationale A form limitation treated as a clinical rule.

options.text: Record it where staff will see it and report the form as a system issue
options.rationale: You solve the problem in front of you and then fix the thing that caused it. The affirmed name and pronouns go somewhere prominent so the next nurse does not have to be corrected, and the form gets raised through practice council, because every patient after this one will hit the same wall.

questions.takeaway: Work around it today, and report it so the next patient does not have to.
questions.strategy: Two options let the form's limits decide the patient's care.

questions.stem: A patient's long term partner, who is not a legal spouse or next of kin, asks to stay during visiting restrictions. The patient wants him there. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Support the patient's designation of who may visit and participate
options.rationale: The patient decides who their support people are. Chosen family is often the real support system when biological family has not been accepting, and hospital visitation policy follows the patient's designation. Asking the parents hands the decision to people the patient did not choose.

options.text: Limit visitation to blood relatives and the legal spouse
options.rationale: Institution as rationale An outdated reading of policy that excludes the actual support system.

options.text: Ask the patient's parents whether they agree
options.rationale: Near miss concept Gives the decision to people the patient did not designate.

options.text: Defer the decision to the charge nurse without consulting the patient
options.rationale: Near miss concept Escalation can be appropriate, and not before asking the patient.

questions.takeaway: The patient names their support people. Biology does not.
questions.strategy: Two options let someone other than the patient decide who supports the patient.

questions.stem: A transgender patient's parent asks the nurse whether the patient is taking hormone therapy. The patient is 24. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Answer, since the parent is listed as the emergency contact
options.rationale: Near miss concept Confuses a contact with an authorized representative.

options.text: Tell the parent to ask the provider
options.rationale: Near miss concept Avoids saying no while implying the answer is obtainable.

options.text: Decline to share any information without the patient's permission
options.rationale: An adult patient's information is the patient's. Gender affirming care is health information like any other, and disclosing it can cost someone their housing or their family. Being an emergency contact is not consent to receive information, and redirecting the question to the provider still implies the information is available for the asking.

options.text: Confirm only the medications the parent already seems to know about
options.rationale: Near miss concept Confirmation is disclosure.

questions.takeaway: Emergency contact is who you call. It is not who gets told.
questions.strategy: Three options disclose, partially disclose, or hand the disclosure to someone else.

questions.stem: A nurse hears a colleague tell another staff member, "You should see what is in room 12, it is really something." The patient in room 12 is transgender. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ignore it, since the colleague never used the patient's name
options.rationale: Near miss concept Room 12 identifies her completely to anyone on the unit.

options.text: Tell the patient what was said so she can decide whether to complain
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hands her an injury she did not have and makes the remedy her work.

options.text: Make a joke to change the subject and move on with the shift
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Avoids the confrontation and signals that it was acceptable.

options.text: Address it with the colleague and report it as a privacy violation
options.rationale: Inviting a colleague to come and look at a patient is a disclosure to someone with no need to know, and it treats a person as a spectacle. That is reportable, not just rude. The patient is not told, because telling her hands her a harm she has not experienced and makes managing it her job. You address it and escalate it.

questions.takeaway: This is reportable conduct, not a question of manners.
questions.strategy: Telling the patient feels like transparency and transfers the burden to her.

questions.stem: The legal name on the chart is Michael. The patient introduces herself as Mia and uses she and her. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Avoid using any name or pronoun to stay neutral
options.rationale: Near miss concept Avoidance reads as discomfort and makes the patient manage your awkwardness.

options.text: Use Mia and she in conversation, and document the affirmed name alongside the legal name
options.rationale: You address people by the name and pronouns they give you. The legal name still has to appear for identification, billing and the armband, and that is a documentation requirement, not a reason to call someone by a name they do not use. Recording both means the next nurse does not have to be corrected.

options.text: Ask the patient which name to use in front of other staff to avoid confusion
options.rationale: Near miss concept Asking is right; doing it publicly outs the patient without consent.

options.text: Use the legal name, because the chart and the armband must match
options.rationale: Institution as rationale Identification needs the legal name on the band, not in conversation.

questions.takeaway: The legal name is for the wristband. The affirmed name is for the person.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options use an administrative requirement as a reason to misgender someone.

questions.topic: a clinical finding that needs context
questions.stem: A transgender woman on long term estrogen presents with calf pain and unilateral swelling. What should the nurse recognize?
questions.objective: a clinical finding that needs context

options.text: Estrogen raises clot risk, so this needs urgent DVT evaluation
options.rationale: Unilateral calf pain with swelling is a possible clot in anyone, and estrogen therapy raises that risk, so her medication history makes this more concerning rather than less. Do not massage the leg, do not ambulate her until it has been evaluated, and watch for sudden dyspnea or pleuritic chest pain. Whether to hold the estrogen is a clinical decision after the evaluation, not a reflex before it.

options.text: The hormone therapy must be stopped before any evaluation
options.rationale: Correct but premature A decision for the team with the patient, after the diagnosis.

options.text: This is most likely a simple muscle strain, given her age
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Explains away a finding in a patient with a specific risk factor.

options.text: Estrogen therapy has no meaningful effect on clotting risk
options.rationale: Near miss concept It increases it, which is the central safety point of this therapy.

questions.takeaway: Estrogen plus a unilateral swollen painful calf is a clot workup, not a strain.
questions.strategy: Knowing the medication changes the pretest probability. That is why the history matters.

questions.stem: A nurse realizes she feels uncomfortable caring for a patient whose identity conflicts with her personal beliefs. What should she do?

options.text: Tell the patient she disagrees with his identity but will still provide the care
options.rationale: Near miss concept Honest and it burdens the patient with managing the relationship.

options.text: Give the same standard of care and reflect on her response privately
options.rationale: Personal beliefs do not alter what a patient is owed. The work is to notice your own reaction and keep it out of the room, which is a professional skill rather than a personal accommodation. Reassignment communicates something to the patient even when nothing is said out loud.

options.text: Avoid discussing anything personal with the patient at all
options.rationale: Near miss concept Withdrawal is noticed, and the history requires personal questions.

options.text: Ask to be reassigned so the patient will receive better care
options.rationale: Near miss concept Framed as being in the patient's interest; patients read reassignment accurately.

questions.takeaway: Your discomfort is yours to manage. It is not information the patient needs.
questions.strategy: Two options hand the nurse's feelings to the patient, in words or by action.

questions.stem: A nurse overhears a colleague repeatedly refer to a transgender patient by the wrong pronoun in the hallway. What should she do?

options.text: Report the colleague to the manager without speaking to her
options.rationale: Correct but premature Escalation before the simplest correction has been tried.

options.text: Correct the colleague loudly so the patient knows someone is on her side
options.rationale: Near miss concept Makes the patient the subject of a public dispute.

options.text: Correct the colleague privately and continue using the patient's pronouns herself
options.rationale: A brief private correction fixes the behavior without a scene, and modeling the right pronouns does more than any conversation. Intent is not the measure; the patient hears it either way. Escalate if it continues, because repeated misgendering is a care quality problem, not a personality one.

options.text: Say nothing, since the colleague did not mean harm
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Protects the colleague's comfort at the patient's expense.

questions.takeaway: Correct it quietly and then model it. Both parts matter.
questions.strategy: Saying nothing and making a scene fail for opposite reasons.

questions.stem: A patient has decided that the lump he found means something is wrong with him. He tells his wife he thinks he is sick, asks whether she agrees, and stays home from work for two days. He has not called a provider. Which stage of illness behavior is this?

options.text: Symptom experience
options.rationale: Correct but premature The interpreting stage; he has already concluded he is ill.

options.text: Assumption of the sick role
options.rationale: Symptom experience is perceiving the symptom and interpreting whether it means illness. Assuming the sick role begins once the person has accepted that he is ill and seeks validation from family or friends, which is where giving up work and asking his wife to agree places him. Medical care contact is reaching out to a provider, and the dependent patient role is accepting the plan of care.

options.text: Medical care contact
options.rationale: Correct but premature That stage starts when he calls someone clinical.

options.text: Dependent patient role
options.rationale: Correct but premature Requires an accepted plan of care.

questions.takeaway: Accepting that you are sick is its own stage, and it happens before anyone clinical is called.
questions.strategy: Sequence items reward reading what the patient has actually concluded, not what he probably will do next.

questions.stem: A nurse provides smoking cessation counseling to a 58 year old patient admitted with an exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. This intervention is an example of which level of prevention?

options.text: Secondary prevention
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is screening for disease in someone without symptoms. He has a diagnosis.

options.text: Tertiary care
options.rationale: Near miss concept A level of CARE, meaning highly specialized services such as a burn center, not a level of prevention.

options.text: Tertiary prevention
options.rationale: The level is set by the patient's disease status, not by the name of the intervention. In a person with no related disease, cessation counseling is primary prevention. In a patient who already has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, the same counseling is limiting progression and complications, which is tertiary prevention.

options.text: Primary prevention
options.rationale: Near miss concept The answer you memorized, applied to the wrong patient.

questions.takeaway: Smoking cessation is primary only when there is no related disease yet.
questions.strategy: Read the patient, not the intervention. And read the noun: tertiary prevention is not tertiary care.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses two patients with the same diagnosis and the same severity whose management of it differs greatly. Which variables influence health? Select all that apply.

options.text: Genetics and age
options.rationale: Both named, and both non-modifiable. Two of the seven, and the ones nursing intervention most often reaches. Culture shapes what health means to a person; socioeconomic status shapes what is available to them. The last of the seven. A plan a patient cannot reach does not work.

options.text: Environment and lifestyle
options.rationale: Both named, and both non-modifiable. Two of the seven, and the ones nursing intervention most often reaches. Culture shapes what health means to a person; socioeconomic status shapes what is available to them. The last of the seven. A plan a patient cannot reach does not work.

options.text: Culture and socioeconomic status
options.rationale: Both named, and both non-modifiable. Two of the seven, and the ones nursing intervention most often reaches. Culture shapes what health means to a person; socioeconomic status shapes what is available to them. The last of the seven. A plan a patient cannot reach does not work.

options.text: Access to health care
options.rationale: Both named, and both non-modifiable. Two of the seven, and the ones nursing intervention most often reaches. Culture shapes what health means to a person; socioeconomic status shapes what is available to them. The last of the seven. A plan a patient cannot reach does not work.

options.text: The severity of the diagnosis itself
options.rationale: Near miss concept The stem holds severity constant between the two patients, so it cannot explain the difference between them.

options.text: The nurse's own health beliefs
options.rationale: Near miss concept They shape the encounter and are not a variable influencing the patient's health.

questions.takeaway: Seven variables influence health: genetics, age, environment, lifestyle, culture, socioeconomic status, and access to health care.
questions.strategy: The stem holds two things constant on purpose. Anything that does not vary cannot explain a difference.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence: A nurse plans care for a community with a high rate of cardiovascular disease. Running a school program that teaches children never to start smoking is [[1]]. Offering blood pressure checks at a community event is [[2]]. Running a cardiac rehabilitation group for people who have had a myocardial infarction is [[3]]. Teaching a patient with diabetes how to inspect his feet is [[4]].

options.text: primary prevention
secondary prevention
tertiary prevention
health promotion
secondary prevention
primary prevention
tertiary prevention
secondary care
tertiary prevention
secondary prevention
restorative care
primary prevention
tertiary prevention
primary prevention
secondary prevention
health education

questions.takeaway: [1] primary prevention: Acts before any disease exists, in people who are currently well. [2] secondary prevention: Screening detects disease early, before symptoms bring someone in. [3] tertiary prevention: The disease has happened. Rehabilitation limits further damage and loss of function. [4] tertiary prevention: He already has diabetes. Foot inspection exists to prevent ulceration and amputation. Primary prevents disease occurring. Secondary detects it early. Tertiary limits complications once it exists.
questions.strategy: Ask one question of each: does the person have the disease yet? No is primary, maybe is secondary, yes is tertiary.

questions.stem: A nurse plans a program for a workplace. Which activity is health promotion rather than illness prevention?

options.text: An on-site influenza vaccination clinic
options.rationale: Near miss concept Illness prevention with a specific focus: one disease, one intervention.

options.text: Mammography screening arranged for eligible staff
options.rationale: Near miss concept Specific and aimed at detecting one disease early.

options.text: A campaign encouraging seatbelt use in company vehicles
options.rationale: Near miss concept Illness prevention. It targets a specific harm, and her slide lists seatbelts under primary prevention.

options.text: A stress management and exercise program open to all staff
options.rationale: Health promotion is broad and aimed at increasing wellbeing and maximizing health potential. It targets no single disease.

questions.takeaway: Health promotion improves wellness and has a broad focus. Illness prevention targets a specific disease or harm.
questions.strategy: Three options name one disease or one harm each. Ask which one has no particular target.

questions.stem: A nurse on a busy oncology unit finds herself irritable with colleagues, dreading her shifts, and no longer moved by patients' distress. She has worked twelve-hour shifts without a break for three months. Which is she most likely experiencing?

options.text: Compassion fatigue
options.rationale: Emotional and physical exhaustion from prolonged caregiving. The decreased empathy alongside irritability and cynicism is the recognizable picture.

options.text: A normal adjustment to a demanding specialty
options.rationale: Near miss concept Normalizes a set of findings her slide names as a syndrome, and it is how the problem goes unaddressed.

options.text: Ineffective coping with the patients' diagnoses
options.rationale: Near miss concept Closer, and it locates the problem in her response to individual patients rather than in cumulative exposure.

options.text: An underlying mood disorder requiring referral
options.rationale: Near miss concept Possible, and the occupational pattern and timing point first to compassion fatigue. Assessment precedes that conclusion.

questions.takeaway: Compassion fatigue: emotional exhaustion, irritability, cynicism, decreased empathy, burnout. Prevention is boundaries, self-care, peer support, mindfulness, debriefing, and counselling when needed.
questions.strategy: One option normalizes it. One reaches for a diagnosis before assessing. Ask what the three months of unbroken shifts adds.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked what makes the WHO definition of health different from earlier definitions. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: It defines health as the ability to fulfill societal and work roles
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is the role performance model, not the WHO definition.

options.text: It defines health as the ability to adapt to environmental change
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is the adaptive model.

options.text: It defines health as a fixed state a person either has or does not have
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reverses a central point. Health is dynamic and constantly changing, and it sits on a continuum.

options.text: It defines health as complete physical, mental, and social wellbeing, not merely the absence of disease
options.rationale: The phrase not merely the absence of disease is what makes it broader, and it is why a person with a chronic condition can still be healthy.
