questions.takeaway: WHO: complete physical, mental, and social wellbeing, not merely the absence of disease. Six dimensions: physical, emotional, intellectual, social, spiritual, environmental.
questions.strategy: Two distractors are models of health offered as the definition. One contradicts the continuum.

questions.stem: A nurse works with a community where many residents have no supermarket within three miles, limited bus services, and high unemployment. Rates of diabetes are well above the national average. Which concept explains the link?

options.text: Social determinants of health
options.rationale: Non-medical conditions where people live, learn, work and age, which shape daily wellbeing and life expectancy. Transportation, food security and employment are her examples.

options.text: Non-modifiable risk factors
options.rationale: Near miss concept Genetics, age, sex and ethnicity. The conditions described are features of a place, and places can change.

options.text: Illness behavior
options.rationale: Near miss concept How individuals monitor and respond to symptoms. The stem describes conditions before anyone becomes symptomatic.

options.text: The clinical model of health
options.rationale: Near miss concept A way of defining health, not an explanation of why a population's rates differ.

questions.takeaway: Social determinants of health are non-medical conditions with major effects on health, daily wellbeing, and life expectancy.
questions.strategy: One distractor treats a feature of a neighborhood as though it were fixed like genetics.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked what Healthy People 2030 sets out to do. Which answer is accurate?

options.text: Improve health and wellbeing, eliminate disparities, promote healthy environments, and increase health equity
options.rationale: The four aims, and the key focus areas run through social determinants, preventive care, community health, and health literacy.

options.text: Set clinical treatment standards for the management of chronic disease
options.rationale: Near miss concept It sets population objectives rather than clinical protocols.

options.text: Define the scope of nursing practice across the states
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is the Nurse Practice Acts, which are state law.

options.text: Establish the accreditation requirements for health care organizations
options.rationale: Near miss concept Accreditation is the work of bodies such as The Joint Commission.

questions.takeaway: Healthy People 2030: improve health and wellbeing, eliminate disparities, promote healthy environments, increase health equity.
questions.strategy: Three distractors name real functions performed by other bodies entirely.

questions.stem: A nursing student discusses health and wellness with her preceptor. Which statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Someone with a chronic illness can still be healthy under most models."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Accurate. Only the clinical model says otherwise.

options.text: "Health sits on a continuum rather than being present or absent."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Accurate, and it runs from high-level wellness through neutral health and illness to death.

options.text: "Learning to manage my blood pressure now counts as primary prevention."
options.rationale: Managing a diagnosed condition is tertiary prevention. Primary acts before disease exists, and hers already does.

options.text: "Illness affects the family as well as the patient."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Accurate. Caregiver burden, financial stress, role adjustment, and emotional distress.

questions.takeaway: Primary prevents disease occurring. Secondary detects it early. Tertiary manages an established condition to limit complications.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate her key takeaways correctly. The fourth misplaces a level of prevention.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked to explain why health is described as dynamic. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: A person moves along a continuum from high-level wellness through neutral health and illness
options.rationale: Health is constantly changing, and the same person occupies different points at different times.

options.text: Health changes only when a new diagnosis is made
options.rationale: Near miss concept Ties health to diagnosis, which is the clinical model rather than the continuum.

options.text: A person is either well or ill, with no state in between
options.rationale: Near miss concept Neutral health sits between wellness and illness on her continuum.

options.text: Health improves steadily with age as a person adapts
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nothing suggests a direction. Movement along the continuum goes both ways.

questions.takeaway: The continuum runs from high-level wellness through neutral health to illness and death, and a person moves along it in both directions.
questions.strategy: Two distractors treat health as a fixed state. One invents a direction of travel.

questions.stem: A patient with hypertension has not filled a prescription for three months. He says he knows high pressure causes strokes, he has seen it happen to his brother, and he believes the medication works. He then says the copay is 60 dollars and he is choosing between the medication and his daughter's school fees. Which component of the health belief model should the nurse target?

options.text: Perceived benefits
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit He states that the medication works.

options.text: Perceived susceptibility
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit He connects it to himself. Also intact.

options.text: Perceived barriers
options.rationale: He has already demonstrated severity, susceptibility and benefit. The only remaining component is the barrier, which here is cost, and it is also the one the nurse can often remove outright through assistance programs, a generic substitution or a social work referral.

options.text: Perceived severity
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit He named a stroke in his own brother. Severity is intact.

questions.takeaway: Barriers is the lever. It is the one you can usually move.
questions.strategy: Read what the patient has ALREADY said. The components he demonstrates are not the answer.

questions.stem: Maria is 68 with well-controlled hypertension. She takes her medication daily, gardens, volunteers at her church, and says she feels healthy and happy despite occasional knee pain. For each model of health, indicate whether it would judge Maria healthy or not healthy.

rows.text: Clinical model
Role performance model
Adaptive model
Eudaimonistic model

questions.takeaway: Clinical model: Health is the absence of disease. She has a diagnosis and knee pain, so this model calls her unhealthy regardless of how she lives. Role performance model: She fulfills her roles: she gardens and volunteers. Function is what this model measures. Adaptive model: She has adapted to a chronic condition and manages it daily. Adaptation is the measure. Eudaimonistic model: She reports satisfaction and meaning through her volunteering. Self-actualization is the measure. Only the clinical model says a person with a chronic condition cannot be healthy. The other three judge function, adaptation, or fulfillment.
questions.strategy: One model disagrees with the other three, and the reason is that it looks only at the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has stopped attending the choir he sang with for twenty years because of breathlessness. He manages his inhalers correctly and says he no longer feels like himself. Which model of health best captures what he has lost?

options.text: Clinical, because his lung disease is progressing
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nothing in the stem says the disease has worsened. He describes a loss that the clinical model cannot see.

options.text: Adaptive, because he has failed to adjust to his diagnosis
options.rationale: Near miss concept He uses his inhalers correctly and has changed his activity. That is adaptation, not failure to adapt.

options.text: Role performance, because he cannot perform his usual activities
options.rationale: Near miss concept The near-miss, and singing in a choir is not a societal or work role. What he lost was meaning rather than function.

options.text: Eudaimonistic, because meaning and life satisfaction have gone
options.rationale: He is managing the disease and performing daily tasks. What has gone is the thing that made his life feel like his own.

questions.takeaway: Eudaimonistic health is self-actualization: satisfaction, meaning, and growth. It is the model that sees what the others miss.
questions.strategy: Two options describe things he is actually doing well. The near-miss turns a source of meaning into a role.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old develops crushing chest pain while mowing the lawn. He sits down, tells his wife it is indigestion, and takes an antacid. Which stage of illness behavior does this represent?

options.text: Assumption of the sick role
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Stage two, where a person accepts being ill and seeks relief from usual duties. He is minimizing rather than accepting.

options.text: Medical care contact
options.rationale: Near miss concept Stage three, and he has contacted nobody.

options.text: Symptom experience
options.rationale: Stage one. He has noticed something is wrong and is interpreting it, which is exactly what this stage is.

options.text: Dependent patient role
options.rationale: Near miss concept Stage four, where the person accepts care from others. He has not entered the system at all.

questions.takeaway: Five stages: symptom experience, assumption of the sick role, medical care contact, dependent patient role, recovery and rehabilitation.
questions.strategy: Every distractor is a later stage. Ask how far into the sequence he has actually travelled.

questions.stem: A self-employed builder has had a persistent cough for six weeks. He tells the nurse he has been calling it a chest cold because he cannot afford to lose a week of work. Which concept explains his delay in seeking care?

options.text: Assumption of the sick role
options.rationale: Near miss concept Stage two, where a person accepts being ill. He is doing the opposite.

options.text: Illness behavior
options.rationale: Illness behavior is how a person monitors, interprets, and responds to symptoms. Calling a six-week cough a chest cold is the interpretation; not seeking care is the response.

options.text: Perceived severity
options.rationale: Near miss concept A Health Belief Model construct about how serious he judges it to be. It is one input into illness behavior rather than the concept itself.

options.text: The dependent patient role
options.rationale: Near miss concept Stage four, where care from others is accepted. He has not entered care.

questions.takeaway: Illness behavior is influenced by culture, family, education, and past experiences.
questions.strategy: Three options name a specific stage or construct. Ask which term covers the whole pattern of interpreting and responding.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old smoker whose father died of lung cancer at 60 tells the nurse he knows smoking is dangerous but does not believe it will happen to him. Which Health Belief Model construct does this reflect?

options.text: Low perceived severity
options.rationale: Near miss concept Severity is how serious he judges the outcome to be. He watched his father die of it, so he is unlikely to underrate its seriousness.

options.text: Low perceived benefits
options.rationale: Near miss concept Benefits concern whether he thinks quitting would help. He has not said quitting would not work.

options.text: Low perceived susceptibility
options.rationale: He accepts the risk exists and does not accept it applies to him. That gap is susceptibility.

options.text: High perceived barriers
options.rationale: Near miss concept Barriers are what stands in the way, such as cost or withdrawal. He has named none.

questions.takeaway: Health Belief Model: perceived susceptibility, perceived severity, perceived benefits, perceived barriers.
questions.strategy: The family history is placed to rule one option out. Someone who watched a parent die of a disease knows how serious it is.

questions.stem: A nurse works with a patient who wants to lose weight and has not managed to change anything in six months. Which barriers to behavior change should the nurse assess? Select all that apply.

options.text: Cost of the changes involved
options.rationale: A named barrier, and gym fees or fresh food can make a plan unreachable. Named, and it is why plans built for someone with free evenings fail. Named, and it includes fear of failing again. Named. A plan he cannot read or interpret is not a plan he can follow.

options.text: Time available to make the change
options.rationale: A named barrier, and gym fees or fresh food can make a plan unreachable. Named, and it is why plans built for someone with free evenings fail. Named, and it includes fear of failing again. Named. A plan he cannot read or interpret is not a plan he can follow.

options.text: Fear about what change might involve
options.rationale: A named barrier, and gym fees or fresh food can make a plan unreachable. Named, and it is why plans built for someone with free evenings fail. Named, and it includes fear of failing again. Named. A plan he cannot read or interpret is not a plan he can follow.

options.text: Health literacy
options.rationale: A named barrier, and gym fees or fresh food can make a plan unreachable. Named, and it is why plans built for someone with free evenings fail. Named, and it includes fear of failing again. Named. A plan he cannot read or interpret is not a plan he can follow.

options.text: His motivation to change
options.rationale: Near miss concept Motivation is one of the four requirements for change, not a barrier. The stem already tells you he wants to.

options.text: His genetic predisposition to weight gain
options.rationale: Near miss concept A non-modifiable risk factor. It affects the difficulty of the goal rather than standing between him and starting.

questions.takeaway: Change requires motivation, knowledge, resources, and support. Barriers include cost, time, fear, and health literacy.
questions.strategy: One distractor names a requirement for change rather than a barrier, and the stem has already established it is present.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews a 52-year-old's risk factors: he smokes 20 a day, drinks heavily at weekends, is sedentary, has a body mass index of 34, has a father who died of myocardial infarction at 55, and is of an ethnicity with raised cardiovascular risk. Which of his risk factors are modifiable? Select all that apply.

options.text: Smoking 20 cigarettes a day
options.rationale: Named as modifiable, and the single change with the largest effect here. Alcohol and drug use are named as modifiable. Activity level can be changed, which makes it modifiable. Weight is named as modifiable.

options.text: Heavy alcohol use
options.rationale: Named as modifiable, and the single change with the largest effect here. Alcohol and drug use are named as modifiable. Activity level can be changed, which makes it modifiable. Weight is named as modifiable.

options.text: Being sedentary
options.rationale: Named as modifiable, and the single change with the largest effect here. Alcohol and drug use are named as modifiable. Activity level can be changed, which makes it modifiable. Weight is named as modifiable.

options.text: A body mass index of 34
options.rationale: Named as modifiable, and the single change with the largest effect here. Alcohol and drug use are named as modifiable. Activity level can be changed, which makes it modifiable. Weight is named as modifiable.

options.text: His father's death from myocardial infarction at 55
options.rationale: Near miss concept Family history is genetics, and genetics is non-modifiable. It raises the urgency of changing the others.

options.text: His ethnicity
options.rationale: Near miss concept Named as non-modifiable, and it is never a target for intervention.

questions.takeaway: Modifiable: smoking, diet, alcohol and drug use, weight. Non-modifiable: age, genetics, biological sex, ethnicity.
questions.strategy: Two of his risk factors are real and cannot be changed. They alter how urgent the others are, not whether they are targets.

questions.stem: 1100: Patient is 61, attends for a routine review. Reports sleeping four to five hours most nights since being moved to night shifts six months ago. Has gained 8 kg in that time. Says he eats from vending machines at work because nothing else is open. Blood pressure 152/94, up from 128/80 a year ago. Smokes 15 a day, unchanged for 20 years. Walks his dog twice daily. Says he has stopped seeing friends because his hours no longer match theirs. Temperature 36.6 C. Attends his annual review every year without fail. Select all of the findings that represent modifiable risks the nurse can address.

options.text: Sleeping four to five hours most nights
options.rationale: Sleep hygiene is named under health promotion, and short sleep affects weight, blood pressure and mood. Weight is a named modifiable risk factor, and the rate of gain makes it recent and reversible. Diet is modifiable, and he has named the barrier himself, which is what makes it addressable. A change from his own baseline, and it is the consequence the other findings are producing. The first named modifiable risk factor, and unchanged does not mean unchangeable. Social isolation affects the social dimension of health and removes the support systems that behavior change requires.

Weight is a named modifiable risk factor, and the rate of gain makes it recent and reversible. Diet is modifiable, and he has named the barrier himself, which is what makes it addressable. A change from his own baseline, and it is the consequence the other findings are producing. The first named modifiable risk factor, and unchanged does not mean unchangeable. Social isolation affects the social dimension of health and removes the support systems that behavior change requires.

options.text: Has stopped seeing friends because his hours no longer match theirs
options.rationale: Sleep hygiene is named under health promotion, and short sleep affects weight, blood pressure and mood. Weight is a named modifiable risk factor, and the rate of gain makes it recent and reversible. Diet is modifiable, and he has named the barrier himself, which is what makes it addressable. A change from his own baseline, and it is the consequence the other findings are producing. The first named modifiable risk factor, and unchanged does not mean unchangeable. Social isolation affects the social dimension of health and removes the support systems that behavior change requires.

options.text: Walks his dog twice daily
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Something he is already doing well. It is a strength, not a risk.

options.text: Temperature 36.6 C
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A normal finding, included to be left alone.

options.text: Attends his annual review every year without fail
options.rationale: Near miss concept A health-seeking behavior and another strength. It is why you are able to catch this at all.

questions.takeaway: Modifiable risks are the ones nursing can act on. Strengths matter too, and they are not risks.
questions.strategy: Two findings describe things he is doing right, and one is normal. A strength offered among risk factors is there to be left alone.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares discharge teaching for a patient newly diagnosed with heart failure. Which content is the priority before he leaves?

options.text: The pathophysiology of how heart failure develops
options.rationale: Near miss concept Interesting and it does not change what he does on Tuesday when his weight is up two kilograms.

options.text: When to notify the provider and how to recognize the signs that matter
options.rationale: Health education exists so patients can make informed decisions. Knowing when to seek help is what prevents the readmission.

options.text: A complete list of his medication side effects
options.rationale: Near miss concept Medication instruction is named content, and an exhaustive list without priorities is not usable at home.

options.text: The names and roles of the team members who cared for him
options.rationale: Near miss concept Courteous, and it does not prevent a complication.

questions.takeaway: Health education asks what the patient needs to know before discharge to stay healthy and prevent complications. When to seek help sits at the top.
questions.strategy: Three options contain real information. Ask which one he will act on at home.

questions.stem: A patient with a new diagnosis of type 2 diabetes attends a follow-up having learned to adjust his diet, check his glucose, and plan around his work shifts. He says it has become routine. Which model of health evaluates him most favorably?

options.text: The clinical model, because his glucose is being monitored
options.rationale: Near miss concept The clinical model measures absence of disease. He has diabetes, so this model does not judge him healthy.

options.text: The adaptive model, because he has adjusted to the change
options.rationale: Adaptive health is the ability to adapt flexibly. Coping with a new diagnosis is her own example of it.

options.text: The role performance model, because he keeps working
options.rationale: Near miss concept Plausible, and the stem emphasizes how he adjusted rather than what roles he fulfills.

options.text: The eudaimonistic model, because he has found meaning
options.rationale: Near miss concept He describes routine, not meaning or growth. This model would need more than competent management.

questions.takeaway: Adaptive health is resilience and flexible adjustment. Her examples are coping with a new diagnosis and adjusting after an amputation.
questions.strategy: The stem emphasizes one particular thing about him. Ask what word describes what he did.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old attends a follow-up three months after being told she has prediabetes. She has not started the exercise plan or changed her diet. She says she understands why it matters, works two cleaning jobs with a two-hour commute, and that the recommended gym costs more than her weekly food budget. Her weight is unchanged and her fasting glucose has risen from 112 to 119 mg/dL. Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem they address, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Build a plan around activity that costs nothing and fits her existing day
Connect her with community food and activity resources she can reach
Re-teach the risks of progressing from prediabetes to diabetes
Document that she has not adhered to the recommended plan
Barriers of cost and time preventing a plan she is motivated to follow
Knowledge deficit about diabetes prevention
Lack of motivation to change her health behaviors
Non-modifiable risk factors driving her rising glucose
Whether she has started and sustained any of the agreed activity
Her fasting glucose at the next visit
Whether she can state three complications of diabetes
Whether she attends her next appointment

questions.takeaway: Motivation and knowledge are both present. What is missing is resources and time, which are two of the four requirements for change. Cost and time are the two barriers she has named. A plan that avoids both is one she can actually start. Advocating for resources is part of the nursing role in risk reduction, and it addresses the barrier rather than the behavior. Measures whether the redesigned plan was actually usable, which is what changed. The outcome the whole intervention exists to move, and it is already trending the wrong way. Change requires motivation, knowledge, resources, and support. When the first two are present and nothing happens, look at the last two.
questions.strategy: Two problem options blame her motivation or her knowledge. She has told you she has both.

questions.stem: A nurse sits down, makes eye contact and asks a newly admitted patient what worries her most about being in the hospital. Which element of Watson's theory does this reflect?

options.text: Providing a supportive, protective and corrective physical environment
options.rationale: Near miss concept The nurse's action is relational, not environmental.

options.text: Using a creative, problem solving caring process to plan care
options.rationale: Near miss concept Systematic problem solving is a different carative factor; this nurse is building trust, not planning.

options.text: Developing a helping and trusting caring relationship
options.rationale: Watson frames caring as the core of nursing rather than an accessory to it. Presence, eye contact and an invitation to say what matters build the relationship that everything clinical then rests on. The other options are also carative factors, and none of them is what this nurse is doing.

options.text: Assisting with gratification of the patient's basic human needs
options.rationale: Near miss concept Meeting physical needs is not what the nurse is doing; she is opening a trusting conversation.

questions.takeaway: Caring is the practice, not the mood.
questions.strategy: When three options are real elements of the same theory, decide by which one the described behavior actually is.

questions.stem: A nurse on an oncology unit tells a colleague that she has stopped feeling anything when patients die, that she is sleeping poorly and that she no longer looks forward to work. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.text: The nurse is showing appropriate professional detachment that protects her from burnout
options.rationale: Near miss concept Numbness is not detachment, and the sleep and satisfaction changes mark it as a problem.

options.text: These are recognized findings of compassion fatigue and the nurse needs support
options.rationale: Emotional exhaustion, numbness, decreased empathy and reduced job satisfaction after repeated exposure to suffering are the defining features of compassion fatigue. Framing decreased empathy as a symptom rather than a character flaw is the whole point of the concept.

options.text: The nurse has developed a values conflict and should consider transferring units
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Names the nurse's situation instead of the recognized syndrome.

options.text: These are findings of second victim syndrome related to an adverse patient event
options.rationale: Near miss concept That follows the nurse's own involvement in an error or adverse event, which the stem does not describe.

questions.takeaway: Decreased empathy is a symptom. It calls for support, not correction.
questions.strategy: When a stem describes a nurse rather than a patient, check which of the three nurse directed stress conditions fits: compassion fatigue, secondary traumatic stress, or second victim.

questions.stem: A hospital reviews patient comments to learn which nursing behaviors patients describe as caring. Which behaviors do patients most often name? Select all that apply.

options.text: Listening carefully
options.rationale: The behavior patients name most, and the one that costs nothing but attention. Named directly, and it turns something done to a patient into something done with them. Named, and it is the thread running through the bathing and hygiene examples. Named. A call light answered quickly says something before anyone speaks. Named, and it is what makes an exposing task tolerable.

options.text: Explaining procedures
options.rationale: The behavior patients name most, and the one that costs nothing but attention. Named directly, and it turns something done to a patient into something done with them. Named, and it is the thread running through the bathing and hygiene examples. Named. A call light answered quickly says something before anyone speaks. Named, and it is what makes an exposing task tolerable.

options.text: Treating them with dignity
options.rationale: The behavior patients name most, and the one that costs nothing but attention. Named directly, and it turns something done to a patient into something done with them. Named, and it is the thread running through the bathing and hygiene examples. Named. A call light answered quickly says something before anyone speaks. Named, and it is what makes an exposing task tolerable.

options.text: Responding promptly
options.rationale: The behavior patients name most, and the one that costs nothing but attention. Named directly, and it turns something done to a patient into something done with them. Named, and it is the thread running through the bathing and hygiene examples. Named. A call light answered quickly says something before anyone speaks. Named, and it is what makes an exposing task tolerable.

options.text: Protecting privacy
options.rationale: The behavior patients name most, and the one that costs nothing but attention. Named directly, and it turns something done to a patient into something done with them. Named, and it is the thread running through the bathing and hygiene examples. Named. A call light answered quickly says something before anyone speaks. Named, and it is what makes an exposing task tolerable.

options.text: Completing tasks without disturbing the patient
options.rationale: Near miss concept Efficient and it is the first nurse in her scenario. Minimal disturbance is not the same as caring.

options.text: Withholding difficult information until the patient seems ready
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Protective in intention and closer to false reassurance than to caring. Patients name honesty and explanation.

questions.takeaway: Patients name: listens carefully, explains procedures, treats with dignity, responds promptly, shows kindness, includes family, protects privacy, advocates.
questions.strategy: Two distractors describe things a nurse might do out of consideration. Ask whether patients actually name them.

questions.stem: A nurse cares for a patient admitted with pneumonia over one shift. For each statement the nurse makes, indicate whether it is therapeutic or a communication block.

rows.text: "I can see this is difficult."
"Everything will be fine."
"What concerns you the most today?"
"Try not to worry about it."
"Tell me more."
Finishing his sentence when he pauses to catch his breath

questions.takeaway: "I can see this is difficult.": Validates the feeling without judging it, and it invites him to say more. "Everything will be fine.": False reassurance. It is meant kindly and it tells him the subject is closed. "What concerns you the most today?": Open-ended, and it lets him set the agenda rather than the nurse. "Try not to worry about it.": Dismisses the worry rather than exploring it, and it asks him to manage his feeling alone. "Tell me more.": The shortest way to keep someone talking, and it commits the nurse to listening. Finishing his sentence when he pauses to catch his breath: Interrupting, and in a breathless patient it also takes away the time he needs to speak. Therapeutic: I can see this is difficult, tell me more, what concerns you most, how can I help. Blocks: false reassurance, don't worry, interrupting.
questions.strategy: The blocks all sound kind. Ask whether the statement opens the conversation or ends it.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence: A nurse reflects on her practice after a shift. Sitting at eye level and listening without interrupting demonstrates [[1]]. Asking a patient what makes taking his medication difficult, rather than whether he took it, is [[2]]. Saying "don't worry, everything will be fine" is an example of [[3]]. According to Watson, caring is best described as [[4]].

options.text: presence
empathy
advocacy
competence
Caritas Coaching
health teaching
therapeutic silence
motivational reassurance
false reassurance
validating feelings
offering self
giving information
the essence of nursing, and both an art and a science
an additional skill applied once clinical tasks are complete
a personality trait some nurses have and others do not
the emotional component of care, separate from the technical

questions.takeaway: [1] presence: Full attention, given deliberately. Sitting, eye contact, minimizing distractions, and not interrupting. [2] Caritas Coaching: Partnering instead of instructing, and helping him find his own solution. Her exact contrast. [3] false reassurance: Named among the things to avoid, alongside don't worry and interrupting. [4] the essence of nursing, and both an art and a science: Watson's position, and the art and science pairing is why competence sits inside caring. Presence is the behavior. Caritas Coaching is the partnership. False reassurance is the block. Watson calls caring the essence of nursing, art and science together.
questions.strategy: Blank 1 has a real near-miss: empathy is the understanding, presence is what you visibly do.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews what professional caring includes beyond compassion. Which elements are part of it? Select all that apply.

options.text: Accountability
options.rationale: Named directly, and it is why caring cannot exist without competence. Named, and it is how respect for the whole person is enacted. Named, and protecting privacy is one of the behaviors patients identify. Named, and it appears in both the professional caring list and the behaviors patients value. Named, and it is what keeps caring from becoming personal preference.

options.rationale: Named directly, and it is why caring cannot exist without competence. Named, and it is how respect for the whole person is enacted. Named, and protecting privacy is one of the behaviors patients identify. Named, and it appears in both the professional caring list and the behaviors patients value. Named, and it is what keeps caring from becoming personal preference.

options.rationale: Named directly, and it is why caring cannot exist without competence. Named, and it is how respect for the whole person is enacted. options.rationale: Named directly, and it is why caring cannot exist without competence. Named, and it is how respect for the whole person is enacted. Named, and protecting privacy is one of the behaviors patients identify. Named, and it appears in both the professional caring list and the behaviors patients value. Named, and it is what keeps caring from becoming personal preference.

options.rationale: Named directly, and it is why caring cannot exist without competence. Named, and it is how respect for the whole person is enacted. Named, and protecting privacy is one of the behaviors patients identify. Named, and it appears in both the professional caring list and the behaviors patients value. Named, and it is what keeps caring from becoming personal preference.

options.text: Emotional involvement in each patient's situation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Empathy is understanding what a patient feels. Becoming emotionally involved is not a professional element and it leads toward compassion fatigue.

questions.takeaway: Professional caring: compassion, respect, accountability, cultural sensitivity, confidentiality, advocacy, ethical practice.
questions.strategy: One distractor sounds like the most caring option on the list and is the one that harms the nurse.

questions.stem: A nurse hears a colleague tell a frightened preoperative patient that there is nothing to worry about and the surgeon is the best in the hospital. What is the problem with this response?

options.text: It gives the patient unrealistic expectations of the surgical outcome
options.rationale: Near miss concept A fair concern about the specific claim, and the broader fault is what the response does to the exchange.

options.text: It breaches confidentiality by discussing the surgeon's reputation
options.rationale: Near miss concept No confidential information is disclosed. The problem is what it does to the patient's ability to speak.

options.text: It is false reassurance, which closes the conversation the patient was trying to start
options.rationale: Named among the things to avoid. It sounds supportive and it tells the patient the subject is finished.

options.text: It should have been delivered by the surgeon rather than the nurse
options.rationale: Near miss concept Addressing fear is squarely nursing work. Handing it to the surgeon avoids it.

questions.takeaway: Avoid: everything will be fine, don't worry, interrupting, and false reassurance.
questions.strategy: One distractor criticizes the content of the claim. Ask what the response does to the patient's next sentence.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked why caring is described as improving outcomes rather than simply being pleasant. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Caring improves trust, communication, and treatment adherence, which change clinical results
options.rationale: Research consistently shows caring relationships improve both patient and nurse outcomes. The mechanism runs through trust and communication.

options.text: Caring improves patient satisfaction scores, which affect hospital reimbursement
options.rationale: Near miss concept True and it is an institutional consequence rather than a clinical one.

options.text: Caring compensates for gaps in clinical competence
options.rationale: Near miss concept Competence is part of caring, not something caring substitutes for.

options.text: Caring reduces the time nurses spend answering questions
options.rationale: Near miss concept The opposite of what presence involves, and efficiency is not the argument.

questions.takeaway: Caring improves trust, communication, healing, satisfaction, emotional wellbeing, treatment adherence, and the nurse-patient relationship.
questions.strategy: One distractor gives a real institutional benefit as though it were the clinical argument.

questions.stem: A nursing student discusses Watson's theory with her preceptor. Which statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Caring is something I can do once I have finished my clinical tasks."
options.rationale: Treats caring as a separate activity. Every nursing skill is also a caring interaction, which means it happens during the tasks rather than after them.

options.text: "Watson describes caring as both an art and a science."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Accurate, and it is why scientific knowledge sits alongside caring in the Caritas Processes.

options.text: "Caring means respecting the whole person, mind, body and spirit."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Accurate, and it is her wording.

options.text: "Caritas Coaching helps patients find their own solutions rather than giving instructions."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Accurate. Partnering rather than directing.

questions.takeaway: Caring is the essence of nursing and happens within every skill, not after the work is done.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate her slides correctly. The fourth makes caring a separate item on the list.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked what patients remember about their hospital stay. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Patients remember the nurses who completed tasks most efficiently
options.rationale: Near miss concept Efficiency is rarely what is described. Patients name listening, explaining, and dignity.

options.text: Patients most accurately recall the clinical details of their treatment
options.rationale: Near miss concept Recall of clinical detail is generally poor, particularly during acute illness.

options.text: Patients may forget what was done and remember how it made them feel
options.rationale: Her closing line, and it is why caring behaviors have outcomes beyond the encounter itself.

options.text: Patients remember the amount of time each nurse spent with them
options.rationale: Near miss concept Presence is not measured in minutes. Sitting down for two minutes is remembered differently from standing for ten.

questions.takeaway: Patients may forget exactly what you did and they remember how you made them feel.
questions.strategy: Two distractors measure caring in efficiency or minutes. Neither is what patients report.

questions.stem: An experienced nurse has become irritable with patients, dreads her shifts, and says she no longer feels anything when a patient dies. Which response by the nurse manager is most appropriate?

options.text: Advise her to set firmer emotional boundaries with her patients
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Implies the problem is her resilience.

options.text: Suggest she use her paid time off and take a restful vacation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Rest helps and she comes back to the same conditions.

options.text: Name what she describes, ask what support she needs, and look at her workload
options.rationale: Emotional numbing, irritability and dread are compassion fatigue and burnout, not a character flaw. It is a workload and system problem as much as a personal one, which is the whole reason clinician wellbeing became the fourth aim. A vacation returns her to the same conditions, and telling her to build boundaries locates the cause in her.

options.text: Monitor her charting closely for errors and document this conversation in her personnel file
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Treats a wellbeing disclosure as a performance matter, which guarantees the next nurse says nothing.

questions.takeaway: Burnout is a system finding. Treating it as a personal failing is why people stop reporting it.
questions.strategy: Three options put the fix entirely on the individual.

questions.stem: Two nurses complete identical admission assessments on a patient with pneumonia. The first works quickly, says little, and leaves. The second introduces herself, sits at eye level, explains each step, and asks what worries the patient most today. Both assessments are clinically complete. What distinguishes the second nurse's care?

options.text: The second nurse gathered more assessment data
options.rationale: Near miss concept Identical assessments. Asking what worries her is presence rather than an extra data point, though it may well produce one.

options.text: The second nurse was more clinically competent
options.rationale: Near miss concept The stem states both assessments were complete. Competence is not what separates them.

options.text: How the care was delivered, which is as much a part of caring as what was done
options.rationale: Caring involves both what nurses do and how they do it. The assessment data is identical; the experience of being assessed is not.

options.text: The second nurse spent longer with the patient
options.rationale: Near miss concept Time is a consequence rather than the distinction. Sitting at eye level and introducing yourself cost seconds.

questions.takeaway: Caring is what nurses do and how they do it. Two technically identical encounters can differ entirely in whether the patient feels cared for.
questions.strategy: The stem tells you both were competent and both were complete. Whatever separates them is not clinical.

questions.stem: A patient with a new cancer diagnosis says she does not know how she will tell her children. The nurse has six other patients and a medication round due. Which response demonstrates presence?

options.text: Offer to arrange a referral to the social worker
options.rationale: Near miss concept An appropriate referral, and offered now it moves her distress to someone else instead of meeting it.

options.text: Say you will come back after the medication round and follow through
options.rationale: Near miss concept Better than dismissing her, and it still asks a frightened woman to hold it for an hour. Presence is a few minutes now.

options.text: Tell her many families find a way and she will too
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic False reassurance. It is meant kindly and it closes the conversation she has just opened.

options.text: Sit down, put the tasks aside for a few minutes, and let her talk
options.rationale: Presence means full attention. Sitting signals you are not about to leave, and sometimes the most therapeutic intervention is simply being present.

questions.takeaway: Presence: sit at eye level, make eye contact, minimize distractions, listen without interrupting, validate feelings.
questions.strategy: Three options are things a considerate nurse might genuinely say. Ask which one meets her now.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure has not been taking his diuretic. Which question reflects Caritas Coaching?

options.text: "Would it help if I explained how the medication works?"
options.rationale: Near miss concept Offers teaching before knowing whether teaching is what is needed.

options.text: "What makes taking the water tablet difficult?"
options.rationale: Opens with the obstacle and assumes he has a reason. Caritas Coaching partners rather than instructs, and it helps patients find their own solutions.

options.text: "Do you understand why the water tablet matters?"
options.rationale: Near miss concept Checks knowledge and implies the problem is his understanding. It also invites a defensive yes.

options.text: "Did you take your medication this week?"
options.rationale: Near miss concept Her own example of the closed question Caritas Coaching replaces. It produces a yes or no and stops there.

questions.takeaway: Caritas Coaching listens first, asks open-ended questions, encourages reflection, supports the patient's goals, builds confidence, and partners.
questions.strategy: One distractor is the exact question her slide contrasts against. Ask which one cannot be answered with a single word.

questions.stem: A nursing student says caring means being kind to patients. Which response by the preceptor is most accurate?

options.text: Caring includes competence, so a nurse who is warm but cannot perform the skill is not providing caring care
options.rationale: The definition names compassion, respect, presence, empathy and competence together. Professional competence and caring work together.

options.text: Kindness is the central element and the clinical skills follow from it
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reverses the relationship. Neither one produces the other, and both are required.

options.text: Kindness matters most with patients who are frightened or distressed
options.rationale: Near miss concept Makes caring conditional on the patient's state, and it applies to every interaction.

options.text: Caring is an attitude, while competence is a separate professional obligation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Separates what her slide joins. Every nursing skill is also a caring interaction.

questions.takeaway: Caring is intentional concern for wellbeing through compassion, respect, presence, empathy, and competence. Competence is part of it, not a separate track.
questions.strategy: Three options treat caring and competence as two different things. Ask what the definition actually contains.

questions.stem: A nurse performs a bed bath for a patient who is embarrassed about needing help. Which actions demonstrate caring during this skill? Select all that apply.

options.text: Explain each step before doing it
options.rationale: Turns something done to him into something he can anticipate and consent to. Protecting privacy and promoting dignity, which is her own example for bathing. Preserves what independence he has, and it treats him as a participant. Privacy is named among the caring behaviors patients value.

options.text: Keep him covered except for the area being washed
options.rationale: Turns something done to him into something he can anticipate and consent to. Protecting privacy and promoting dignity, which is her own example for bathing. Preserves what independence he has, and it treats him as a participant. Privacy is named among the caring behaviors patients value.

options.text: Ask what he would prefer to do himself
options.rationale: Turns something done to him into something he can anticipate and consent to. Protecting privacy and promoting dignity, which is her own example for bathing. Preserves what independence he has, and it treats him as a participant. Privacy is named among the caring behaviors patients value.

options.text: Close the door and the curtain before starting
options.rationale: Turns something done to him into something he can anticipate and consent to. Protecting privacy and promoting dignity, which is her own example for bathing. Preserves what independence he has, and it treats him as a participant. Privacy is named among the caring behaviors patients value.

options.text: Work quickly so the embarrassing part is over sooner
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sounds considerate and produces the first nurse in her scenario: efficient, minimal conversation, no presence.

options.text: Tell him there is nothing to be embarrassed about
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dismisses the feeling rather than validating it. His embarrassment is real whether or not it is necessary.

questions.takeaway: Every nursing skill is also a caring interaction. For bathing, that means privacy and dignity specifically.
questions.strategy: Two distractors are kindly meant. One rushes, one tells him how to feel.

questions.stem: A nurse administering an intravenous antibiotic explains what it is for, what side effects to report, and answers the patient's questions while the infusion runs. Which principle does this demonstrate?

options.text: Caring behaviors are most important during invasive procedures
options.rationale: Near miss concept Ranks the skills, and her slide names vital signs, medication, bathing, and wound care alike.

options.text: Medication administration requires verbal consent for each dose
options.rationale: Near miss concept Explaining is not the same as obtaining consent, and no such requirement is described.

options.text: Patient education should be scheduled separately from procedures
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reverses her point. Teaching while administering is her own example.

options.text: Every nursing skill is also a caring interaction
options.rationale: Caring is not a separate activity performed when there is time. The medication round became teaching and presence without adding a task.

questions.takeaway: Caring should be present during every skill. Vital signs, medication, bathing and wound care are all opportunities.
questions.strategy: One distractor makes caring a separate scheduled activity. One reserves it for the invasive tasks.

questions.stem: A nurse asks a patient what has been hardest about managing his diet since his diagnosis. He describes his shift pattern and the food available at work. Together they agree he will eat his main meal before his shift rather than during it. Which describes what the nurse has done?

options.text: Negotiated a compromise between his preference and the plan
options.rationale: Near miss concept Closer, and nothing was traded away. The dietary goal is unchanged; only the timing moved.

options.text: Partnered with him so he could find a solution that fits his life
options.rationale: Caritas Coaching helps patients discover their own strengths and solutions. The plan came from his information, not from a leaflet.

options.text: Assessed his adherence to the prescribed regimen
options.rationale: Near miss concept Adherence assessment asks whether he is doing it. She asked what was in the way, which is a different question.

options.text: Provided health teaching about dietary management
options.rationale: Near miss concept She supplied no dietary information. The content came from him.

questions.takeaway: Caritas Coaching: listen first, ask open questions, encourage reflection, support the patient's goals, build confidence, partner.
questions.strategy: The near-miss calls it a compromise. Check whether anything clinical was actually given up.

questions.stem: A nurse taking a patient's vital signs enters, applies the cuff, records the readings, and leaves without speaking. The readings are accurate. Which principle has been missed?

options.text: The readings should be verified with the patient before recording
options.rationale: Near miss concept No such requirement, and verification is not what was missing.

options.text: Caring should be present during every skill, including routine ones
options.rationale: Her example for vital signs is to introduce yourself and explain what you are doing. The task was done and the interaction was not.

options.text: Vital signs should be explained because patients have a right to their results
options.rationale: Near miss concept A reasonable position and not the principle here. The point is the interaction, not the disclosure.

options.text: Routine tasks may be delegated so the nurse can focus on caring
options.rationale: Near miss concept Treats caring as something that happens elsewhere, when the point is that it happens here.

questions.takeaway: Every nursing skill is also a caring interaction. For vital signs, introduce yourself and explain what you are doing.
questions.strategy: One distractor suggests delegating the routine work so caring can happen separately, which inverts the whole principle.

questions.stem: 1430: Patient is 54, admitted three days ago with pancreatitis. Sitting on the edge of the bed facing the window. Answers questions in single words. Has not touched the lunch tray. Says he is 'fine' when asked, then adds that his wife has not visited since admission. Wound site clean and dry. Pain reported as 2 of 10. Declines to discuss discharge planning, saying there is no point. Vital signs stable. Ambulated in the corridor this morning with the physiotherapist. Select all of the findings that indicate a need for therapeutic presence.

options.text: Sitting on the edge of the bed facing the window
options.rationale: Turned away from the room and from people. Nonverbal behavior is part of what you assess. Withdrawal from conversation, and it is the finding that tells you asking more questions will not work. A change in a basic behavior, and in this context it belongs with the withdrawal rather than with his pancreatitis. He offered something after saying he was fine. That second sentence is an opening, and it is the one to stay with. There is no point is a statement about hopelessness rather than about discharge. It needs exploring, not rescheduling.

Withdrawal from conversation, and it is the finding that tells you asking more questions will not work. A change in a basic behavior, and in this context it belongs with the withdrawal rather than with his pancreatitis. He offered something after saying he was fine. Withdrawal from conversation, and it is the finding that tells you asking more questions will not work. A change in a basic behavior, and in this context it belongs with the withdrawal rather than with his pancreatitis. He offered something after saying he was fine. That second sentence is an opening, and it is the one to stay with. There is no point is a statement about hopelessness rather than about discharge. It needs exploring, not rescheduling.

options.text: Wound site clean and dry
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A normal finding. The physical recovery is going well.

options.text: Pain reported as 2 of 10
options.rationale: Near miss concept Controlled pain, and it rules out discomfort as the explanation for the withdrawal.

options.text: Ambulated in the corridor this morning with the physiotherapist
options.rationale: Near miss concept He is participating in his physical care. A strength, included to be left alone.

questions.takeaway: Presence is indicated when a patient is saying something the clinical findings cannot explain. Listen for the sentence that comes after 'I'm fine'.
questions.strategy: Three findings are normal or positive, and one of them actively rules out the easy explanation. If his pain is 2 of 10, the withdrawal is not about pain.

questions.stem: A nurse applies Watson's Caritas Processes while caring for a patient having a wound dressing changed. Which actions reflect those principles? Select all that apply.

options.text: Explaining each step as the dressing is changed
options.rationale: Teaching and learning together, which involves the patient in his own care rather than performing it on him. Creating a healing environment that promotes comfort, dignity and safety. Recognizing the spiritual and personal meaning of health, illness and healing. Using scientific knowledge alongside caring and clinical judgment, which is why competence is inside the theory.

options.text: Ensuring his pain is controlled before starting
options.rationale: Teaching and learning together, which involves the patient in his own care rather than performing it on him. Creating a healing environment that promotes comfort, dignity and safety. Recognizing the spiritual and personal meaning of health, illness and healing. Using scientific knowledge alongside caring and clinical judgment, which is why competence is inside the theory.

options.text: Asking what this wound has meant for him
options.rationale: Teaching and learning together, which involves the patient in his own care rather than performing it on him. Creating a healing environment that promotes comfort, dignity and safety. Recognizing the spiritual and personal meaning of health, illness and healing. Using scientific knowledge alongside caring and clinical judgment, which is why competence is inside the theory.

options.text: Using current evidence to select the dressing
options.rationale: Teaching and learning together, which involves the patient in his own care rather than performing it on him. Creating a healing environment that promotes comfort, dignity and safety. Recognizing the spiritual and personal meaning of health, illness and healing. Using scientific knowledge alongside caring and clinical judgment, which is why competence is inside the theory.

options.text: Working in silence so the procedure finishes faster
options.rationale: Near miss concept Efficiency offered in place of presence, and it is the first nurse from her pneumonia scenario.

options.text: Telling him the wound looks much better than it does
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Kindly meant and it is false reassurance, and it also breaches the honesty that trust depends on.

questions.takeaway: The Caritas Processes cover loving kindness, authentic presence, honoring beliefs, supporting healing, scientific knowledge, a healing environment, teaching together, addressing needs, and personal meaning.
questions.strategy: Two distractors are things a nurse might do to be efficient or to be kind. Neither is in the theory.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with newly diagnosed heart failure is readmitted three weeks after discharge with fluid overload. He tells the nurse he stopped weighing himself because the scale 'just made him feel worse'. He can recite the discharge instructions accurately. He lives alone and says his daughter phones but he does not like to bother her with it. He has not mentioned any of this to his provider. Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem they address, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Ask what the daily weight has come to mean to him
Work with him to agree a monitoring plan he is willing to follow
Re-teach the importance of daily weights before discharge
Reassure him that many patients find self-monitoring difficult
The monitoring carries a meaning that makes him avoid it
Knowledge deficit regarding heart failure self-management
Nonadherence with the prescribed monitoring regimen
Lack of social support at home
Whether he is recording weights in the way he agreed
Whether he raises a change in weight with anyone before it becomes an admission
Whether he can state his target weight range
Whether his daughter attends the next appointment

questions.takeaway: He told you the scale made him feel worse. That is about what the number represents, not about whether he understands it. Recognizing the personal meaning of illness. The scale is not a measurement problem, and you cannot solve it until you know what it represents. Caritas Coaching partners rather than instructs, and a plan he helped build is one he may actually use. Measures whether the plan he helped design is one he can use. The behavior the whole intervention exists to produce, and the one that prevents the next readmission. When a patient knows exactly what to do and does not do it, the obstacle is usually what the task means to him.
questions.strategy: Two problem options name knowledge or adherence. He can recite the instructions, which rules the first out and makes the second a description rather than an explanation.

questions.stem: A nurse finishes a difficult conversation with a family and notices she has been thinking about it for two days. Which Caritas principle addresses this?

options.text: Being authentically present with patients and families
options.rationale: Near miss concept She was present, which is part of why the conversation stayed with her.

options.text: Honoring each person's beliefs, values and emotions
options.rationale: Near miss concept Directed at the patient's beliefs rather than at the nurse's own state.

options.text: Creating a healing environment for patients
options.rationale: Near miss concept Concerns the patient's surroundings, comfort, dignity and safety.

options.text: Practicing loving kindness toward yourself as well as others
options.rationale: The first Caritas Process names both directions. A nurse who extends nothing to herself has nothing left to extend.

questions.takeaway: The first Caritas Process is loving kindness toward yourself and others. Self-directed care is inside the theory, not outside it.
questions.strategy: Three options are genuine Caritas Processes directed outward. Ask who this one is about.

questions.topic: goals of care across the trajectory
questions.stem: Match each situation to the care goal that fits it best.
questions.objective: goals of care across the trajectory

rows.text: A patient with type 2 diabetes aiming to prevent complications
A patient with end stage heart failure declining further hospitalization
A healthy adult with community acquired pneumonia
A patient with rheumatoid arthritis wanting to keep working

questions.takeaway: Acute illness aims at cure. Chronic illness aims at control and function, because the disease is not leaving, and the patient defines what function means to him. At the end of the trajectory the goal becomes comfort. The same patient can move between these, and the mistake is pursuing cure in a chronic illness, which produces a plan nobody can live with. In chronic illness the outcome is function, and the patient decides what function means.
questions.strategy: Ask what is achievable for this disease, then ask what the patient wants from the time he has.

questions.stem: A patient with advanced Parkinson disease is cared for at home by his wife. Select all of the findings that suggest caregiver strain.

options.text: She has lost weight and reports sleeping poorly
options.rationale: Caregiver strain shows as the caregiver's own life and health contracting: withdrawal from activities, physical decline, emotional lability and deferred care for herself. Asking good questions is engagement, and arranging respite is exactly what you would hope for. The caregiver is a patient too, and nobody screens her unless you do.

options.text: She becomes tearful when asked how she is doing
options.rationale: Caregiver strain shows as the caregiver's own life and health contracting: withdrawal from activities, physical decline, emotional lability and deferred care for herself. Asking good questions is engagement, and arranging respite is exactly what you would hope for. The caregiver is a patient too, and nobody screens her unless you do.

options.text: She has arranged for a neighbor to sit with him weekly
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Respite use is a protective factor.

options.text: She asks detailed questions about his medication schedule
options.rationale: Near miss concept Engagement and competence, not strain.

options.text: She says she has not seen her own doctor in over a year
options.rationale: Caregiver strain shows as the caregiver's own life and health contracting: withdrawal from activities, physical decline, emotional lability and deferred care for herself. Asking good questions is engagement, and arranging respite is exactly what you would hope for. The caregiver is a patient too, and nobody screens her unless you do.

options.text: She has stopped attending the activities she used to enjoy
options.rationale: Caregiver strain shows as the caregiver's own life and health contracting: withdrawal from activities, physical decline, emotional lability and deferred care for herself. Asking good questions is engagement, and arranging respite is exactly what you would hope for. The caregiver is a patient too, and nobody screens her unless you do.

questions.takeaway: Ask the caregiver how she is. Her answer is an assessment finding.
questions.strategy: Two options are signs she is coping well. Do not read all involvement as strain.

questions.stem: Which assessment best captures how chronic illness is affecting a patient's life?

options.text: The trend in his most recent laboratory values
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Useful for management and silent on function.

options.text: Which daily activities and valued roles he can still do
options.rationale: In chronic illness, function is the outcome that matters, because the disease is not going away. Diagnoses, labs and pill counts describe the illness; function describes the life. Two patients with identical problem lists can be living completely differently, and only one of those facts tells you what to work on.

options.text: How many medications he must take each day
options.rationale: Near miss concept Relevant to polypharmacy risk, not to function.

options.text: The number of diagnoses listed on his current problem list
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data A count that says nothing about how he lives.

questions.takeaway: Count what he can still do, not what he has been diagnosed with.
questions.strategy: Three options measure the disease. One measures the person.

questions.stem: Which factor should the nurse address to reduce a chronically ill patient's risk of readmission?

options.text: The total number of days the patient spent in the hospital this admission
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Associated with severity and not itself the mechanism.

options.text: The specific diagnosis listed on the discharge summary
options.rationale: Near miss concept Some diagnoses readmit more, and the mechanism is still the gap.

options.text: The patient's age and the number of his comorbidities
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data A risk marker, not a modifiable cause.

options.text: Gaps between the discharge plan and what he can do at home
options.rationale: Readmissions come from the gap: the plan assumes he can afford the medication, get to the pharmacy, read the instructions, remember the schedule, and has someone to help. Any one of those failing sends him back. That is why discharge planning is an assessment of circumstances, not a handout.

questions.takeaway: Ask what will actually happen at his house on Thursday. That is the discharge assessment.
questions.strategy: Three options are characteristics you cannot change. One is something nursing can fix.

questions.stem: Select all of the measures that support self management in a patient with a chronic illness.

options.text: Set goals collaboratively, starting from what the patient says matters most
options.rationale: Chronic illness is managed by the patient on the days you are not there, so the goal has to be theirs and the plan has to survive a bad day. Cost is a clinical variable, because a medication he cannot afford is a medication he will not take. Teaching everything at once is how nothing is retained, and choosing the goal for him is the surest way to lose the adherence you were trying to build.

options.text: Help the patient build an action plan for the days when symptoms worsen
options.rationale: Chronic illness is managed by the patient on the days you are not there, so the goal has to be theirs and the plan has to survive a bad day. Cost is a clinical variable, because a medication he cannot afford is a medication he will not take. Teaching everything at once is how nothing is retained, and choosing the goal for him is the surest way to lose the adherence you were trying to build.

options.text: Provide the complete teaching plan in one session before discharge
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome Volume defeats retention; short segments with teach back work.

options.text: Simplify the regimen and address cost and access barriers
options.rationale: Chronic illness is managed by the patient on the days you are not there, so the goal has to be theirs and the plan has to survive a bad day. Cost is a clinical variable, because a medication he cannot afford is a medication he will not take. Teaching everything at once is how nothing is retained, and choosing the goal for him is the surest way to lose the adherence you were trying to build.

options.text: Teach in short segments and use teach back to confirm understanding
options.rationale: Chronic illness is managed by the patient on the days you are not there, so the goal has to be theirs and the plan has to survive a bad day. Cost is a clinical variable, because a medication he cannot afford is a medication he will not take. Teaching everything at once is how nothing is retained, and choosing the goal for him is the surest way to lose the adherence you were trying to build.

options.text: Tell the patient which goal to pursue first, since you know the condition
options.rationale: Near miss concept Collaborative goals are the ones patients act on.

questions.takeaway: Cost and access are clinical variables. A prescription he cannot fill is not a treatment.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options take the work back from the patient who has to do it.

questions.stem: Select all of the statements that reflect how chronic illness is understood.

options.text: It follows a trajectory with stable periods and exacerbations
options.rationale: The shift from cure to management is what chronic illness care turns on, and the losses that matter most to patients are usually about role and identity rather than a laboratory value. Exacerbations are part of the trajectory and treating them as adherence failures is both wrong and corrosive to the relationship. There is often no previous baseline to return to, which is why the goal is the best achievable function.

options.text: Each exacerbation reflects a failure of the patient's adherence
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Exacerbations are part of the trajectory; blame damages the alliance.

options.text: The goal of care is to return the patient to the previous baseline
options.rationale: Near miss concept Often unattainable; the goal is optimal function from here.

options.text: It involves permanent changes that are managed rather than cured
options.rationale: The shift from cure to management is what chronic illness care turns on, and the losses that matter most to patients are usually about role and identity rather than a laboratory value. Exacerbations are part of the trajectory and treating them as adherence failures is both wrong and corrosive to the relationship. There is often no previous baseline to return to, which is why the goal is the best achievable function.

options.text: Care is directed at function, symptom control and quality of life
options.rationale: The shift from cure to management is what chronic illness care turns on, and the losses that matter most to patients are usually about role and identity rather than a laboratory value. Exacerbations are part of the trajectory and treating them as adherence failures is both wrong and corrosive to the relationship. There is often no previous baseline to return to, which is why the goal is the best achievable function.

options.text: It affects roles, identity and family as much as the body
options.rationale: The shift from cure to management is what chronic illness care turns on, and the losses that matter most to patients are usually about role and identity rather than a laboratory value. Exacerbations are part of the trajectory and treating them as adherence failures is both wrong and corrosive to the relationship. There is often no previous baseline to return to, which is why the goal is the best achievable function.

questions.takeaway: Not every exacerbation is a failure. Most are the disease doing what the disease does.
questions.strategy: One wrong option blames the patient; the other sets a goal that may not exist.

questions.stem: A patient who uses a wheelchair is admitted for pneumonia. Which approach reflects appropriate care?

options.text: Ask how he usually transfers and manages care, and plan from that
options.rationale: A long standing disability is not a new deficit, and the patient is the expert on his own method. He has been transferring himself for years. The nursing concern is the pneumonia and anything that has changed from his baseline, not the wheelchair itself.

options.text: Encourage him to let staff do everything so he can rest and recover
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Well meant, and a week of this costs him independence.

options.text: Assume he needs total assistance with all activities of daily living
options.rationale: Near miss concept Treats a wheelchair as a global dependency.

options.text: Document the wheelchair as a mobility deficit needing a therapy consult
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Pathologizes his established baseline.

questions.takeaway: A stable disability is a baseline, not a problem to solve.
questions.strategy: Two options take away function he already has.

questions.stem: Select all of the nursing actions that build a chronically ill patient's confidence in managing his own care.

options.text: Break the regimen into one change at a time
options.rationale: Self efficacy is built by succeeding at something small and seeing that you did. One change at a time, demonstrated rather than described, with the successes named out loud and the goals chosen together. Threatening consequences raises fear without raising capability, which usually produces avoidance. All the teaching on discharge day is the least retained teaching there is.

options.text: Describe in detail what will happen if he does not comply
options.rationale: Near miss concept Raises perceived severity without raising self efficacy, which tends to produce avoidance.

options.text: Point out specific successes he has already had
options.rationale: Self efficacy is built by succeeding at something small and seeing that you did. One change at a time, demonstrated rather than described, with the successes named out loud and the goals chosen together. Threatening consequences raises fear without raising capability, which usually produces avoidance. All the teaching on discharge day is the least retained teaching there is.

options.text: Set goals with him rather than for him
options.rationale: Self efficacy is built by succeeding at something small and seeing that you did. One change at a time, demonstrated rather than described, with the successes named out loud and the goals chosen together. Threatening consequences raises fear without raising capability, which usually produces avoidance. All the teaching on discharge day is the least retained teaching there is.

options.text: Provide all the teaching at once on the day of discharge
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome Completes the teaching requirement at the moment of lowest retention.

options.text: Have the patient demonstrate the skill rather than describe it
options.rationale: Self efficacy is built by succeeding at something small and seeing that you did. One change at a time, demonstrated rather than described, with the successes named out loud and the goals chosen together. Threatening consequences raises fear without raising capability, which usually produces avoidance. All the teaching on discharge day is the least retained teaching there is.

questions.takeaway: Confidence comes from a success he can point to, not from understanding the risk.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options are common practice and neither builds capability.

questions.stem: A patient has heart failure, chronic kidney disease stage 4, osteoarthritis and type 2 diabetes. Select all of the accurate nursing conclusions.

options.text: Treating each condition to its own guideline target may produce an unmanageable regimen
options.rationale: Multimorbidity is not four separate problems; the treatments collide. Guidelines are written for one disease at a time, and stacking four of them produces a pill burden and a set of contradictions no patient can follow. The resolution is prioritizing with the patient around what she wants, which is why what matters most is the first of the four Ms.

options.text: Nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs for her arthritis threaten both her kidneys and her heart failure
options.rationale: Multimorbidity is not four separate problems; the treatments collide. Guidelines are written for one disease at a time, and stacking four of them produces a pill burden and a set of contradictions no patient can follow. The resolution is prioritizing with the patient around what she wants, which is why what matters most is the first of the four Ms.

options.text: Her goals should be negotiated around what matters most to her
options.rationale: Multimorbidity is not four separate problems; the treatments collide. Guidelines are written for one disease at a time, and stacking four of them produces a pill burden and a set of contradictions no patient can follow. The resolution is prioritizing with the patient around what she wants, which is why what matters most is the first of the four Ms.

options.text: Her care will be simplest if every guideline target is met
options.rationale: Absolute language Meeting every target simultaneously is usually impossible and often harmful.

options.text: Each specialist should optimize their own condition independently
options.rationale: Near miss concept Independent optimization is what creates the collisions.

options.text: Diuresis adequate for her heart failure may worsen her kidney function
options.rationale: Multimorbidity is not four separate problems; the treatments collide. Guidelines are written for one disease at a time, and stacking four of them produces a pill burden and a set of contradictions no patient can follow. The resolution is prioritizing with the patient around what she wants, which is why what matters most is the first of the four Ms.

questions.takeaway: Treating each disease perfectly is how you harm a patient who has four of them.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options treat the conditions as independent, which is the central error.
