questions.topic: the older adult with multiple conditions
questions.stem: A 78 year old has heart failure, diabetes, osteoarthritis and chronic kidney disease, and takes 11 medications. What should the nurse recognize as the central risk?
questions.objective: the older adult with multiple conditions

options.text: The number of diagnoses means his overall prognosis is poor
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Counts diagnoses instead of assessing function.

options.text: Each condition must be managed strictly by its own guideline
options.rationale: Near miss concept Guidelines are written for single diseases and collide in a patient like this.

options.text: The conditions and treatments interact; helping one can worsen another
options.rationale: Multimorbidity is not four separate problems. A nonsteroidal for the arthritis hurts the kidneys and the heart failure. Diuresing hard enough to clear the congestion drops renal perfusion and injures the kidneys, and easing off to protect them lets the congestion come back; add a RAAS blocker on top of chronic kidney disease and the potassium climbs. Following every single disease guideline at once produces a drug list nobody can take safely, which is why the goal is negotiated around what the patient wants rather than optimized disease by disease.

options.text: He is too old to benefit from aggressive disease management
options.rationale: Near miss concept Age alone is not a treatment decision.

questions.takeaway: Treating each disease perfectly is how you harm a patient who has four of them.
questions.strategy: The option that sounds most rigorous, follow every guideline, is the trap.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure has been readmitted twice in three months. Which nursing approach is most likely to reduce the next admission?

options.text: Give a detailed heart failure pamphlet to review carefully at home after discharge
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome Delivers information and establishes nothing about what he will do.

options.text: Stress how serious the consequences of nonadherence will be
options.rationale: Near miss concept Raising perceived severity without raising self efficacy usually increases avoidance.

options.text: Arrange more frequent clinic appointments with the cardiologist
options.rationale: Near miss concept Useful, and it does not help him on the day between visits.

options.text: Build a daily self monitoring routine and agree on when to call
options.rationale: Chronic disease is managed at home by the patient, not in the clinic by you. A concrete routine, weigh yourself at the same time each morning, call for a gain of 2 to 3 pounds in a day, is something he can act on. Information alone changes little, and raising fear tends to raise avoidance rather than adherence.

questions.takeaway: Self management means the patient knows the number that makes him pick up the phone.
questions.strategy: Information and appointments both keep the control with the system.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has had three exacerbations this year, each leaving him weaker than before. How should the nurse understand this pattern?

options.text: Evidence that he is not adhering to his prescribed treatment plan
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Assumes a cause the stem does not support.

options.text: A stepwise decline, with each flare resetting him to a lower baseline
options.rationale: Many chronic illnesses decline in steps rather than a smooth slope: the patient is stable, has a crisis, partially recovers, and settles lower than before. Recognizing the pattern changes the conversation, because the window for advance care planning and for maximizing function is between the steps, not during them.

options.text: An expected part of normal aging rather than disease progression
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Attributes disease progression to age.

options.text: A normal fluctuation that will return to his old baseline in time
options.rationale: Near miss concept Describes an acute illness, which this is not.

questions.takeaway: He does not come all the way back. Each exacerbation costs him a piece of the baseline.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options blame the patient or his age for the disease's own course.

questions.stem: A patient with advanced heart failure asks about palliative care. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: It replaces the patient's ongoing cardiology care
options.rationale: Near miss concept It is added to it.

options.text: It eases symptoms and can be given alongside active treatment
options.rationale: Palliative care is symptom and quality of life care that runs alongside everything else, from diagnosis onward. Hospice is the subset for a prognosis of about six months when the goal has shifted away from life prolonging treatment. Conflating them is why patients refuse palliative care: they hear that treatment is ending.

options.text: It requires a prognosis of six months or less to begin
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is the hospice criterion.

options.text: It begins only once curative treatment has been stopped
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is closer to hospice, and it is the misconception that makes patients refuse.

questions.takeaway: Palliative is any stage, alongside treatment. Hospice is the subset with a prognosis.
questions.strategy: Three distractors are all descriptions of hospice offered as definitions of palliative care.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease says he wants to be able to walk to his mailbox without stopping. Which outcome statement best reflects chronic illness care?

options.text: The patient will verbalize understanding of his disease process
options.rationale: Near miss concept Unmeasurable, and not what he asked for.

options.text: The patient's oxygen saturation will stay above 92% at all times
options.rationale: Near miss concept A number rather than a function, and his target may be lower by design.

options.text: The patient's forced expiratory volume will improve by 10%
options.rationale: Near miss concept Often not achievable in COPD, and function improves without it.

options.text: The patient will walk 100 feet without resting within 4 weeks
options.rationale: He told you the goal, and a good outcome translates it into something measurable without replacing it. Chronic illness care is judged on function, because the disease is not reversing. A saturation target is not what he came for and is not fully controllable. Verbalizing understanding is unmeasurable. A lung function improvement is often not achievable in COPD and has little to do with reaching his mailbox.

questions.takeaway: Translate the patient's own goal into something you can measure. Do not substitute your own.
questions.strategy: Three distractors are clinical targets. Only one is the life he described.

questions.stem: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis says, "I just want you to fix this." Which response best reflects a chronic illness framework?

options.text: "That is a question to discuss with your rheumatologist at the next scheduled visit."
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Deflects a conversation that is squarely nursing's.

options.text: "Try to stay positive. Many people live full lives with this condition."
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Assigns him a mood and dismisses the loss.

options.text: "We cannot cure it, but we can work toward what matters most to you."
options.rationale: Chronic illness care changes the goal from cure to function and quality of life, and the patient defines what function means. Saying so plainly respects him more than optimism does, and the follow up question hands him back the control the diagnosis just took.

options.text: "The newer medications work very well for most people who have this."
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic False reassurance that sidesteps what he asked.

questions.takeaway: The goal moves from cure to function. Say it honestly and then ask what function means to him.
questions.strategy: False reassurance and redirection both avoid the sentence he actually needs to hear.

questions.stem: A patient with diabetes has not been checking his glucose. Which response is most likely to help?

options.text: "I will ask your provider to simplify the regimen."
options.rationale: Correct but premature A good intervention, chosen before you know what the problem is.

options.text: "You know this is how people lose their feet."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Raises severity without raising his ability to act, which tends to produce avoidance.

options.text: "What gets in the way of checking?"
options.rationale: What gets in the way asks about the barrier without asking him to defend himself. The answer is usually concrete and fixable: the strips cost too much, the meter is in a drawer he cannot reach, he is embarrassed to do it at work. Why puts him on the defensive, and fear changes behavior far less reliably than removing the obstacle does.

options.text: "Why aren't you checking your sugar?"
options.rationale: Near miss concept Same information sought, and the word why makes it an accusation.

questions.takeaway: Ask what gets in the way. Why makes him argue; what makes him think.
questions.strategy: Nonadherence is almost always a barrier, not a choice. Find the barrier.

questions.stem: The wife of a patient with advanced dementia says, "I cannot do this anymore," then immediately adds that she did not mean it. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Take it seriously, explore her situation, and discuss respite options
options.rationale: People retract these statements because saying them feels like failure, and the retraction is not a withdrawal of the message. She is telling you she is at the edge, which matters for her health and for his safety, because caregiver exhaustion is a risk factor for neglect and for injury to both of them. Explore it, and bring respite and support into the conversation.

options.text: Suggest she consider long term placement for her husband soon
options.rationale: Correct but premature May become the answer, and it is not the response to a first disclosure.

options.text: Reassure her that she is doing a wonderful job as his caregiver
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Praise that closes the subject she just opened.

options.text: Accept her correction and move on to the planned discharge teaching
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome Takes the retraction at face value and completes the paperwork.

questions.takeaway: The retraction does not cancel the disclosure. She told you where she is.
questions.strategy: Praise and acceptance both let everyone off the hook, including you.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure is readmitted for the third time in four months. He says he ran out of his diuretic ten days ago because he could not afford the refill, and did not want to bother anyone. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Arrange more frequent clinic follow up visits for the first months after discharge
options.rationale: Near miss concept Useful and it does not put the medication in his hand.

options.text: Reinforce the importance of taking medications as prescribed
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome He knows; he could not pay.

options.text: Involve social work about cost and address his reluctance to ask
options.rationale: He has named the barrier, and it is money, not understanding. Teaching him again about adherence answers a question he did not ask. The second part matters as much: he did not want to bother anyone, so even with a solved cost problem he may not call next time, and that is worth naming directly. Calling this nonadherence hides a solvable social problem behind a label.

options.text: Document medication nonadherence as the cause of readmission
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism A judgment that conceals a cost barrier and a help seeking barrier.

questions.takeaway: Nonadherence is almost always a barrier. He told you which one.
questions.strategy: When a patient volunteers the reason, the answer is to fix that reason, not to teach harder.

questions.stem: An 80 year old tells the nurse she has been more forgetful and tired for two months. The provider's note reads "age related changes." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Reinforce the provider's explanation to reassure the patient
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Comfortable for everyone and closes a workup that has not happened.

options.text: Document her concern and monitor her closely over the next several clinic visits
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Charts a symptom and waits.

options.text: Suggest memory exercises and a more regular sleep schedule
options.rationale: Correct but premature Treats a symptom whose cause has not been looked for.

options.text: Pursue the symptoms, since new fatigue and memory loss are not aging
options.rationale: Ageism in health care looks exactly like this: a real symptom gets filed under getting older and nobody looks further. Two months of new fatigue and forgetfulness could be thyroid disease, anemia, depression, B12 deficiency, medication effect or early dementia, all of which are worth finding. Aging is a diagnosis of exclusion and usually not a diagnosis at all.

questions.takeaway: Age explains a slow decline over years, never a change over two months.
questions.strategy: The note is the trap. A label already written in the chart is still a label.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has an oxygen saturation of 89 percent. His baseline is 88 to 90 percent. He denies increased dyspnea. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Recognize this as his baseline and assess for change from it
options.rationale: In chronic disease, normal is whatever this patient usually runs. A saturation that would alarm you in a healthy adult is his Tuesday. The clinically useful question is always whether anything has changed. Driving his saturation up with high flow oxygen worsens the match between ventilation and blood flow and shifts carbon dioxide off hemoglobin, so his carbon dioxide climbs.

options.text: Notify the provider that the patient has new hypoxemia
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reports an unchanged baseline as a new finding.

options.text: Place the patient on bedrest until the saturation improves
options.rationale: Near miss concept Immobilizes him for a number that is not going to change.

options.text: Apply high flow oxygen to raise the saturation above 94% right away
options.rationale: Near miss concept Risks carbon dioxide retention, and his target is lower by design.

questions.takeaway: Chronic disease moves the baseline. Compare to his normal, not to the population normal.
questions.strategy: Two options treat a number that is normal for this patient as an emergency.

questions.stem: Select all of the areas a nurse should include in a cultural assessment.

options.text: Use of traditional remedies or healers alongside prescribed treatment
options.rationale: Cultural assessment is asking, not categorizing. Decision making structure, diet, beliefs about causation and concurrent remedies all change the plan, and the last one matters clinically because herbal products interact with prescribed drugs. Assuming from nationality is stereotyping, and judging the validity of a practice ends the conversation that was revealing it.

options.text: An assumption about the patient's beliefs based on her country of origin
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Stereotyping, which is the opposite of cultural humility.

options.text: Whether the patient's practices are medically valid
options.rationale: Near miss concept Judging validity stops disclosure; you need the information more than the verdict.

options.text: Who the patient wants included in health decisions
options.rationale: Cultural assessment is asking, not categorizing. Decision making structure, diet, beliefs about causation and concurrent remedies all change the plan, and the last one matters clinically because herbal products interact with prescribed drugs. Assuming from nationality is stereotyping, and judging the validity of a practice ends the conversation that was revealing it.

options.text: Health beliefs about the cause of the illness
options.rationale: Cultural assessment is asking, not categorizing. Decision making structure, diet, beliefs about causation and concurrent remedies all change the plan, and the last one matters clinically because herbal products interact with prescribed drugs. Assuming from nationality is stereotyping, and judging the validity of a practice ends the conversation that was revealing it.

options.text: Dietary practices and restrictions relevant to the plan of care
options.rationale: Cultural assessment is asking, not categorizing. Decision making structure, diet, beliefs about causation and concurrent remedies all change the plan, and the last one matters clinically because herbal products interact with prescribed drugs. Assuming from nationality is stereotyping, and judging the validity of a practice ends the conversation that was revealing it.

questions.takeaway: Ask about traditional remedies without judgment. You need to know what is actually being taken.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options substitute the nurse's framework for the patient's account.

questions.stem: A nurse has read extensively about the health beliefs of the cultural group her patient belongs to and applies that knowledge in planning care. The patient later says the nurse keeps assuming things about his family that are not true of him. Which construct of cultural competence has the nurse underused?

options.text: Cultural knowledge
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit She has it. The stem says she read extensively.

options.text: Cultural desire
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit She is actively trying, which is desire.

options.text: Cultural awareness
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is inward, about her own biases, and is not what the patient is describing.

options.text: Cultural encounters
options.rationale: Encounters are direct interactions with individuals from the group, and they are the construct that corrects knowledge before it hardens into stereotype. The nurse has knowledge and is willing; what is missing is checking the general against this particular person.

questions.takeaway: Knowledge without encounters becomes stereotype. Nothing else corrects it.
questions.strategy: When a stem shows a nurse who studied the group and misread the individual, the answer is the construct that connects the two.

questions.stem: Place the steps of the LEARN model in the order the nurse should use them when a patient's cultural practice conflicts with the prescribed plan.

options.text: Explain your own perception of the problem
Recommend a course of action that involves the patient
Acknowledge the differences and the similarities
Listen to the patient's perception of the problem
Negotiate a plan that keeps selected aspects of the patient's practice

questions.takeaway: Listening comes first. If you explain before you listen, what follows is persuasion with a negotiation label on it. Acknowledging builds on the similarities, not only the differences. LEARN starts with L. That is the step people invert.
questions.strategy: Any ordering item about a communication model is testing whether you listen before you speak.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence: A nurse prepares for a difficult conversation with a patient whose beliefs about his treatment differ from her own. Saying "tell me more about what you think is causing this" is the [[1]] step of LEARN. Pointing out that they both want him to avoid another admission is the [[2]] step. Agreeing a plan that keeps his traditional remedies alongside the prescribed treatment is the [[3]] step. A nurse who examines her own assumptions before entering the room is demonstrating [[4]].

options.text: Listen
Explain
Acknowledge
Negotiate
Acknowledge
Recommend
Listen
Explain
Negotiate
Recommend
Acknowledge
Explain
cultural awareness
cultural knowledge
cultural skill
cultural desire

questions.takeaway: [1] Listen: Listen to the patient's perception of the problem, nonjudgmentally, using encouraging comments such as tell me more. [2] Acknowledge: Recognize the differences and build on the similarities. Naming a shared goal is exactly that. [3] Negotiate: Negotiate a treatment plan, incorporating selected aspects of the patient's culture into it. [4] cultural awareness: The first Campinha-Bacote construct, and it is self-examination before anything else. LEARN: Listen, Explain, Acknowledge, Recommend, Negotiate. Campinha-Bacote: awareness, knowledge, skill, encounters, desire.
questions.strategy: Recommend and Negotiate are the pair that gets confused. Recommending offers options; negotiating lands on a plan the patient accepts.

questions.stem: A nurse reads that a particular cultural group commonly involves family elders in medical decisions. She assumes her patient from that background will want his father present and arranges it without asking. What error has she made?

options.text: She applied group knowledge to an individual without checking
options.rationale: Cultural knowledge is a genuine construct and becomes stereotyping the moment it is applied without asking. Culturally congruent care is based on the individual's beliefs, practices and values.

options.text: She should not have read about cultural practices at all
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cultural knowledge is part of competence. The problem is applying it without verifying it.

options.text: She demonstrated a lack of cultural awareness
options.rationale: Near miss concept Awareness is self-examination. She may lack it, and what the stem shows is misapplied knowledge.

options.text: She failed to obtain the patient's consent for the arrangement
options.rationale: Near miss concept Consent is a real issue here, and it is a consequence of the underlying error rather than the error itself.

questions.takeaway: Culturally congruent care is based on the individual's beliefs, practices and values. Group knowledge tells you what to ask about, not what to assume.
questions.strategy: One distractor concludes that learning about cultures is itself the mistake. Ask what turned useful knowledge into an error.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the five social determinants of health domains from Healthy People 2030. Which are included? Select all that apply.

options.text: Economic stability
options.rationale: Income, employment and the ability to meet basic needs. Named, and it connects to health literacy and to lifetime earning. Named, and it covers insurance, transport and having a usual provider. Named, and it covers housing, food access and safety. Named, and it covers support networks, discrimination and civic participation.

options.text: Education access and quality
options.rationale: Income, employment and the ability to meet basic needs. Named, and it connects to health literacy and to lifetime earning. Named, and it covers insurance, transport and having a usual provider. Named, and it covers housing, food access and safety. Named, and it covers support networks, discrimination and civic participation.

options.text: Health care access and quality
options.rationale: Income, employment and the ability to meet basic needs. Named, and it connects to health literacy and to lifetime earning. Named, and it covers insurance, transport and having a usual provider. Named, and it covers housing, food access and safety. Named, and it covers support networks, discrimination and civic participation.

options.text: Neighborhood and built environment
options.rationale: Income, employment and the ability to meet basic needs. Named, and it connects to health literacy and to lifetime earning. Named, and it covers insurance, transport and having a usual provider. Named, and it covers housing, food access and safety. Named, and it covers support networks, discrimination and civic participation.

options.text: Social and community context
options.rationale: Income, employment and the ability to meet basic needs. Named, and it connects to health literacy and to lifetime earning. Named, and it covers insurance, transport and having a usual provider. Named, and it covers housing, food access and safety. Named, and it covers support networks, discrimination and civic participation.

options.text: Genetic predisposition to disease
options.rationale: Near miss concept A genuine influence on health, and it is a biological factor rather than a social determinant. Determinants are non-medical conditions.

questions.takeaway: Five domains: economic stability, education, health care access, neighborhood and built environment, social and community context.
questions.strategy: One distractor names a real health influence that is biological rather than social. Determinants are non-medical by definition.

questions.stem: Four patients attend the same clinic, all with type 2 diabetes diagnosed within the past year. For each patient, indicate the barrier most likely to affect their diabetes management.

rows.text: A 25-year-old who is unhoused and uses a shelter
An 85-year-old retired nurse in rural Alabama, 50 miles from the nearest endocrinologist
A 32-year-old executive whose church community treats illness as a private matter she does not discuss
An undocumented mother who avoids clinics for fear of immigration consequences

questions.takeaway: A 25-year-old who is unhoused and uses a shelter: Housing and income shape everything else, including whether insulin can be stored and meals eaten on time. An 85-year-old retired nurse in rural Alabama, 50 miles from the nearest endocrinologist: She has the knowledge and the means. What she lacks is a service she can physically reach. A 32-year-old executive whose church community treats illness as a private matter she does not discuss: Resources and access are not the problem. Her support network is a place she cannot bring this. An undocumented mother who avoids clinics for fear of immigration consequences: The service exists and she cannot safely use it. Fear functions as an access barrier. The same diagnosis meets four different lives. Intersectionality is why identical treatment plans produce different outcomes.
questions.strategy: Two patients share a domain for opposite reasons: one cannot reach the service, the other cannot safely use it.

questions.stem: A hospital implements core measures for the management of myocardial infarction. A nurse asks what these are intended to achieve. Which response is accurate?

options.text: Individualized protocols adapted to each patient's cultural preferences
options.rationale: Near miss concept The opposite of what they are. Their value comes from being applied consistently.

options.text: Internal quality targets set by each hospital for its own improvement
options.rationale: Near miss concept Externally set by CMS and The Joint Commission rather than by the organization.

options.text: Evidence-based standards applied to every patient, intended to reduce disparities in care
options.rationale: Set by CMS and The Joint Commission, and the aim is to standardize care regardless of background so that outcomes depend less on who the patient is.

options.text: Guidelines for nurses working with patients who need interpreters
options.rationale: Near miss concept Interpreter use is a cultural skill. Core measures are clinical standards of care.

questions.takeaway: Core measures are evidence-based, scientifically researched standards set by CMS and The Joint Commission, aimed at reducing disparities and standardizing care regardless of background.
questions.strategy: One distractor makes them individualized, which is the opposite of the mechanism. Standardization is how they reduce disparity.

questions.stem: A nursing student discusses cultural care with her preceptor. Which statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Once I have learned about a culture, I can apply that knowledge to patients from that background."
options.rationale: Cultural competence is an ongoing process rather than a finished state, and culturally congruent care is based on the individual rather than the group.

options.text: "Self-awareness is where cultural competence starts."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Accurate, and it matches both her key points and the first Campinha-Bacote construct.

options.text: "Disease is the biological process and illness is how the person and family react to it."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Accurate, and it includes cultural stigma and socially constructed meaning.

options.text: "Implicit bias is unconscious, and I am still responsible for managing it."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Accurate. Outside our control to have, within our responsibility to recognize.

questions.takeaway: Cultural competence is an ongoing process, not an achievement. Group knowledge tells you what to ask, never what to assume.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate her slides correctly. The fourth treats competence as something that can be completed.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked where cultural competence begins. Which answer is most accurate?

options.text: With learning the health beliefs of the groups served by the hospital
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cultural knowledge is a genuine construct and it is the second one. Knowledge without awareness becomes assumption.

options.text: With building experience through repeated cross-cultural encounters
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cultural encounters is a construct, and encounters without self-examination tend to confirm what you already believed.

options.text: With self-awareness, examining one's own beliefs and assumptions
options.rationale: Cultural awareness is the first Campinha-Bacote construct and her stated key point. Self-exploration precedes the encounter.

options.text: With a genuine wish to provide equitable care
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cultural desire is a construct and arguably what motivates the rest. It is not where the process starts.

questions.takeaway: Campinha-Bacote: awareness, knowledge, skill, encounters, desire. Self-awareness is the starting point.
questions.strategy: All four options name real constructs from the same model. Ask which one comes first.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews health disparity data showing that rural patients have higher mortality and worse access to substance use treatment than urban patients. Which term describes this?

options.text: A social determinant of health
options.rationale: Near miss concept Determinants are the conditions producing the difference. The difference itself is the disparity.

options.text: Implicit bias operating at a system level
options.rationale: Near miss concept Bias may contribute, and the data describes an outcome gap rather than a mechanism.

options.text: A failure of cultural competence among rural providers
options.rationale: Near miss concept Assigns a cause the data does not support, and rural disparities trace largely to access and resources.

options.text: A health disparity, a measurable difference between population groups
options.rationale: Measurable, between defined groups, and the measurability is what allows it to be tracked and targeted.

questions.takeaway: A health disparity is a measurable difference in health between specific population groups. Social determinants are the conditions that produce it.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is social determinants. One names the cause, the other names the gap.

questions.stem: A patient speaks limited English. Her adult daughter offers to interpret for the discharge teaching. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Accept the daughter's offer, since she knows her mother best
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Convenient and willing, and it compromises accuracy and the patient's privacy.

options.text: Use a professional interpreter, and invite the daughter to stay as family
options.rationale: Family interpreters filter. They soften bad news, skip what embarrasses them, and may not know the clinical vocabulary, and the patient may not disclose with a relative speaking for her. Effective communication is a legal and ethical requirement, not a courtesy. The daughter is still welcome in the room as a daughter.

options.text: Use the daughter for simple instructions and an interpreter for complex ones
options.rationale: Near miss concept Who decides which is simple? Errors hide in the instructions that sounded easy.

options.text: Write the instructions down and let the family translate at home
options.rationale: Near miss concept Removes any chance for her to ask a question.

questions.takeaway: A family member is support, not a language service.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options use a family member for some or all of the teaching.

questions.stem: A patient's family asks that the patient not be told her cancer diagnosis, saying that in their culture the family carries bad news. The patient is competent and has not said what she wants. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ask the patient how much she wants to know and whom she wants involved
options.rationale: Cultural humility means asking rather than assuming, and that cuts both ways: you do not assume the family speaks for her, and you do not assume she wants the Western default of full individual disclosure. Many patients do choose to delegate information to family, and that is her decision to make. Asking her settles it without overriding anyone.

options.text: Ask the provider to decide how the family's request should be handled
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Finding out what the patient wants is nursing work, not a referral.

options.text: Tell the patient the diagnosis, since she has a legal right to know it
options.rationale: Near miss concept She has the right to information and also the right to decline it.

options.text: Follow the family's request, since honoring culture is patient centered
options.rationale: Near miss concept Respects a generalization about her culture instead of asking her.

questions.takeaway: Ask the patient what she wants. A culture does not consent; a person does.
questions.strategy: Two options are each defensible on principle, and both skip the one person who can resolve it.

questions.stem: 0800: Patient is 27, diagnosed with type 2 diabetes two years ago and now requires insulin. Admitted with a blood glucose of 322 mg/dL; her target range is 80 to 130. HbA1c 11%, target 7% or less. Became unhoused after losing her job and health insurance. Currently living in shelter-provided housing. Third emergency department visit for the same reason in six months. Previous providers documented that she verbalized understanding of her diabetes management but has difficulty following her treatment plan. Alert and oriented. Answers questions readily. Select all of the findings that represent social determinants affecting her ability to manage her diabetes.

options.text: Became unhoused after losing her job
options.rationale: Economic stability, and it is the event that set the rest in motion. Health care access. Insulin and supplies both depend on it. Neighborhood and built environment. Shelter living affects refrigeration for insulin, meal timing, and where syringes can be kept safely. The pattern that says the plan is failing repeatedly, and repeated presentation is how a determinant shows up clinically.

options.text: Lost her health insurance
options.rationale: Economic stability, and it is the event that set the rest in motion. Health care access. Insulin and supplies both depend on it. Neighborhood and built environment. Shelter living affects refrigeration for insulin, meal timing, and where syringes can be kept safely. The pattern that says the plan is failing repeatedly, and repeated presentation is how a determinant shows up clinically.

options.text: Living in shelter-provided housing
options.rationale: Economic stability, and it is the event that set the rest in motion. Health care access. Insulin and supplies both depend on it. Neighborhood and built environment. Shelter living affects refrigeration for insulin, meal timing, and where syringes can be kept safely. The pattern that says the plan is failing repeatedly, and repeated presentation is how a determinant shows up clinically.

options.text: Third emergency department visit for the same reason in six months
options.rationale: Economic stability, and it is the event that set the rest in motion. Health care access. Insulin and supplies both depend on it. Neighborhood and built environment. Shelter living affects refrigeration for insulin, meal timing, and where syringes can be kept safely. The pattern that says the plan is failing repeatedly, and repeated presentation is how a determinant shows up clinically.

options.text: Blood glucose 322 mg/dL
options.rationale: Near miss concept A clinical value describing the disease. It is the consequence of the determinants rather than one of them.

options.text: HbA1c 11%
options.rationale: Near miss concept Also a clinical measure, and it tells you the problem has been sustained for months rather than naming its cause.

options.text: Verbalized understanding of her diabetes management
options.rationale: Near miss concept Documented knowledge. It is the finding that rules out a knowledge deficit, which makes it important and not a determinant.

options.text: Alert and oriented, answers questions readily
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A normal finding, and it removes cognition as an explanation.

questions.takeaway: Social determinants are the non-medical conditions where a person lives, learns, works and ages. The glucose is what they produce, not what they are.
questions.strategy: Two findings are laboratory values and two rule out the easy explanations. If she understands and is oriented, the barrier is elsewhere.

questions.stem: A nursing student caring for the patient above teaches her the importance of taking insulin as prescribed and how to make healthy food choices. The patient nods and says she has no questions. Which assessment should the student have made first?

options.text: Her level of health literacy before beginning the teaching
options.rationale: Near miss concept A reasonable step in general, and the record already documents verbalized understanding. Literacy is not what is unexplained here.

options.text: What gets in the way of following the plan where she currently lives
options.rationale: Previous providers documented that she understands the management. Teaching again addresses a gap that has already been ruled out; the barrier is in her circumstances.

options.text: Whether she has been storing her insulin correctly
options.rationale: Near miss concept A specific and useful question, and it is one of several barriers rather than the assessment that would find them.

options.text: Her readiness to learn about diabetes management
options.rationale: Near miss concept Readiness matters before teaching, and the deeper problem is that teaching is the wrong intervention for this patient today.

questions.takeaway: When the record says a patient understands and still cannot follow the plan, the barrier is not knowledge. Ask what is in the way.
questions.strategy: One distractor names a real barrier rather than the assessment that uncovers barriers. Ask which question would find whatever is actually stopping her.

questions.stem: The nurse asks the same patient how she stores her insulin. She explains the shelter has one shared refrigerator that is often full, meals are served at fixed times she cannot always attend, and she keeps her supplies in a locker. Which conclusion is most accurate?

options.text: Her housing situation directly affects insulin storage, meal timing, and medication access
options.rationale: Every element of her regimen depends on conditions she does not control. Neighborhood and built environment is a determinant with concrete clinical consequences.

options.text: She is nonadherent with the prescribed diabetes regimen
options.rationale: Near miss concept Describes the outcome and blames her for it. The stem has just explained what stands in the way.

options.text: She requires more intensive education about insulin storage requirements
options.rationale: Near miss concept She has just described the problem accurately, which means she understands the requirement and cannot meet it.

options.text: A referral to a diabetes specialist is the priority
options.rationale: Near miss concept Specialist input may help eventually, and it does not change a shared refrigerator or fixed mealtimes.

questions.takeaway: Housing instability affects insulin storage, meal timing, and medication adherence directly. The regimen assumes conditions she does not have.
questions.strategy: One distractor labels her. One sends her to a specialist for a problem the specialist cannot change.

questions.stem: A nurse notices she assumed a patient would decline a blood transfusion because of his surname. She stops and asks him directly. Which describes what she recognized in herself?

options.text: Stereotyping, an assumed belief about a group of people
options.rationale: Near miss concept Close, and stereotyping is the assumed belief itself. What she caught was the unconscious process that produced it before she was aware of it.

options.text: Cultural knowledge applied to an individual patient
options.rationale: Near miss concept Knowledge about a group applied without checking becomes the problem rather than the solution.

options.text: A failure of cultural desire
options.rationale: Near miss concept Desire is the genuine wish to engage. Hers is evident in stopping to ask.

options.text: Implicit bias, which is unconscious and shaped by her background
options.rationale: Unconscious, outside our control, and it drives quick judgments. She is responsible for recognizing and managing it, which is what she did.

questions.takeaway: Implicit bias is unconscious and outside our control. Recognizing and managing it is the part we are responsible for.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is stereotyping. One names the unconscious process, the other names the belief it produces.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked what intersectionality adds to understanding a patient's health. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Identities accumulate, so more marginalized identities produce proportionally worse outcomes
options.rationale: Near miss concept Treats them as additive. The framework describes interlocking systems rather than a running total.

options.text: Overlapping identities interact, so privilege and oppression work as interlocking systems
options.rationale: The identities do not simply add up. A person can hold advantage in one dimension and disadvantage in another, and the combination shapes the outcome.

options.text: The most significant identity should be identified and addressed first
options.rationale: Near miss concept Ranking identities misses the point that they operate together and cannot be separated.

options.text: Patients with shared identities will have comparable health experiences
options.rationale: Near miss concept Contradicts the framework, and it is the assumption that produces stereotyping.

questions.takeaway: Intersectionality: social identities overlap, and privilege and oppression interlock rather than adding up.
questions.strategy: One distractor turns it into arithmetic. One turns it into a ranking. Both simplify what the framework exists to describe.

questions.stem: A nurse works with a patient whose first language is not English. She speaks slowly, uses simple words, and asks the patient's adult son to interpret the consent discussion. Which action requires correction?

options.text: Speaking slowly during the conversation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reasonable, and it helps when someone is working in a second language.

options.text: Using plain language rather than clinical terms
options.rationale: Near miss concept A named cultural skill, and it applies regardless of language.

options.text: Continuing the conversation in English with support
options.rationale: Near miss concept Not itself wrong. What is wrong is who was asked to bridge the gap for a consent discussion.

options.text: Using the patient's son as the interpreter for the consent discussion
options.rationale: Working with interpreters is a named cultural skill, and family members bring their own views, may edit what is said, and are not accountable for accuracy.

questions.takeaway: Working with qualified interpreters is a cultural skill. Family members are not interpreters, particularly for consent.
questions.strategy: Three options describe reasonable communication technique. Ask who is being asked to carry the responsibility.

questions.stem: A patient says she has been managing her blood pressure with a herbal preparation her mother used, and has not started the prescribed medication. Which response reflects the LEARN model?

options.text: "That preparation has not been shown to lower blood pressure."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Explaining your own perception before hearing hers, which inverts the order and usually ends the conversation.

options.text: "We can keep the herbal preparation if you also take the medication."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Negotiation offered as the opening move. It may well be where you end up, and arriving there first skips the steps that make it stick.

options.text: "Tell me more about what the preparation does for you."
options.rationale: Listen is the first step, nonjudgmentally, using encouraging comments such as tell me more. You cannot negotiate a plan before you know what you are negotiating with.

options.text: "What matters is that your blood pressure comes down, however we do it."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sounds flexible and it dismisses the thing she has just told you matters to her.

questions.takeaway: LEARN begins with Listen: the patient's perception of the problem, nonjudgmentally, before you offer yours.
questions.strategy: Two distractors are steps from later in the model offered too early. Ask what has to happen before you can negotiate anything.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews projected United States demographic change by 2060. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: The Asian population is projected to halve
options.rationale: Near miss concept Projected to double.

options.text: The racial and ethnic minority population is projected to reach 32%
options.rationale: Her figure, and it is why culturally congruent care stops being a specialty skill and becomes routine practice.

options.text: The population aged 65 and over is projected to remain stable
options.rationale: Near miss concept Projected to grow from 49 million in 2016 to 95 million in 2060, roughly doubling.

options.text: The multiracial population is projected to decline
options.rationale: Near miss concept Projected to grow by 200%, which is the largest proportional change on her slide.

questions.takeaway: By 2060: racial and ethnic minority population 32%, multiracial up 200%, Asian population doubling, and those aged 65 and over from 49 million to 95 million.
questions.strategy: Three distractors reverse the direction of a projected change. Every figure on her slide is growth.

questions.stem: A patient with a new diagnosis of epilepsy tells the nurse she has not told anyone in her community because of how the condition is viewed there. Which concept best describes what she is experiencing?

options.text: Illness, which includes the socially constructed meaning of the condition
options.rationale: Disease is the biological malfunction; illness is the individual and family reaction to it. Cultural stigma is part of the illness experience, not part of the pathology.

options.text: Acculturation to her community's health beliefs
options.rationale: Near miss concept Acculturation is adopting a new culture while keeping your own. Nothing here describes a cultural transition.

options.text: Implicit bias operating within her community
options.rationale: Near miss concept Community attitudes are involved, and implicit bias describes unconscious processes in the person providing care.

options.text: Disease, since epilepsy is a neurological disorder
options.rationale: Near miss concept Describes the biological process. She is describing what having it means where she lives.

questions.takeaway: Disease is the biological or psychological malfunction. Illness is the individual and family reaction, including cultural stigma and socially constructed meaning.
questions.strategy: One distractor names the pathology. One misapplies a term about the nurse to the community.

questions.stem: A patient who moved to the United States twelve years ago celebrates both his country of origin's holidays and American ones, cooks traditional food, and speaks both languages at home. Which term describes this?

options.text: Assimilation
options.rationale: Near miss concept The near-miss. Assimilation replaces the original culture rather than adding to it, and his has not been replaced.

options.text: Acculturation
options.rationale: Adopting aspects of a new culture while retaining one's own. The original practices survive, which is the giveaway.

options.text: Cultural competence
options.rationale: Near miss concept A capability of health care professionals, not a description of a patient's cultural position.

options.text: Intersectionality
options.rationale: Near miss concept Describes how overlapping identities interact, not how a person relates to a new culture.

questions.takeaway: Acculturation keeps your own culture while adopting a new one. Assimilation replaces it. The test is whether the original practices survive.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is assimilation. Check whether anything was given up.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to take a history from a patient whose background differs from her own. Which actions demonstrate cultural skill? Select all that apply.

options.text: Self-exploration before the encounter
options.rationale: Named first, and it is where awareness becomes practice. Named, and it starts the encounter on the patient's terms. Named, and it determines how everything afterwards is communicated. Named, and teach-back is what tells you whether anything landed. Named. Working with interpreters is a specific skill.

options.text: Asking the patient's preferred name and goals for the visit
options.rationale: Named first, and it is where awareness becomes practice. Named, and it starts the encounter on the patient's terms. Named, and it determines how everything afterwards is communicated. Named, and teach-back is what tells you whether anything landed. Named. Working with interpreters is a specific skill.

options.text: Assessing health literacy
options.rationale: Named first, and it is where awareness becomes practice. Named, and it starts the encounter on the patient's terms. Named, and it determines how everything afterwards is communicated. Named, and teach-back is what tells you whether anything landed. Named. Working with interpreters is a specific skill.

options.text: Using teach-back and plain language
options.rationale: Named first, and it is where awareness becomes practice. Named, and it starts the encounter on the patient's terms. Named, and it determines how everything afterwards is communicated. Named, and teach-back is what tells you whether anything landed. Named. Working with interpreters is a specific skill.

options.text: Arranging a qualified interpreter when needed
options.rationale: Named first, and it is where awareness becomes practice. Named, and it starts the encounter on the patient's terms. Named, and it determines how everything afterwards is communicated. Named, and teach-back is what tells you whether anything landed. Named. Working with interpreters is a specific skill.

options.text: Reading about the patient's culture and planning the encounter around what you find
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cultural knowledge is a separate construct, and used this way it produces the assumption that skill is meant to prevent.

questions.takeaway: Cultural skill: self-exploration, preferred name and goals, storytelling, history, health literacy, culturally based assessment, teach-back, plain language, interpreters.
questions.strategy: One distractor turns knowledge into a script for the encounter, which is how competence becomes stereotyping.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old attends a follow-up after a myocardial infarction. He has not started the prescribed statin. He says his brother took one and 'it ruined his muscles', and that in his family people manage heart trouble with diet and rest. He can describe his own risk factors accurately. He has attended every appointment since discharge. Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem they address, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Ask what he understands about what happened to his brother
Work with him toward a plan that keeps the diet changes and addresses the statin concern
Explain the evidence for statins after myocardial infarction
Document that the patient declines the prescribed statin
A health belief formed from family experience that conflicts with the plan
Knowledge deficit about his cardiac risk factors
Nonadherence to the prescribed medication regimen
Lack of engagement with his follow-up care
Whether he has started and continued the agreed medication plan
Whether he raises further concerns rather than stopping silently
Whether his cholesterol has fallen at the next visit
Whether he can list three benefits of statin therapy

questions.takeaway: He has a specific reason rooted in what happened to his brother and how his family manages heart trouble. That is a belief, not a gap. Listen, the first LEARN step. His belief has a specific source, and you cannot address it until you know what it is. Negotiate, the final LEARN step. Incorporating selected aspects of the patient's own approach is what makes a plan he will follow. Measures whether the negotiated plan was one he could accept. The relationship outcome. A patient who tells you when something worries him is one you can work with. Health beliefs come from somewhere specific. LEARN starts with listening because you cannot negotiate with a belief you have not heard.
questions.strategy: The stem rules out two distractors explicitly: he describes his risk factors accurately and he attends every appointment.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old with heart failure is readmitted with an ejection fraction of 30% and a weight four pounds above his dry weight after three days. During the admission interview he makes the statements below. A patient's worldview sits in layers, with only the state of health visible at the surface. For each finding, indicate which layer of this patient's worldview it reveals.

rows.text: Ejection fraction 30%, weight four pounds above dry weight in three days
Salts his food at the table because without it "everything tastes like paper"
Says the men in his family "do not make a fuss" and that doctors are for the seriously ill
Has not filled the new prescription, saying he does not believe a tablet changes how a heart wears out
Says that since his wife died he is not certain what he is staying well for

questions.takeaway: The state of health is the only layer that shows up in the chart: the ejection fraction and the weight gain. Salting his food is behavior, one layer down. Two findings sit deeper still, in what he believes about illness and about what medicine can do, and those are the beliefs driving the behavior. The deepest is meaning, and it is the one that explains why nothing above it has moved. A nurse who works only at the surface will treat the weight and discharge him into the same beliefs that produced it. Readmission is usually a problem at a layer below the one in the chart. The visible finding is the end of the story, not the start of it.
questions.strategy: Two rows share a layer, so you cannot answer by assigning one row per column. Separate what he DOES from what he BELIEVES: salting food is behavior, but not filling a prescription because tablets cannot fix a worn heart is a belief that happens to produce behavior.

questions.stem: A patient with a newly diagnosed operable cancer declines surgery, saying his family has always held that illness is endured rather than cut out. He states the risks and the survival figures back to the nurse accurately and without hesitation. The nurse notices she is irritated and is thinking that he is throwing his life away. Which action should she take first?

options.text: Review the survival figures with him again and confirm he understands what declining means
options.rationale: Near miss concept The stem already rules this out: he restates the risks and the figures accurately. Repeating information he has demonstrably absorbed treats a value as a knowledge deficit, and it is the move that makes a patient stop talking.

options.text: Arrange a palliative care consultation so his decision is supported
options.rationale: Correct but premature A reasonable step later and it accepts the decision as settled before anyone has understood it. Consulting is part of planning, which comes after the nurse has examined what she is bringing to the conversation.

options.text: Examine her own reaction, recognizing that her beliefs about surgery were socialized the same way his were
options.rationale: His decision is informed, so the gap is not information. Both his position and the nurse's reaction to it were socialized through the same channels: family, community, schooling, and the health care system itself. Implicit bias is unconscious and outside her control, but recognizing and managing it is her responsibility, and self-exploration before the encounter is the cultural skill that makes the rest possible.

options.text: Document that the patient has declined surgery after demonstrating understanding of the risks
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Accurate charting, and it closes the encounter at the moment the nurse's own reaction has become the obstacle. Her irritation never gets examined and will be in the room at the next conversation.

questions.takeaway: When a patient's decision irritates you and the decision is informed, the finding is about you. Examine it before you act, because you will act on it either way.
questions.strategy: The stem plants two details that kill the obvious answers: he restates the figures accurately, and the nurse notices her own irritation. Each one is there to eliminate a specific option.

chapters.title: Fluid, Electrolyte and Acid Base Balance

members.title: Fluid, Electrolyte and Acid Base Balance
Fluid, Electrolyte and Acid Base Balance
Fluid, Electrolyte and Acid Base Balance

questions.stem: Classify each arterial blood gas result.

rows.text: pH 7.28, PaCO2 56, HCO3 25
pH 7.51, PaCO2 42, HCO3 33
pH 7.50, PaCO2 29, HCO3 23
pH 7.26, PaCO2 38, HCO3 15

questions.takeaway: Find the abnormal pH, then find which value moved with it. ROME: respiratory opposite, so pH and carbon dioxide move in opposite directions; metabolic equal, so pH and bicarbonate move in the same direction. ROME settles every one of these in about five seconds.
questions.strategy: Read the pH first, then look only at which of the two drivers is abnormal.

questions.stem: Select all of the findings consistent with extracellular fluid volume deficit.

options.text: Distended neck veins at 45 degrees
options.rationale: Near miss concept A volume finding, in the wrong direction.

options.text: Dry mucous membranes
options.rationale: Deficit presents with orthostatic change, dry mucous membranes, falling urine output and rapid weight loss. Distended neck veins and crackles are findings of excess. A change of about 1 kg in 24 hours is a liter of fluid in either direction.

options.text: Urine output of 18 mL per hour

options.text: Crackles in the lung bases
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fluid in the lungs means too much volume, not too little.

questions.takeaway: Weight moves faster and more reliably than any other volume indicator.
questions.strategy: Two options here belong to the opposite imbalance. Sort by direction before you sort by severity.

questions.stem: Select all of the statements about intravenous solutions that are accurate.

options.text: Hypotonic solutions are contraindicated in head trauma and raised intracranial pressure
options.rationale: Isotonic expands volume without shifting water. Hypotonic drives water into cells, which is why it is dangerous when the brain is already swollen. Hypertonic pulls water out of cells and goes in slowly with close monitoring. Lactated Ringer at 273 is isotonic, because the isotonic band is wide, roughly 250 to 375 mOsm per L.

options.text: Hypertonic saline can be given by rapid intravenous push in symptomatic hyponatremia
options.rationale: Near miss concept It goes in slowly on a pump with frequent sodium checks; fast correction causes brain injury.

options.text: 3 percent sodium chloride is hypertonic and pulls water out of cells
options.rationale: Isotonic expands volume without shifting water. Hypotonic drives water into cells, which is why it is dangerous when the brain is already swollen. Hypertonic pulls water out of cells and goes in slowly with close monitoring. Lactated Ringer at 273 is isotonic, because the isotonic band is wide, roughly 250 to 375 mOsm per L.

options.text: Lactated Ringer solution is hypotonic because its osmolarity is below 285
options.rationale: Near miss concept 273 sits inside the isotonic band of roughly 250 to 375; 285 is plasma, not the cutoff.

options.text: 0.45 percent sodium chloride is hypotonic and moves water into cells
options.rationale: Isotonic expands volume without shifting water. Hypotonic drives water into cells, which is why it is dangerous when the brain is already swollen. Hypertonic pulls water out of cells and goes in slowly with close monitoring. Lactated Ringer at 273 is isotonic, because the isotonic band is wide, roughly 250 to 375 mOsm per L.

options.text: 0.9 percent sodium chloride is isotonic and stays in the vascular space
options.rationale: Isotonic expands volume without shifting water. Hypotonic drives water into cells, which is why it is dangerous when the brain is already swollen. Hypertonic pulls water out of cells and goes in slowly with close monitoring. Lactated Ringer at 273 is isotonic, because the isotonic band is wide, roughly 250 to 375 mOsm per L.

questions.takeaway: Hypotonic fluid in a head injury swells the one organ that has nowhere to swell into.
questions.strategy: One wrong option tests the isotonic band too narrowly; the other tests infusion speed.

questions.stem: Select all of the measures that give the most reliable picture of a patient's fluid balance.

options.text: A single hematocrit value drawn on admission
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data One value cannot separate hemodilution from anemia; the trend might.

options.text: Daily weight on the same scale at the same time
options.rationale: Weight is the most reliable single measure, because a kilogram is a liter and it cannot be argued with, and it works best alongside intake and output and the physical findings. A single hematocrit cannot distinguish dilution from anemia, and thirst is blunted in older adults, which is precisely the group most likely to be dry.

options.text: Blood pressure trends, with orthostatic checks if needed
options.rationale: Weight is the most reliable single measure, because a kilogram is a liter and it cannot be argued with, and it works best alongside intake and output and the physical findings. A single hematocrit cannot distinguish dilution from anemia, and thirst is blunted in older adults, which is precisely the group most likely to be dry.

options.text: The patient's own report of how thirsty he feels
options.rationale: Near miss concept Thirst is blunted with age and absent in many dehydrated older adults.

options.text: Strict intake and output including all sources
options.rationale: Weight is the most reliable single measure, because a kilogram is a liter and it cannot be argued with, and it works best alongside intake and output and the physical findings. A single hematocrit cannot distinguish dilution from anemia, and thirst is blunted in older adults, which is precisely the group most likely to be dry.

options.text: Lung sounds, neck veins and the presence of edema
options.rationale: Weight is the most reliable single measure, because a kilogram is a liter and it cannot be argued with, and it works best alongside intake and output and the physical findings. A single hematocrit cannot distinguish dilution from anemia, and thirst is blunted in older adults, which is precisely the group most likely to be dry.

questions.takeaway: Weight is the honest number. Everything else interprets it.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options rely on a single value or a sensation that is unreliable in the patients who need it most.

questions.stem: Select all of the findings consistent with hypokalemia.

options.text: Flattened T waves on the electrocardiogram
options.rationale: Potassium drives excitability, so too little makes muscle, including smooth muscle, sluggish: weakness, an ileus, flat T waves and sometimes a U wave. Too much makes everything irritable and peaks the T waves. Hyperactive reflexes belong with hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia, not with low potassium.

options.text: Generalized muscle weakness
options.rationale: Potassium drives excitability, so too little makes muscle, including smooth muscle, sluggish: weakness, an ileus, flat T waves and sometimes a U wave. Too much makes everything irritable and peaks the T waves. Hyperactive reflexes belong with hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia, not with low potassium.

options.text: Peaked T waves on the electrocardiogram
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hyperkalemia, which is the mirror image.

options.text: Decreased bowel sounds and ileus
options.rationale: Potassium drives excitability, so too little makes muscle, including smooth muscle, sluggish: weakness, an ileus, flat T waves and sometimes a U wave. Too much makes everything irritable and peaks the T waves. Hyperactive reflexes belong with hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia, not with low potassium.

options.text: Leg cramps and paresthesia
options.rationale: Potassium drives excitability, so too little makes muscle, including smooth muscle, sluggish: weakness, an ileus, flat T waves and sometimes a U wave. Too much makes everything irritable and peaks the T waves. Hyperactive reflexes belong with hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia, not with low potassium.

options.text: Hyperactive deep tendon reflexes
options.rationale: Near miss concept Points to low calcium or low magnesium.

questions.takeaway: Flat T for low potassium, peaked T for high. The wave flattens as the level falls and spikes as it rises.
questions.strategy: One wrong option is the opposite potassium problem; the other belongs to a different electrolyte.

questions.stem: Select all of the statements that correctly match an intravenous complication to its nursing response.

options.text: Circulatory overload: slow the rate, raise the head of the bed and notify the provider
options.rationale: Site problems take the catheter out; volume problems change the rate and keep the line. The vesicant is the exception where the catheter stays, because the protocol aspirates residual drug and instills an antidote through it. Flushing a suspected infiltration pushes more fluid into tissue, and laying an overloaded patient flat worsens the pulmonary congestion.

options.text: Phlebitis: discontinue the catheter and restart in another extremity
options.rationale: Site problems take the catheter out; volume problems change the rate and keep the line. The vesicant is the exception where the catheter stays, because the protocol aspirates residual drug and instills an antidote through it. Flushing a suspected infiltration pushes more fluid into tissue, and laying an overloaded patient flat worsens the pulmonary congestion.

options.text: Extravasation of a vesicant: stop the infusion and leave the catheter in place
options.rationale: Site problems take the catheter out; volume problems change the rate and keep the line. The vesicant is the exception where the catheter stays, because the protocol aspirates residual drug and instills an antidote through it. Flushing a suspected infiltration pushes more fluid into tissue, and laying an overloaded patient flat worsens the pulmonary congestion.

options.text: Circulatory overload: remove the catheter and lay the patient flat
options.rationale: Near miss concept Discards access you need and worsens the congestion.

options.text: Infiltration: flush the catheter to confirm patency
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pushes more fluid into already infiltrated tissue.

options.text: Infiltration: stop the infusion and remove the catheter
options.rationale: Site problems take the catheter out; volume problems change the rate and keep the line. The vesicant is the exception where the catheter stays, because the protocol aspirates residual drug and instills an antidote through it. Flushing a suspected infiltration pushes more fluid into tissue, and laying an overloaded patient flat worsens the pulmonary congestion.

questions.takeaway: Vesicant extravasation is the one infiltration where the catheter stays in.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options do the opposite of what the complication requires.

questions.stem: An arterial blood gas shows pH 7.37, PaCO2 58, HCO3 34. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: Fully compensated respiratory acidosis
options.rationale: The pH is back inside the normal range, so compensation is full. Both the carbon dioxide and the bicarbonate are abnormal, which tells you one is the problem and the other is the compensation. The pH of 7.37 sits on the acidic half of normal, which points to the acidosis as the primary problem, so respiratory is the cause and the kidneys retained bicarbonate to fix it.

options.text: Partially compensated metabolic alkalosis
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would put the pH on the alkalotic side of normal, above 7.40.

options.text: Uncompensated respiratory acidosis
options.rationale: Near miss concept Uncompensated means the bicarbonate has not moved; here it is 34.

options.text: A normal gas requiring no action
options.rationale: Near miss concept The pH is normal and both drivers are well outside their ranges.

questions.takeaway: Normal pH with two abnormal values means full compensation. Which half of normal the pH sits on names the primary problem.
questions.strategy: Three options misread either the compensation or which value is primary.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease who has been vomiting for two days has pH 7.47, PaCO2 56 and HCO3 38. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: A primary respiratory alkalosis from anxious overbreathing
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would require a low carbon dioxide; his is 56.

options.text: A normal blood gas for a patient with chronic lung disease
options.rationale: Near miss concept His compensated baseline would sit near 7.37; 7.47 is a change.

options.text: Metabolic alkalosis from vomiting on top of chronic CO2 retention
options.rationale: His baseline is a high carbon dioxide with a high bicarbonate holding the pH near normal. Then vomiting stripped hydrogen and chloride, pushing the bicarbonate higher still and tipping the pH alkalotic. The giveaway is that the pH is above 7.45 while the carbon dioxide is high: respiratory acidosis alone can never make a patient alkalotic, so something else must be driving it.

options.text: An acute respiratory acidosis with full renal compensation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Compensation never overshoots into alkalosis; it brings the pH toward normal.

questions.takeaway: A high carbon dioxide with an alkalotic pH means there are two processes, not one.
questions.strategy: When the pH points the opposite way from the obvious driver, look for a second disorder.

questions.stem: A patient has a serum sodium of 124 mmol/L, concentrated urine and no edema. Which hormonal problem does this suggest?

options.text: Excess antidiuretic hormone, which retains water without retaining sodium
options.rationale: ADH holds water alone, so the retained water dilutes the sodium while the urine comes out concentrated, and there is no edema because the water distributes everywhere rather than pooling. Aldosterone holds sodium with the water, so volume rises and sodium stays normal. ANP does the opposite of both. A deficiency of ADH is diabetes insipidus, with huge volumes of dilute urine.

options.text: Excess aldosterone, which retains sodium and water together
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would raise volume and leave the sodium near normal, often with hypertension.

options.text: Deficient antidiuretic hormone, which produces dilute urine
options.rationale: Near miss concept The urine here is concentrated, which is the opposite finding.

options.text: Excess atrial natriuretic peptide, which excretes sodium and water
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would produce dilute urine and volume loss.

questions.takeaway: ADH holds water only. That is why its excess causes hyponatremia and its lack causes diabetes insipidus.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the hormone moves water alone or sodium with it. That predicts the serum sodium.

questions.stem: A patient with a serum sodium of 119 mmol/L becomes increasingly confused and then has a generalized seizure. Which explains the neurologic findings?

options.text: Water shifting into brain cells because the extracellular fluid is dilute
options.rationale: Sodium holds water where it is. When the extracellular sodium falls, the extracellular fluid becomes relatively dilute and water moves into the cells, including brain cells. The swelling produces confusion and then seizures, which is why the endpoint of hyponatremia is neurologic.

options.text: Water shifting out of brain cells because the extracellular fluid is concentrated
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is hypernatremia, and it also ends in seizures, which is what makes it attractive.

options.text: Direct sodium toxicity to the cerebral cortex
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sodium is not a poison here. The damage is water moving, not sodium acting.

options.text: Reduced cerebral perfusion from the associated hypovolemia
options.rationale: Near miss concept Volume may be low, high or normal in hyponatremia.

questions.takeaway: Sodium is a brain problem. Reason from where the water goes.
questions.strategy: Osmosis questions are answered by asking which side has more particles, not by matching the word low to the word decreased.

questions.stem: Classify each set of findings by the electrolyte imbalance it fits best.

rows.text: Tall peaked T waves with diarrhea
Positive Trousseau sign with tingling around the mouth
Absent reflexes, drowsiness and a respiratory rate of 9 breaths per minute
A prominent U wave with leg cramps
Flaccid weakness that ascends from the legs
Constipation, confusion and depressed reflexes with a risk of leg clots

questions.takeaway: Potassium is the heart and the gut: low gives flat T, U wave, cramps and a slow gut; high gives peaked T, diarrhea and an ascending flaccid weakness. Calcium and magnesium are brakes: low calcium gives tingling, tetany and Trousseau; high calcium slows everything and adds clots and stones; high magnesium depresses reflexes and breathing. Potassium shows on the ECG and in the gut. Calcium and magnesium show in the nerves and reflexes.
questions.strategy: Sort by system first (ECG and gut for potassium, nerves for calcium and magnesium), then by direction (excited or slowed).

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching staff on a long term care unit about preventing fluid volume deficit in residents. Select all of the statements that are accurate.

options.text: Skin turgor on the back of the hand is the most reliable sign of hydration
options.rationale: Near miss concept Aging skin tents on the hand even when hydrated; the sternum is used.

options.text: Fluids should be offered on a schedule rather than when the resident asks
options.rationale: Older adults start with less water (about 50 to 55 percent of body weight), feel thirst later and lose more water through kidneys that concentrate poorly. The safe response is scheduled fluids rather than waiting for thirst, and turgor checked on the sternum.

options.text: Aging kidneys concentrate urine poorly
options.rationale: Older adults start with less water (about 50 to 55 percent of body weight), feel thirst later and lose more water through kidneys that concentrate poorly. The safe response is scheduled fluids rather than waiting for thirst, and turgor checked on the sternum.

options.text: A resident who denies thirst has an adequate intake
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data A weak thirst alarm means a denial of thirst says little about intake.

options.text: Older adults have less total body water than younger adults
options.rationale: Older adults start with less water (about 50 to 55 percent of body weight), feel thirst later and lose more water through kidneys that concentrate poorly. The safe response is scheduled fluids rather than waiting for thirst, and turgor checked on the sternum.

options.text: The thirst alarm is weaker with aging
options.rationale: Older adults start with less water (about 50 to 55 percent of body weight), feel thirst later and lose more water through kidneys that concentrate poorly. The safe response is scheduled fluids rather than waiting for thirst, and turgor checked on the sternum.

questions.takeaway: Less water, weaker thirst, leakier kidneys. Offer fluids on a schedule.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options rely on a signal that aging blunts: skin elasticity and thirst.

questions.stem: The nurse is delegating daily weights for a patient with fluid volume excess to a UAP. Select all of the instructions that are appropriate.

options.text: Decide whether to call the provider based on the amount of gain
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Interpreting the trend and deciding to report it is the nurse's job, not the UAP's.

options.text: Weigh only on days the patient looks more swollen
options.rationale: Near miss concept Edema lags behind fluid gain; daily weights are scheduled, not triggered by appearance.

options.text: Weigh in the same type of clothing
options.rationale: Daily weight is only useful when the conditions match: same time, same scale, same clothing, before breakfast and after voiding. Weighing is a stable routine task the UAP can do. Deciding what the number means and what to do about it stays with the nurse.

options.text: Use the same scale each day
