options.rationale: Daily weight is only useful when the conditions match: same time, same scale, same clothing, before breakfast and after voiding. Weighing is a stable routine task the UAP can do. Deciding what the number means and what to do about it stays with the nurse.

options.text: Weigh before breakfast and after the patient voids
options.rationale: Daily weight is only useful when the conditions match: same time, same scale, same clothing, before breakfast and after voiding. Weighing is a stable routine task the UAP can do. Deciding what the number means and what to do about it stays with the nurse.

options.text: Weigh at the same time each day
options.rationale: Daily weight is only useful when the conditions match: same time, same scale, same clothing, before breakfast and after voiding. Weighing is a stable routine task the UAP can do. Deciding what the number means and what to do about it stays with the nurse.

questions.takeaway: Same time, same scale, same clothing, before breakfast after voiding. The UAP reports; the nurse interprets.
questions.strategy: In delegation questions, the UAP collects the data and the nurse judges it.

questions.stem: A patient with kidney failure has a serum potassium of 6.6 mEq/L. Select all of the findings the nurse should expect.

options.text: Tall peaked T waves and a widening QRS
options.rationale: Potassium runs the opposite way in muscle from calcium and magnesium. A high level excites first (tingling, twitching, a hyperactive gut and diarrhea), then paralyzes, with weakness that climbs from the legs. The heart shows tall peaked T waves and a widening QRS on the way to ventricular fibrillation, so the patient goes on a monitor.

options.text: Tingling and twitching early on
options.rationale: Potassium runs the opposite way in muscle from calcium and magnesium. A high level excites first (tingling, twitching, a hyperactive gut and diarrhea), then paralyzes, with weakness that climbs from the legs. The heart shows tall peaked T waves and a widening QRS on the way to ventricular fibrillation, so the patient goes on a monitor.

options.text: A prominent U wave
options.rationale: Near miss concept The U wave belongs to low potassium, with a flat T.

options.text: Diarrhea with hyperactive bowel sounds
options.rationale: Potassium runs the opposite way in muscle from calcium and magnesium. A high level excites first (tingling, twitching, a hyperactive gut and diarrhea), then paralyzes, with weakness that climbs from the legs. The heart shows tall peaked T waves and a widening QRS on the way to ventricular fibrillation, so the patient goes on a monitor.

options.text: Constipation and hypoactive bowel sounds
options.rationale: Near miss concept A slow gut is low potassium; high potassium speeds it up.

options.text: Flaccid muscle weakness that ascends from the legs
options.rationale: Potassium runs the opposite way in muscle from calcium and magnesium. A high level excites first (tingling, twitching, a hyperactive gut and diarrhea), then paralyzes, with weakness that climbs from the legs. The heart shows tall peaked T waves and a widening QRS on the way to ventricular fibrillation, so the patient goes on a monitor.

questions.takeaway: High potassium excites, then paralyzes. MURDER: muscle weakness, urine changes, respiratory distress, decreased contractility, ECG changes, reflexes.
questions.strategy: The two wrong options are the low potassium picture. If an option would fit the mirror image, cross it off.

questions.stem: A patient with a potassium of 2.9 mEq/L has an order for IV potassium chloride through a peripheral line. Select all of the actions that are correct.

options.text: Confirm a urine output of at least 30 mL per hour before starting
options.rationale: IV potassium is high alert: always diluted, always on a pump, 5 to 10 mEq per hour peripherally, never IV push, IM or subcutaneous. A patient who cannot make urine cannot clear it, so output is confirmed first. Concentrated potassium irritates veins, so the site is checked hourly for burning.

options.text: Give the first dose by slow IV push because the level is critically low
options.rationale: Correct but premature A critical level is never a reason to push potassium. Potassium by push is lethal.

options.text: Infuse the diluted potassium on an infusion pump
options.rationale: IV potassium is high alert: always diluted, always on a pump, 5 to 10 mEq per hour peripherally, never IV push, IM or subcutaneous. A patient who cannot make urine cannot clear it, so output is confirmed first. Concentrated potassium irritates veins, so the site is checked hourly for burning.

options.text: Ask for the dose to be given intramuscularly if the IV site is lost
options.rationale: Near miss concept Potassium is never given IM or subcutaneously; a lost site means new IV access.

options.text: Keep the peripheral rate at 5 to 10 mEq per hour
options.rationale: IV potassium is high alert: always diluted, always on a pump, 5 to 10 mEq per hour peripherally, never IV push, IM or subcutaneous. A patient who cannot make urine cannot clear it, so output is confirmed first. Concentrated potassium irritates veins, so the site is checked hourly for burning.

options.text: Increase the rate to 20 mEq per hour because the patient is on a cardiac monitor
options.rationale: Institution as rationale A monitor shows harm; it does not prevent it. The peripheral limit is 10 mEq per hour.

options.text: Check the IV site hourly and ask about burning
options.rationale: IV potassium is high alert: always diluted, always on a pump, 5 to 10 mEq per hour peripherally, never IV push, IM or subcutaneous. A patient who cannot make urine cannot clear it, so output is confirmed first. Concentrated potassium irritates veins, so the site is checked hourly for burning.

questions.takeaway: Diluted, on a pump, 5 to 10 mEq an hour, urine output first, site checked hourly. Never push, IM or subcutaneous.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option offers a reason to break a rule: a critical level, lost access, a monitor. None of them changes the rule.

questions.stem: A patient has a serum calcium of 12.0 mg/dL with weakness, constipation and new confusion. Select all of the actions the nurse should anticipate.

options.text: Assess the calves for signs of clots
options.rationale: High calcium slows everything: weakness, depressed reflexes, confusion, constipation. Treatment stops the calcium coming in and washes it out with 0.9% sodium chloride plus furosemide. Hypercalcemia also raises the risk of clots in the legs, so the calves are assessed, and the heart is monitored because late hypercalcemia can slow it.

options.text: Stop any calcium sources
options.rationale: High calcium slows everything: weakness, depressed reflexes, confusion, constipation. Treatment stops the calcium coming in and washes it out with 0.9% sodium chloride plus furosemide. Hypercalcemia also raises the risk of clots in the legs, so the calves are assessed, and the heart is monitored because late hypercalcemia can slow it.

options.text: Give the ordered furosemide
options.rationale: High calcium slows everything: weakness, depressed reflexes, confusion, constipation. Treatment stops the calcium coming in and washes it out with 0.9% sodium chloride plus furosemide. Hypercalcemia also raises the risk of clots in the legs, so the calves are assessed, and the heart is monitored because late hypercalcemia can slow it.

options.text: Give IV calcium to stabilize the heart
options.rationale: Near miss concept IV calcium is the antidote for high magnesium and the heart protector in high potassium; here it adds to the problem.

options.text: Infuse 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: High calcium slows everything: weakness, depressed reflexes, confusion, constipation. Treatment stops the calcium coming in and washes it out with 0.9% sodium chloride plus furosemide. Hypercalcemia also raises the risk of clots in the legs, so the calves are assessed, and the heart is monitored because late hypercalcemia can slow it.

options.text: Monitor for hyperactive deep tendon reflexes
options.rationale: Near miss concept High calcium depresses reflexes; hyperactive reflexes go with low calcium.

questions.takeaway: STONE adds the calves. Stop calcium, give saline plus furosemide, and assess the legs.
questions.strategy: Low calcium excites and high calcium slows. Any option that describes excitement belongs to the other imbalance.

questions.stem: A patient has a serum calcium of 7.4 mg/dL. The nurse inflates a blood pressure cuff on the upper arm above systolic pressure. Which finding is a positive Trousseau sign?

options.text: Facial twitching when the cheek is tapped over the facial nerve
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is Chvostek sign, elicited by tapping the cheek, not by the cuff.

options.text: Hyperactive deep tendon reflexes
options.rationale: Near miss concept A finding of low calcium and low magnesium, tested with a reflex hammer, not the cuff.

options.text: Tremor of the hands at rest
options.rationale: Near miss concept Tremor is listed with low magnesium and is not what the cuff test elicits.

options.text: Carpal spasm of the hand while the cuff is inflated
options.rationale: Calcium acts as a brake on nerves, so a low level makes them fire too easily. Trousseau sign is elicited with the cuff: the hand and wrist spasm while it is inflated. Chvostek sign is elicited by tapping the cheek over the facial nerve, and it points to low calcium or low magnesium. Hyperactive reflexes and tremor also go with low calcium and low magnesium, but neither is the cuff test.

questions.takeaway: Trousseau is the cuff test and Chvostek is the cheek tap. Both point to low calcium, and Chvostek also to low magnesium.
questions.strategy: Match the sign to the maneuver that elicits it before thinking about which electrolyte it points to.

questions.stem: A patient with a magnesium of 1.0 mEq/L, tremor and hyperactive reflexes is receiving IV magnesium sulfate. Which assessment should the nurse repeat most often during the infusion?

options.text: Bowel sounds
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Not the early warning for magnesium toxicity.

options.text: Capillary refill in the fingers
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Reflects perfusion, not magnesium level.

options.text: The patellar (knee jerk) reflex
options.rationale: Replacement aims to calm the overactive reflexes, but too much magnesium depresses them. The patellar reflex fades first, before breathing slows and before the heart slows, so frequent reflex checks catch toxicity at the earliest, safest point.

options.text: Skin turgor over the sternum
options.rationale: Near miss concept A fluid status check, unrelated to magnesium toxicity.

questions.takeaway: IV magnesium means frequent deep tendon reflex checks. The knee jerk is the early warning.
questions.strategy: Pick the assessment that changes first when the drug goes too far.

questions.stem: A patient's magnesium infusion has been stopped because the knee jerk reflex is absent and the respiratory rate is 10 breaths per minute. Which medication should the nurse have ready?

options.text: Furosemide
options.rationale: Near miss concept Used to wash out calcium or remove fluid, not the antidote for magnesium.

options.text: Regular insulin with dextrose
options.rationale: Near miss concept Shifts potassium, not magnesium.

options.text: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate
options.rationale: Near miss concept A potassium binder.

options.text: IV calcium
options.rationale: High magnesium depresses nerves, breathing and eventually the heart. After stopping every magnesium source and supporting breathing, IV calcium is the antidote.

questions.takeaway: SLOW ends at the heart. Stop the magnesium, watch the breathing, and give IV calcium as the antidote.
questions.strategy: Three options are real treatments for other electrolyte problems. Match the antidote to the electrolyte.

questions.stem: A patient admitted after three days of vomiting has a hematocrit that is higher than the patient's baseline, along with dry mucous membranes and a heart rate of 110 beats per minute. After 24 hours of IV isotonic fluid, the hematocrit falls toward baseline. How should the nurse interpret these results?

options.text: The admission value reflected fluid loss concentrating the blood, and the fall reflects rehydration
options.rationale: In deficit, the water leaves and the cells stay, so the hemoglobin, hematocrit and osmolarity rise (hemoconcentration). Replacing the water brings them back down. In excess, the opposite happens and the hematocrit falls below baseline.

options.text: The admission value showed the body was making extra red cells, and the fall shows bleeding
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism No cells were added; the water was lost. A fall with rehydration is not bleeding.

options.text: The fall shows the IV fluid has caused fluid volume excess
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dilution of an excess lowers the hematocrit too, but a fall back toward baseline in a dehydrated patient is the goal.

options.text: Both values are lab error, because the hematocrit does not change with fluid status
options.rationale: Absolute language The hematocrit is one of the lab values that moves with fluid status.

questions.takeaway: Deficit concentrates the labs; excess dilutes them.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the cells changed or the water changed. In a vomiting patient, it is the water.

questions.stem: A patient's blood suddenly gains extra acid from a burst of muscle activity. Within seconds, the pH changes far less than expected. Which describes what the chemical buffers did?

options.text: They breathed off the extra acid as carbon dioxide through the lungs
options.rationale: Near miss concept Changing ventilation is respiratory regulation, a separate system that works over seconds to minutes. A buffer is a chemical in the fluid, not an organ, so an option that names the lungs is not describing a buffer.

options.text: They made the kidneys excrete the extra acid as ammonium in the urine
options.rationale: Near miss concept Ammonium formation is a kidney mechanism and takes hours to days. The stem says the pH held within seconds, which is too fast for the kidneys.

options.text: They bound the extra hydrogen ions, and can release them if the pH rises
options.rationale: A buffer is a chemical that prevents sudden changes in pH. The test question is: did something in the fluid itself grab or release hydrogen ions within seconds? Here the pH held within seconds of the acid load, so a buffer bound the extra hydrogen ions. Buffers work both ways: they act as a base when the fluid is too acidic and as an acid when it is too basic. Bicarbonate is the main buffer outside cells, phosphate works mainly inside cells, and proteins such as hemoglobin pull hydrogen ions out of the blood inside red cells. Breathing off carbon dioxide is the lungs, which respond over seconds to minutes. Ammonium excretion is the kidneys, which take hours to days. Neither organ is a buffer, and no buffer raises the pH permanently.

options.text: They converted the acid into new bicarbonate that permanently raises the pH
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism A buffer does not create base or push the pH up for good. It only damps sudden change, and it can act as an acid or a base depending on the fluid pH.

questions.takeaway: Buffers are chemicals that bind or release hydrogen ions within seconds to blunt a sudden pH change; they do not fix the cause.
questions.strategy: The stem asks what the chemical buffers did, and the pH held "within seconds." That rules out the kidneys on speed, and it rules out the lungs because a buffer is a chemical in the fluid, not an organ.

questions.stem: Match each feature to the acid base regulatory mechanism it describes.

rows.text: Fastest of the three to act on a pH change
Hemoglobin binds excess hydrogen ions inside red blood cells
Changes the rate and depth of breathing to adjust carbon dioxide
Responds within minutes but is easily overwhelmed
Takes 24 to 48 hours to respond fully
Traps hydrogen ions in urine using phosphate and ammonia
Most powerful and longest lasting of the three

questions.takeaway: Sort by speed and by tool. Chemical buffers are chemicals already in the fluid, so they act in seconds and are the fastest of the three. Hemoglobin is a protein buffer: it binds hydrogen ions inside red cells, which pulls acid out of the blood, so that row is a buffer and not a lung function even though red cells carry gases. The lungs work by breathing: more carbon dioxide or hydrogen ions trigger faster, deeper breathing, and less triggers slower breathing. That response comes within minutes but is limited and easily overwhelmed. The kidneys reabsorb or excrete bicarbonate and trap hydrogen ions in urine with phosphate and ammonia. They need 24 to 48 hours to respond fully, but they are the most powerful and longest lasting mechanism. Buffers act in seconds, lungs in minutes, kidneys in hours to days but most powerfully.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out "Lungs" for the hemoglobin row is that hemoglobin is binding hydrogen ions, which is a chemical buffer job, not a breathing job. Sort the rest by speed.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence: The main base in body fluid is [[1]], and it is regulated mainly by the [[2]]. The main acid is carbonic acid, which is closely tied to carbon dioxide and regulated by the [[3]]. A normal pH depends on keeping about [[4]] of carbonic acid to bicarbonate.

options.text: bicarbonate
phosphate
hemoglobin
ammonia
kidneys
lungs
liver
red blood cells
lungs
kidneys
pancreas
intracellular buffers
1 part to 20 parts
1 part to 1 part
20 parts to 1 part
1 part to 5 parts

questions.takeaway: [1] bicarbonate: a base binds hydrogen ions and lowers the free hydrogen in solution. Bicarbonate is the main base in body fluid. Phosphate and hemoglobin are buffers with smaller roles, and ammonia is a kidney tool for trapping acid in urine. [2] kidneys: the kidneys reabsorb or excrete bicarbonate depending on hydrogen ion levels, so they control the base side. [3] lungs: carbonic acid rises and falls with carbon dioxide, and breathing controls carbon dioxide, so the lungs control the acid side. [4] 1 part to 20 parts: normal blood holds about 1 part carbonic acid to 20 parts bicarbonate. The ratio, not either number alone, keeps the pH in range. Reversing it to 20 to 1 would describe a severely acidic blood. Lungs handle the acid side (carbon dioxide), kidneys handle the base side (bicarbonate), and pH depends on their 1 to 20 ratio.
questions.strategy: Anchor on one fact: carbon dioxide is the acid and the lungs move carbon dioxide. Everything else falls into the opposite slot.

questions.stem: Classify the compensation status of each arterial blood gas.

rows.text: pH 7.30, PaCO2 56 mm Hg, HCO3 25 mEq/L
pH 7.48, PaCO2 41 mm Hg, HCO3 32 mEq/L
pH 7.32, PaCO2 55 mm Hg, HCO3 30 mEq/L
pH 7.29, PaCO2 30 mm Hg, HCO3 15 mEq/L
pH 7.44, PaCO2 30 mm Hg, HCO3 20 mEq/L
pH 7.36, PaCO2 52 mm Hg, HCO3 31 mEq/L

questions.takeaway: Compensation is the body moving the pH back toward normal with the system that did not cause the problem. Ask two questions: is the pH normal, and is the second system abnormal? Uncompensated means the pH and the primary value are abnormal while the other system is still normal. pH 7.30 with PaCO2 56 mm Hg and HCO3 25 mEq/L is a respiratory acidosis with a normal bicarbonate. pH 7.48 with HCO3 32 mEq/L and PaCO2 41 mm Hg is a metabolic alkalosis with a normal carbon dioxide. Partially compensated means the pH is still abnormal but both PaCO2 and HCO3 are abnormal. pH 7.32 with a high PaCO2 and a high HCO3 is respiratory acidosis with the kidneys holding bicarbonate. pH 7.29 with HCO3 15 mEq/L and PaCO2 30 mm Hg is metabolic acidosis with the lungs blowing off carbon dioxide. Fully compensated means the pH is back in the 7.35 to 7.45 range while both drivers stay abnormal. pH 7.44 with a low PaCO2 and a low HCO3 sits on the alkaline half, so it is a compensated respiratory alkalosis. pH 7.36 with a high PaCO2 and a high HCO3 sits on the acid half, so it is a compensated respiratory acidosis. One abnormal driver is uncompensated; two abnormal drivers with an abnormal pH is partial; two abnormal drivers with a normal pH is full.
questions.strategy: The pH alone cannot separate uncompensated from partial. The detail that decides it is whether the second value is still inside its normal range.

questions.topic: what the pH alone tells you
questions.stem: The first value the nurse reads on a new arterial blood gas is a pH of 7.31. The other values have not been reviewed yet. What can the nurse conclude from the pH alone?
questions.objective: what the pH alone tells you

options.text: The blood is acidotic, but the cause is not known yet
options.rationale: The pH shows the overall acid base status, meaning direction only. A pH below 7.35 is acidosis, 7.35 to 7.45 is normal, and above 7.45 is alkalosis. The test question for any conclusion is: which value would prove it? Respiratory acidosis is proven by a high PaCO2 and metabolic acidosis by a low HCO3, and the stem says neither has been read. Compensation status is proven only by comparing both drivers. So from 7.31 alone, the nurse knows only that the blood is acidotic.

options.text: The patient has a respiratory acidosis from retained carbon dioxide
options.rationale: Correct but premature Respiratory acidosis needs a PaCO2 above 45 mm Hg. The PaCO2 has not been read, so naming the cause now skips step two.

options.text: The patient has a metabolic acidosis from a bicarbonate loss
options.rationale: Correct but premature Metabolic acidosis needs an HCO3 below 22 mEq/L. Without that value the cause is a guess.

options.text: The kidneys have not yet started to compensate for the problem
options.rationale: Correct but premature Compensation is step three and depends on both PaCO2 and HCO3. An abnormal pH happens with uncompensated and partially compensated results alike.

questions.takeaway: The pH identifies the direction, not the cause.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out every cause option is "the other values have not been reviewed yet." Each wrong option needs a value the nurse does not have.

questions.topic: assessment findings of acidosis and alkalosis
questions.stem: Classify each assessment finding as more consistent with acidosis or with alkalosis.
questions.objective: assessment findings of acidosis and alkalosis

rows.text: Hyporeflexia with flaccid muscle weakness
Positive Chvostek and Trousseau signs
Tall T waves, a wide QRS and a slow heart rate
Agitation with muscle twitching and cramping
Warm, flushed, dry skin with deep rapid breathing
Fast heart rate with a higher risk of digoxin toxicity
Lethargy progressing to stupor

questions.takeaway: Acidosis depresses and alkalosis excites. Ask of each finding: is the nerve, muscle or heart slowed, or overexcited? Hyporeflexia and flaccid weakness are slowed muscles, so acidosis. Lethargy to stupor is a depressed brain, so acidosis. Tall T waves, a wide QRS and bradycardia reflect the hyperkalemia that acidosis causes, so acidosis. Warm, flushed, dry skin with deep rapid Kussmaul breathing fits metabolic acidosis. Chvostek and Trousseau signs are nerve twitching and spasm, so alkalosis. Agitation, twitching and cramping are overexcited nerves and muscles, so alkalosis. A fast heart rate and digoxin toxicity risk fit alkalosis, where the overexcited heart and the shift of potassium into cells go with a higher risk of digoxin toxicity. Acidosis slows the brain, muscles and heart; alkalosis overexcites them.
questions.strategy: The detail that tips the deep rapid breathing row is the warm, flushed, dry skin, which marks metabolic acidosis rather than anxious overbreathing.

questions.stem: A patient in acidosis has a serum potassium of 6.0 mEq/L. The patient has had no potassium supplements, and the potassium was normal before the acidosis began. Which explains the high potassium?

options.text: Acid damages cell membranes, so cells break open and spill potassium
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Cell injury can release potassium, but that is not the acid base mechanism. In acidosis the cells are intact and trading ions with the blood.

options.text: The lungs retain potassium along with the carbon dioxide they hold
options.rationale: Near miss concept The lungs move gases, not electrolytes. Potassium is not exhaled or retained by breathing.

options.text: Bicarbonate carries potassium out of cells as it enters the blood
options.rationale: Near miss concept In acidosis bicarbonate is low or used up. The ion moving into cells is hydrogen, not bicarbonate.

options.text: Hydrogen ions move into cells, and potassium moves out to balance charge
options.rationale: Intracellular buffering means the cells soak up extra hydrogen ions to protect the blood pH. The test question is: what has to leave the cell when a positive hydrogen ion enters? Another positive ion, potassium, moves out to keep the cell electrically neutral. That raises the serum potassium even when total body potassium has not changed, which is called relative hyperkalemia. Here the potassium was normal before the acidosis and no supplements were given, so the shift explains the rise. The reverse happens in alkalosis: potassium moves into cells and serum potassium falls.

questions.takeaway: Acidosis pushes potassium out of cells (hyperkalemia); alkalosis pulls it in (hypokalemia).
questions.strategy: The detail that points to a shift rather than intake is "no potassium supplements" with a normal level before the acidosis.

questions.stem: Classify each cause by the acid base imbalance it is most likely to produce.

rows.text: Several days of starvation
Kidney failure
Slow, shallow breathing after an opioid dose
An airway blocked by thick secretions
Prolonged nasogastric suctioning
Frequent large doses of antacids
Fast breathing during a panic attack
A first trip to a high altitude

questions.takeaway: First ask whether the cause changes breathing. If it does, the problem is respiratory; if it does not, it is metabolic. Then ask whether acid is gained or lost. Starvation overproduces acid, and kidney failure both under eliminates acid and underproduces bicarbonate, so both are metabolic acidosis. Opioid respiratory depression and an obstructed airway both retain carbon dioxide, so both are respiratory acidosis. Nasogastric suctioning removes stomach acid, an acid deficit, and antacids add base, a base excess, so both are metabolic alkalosis. Panic breathing and high altitude both drive fast breathing that blows off carbon dioxide, so both are respiratory alkalosis. Breathing causes are respiratory; everything else is metabolic. Then ask whether acid is gained or lost.
questions.strategy: The detail that places nasogastric suctioning under alkalosis is the site: stomach contents are acid, so removing them leaves an acid deficit. The opioid and blocked airway rows are respiratory because they change breathing.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence: In an adult, about [[1]] of total body water is inside the cells. Of the fluid outside the cells, the largest share is [[2]]. Compared with a younger adult, an older adult has [[3]] total body water. A person with more body fat and less muscle has [[4]] water as a share of body weight.

options.text: two thirds
one third
one half
four fifths
plasma
interstitial fluid
transcellular fluid
intracellular fluid
more
the same
less
more in the cells but less in the blood
more
less
the same
a changing amount of

questions.takeaway: [1] two thirds: Intracellular fluid (ICF) is the water inside cells. Ask where most water lives: about two thirds is in the cells and one third is outside them as extracellular fluid (ECF). One third is the ECF share, so it is the near miss. [2] interstitial fluid: Interstitial fluid is the water between cells, around the tissues. Of the ECF, about 80 percent is interstitial and only about 20 percent is plasma, the fluid part of blood. Plasma is the tempting pick because it is what we measure, but it is the smaller part. Intracellular fluid is wrong because it is not outside the cells at all. [3] less: Total body water is about 55 to 60 percent of body weight in younger adults and 50 to 55 percent in older adults. Ask what aging does: water drops, which leaves less reserve when fluid is lost. [4] less: Fat holds little water and muscle holds a lot. A body with more fat and less muscle therefore has a lower water percentage, so body water runs lower as the share of fat rises. Two thirds of body water is in the cells; outside the cells, most is interstitial, not plasma. Age and fat both lower the total.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out plasma in blank 2 is the phrase largest share: plasma is only about one fifth of the ECF.

questions.stem: For each statement, select the hormone it describes.

rows.text: Released when serum osmolarity rises
Released when serum sodium falls
Released by the heart when blood volume and pressure are high
Holds sodium and water while the kidneys excrete potassium
Makes the kidneys hold water so the urine becomes concentrated
Makes the kidneys excrete sodium and water

questions.takeaway: Sort each hormone by its trigger and by what it makes the kidney keep or lose. Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) comes from the posterior pituitary. Its trigger is high osmolarity, meaning the blood is too concentrated. It makes the kidneys hold water, so the blood dilutes and the urine becomes concentrated. It saves water, not sodium. Aldosterone comes from the adrenal cortex. Its trigger is low sodium. It makes the kidneys reabsorb sodium, water follows, and potassium is excreted in trade. Natriuretic peptide comes from the heart. Its trigger is stretch from high volume or pressure. It does the opposite of aldosterone: the kidneys excrete sodium and water to unload the circulation. Rows 1 and 5 are ADH, rows 2 and 4 are aldosterone, rows 3 and 6 are natriuretic peptide. ADH saves water for concentrated blood. Aldosterone saves sodium and dumps potassium. Natriuretic peptide dumps sodium and water when the heart is stretched.
questions.strategy: Ask two things of each row: what was the trigger, and is the kidney saving or losing? The near miss is ADH versus aldosterone: only aldosterone moves sodium and potassium.

questions.stem: A patient has a large hemorrhage and the blood pressure falls. Place the steps of the body's response in the order they occur.

options.text: Angiotensin I forms
Blood volume and blood pressure rise
The kidneys secrete renin
Blood vessels constrict and aldosterone release increases
Angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II

questions.takeaway: The renin angiotensin aldosterone system (RAAS) is the kidney's way of raising pressure and volume. Its triggers are low blood pressure, low blood volume, low oxygen and low sodium; a hemorrhage gives the first two. First, the kidneys sense the low flow and secrete renin. Renin leads to angiotensin I, which is inactive. Next, angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE), an enzyme mostly in the lungs, converts it to angiotensin II, the active form. Angiotensin II then acts: blood vessels constrict, urine output falls and aldosterone release rises, so sodium and water are held. The result comes last: blood volume and pressure rise. Renin, then angiotensin I, then ACE makes angiotensin II, which squeezes vessels and calls aldosterone. Volume and pressure rise last.
questions.strategy: Anchor the ends first: renin starts it because the kidney senses the drop, and the rise in pressure is the result. ACE must sit between angiotensin I and II because it converts one to the other.

questions.stem: A patient with right sided heart failure has new pitting edema in both ankles. The serum albumin is normal. Which process best explains the edema?

options.text: Low oncotic pressure lets water leave the vessels
options.rationale: Near miss concept Low oncotic pressure does cause edema, but it comes from low albumin. This patient's albumin is normal, so this cause is ruled out.

options.text: Water moves into cells by osmosis toward more solute
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Osmosis moves water toward more solute, often into or out of cells. Edema is fluid in the spaces between cells, not swelling of the cells.

options.text: Raised capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid into tissue
options.rationale: Filtration is fluid moving across a membrane because of a pressure difference, from high pressure to low. The test question is: is something pushing on the fluid? In right sided heart failure, blood backs up into the veins, so pressure inside the capillaries rises. That raised hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out into the tissues, and gravity puts it in the ankles. Low oncotic pressure, from low albumin, is the other common cause of edema, but the normal albumin rules it out. Osmosis and diffusion are real processes but describe water following solute and solute moving down a gradient, not pressure forcing fluid out.

options.text: Sodium diffuses out of the vessels and pulls water along
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Diffusion moves solutes, not water, from high to low concentration. It does not explain fluid being forced out of the vessels by a failing heart.

questions.takeaway: Edema from heart failure is filtration: backed up pressure pushes fluid out of the capillaries.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out low oncotic pressure is the normal serum albumin. With albumin normal, look for a pressure problem.

questions.stem: A patient with untreated diabetes has a very high blood glucose. The glucose level inside the cells is much lower than in the blood, yet little glucose enters the cells until insulin is given. Which statement explains this?

options.text: Glucose needs help crossing the membrane, and insulin provides it
options.rationale: Diffusion is solute moving from an area of high concentration to low; a steeper gradient makes it faster. Facilitated diffusion is diffusion that still runs downhill but needs help getting through the membrane. The test question: does the solute have a gradient in its favor but still not cross on its own? Here glucose is far higher in the blood than in the cells, so the gradient favors entry, yet it barely moves until insulin arrives. Insulin is the helper that lets glucose cross. Osmosis moves water only, filtration is pressure driven fluid movement, and diffusion does not run low to high.

options.text: Glucose moves only by osmosis, and osmosis has stopped working
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Osmosis moves water, not solutes like glucose. It cannot be the process that carries glucose into cells.

options.text: Glucose enters only when hydrostatic pressure pushes it inward
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Hydrostatic pressure drives filtration of fluid across capillaries. It does not explain why glucose waits for insulin.

options.text: Glucose moves from low to high concentration, so it stays out
options.rationale: Near miss concept Diffusion runs from high to low concentration, not low to high. Here the gradient favors entry, so direction is not the barrier.

questions.takeaway: Facilitated diffusion still runs high to low, but the solute needs help through the membrane; insulin helps glucose.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out a gradient problem is that glucose is higher outside the cells. If the gradient is right and it still will not cross, it needs help.

questions.stem: For each imbalance, select its effect on nerve and muscle cells.

rows.text: Hypocalcemia
Hypercalcemia
Hypomagnesemia
Hypermagnesemia
Hypokalemia
Hyperkalemia

questions.takeaway: Excitability means how easily a nerve or muscle cell fires. Calcium works like a brake on the cell membrane. Low calcium takes the brake off, so cells fire too easily: tingling, spasms, tetany. High calcium presses the brake: weakness, low reflexes, slow gut. Magnesium behaves the same way as calcium: low magnesium raises excitability (hyperreflexia, cramps, seizures) and high magnesium lowers it (weak or absent reflexes, drowsiness). Potassium runs the other way. Low potassium makes cells less responsive to a stimulus, so muscles are weak and reflexes drop. High potassium makes cells respond to a weaker stimulus, so early signs are tingling and twitching before weakness sets in. So hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia and hyperkalemia increase excitability; hypercalcemia, hypermagnesemia and hypokalemia decrease it. Calcium and magnesium: low fires, high stalls. Potassium is reversed: low stalls, high fires.
questions.strategy: The trap is assuming every low value acts the same. Low potassium and low calcium can both cause cramps, but low potassium lowers excitability while low calcium raises it.

questions.stem: A patient with hypernatremia from fluid loss has an order for dextrose 5 percent in 0.45 percent sodium chloride. A student says, "This bag is hypertonic, so it will pull water out of the cells." Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: Correct, so it should run fast to restore volume quickly
options.rationale: Near miss concept Running fluid fast is the wrong idea in hypernatremia. Rapid correction can cause cerebral edema, so sodium is lowered gradually.

options.text: Correct, which is why it is used only for hyponatremia
options.rationale: Near miss concept It is ordered here for hypernatremia from fluid loss, so it is not limited to hyponatremia. The student's premise about tonicity is also only half true.

options.text: It is isotonic in the bag and stays in the vascular space
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Isotonic fluid, like 0.9 percent saline, has about the same concentration as plasma. This bag measures higher because of the dextrose, so it is not isotonic.

options.text: It is hypertonic in the bag but hypotonic once dextrose is used
options.rationale: Tonicity is how concentrated a fluid is compared with plasma. Hypertonic pulls water out of cells; hypotonic pushes water into cells. The test question for a dextrose solution: what is left after the dextrose is used? In the bag, the dextrose plus the half strength saline makes the fluid hypertonic. Once infused, the body metabolizes the dextrose, leaving free water and 0.45 percent saline, which is hypotonic. That is the goal in hypernatremia from fluid loss: replace free water and let it move back into shrunken cells. The correction must be gradual, because lowering sodium too fast swells brain cells.

questions.takeaway: Dextrose solutions act on the body after the dextrose is gone: D5 in 0.45 percent saline ends up hypotonic.
questions.strategy: The detail that decides it is the dextrose. Judge the fluid by what remains after the sugar is metabolized, not by the label on the bag.

questions.stem: A patient with diabetes and chronic kidney disease has a potassium of 5.6 mEq/L. Select all of the items on the medication and diet list that could be raising the potassium.

options.text: Lisinopril, an ACE inhibitor
options.rationale: Hyperkalemia, a potassium above 5.0 mEq/L, usually comes from the kidneys not excreting enough. The test question for each item: does it cut potassium excretion or add potassium? Kidney disease and diabetes already raise the risk. An ACE inhibitor such as lisinopril and an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) such as losartan both reduce aldosterone, and aldosterone is what makes the kidneys excrete potassium, so both raise it. Spironolactone is a potassium sparing diuretic: it removes fluid while holding potassium. Salt substitutes are made with potassium, so they add it. Furosemide and prednisone both push potassium down and are hypokalemia risks.

options.text: Spironolactone, a potassium sparing diuretic
options.rationale: Hyperkalemia, a potassium above 5.0 mEq/L, usually comes from the kidneys not excreting enough. The test question for each item: does it cut potassium excretion or add potassium? Kidney disease and diabetes already raise the risk. An ACE inhibitor such as lisinopril and an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) such as losartan both reduce aldosterone, and aldosterone is what makes the kidneys excrete potassium, so both raise it. Spironolactone is a potassium sparing diuretic: it removes fluid while holding potassium. Salt substitutes are made with potassium, so they add it. Furosemide and prednisone both push potassium down and are hypokalemia risks.

options.text: Furosemide, a loop diuretic
options.rationale: Near miss concept A loop diuretic makes the kidneys lose potassium. It lowers potassium and is a cause of hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia.

options.text: A salt substitute used to season food
options.rationale: Hyperkalemia, a potassium above 5.0 mEq/L, usually comes from the kidneys not excreting enough. The test question for each item: does it cut potassium excretion or add potassium? Kidney disease and diabetes already raise the risk. An ACE inhibitor such as lisinopril and an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) such as losartan both reduce aldosterone, and aldosterone is what makes the kidneys excrete potassium, so both raise it. Spironolactone is a potassium sparing diuretic: it removes fluid while holding potassium. Salt substitutes are made with potassium, so they add it. Furosemide and prednisone both push potassium down and are hypokalemia risks.

options.text: Losartan, an angiotensin receptor blocker
options.rationale: Hyperkalemia, a potassium above 5.0 mEq/L, usually comes from the kidneys not excreting enough. The test question for each item: does it cut potassium excretion or add potassium? Kidney disease and diabetes already raise the risk. An ACE inhibitor such as lisinopril and an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) such as losartan both reduce aldosterone, and aldosterone is what makes the kidneys excrete potassium, so both raise it. Spironolactone is a potassium sparing diuretic: it removes fluid while holding potassium. Salt substitutes are made with potassium, so they add it. Furosemide and prednisone both push potassium down and are hypokalemia risks.

options.text: Prednisone, a corticosteroid taken daily
options.rationale: Near miss concept Corticosteroids are a risk factor for low potassium. They do not explain a high level.

questions.takeaway: Drugs that block aldosterone or spare potassium, plus salt substitutes, raise potassium. Loop diuretics and steroids lower it.
questions.strategy: Sort each item by direction: does it hold potassium or waste it? The planted detail is chronic kidney disease, which means the kidneys cannot clear any extra.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence: When serum calcium falls, [[1]] raises it by pulling calcium from bone and reducing kidney excretion. [[2]] raises calcium by increasing its absorption from the gut. When serum calcium is high, [[3]] lowers it by moving calcium into bone. Removal of the parathyroid glands puts the patient at risk for [[4]].

options.text: calcitonin
parathyroid hormone
vitamin D
aldosterone
Vitamin D
Calcitonin
Parathyroid hormone
Antidiuretic hormone
parathyroid hormone
vitamin D
calcitonin
natriuretic peptide
hypercalcemia
hypocalcemia
hyperkalemia
hypermagnesemia

questions.takeaway: [1] parathyroid hormone: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) is the main hormone that raises calcium. It pulls calcium out of bone, activates vitamin D and makes the kidneys keep calcium. Calcitonin does the reverse. [2] Vitamin D: Vitamin D raises calcium from the other direction, by helping the gut absorb calcium from food. The clue is gut absorption; PTH acts on bone and kidney. [3] calcitonin: Calcitonin is the hormone that lowers calcium. It moves calcium into storage in bone. That is why calcitonin is a treatment for hypercalcemia. [4] hypocalcemia: Without the parathyroid glands there is no PTH, so nothing pulls calcium up when it falls. Parathyroid damage or removal, including during thyroid surgery, is a classic cause of low calcium. PTH and vitamin D raise calcium; calcitonin lowers it. No parathyroid glands means low calcium.
questions.strategy: Assign direction first: two raise, one lowers. Then split the two raisers by site: bone and kidney for PTH, gut for vitamin D.

questions.topic: causes of dehydration and fluid overload
questions.stem: For each condition, select the fluid imbalance it is most likely to cause.
questions.objective: causes of dehydration and fluid overload

rows.text: Continuous gastric suction
Long term corticosteroid therapy
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH)
A new ileostomy with high output
A psychiatric disorder with compulsive water drinking
Profuse sweating

questions.takeaway: Dehydration is fluid intake or retention that is less than the body needs. Fluid overload is intake or retention that is more than the body needs. The test question for each row: is fluid leaving, or is it coming in or being held? Gastric suction removes fluid from the stomach, an ileostomy drains liquid stool from the small bowel, and profuse sweating loses water through the skin; all three are losses, so dehydration. Long term corticosteroids make the kidneys hold sodium and water. SIADH means too much antidiuretic hormone, so the kidneys hold water they should release. Compulsive water drinking (polydipsia) takes in more water than the kidneys can clear. Those three cause fluid overload. Losses through the gut, drains or skin cause dehydration. Too much intake or a body holding fluid causes overload.
questions.strategy: Ask whether each condition takes fluid out or keeps it in. SIADH is the near miss: the word hormone sounds like regulation, but too much ADH means water is held.

questions.stem: A patient with severe dehydration and a low serum albumin received a bolus of 0.9 percent sodium chloride. The provider now orders IV albumin. What does the albumin add that the saline does not?

options.text: It replaces water inside the cells as well as outside them
options.rationale: Near miss concept Replacing fluid in and out of cells describes crystalloids like the saline already given. Albumin is a colloid and works inside the vessels.

options.text: It raises oncotic pressure, so water stays in the vessels
options.rationale: Crystalloids are IV fluids of water and small solutes, such as 0.9 percent saline, lactated Ringer's, 0.45 percent saline and D5W. They spread through both the ECF and ICF. Colloids are fluids with large molecules, such as albumin and blood products, that stay in the vessels. Oncotic pressure is the pull that these large proteins create to hold water inside the blood vessels. The test question: does the fluid add protein that keeps water in the vascular space? Albumin does. A patient with low albumin cannot hold water in the vessels well, so the albumin raises oncotic pressure, keeps water in and expands plasma volume.

options.text: It lowers oncotic pressure, so water moves into the tissues
options.rationale: Near miss concept This reverses the effect. Lower oncotic pressure would let water leak out of the vessels, which is the problem albumin is meant to fix.

options.text: It supplies sodium to correct a low serum sodium level
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Albumin is a protein, not a sodium source. Nothing in the stem points to a low sodium.

questions.takeaway: Crystalloids spread water everywhere. Colloids like albumin raise oncotic pressure and keep water in the vessels.
questions.strategy: The planted detail is the low serum albumin. It tells you the problem is holding water inside the vessels, which is the job of a colloid.

questions.stem: A patient with liver disease has pitting edema of the legs and ascites, yet the blood pressure is 94/58 and the heart rate is 104. How should the nurse interpret this combination?

options.text: The findings conflict, so one measurement is probably in error
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dismisses a real and common pattern.

options.text: Low albumin lets fluid leave vessels: edematous yet volume depleted
options.rationale: Albumin creates the oncotic pressure that pulls fluid back into the capillary. When it falls, fluid stays in the interstitium. The patient looks wet and the vascular space is dry, which is why the pressure is low and the rate is up.

options.text: The edema means fluid overload, and the low pressure is unrelated
options.rationale: Near miss concept Treats edema as proof of intravascular volume.

options.text: The edema is positional and will resolve once the legs are elevated
options.rationale: Near miss concept Does not account for the ascites or the vital signs.

questions.takeaway: Edema is not the same as volume. Ask where the fluid actually is.
questions.strategy: When a stem gives you findings that seem to contradict, look for a third variable. Here it is albumin.

questions.stem: A patient has a potassium of 2.8 and an order for 40 mEq of potassium chloride in 100 mL to run over one hour through a peripheral line. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give it by slow intravenous push over 10 minutes
options.rationale: Near miss concept Potassium by push is lethal; there is no slow enough.

options.text: Give it and request a central line for later doses
options.rationale: Near miss concept Gives the dangerous dose now and fixes the access later.

options.text: Give it as ordered on a pump with cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Near miss concept A pump and a monitor do not make an unsafe rate safe.

options.text: Question it; the concentration and rate are unsafe peripherally
options.rationale: Her deck gives 5 to 10 mEq per hour; this order is 40 in one hour, four to eight times that. Concentrated potassium peripherally also causes severe pain and phlebitis and risks extravasation of a vesicant. Potassium is never pushed, under any circumstances. Confirm urine output, question the order, and expect a lower rate, a more dilute solution, or central access.

questions.takeaway: Potassium is never pushed, and the rate is part of the order. Both are worth a phone call.
questions.strategy: Two options give a dangerous order with a safety measure attached. The measures do not make the rate safe.

questions.stem: A patient receiving intravenous magnesium has diminished deep tendon reflexes, a blood pressure of 92/54 and a respiratory rate of 10. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Prepare for intubation and mechanical ventilation
options.rationale: Correct but premature Appropriate next, once the source is off.

options.text: Obtain a stat serum magnesium level
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Confirms a diagnosis the clinical picture has already made.

options.text: Stop the magnesium infusion
options.rationale: Loss of deep tendon reflexes is the early warning of hypermagnesemia, which is why reflexes are checked on every magnesium infusion. This patient has moved past that: with hypotension and a respiratory rate of 10 the depression is already here. Stopping the infusion is still the first action, because calcium and ventilatory support accomplish nothing while magnesium keeps running in.

options.text: Administer intravenous calcium gluconate per protocol
options.rationale: Correct but premature The right antidote, given while the magnesium is still running in.

questions.takeaway: Reflexes warn you first. Once the rate falls, the warning was already missed.
questions.strategy: Stop the cause, then give the antidote. Testing confirms what the patient is already showing you.

questions.topic: fluid status in a complicated patient
questions.stem: A patient with cirrhosis has ascites, 3 plus leg edema, sodium 128, albumin 2.1, blood pressure 88/54 and urine output 18 mL per hour. Select all of the accurate nursing conclusions.
questions.objective: fluid status in a complicated patient

options.text: He can be edematous and intravascularly depleted at the same time
options.rationale: Albumin creates the oncotic pressure that holds fluid in the capillary. At 2.1 it cannot, so he looks wet and the vascular space is dry, which is why the pressure is low and the kidneys are not being perfused. Diuresing hard pulls from the only compartment that is already empty. His hyponatremia is dilutional, so the treatment is water restriction, not sodium.

options.text: The edema proves he is fluid overloaded and needs a large diuretic dose
options.rationale: Near miss concept Total body water is high and the circulating volume is low; this is the central error in this patient.

options.text: The sodium of 128 means he needs intravenous sodium replacement
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dilutional hyponatremia is managed by restricting water, not giving sodium.

options.text: The low albumin lets fluid leave the vascular space and stay in the interstitium
options.rationale: Albumin creates the oncotic pressure that holds fluid in the capillary. At 2.1 it cannot, so he looks wet and the vascular space is dry, which is why the pressure is low and the kidneys are not being perfused. Diuresing hard pulls from the only compartment that is already empty. His hyponatremia is dilutional, so the treatment is water restriction, not sodium.

options.text: Aggressive diuresis without attention to the pressure could worsen kidney function
options.rationale: Albumin creates the oncotic pressure that holds fluid in the capillary. At 2.1 it cannot, so he looks wet and the vascular space is dry, which is why the pressure is low and the kidneys are not being perfused. Diuresing hard pulls from the only compartment that is already empty. His hyponatremia is dilutional, so the treatment is water restriction, not sodium.

options.text: The low urine output likely reflects poor renal perfusion rather than kidney disease alone
options.rationale: Albumin creates the oncotic pressure that holds fluid in the capillary. At 2.1 it cannot, so he looks wet and the vascular space is dry, which is why the pressure is low and the kidneys are not being perfused. Diuresing hard pulls from the only compartment that is already empty. His hyponatremia is dilutional, so the treatment is water restriction, not sodium.

questions.takeaway: Edema is not volume. Ask where the fluid actually is before you reach for a diuretic.
questions.strategy: Two options treat the visible finding instead of the compartment that matters.

questions.stem: A patient admitted with a sodium of 112 and seizures has received hypertonic saline. Six hours later the sodium is 126. What should the nurse recognize?

options.text: The correction is too slow, and the infusion rate should be increased
options.rationale: Near miss concept Backwards, and dangerous.

options.text: The correction is too fast; notify the provider before giving more
options.rationale: Fourteen points in six hours is far faster than the roughly 8 to 10 per 24 hours that is considered safe. The brain adapted to a dilute environment over days, and pulling water out too quickly causes osmotic demyelination, which is often permanent and sometimes appears days later, after everyone has relaxed. Faster is not better in either direction with sodium.

options.text: The sodium should be brought up to 135 within the next 6 hours
options.rationale: Near miss concept That would nearly double an already excessive rate.

options.text: The correction is appropriate, since the sodium is approaching normal
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Reads a normalizing number as a good outcome and ignores the rate.

questions.takeaway: About 8 to 10 points in 24 hours. Faster correction injures the brain you were saving.
questions.strategy: The temptation is to read movement toward normal as success. With sodium, the rate is the danger.

questions.stem: An older adult who lives alone is admitted with a sodium of 158 mmol/L. He is lethargic and has dry mucous membranes. What is the priority nursing concern?

options.text: Safety and neurologic status, with gradual correction of the sodium
options.rationale: Hypernatremia in an older adult is usually a water problem, not a salt problem: reduced thirst sensation plus poor access means water loss. The brain adapts to a concentrated extracellular space, so correcting fast pulls water into brain cells and causes cerebral edema. Sodium is corrected slowly in both directions.

options.text: Rapid intravenous correction of the sodium back to a normal range
options.rationale: Near miss concept The right target, reached at a speed that causes brain injury.

options.text: Strict fluid restriction until the sodium level returns to normal
options.rationale: Near miss concept Restricting water in a water deficit.

options.text: A low sodium diet and removal of the salt shaker from meal trays
options.rationale: Near miss concept Treats it as a salt excess.

questions.takeaway: Correct sodium slowly, whichever way it is wrong.
questions.strategy: Any option with rapid correction of sodium is wrong, high or low.

questions.topic: reading an electrolyte panel as a set
questions.stem: A patient on a thiazide diuretic for three weeks has sodium 131, potassium 3.0, chloride 94, bicarbonate 31 and magnesium 1.4. She reports weakness and leg cramps. Which finding should the nurse address first with the provider?
questions.objective: reading an electrolyte panel as a set

options.text: The sodium of 131, because hyponatremia can cause seizures
options.rationale: Near miss concept Mild and asymptomatic at this level; seizures come far lower.

options.text: The bicarbonate of 31, because the alkalosis drives the weakness
options.rationale: Near miss concept A consequence of the chloride and volume loss, not the lever to pull.

options.text: The potassium of 3.0, because it is causing her muscle symptoms
options.rationale: Near miss concept It is causing the symptoms and it will not stay corrected until the magnesium is fixed.

options.text: The magnesium of 1.4, since low magnesium blocks potassium repair
options.rationale: This is the whole panel telling one story: a thiazide wasting sodium, potassium, chloride and magnesium, with a contraction alkalosis behind it. The trap is treating the potassium alone. Low magnesium makes the kidney keep dumping potassium, so the replacement does not hold and the level keeps falling back. You fix the magnesium or you repeat the potassium forever.

questions.takeaway: Low potassium that will not correct is a magnesium problem. Check it before you replace anything.
questions.strategy: Read every value as one story before you pick the worst number.

questions.stem: A patient with acute kidney injury has a potassium of 6.7 mEq/L. The monitor shows tall peaked T waves. Which order should the nurse anticipate first?

options.text: Intravenous furosemide
options.rationale: Near miss concept A legitimate way to remove potassium when urine output is adequate, and far too slow for a heart that is already showing electrocardiogram changes.

options.text: Intravenous calcium gluconate
options.rationale: Calcium does not lower the potassium. It stabilizes the cardiac membrane and buys time while the measures that actually shift or remove potassium take effect. With electrocardiogram changes already present, protecting the heart comes first.

options.text: Oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate
options.rationale: Near miss concept Removes potassium, and far too slowly for peaked T waves.

options.text: A potassium restricted diet
options.rationale: Correct but premature Prevention, not treatment of an acute arrhythmia risk.

questions.takeaway: Calcium protects the heart. Insulin and glucose shift it. Binders and dialysis remove it.
questions.strategy: When the electrocardiogram has already changed, choose the intervention that protects the myocardium rather than the one that lowers the number.

questions.stem: A patient 12 hours after thyroid surgery reports tingling around the mouth and in the fingertips. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Encourage oral intake of dairy products
options.rationale: Correct but premature Far too slow, and the level has not been checked.

options.text: Reassure the patient that this is expected after neck surgery
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Dismisses the earliest sign of a complication that ends in laryngospasm.

options.text: Administer the ordered analgesic
options.rationale: Near miss concept This is paresthesia, not pain.

options.text: Assess for Chvostek and Trousseau signs and notify the provider
options.rationale: The parathyroid glands sit on the thyroid and can be bruised or removed during the surgery, which drops calcium. Perioral and fingertip tingling is the earliest sign, and it progresses to tetany, laryngospasm and seizures. Chvostek is a facial twitch on tapping the nerve, Trousseau is carpal spasm with a blood pressure cuff inflated.

questions.takeaway: Tingling around the mouth after thyroid surgery is low calcium until proven otherwise.
questions.strategy: Normalizing this as expected is the error, because the next step is airway.

questions.stem: A patient after major abdominal surgery has generalized edema, a weight gain of 3 kg, blood pressure of 92/56, heart rate of 118 and urine output of 15 mL per hour. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: Acute kidney injury unrelated to the patient's volume status
options.rationale: Near miss concept The oliguria is prerenal here, driven by the depleted vascular space.

options.text: Heart failure from fluid overload given during the surgery
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would show high filling pressures and distended neck veins, not hypotension with tachycardia.

options.text: Third spacing: fluid in the tissues, vascular space depleted
options.rationale: The fluid is in the patient, just not where it can perfuse anything. Capillaries leak after surgery, trauma, burns and sepsis, so the weight goes up and the circulating volume goes down at the same time. Diuresing this patient empties the one compartment that is already dry. The fluid returns on its own during the reabsorption phase, and that is when overload becomes the risk.

options.text: Fluid volume excess that should be treated with a diuretic
options.rationale: Near miss concept Treats the weight and worsens the perfusion.

questions.takeaway: Edema plus hypotension plus oliguria is fluid in the wrong compartment, not too much fluid.
questions.strategy: The weight gain is designed to pull you toward a diuretic.

questions.stem: Thirty minutes into an infusion of isotonic saline, a patient develops crackles in both lung bases, shortness of breath and distended neck veins. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Place the patient flat and elevate the legs to redistribute the fluid
options.rationale: Near miss concept Increases venous return to a heart that cannot handle it.

options.text: Document the findings and notify the provider at the end of the assessment
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Delays the one action that reduces the load.

options.text: Stop the infusion, remove the catheter and restart in a new site
options.rationale: Near miss concept The correct response to infiltration or phlebitis, applied to an overload.

options.text: Slow the infusion rate and reassess
options.rationale: This is circulatory overload. The first action is to reduce the rate, then raise the head of the bed, give oxygen and diuretics per order, and notify the provider. Removing the catheter discards the access you may need, and laying the patient flat worsens the pulmonary congestion.

questions.takeaway: Slow the rate first. The line stays; the rate changes.
questions.strategy: In an infusion complication, ask whether the problem is the SITE or the VOLUME. Only site problems take the catheter out.

questions.stem: A patient admitted with severe diarrhea has deep rapid respirations, a pH of 7.27 and a bicarbonate of 14. The respiratory rate is 32. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Administer oxygen and prepare to assist ventilation to slow the respiratory rate
options.rationale: Near miss concept Treats the compensation as the pathology.

options.text: Treat the underlying cause and recognize the respiratory pattern as compensation
options.rationale: Deep rapid respirations in metabolic acidosis are Kussmaul breathing, which is the lungs blowing off carbon dioxide to raise the pH. Slowing that pattern removes the compensation and drops the pH further. The treatment is the diarrhea and the fluid and bicarbonate loss.

options.text: Encourage pursed lip breathing to slow the respiratory rate
options.rationale: Near miss concept A useful technique in obstructive disease, harmful here.

options.text: Request an order for a sedative to reduce the work of breathing
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would remove the compensation entirely.

questions.takeaway: Kussmaul respirations are compensation, not a respiratory problem.
questions.strategy: When a breathing pattern is the only thing keeping the pH survivable, do not treat the pattern.

questions.stem: A nurse finds redness along the vein above an intravenous site, with warmth and a palpable cord. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Slow the infusion rate and continue to monitor the site
options.rationale: Near miss concept The correct response to circulatory overload.

options.text: Flush the catheter to confirm it is still patent
options.rationale: Near miss concept Patency is not the question when the vein is inflamed.

options.text: Discontinue the catheter, apply warmth, and restart in another extremity
options.rationale: Redness tracking along the vein with warmth and a palpable cord is phlebitis, which is inflammation of the vein wall. That is a site problem, so the catheter comes out and the new one goes in a different extremity. Infiltration gives you cool, pale, swollen tissue instead, and circulatory overload is a volume problem where the line stays and the rate changes.

options.text: Apply a cold compress and continue the infusion at the current rate
options.rationale: Near miss concept Leaves an inflamed vein in use.

questions.takeaway: Site problems take the catheter out. Volume problems change the rate.
questions.strategy: Sort the intravenous complications by whether the trouble is in the vein or in the patient.

questions.stem: A provider orders 40 mEq of potassium chloride intravenously for a patient whose serum potassium is 2.9 mEq/L. Before beginning the infusion, which assessment is essential?

options.text: Bowel sounds present in all four quadrants
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Relevant to oral potassium tolerance, not to the intravenous safety check.

options.text: A serum sodium within normal limits today
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sodium does not determine whether potassium can be given safely; adequate kidney output does.

options.text: A blood pressure that remains within the patient's usual baseline
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Reasonable monitoring unrelated to potassium handling.

options.text: Urine output of at least 30 mL per hour
options.rationale: Potassium is excreted by the kidneys. Giving it to a patient who is not producing urine can drive the level into a lethal range. Confirming output is the safety check that precedes the infusion. Potassium is never given by intravenous push and is always given on a pump.

questions.takeaway: Check urine output before giving potassium. Never push it.
questions.strategy: The safety check that belongs to a drug is usually tied to how the body gets rid of it.

questions.stem: Two patients each have a serum sodium of 128 mEq/L. Patient A has vomited for two days and has a weak, thready pulse of 112 beats per minute and a blood pressure that drops on standing. Patient B has heart failure, a bounding pulse, crackles in both bases and a weight gain of 2 kg in two days. Which plan fits both patients correctly?

options.text: Fluid restriction for both, because a low sodium always means too much water
options.rationale: Absolute language Right for the diluted patient only; restricting fluid in Patient A deepens a volume loss that is already dropping the pressure.

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride for both, because a low sodium always needs salt replaced
options.rationale: Absolute language Right for the patient who lost sodium with fluid; salt water in Patient B adds volume to lungs that are already wet.

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride for Patient A and fluid restriction for Patient B
options.rationale: The sodium number is the same, but the cause is not. Patient A lost sodium and water (thready pulse, orthostatic drop), so the volume and the sodium both need replacing with isotonic saline. Patient B has dilution (bounding pulse, crackles, weight gain), so the fix is less water, not more salt. Both still need neuro checks and seizure safety.

options.text: Fluid restriction for Patient A and 0.9% sodium chloride for Patient B
options.rationale: Near miss concept The right two treatments assigned to the wrong two patients.

questions.takeaway: Low sodium is not always treated with salt. The pulse tells you whether it is loss or dilution.
questions.strategy: When two patients share a lab value, the answer lives in the findings that differ. Read the pulse and the weight before the sodium.

questions.stem: A patient has a potassium of 6.5 mEq/L, peaked T waves, and maintenance IV fluid with potassium chloride infusing. Place the nurse's actions in the order they should occur.

options.text: Give the ordered sodium polystyrene sulfonate
Check the blood glucose
Stop the potassium infusion and place the patient on telemetry
Give the ordered regular insulin with dextrose
Give the ordered IV calcium

questions.takeaway: Stop, protect, shift, remove. Nothing else helps while potassium is still running in, so every source stops and the heart is watched. IV calcium protects the myocardium within minutes but does not lower the level. Insulin with dextrose shifts potassium into the cells, and because insulin can still drop the glucose, the glucose is checked next. A binder removes potassium from the body last, because it is the slowest. Stop, protect, shift, remove. Each step does a different job.
questions.strategy: Order by speed of danger: stop the input, then protect the heart, then fix the number fastest to slowest.

questions.stem: Forty minutes after receiving regular insulin with dextrose for a potassium of 6.4 mEq/L, a patient becomes sweaty, shaky and anxious. The potassium has not been redrawn. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Redraw the potassium to see whether the treatment worked
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question The potassium recheck is due, but it does not explain sweating and shaking.

options.text: Check the blood glucose
options.rationale: Insulin moves potassium into cells by moving glucose with it, and the dextrose does not always keep up. Sweating, shaking and anxiety after insulin are hypoglycemia until a glucose check says otherwise, which is why the glucose check is part of the hyperkalemia sequence.

options.text: Reassure the patient that anxiety is common during treatment
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Labels a physical warning sign as emotion and delays the fingerstick.

options.text: Give the next ordered dose of IV calcium
options.rationale: Near miss concept Calcium protects the heart; it does nothing for the problem the symptoms point to.

questions.takeaway: After insulin for hyperkalemia, a sweaty, shaky patient is low on glucose until proven otherwise.
questions.strategy: Ask what the last drug given can cause. The symptoms point to the insulin, not the potassium.

questions.stem: A patient treated two hours ago for hyperkalemia with IV calcium, regular insulin with dextrose and a binder now has a potassium of 3.2 mEq/L. Which finding requires follow up?

options.text: The peaked T waves seen on admission have now resolved
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Resolution of peaked T waves is the goal of treatment.

options.text: A blood glucose of 112 mg/dL one hour after the dextrose
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data A normal glucose after insulin with dextrose is the outcome you want.

options.text: A regular heart rate of 78 beats per minute on the monitor
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A regular rate in the normal range is reassuring.

options.text: New flat T waves with a U wave and new leg weakness
options.rationale: Shifting and removing potassium can overshoot. Flat T waves, a U wave and weakness are the low potassium picture, so the patient has swung into rebound hypokalemia, which is just as able to cause a fatal dysrhythmia. Report it and keep the monitor on.

questions.takeaway: During treatment for an imbalance, the finding that needs follow up is the one that signals the opposite imbalance.
questions.strategy: Three options describe treatment working. Find the one that describes treatment going too far.

questions.topic: what IV calcium does in hyperkalemia
questions.stem: A patient with a potassium of 6.8 mEq/L received IV calcium, and the peaked T waves have settled. A nursing student says, "The potassium problem is handled now." Which response by the nurse is accurate?
questions.objective: what IV calcium does in hyperkalemia

options.text: “Calcium protects the heart, but the potassium stays high until it is lowered.”
options.rationale: IV calcium steadies the cardiac membrane while the potassium is still dangerously high. It buys time and nothing more. The level comes down only when insulin with dextrose shifts potassium into the cells and binders, diuretics or dialysis remove it.

options.text: “Yes, calcium binds the potassium so the kidneys can excrete all of it.”
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Calcium does not bind or remove potassium; binders do that.

options.text: “Yes, the ECG is the best potassium measure, so telemetry can stop now.”
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome A calmer ECG is not a lower level; removing the monitor is premature and unsafe.

options.text: “Calcium lowered the potassium, but a low potassium diet is still needed.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Restriction is reasonable later, but the premise that calcium lowered the level is wrong.

questions.takeaway: IV calcium does not lower potassium. It only steadies the heart.
questions.strategy: When an option says a drug fixed the number, ask what the drug actually does. Here it protects; it does not lower.

questions.stem: A patient with a potassium of 3.3 mEq/L is prescribed oral potassium chloride and reports stomach upset after taking the first dose with water on an empty stomach. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Hold the potassium until the next lab result
options.rationale: Correct but premature Leaves a low potassium untreated over a fixable side effect.

options.text: Ask the provider to change the order to IV potassium
options.rationale: Near miss concept Escalates to the high alert route when the oral route only needs a change in timing.

options.text: Give future doses with food
options.rationale: Oral potassium irritates the stomach. Giving it with food is the standard fix and keeps the patient on the safer route. IV potassium is reserved for when oral replacement is not enough or not possible.

options.text: Give the dose with extra water and have the patient lie flat afterward
options.rationale: Near miss concept More water helps a little; lying flat does nothing for the stomach.

questions.takeaway: Oral potassium goes with food.
questions.strategy: Prefer the answer that solves the problem on the current, safer route before escalating.

questions.stem: A patient with a potassium of 3.0 mEq/L reports leg cramps and feels weak in both legs, and wants to walk to the bathroom alone. Which nursing action is the priority?

options.text: Encourage the patient to walk to strengthen the leg muscles
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit The weakness is from the potassium, not deconditioning; walking alone invites a fall.

options.text: Implement fall precautions and assist the patient to the bathroom
options.rationale: Low potassium weakens skeletal muscle and causes cramps, so the immediate risk at the bedside is a fall. Fall precautions sit alongside monitoring and replacement in the priority care for hypokalemia.

options.text: Apply warm packs to the calves for the cramps
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question May ease comfort but ignores the safety risk of weak legs.

options.text: Document the cramps as an expected finding and recheck tomorrow
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Recording a finding does not protect a weak patient walking alone.

questions.takeaway: Low potassium means weak legs. Weak legs mean fall precautions.
questions.strategy: Translate the finding into the harm it can cause in the next five minutes.

questions.stem: Eighteen hours after thyroid surgery, a patient who reported lip tingling an hour ago now has high pitched, noisy breathing on inspiration and is anxious. The oxygen saturation is 91 percent. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Call the rapid response team
options.rationale: Perioral tingling after thyroid surgery signals low calcium. Stridor means it has progressed to laryngospasm, which closes the airway. The tingling gets reported; the stridor gets the rapid response team now, with airway support while calcium is replaced.

options.text: Tap the cheek in front of the ear to check for a Chvostek sign
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Confirms low calcium the airway is already telling you about.

options.text: Draw a serum calcium level
options.rationale: Correct but premature The level will be needed, but it does not open a closing airway.

options.text: Document the finding and recheck in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Stridor can progress to complete obstruction in minutes.

questions.takeaway: Tingling gets reported. Stridor is laryngospasm: call the rapid response team.
questions.strategy: Airway beats confirmation. When a finding threatens the airway, skip the test that proves what you already know.

questions.stem: A patient has a serum calcium of 7.4 mg/dL, a prolonged QT interval and muscle cramps. Calcium replacement has been ordered. Which room arrangement best supports this patient's safety?

options.text: A room near the busy nurses' station with the door open and lights on
options.rationale: Institution as rationale Visibility helps staff, but noise and light stimulate nerves that are already firing too easily.

options.text: A quiet room with seizure precautions and gentle handling during care
options.rationale: Low calcium removes a brake on the nerves, so stimulation can trigger tetany, seizures or laryngospasm. Priority care is airway and seizure safety, a quiet room, gentle movement and calcium replacement, with the heart monitored because of the prolonged QT.

options.text: A shared room so a roommate can call for help
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic A roommate is not a safety plan and adds stimulation.
