options.text: A room with the bed in a low position and bed rails down to allow ambulation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fall safety is reasonable, but it misses the seizure and airway risk that define low calcium.

questions.takeaway: Low calcium: quiet room, move gently, protect the airway, prepare for seizures.
questions.strategy: Match the environment to the mechanism. An overexcited nervous system needs less stimulation.

questions.topic: assessing turgor in the older adult
questions.stem: An 86 year old patient admitted with poor intake has skin on the back of the hand that stays tented after a pinch. The mucous membranes are moist and the heart rate and blood pressure match the patient's baseline. What should the nurse do next?
questions.objective: assessing turgor in the older adult

options.text: Recheck skin turgor over the sternum
options.rationale: Aging skin loses elasticity and tents on the hand even when the patient is hydrated. In older adults turgor is checked over the sternum, and it is read alongside vital signs, mucous membranes, intake and output and daily weight.

options.text: Report severe dehydration and request IV fluids
options.rationale: Most dramatic finding Acts on a sign that misleads in aging skin while every other finding is reassuring.

options.text: Encourage fluids only if the patient says they are thirsty
options.rationale: Near miss concept Older adults have a weaker thirst alarm; fluids are offered on a schedule, not on request.

options.text: Document poor turgor as the main finding of the fluid assessment
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Records the misleading sign instead of checking it where it is reliable.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult, check turgor on the sternum. The hand lies.
questions.strategy: When one finding conflicts with the rest of the picture, ask whether the method of getting that finding is valid for this patient.

questions.topic: new confusion in the older adult
questions.stem: A 79 year old patient was alert and oriented yesterday. Tonight the patient is pulling at the IV, does not know the date, and has drunk little today. What should the nurse do first?
questions.objective: new confusion in the older adult

options.text: Apply soft wrist restraints to protect the IV site
options.rationale: Correct but premature Restraint treats the behavior and skips the cause; it is never the first move.

options.text: Reorient the patient and document the new confusion
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Reorienting is kind, but new confusion is a change in condition that needs assessment.

options.text: Request an order for a sedative to calm the patient
options.rationale: Correct but premature Sedation masks the very change you need to explain and can worsen confusion.

options.text: Check orthostatic vital signs and review intake and labs
options.rationale: New confusion in an older adult may be the first sign of a fluid or electrolyte imbalance. Older adults have less body water, a weaker thirst alarm and kidneys that concentrate poorly, so a day of poor intake can tip them into deficit. Assess vital signs, orthostatics, intake and labs before anything else.

questions.takeaway: New confusion is a change in condition. Assess before you restrain, sedate or reorient.
questions.strategy: Assessment before intervention. Choose the answer that looks for the cause.

questions.topic: fluid volume deficit and fall risk
questions.stem: A patient with two days of diarrhea has a heart rate of 108 beats per minute and a blood pressure of 112/70 lying and 90/58 standing, with dizziness on standing. The patient asks to walk to the bathroom. What should the nurse do?
questions.objective: fluid volume deficit and fall risk

options.text: Allow the patient to walk alone, since the lying blood pressure is normal
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data The lying pressure is normal, but the standing drop is what causes falls.

options.text: Insert an indwelling urinary catheter to avoid getting up
options.rationale: Near miss concept An invasive device with infection risk is not a fall precaution.

options.text: Have the patient sit before standing, rise slowly, and walk with assistance
options.rationale: A fast heart rate with an orthostatic drop is fluid volume deficit. Restoring volume is one priority; preventing falls is the other. Slow position changes, dangling first and assistance protect the patient while volume is replaced.

options.text: Keep the patient on bed rest until the diarrhea stops
options.rationale: Absolute language Prolonged bed rest brings its own harm; the patient can move safely with support.

questions.takeaway: Deficit means orthostatic hypotension. Slow position changes and assist.
questions.strategy: Read the standing numbers, not the lying ones. The fall happens on the way up.

questions.stem: A patient with mild fluid volume deficit after a day of vomiting is now alert, swallowing well and has kept down sips of water for two hours. Which plan should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Encourage oral fluids and monitor intake, output and weight
options.rationale: Oral fluids are first when the patient is alert, able to swallow and tolerating them. IV isotonic crystalloid such as 0.9% sodium chloride or lactated Ringer's is used when oral intake is not possible or the deficit is severe. The response is tracked by intake and output and daily weight.

options.text: Start IV 0.9% sodium chloride at a rapid rate
options.rationale: Most dramatic finding IV isotonic fluid is for a patient who cannot take oral fluids or has a severe deficit.

options.text: Keep the patient on nothing by mouth for 24 hours
options.rationale: Near miss concept Prolonged NPO is itself a cause of fluid deficit.

options.text: Start IV 3% sodium chloride to restore volume quickly
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe hyponatremia, not routine volume replacement.

questions.takeaway: Alert, swallowing and tolerating: oral fluids first.
questions.strategy: Choose the least invasive route that meets the need.

questions.topic: early pulmonary edema in fluid volume excess
questions.stem: A patient with heart failure says, "I feel fine, just a little tired." The nurse hears new crackles in both lung bases that were not present this morning, and the weight is up 1.5 kg since yesterday. What should the nurse do first?
questions.objective: early pulmonary edema in fluid volume excess

options.text: Reassess at the next scheduled check, since the patient has no complaints of breathlessness
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic How the patient feels does not change the finding; crackles are the early sign.

options.text: Encourage coughing and deep breathing to clear the new crackles
options.rationale: Near miss concept Crackles from fluid do not clear with coughing; this treats it as secretions.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed, do a focused assessment and call the provider
options.rationale: New crackles in an overloaded patient are the early sign of pulmonary edema, and the 1.5 kg gain is about 1.5 L of retained fluid. Sitting the patient up eases breathing, the focused assessment (vital signs, oxygen saturation, neck veins, edema) gives the provider the full picture, and the report starts treatment such as a diuretic and fluid and sodium restriction.

options.text: Document the crackles and the weight change in the nursing notes
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Recording an early sign of pulmonary edema without reporting it lets it progress.

questions.takeaway: New crackles in overload are early pulmonary edema, even when the patient feels fine.
questions.strategy: The patient's comfort is not the finding. Act on the objective change.

questions.stem: A UAP reports that a patient with kidney failure weighs 2 kg more than yesterday, weighed on the same scale at the same time. Ankle edema looks unchanged. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: The gain is not significant, because the ankle edema is unchanged
options.rationale: Near miss concept Edema lags behind fluid gain; weight is the faster, more reliable sign.

options.text: About 2 L of fluid has been retained; assess and report the gain
options.rationale: A sudden change of 1 kg is about 1 L of fluid, so 2 kg overnight is about 2 L retained. Weighing is a stable routine task for the UAP; interpreting the trend and acting on it belongs to the nurse, so the nurse assesses lung sounds, vital signs and edema and reports.

options.text: The UAP should repeat the weight after breakfast to confirm it before anyone acts
options.rationale: Near miss concept Weighing after breakfast adds the meal and breaks the before breakfast routine.

options.text: The gain most likely reflects better appetite and new tissue gain
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Nobody gains 2 kg of tissue overnight.

questions.takeaway: 1 kg is about 1 L. The UAP weighs; you interpret.
questions.strategy: Trust weight over edema. Edema is a late, rough measure; weight is the honest number.

questions.stem: A patient who received IV morphine for postoperative pain is hard to arouse. The respiratory rate is 8 breaths per minute and the SaO2 is 89 percent. An arterial blood gas shows pH 7.28, PaCO2 55 mm Hg and HCO3 24 mEq/L. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Request an order for IV sodium bicarbonate to raise the pH
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question IV bicarbonate is a metabolic acidosis treatment, reserved for a pH below 7.2. This acidosis comes from retained carbon dioxide with a normal HCO3, so bicarbonate does not touch the cause.

options.text: Rouse the patient, coach deep breaths and apply oxygen
options.rationale: Respiratory acidosis means retained carbon dioxide is lowering the pH: here pH 7.28 is low, PaCO2 55 mm Hg is high, and HCO3 24 mEq/L is normal, so it is uncompensated. The test question for the first action is: what removes the cause fastest? The cause is slow, shallow breathing from the opioid. Rousing the patient and coaching deep breaths increases ventilation and blows off carbon dioxide, and oxygen treats the SaO2 of 89 percent. Respiratory acidosis care is oxygen, pulmonary hygiene and, if severe, mechanical ventilation. Bicarbonate treats a metabolic problem, a repeat gas has nothing to evaluate yet, and documenting is not an intervention.

options.text: Recheck the blood gas in two hours to see if the kidneys compensate
options.rationale: Correct but premature Repeat gases evaluate treatment, but no treatment has started. Kidney compensation takes 24 to 48 hours, far too slow for a patient breathing 8 times a minute.

options.text: Document the uncompensated respiratory acidosis and continue to observe
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting The interpretation is accurate, but writing it down does nothing for a patient who is hypoventilating and hypoxic right now.

questions.takeaway: Respiratory acidosis is a ventilation problem; the first fix is more breathing, not more base.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out bicarbonate is the normal HCO3 of 24 mEq/L, which shows the problem is carbon dioxide, not a missing base.

questions.topic: oxygenation read separately from acid base
questions.stem: A patient with pneumonia is short of breath. The arterial blood gas shows pH 7.41, PaCO2 39 mm Hg, HCO3 24 mEq/L, PaO2 61 mm Hg and SaO2 89 percent. How should the nurse interpret these results?
questions.objective: oxygenation read separately from acid base

options.text: A normal blood gas that needs no change in care
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data The pH, PaCO2 and HCO3 are normal, but the PaO2 is below 80 mm Hg and the SaO2 is below 95 percent. Oxygenation is a separate question, and it is failing.

options.text: A fully compensated acid base disorder with good oxygenation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Full compensation needs a normal pH with both PaCO2 and HCO3 abnormal. Here both are normal, and the oxygen values are low, not good.

options.text: A normal acid base balance with impaired oxygenation
options.rationale: A blood gas answers three questions: is the blood acidic or alkaline, is the patient ventilating, and is the patient oxygenating? pH, PaCO2 and HCO3 answer the first two. PaO2, the oxygen dissolved in arterial blood, and SaO2, the percent of hemoglobin carrying oxygen, answer the third and are read separately. Here pH 7.41, PaCO2 39 mm Hg and HCO3 24 mEq/L are all normal, so acid base balance is normal and there is nothing to compensate. But PaO2 61 mm Hg is below the 80 to 100 mm Hg range and SaO2 89 percent is below 95 to 100 percent, so oxygenation is impaired. That fits a short of breath patient with pneumonia.

options.text: An early respiratory alkalosis from fast breathing
options.rationale: Near miss concept Respiratory alkalosis needs a pH above 7.45 and a PaCO2 below 35 mm Hg. Both are normal here.

questions.takeaway: A normal pH, PaCO2 and HCO3 do not mean a normal blood gas. Check PaO2 and SaO2 as a separate question.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out full compensation is that PaCO2 and HCO3 are both normal. The detail that rules out "normal gas" is the PaO2 of 61 mm Hg.

questions.topic: acidosis with hyperkalemia: assess the heart first
questions.stem: A patient admitted after drinking methanol is lethargic with deep, rapid respirations and warm, flushed skin. The pH is 7.16, HCO3 11 mEq/L and potassium 6.3 mEq/L. The heart rate is 46 beats per minute and the blood pressure is 86/50 mm Hg. Which assessment should the nurse complete first?
questions.objective: acidosis with hyperkalemia: assess the heart first

options.text: Place the patient on a cardiac monitor and check the rhythm
options.rationale: Methanol causes metabolic acidosis by adding acid. Excess hydrogen ions enter cells and push potassium out, giving hyperkalemia, here 6.3 mEq/L. The test question for the first assessment is: which system can stop working in minutes? A heart rate of 46 beats per minute and a blood pressure of 86/50 mm Hg show the heart is already affected, and acidosis with hyperkalemia can progress from bradycardia to heart block and cardiac arrest. The cardiovascular system is assessed first, so the monitor goes on. The deep breathing is compensation, the lethargy is expected CNS depression, and reflex changes are expected muscle findings. All matter, but none outranks the rhythm.

options.text: Count the respiratory rate and depth for a full minute
options.rationale: Most dramatic finding The deep, rapid breathing is the most visible finding, but it is Kussmaul compensation for the metabolic acidosis. It is helping, and it is not what will cause arrest.

options.text: Complete a full neurologic check of the level of consciousness
options.rationale: Correct but premature Lethargy is expected CNS depression in acidosis and needs tracking, but it is not the finding that can kill within minutes.

options.text: Check deep tendon reflexes and muscle strength in all limbs
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Hyporeflexia and weakness are expected in acidosis, and finding them would not change the immediate priority.

questions.takeaway: In acidosis, assess the cardiovascular system first: hyperkalemia can trigger cardiac arrest.
questions.strategy: The detail that makes the heart the priority is the combination of potassium 6.3 mEq/L with a heart rate of 46 beats per minute. The breathing pattern is the dramatic distractor.

questions.stem: A patient has had a nasogastric tube to suction for four days after bowel surgery. The patient reports dizziness on standing, has muscle twitching and hyperactive reflexes, and the blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg. The arterial blood gas shows pH 7.52, PaCO2 43 mm Hg and HCO3 34 mEq/L. Serum potassium is 3.1 mEq/L. Select 2 actions the nurse should take, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters to monitor.

options.text: Give IV fluids and electrolyte replacement as ordered
Institute fall precautions before the patient gets up
Coach the patient to breathe slowly into a paper bag
Offer an antacid to settle the stomach
Request an order for IV sodium bicarbonate
Metabolic alkalosis
Respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis
Fully compensated respiratory acidosis
Serum potassium
Repeat pH and HCO3
PaO2
Blood glucose
Urine ketones

questions.takeaway: Condition: metabolic alkalosis means too much base or too little acid with a pH above 7.45. pH 7.52 is high, HCO3 34 mEq/L is high and moves the same way as the pH, and PaCO2 43 mm Hg is normal, so it is an uncompensated metabolic alkalosis. Suction removes stomach acid, an acid deficit. Respiratory alkalosis would need a low PaCO2. Metabolic acidosis would need a low pH. Compensated respiratory acidosis would need a normal pH. Actions: alkalosis care aims to prevent further loss of hydrogen, potassium, calcium and chloride, so IV fluids and electrolyte replacement replace what the suction removed. Dizziness on standing and a low blood pressure raise fall risk, so fall precautions come before the patient gets up. A paper bag treats anxious overbreathing, which this patient does not have. An antacid and sodium bicarbonate both add base and would worsen the alkalosis. Parameters: potassium is low because alkalosis shifts potassium into cells and suction removes more, so it must be tracked. A repeat pH and HCO3 show whether treatment is correcting the alkalosis. PaO2 is an oxygenation value, and glucose and ketones relate to diabetic acidosis, not this problem. Metabolic alkalosis from acid loss: replace fluid and electrolytes, prevent falls, and never add base.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out respiratory alkalosis is the normal PaCO2 of 43 mm Hg. The detail that makes fall precautions a key action is dizziness on standing with a blood pressure of 96/58 mm Hg.

questions.stem: A patient who just heard frightening news is breathing 34 times a minute and reports tingling in both hands. The SaO2 is 99 percent. The arterial blood gas shows pH 7.50, PaCO2 29 mm Hg and HCO3 24 mEq/L. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Request an order for IV fluids and potassium replacement
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Fluids and electrolyte replacement are metabolic alkalosis care. The HCO3 of 24 mEq/L is normal, so this is not a metabolic problem.

options.text: Prepare equipment for possible mechanical ventilation
options.rationale: Most dramatic finding Mechanical ventilation is for severe respiratory acidosis with failed breathing. This patient is breathing too much, with an SaO2 of 99 percent.

options.text: Request an order for IV calcium to stop the tingling
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question The tingling comes from nerve overexcitement in alkalosis. It resolves when the carbon dioxide rises again, so treating the symptom misses the cause.

options.text: Stay with the patient and coach slow breaths into a paper bag
options.rationale: Respiratory alkalosis means carbon dioxide is blown off faster than it is made, so the pH rises. Here pH 7.50 is high and PaCO2 29 mm Hg is low and moves the opposite way, while HCO3 24 mEq/L is normal, so it is uncompensated. The test question for treatment is: what is driving the fast breathing? Here it is fear. Calm reassurance and slow breathing into a paper bag let the patient rebreathe carbon dioxide, which lowers the pH back toward normal. Electrolyte replacement treats metabolic alkalosis, ventilation equipment treats failed breathing, and calcium treats a symptom instead of the cause.

questions.takeaway: Anxiety driven respiratory alkalosis is treated by calming the patient and slowing the breathing.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out a ventilation emergency is the SaO2 of 99 percent. The detail that rules out a metabolic cause is the normal HCO3.

questions.stem: A patient takes digoxin and a high dose loop diuretic for heart failure. The patient now reports nausea and has a new irregular pulse of 112 beats per minute. The pH is 7.50, HCO3 32 mEq/L and potassium 3.0 mEq/L. The morning digoxin dose is due. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the digoxin and offer an antacid for the nausea
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Treating nausea is reasonable, but an antacid adds base and worsens the alkalosis. Giving digoxin ignores signs of toxicity.

options.text: Hold the digoxin and report the findings to the provider
options.rationale: High dose loop diuretics cause metabolic alkalosis through acid loss. Here pH 7.50 and HCO3 32 mEq/L are both high. In alkalosis potassium shifts into cells, giving hypokalemia, here 3.0 mEq/L, and alkalosis raises the risk of digoxin toxicity. The test question is: is this patient showing signs that the drug is already harmful? Nausea and a new irregular, fast pulse say yes. Alkalosis care includes stopping or adjusting the causative treatment, so the nurse holds the digoxin and reports the full picture. An antacid adds base, giving digoxin first ignores the warning signs, and pushing the diuretic feeds the cause.

options.text: Give the digoxin and recheck the potassium in the morning
options.rationale: Correct but premature Rechecking the potassium is useful, but the irregular pulse and nausea are already present, so the drug should not be given first.

options.text: Give the diuretic first to reduce the heart failure symptoms
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question A high dose loop diuretic is one cause of this metabolic alkalosis. Giving more of it before the provider weighs in can deepen the alkalosis and the potassium loss.

questions.takeaway: Alkalosis with low potassium raises digoxin toxicity risk; hold the dose and report when toxicity signs appear.
questions.strategy: The detail that makes holding the dose correct is the new irregular pulse with nausea in a patient whose potassium is 3.0 mEq/L.

questions.topic: older adult acid base history and assessment
questions.stem: An older adult with chronic kidney disease and heart failure is admitted with new confusion. The patient takes a diuretic and a daily aspirin and often uses antacids. An acid base imbalance is suspected. Select all of the actions that are appropriate for the nurse's history and assessment.
questions.objective: older adult acid base history and assessment

options.text: Ask about every prescribed and over the counter drug the patient uses
options.rationale: Older adults are at greater risk because chronic kidney, lung and heart disease are common, and because many take drugs that disrupt acid base balance, such as diuretics, aspirin and antacids. For each option ask: does it uncover a cause or show how the patient is coping? Asking about all prescribed and over the counter drugs finds the drug causes, and this patient takes all three. Recent fluid intake and urination changes point to fluid loss and kidney function. Comparing mental status with the patient's own baseline separates a new change from long standing status. Whether the patient can complete a sentence shows the work of breathing and how well the lungs can compensate. Accepting new confusion as aging misses the problem, and skipping over the counter drugs misses two likely causes.

options.text: Ask about recent fluid intake and any change in urination
options.rationale: Older adults are at greater risk because chronic kidney, lung and heart disease are common, and because many take drugs that disrupt acid base balance, such as diuretics, aspirin and antacids. For each option ask: does it uncover a cause or show how the patient is coping? Asking about all prescribed and over the counter drugs finds the drug causes, and this patient takes all three. Recent fluid intake and urination changes point to fluid loss and kidney function. Comparing mental status with the patient's own baseline separates a new change from long standing status. Whether the patient can complete a sentence shows the work of breathing and how well the lungs can compensate. Accepting new confusion as aging misses the problem, and skipping over the counter drugs misses two likely causes.

options.text: Compare the current mental status with the patient's own baseline
options.rationale: Older adults are at greater risk because chronic kidney, lung and heart disease are common, and because many take drugs that disrupt acid base balance, such as diuretics, aspirin and antacids. For each option ask: does it uncover a cause or show how the patient is coping? Asking about all prescribed and over the counter drugs finds the drug causes, and this patient takes all three. Recent fluid intake and urination changes point to fluid loss and kidney function. Comparing mental status with the patient's own baseline separates a new change from long standing status. Whether the patient can complete a sentence shows the work of breathing and how well the lungs can compensate. Accepting new confusion as aging misses the problem, and skipping over the counter drugs misses two likely causes.

options.text: Note whether the patient can complete a sentence without stopping to breathe
options.rationale: Older adults are at greater risk because chronic kidney, lung and heart disease are common, and because many take drugs that disrupt acid base balance, such as diuretics, aspirin and antacids. For each option ask: does it uncover a cause or show how the patient is coping? Asking about all prescribed and over the counter drugs finds the drug causes, and this patient takes all three. Recent fluid intake and urination changes point to fluid loss and kidney function. Comparing mental status with the patient's own baseline separates a new change from long standing status. Whether the patient can complete a sentence shows the work of breathing and how well the lungs can compensate. Accepting new confusion as aging misses the problem, and skipping over the counter drugs misses two likely causes.

options.text: Accept the confusion as an expected change of normal aging
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem The confusion is new. A change from baseline is a warning sign in an older adult and can be an early sign of acid base imbalance.

options.text: Skip questions about aspirin and antacids because they are over the counter
options.rationale: Absolute language Aspirin and antacids are both drugs that can disrupt acid base balance, and older adults often take them. Over the counter does not mean harmless.

questions.takeaway: In older adults, ask about every drug including over the counter ones and judge mental status against the patient's own baseline.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out "normal aging" is the word "new" in front of confusion.

questions.stem: A patient with type 1 diabetes is admitted with diabetic ketoacidosis. The pH is 7.26, HCO3 15 mEq/L and the mucous membranes are dry. The admission orders include an IV insulin infusion, IV fluid, cardiac monitoring and IV sodium bicarbonate. Which order should the nurse clarify with the provider?

options.text: The IV insulin infusion
options.rationale: Near miss concept Insulin stops the overproduction of ketoacids in diabetic ketoacidosis. It treats the underlying cause, so it is expected.

options.text: The IV fluid
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hydration is a core treatment for metabolic acidosis, and the dry mucous membranes show this patient needs it.

options.text: The IV sodium bicarbonate
options.rationale: Metabolic acidosis care treats the underlying problem: hydration, insulin if the cause is diabetic ketoacidosis, and antidiarrheal agents if the cause is diarrhea. IV bicarbonate is reserved for a pH below 7.2. The test question for each order is: does it fit this cause and this severity? Insulin and fluid fit the cause. Cardiac monitoring fits the hyperkalemia risk that acidosis carries. The pH here is 7.26, above the 7.2 threshold, so the bicarbonate is the order to clarify.

options.text: The cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Near miss concept Acidosis can cause hyperkalemia and rhythm changes, so watching the heart is a priority, not an excess.

questions.takeaway: Treat the cause of metabolic acidosis; IV bicarbonate is for a pH below 7.2.
questions.strategy: The detail that makes bicarbonate the outlier is the pH of 7.26, which is acidotic but above 7.2.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence: A patient with three broken ribs takes shallow breaths to avoid pain. After two days, the arterial blood gas shows pH 7.31, PaCO2 56 mm Hg and HCO3 30 mEq/L. The nurse interprets this as [[1]] [[2]]. The raised HCO3 shows that the [[3]]. The nursing priority is to [[4]].

options.text: partially compensated
uncompensated
fully compensated
mixed
respiratory acidosis
metabolic acidosis
metabolic alkalosis
respiratory alkalosis
kidneys are retaining bicarbonate
lungs are blowing off carbon dioxide
patient is losing stomach acid
buffers have stopped working
position upright and coach deep breathing
request IV sodium bicarbonate
have the patient breathe into a paper bag
restrict fluids to limit lung congestion

questions.takeaway: [2] respiratory acidosis: pH 7.31 is low and PaCO2 56 mm Hg is high, moving opposite to the pH, so carbon dioxide is the cause. Shallow breathing from rib pain is inadequate chest expansion, a cause of carbon dioxide retention. Metabolic acidosis would need a low HCO3, and both alkaloses need a high pH. [1] partially compensated: the pH is still abnormal, and both PaCO2 and HCO3 are abnormal. Uncompensated would need a normal HCO3. Fully compensated would need a pH back in 7.35 to 7.45. Mixed would mean two primary problems pushing the pH, but the high HCO3 is pulling the pH toward normal, which is compensation. [3] kidneys are retaining bicarbonate: kidneys correct a respiratory problem, and after two days they have had time to start. The lungs are the failing system, nothing suggests stomach losses, and the buffers are not the system that changes HCO3 over days. [4] position upright and coach deep breathing: respiratory acidosis care is pulmonary hygiene, positioning and breathing techniques, which expand the chest and blow off carbon dioxide. Bicarbonate is for metabolic acidosis with a pH below 7.2, a paper bag would retain more carbon dioxide, and restricting fluid does nothing for ventilation. A high PaCO2 with a high HCO3 and a still low pH is a respiratory acidosis the kidneys are partly correcting; fix the breathing.
questions.strategy: The detail that sets the compensation status is "after two days," long enough for the kidneys to begin raising HCO3 but not to bring the pH back to normal.

questions.stem: An 87 year old patient takes a diuretic, a daily laxative and a blood pressure medicine. In the past 24 hours the patient drank about 600 mL and passed 420 mL of dark amber urine. The patient is alert but slower to answer than usual. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Send a urine specimen for culture to check for infection
options.rationale: Correct but premature Dark urine can come with infection, but here the intake is low and the output is concentrated. Fluid status is the first problem to assess and report.

options.text: Document the output as expected for the patient's age
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Aging does reduce the kidney's concentrating ability, but an output under 500 mL a day is never expected. It signals a deficit.

options.text: Assess fluid status and report the low output and slowed answers
options.rationale: Older adults have less body water, a weaker thirst reflex and kidneys that filter and concentrate less well. Diuretics, laxatives and blood pressure drugs all add to the risk of a deficit. A daily urine output under 500 mL is a concerning sign of dehydration, and concentrated dark urine fits. In an older adult, a change in mental status, even subtle slowing, may be the first sign of a fluid or electrolyte imbalance. The test question: is there a new finding that points to a body short on fluid? Yes, three of them together, so the nurse assesses fluid status (orthostatic vital signs, mucous membranes, sternal turgor, labs) and reports to the provider.

options.text: Hold the evening laxative and recheck the output tomorrow
options.rationale: Correct but premature The laxative adds risk, but holding one dose and waiting a day leaves the deficit and the mental change unaddressed.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult, low output plus a subtle mental change is a fluid problem until proven otherwise.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out documenting it as age related is the 420 mL output, which is below the 500 mL a day concern line. The subtle slowing confirms it.

questions.stem: An 89 year old patient on a medical unit has had a fever of 38.9 C for two days and has drunk very little. The patient was agitated this morning and is now drowsy, with muscle twitching. Serum sodium is 156 mEq/L. Skin over the sternum stays tented and the mucous membranes are dry. Select 2 actions the nurse should take, the 1 condition the findings point to, and 2 parameters to monitor.

options.text: Give the ordered hypotonic IV fluid at the prescribed gradual rate
Offer water on a set schedule once swallowing is safe
Give 3 percent sodium chloride to restore volume quickly
Restrict oral fluids to prevent cerebral edema
Give furosemide to remove the excess sodium
Hypernatremia from water loss
Hyponatremia from excess water
Fluid overload
Hypercalcemia from dehydration
Serum sodium trend, checking that it falls gradually
Level of consciousness and neurologic checks
Chvostek and Trousseau signs
Bowel sounds in all four quadrants

questions.takeaway: Condition: Hypernatremia is a sodium above 145 mEq/L. Water leaves the cells and they shrink, so the brain shows agitation and confusion that progress to lethargy, and muscles twitch and then weaken. Fever and poor intake cause it by losing water, and the tented sternal skin and dry mucosa confirm a deficit. Hyponatremia needs a sodium below 135, and fluid overload would show edema, crackles and a bounding pulse, not dry tissue. Hypercalcemia can follow dehydration, but no calcium value is given and twitching is not its pattern. Actions: The goal is to replace free water and lower sodium gradually. Hypotonic fluid puts water back into the shrunken cells, and the prescribed slow rate prevents cerebral edema from too fast a shift. Older adults have a weak thirst reflex, so water is offered on a schedule rather than when asked for, once the drowsy patient can swallow safely. 3 percent saline is hypertonic and would raise sodium. Restricting fluid worsens a water deficit. Furosemide is used only when the cause is kidney related, which this is not. Parameters: The sodium trend shows whether treatment is working and whether it is falling too fast. Neurologic checks show both improvement and the warning signs of cerebral edema. Chvostek and Trousseau signs test for low calcium, and bowel sounds are not the key measure here. Hypernatremia from water loss: replace free water slowly, offer water on a schedule, and watch sodium and the brain.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out fluid overload is the dry mucosa and tented sternal skin. The detail that rules out a fast fix is the brain: sodium must fall gradually.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure takes furosemide twice daily. The potassium is 3.1 mEq/L, and bowel sounds are hypoactive. Distended neck veins and leg edema persist, so the provider plans to add a second diuretic. Which choice fits this patient best?

options.text: Spironolactone, because it removes fluid while saving potassium
options.rationale: Hypokalemia is a potassium below 3.5 mEq/L, and loop and thiazide diuretics are common causes because they make the kidneys excrete potassium. The care plan for hypokalemia includes avoiding loop and thiazide diuretics and considering a potassium sparing diuretic. The test question for each option: does it remove fluid without wasting more potassium? Spironolactone is potassium sparing, so it treats the persistent edema while helping the potassium recover. A thiazide or more furosemide would deepen the deficit, and refusing all diuretics leaves the edema untreated.

options.text: Hydrochlorothiazide, because it removes fluid with once daily dosing
options.rationale: Near miss concept A thiazide removes fluid but also wastes potassium, like furosemide. Adding it would push the low potassium lower.

options.text: A higher furosemide dose, because the edema is the main problem
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question More furosemide treats the edema but costs more potassium. The low potassium and cramps rule it out.

options.text: No added diuretic, because every diuretic lowers potassium further
options.rationale: Absolute language Not every diuretic lowers potassium. Potassium sparing diuretics remove fluid while holding potassium.

questions.takeaway: Low potassium on a loop diuretic: the add on should be potassium sparing, such as spironolactone.
questions.strategy: The planted detail is the potassium of 3.1 with hypoactive bowel sounds. It turns a fluid question into a potassium question.

questions.stem: A patient with a very high blood glucose is started on a rapid IV insulin infusion. No other IV fluid is running. The potassium was 4.6 mEq/L before the infusion and is 3.2 mEq/L three hours later. The patient has not vomited, has no diarrhea and is not on a diuretic. Which explanation fits?

options.text: The kidneys are excreting potassium faster than normal
options.rationale: Near miss concept Kidney loss is a common cause of low potassium, but nothing in the stem suggests extra excretion, such as a diuretic. The timing ties the drop to the insulin.

options.text: The IV fluid has diluted the potassium in the blood
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dilution is a real cause of low potassium, but the insulin runs alone with no other IV fluid, so there is not enough volume to dilute the blood.

options.text: Aldosterone release has increased potassium loss in urine
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Aldosterone does increase potassium excretion, but nothing here would trigger it, and it would not explain a drop timed to the insulin.

options.text: Insulin has moved potassium from the blood into the cells
options.rationale: Hypokalemia has three kinds of cause: actual loss from the body, dilution by excess water, and a shift of potassium into the cells. The test question: did potassium leave the body, get watered down, or move inside the cells? The stem rules out loss through vomiting, diarrhea and diuretics. It rules out dilution because no other IV fluid runs. What remains is the rapid insulin infusion, which drives potassium from the blood into the cells along with glucose. The total body potassium has not changed, but the serum level has dropped, and the heart responds to the serum level.

questions.takeaway: Rapid insulin shifts potassium into the cells and can cause hypokalemia without any loss from the body.
questions.strategy: The planted details are no vomiting, diarrhea or diuretic, which rule out loss, and no other IV fluid, which rules out dilution. Only the shift is left.

questions.stem: A patient with lung cancer has a serum calcium of 12.6 mg/dL, hypoactive bowel sounds, decreased deep tendon reflexes and lethargy. The patient takes hydrochlorothiazide at home and has been on bed rest for a week. Orders include IV 0.9 percent sodium chloride and calcitonin. Which additional action should the nurse plan?

options.text: Give a calcium supplement with meals to protect the bones
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Calcium supplements protect bone in low calcium. In hypercalcemia every calcium source is stopped, so this adds to the problem.

options.text: Ask the provider about stopping the hydrochlorothiazide
options.rationale: Hypercalcemia is a serum calcium above 10.5 mg/dL. High calcium makes nerves, muscles and the gut less excitable, which explains the slow bowel, weak reflexes and lethargy. Its causes include malignancy, thiazide diuretics, immobility, dehydration and excess calcium or vitamin D. The test question for each option: does it remove a cause or calcium source? Thiazide diuretics make the kidneys hold calcium, so stopping hydrochlorothiazide is part of the plan. That needs a provider order, so the nurse asks. The saline and calcitonin already ordered increase excretion and lower the level; bisphosphonates and a loop diuretic may also be used.

options.text: Keep the patient on strict bed rest to prevent falls
options.rationale: Correct but premature Weak reflexes and lethargy do raise fall risk, but immobility is itself a cause of high calcium. Safe, assisted movement fits better than strict bed rest.

options.text: Check Chvostek and Trousseau signs every 4 hours
options.rationale: Near miss concept Chvostek and Trousseau signs detect low calcium. Hypercalcemia has no classic bedside sign, so these checks do not track this problem.

questions.takeaway: In hypercalcemia, look for and remove causes: calcium sources, thiazides and immobility.
questions.strategy: The planted details are the home thiazide and the week of bed rest. Both are causes of high calcium, which rules out bed rest and points to the thiazide.

questions.stem: A patient with alcohol use disorder has eaten poorly for weeks and takes a loop diuretic. The magnesium is 1.1 mEq/L. Select all of the findings the nurse should expect.

options.text: Hyperactive deep tendon reflexes
options.rationale: Hypomagnesemia is a magnesium below 1.3 mEq/L. Poor intake, alcoholism and loop or thiazide diuretics are common causes, and this patient has all three. Low magnesium raises nerve and muscle excitability, so the test question for each finding is: does it show an overactive nerve or muscle? Hyperactive reflexes, cramps and tingling do. The heart becomes irritable, giving a prolonged QT and ectopic (extra) beats. The gut is the exception that trips students: low magnesium slows motility, causing nausea, constipation and possible ileus. Drowsiness, absent reflexes, bradycardia and hypotension are the slowed picture of high magnesium.

options.text: A prolonged QT interval with extra beats
options.rationale: Hypomagnesemia is a magnesium below 1.3 mEq/L. Poor intake, alcoholism and loop or thiazide diuretics are common causes, and this patient has all three. Low magnesium raises nerve and muscle excitability, so the test question for each finding is: does it show an overactive nerve or muscle? Hyperactive reflexes, cramps and tingling do. The heart becomes irritable, giving a prolonged QT and ectopic (extra) beats. The gut is the exception that trips students: low magnesium slows motility, causing nausea, constipation and possible ileus. Drowsiness, absent reflexes, bradycardia and hypotension are the slowed picture of high magnesium.

options.text: Muscle cramps and tingling
options.rationale: Hypomagnesemia is a magnesium below 1.3 mEq/L. Poor intake, alcoholism and loop or thiazide diuretics are common causes, and this patient has all three. Low magnesium raises nerve and muscle excitability, so the test question for each finding is: does it show an overactive nerve or muscle? Hyperactive reflexes, cramps and tingling do. The heart becomes irritable, giving a prolonged QT and ectopic (extra) beats. The gut is the exception that trips students: low magnesium slows motility, causing nausea, constipation and possible ileus. Drowsiness, absent reflexes, bradycardia and hypotension are the slowed picture of high magnesium.

options.text: Drowsiness and absent reflexes
options.rationale: Near miss concept Drowsiness and absent reflexes come from high magnesium, which slows nerves. Low magnesium does the opposite.

options.text: Constipation with slowed bowel sounds
options.rationale: Hypomagnesemia is a magnesium below 1.3 mEq/L. Poor intake, alcoholism and loop or thiazide diuretics are common causes, and this patient has all three. Low magnesium raises nerve and muscle excitability, so the test question for each finding is: does it show an overactive nerve or muscle? Hyperactive reflexes, cramps and tingling do. The heart becomes irritable, giving a prolonged QT and ectopic (extra) beats. The gut is the exception that trips students: low magnesium slows motility, causing nausea, constipation and possible ileus. Drowsiness, absent reflexes, bradycardia and hypotension are the slowed picture of high magnesium.

options.text: Bradycardia and low blood pressure
options.rationale: Near miss concept Bradycardia and hypotension are signs of high magnesium. Low magnesium causes dysrhythmias and extra beats instead.

questions.takeaway: Low magnesium: brisk reflexes, cramps, irritable heart, but a slow gut.
questions.strategy: Sort by direction: low magnesium speeds nerves and the heart. The trap is constipation, which looks like a slowed finding but belongs to low magnesium.

questions.stem: A patient with a potassium of 2.5 mEq/L has flaccid weakness in the arms and legs. Over the last hour, breathing has become shallow and the oxygen saturation has fallen from 96 to 89 percent. IV potassium is infusing on a pump at the ordered rate. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Increase the potassium infusion rate to correct the level faster
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope The rate is set by the order, and faster potassium can cause deadly dysrhythmias. The safe rate stays slow.

options.text: Implement fall precautions and keep the bed in low position
options.rationale: Correct but premature Fall precautions are part of hypokalemia care, but a falling oxygen saturation is an airway and breathing problem that comes first.

options.text: Assess breathing, raise the head of the bed and call for help
options.rationale: Severe hypokalemia weakens all skeletal muscle, including the muscles of breathing, so shallow breathing and a falling oxygen saturation mean respiratory weakness. Monitoring oxygen saturation is part of hypokalemia care for this reason. The test question is ABC priority: is airway or breathing at risk right now? Yes: the saturation has dropped from 96 to 89 percent in an hour. The nurse assesses breathing, positions the patient upright to ease breathing and calls for help. The potassium keeps running at the safe ordered rate; raising it can trigger dysrhythmias. Fall precautions and a repeat level matter, but neither protects breathing.

options.text: Recheck the potassium level before taking any further action
options.rationale: Correct but premature A new level will help guide treatment, but waiting for it delays care for a patient whose breathing is failing now.

questions.takeaway: Severe low potassium can weaken the breathing muscles; a falling saturation outranks every other hypokalemia task.
questions.strategy: The planted detail is the saturation drop from 96 to 89 percent. It turns a muscle weakness question into a breathing question.

questions.stem: Select all of the findings that should raise concern for elder mistreatment.

options.text: A caregiver who answers all questions and will not leave the room
options.rationale: Injuries of different ages, a caregiver who controls the interview, neglect findings in someone who has help, and financial exploitation. Mistreatment includes neglect and financial abuse, not only physical injury. Nurses are mandated reporters and the threshold is reasonable suspicion, so the next step is interviewing her alone and reporting.

options.text: A caregiver who asks detailed questions about the medication schedule
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Engagement and competence, which is protective.

options.text: Poor hygiene and untreated pressure injuries in a patient with a caregiver
options.rationale: Injuries of different ages, a caregiver who controls the interview, neglect findings in someone who has help, and financial exploitation. Mistreatment includes neglect and financial abuse, not only physical injury. Nurses are mandated reporters and the threshold is reasonable suspicion, so the next step is interviewing her alone and reporting.

options.text: Unexplained depletion of the patient's financial resources
options.rationale: Injuries of different ages, a caregiver who controls the interview, neglect findings in someone who has help, and financial exploitation. Mistreatment includes neglect and financial abuse, not only physical injury. Nurses are mandated reporters and the threshold is reasonable suspicion, so the next step is interviewing her alone and reporting.

options.text: A patient who declines a bath because she is tired
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data A reasonable refusal with a reason given.

options.text: Bruises at several different stages of healing
options.rationale: Injuries of different ages, a caregiver who controls the interview, neglect findings in someone who has help, and financial exploitation. Mistreatment includes neglect and financial abuse, not only physical injury. Nurses are mandated reporters and the threshold is reasonable suspicion, so the next step is interviewing her alone and reporting.

questions.takeaway: Interview the patient alone. She cannot answer honestly with him in the room.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options describe ordinary behavior, one by the patient and one by an engaged caregiver.

questions.stem: Select all of the findings that are expected changes of aging rather than disease.

options.text: High frequency hearing loss
options.rationale: Expected changes come on over years and are symmetric and gradual. The two wrong options are both acute or progressive and both are findings that get dismissed as aging more often than almost anything else, which is how infection and malnutrition go unnoticed. Sudden is never normal aging.

options.text: Reduced skin elasticity, making turgor an unreliable hydration sign
options.rationale: Expected changes come on over years and are symmetric and gradual. The two wrong options are both acute or progressive and both are findings that get dismissed as aging more often than almost anything else, which is how infection and malnutrition go unnoticed. Sudden is never normal aging.

options.text: Presbyopia requiring reading glasses
options.rationale: Expected changes come on over years and are symmetric and gradual. The two wrong options are both acute or progressive and both are findings that get dismissed as aging more often than almost anything else, which is how infection and malnutrition go unnoticed. Sudden is never normal aging.

options.text: Confusion developing over two days
options.rationale: Near miss concept Acute confusion is delirium and has a cause worth finding.

options.text: Unintentional weight loss of 8 percent in three months
options.rationale: Near miss concept A measurable involuntary loss is always investigated.

options.text: A slower gait with a wider stance
options.rationale: Expected changes come on over years and are symmetric and gradual. The two wrong options are both acute or progressive and both are findings that get dismissed as aging more often than almost anything else, which is how infection and malnutrition go unnoticed. Sudden is never normal aging.

questions.takeaway: Gradual over years is aging. Days or a measurable loss is disease.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options have a time frame attached, which is the tell.

questions.stem: Select all of the measures that reduce delirium risk in a hospitalized older adult.

options.text: Insert a urinary catheter to reduce the need to get up
options.rationale: Near miss concept An infection risk and an immobilizer, and a known delirium contributor.

options.text: Ensure glasses and hearing aids are in place and working
options.rationale: Delirium prevention is sensory input, sleep, movement, hydration and fewer culprit drugs. Restraints make delirium worse rather than safer, and patients injure themselves trying to escape them. A catheter adds an infection risk and removes a reason to get up, and both appear repeatedly as practices that worsen the outcome they were meant to protect.

options.text: Use physical restraints at night to prevent wandering
options.rationale: Near miss concept Worsens delirium and causes escape injuries.

options.text: Mobilize early and daily
options.rationale: Delirium prevention is sensory input, sleep, movement, hydration and fewer culprit drugs. Restraints make delirium worse rather than safer, and patients injure themselves trying to escape them. A catheter adds an infection risk and removes a reason to get up, and both appear repeatedly as practices that worsen the outcome they were meant to protect.

options.text: Protect sleep by clustering care and reducing night time noise and light
options.rationale: Delirium prevention is sensory input, sleep, movement, hydration and fewer culprit drugs. Restraints make delirium worse rather than safer, and patients injure themselves trying to escape them. A catheter adds an infection risk and removes a reason to get up, and both appear repeatedly as practices that worsen the outcome they were meant to protect.

options.text: Review and minimize medications with anticholinergic or sedative effects
options.rationale: Delirium prevention is sensory input, sleep, movement, hydration and fewer culprit drugs. Restraints make delirium worse rather than safer, and patients injure themselves trying to escape them. A catheter adds an infection risk and removes a reason to get up, and both appear repeatedly as practices that worsen the outcome they were meant to protect.

questions.takeaway: Restraints and catheters both make delirium worse. They are the two interventions that feel protective.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options are convenience measures that are independent risk factors for delirium.

questions.stem: Select all of the nursing actions that reflect the Age Friendly 4 Ms framework.

options.text: Keeping her in bed to prevent falls during the admission
options.rationale: Near miss concept Trades mobility for one risk and causes several others.

options.text: Screening for delirium, dementia and depression
options.rationale: What Matters, Medication, Mentation, Mobility, and the first one orders the other three. Each correct option is one of the four. Setting goals from the diagnosis rather than from the patient inverts the framework, and immobilizing her to prevent falls defeats the mobility element entirely.

options.text: Reviewing the medication list for drugs that impair cognition or mobility
options.rationale: What Matters, Medication, Mentation, Mobility, and the first one orders the other three. Each correct option is one of the four. Setting goals from the diagnosis rather than from the patient inverts the framework, and immobilizing her to prevent falls defeats the mobility element entirely.

options.text: Getting the patient up and walking on the first day
options.rationale: What Matters, Medication, Mentation, Mobility, and the first one orders the other three. Each correct option is one of the four. Setting goals from the diagnosis rather than from the patient inverts the framework, and immobilizing her to prevent falls defeats the mobility element entirely.

options.text: Asking the patient what matters most to her for this admission
options.rationale: What Matters, Medication, Mentation, Mobility, and the first one orders the other three. Each correct option is one of the four. Setting goals from the diagnosis rather than from the patient inverts the framework, and immobilizing her to prevent falls defeats the mobility element entirely.

options.text: Deciding the goals of care based on her diagnosis
options.rationale: Near miss concept The diagnosis informs the plan; what matters to her sets the goal.

questions.takeaway: What Matters is not one of four equal items. It is the one that aims the other three.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options replace the patient's priorities or remove her function.

questions.stem: Classify each finding by the condition it most suggests.

rows.text: Answers "I do not know" to most questions and makes little effort
Gradual decline over two years with preserved alertness
Onset over several weeks with impaired concentration and a flat affect
Onset over hours with a fluctuating course and inattention

questions.takeaway: Onset and course separate these three. Delirium is acute, fluctuating and inattentive, and it is potentially reversible. Dementia is gradual and progressive with alertness preserved until late. Depression develops over weeks, impairs concentration, and produces the patient who stops trying rather than the one who guesses wrong. Ask how fast it came on. That one question sorts all three.
questions.strategy: A patient who gives up on the question looks demented and is more often depressed. That is the discrimination the item is built on.

questions.stem: A nurse is using the 4 Ms framework to plan care for an 84 year old admitted with a hip fracture. Which element should direct the rest of the plan?

options.text: Medication
options.rationale: Near miss concept An element, and it serves the goal rather than setting it.

options.text: What Matters
options.rationale: What Matters comes first and the other three serve it. Medication, mentation and mobility are where the nursing work happens, and what the patient is actually trying to get back to is what decides how that work is aimed. A plan built on mobility alone can be technically excellent and still miss the point of her admission.

options.text: Mentation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Where delirium, dementia and depression are screened.

options.text: Mobility
options.rationale: Near miss concept The obvious choice after a hip fracture, and still a means rather than the aim.

questions.takeaway: What Matters is not one of four equal items. It is the one that orders the other three.
questions.strategy: When a framework has a first element by design, the item is usually asking whether you know the order rather than the list.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the medication list of an 82 year old and notes diphenhydramine taken nightly for sleep. Why is this a concern?

options.text: It is habit forming and causes physical dependence in older adults
options.rationale: Near miss concept Tolerance develops; physical dependence is not the Beers concern.

options.text: It interacts dangerously with most antihypertensive medications
options.rationale: Near miss concept Not the reason it is flagged; the anticholinergic burden is.

options.text: It is on the Beers Criteria because of its anticholinergic effects
options.rationale: Near miss concept True of the sedation and not why the drug is on the list.

options.text: It loses its effectiveness after about two weeks of nightly use
options.rationale: The Beers Criteria flags drugs whose risk outweighs their benefit in older adults. Anticholinergics like diphenhydramine cause exactly the problems that get mistaken for aging: confusion, falls, urinary retention, constipation and oversedation. The patient bought it over the counter, so it may not be on any list the team sees.

questions.takeaway: Beers drugs cause the symptoms people blame on getting old.
questions.strategy: An over the counter sleep aid in an older adult is a medication problem wearing a disguise.

questions.stem: A nurse uses the SPICES tool on admission for an 80 year old. Which set of findings does the tool screen for?

options.text: Sleep, eating problems, incontinence, confusion, falls and skin breakdown
options.rationale: SPICES screens six conditions that are common in older adults and that feed each other: each element is both a finding and a risk factor for the others. Poor sleep worsens confusion, confusion raises fall risk, immobility after a fall breaks down skin. Finding one tells you to look for the rest.

options.text: Strength, pain, independence, cognition, elimination and home safety
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fits the letters and is not the tool.

options.text: Sleep, pain, fluid intake, cognition, exercise and social isolation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fits the letters. Six things a nurse would ask about, and not this tool.

options.text: Sensory loss, pressure injury, immobility, continence and caregiver support
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reads like geriatrics and is made up.

questions.takeaway: Six items that cause each other. Find one, screen for all six.
questions.strategy: The distractors here are plausible nursing words arranged into the same acronym. Know the actual expansion.

questions.stem: A nurse performs the Timed Up and Go with an older adult: stand from the chair, walk 10 feet, turn, return and sit. It takes 19 seconds. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: Normal, since the patient completed the task without any assistance
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome Completion is not the measure. The clock is.

options.text: Elevated fall risk needing a prevention plan and a gait evaluation
options.rationale: Most healthy older adults finish in about 10 seconds. Nineteen is well past that, and the value of the test is that it gives you a number instead of an impression. Completing the task is not the outcome; how long it took is.

options.text: Invalid, because the test requires the patient's usual assistive device
options.rationale: Near miss concept A device may be used if the patient normally uses one. Its absence does not void the test.

options.text: Normal performance for an adult older than 75 years of age
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Age does not buy extra seconds; the benchmark is the same.

questions.takeaway: Around 10 seconds is the benchmark. Slower means higher risk, not just slower.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options grade this as a pass because the patient finished.

questions.stem: A 76 year old and a 32 year old both receive the same standard adult dose of a medication cleared by the liver and kidneys. On day three the older patient shows signs of toxicity. What best explains this?

options.text: Increased receptor sensitivity produces a stronger first dose effect
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sensitivity does change; a first dose effect would have appeared on day one.

options.text: Slower liver metabolism and kidney clearance let the drug accumulate
options.rationale: Aging alters absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion. The clinically important change is slower clearance, which means a standard dose behaves like a larger one over several days. The toxicity on day three rather than day one is the clue that this is accumulation.

options.text: The older patient most likely received an incorrect dose by mistake
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Blames an error instead of explaining the physiology.

options.text: Older adults absorb medications more rapidly from the stomach and bowel
options.rationale: Near miss concept The direction is backwards. Aging slows gastric emptying and reduces splanchnic blood flow, so absorption is delayed rather than accelerated.

questions.takeaway: Same drug, same dose, different response, and the difference shows up over days.
questions.strategy: The timing in the stem tells you the mechanism. Day three points at accumulation, not at a first dose effect.

questions.stem: A nurse is completing a medication reconciliation for a 77 year old. Select all of the items that should be counted when assessing for polypharmacy.

options.text: An over the counter antihistamine taken most nights for sleep
options.rationale: Polypharmacy is five or more medications taken concurrently, and the count includes over the counter products and supplements. Counting only the prescriptions is the error, and the antihistamine is exactly the kind of agent that produces falls, confusion, urinary retention and oversedation in an older adult.

options.text: Four prescription medications from two different providers
options.rationale: Polypharmacy is five or more medications taken concurrently, and the count includes over the counter products and supplements. Counting only the prescriptions is the error, and the antihistamine is exactly the kind of agent that produces falls, confusion, urinary retention and oversedation in an older adult.

options.text: A topical analgesic cream used as needed
options.rationale: Polypharmacy is five or more medications taken concurrently, and the count includes over the counter products and supplements. Counting only the prescriptions is the error, and the antihistamine is exactly the kind of agent that produces falls, confusion, urinary retention and oversedation in an older adult.

options.text: A prescription inhaler used twice daily
options.rationale: Polypharmacy is five or more medications taken concurrently, and the count includes over the counter products and supplements. Counting only the prescriptions is the error, and the antihistamine is exactly the kind of agent that produces falls, confusion, urinary retention and oversedation in an older adult.

options.text: A daily multivitamin
options.rationale: Polypharmacy is five or more medications taken concurrently, and the count includes over the counter products and supplements. Counting only the prescriptions is the error, and the antihistamine is exactly the kind of agent that produces falls, confusion, urinary retention and oversedation in an older adult.

options.text: An herbal supplement for joint pain
options.rationale: Polypharmacy is five or more medications taken concurrently, and the count includes over the counter products and supplements. Counting only the prescriptions is the error, and the antihistamine is exactly the kind of agent that produces falls, confusion, urinary retention and oversedation in an older adult.

questions.takeaway: Count everything the patient takes, not everything a provider prescribed.
questions.strategy: When every option looks includable, check whether the item is testing an inclusive definition.

questions.stem: An older adult scores high on the Geriatric Depression Scale and also performs poorly on a cognitive screen. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: Depression can impair memory, so cognition may improve with treatment
options.rationale: Depression impairs concentration, and a patient who cannot concentrate scores badly on a memory test. That is pseudodementia, and it is reversible in a way dementia is not. Treating the depression and retesting is how you tell them apart, which is why labeling this dementia now would be a costly mistake.

options.text: The cognitive screen is invalid whenever depression is also present
options.rationale: Near miss concept Not invalid, just confounded, which is why you retest after treatment.

options.text: Two abnormal screening results together confirm a dementia diagnosis
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Screens are not diagnostic, and depression explains both results.

options.text: Depression in older adults does not affect results of cognitive testing
options.rationale: Near miss concept It affects it substantially, which is the whole point of the pairing.

questions.takeaway: Treat the depression, then retest the cognition. The order matters.
questions.strategy: Screens do not diagnose. They tell you what to look at next.

questions.stem: An older woman arrives with several bruises at different stages of healing. Her son answers every question for her and says she bruises easily. She avoids eye contact. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Interview the patient alone and report suspected mistreatment per policy
options.rationale: Bruises of different ages, a caregiver who answers for the patient and a patient who will not look at you is a pattern. You separate them, because she cannot speak freely with him in the room. Nurses are mandated reporters and the threshold is reasonable suspicion, not proof; Adult Protective Services investigates, you do not.

options.text: Document the son's explanation and continue with the admission
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Records his version and leaves her with him.

options.text: Wait for more definitive evidence before involving anyone
options.rationale: Near miss concept Mandated reporting runs on suspicion; gathering proof is the investigator's job.

options.text: Confront the son about the inconsistency in front of the patient
options.rationale: Near miss concept Tips him off and raises the risk to her when they go home.

questions.takeaway: Suspicion is the threshold. You are not required to be sure.
questions.strategy: Confronting the caregiver endangers her after you leave.

questions.stem: A 79 year old admitted for cellulitis has become incontinent, has lost 2 kg, is now confused in the evenings and has a new stage 1 pressure injury after five days. The family asks whether she will need to go to a nursing home. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: “These changes are common at her age and mean she cannot live alone.”
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Age used as the explanation, with a placement conclusion attached.

options.text: “Several of these may be reversible; let us not decide placement now.”
options.rationale: Every finding listed is one of the seven acute care adverse events: incontinence, malnutrition, delirium, tissue integrity. They are produced by the hospitalization itself, and restorative care targets the prior level of independence. A permanent placement decision made at the point of maximum deconditioning uses the wrong baseline.

options.text: “I will ask the case manager to start looking at nursing homes today.”
options.rationale: Correct but premature Acts on the lowest point as though it were the baseline.

options.text: “We will need to watch her for several months before anyone decides.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept The right instinct with the wrong timeline; recovery planning starts now.

questions.takeaway: When an older adult declines in hospital, suspect the hospital first.
questions.strategy: A stem that lists several adverse events at once is testing whether you recognize them as iatrogenic rather than as decline.

questions.stem: An independent 82 year old is admitted for pneumonia. By day 4 she is on bedrest with a urinary catheter, has had three nights of interrupted sleep, and now needs help to stand. The pneumonia is improving. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: Early dementia that the hospitalization has unmasked
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism This is physical function, not cognition.

options.text: An expected consequence of being this ill at her age
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Common is not the same as expected or acceptable.

options.text: Hospital acquired functional decline to reverse now
options.rationale: The infection is getting better and the patient is getting worse, which tells you the harm is coming from the care rather than the disease. Bedrest, a catheter she probably does not need, and broken sleep are the three classic drivers. Most of it is reversible if you act during the admission: get the catheter out, get her up, cluster care to protect sleep. Waiting for discharge is how a woman who walked in needs placement.

options.text: Deconditioning that will resolve on its own at home
options.rationale: Near miss concept Often it does not; a third of older adults never regain the function they lose in hospital.

questions.takeaway: When the illness improves and the function declines, the hospital is the cause.
questions.strategy: The detail that the pneumonia is improving is the whole clue.

questions.stem: A 79 year old admitted three days ago for pneumonia is described in report as pleasantly confused and oriented to person only. The daughter states that her mother does the crossword every morning at home and manages her own finances. The patient has had no bowel movement since admission, was started on a sleep aid on admission, and has been on bed rest. She is more confused in the evenings and cannot follow a two step instruction. What should the nurse conclude?

options.text: This is likely depression related to the acute illness and loss of independence
options.rationale: Near miss concept Possible over time, but it does not explain a three day change with an active infection.

options.text: This is an expected response to hospitalization in a patient of this age
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Age offered as an explanation. This is the error the item is built on.

options.text: This is likely delirium and the nurse should look for a reversible cause
options.rationale: Acute onset, fluctuating course and inattention in a hospitalized older adult with an active infection is delirium until proven otherwise. The daughter's sentence establishes a baseline that nobody in the chart had established. Three candidate causes are already in the stem: the new sedative, three days without a bowel movement, and immobility.

options.text: This is likely early dementia that the family has not previously recognized
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dementia is gradual. A week ago she was paying bills.

questions.takeaway: When a chart gives you a label instead of a timeline, go find the timeline.
questions.strategy: Family is often the only source of baseline. A reported baseline that nobody documented is not a baseline.

questions.stem: An 84 year old takes amitriptyline for sleep, diphenhydramine for allergies, oxybutynin for urinary urgency, lisinopril, and a daily multivitamin. She reports dry mouth, constipation, confusion and two near falls. Select all of the accurate nursing conclusions.

options.text: The medication list should be reviewed against the Beers Criteria
options.rationale: Amitriptyline, diphenhydramine and oxybutynin are all anticholinergic, and the effects add up: dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, confusion and falls. All three appear on the Beers Criteria as potentially inappropriate in older adults. Treating each symptom separately adds drugs to a list that is already the problem, which is the prescribing cascade.

options.text: Her symptoms should be reported rather than attributed to aging
options.rationale: Amitriptyline, diphenhydramine and oxybutynin are all anticholinergic, and the effects add up: dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, confusion and falls. All three appear on the Beers Criteria as potentially inappropriate in older adults. Treating each symptom separately adds drugs to a list that is already the problem, which is the prescribing cascade.

options.text: Adding a stool softener and an artificial saliva product is the priority intervention
options.rationale: Near miss concept Treats the symptoms of the drugs instead of reviewing the drugs; this is the prescribing cascade.

options.text: Three of her medications carry significant anticholinergic effects
options.rationale: Amitriptyline, diphenhydramine and oxybutynin are all anticholinergic, and the effects add up: dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, confusion and falls. All three appear on the Beers Criteria as potentially inappropriate in older adults. Treating each symptom separately adds drugs to a list that is already the problem, which is the prescribing cascade.

options.text: The multivitamin is the most likely cause of her confusion
options.rationale: Near miss concept Inert here; three genuine culprits are on the list.

options.text: The anticholinergic burden can account for all four of her symptoms
options.rationale: Amitriptyline, diphenhydramine and oxybutynin are all anticholinergic, and the effects add up: dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, confusion and falls. All three appear on the Beers Criteria as potentially inappropriate in older adults. Treating each symptom separately adds drugs to a list that is already the problem, which is the prescribing cascade.

questions.takeaway: Count the anticholinergics before you treat any single symptom. The burden is the diagnosis.
questions.strategy: Treating a drug side effect with another drug is the cascade. Look at the list first.

questions.stem: An 88 year old nursing home resident has eaten little for two days, is newly confused with her orientation drifting in and out through the day, and fell last night. Temperature is 36.9, heart rate 94, blood pressure 118/70, respirations 22, oxygen saturation 95 percent. What should the nurse suspect first?

options.text: Depression presenting as reduced intake
options.rationale: Near miss concept Possible and it develops over weeks and does not explain the tachypnea.

options.text: Dehydration from inadequate oral intake alone
options.rationale: Near miss concept Likely present as a consequence, and it is not the cause to chase first.

options.text: Progression of her underlying dementia
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Dementia does not produce a two day decline with a fall and anorexia.

options.text: Infection, most likely urinary or pulmonary
options.rationale: Four findings point the same way: anorexia, new fluctuating confusion, a fall and a respiratory rate of 22. The vital signs look reassuring, and in an older adult they are the least reliable part of the picture, because the fever and the white count often never arrive. A respiratory rate above 20 is the vital sign that does still move, and it is the one most often not counted.

questions.takeaway: Respiratory rate is the vital sign that still tells the truth in an older adult. Count it for a full minute.
questions.strategy: Dementia progresses over months. Four findings in two days is an acute illness.

questions.topic: pain in the older adult with dementia
questions.stem: A patient with advanced dementia cannot report pain. She is grimacing, resisting care, calling out, and has been rubbing her hip since a fall two days ago. The chart notes agitation. What should the nurse do?
questions.objective: pain in the older adult with dementia

options.text: Request an order for an antipsychotic to manage the agitation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Chemically restrains a patient whose problem is probably a fractured hip.

options.text: Reduce stimulation in the room and reapproach the care later
options.rationale: Correct but premature Reasonable for overload, and it does nothing for pain.

options.text: Assess with a behavioral pain tool and discuss scheduled analgesia
options.rationale: Grimacing, resisting care, vocalizing and guarding a body part are pain behaviors, and in advanced dementia they are the only pain report you will get. A behavioral tool such as PAINAD scores them. Agitation in a patient who recently fell and is rubbing her hip is pain until treated, and an analgesic trial is both the treatment and the diagnostic test. Sedating her instead treats your difficulty rather than hers.

options.text: Document the behaviors as expected progression of her dementia
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Attributes a treatable finding to the diagnosis.

questions.takeaway: Agitation in advanced dementia is pain until an analgesic trial says otherwise.
questions.strategy: The word agitation in a chart is often a pain assessment that never happened.
