questions.stem: A nurse assesses an 81 year old admitted for an elective knee replacement. Select all of the findings that require further assessment rather than being attributed to aging.

options.text: Asymmetric deep tendon reflexes
options.rationale: Reduced bowel sounds, an increased anteroposterior diameter and slowed response to multiple stimuli are expected aging changes. Absent bowel sounds are not. Incontinence is abnormal at any age no matter how long it has been present, and asymmetric reflexes are abnormal at any age even though a symmetrically diminished ankle reflex can be expected.

options.text: Reduced bowel sounds
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem The near miss that makes absent bowel sounds work as a distractor.

options.text: Absent bowel sounds in all four quadrants
options.rationale: Reduced bowel sounds, an increased anteroposterior diameter and slowed response to multiple stimuli are expected aging changes. Absent bowel sounds are not. Incontinence is abnormal at any age no matter how long it has been present, and asymmetric reflexes are abnormal at any age even though a symmetrically diminished ankle reflex can be expected.

options.text: An increased anteroposterior chest diameter
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A normal aging change in the thorax.

options.text: Urinary incontinence that began two years ago
options.rationale: Reduced bowel sounds, an increased anteroposterior diameter and slowed response to multiple stimuli are expected aging changes. Absent bowel sounds are not. Incontinence is abnormal at any age no matter how long it has been present, and asymmetric reflexes are abnormal at any age even though a symmetrically diminished ankle reflex can be expected.

options.text: Slowed reaction time when given two instructions at once
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Expected, and the reason you give one instruction at a time.

questions.takeaway: Reduced is expected. Absent is not. Incontinence is never normal aging.
questions.strategy: Expected changes are gradual and symmetric. Sudden and one sided are not.

questions.stem: Which finding in an 82 year old patient requires further assessment rather than being accepted as a change of aging?

options.text: A slower gait with a wider stance when walking
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Normal aging, and a fall risk worth addressing, not an acute finding.

options.text: A temperature of 37.9 °C with new confusion
options.rationale: Older adults blunt the fever response, so a temperature that looks unimpressive can accompany serious infection, and new confusion is often the first sign. Slower gait, presbyopia and decreased elasticity are expected changes. Confusion is never an expected change of aging.

options.text: Presbyopia that requires reading glasses for print
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Universal aging change.

options.text: Decreased skin elasticity over the forearms
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Normal, and it also makes turgor an unreliable hydration sign.

questions.takeaway: New confusion in an older adult is a symptom, not a personality.
questions.strategy: Expected versus unexpected is one of the highest yield sorts on this exam. Learn which changes are normal so the abnormal one stands out.

questions.stem: A patient reports feeling dizzy and says she needs to get to the bathroom now. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Check the blood pressure and heart rate while the patient remains seated
options.rationale: Dizziness in a patient about to stand is the setup for a fall, and it may be orthostatic hypotension or an arrhythmia. You assess before you move her, because what you find changes how you move her. Helping her up is compassionate and bypasses the finding.

options.text: Bring a bedside commode to the chair
options.rationale: Correct but premature A reasonable plan once you know why she is dizzy.

options.text: Raise the bed rails and tell the patient to wait for help
options.rationale: Near miss concept Restricts her and does not address the dizziness; rails are also a fall hazard in some patients.

options.text: Assist the patient to the bathroom and stay with her
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Responsive and skips the assessment that tells you whether she can stand safely.

questions.takeaway: Assess before you intervene, especially when the intervention involves standing a dizzy patient up.
questions.strategy: The kind option is the trap here. So is the restrictive one.

questions.stem: An 84 year old on a medical unit has had two near falls in 24 hours. Her medications include a new diuretic and a sleep aid, she reports dizziness on standing, and there is a scatter rug beside the chair her family brought from home. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Remove the scatter rug and ask the family not to bring items from home
options.rationale: Correct but premature Correct action performed before the assessment that should precede it.

options.text: Place a bed alarm and move the patient closer to the nurses station
options.rationale: Correct but premature Monitoring without addressing the cause.

options.text: Apply a gait belt and instruct the patient not to get up without assistance
options.rationale: Correct but premature Restricting mobility to manage a risk you have not identified.

options.text: Assess orthostatic blood pressures and review the medication list
options.rationale: Intrinsic risk usually outweighs what is underfoot. The stem has already handed you a diuretic, a sedative and orthostatic symptoms, which together explain the near falls far better than the rug. Assessment precedes intervention, and the environmental fix without the workup is the classic wrong answer.

questions.takeaway: A fall is a clinical clue, not an accident.
questions.strategy: The environmental option is almost always the distractor when a medication and a symptom are sitting in the stem.

questions.stem: A patient with advanced Alzheimer disease asks the nurse repeatedly when her husband is coming to visit. Her husband died six years ago. What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: "I will check the visitor list and let you know when someone is coming."
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Deflects rather than engaging the feeling.

options.text: "He is not able to come today, but your daughter will be here this afternoon."
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic A lie that will need repeating, and it closes the subject.

options.text: "Tell me about your husband. What do you miss most about him?"
options.rationale: In irreversible confusion you validate the feeling rather than correcting the facts. Telling her repeatedly that her husband is dead re inflicts the loss every time and does not improve orientation. Reality orientation is for reversible confusion such as delirium, where the person can retain the information once the cause is treated.

options.text: "Your husband died six years ago. Today is Tuesday and you are in the hospital."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Correct technique, wrong patient. This is reality orientation.

questions.takeaway: Reversible confusion gets orientation. Irreversible confusion gets validation.
questions.strategy: Ask one question first: can this person hold the correction? If not, orientation is cruelty with a clinical name.

questions.stem: A competent 90 year old with heart failure declines further hospitalizations and says she wants to stay home even if it shortens her life. Her son insists she is not thinking clearly and wants her admitted next time. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Arrange a cognitive assessment to verify she can make this decision
options.rationale: Near miss concept Appropriate if there were any sign of impairment; ordering it because a relative objects weaponizes the assessment.

options.text: Encourage her to accept admission to reassure her son
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Prioritizes his comfort over her autonomy.

options.text: Support her stated wishes and help document them in an advance directive
options.rationale: Capacity is the question, and nothing in the stem suggests she lacks it. Disagreeing with a family member is not evidence of impaired capacity, and declining burdensome treatment for a progressive illness is a coherent choice many people make. The nursing work is getting it written down so it holds when she cannot speak, and including the son in that conversation so he hears it from her.

options.text: Explain to the son that he can pursue guardianship if he disagrees
options.rationale: Near miss concept Points a family member toward overriding a competent patient.

questions.takeaway: A decision a family dislikes is not evidence of incapacity.
questions.strategy: The cognitive assessment option is attractive because it sounds thorough. Ask what would trigger it other than the disagreement.

chapters.title: Clinical Judgment and the Nursing Process

members.title: Clinical Judgment and the Nursing Process
Clinical Judgment and the Nursing Process
Clinical Judgment and the Nursing Process
Clinical Judgment and the Nursing Process
Clinical Judgment and the Nursing Process

questions.stem: A nurse identifies that a patient with heart failure is at risk for readmission. Which outcome statement is written correctly for this problem?

options.text: The patient will understand why monitoring his weight each day matters
options.rationale: Near miss concept “Understand” cannot be observed or measured, and there is no time frame.

options.text: The patient will weigh daily and report a 2 to 3 pound overnight gain
options.rationale: An outcome is patient centered, observable, measurable and has a deadline. This one names what he does, with a number that triggers the call, by a specific time. Understand cannot be measured. The nurse teaching is an intervention. Not being readmitted is an outcome nobody can evaluate at discharge and depends on things outside his control.

options.text: The nurse will teach the patient all about daily weights and their purpose before discharge today
options.rationale: Near miss concept This is a nursing intervention, not a patient outcome.

options.text: The patient will not be readmitted for heart failure within 30 days
options.rationale: Near miss concept Readmission is a system level result the patient cannot directly perform; it is not a measurable patient behavior with a time frame.

questions.takeaway: If you cannot watch it happen, it is not an outcome.
questions.strategy: Three distractors fail in three different standard ways: unmeasurable verb, nurse focused, and not evaluable in the time frame.

questions.stem: Match each nurse action to the step of the clinical judgment model it represents.

rows.text: Compares the urine output four hours after the bolus against the stated goal
Concludes that the falling output and the dry mucous membranes belong to the same problem
Selects a fluid bolus and increased monitoring from among the available options
Decides that dehydration is a more likely explanation than obstruction because the bladder scan is empty
Notes that the urine output has fallen below 30 mL per hour for two consecutive hours

questions.takeaway: Recognizing is noticing a cue. Analyzing is clustering cues into a meaning. Prioritizing hypotheses is choosing between competing explanations. Generating solutions is selecting the plan. Evaluating is measuring the result against the goal. Analyze clusters the data. Prioritize hypotheses chooses between explanations. They are not the same step.
questions.strategy: The verb in each row tells you the step: notes, concludes, decides between, selects, compares.

questions.stem: Which statement is written correctly as a nursing diagnosis?

options.text: Pneumonia related to streptococcal infection as evidenced by a lobar infiltrate on x ray
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Pneumonia is a medical diagnosis, not a nursing diagnosis.

options.text: Risk for impaired gas exchange related to fluid as evidenced by crackles and a saturation of 88 percent
options.rationale: Near miss concept A risk diagnosis has no “as evidenced by” clause, because the problem has not occurred yet. These findings show an actual problem.

options.text: Needs supplemental oxygen related to a low saturation as evidenced by crackles and dyspnea
options.rationale: Near miss concept A need for oxygen is a treatment, not a human response, so it cannot be the diagnostic label.

options.text: Impaired gas exchange related to alveolar fluid as evidenced by crackles and a saturation of 88 percent
options.rationale: A nursing diagnosis names a human response the nurse can treat, links it to an etiology the nurse can influence, and supports it with assessment data. A medical diagnosis is not a nursing diagnosis, a risk diagnosis has risk factors rather than evidence because the problem has not occurred yet, and a needs statement is an intervention dressed as a diagnosis.

questions.takeaway: Human response, etiology you can act on, and data. A medical label is none of those.
questions.strategy: The nursing diagnosis item almost always offers one medical diagnosis and one intervention. Eliminate those two first.

questions.stem: A nurse is choosing among options on an examination item about a deteriorating patient. Select all of the option features that should raise suspicion.

options.text: The option is correct but belongs later in the sequence
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting, correct but premature, absolute language and a label that explains a finding away are all recurring distractor shapes. Naming a diagnosis is not itself a trap: plenty of correct answers do it. The trap is the label used to dismiss a finding rather than account for it. Assessing airway and breathing and reporting a change are usually right, and an option is not suspicious just because it is common.

options.text: The option uses the words always or never
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting, correct but premature, absolute language and a label that explains a finding away are all recurring distractor shapes. Naming a diagnosis is not itself a trap: plenty of correct answers do it. The trap is the label used to dismiss a finding rather than account for it. Assessing airway and breathing and reporting a change are usually right, and an option is not suspicious just because it is common.

options.text: The option offers a label that explains the finding away, such as calling new confusion sundowning
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting, correct but premature, absolute language and a label that explains a finding away are all recurring distractor shapes. Naming a diagnosis is not itself a trap: plenty of correct answers do it. The trap is the label used to dismiss a finding rather than account for it. Assessing airway and breathing and reporting a change are usually right, and an option is not suspicious just because it is common.

options.text: The option reports a change in the patient's condition to the provider
options.rationale: Near miss concept Appropriate; it only becomes wrong when something must be done first.

options.text: The option directs the nurse to assess the airway and breathing
options.rationale: Near miss concept Almost always the right move.

options.text: The option documents the finding instead of acting on it
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting, correct but premature, absolute language and a label that explains a finding away are all recurring distractor shapes. Naming a diagnosis is not itself a trap: plenty of correct answers do it. The trap is the label used to dismiss a finding rather than account for it. Assessing airway and breathing and reporting a change are usually right, and an option is not suspicious just because it is common.

questions.takeaway: Learn the shape of a wrong answer and you will find it before you know the content.
questions.strategy: Two options here describe correct nursing. Do not reject an option for looking familiar.

questions.stem: A nurse caring for a patient 6 hours after abdominal surgery notes the heart rate has climbed from 78 to 104 over three hours while the blood pressure has held at 118/70, the dressing is dry and intact, and the patient rates pain 2 of 10. The nurse puts these findings together and determines that the cluster represents early compensation for volume loss. Which step of the clinical judgment measurement model has the nurse just completed?

options.text: Take action
options.rationale: Correct but premature Nothing has been carried out.

options.text: Generate solutions
options.rationale: Correct but premature No outcome or intervention has been chosen yet.

options.text: Prioritize hypotheses
options.rationale: Near miss concept That step ranks several competing explanations by likelihood AND urgency. She named one meaning, she did not rank a set.

options.text: Analyze cues
options.rationale: Putting separate findings together and assigning them a meaning is analysis. The nurse already recognized the cues when she noticed the trend; she has not yet ranked this explanation against other possible ones, and she has not planned anything.

options.text: Recognize cues
options.rationale: Correct but premature She did this earlier, when she saw the trend. The stem has moved past it.

questions.takeaway: Noticing is recognizing. Deciding what it means is analyzing.
questions.strategy: Name what the nurse actually DID in the stem, not what she will do next.

questions.stem: A nurse finds her patient's respiratory rate has risen from 18 to 28, he is using his neck muscles to breathe, and he can no longer finish a sentence. Yesterday he spoke in full sentences. She concludes his breathing is deteriorating and calls the provider. Which term names what she has demonstrated?

options.text: The nursing process, the systematic method for planning and delivering care
options.rationale: Near miss concept The framework she worked inside, rather than the capability she showed.

options.text: Clinical judgment, the observed outcome of critical thinking and decision making
options.rationale: Judgment is what you can see: she reached a conclusion and acted on it. The thinking that produced it happened out of sight.

options.text: Critical thinking, the mental process of gathering and questioning information
options.rationale: Near miss concept One of the two processes feeding the judgment, and it is not itself observable.

options.text: Clinical reasoning, the process of making informed and responsible decisions
options.rationale: Near miss concept The other underlying process. It also sits below the surface.

questions.takeaway: Critical thinking and clinical reasoning are the processes. Clinical judgment is the observed outcome of both.
questions.strategy: The distinguishing word is observed. Two options name processes you cannot see; one names a framework.

questions.stem: A student asks why the nursing process and the clinical judgment model are both taught. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: The nursing process is used in practice and the model is used only for examinations
options.rationale: Near miss concept The model describes real cognitive work. It is measured on the NCLEX because it happens at the bedside.

options.text: The clinical judgment model has replaced the nursing process in current practice
options.rationale: Near miss concept Neither replaces the other. They run in parallel and map onto each other step by step.

options.text: The nursing process describes what nurses do; the model describes how nurses think while doing it
options.rationale: Her own framing. One organizes the work into steps, the other describes the reasoning running underneath.

options.text: The nursing process applies to stable patients and the model to emergencies
options.rationale: Near miss concept The nursing process is used with every patient, in every setting, every shift.

questions.takeaway: The nursing process is what nurses do. The clinical judgment model is how nurses think.
questions.strategy: Two distractors put the two in competition. Ask what each one is describing.

questions.stem: A nurse caring for a confused older adult lists four possible causes: low oxygen, a new medication, infection, and dehydration. She decides the oxygen saturation must be checked first. Which step of the clinical judgment model is this?

options.text: Generating solutions
options.rationale: Near miss concept She has not yet decided what to do about any of them.

options.text: Recognizing cues
options.rationale: Near miss concept The data gathering is complete. She is working with what she found.

options.text: Analyzing cues
options.rationale: Near miss concept Analysis produced the four possibilities. Choosing between them is the next step.

options.text: Prioritizing hypotheses
options.rationale: Four competing explanations ranked by likelihood and urgency. Ranking is what this step means, and the ABCs put oxygenation first.

questions.takeaway: Prioritizing hypotheses ranks competing explanations by likelihood and urgency, using the ABCs, Maslow, acute against chronic, and risk of deterioration.
questions.strategy: The giveaway is that there are four explanations and she is putting one first. Ranking needs competitors.

questions.stem: A nurse builds an assessment database for a newly admitted patient. Which sources contribute to it? Select all that apply.

options.text: The patient's own account of the problem
options.rationale: Subjective data, and the patient is the primary source. Objective data, measured or observed directly. Named, and they often hold the baseline the patient cannot describe. Named, and reviewing it is part of preparing for the interview. Named, and it is part of the database rather than separate from it.

options.text: The nurse's physical examination findings
options.rationale: Subjective data, and the patient is the primary source. Objective data, measured or observed directly. Named, and they often hold the baseline the patient cannot describe. Named, and reviewing it is part of preparing for the interview. Named, and it is part of the database rather than separate from it.

options.text: Family caregivers and significant others
options.rationale: Subjective data, and the patient is the primary source. Objective data, measured or observed directly. Named, and they often hold the baseline the patient cannot describe. Named, and reviewing it is part of preparing for the interview. Named, and it is part of the database rather than separate from it.

options.text: The health record and previous notes
options.rationale: Subjective data, and the patient is the primary source. Objective data, measured or observed directly. Named, and they often hold the baseline the patient cannot describe. Named, and reviewing it is part of preparing for the interview. Named, and it is part of the database rather than separate from it.

options.text: Diagnostic and laboratory data
options.rationale: Subjective data, and the patient is the primary source. Objective data, measured or observed directly. Named, and they often hold the baseline the patient cannot describe. Named, and reviewing it is part of preparing for the interview. Named, and it is part of the database rather than separate from it.

options.text: The nurse's impression of how motivated the patient seems
options.rationale: Near miss concept A judgment about the patient rather than data. It belongs nowhere in the database, and it shapes care if left unexamined.

questions.takeaway: The database draws on scientific data and theory, patient subjective and objective data, family and significant others, the health care team, health records, and diagnostic data.
questions.strategy: One distractor is an inference about the patient dressed as an observation.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the care plan for a patient two days after abdominal surgery. For each item, indicate which type of diagnosis or problem it represents.

rows.text: Perforated appendix
Acute pain related to the surgical incision
Monitoring for postoperative hemorrhage
Impaired physical mobility related to incisional pain
Type 2 diabetes mellitus
Monitoring for hypoglycemia during the insulin infusion

questions.takeaway: Perforated appendix: Identifies the disease, and it is what physicians and advanced practice providers treat. Acute pain related to the surgical incision: Classifies his response to the illness, and nurses treat it independently. Monitoring for postoperative hemorrhage: The nurse monitors and the provider treats. Both are required, and the focus is preventing a potential complication. Impaired physical mobility related to incisional pain: A human response the nurse can act on directly through positioning, analgesia timing and assisted movement. Type 2 diabetes mellitus: A disease process, diagnosed and medically managed. Monitoring for hypoglycemia during the insulin infusion: Nursing surveillance of a potential complication that needs medical intervention if it occurs. Medical diagnoses name the disease. Nursing diagnoses name the patient's response. Collaborative problems need both, and the nursing role is monitoring for complications.
questions.strategy: The word monitoring signals a collaborative problem. Ask whether the nurse can treat it alone.

questions.stem: A nurse manager reviews a care plan on which every high-priority diagnosis is physiological. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Classifying only physiological diagnoses as high priority is an error to avoid
options.rationale: Her slide says this directly. A psychosocial problem can be the most urgent thing for a particular patient at a particular moment.

options.text: Psychosocial diagnoses should be addressed only after discharge planning begins
options.rationale: Near miss concept Delays them indefinitely, and nothing supports the timing.

options.text: Priority should be determined by the order in which problems were identified
options.rationale: Near miss concept Order of discovery has nothing to do with urgency.

options.text: Physiological diagnoses are always ranked above psychosocial ones
options.rationale: Absolute language The rule of thumb, stated as an absolute. Her slide explicitly warns against applying it that way.

questions.takeaway: Avoid classifying only physiological nursing diagnoses as high priority. Consider each patient's unique situation.
questions.strategy: One distractor is the general rule stated without the caveat her slide attaches to it.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence: A nurse writes outcomes for a patient recovering from a stroke. Saying exactly what the patient will do, rather than that he will improve, makes the outcome [[1]]. Adding that he will walk 20 feet makes it [[2]]. Checking that the goal fits a patient who could walk 10 feet yesterday makes it [[3]]. Adding by the end of the week makes it [[4]].

options.text: specific
measurable
relevant
achievable
measurable
specific
time-bound
achievable
achievable
relevant
measurable
specific
time-bound
achievable
relevant
measurable

questions.takeaway: [1] specific: Says exactly what should happen, with no room for interpretation. [2] measurable: A number you can check against. Twenty feet either happened or it did not. [3] achievable: Realistic for this patient, judged against what he could do yesterday. [4] time-bound: A deadline, without which an outcome can never be judged unmet. SMART: Specific is what, Measurable is how much, Achievable is whether he can, Relevant is whether it matters, Time-bound is when.
questions.strategy: Specific and measurable are the pair that gets confused. Specific names the action; measurable attaches a number.

questions.stem: After an outcome is not met, a nurse reconsiders whether the nursing diagnosis she wrote is still accurate. Which step of the clinical judgment model has she returned to?

options.text: Generating solutions
options.rationale: Near miss concept Choosing new interventions is generating solutions. She is questioning the problem, not the plan.

options.text: Prioritizing hypotheses
options.rationale: Near miss concept Ranking competing explanations. She is asking whether the one she chose was right at all.

options.text: Analyzing cues
options.rationale: Questioning whether the problem was named correctly is a return to interpretation, one step further back than revising the plan.

options.text: Evaluating outcomes
options.rationale: Near miss concept That step produced the verdict. Acting on it is what comes next.

questions.takeaway: Revising the plan can send you back to different steps. New data goes to recognizing cues; a wrong diagnosis goes to analyzing cues; a wrong intervention goes to generating solutions.
questions.strategy: Three distractors are also steps you can return to. Ask which part of the plan she is questioning.

questions.stem: A nurse receives report on four patients. Place them in the order they should be seen, most urgent first.

options.text: A patient with type 2 diabetes whose morning glucose is 212 mg/dL
A patient with pneumonia whose oxygen saturation has fallen from 94 to 86 percent on 2 L nasal cannula
A patient with heart failure who gained 1.4 kg overnight and has new basilar crackles
A patient two hours after a stroke whose blood pressure is 188/96 and who is newly unable to say her own name

questions.takeaway: Airway and breathing first: a falling saturation on oxygen is an unstable oxygenation problem. New aphasia after a stroke is a change in neurologic status and comes next. The weight gain with crackles is real and developing over hours. A glucose of 212 is abnormal, expected in this population and the least urgent. Unstable before stable, new before known, ABCs before numbers.
questions.strategy: Rank by the airway, breathing, circulation sequence first, then break ties with new versus known and with how fast the finding is moving.

questions.stem: A nurse receives report on four patients. Which patient should the nurse assess first?

options.text: A patient with a potassium of 5.9 mEq/L who reports tingling in the fingertips
options.rationale: Most dramatic finding The most alarming lab on the page, and genuinely urgent, but the patient is still moving air and talking.

options.text: A patient two days after a hip replacement whose pain is 8 of 10 and whose last analgesic was four hours ago
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic The most emotionally compelling option. Pain is not an airway problem.

options.text: A patient with pneumonia whose respiratory rate is 28 and who can speak only three words between breaths
options.rationale: Three word sentences with a rate of 28 is failing ventilation, which is a B problem and outranks everything else here. The potassium is dangerous and is the next one to see, the pain is real but stable, and the fever in an alert patient who is drinking is the least urgent.

options.text: A patient with a temperature of 102.6 F who is alert and drinking fluids
options.rationale: Most dramatic finding A big number attached to a stable patient.

questions.takeaway: Severity of suffering does not set priority. Speed of deterioration does.
questions.strategy: Run the stack and stop at the first rule that separates them. Airway and breathing end the question before Maslow is needed.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure was started on a diuretic with the outcome that he would lose at least 1 kg in 24 hours. At 24 hours the weight is down 0.4 kg, the crackles are unchanged and the patient reports the same shortness of breath on exertion. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Treat the results as new assessment data and revise the plan with the provider
options.rationale: Evaluation does not close the loop, it restarts it. A partially met outcome with unchanged clinical findings is new assessment data that should drive a revision now, not another 24 hours of the same plan.

options.text: Document the outcome as partially met and continue the current plan unchanged
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Accurate charting attached to inaction.

options.text: Reinforce teaching about daily weights and the 1.5 L fluid restriction today
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question A good nursing action that does not address why the diuresis is inadequate.

options.text: Document the outcome as not met and reevaluate after 24 more hours on this plan
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Another day of a plan that is already failing.

questions.takeaway: Evaluation data is assessment data. The cycle restarts rather than ending.
questions.strategy: When an outcome is not met and the findings have not moved, the answer that merely records or waits is almost never right.

questions.stem: A patient's plan of care includes a goal of ambulating 50 feet twice daily. Select all of the findings that indicate the plan needs revision.

options.text: He refuses consistently and says the goal was never discussed with him
options.rationale: Evaluation revises the plan in both directions. A goal he has outgrown needs raising, a goal producing symptoms needs lowering, a goal he never agreed to needs renegotiating, and a goal requiring two staff every time is not a goal he is achieving. The last two options describe the plan working as written.

options.text: He walks 50 feet twice daily with a walker and no symptoms
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit The goal is being met with an appropriate device.

options.text: He reports mild fatigue that resolves within two minutes of sitting
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Prompt recovery is the definition of adequate activity tolerance.

options.text: He has met the goal for three days and asks for more
options.rationale: Evaluation revises the plan in both directions. A goal he has outgrown needs raising, a goal producing symptoms needs lowering, a goal he never agreed to needs renegotiating, and a goal requiring two staff every time is not a goal he is achieving. The last two options describe the plan working as written.

options.text: He can walk 50 feet only with two staff members assisting
options.rationale: Evaluation revises the plan in both directions. A goal he has outgrown needs raising, a goal producing symptoms needs lowering, a goal he never agreed to needs renegotiating, and a goal requiring two staff every time is not a goal he is achieving. The last two options describe the plan working as written.

options.text: He becomes dizzy and his heart rate does not recover after walking
options.rationale: Evaluation revises the plan in both directions. A goal he has outgrown needs raising, a goal producing symptoms needs lowering, a goal he never agreed to needs renegotiating, and a goal requiring two staff every time is not a goal he is achieving. The last two options describe the plan working as written.

questions.takeaway: A goal that has been met is as much a reason to revise as a goal that failed.
questions.strategy: Two options describe exactly the outcome the plan was aiming for.

questions.topic: recognizing and acting on a change
questions.stem: A patient two days after surgery becomes restless and reports feeling short of breath. Place the nurse's actions in the order they should occur.
questions.objective: recognizing and acting on a change

options.text: Review the chart for risk factors such as immobility and recent surgery
Notify the provider with a structured report of the findings
Raise the head of the bed and assess respiratory effort and oxygen saturation
Apply oxygen and obtain a full set of vital signs
Document the episode and the response to intervention

questions.takeaway: Position and assess first, because that costs seconds and tells you how bad this is. Then intervene and complete the data set. The chart review happens before the call, not after, because the provider will ask and because immobility plus recent surgery turns restlessness and dyspnea into a suspected pulmonary embolism. Documentation closes it. Gather what the provider will ask for before you call. It changes the call from a symptom report into a clinical picture.
questions.strategy: Restlessness is an early hypoxia sign and it is read as anxiety more often than any other finding in nursing.

questions.stem: A nurse has four things to do. A patient with pneumonia has a saturation of 91 percent on 2 L and is working harder than an hour ago. A patient with a potassium of 6.1 has an order for insulin and dextrose. A patient who fell yesterday is asking to get up to the bathroom. A patient's family is waiting to discuss discharge. Which does the nurse do first?

options.text: Assess the pneumonia patient, whose breathing is getting harder
options.rationale: The saturation is only slightly low, which is the distractor. The finding that matters is the trend: he is working harder than he was, and increased work of breathing precedes the saturation falling, not the other way round. A potassium of 6.1 is dangerous and the treatment is already ordered and takes minutes to prepare; airway and breathing outrank it, and you can delegate neither assessment nor the toileting judgment.

options.text: Give the ordered insulin and dextrose for the potassium of 6.1
options.rationale: Near miss concept A potassium of 6.1 is serious, but the treatment is scheduled and the patient is not described as unstable. Worsening work of breathing is a change in an airway and breathing problem now.

options.text: Help the patient who fell yesterday get safely to the bathroom
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome The fall risk is real and can be handled with a quick delegation or call light plan; it does not outrank a breathing change.

options.text: Meet the waiting family, since discharge delays affect everyone
options.rationale: Near miss concept Family communication matters but is not physiologically urgent.

questions.takeaway: A number that is almost normal plus a trend that is worsening beats a bad number that is already being treated.
questions.strategy: When two options are both ABC problems, the tiebreaker is which one is actively deteriorating.

questions.stem: A nurse has four things to do at the start of the shift. Which should be done first?

options.text: Suction a patient with gurgling respirations and a weak cough
options.rationale: Gurgling respirations with a weak cough is an airway that the patient cannot clear. Airway outranks the insulin, the repositioning and the call, all of which are real nursing and none of which is an airway.

options.text: Reposition a patient who has been supine for two hours
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome Prevention, correctly scheduled, lower priority.

options.text: Call a family member who asked to be updated on the plan of care
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Important to the family and lowest in this set.

options.text: Administer scheduled insulin before a tray arrives
options.rationale: Correct but premature Time sensitive and not an airway.

questions.takeaway: Airway wins. Every time, without a tiebreaker.
questions.strategy: When one option is an airway problem, the question is already answered. Resist ranking the other three.

questions.stem: A nurse has twice reported a patient's worsening restlessness and falling oxygen saturation to the provider, who each time ordered continued monitoring. The saturation is now 88 percent on 4 L and the patient is using accessory muscles. What should the nurse do next?

options.text: Increase the oxygen and reassess in 15 minutes before calling the provider again
options.rationale: Correct but premature Titrating oxygen without an order and buying 15 more minutes delays the escalation this patient already needs.

options.text: Document both earlier calls and the current findings in detail in the medical record
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Charting the deterioration is not treating it. Document after you act.

options.text: Tell the provider this is a safety concern and escalate through the chain of command
options.rationale: CUS exists for exactly this moment. Concerned and uncomfortable have already been expressed twice without action, so the nurse names it as a safety issue and escalates. The patient is deteriorating and a third identical report predicts a third identical outcome.

options.text: Repeat the SBAR report to the same provider again with the updated saturation and new findings
options.rationale: Near miss concept SBAR is the right structure and the wrong step; it has already failed twice.

questions.takeaway: When SBAR has not produced action, the next tool is not a louder SBAR.
questions.strategy: A stem that tells you the nurse has already reported more than once is pointing at CUS and the chain of command.

questions.stem: A patient's blood pressure has dropped from 128/76 to 96/58 over two hours. He is alert, his skin is warm and dry, and his urine output is 40 mL per hour. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Notify the provider immediately, because the systolic pressure has fallen more than 30 points
options.rationale: Near miss concept Defensible, and a trend with intact perfusion is reported on the next round, not as an emergency.

options.text: Continue to monitor closely and reassess the trend, because perfusion indicators remain adequate
options.rationale: The pressure moved and the patient has not. Mentation, skin and urine output are the three bedside measures of whether organs are being perfused, and all three are intact, which means the number changed but the perfusion did not. You watch closely and reassess. If mentation dulls, the skin turns cool, or the output falls below 30 mL per hour, that is a different patient and a different answer.

options.text: Give a fluid bolus from the maintenance order to restore the pressure
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope A maintenance order is not a bolus order.

options.text: Place the patient in Trendelenburg position
options.rationale: Near miss concept Abandoned practice; it worsens ventilation and does not improve perfusion.

questions.takeaway: Treat the patient, not the number, and the patient is told by mentation, skin and urine output.
questions.strategy: Say out loud what would have to change for you to escalate. If you can name it, you are monitoring rather than ignoring.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews a patient's record. Select all of the findings that require action before the end of the shift.

options.text: A potassium of 3.1 with an order for replacement
options.rationale: Recognizing cues means sorting what has to change from what can be watched. A low potassium with an order waiting, output under 30 mL per hour, an allergy collision and a drifting saturation all need something done. A hemoglobin of 11.8 after surgery and a pressure of 138/84 in a hypertensive patient are findings to note, not to act on tonight.

options.text: A hemoglobin of 11.8 in a postoperative patient
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Mild and expected after surgery; it is monitored rather than treated.

options.text: A new order for an antibiotic the patient is allergic to
options.rationale: Recognizing cues means sorting what has to change from what can be watched. A low potassium with an order waiting, output under 30 mL per hour, an allergy collision and a drifting saturation all need something done. A hemoglobin of 11.8 after surgery and a pressure of 138/84 in a hypertensive patient are findings to note, not to act on tonight.

options.text: A urine output of 22 mL per hour for the last three hours
options.rationale: Recognizing cues means sorting what has to change from what can be watched. A low potassium with an order waiting, output under 30 mL per hour, an allergy collision and a drifting saturation all need something done. A hemoglobin of 11.8 after surgery and a pressure of 138/84 in a hypertensive patient are findings to note, not to act on tonight.

options.text: An oxygen saturation that has drifted from 96 to 91 percent
options.rationale: Recognizing cues means sorting what has to change from what can be watched. A low potassium with an order waiting, output under 30 mL per hour, an allergy collision and a drifting saturation all need something done. A hemoglobin of 11.8 after surgery and a pressure of 138/84 in a hypertensive patient are findings to note, not to act on tonight.

options.text: A blood pressure of 138/84 in a patient with hypertension
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Above the 130/80 goal but not an acute change, so it belongs in the long term plan rather than tonight's.

questions.takeaway: An order that conflicts with a documented allergy is a cue, and the catch is noticing it in the chart rather than at the bedside.
questions.strategy: Two options are abnormal numbers that are expected for the patient described.

questions.stem: A nurse cares for a post-operative patient who reports incisional pain at 5 of 10. The wound edges are slightly separated and the temperature is 99.5 F. For each nurse activity, indicate which step of the clinical judgment model it represents.

rows.text: Notes the wound separation, the drainage and the elevated temperature
Compares the findings with normal wound healing and clusters them toward risk for infection
Decides to increase wound checks to every four hours and sets a threshold for calling the provider
Performs the wound care, documents, and communicates the change at handoff
Reassesses 24 hours later, finds no further separation and a normal temperature

questions.takeaway: Notes the wound separation, the drainage and the elevated temperature: Gathering the findings that matter, without yet saying what they mean. Compares the findings with normal wound healing and clusters them toward risk for infection: Interpreting the data, grouping it, and asking what is expected against what is not. Decides to increase wound checks to every four hours and sets a threshold for calling the provider: Choosing what could be done and when to escalate, before anything is carried out. Performs the wound care, documents, and communicates the change at handoff: Carrying out the plan, including the communication that is part of it. Reassesses 24 hours later, finds no further separation and a normal temperature: Measuring the result against what was expected, and deciding whether to continue. Six steps: recognize cues, analyze cues, prioritize hypotheses, generate solutions, take action, evaluate outcomes.
questions.strategy: The step missing from these five is prioritizing hypotheses, which needs competing explanations to rank.

questions.stem: A nurse gives a scheduled analgesic, then returns 40 minutes later and finds the pain is now 7 of 10 rather than the expected 3. Which step does she return to?

options.text: Recognizing cues, because the new finding restarts the cycle
options.rationale: Evaluation data becomes new assessment data. An unmet outcome sends you back to gathering, not forward.

options.text: Taking action, by giving a further dose
options.rationale: Near miss concept Acting again before knowing why the first action failed, and the reason may not be the dose.

options.text: Evaluating outcomes, by documenting that the goal was not met
options.rationale: Near miss concept She has already evaluated. The question is what happens after that verdict.

options.text: Generating solutions, by choosing a different analgesic
options.rationale: Near miss concept Changing the plan before reassessing skips the step that would tell you what to change it to.

questions.takeaway: The cycle is not one-way. Evaluation data becomes new assessment data, and the process begins its next loop immediately.
questions.strategy: Two distractors jump forward to fixing it. Ask what you need before you can choose a new plan.

questions.stem: A nurse begins an admission interview by introducing herself, explaining the purpose and confidentiality, and asking what the patient most wants to cover. Which phase is this?

options.text: Working phase
options.rationale: Near miss concept Data collection, which begins after the ground rules are set.

options.text: Orientation
options.rationale: Introduce yourself, explain purpose and confidentiality, and set an agenda around the patient's priorities so he becomes an active partner.

options.text: Preparation
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting The near-miss. Preparation is reviewing the record before the encounter, and it happens before the patient is in the room.

options.text: Termination
options.rationale: Near miss concept Summarizing, checking accuracy, inviting final questions, and saying when you will return.

questions.takeaway: Three phases: orientation, working phase, termination. Preparation happens before the interview begins.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is preparation, which is real and happens before you walk in.

questions.stem: A nurse completes an admission assessment on a 54-year-old with abdominal pain. For each finding, indicate whether it is subjective or objective data.

rows.text: The patient rates his pain at 7 of 10
Temperature 38.2 C
He says the pain is worse after eating
The abdomen is distended and firm on palpation
He reports feeling frightened about what this means
He is guarding the abdomen and grimacing when he moves

questions.takeaway: The patient rates his pain at 7 of 10: His own report of his experience. Attaching a number does not make it measurable by anyone else. Temperature 38.2 C: Measured, and reproducible by anyone with the same equipment. He says the pain is worse after eating: His account of a pattern only he can perceive. The abdomen is distended and firm on palpation: Observed and felt by the examiner. He reports feeling frightened about what this means: An emotion, reported. Real data, and only he has access to it. He is guarding the abdomen and grimacing when he moves: Observation of behavior. You are recording what you see, not what he tells you he feels. Subjective is what the patient reports. Objective is what you measure or observe. A pain score is subjective; guarding is objective.
questions.strategy: Two rows are about pain and they fall on opposite sides. What he says about it is subjective; what you watch him do is objective.

questions.stem: A patient tells the nurse he is fine, while sitting rigidly, guarding his abdomen, and grimacing when he shifts position. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.text: Record that the patient denies pain
options.rationale: Near miss concept Documents one source and discards the other. The two findings together are the finding.

options.text: Record the objective findings and disregard his statement
options.rationale: Near miss concept The reverse error. His account is data even when it conflicts with what you see.

options.text: Name the discrepancy and invite him to say more about it
options.rationale: Validating is part of the working phase. Clarifying and summarizing checks your understanding rather than choosing which piece of data to believe.

options.text: Ask a direct closed question about whether he has pain
options.rationale: Near miss concept Rushing to yes or no questions can mask the real problem, which is exactly what her slide warns against.

questions.takeaway: When subjective and objective data conflict, the conflict is the finding. Clarify and validate rather than choosing a side.
questions.strategy: Two distractors pick one source and discard the other. One narrows the question too soon.

questions.stem: During an interview a patient pauses after describing his symptoms. The nurse says nothing, nods, and waits. Which technique is she using?

options.text: Back-channeling, which encourages him to continue without directing him
options.rationale: A named interview technique. Small signals that you are listening keep the account going without steering it.

options.text: Probing, to obtain more specific detail
options.rationale: Near miss concept Probing asks a follow-up question. She has asked nothing.

options.text: Closed-ended questioning, to confirm what he has said
options.rationale: Near miss concept A closed question invites yes or no. Silence with a nod invites him to keep going.

options.text: A leading question, to guide him toward the relevant information
options.rationale: Near miss concept Leading questions are named among the things to avoid, and she has not asked anything.

questions.takeaway: Interview techniques: observation, open-ended questions, direct closed-ended questions, back-channeling, probing, and avoiding leading questions.
questions.strategy: Three distractors describe something the nurse says. She has said nothing.

questions.stem: A nurse finds that a patient cannot explain his diuretic, has not weighed himself since discharge, and cannot name foods high in sodium. She groups these and names the problem. Which step has she completed?

options.text: Prioritizing hypotheses, by selecting the most urgent problem
options.rationale: Near miss concept Only one problem has been named. Prioritizing needs competitors.

options.text: Analyzing cues, by clustering the data into a pattern and stating the problem
options.rationale: Analysis interprets the data, clusters it, and names what it amounts to. Three separate gaps became one problem.

options.text: Recognizing cues, by identifying the relevant findings
options.rationale: Near miss concept Recognizing produced the three findings. Grouping and naming them is the next step.

options.text: Generating solutions, by planning the teaching he needs
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nothing has been planned yet.

questions.takeaway: Analyzing cues means data interpretation, clustering, and finding patterns. Naming the problem is where it lands.
questions.strategy: Three findings became one named problem. That move from data to meaning is analysis.

questions.stem: A nurse writes a nursing diagnosis for a patient who developed a pressure injury during a five-day period of bed rest. Which related factor is appropriate?

options.text: Related to inadequate repositioning by the previous shift
options.rationale: Near miss concept Implies legal liability and names a colleague. A related factor must not do either.

options.text: Related to a stage 2 pressure injury
options.rationale: Near miss concept The injury is the problem, not the factor related to it. This restates the diagnosis as its own cause.

options.text: Related to the patient's refusal to be turned
options.rationale: Near miss concept Blames the patient, and refusal would itself need assessment rather than being used as a cause.

options.text: Related to prolonged immobility
options.rationale: Names the cause in a way the nurse can act on, and it assigns no blame to anyone.

questions.takeaway: The related factor names the cause after the words related to. It must be something nursing can address, and it must not imply blame or legal liability.
questions.strategy: Two distractors assign fault. One uses the problem as its own cause.

questions.stem: A nurse identifies four problems for a patient: impaired gas exchange with a saturation of 88%, acute pain at 6 of 10, anxiety about the diagnosis, and risk for constipation. Which is the priority?

options.text: Acute pain
options.rationale: Near miss concept Real, actual, and distressing. It does not threaten airway, breathing or circulation.

options.text: Risk for constipation
options.rationale: Near miss concept A potential problem. Actual problems outrank potential ones.

options.text: Impaired gas exchange
options.rationale: The ABCs place breathing above everything else, and 88% is a current physiological threat rather than a potential one.

options.text: Anxiety about the diagnosis
options.rationale: Near miss concept A genuine problem, and her slide warns against dismissing psychosocial diagnoses. It still ranks below hypoxia.

questions.takeaway: Priority concepts: the ABCs, Maslow, acute against chronic, actual against potential, and risk of deterioration.
questions.strategy: All four are legitimate problems. Ask which one is both actual and threatens the ABCs.

questions.stem: A nurse writes an expected outcome for a patient learning insulin injection. Which outcome is written correctly?

options.text: The patient will feel confident about managing his insulin at home
options.rationale: Near miss concept Confidence matters and it is not measurable. Nothing tells you whether it was met.

options.text: The patient will understand how to inject his insulin
options.rationale: Near miss concept Understanding cannot be observed, and two nurses would judge it differently.

options.text: The patient will demonstrate correct injection technique unaided before discharge
options.rationale: Specific, measurable by observation, achievable, relevant to the priority problem, and time-bound.

options.text: The nurse will teach the patient correct injection technique
options.rationale: Near miss concept Describes what the nurse does. An outcome states what the patient will achieve.

questions.takeaway: SMART outcomes: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. Write what the patient will do, not what the nurse will do.
questions.strategy: One distractor uses a verb you cannot observe. One describes the nurse's activity instead of the patient's.

questions.stem: A patient recovering from a stroke has difficulty swallowing, cannot manage stairs at home, and struggles to make himself understood. Which consultation should the nurse arrange for the swallowing difficulty?

options.text: Occupational therapist
options.rationale: Near miss concept Occupational therapy addresses daily activities and adaptation, which is relevant to other parts of his care.

options.text: Speech and language pathologist
options.rationale: Swallowing assessment and management sits with the speech and language pathologist, alongside communication.

options.text: Physical therapist
options.rationale: Near miss concept Physical therapy addresses the stairs and mobility.

options.text: Registered dietitian nutritionist
options.rationale: Near miss concept The near-miss. The dietitian determines what he should eat; the speech pathologist determines whether he can swallow it safely.

questions.takeaway: Consult the professional whose scope matches the problem. Swallowing and communication go to speech and language pathology.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is the dietitian. One decides what the diet should be, the other decides whether swallowing is safe at all.

questions.stem: A nurse plans care for a patient with four identified problems and a heavy assignment. Which principles guide how she establishes priorities? Select all that apply.

options.text: Rank problems as high, intermediate or low using the ABCs
options.rationale: Airway, breathing and circulation order the physiological problems. Named, and it orders needs by how fundamental they are. Named, and it is why two patients with identical problem lists may be prioritized differently. Named under establishing priorities, because a plan she never reaches is not a priority.

options.text: Apply Maslow's hierarchy to the identified problems
options.rationale: Airway, breathing and circulation order the physiological problems. Named, and it orders needs by how fundamental they are. Named, and it is why two patients with identical problem lists may be prioritized differently. Named under establishing priorities, because a plan she never reaches is not a priority.

options.text: Consider this patient's unique situation
options.rationale: Airway, breathing and circulation order the physiological problems. Named, and it orders needs by how fundamental they are. Named, and it is why two patients with identical problem lists may be prioritized differently. Named under establishing priorities, because a plan she never reaches is not a priority.

options.text: Manage her time and protect it from interruptions
options.rationale: Airway, breathing and circulation order the physiological problems. Named, and it orders needs by how fundamental they are. Named, and it is why two patients with identical problem lists may be prioritized differently. Named under establishing priorities, because a plan she never reaches is not a priority.

options.text: Address problems in the order they were identified
options.rationale: Near miss concept Order of discovery has nothing to do with urgency.

options.text: Treat every physiological problem as higher priority than any psychosocial one
options.rationale: Near miss concept Her slide warns against exactly this. Physiological problems usually rank high, and always is what makes it wrong.

questions.takeaway: Establishing priorities: the ABCs, Maslow, the patient's unique situation, and time management. Avoid ranking only physiological diagnoses as high priority.
questions.strategy: One distractor states a good rule of thumb as an absolute. That word is what makes it the wrong answer.

questions.stem: A nurse writes an outcome that a patient will ambulate 50 feet twice daily by tomorrow. He walked 10 feet once today with two assistants. Which element of the outcome is the problem?

options.text: It is not achievable for this patient at this point
options.rationale: Achievable asks whether it is realistic for this patient. The gap between 10 feet with two assistants and 50 feet twice daily makes failure certain.

options.text: It is not measurable
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fifty feet and twice daily are both countable.

options.text: It is not time-bound
options.rationale: Near miss concept By tomorrow is a deadline.

options.text: It is not specific enough about the activity
options.rationale: Near miss concept Ambulate 50 feet twice daily is entirely specific.

questions.takeaway: An outcome that cannot be reached is not a goal, it is a guaranteed failure. Achievable is judged against what this patient can do now.
questions.strategy: Three elements are plainly present in the outcome as written. Check each against the wording before choosing.

questions.stem: A nurse begins a planned bed bath and the patient becomes short of breath and asks to sit forward. He was assessed as stable at the start of the shift. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Continue with the head of the bed raised and monitor him
options.rationale: Near miss concept Better, and it still continues a non-urgent task through an unexplained change in breathing.

options.text: Stop, reassess, and act on the new finding before continuing
options.rationale: Implementation requires ongoing reassessment while performing care. A plan made an hour ago does not override what is happening now.

options.text: Complete the bath quickly so he can rest afterwards
options.rationale: Near miss concept Prioritizes finishing the task over a change in his condition.

options.text: Document that the bath was not tolerated and reschedule it
options.rationale: Near miss concept Records the event and leaves the breathlessness unassessed.

questions.takeaway: Implementation requires ongoing reassessment during care. A change mid-task sends you back to assessment.
questions.strategy: Two distractors continue the task in some form. Ask what has changed since the plan was made.

questions.stem: A nurse gathers her equipment, reviews the steps, and confirms the patient's identity and allergies before starting a procedure she has performed many times. Which principle does this reflect?

options.text: Individualization takes precedence over standardization
options.rationale: Near miss concept A real tension in implementation, and nothing here is being individualized.

options.text: Standard interventions ensure evidence-based care
options.rationale: Near miss concept Standard interventions concern what the care is, not how she readies herself to give it.

options.text: Preparation reduces adverse events
options.rationale: Named directly. Familiarity with a procedure is not a substitute for preparing for this instance of it.

options.text: Care coordination requires appropriate use of resources
options.rationale: Near miss concept Coordination concerns communication, time management and resources across the whole assignment.

questions.takeaway: Preparation reduces adverse events. Care coordination skills are communication, time management, and appropriate use of resources.
questions.strategy: Three distractors name real implementation principles that describe something other than what she did.

questions.stem: 1015: Nurse enters to perform a scheduled dressing change on a 66-year-old, second day after bowel surgery. Supplies gathered and identity confirmed. Patient states the pain is 8 of 10 and he has not had analgesia since 0400. He is diaphoretic. Respiratory rate 24, up from 16 at 0800. Wound edges approximated, no drainage. Temperature 36.9 C. He says he would rather wait. Blood pressure 138/84. Select all of the findings that should stop the nurse proceeding with the dressing change now.

options.text: Pain 8 of 10 with no analgesia since 0400
options.rationale: Six hours without analgesia at 8 of 10. Performing a painful procedure on top of uncontrolled pain is avoidable harm. A finding with several possible causes, none of which should be worked through during a dressing change. A change from his own baseline within two hours. It may be pain, and it may not. The patient declining is sufficient on its own, and here he is also telling you something the numbers support.

options.text: Diaphoretic
options.rationale: Six hours without analgesia at 8 of 10. Performing a painful procedure on top of uncontrolled pain is avoidable harm. A finding with several possible causes, none of which should be worked through during a dressing change. A change from his own baseline within two hours. It may be pain, and it may not. The patient declining is sufficient on its own, and here he is also telling you something the numbers support.

options.text: Respiratory rate 24, up from 16 at 0800
options.rationale: Six hours without analgesia at 8 of 10. Performing a painful procedure on top of uncontrolled pain is avoidable harm. A finding with several possible causes, none of which should be worked through during a dressing change. A change from his own baseline within two hours. It may be pain, and it may not. The patient declining is sufficient on its own, and here he is also telling you something the numbers support.

options.text: He says he would rather wait
options.rationale: Six hours without analgesia at 8 of 10. Performing a painful procedure on top of uncontrolled pain is avoidable harm. A finding with several possible causes, none of which should be worked through during a dressing change. A change from his own baseline within two hours. It may be pain, and it may not. The patient declining is sufficient on its own, and here he is also telling you something the numbers support.

options.text: Wound edges approximated, no drainage
options.rationale: Near miss concept A reassuring finding, and it is why this dressing change is not urgent.

options.text: Temperature 36.9 C
options.rationale: Near miss concept Normal, and it makes infection less likely as the cause of the other findings.

options.text: Blood pressure 138/84
options.rationale: Near miss concept Acceptable, and it does not by itself require action.

options.text: Supplies gathered and identity confirmed
options.rationale: Near miss concept Correct preparation. Preparing well does not oblige you to proceed.

questions.takeaway: Ongoing reassessment during implementation means the plan can be stopped. A prepared nurse is still allowed to change her mind.
questions.strategy: One finding tells you the task is not urgent. Another shows the preparation was correct, which is a reason to feel committed and not a reason to proceed.

questions.stem: A nurse follows a standard turning schedule but adapts it for a patient who cannot lie on his left side after surgery. Which implementation principle does this show?

options.text: Standard interventions provide evidence-based care and must still be individualized
options.rationale: Both halves are named on her slide. The standard gives the evidence base; the individual gives the constraints.

options.text: Nurses should develop an original plan for every patient
options.rationale: Near miss concept Discards the evidence base that standard interventions carry.

options.text: Deviation from a standard requires a provider order
options.rationale: Near miss concept Adapting how nursing care is delivered sits within nursing judgment.

options.text: Standard interventions should be followed exactly to ensure consistency
options.rationale: Near miss concept Removes individualization, which her slide names explicitly as a requirement.

questions.takeaway: Standard interventions help nurses provide evidence-based care, and care should be individualized. Both are required.
questions.strategy: Two distractors take one half of the principle and discard the other.

questions.stem: A nurse hands over a patient whose condition changed during the shift. Which activities are part of implementation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Communicating the change at handoff
options.rationale: Care coordination skills include communication, and handoff is where it matters most. Part of carrying out the plan, and it is how the next nurse can act on what happened. Teaching is an intervention delivered rather than a separate activity. The most visible form of taking action. Named directly. Implementation requires ongoing reassessment.

options.text: Documenting the findings and the care given
options.rationale: Care coordination skills include communication, and handoff is where it matters most. Part of carrying out the plan, and it is how the next nurse can act on what happened. Teaching is an intervention delivered rather than a separate activity. The most visible form of taking action. Named directly. Implementation requires ongoing reassessment.

options.text: Beginning patient and family teaching
options.rationale: Care coordination skills include communication, and handoff is where it matters most. Part of carrying out the plan, and it is how the next nurse can act on what happened. Teaching is an intervention delivered rather than a separate activity. The most visible form of taking action. Named directly. Implementation requires ongoing reassessment.

options.text: Performing the wound care per protocol
options.rationale: Care coordination skills include communication, and handoff is where it matters most. Part of carrying out the plan, and it is how the next nurse can act on what happened. Teaching is an intervention delivered rather than a separate activity. The most visible form of taking action. Named directly. Implementation requires ongoing reassessment.

options.text: Reassessing the patient while performing the care
options.rationale: Care coordination skills include communication, and handoff is where it matters most. Part of carrying out the plan, and it is how the next nurse can act on what happened. Teaching is an intervention delivered rather than a separate activity. The most visible form of taking action. Named directly. Implementation requires ongoing reassessment.

options.text: Writing the expected outcome the care is aimed at
options.rationale: Near miss concept Outcomes are written during planning, before implementation begins.

questions.takeaway: Implementation: carry out the plan, individualize it, reassess while performing care, prepare properly, and coordinate through communication, time management and resources.
questions.strategy: One distractor belongs to the step before. Ask when the outcome was written.

questions.stem: An outcome states that a patient will walk 100 feet twice daily by day four. On day four he walks 60 feet once, having managed 20 feet on day one. Which evaluation is accurate?

options.text: Met, because he has made significant progress
options.rationale: Near miss concept The outcome named 100 feet twice daily. Progress is not the same as achievement.

options.text: Partially met, because he improved substantially without reaching the stated target
options.rationale: Three verdicts exist: met, partially met, not met. Real progress that falls short of the target is what partially met describes.

options.text: Cannot be evaluated until he reaches his baseline
options.rationale: Near miss concept The outcome had a deadline, and day four has arrived.

options.text: Not met, because he did not reach 100 feet twice daily
options.rationale: Near miss concept Technically accurate about the target and it discards a tripling of his distance, which the plan revision needs to know.

questions.takeaway: Evaluation asks whether the goal was met, partially met, or not met, and what data supports that conclusion.
questions.strategy: The middle verdict exists precisely for this situation. Two options collapse it into all or nothing.

questions.stem: A patient's mobility outcome was not met. Which actions does the nurse take when revising the plan? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reassess the patient for new or overlooked data
options.rationale: Named first. Something may have been missed, or may have changed since the plan was written. Named, and it is the step students skip. The plan may be failing because the problem was named wrongly. Named, and sometimes only the deadline was wrong. Named, and it is what most people think of first.

options.text: Reconsider whether the nursing diagnosis is still the priority
options.rationale: Named first. Something may have been missed, or may have changed since the plan was written. Named, and it is the step students skip. The plan may be failing because the problem was named wrongly. Named, and sometimes only the deadline was wrong. Named, and it is what most people think of first.

options.text: Adjust the goal, the outcome, or the target timeframe
options.rationale: Named first. Something may have been missed, or may have changed since the plan was written. Named, and it is the step students skip. The plan may be failing because the problem was named wrongly. Named, and sometimes only the deadline was wrong. Named, and it is what most people think of first.

options.text: Select new or additional interventions
options.rationale: Named first. Something may have been missed, or may have changed since the plan was written. Named, and it is the step students skip. The plan may be failing because the problem was named wrongly. Named, and sometimes only the deadline was wrong. Named, and it is what most people think of first.

options.text: Document that the patient was nonadherent with the mobility plan
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Attributes the failure to the patient and closes the revision before it starts.

options.text: Continue the current plan for a further 48 hours before changing anything
options.rationale: Near miss concept Delays a revision the evaluation has already shown is needed.

questions.takeaway: When an outcome is not met: reassess for new data, reconsider the diagnosis, adjust goals or timeframes, and select new interventions.
questions.strategy: One distractor blames the patient. One waits. Neither is among the four named steps.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old was admitted with pneumonia. An outcome stated he would maintain an oxygen saturation above 92% on room air by day three. On day three his saturation is 89% on room air and 94% on 2 L by nasal cannula. He is completing his antibiotics, his temperature is normal, and his chest sounds have improved. He has been on bed rest since admission and has not mobilized. Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 conclusion she reaches, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Reassess for factors the original plan did not account for
Add mobilization and deep breathing to the plan of care
Document that the outcome was not met and continue the current plan
Extend the target date by a further three days
The outcome was not met, and the plan omitted a contributing factor
The outcome was met, since his saturation is 94%
The outcome was partially met and the plan should continue unchanged
The antibiotic regimen has failed and should be reviewed
Oxygen saturation on room air after mobilization begins
Distance mobilized and frequency of deep breathing exercises
White cell count at the next blood test
Whether he can describe the purpose of deep breathing

questions.takeaway: He needs oxygen to reach 94%, so the outcome as written was not achieved. The infection is treated and the immobility is not. The first step when an outcome is not met. His infection is resolving, so something else is keeping his saturation down. Selecting new or additional interventions. Three days of bed rest is the factor the original plan missed. The original outcome, remeasured under the same conditions, after the new intervention. Measures whether the added intervention is actually happening, which has to be true before it can work. An unmet outcome is information. Reassess for what the plan missed before assuming the plan needs longer.
questions.strategy: The outcome specified room air, which is what makes 94% on oxygen a non-achievement. Two distractors track the infection, which is already resolving.

questions.stem: A nurse evaluates whether a patient met the outcome of demonstrating correct inhaler technique. Which method is appropriate?

options.text: Observe him use the inhaler and compare against the correct steps
options.rationale: A psychomotor outcome is evaluated by watching it performed. Asking whether he understands does not show that he can.

options.text: Ask him to describe the steps in the correct order
options.rationale: Near miss concept The near-miss. Describing shows knowledge; the outcome required performance.

options.text: Confirm that the teaching session was completed and documented
options.rationale: Near miss concept Records what the nurse did. It says nothing about what the patient achieved.

options.text: Ask him whether he feels confident using the inhaler
options.rationale: Near miss concept Confidence is not competence, and the outcome specified demonstration.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate an outcome by the method the outcome specified. Demonstration is evaluated by watching.
questions.strategy: One distractor offers what the nurse did as evidence of what the patient achieved. The near-miss tests knowledge instead of performance.

questions.stem: A nurse admits a 68-year-old whose legs have been swelling for two weeks. For each piece of information gathered during the interview, indicate which component of the nursing health history it belongs to.

rows.text: "I came in because my legs have been swelling for about two weeks"
The swelling worsens through the day and is nearly gone by morning; he has begun stopping halfway up the stairs to catch his breath
Myocardial infarction six years ago; his mother died of heart failure at 70
Lives alone on the second floor with no elevator; his daughter shops for him weekly
Stopped driving last year and now depends on that daughter to reach appointments
Denies headache, visual change, abdominal pain or any change in urination

questions.takeaway: The chief concern is the reason in the patient's own words.
