The present illness is the story of that concern: onset, pattern, and what has come with it, which is where the exertional breathlessness belongs because it is part of the same episode. Past health history reaches back beyond this episode and carries family history with it. Psychosocial history is who he is outside the diagnosis, and it is the component that determines whether a discharge plan can work. Review of systems is the deliberate screen of systems not yet covered, and a documented set of denials is a finding rather than empty space. Exertional breathlessness in a patient presenting with leg swelling is present illness, not review of systems. If it belongs to the same story as the chief concern, it is present illness.
questions.strategy: Two rows are psychosocial, so one row per column will not work. The row most people misplace is the breathlessness: it reads like a respiratory screening item, and it is part of the presenting episode.

questions.stem: A nurse admits a patient for a planned hip replacement. She documents the hip pain, the current medication list, allergies and a full review of systems, then ends the interview. Which omission is most likely to result in a failed discharge?

options.text: Patient expectations
options.rationale: Near miss concept A genuine component, and one students also skip. What a patient expects shapes whether he judges the surgery a success, and it is not what determines whether he can physically manage at home on day three.

options.text: Observation of patient behavior
options.rationale: Near miss concept Part of the history and most valuable where the spoken account and the presentation disagree. This patient's account is not in question.

options.text: Past health history
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Nearly covered already: she took medications and allergies, which is most of what past health history contributes preoperatively, and what it adds bears on the anesthetic rather than on the discharge.

options.text: Psychosocial history
options.rationale: Psychosocial history is where stairs, who is at home, who can help in the first fortnight and what support exists come from. A hip replacement is discharged into a home, and the plan either fits that home or produces a readmission. Discovering on the morning of discharge that the patient lives alone above two flights is not a scheduling problem; it is an assessment that was never done.

questions.takeaway: Ask the discharge questions on admission. By the time discharge arrives the answers can no longer change anything.
questions.strategy: All four are real components, so completeness will not separate them. The stem narrows it to a failed discharge, so test each against one question: does this tell me whether he can manage at home?

questions.stem: Before accessing a needleless connector, what should the nurse do?

options.text: Wipe the hub once with alcohol and connect right away
options.rationale: Near miss concept No friction time and no drying time.

options.text: Scrub the hub with antiseptic for 15 seconds and let it dry
options.rationale: The connector is the doorway into a central vein. Fifteen seconds of friction plus drying time is what removes the organisms sitting on it; a single swipe moves them around. This is one of the highest yield infection prevention steps on a line and one of the most frequently shortcut.

options.text: Flush the line first, then scrub the hub briefly with alcohol before connecting
options.rationale: Near miss concept Flushing through an unscrubbed hub pushes organisms inward.

options.text: Replace the needleless connector before every single use
options.rationale: Near miss concept Connectors are changed on a schedule, not every access, and this does not replace scrubbing.

questions.takeaway: Fifteen seconds of scrubbing, then let it dry. A quick wipe does nothing.
questions.strategy: Two options either shorten the scrub or do something before it.

questions.stem: Select all of the nursing actions when a transfusion reaction is suspected.

options.text: Assess and document vital signs and the patient's symptoms
options.rationale: Stop first, then keep the access with new tubing, because any saline run through the old tubing pushes more blood into the patient. Both wrong options continue the exposure: slowing the rate still gives blood, and flushing the line delivers whatever volume is sitting in it. The unit and tubing go back to the blood bank as evidence.

options.text: Notify the provider and the blood bank and return the unit and tubing
options.rationale: Stop first, then keep the access with new tubing, because any saline run through the old tubing pushes more blood into the patient. Both wrong options continue the exposure: slowing the rate still gives blood, and flushing the line delivers whatever volume is sitting in it. The unit and tubing go back to the blood bank as evidence.

options.text: Keep the intravenous line open with normal saline using new tubing
options.rationale: Stop first, then keep the access with new tubing, because any saline run through the old tubing pushes more blood into the patient. Both wrong options continue the exposure: slowing the rate still gives blood, and flushing the line delivers whatever volume is sitting in it. The unit and tubing go back to the blood bank as evidence.

options.text: Slow the transfusion and continue while monitoring closely
options.rationale: Near miss concept You cannot risk a hemolytic reaction; it stops.

options.text: Stop the transfusion immediately
options.rationale: Stop first, then keep the access with new tubing, because any saline run through the old tubing pushes more blood into the patient. Both wrong options continue the exposure: slowing the rate still gives blood, and flushing the line delivers whatever volume is sitting in it. The unit and tubing go back to the blood bank as evidence.

options.text: Flush the existing blood tubing with saline to clear the line
options.rationale: Near miss concept That pushes the residual blood into the patient.

questions.takeaway: New tubing. Flushing the old line gives him more of the blood you just stopped.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options keep delivering the product the reaction is to.

questions.stem: An order reads 1 unit of packed red blood cells over 3 hours. The unit contains 300 mL and the blood set delivers 10 drops per mL. What is the drip rate?

options.text: 17 drops per minute
options.rationale: 300 mL over 180 minutes is 1.67 mL per minute, times 10 drops per mL gives 16.7, which rounds to 17. Work in minutes, not hours, and round to a whole drop. Remember the other limit on blood: the unit has to be in within 4 hours of leaving the blood bank, so a 3 hour order is already close to the ceiling.

options.text: 33 drops per minute
options.rationale: Near miss concept What you get running the unit over 90 minutes.

options.text: 50 drops per minute
options.rationale: Near miss concept What you get running the unit over 1 hour.

options.text: 10 drops per minute
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is the drop factor, not the rate.

questions.takeaway: Volume over total minutes, times the drop factor. Blood sets are usually 10 drops per mL.
questions.strategy: Most errors here come from dividing by hours instead of minutes, or using a 15 drop factor out of habit.

questions.stem: Match each therapy to the appropriate access device.

rows.text: Two days of isotonic fluid in the emergency department
Total parenteral nutrition for an indefinite period
Intermittent chemotherapy over the next year
Ten days of intravenous antibiotics, non vesicant

questions.takeaway: Four things decide the device: how long the therapy runs, the osmolarity and vesicant status of the solution, the condition of the veins, and the patient's own situation. Ports have the lowest infection risk and suit intermittent long term therapy because there is nothing outside the skin between accesses. A midline suits roughly one to two weeks. Past that, the conversation is about a PICC rather than another peripheral stick.
questions.strategy: Ask how long, how caustic, and how often.

questions.stem: Select all of the instructions for a patient going home with a PICC.

options.text: Cover the site for showering and do not submerge the arm
options.rationale: The dressing is the barrier, so wet or loose means it gets changed. A cuff on that arm can damage the catheter, and a blood draw can shear it. Resistance on flushing means stop and call, because forcing it can dislodge a clot or rupture the line. Heavy lifting over about 10 pounds is restricted on that arm.

options.text: Report fever, chills, redness, swelling or arm pain right away
options.rationale: The dressing is the barrier, so wet or loose means it gets changed. A cuff on that arm can damage the catheter, and a blood draw can shear it. Resistance on flushing means stop and call, because forcing it can dislodge a clot or rupture the line. Heavy lifting over about 10 pounds is restricted on that arm.

options.text: No blood pressure cuffs or blood draws on that arm
options.rationale: The dressing is the barrier, so wet or loose means it gets changed. A cuff on that arm can damage the catheter, and a blood draw can shear it. Resistance on flushing means stop and call, because forcing it can dislodge a clot or rupture the line. Heavy lifting over about 10 pounds is restricted on that arm.

options.text: Flush the line harder if you feel resistance
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dangerous. Resistance means stop and call.

options.text: Keep the dressing clean, dry and intact
options.rationale: The dressing is the barrier, so wet or loose means it gets changed. A cuff on that arm can damage the catheter, and a blood draw can shear it. Resistance on flushing means stop and call, because forcing it can dislodge a clot or rupture the line. Heavy lifting over about 10 pounds is restricted on that arm.

options.text: Lift normally with that arm to maintain strength
options.rationale: Near miss concept Heavy lifting with that arm is restricted.

questions.takeaway: Resistance means stop. Never force a flush.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options apply force to a catheter that is telling you not to.

questions.stem: Select all of the sites the nurse should avoid for a short peripheral intravenous catheter.

options.text: A paralyzed extremity
options.rationale: Avoid an arm with compromised lymphatic drainage, a dialysis access you could destroy, a limb that cannot report pain or move, and anything downstream of a site that already failed. Also avoid the antecubital fossa for short peripheral lines and the lower extremities in adults. The forearm is the preferred territory.

options.text: The arm on the side of a previous mastectomy with node dissection
options.rationale: Avoid an arm with compromised lymphatic drainage, a dialysis access you could destroy, a limb that cannot report pain or move, and anything downstream of a site that already failed. Also avoid the antecubital fossa for short peripheral lines and the lower extremities in adults. The forearm is the preferred territory.

options.text: A site distal to a previous infiltration
options.rationale: Avoid an arm with compromised lymphatic drainage, a dialysis access you could destroy, a limb that cannot report pain or move, and anything downstream of a site that already failed. Also avoid the antecubital fossa for short peripheral lines and the lower extremities in adults. The forearm is the preferred territory.

options.text: An arm with an arteriovenous fistula
options.rationale: Avoid an arm with compromised lymphatic drainage, a dialysis access you could destroy, a limb that cannot report pain or move, and anything downstream of a site that already failed. Also avoid the antecubital fossa for short peripheral lines and the lower extremities in adults. The forearm is the preferred territory.

options.text: A soft, straight, resilient vein in the forearm
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit This is what you are palpating for.

options.text: The forearm cephalic vein on the nondominant arm
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit The preferred location, not one to avoid.

questions.takeaway: Go distal first and move proximally on the next attempt, so you never work below a vein you already used.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options describe exactly the site you want.

questions.stem: A patient becomes flushed with a pounding headache and chest tightness moments after an intravenous medication is given. What happened and what prevents it?

options.text: An allergic reaction, prevented by premedicating with an antihistamine
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would more typically bring urticaria, wheeze or angioedema.

options.text: Speed shock from too rapid a rate, prevented by a pump and rate check
options.rationale: Speed shock is a systemic reaction to a drug hitting the circulation faster than the body can distribute it: flushing, headache, chest tightness, and then shock. The prevention is mechanical. Use a pump, confirm the rate before you start, and never bolus a concentrated medication.

options.text: Infiltration of the drug into tissue, prevented by checking for a blood return first
options.rationale: Near miss concept A local problem at the site, not a systemic reaction.

options.text: An air embolism, prevented by fully priming the tubing before use
options.rationale: Near miss concept Brings sudden dyspnea and hypotension rather than flushing and headache.

questions.takeaway: The rate is part of the order. Giving the right drug too fast is still a medication error.
questions.strategy: Timing is the clue: moments after, with no rash and no respiratory obstruction.

questions.stem: Select all of the measures that reduce central line associated bloodstream infection.

options.text: Review the necessity of the line daily and advocate for removal when it is no longer needed
options.rationale: The bundle is hand hygiene, hub disinfection, dressing integrity and daily review of necessity, and the last one is the most powerful because a line that is out cannot become infected. Letting the antiseptic dry is what makes it work. A damp or loose dressing is a problem before it is soiled, and every extra entry into the line is another chance to introduce organisms.

options.text: Scrub the hub with the approved antiseptic and let it dry
options.rationale: The bundle is hand hygiene, hub disinfection, dressing integrity and daily review of necessity, and the last one is the most powerful because a line that is out cannot become infected. Letting the antiseptic dry is what makes it work. A damp or loose dressing is a problem before it is soiled, and every extra entry into the line is another chance to introduce organisms.

options.text: Change the dressing on schedule and whenever it is damp, loose or soiled
options.rationale: The bundle is hand hygiene, hub disinfection, dressing integrity and daily review of necessity, and the last one is the most powerful because a line that is out cannot become infected. Letting the antiseptic dry is what makes it work. A damp or loose dressing is a problem before it is soiled, and every extra entry into the line is another chance to introduce organisms.

options.text: Change the dressing only when it is visibly soiled
options.rationale: Near miss concept Damp or loose is enough; a compromised dressing is a portal.

options.text: Perform hand hygiene before every access
options.rationale: The bundle is hand hygiene, hub disinfection, dressing integrity and daily review of necessity, and the last one is the most powerful because a line that is out cannot become infected. Letting the antiseptic dry is what makes it work. A damp or loose dressing is a problem before it is soiled, and every extra entry into the line is another chance to introduce organisms.

options.text: Use the central line for all blood draws to spare the patient's veins
options.rationale: Near miss concept Each access is another infection opportunity; minimize entries.

questions.takeaway: The strongest prevention is getting the line out. Ask every day whether it is still needed.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options reduce work at the cost of extra risk.

questions.stem: After inserting a peripheral intravenous catheter, what should the nurse document?

options.text: Insertion time, the patient's name and the solution started
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome Minimal, and it leaves out everything clinically useful.

options.text: Site, gauge, attempts, vein condition, dressing and tolerance
options.rationale: The next nurse needs to know what is in the patient, where, how old it is and how hard it was to get. Number of attempts matters because it predicts the next insertion and flags a patient who needs ultrasound or a vascular access consult early rather than after six more sticks.

options.text: The solution hanging, the rate and the pump settings used
options.rationale: Near miss concept Part of the infusion record and not the insertion record.

options.text: That the procedure was completed without any difficulty
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting An evaluation with no data behind it.

questions.takeaway: Record the number of attempts. It is the field that saves the patient the next six sticks.
questions.strategy: Three options document that something happened rather than what was done.

questions.stem: Select all of the practices that make intravenous therapy safer.

options.text: Label all lines and tubing with the drug and the date
options.rationale: Tracing the line is the habit that prevents a wrong route error, and labeling is what makes tracing possible on a patient with six infusions. Vesicants go through the most reliable access available, generally a central line, not the most distal small vein. Potassium is never given by push, which is one of a very small number of absolute never rules in medication administration.

options.text: Use a smart pump with the drug library and respond to alerts rather than overriding them
options.rationale: Tracing the line is the habit that prevents a wrong route error, and labeling is what makes tracing possible on a patient with six infusions. Vesicants go through the most reliable access available, generally a central line, not the most distal small vein. Potassium is never given by push, which is one of a very small number of absolute never rules in medication administration.

options.text: Choose the most distal peripheral vein available for a vesicant to limit vein damage
options.rationale: Near miss concept A vesicant needs the most secure access available, usually central; a small distal vein is the worst place for it.

options.text: Verify compatibility before infusing two medications through one line
options.rationale: Tracing the line is the habit that prevents a wrong route error, and labeling is what makes tracing possible on a patient with six infusions. Vesicants go through the most reliable access available, generally a central line, not the most distal small vein. Potassium is never given by push, which is one of a very small number of absolute never rules in medication administration.

options.text: Trace the line from the bag to the patient before any infusion change
options.rationale: Tracing the line is the habit that prevents a wrong route error, and labeling is what makes tracing possible on a patient with six infusions. Vesicants go through the most reliable access available, generally a central line, not the most distal small vein. Potassium is never given by push, which is one of a very small number of absolute never rules in medication administration.

options.text: Infuse potassium chloride by rapid intravenous push for a critically low level
options.rationale: Absolute language Always diluted and infused by pump; push is fatal.

questions.takeaway: Potassium is never pushed. That rule has no exception and it kills people when it is broken.
questions.strategy: One wrong option picks the worst site for a vesicant; the other violates an absolute rule.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses an intravenous site and finds redness tracking up the vein with warmth and a palpable cord. Which complication is this, and what is the grading scale based on?

options.text: Extravasation, graded by the volume of vesicant that escaped
options.rationale: Near miss concept Extravasation is infiltration of a vesicant; nothing here says vesicant.

options.text: Thrombosis, graded by how much the infusion flow has slowed
options.rationale: Near miss concept Thrombosis gives a swollen painful limb with reduced flow, not a surface streak.

options.text: Phlebitis, graded 0 to 4 by the streak and a palpable cord
options.rationale: Phlebitis is inflammation of the vein wall: red, warm, painful, with a streak along the vein and eventually a palpable cord. Grade 4 adds a cord longer than an inch with purulent drainage. It can be mechanical from catheter movement, chemical from an irritating solution, or bacterial from poor asepsis. Infiltration is the cool pale swollen one, graded by edema.

options.text: Infiltration, graded 0 to 4 by the amount of edema and the skin changes
options.rationale: Near miss concept Correct description of infiltration and its scale, applied to the wrong findings.

questions.takeaway: Red, warm and streaking is the vein. Cool, pale and swollen is the tissue.
questions.strategy: Two complications, two scales, two opposite sets of findings.

questions.stem: Which infusion task may the registered nurse delegate to assistive personnel?

options.text: Assessing the patient's response to the infusion
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Interpretation and clinical judgment, which never move.

options.text: Reporting the appearance of the intravenous site
options.rationale: Assistive personnel take vital signs, report what a site looks like and attend to comfort. Flushing an established line, hanging non high alert fluids and, in many states, peripheral insertion may go to an LPN or LVN where the practice act allows. What never moves is assessment, interpretation, teaching, starting blood products and titrating high alert drugs. The registered nurse keeps accountability regardless of who performed the task.

options.text: Hanging a bag of maintenance fluid
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Also within LPN scope in many states, and above assistive personnel.

options.text: Flushing an established peripheral line
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope An LPN or LVN task where the practice act allows, not assistive personnel.

questions.takeaway: They can tell you what it looks like. You decide what it means.
questions.strategy: Two of the wrong options belong to the LPN, not the assistive personnel, which is the distinction being tested.

questions.stem: An order reads 1,000 mL of 0.9 percent sodium chloride over 8 hours. The administration set delivers 15 drops per mL. What is the drip rate?

options.text: 21 drops per minute
options.rationale: Near miss concept What you get with a drop factor of 10 instead of 15.

options.text: 15 drops per minute
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is the drop factor itself, not the rate.

options.text: 63 drops per minute
options.rationale: Near miss concept Double the correct answer, from using 4 hours.

options.text: 31 drops per minute
options.rationale: Volume divided by time in minutes, multiplied by the drop factor. 1,000 mL over 480 minutes is 2.08 mL per minute; times 15 drops per mL gives 31.25, which rounds to 31 drops per minute. Round to a whole drop, because you cannot count a fraction of one.

questions.takeaway: Total volume divided by total minutes, times the drop factor. Round to a whole drop.
questions.strategy: Work in minutes, not hours. The most common error is dividing by 8 instead of 480.

questions.stem: Select all of the requirements before starting a unit of packed red blood cells.

options.text: Baseline vital signs recorded before the infusion begins
options.rationale: Two nurse verification of the label against the band, the ABO and Rh type, the unit number and the expiration date. An 18 to 20 gauge line so the cells flow without hemolyzing. Normal saline only. Baseline vitals, recheck at 15 minutes, then every 30 to 60 minutes. Each unit goes in within 4 hours.

options.text: Two licensed nurses independently verify the product against the patient's identification band
options.rationale: Two nurse verification of the label against the band, the ABO and Rh type, the unit number and the expiration date. An 18 to 20 gauge line so the cells flow without hemolyzing. Normal saline only. Baseline vitals, recheck at 15 minutes, then every 30 to 60 minutes. Each unit goes in within 4 hours.

options.text: Lactated Ringer solution primed through the tubing
options.rationale: Near miss concept The calcium in lactated Ringer can clot the blood in the line.

options.text: An 18 to 20 gauge intravenous catheter
options.rationale: Two nurse verification of the label against the band, the ABO and Rh type, the unit number and the expiration date. An 18 to 20 gauge line so the cells flow without hemolyzing. Normal saline only. Baseline vitals, recheck at 15 minutes, then every 30 to 60 minutes. Each unit goes in within 4 hours.

options.text: The unit infused over no more than 6 hours
options.rationale: Near miss concept Four hours. Past that the unit is a bacterial growth medium at room temperature.

options.text: 0.9 percent sodium chloride as the only compatible solution
options.rationale: Two nurse verification of the label against the band, the ABO and Rh type, the unit number and the expiration date. An 18 to 20 gauge line so the cells flow without hemolyzing. Normal saline only. Baseline vitals, recheck at 15 minutes, then every 30 to 60 minutes. Each unit goes in within 4 hours.

questions.takeaway: Saline only, 4 hours maximum, two nurses at the bedside.
questions.strategy: The two wrong options each change one number or one solution, which is exactly how a real error happens.

questions.stem: Classify each solution as it is listed on the course slides.

rows.text: Lactated Ringer solution
0.225 percent sodium chloride
10 percent dextrose in water
5 percent dextrose in water
5 percent dextrose in 0.9 percent sodium chloride
0.45 percent sodium chloride

questions.takeaway: Classify by the slide's lists, not by the number. Lactated Ringer sits at about 273 mOsm per L, just under the 275 to 295 plasma range on one slide, but every source calls it isotonic. D5W is listed as isotonic in the bag even though it acts hypotonic in the body. Adding dextrose to saline or Ringer makes the bag hypertonic, so D5NS and D5LR sit with 3 percent sodium chloride and D10W. Isotonic: NS, LR, D5W. Hypotonic: 0.45 and 0.225 NS. Hypertonic: 3 percent NaCl, D10W, D5NS, D5LR.
questions.strategy: The two that trip students are LR, which the number calls hypotonic, and D5NS, which sounds like plain saline.

questions.stem: An order reads 1,200 mL of 0.9 percent sodium chloride over 24 hours. No pump is available, so the nurse uses a microdrip set that delivers 60 drops per mL. What is the drip rate?

options.text: 20 drops per minute
options.rationale: Near miss concept This divides 1,200 by 60 without using the time correctly; with a 60 drop set the answer must equal the mL per hour.

options.text: 12 drops per minute
options.rationale: Near miss concept This uses a 15 drop per mL factor or drops the conversion; with microdrip the answer equals the mL per hour.

options.text: 50 drops per minute
options.rationale: 1,200 mL over 24 hours is 50 mL per hour. With microdrip, 1,200 times 60 divided by 1,440 minutes is 50 drops per minute. Because a microdrip set delivers 60 drops per mL and an hour has 60 minutes, the two 60s cancel and drops per minute always equals mL per hour.

options.text: 3,000 drops per minute
options.rationale: Near miss concept This multiplies by 60 drops per mL but divides by hours instead of minutes.

questions.takeaway: Microdrip: drops per minute equals mL per hour.
questions.strategy: Work the pump rate first; with a 60 drop set it is already your answer, and it checks your math.

questions.stem: Select all of the statements about blood product handling that are correct.

options.text: Platelets are stored at room temperature
options.rationale: Each product has its own clock: packed red cells within 4 hours of issue, FFP within 24 hours of thawing, cryoprecipitate within 6 hours. Platelets are stored at room temperature, not refrigerated. Blood runs only with normal saline because D5W lyses red cells, and no drug ever goes into the bag.

options.text: Fresh frozen plasma is given within 24 hours of thawing
options.rationale: Each product has its own clock: packed red cells within 4 hours of issue, FFP within 24 hours of thawing, cryoprecipitate within 6 hours. Platelets are stored at room temperature, not refrigerated. Blood runs only with normal saline because D5W lyses red cells, and no drug ever goes into the bag.

options.text: The 4 hour limit on a unit of packed red cells starts when the unit is hung
options.rationale: Near miss concept The clock starts at issue from the blood bank, so time spent walking and checking counts.

options.text: An ordered antibiotic may be added to the blood bag to save a second line
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nothing is ever added to blood.

options.text: Cryoprecipitate is given within 6 hours
options.rationale: Each product has its own clock: packed red cells within 4 hours of issue, FFP within 24 hours of thawing, cryoprecipitate within 6 hours. Platelets are stored at room temperature, not refrigerated. Blood runs only with normal saline because D5W lyses red cells, and no drug ever goes into the bag.

options.text: 5 percent dextrose in water may be used to flush a blood set
options.rationale: Near miss concept D5W hemolyzes red cells; 0.9 percent sodium chloride is the only fluid with blood.

questions.takeaway: Red cells 4 hours from issue, FFP 24 hours from thaw, cryo 6 hours, platelets at room temperature.
questions.strategy: The hung versus issued wording is the near miss; read when each clock starts.

questions.stem: Four patients have central access. Which device carries the highest risk of catheter related bloodstream infection?

options.text: An implanted port accessed with a Huber needle
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit The port has the lowest infection risk because nothing sits outside the skin between accesses.

options.text: A nontunneled central venous catheter
options.rationale: On the sheet, the nontunneled CVC has the highest CRBSI risk and the implanted port the lowest, accessed with a Huber needle. The more direct the path from skin to vein, the easier it is for organisms to follow it.

options.text: A PICC in the upper arm
options.rationale: Near miss concept A PICC is central, but the sheet singles out the nontunneled CVC as highest risk.

options.text: A tunneled central venous catheter
options.rationale: Near miss concept Tunneling puts distance between the skin and the vein; it lowers risk compared with a nontunneled line.

questions.takeaway: Nontunneled CVC highest risk; implanted port lowest.
questions.strategy: Rank by the distance and barrier between the skin and the vein.

questions.topic: preventing air embolism at central line removal
questions.stem: A nurse is removing a nontunneled central venous catheter. Select all of the actions that prevent air embolism or confirm a safe removal.
questions.objective: preventing air embolism at central line removal

options.text: Position the patient flat
options.rationale: Flat positioning and breath holding raise the pressure in the central veins at the moment the catheter comes out, so air is pushed away rather than pulled in. An occlusive dressing seals the tract. Checking the tip confirms nothing was left behind.

options.text: Have the patient sit upright with the legs dangling
options.rationale: Near miss concept Upright lowers the pressure in the central veins and makes it easier for air to be drawn in.

options.text: Have the patient hold the breath as the catheter is withdrawn
options.rationale: Flat positioning and breath holding raise the pressure in the central veins at the moment the catheter comes out, so air is pushed away rather than pulled in. An occlusive dressing seals the tract. Checking the tip confirms nothing was left behind.

options.text: Cover the site with an occlusive dressing
options.rationale: Flat positioning and breath holding raise the pressure in the central veins at the moment the catheter comes out, so air is pushed away rather than pulled in. An occlusive dressing seals the tract. Checking the tip confirms nothing was left behind.

options.text: Check that the catheter tip came out intact
options.rationale: Flat positioning and breath holding raise the pressure in the central veins at the moment the catheter comes out, so air is pushed away rather than pulled in. An occlusive dressing seals the tract. Checking the tip confirms nothing was left behind.

options.text: Cover the site with a dry gauze dressing so it can breathe
options.rationale: Near miss concept A breathable dressing leaves a path for air to enter the vein; the dressing must be occlusive.

questions.takeaway: CVC out: flat, hold the breath, occlusive dressing, tip intact.
questions.strategy: Any option that lets air near the open vein is wrong.

questions.stem: A nurse removed a peripheral IV for infiltration. Which entry is the best documentation?

options.text: 1400: Left hand site cool, pale, 3 cm edema. Stopped, removed intact, elevated. Grade 2. Provider notified.
options.rationale: A complication note records what you saw, what you did and the result: the site findings, the grade, the interventions, that the catheter came out intact and who was notified. At removal you always document the time, site appearance, tip intact and the patient's tolerance.

options.text: 1400: IV infiltrated in left hand and was removed per protocol. Will restart in other arm when able.
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism This entry has no assessment data, grade, actions taken or notification.

options.text: 1400: Patient complained of IV pain and swelling in left hand. IV removed per protocol. Patient comfortable.
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data It records the complaint and removal but not the findings, grade, elevation or notification.

options.text: 1400: Infiltration grade 2 in left hand. Catheter removed. Patient tolerated removal well. Will monitor site.
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism It gives a grade without the findings that support it and omits the actions and notification.

questions.takeaway: Findings, grade, actions, tip intact, who was notified.
questions.strategy: The best note lets the next nurse picture the site without seeing it.

questions.stem: A nurse is starting an intravenous line on an 86 year old with thin skin and fragile veins. Which approach is best?

options.text: Use an 18 gauge catheter so a second attempt is less likely
options.rationale: Near miss concept A large catheter in a fragile vein is what causes the second attempt.

options.text: Apply a cold compress to make the vein stand out more clearly
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cold constricts. Warmth dilates.

options.text: Use a 22 or 24 gauge, a loose tourniquet and gentle traction
options.rationale: Older veins roll, and older skin tears. The smallest effective gauge, a loose tourniquet and gentle traction to anchor the vein reduce both problems. Warm compresses dilate; cold does the opposite. Dorsal hand veins are avoided when possible because the skin there is thinnest and the vein is least supported.

options.text: Use a dorsal hand vein, since it is easiest to see and reach
options.rationale: Near miss concept Visible and the worst supported, with the thinnest skin over it.

questions.takeaway: Smallest gauge that does the job, and warmth rather than cold.
questions.strategy: The gauge option is seductive: bigger is not more reliable in a vein that will blow.

questions.stem: A patient is to receive total parenteral nutrition with an osmolarity of 1,100 mOsm per L. Which access is appropriate?

options.text: A midline catheter in the upper arm
options.rationale: Near miss concept Long dwell time, and the tip still ends in a peripheral vein, so no vesicants and no parenteral nutrition.

options.text: A 20 gauge short peripheral intravenous catheter in the forearm
options.rationale: Near miss concept Well over the roughly 900 mOsm per L peripheral limit; this sclerose the vein.

options.text: A 22 gauge catheter in the dorsal hand, rotated every 72 hours
options.rationale: Near miss concept Smaller and more fragile, and rotation does not raise the osmolarity limit.

options.text: A central venous access device such as a PICC
options.rationale: Osmolarity decides the device. Short peripheral lines take solutions under about 900 mOsm per L, midlines under about 600, and anything above that needs a central tip sitting in high flow blood that dilutes it immediately. Total parenteral nutrition and vesicants are central line therapy. A PICC is a central line even though it is inserted peripherally, because the tip defines the category.

questions.takeaway: The tip location decides central versus peripheral, not where the needle went in.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options are peripheral devices with longer dwell times, which is not the same as tolerating a higher osmolarity.

questions.stem: A patient in cardiac arrest has no intravenous access after repeated attempts. What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Waiting for a central line to be placed before any medication is given
options.rationale: Correct but premature Minutes the patient does not have.

options.text: Administering medications by the intramuscular route instead
options.rationale: Near miss concept Absorption depends on perfusion, which has stopped.

options.text: Subcutaneous hypodermoclysis for rapid volume replacement
options.rationale: Near miss concept About 1 mL per minute, for mild dehydration in a stable patient.

options.text: Intraosseous access, which can deliver all intravenous fluids, medications and blood products
options.rationale: The marrow cavity is a non collapsible vein. Intraosseous access goes in within seconds at the proximal tibia, distal femur or humeral head, takes everything an intravenous line takes, and is limited to about 24 hours. Hypodermoclysis is slow and suits mild dehydration in a stable patient, which is the opposite of an arrest.

questions.takeaway: In an arrest, intraosseous beats waiting for a central line.
questions.strategy: Two options deliver drugs through tissue that is not being perfused during an arrest.

questions.stem: A nurse preps an intravenous site with chlorhexidine. Which action is correct?

options.text: Apply it, let it dry, then repalpate the vein with a gloved finger to confirm landmarks
options.rationale: Near miss concept Recontaminates the site with an unsterile finger.

options.text: Scrub back and forth for 30 seconds and let it air dry completely
options.rationale: Chlorhexidine works through mechanical friction plus contact time. Scrubbing back and forth lifts organisms out of the skin; full air drying is when the antimicrobial effect actually happens. Do not blot, do not fan, and do not repalpate after prepping, because an unsterile finger undoes all of it.

options.text: Apply in circles from the center outward, then blot dry with gauze
options.rationale: Near miss concept The circular technique belongs to povidone iodine, and blotting removes the antiseptic.

options.text: Apply it and fan the area to speed drying before inserting
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cuts the contact time the prep depends on.

questions.takeaway: Friction, then full drying, then nothing touches it.
questions.strategy: Three wrong options each shortcut one of the three requirements.

questions.stem: A patient with severe hyponatremia and confusion has an order for 3 percent sodium chloride. Which nursing action is most important?

options.text: Infuse it by gravity so the rate can be adjusted at the bedside
options.rationale: Near miss concept Gravity rates drift; 3 percent sodium chloride is given only by pump and protocol.

options.text: Use a pump per protocol; monitor sodium, neuro status and lungs
options.rationale: Hypertonic fluid pulls water out of cells into the vessels, so it can shrink swollen brain cells but also overload the circulation and push sodium too high. That is why it runs by pump and protocol, with sodium, neurologic status and lung sounds watched. Correct slowly: too fast a rise causes osmotic demyelination, a permanent brain injury.

options.text: Run it rapidly to correct the sodium before confusion worsens
options.rationale: Most dramatic finding The confusion pulls you toward speed, but correcting sodium too fast causes permanent brain injury.

options.text: Hold it until the sodium falls further, reserving it for seizures
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Withholding an ordered therapy because of your own threshold is not the nurse's call; severe hyponatremia with confusion is the indication.

questions.takeaway: 3 percent sodium chloride: pump, protocol, slow correction.
questions.strategy: The urgent sounding option is the trap when the therapy itself is dangerous at speed.

questions.stem: A patient has an order for 1 unit of packed red blood cells. Place the nursing actions in order.

options.text: Obtain baseline temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure and SpO2
Confirm the order and that the type and crossmatch are done
Stay with the patient for the first 15 minutes and recheck vital signs at 15 minutes
Confirm written consent is on file
Two licensed nurses match the unit to the ID band at the bedside and both sign
Start an 18 to 20 gauge IV and prime a filter blood set with 0.9 percent sodium chloride

questions.takeaway: Everything before the two nurse check happens before the blood leaves the bank, because each unit must be finished within 4 hours of issue and the clock starts at issue, not at hanging. Consent and baseline vital signs come first so a later change can be recognized as a reaction. The first 15 minutes are when the worst reactions show, so you stay. Consent, access and baseline vital signs before you pick up the blood.
questions.strategy: Ask which steps can happen while the blood is still in the bank. Those all go first.

questions.stem: A patient with a hemoglobin of 7.1 g per dL receives 2 units of packed red blood cells with no reaction. Which posttransfusion hemoglobin does the nurse expect?

options.text: About 7.5 g per dL
options.rationale: Near miss concept This expects almost no rise; each unit raises hemoglobin about 1 g per dL.

options.text: About 13 g per dL
options.rationale: Near miss concept This assumes about 3 g per dL per unit, which overstates the response.

options.text: About 9 g per dL
options.rationale: Each unit of packed red cells raises hemoglobin about 1 g per dL, so 2 units should bring 7.1 to about 9. A much smaller rise than expected is a finding worth reporting, because it suggests ongoing loss or destruction.

options.text: About 11 g per dL
options.rationale: Near miss concept This doubles the expected rise per unit.

questions.takeaway: One unit, about 1 g per dL.
questions.strategy: Know the expected response so you can recognize the unexpected one.

questions.stem: A nurse has just started a unit of packed red blood cells and is called to another patient's room. Which action is appropriate?

options.text: Stay for the first 15 minutes and ask another nurse to go
options.rationale: The first 15 minutes are when the most dangerous reactions appear, so the RN stays, then takes vital signs at 15 minutes and every 30 to 60 minutes after. Identifying a reaction is assessment, and assessment is not delegated.

options.text: Have assistive personnel sit with the patient and report changes
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Watching for a reaction is assessment, which stays with the RN and cannot go to assistive personnel.

options.text: Slow the transfusion rate until the nurse is able to come back to the room
options.rationale: Near miss concept A slower rate does not prevent a reaction, and it eats into the 4 hour window that started at issue.

options.text: Ask the patient to use the call light if symptoms develop
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome A patient cannot be relied on to recognize early hypotension or a rising temperature.

questions.takeaway: The RN watches the first 15 minutes. Nobody else.
questions.strategy: Delegation questions turn on one word: is the task assessment? If yes, it stays with the RN.

questions.stem: A nurse has made two unsuccessful attempts to start a peripheral IV in a patient's left forearm. What should the nurse do next?

options.text: Try a third time in a vein distal to the failed attempts
options.rationale: Near miss concept Distal first is right for a first stick, but a new puncture below an old one leaks out of the old hole, and the attempt limit is already reached.

options.text: Escalate to another skilled clinician or the vascular access team
options.rationale: Limit yourself to two attempts, then escalate. Each further stick damages veins the patient may need later. When you do start, begin with the most distal appropriate vein and move up the arm, because a new IV above an old puncture will not leak out of the old hole.

options.text: Try the antecubital fossa, since the vein is larger
options.rationale: Near miss concept The antecubital fossa is avoided for short peripheral lines, and the attempt limit still applies.

options.text: Try a third time in the right forearm, since it has not been used
options.rationale: Correct but premature A fresh arm is tempting, but the limit is two attempts, then you escalate.

questions.takeaway: Two attempts, then escalate.
questions.strategy: The fresh arm option is the trap: it sounds reasonable, but the rule is about attempts, not arms.

questions.stem: After cleaning the IV site with chlorhexidine, what should the nurse do?

options.text: Blot it dry with sterile gauze.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Blotting removes the antiseptic.

options.text: Fan it dry to speed it up.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fanning can contaminate the site.

options.text: Repalpate the vein to confirm it.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Repalpating contaminates the prepared site.

options.text: Let it air dry without touching.
options.rationale: Chlorhexidine is scrubbed back and forth for 30 seconds, then left to air dry with no blotting or fanning. The site is not repalpated after the prep.

questions.takeaway: Do not repalpate after the skin prep.
questions.strategy: Reject anything that touches the prepared site.

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate the complication.

rows.text: Sudden dyspnea, chest pain and a mill wheel murmur
Warm, red site with a red streak and a palpable cord
Flushing, headache and chest tightness after a drug was pushed too fast
Cool, pale, swollen site with a slow drip

questions.takeaway: Infiltration is cool and pale; phlebitis is warm and red. Air embolism causes sudden dyspnea, chest pain, low blood pressure and a mill wheel murmur. Speed shock follows a drug given too fast. Infiltration is cool; phlebitis is warm.
questions.strategy: Use temperature and color to separate the local complications.

questions.stem: For each statement, indicate the device it describes.

rows.text: Tip in the lower superior vena cava and confirmed by x ray before first use
Accessed only with a noncoring needle
Placed in the proximal tibia when no vein can be found in an emergency
Tip ends below the axilla and vesicants are not given

questions.takeaway: A midline is not central and cannot take vesicants. A PICC is central with its tip in the lower SVC. An implanted port has the lowest infection risk and uses only a noncoring (Huber) needle. Intraosseous access is for emergencies, up to 24 hours. Tip location defines central.
questions.strategy: Ask where the tip ends for each device.

questions.stem: Why is 5% dextrose in water not used as a volume expander?

options.text: It is hypertonic and pulls water out of the cells.
options.rationale: Near miss concept D5W is isotonic in the bag and acts hypotonic in the body.

options.text: It causes the red blood cells to clump and clot.
options.rationale: Near miss concept D5W hemolyzes red cells, which is why it is never used with blood, but that is not why it fails as a volume expander.

options.text: Cells use the dextrose, leaving water that enters cells.
options.rationale: D5W is isotonic in the bag but acts hypotonic: dextrose is metabolized and free water enters cells. It is not a volume expander and is avoided with increased ICP.

options.text: It raises the blood glucose too high to be safe.
options.rationale: Near miss concept The main issue is where the water goes.

questions.takeaway: D5W is isotonic in the bag, hypotonic in the body.
questions.strategy: Follow what happens to the dextrose once it is in the body.

questions.stem: For each IV solution, indicate its tonicity.

rows.text: 0.9% sodium chloride
0.45% sodium chloride
3% sodium chloride
10% dextrose in water
Lactated Ringer solution

questions.takeaway: Isotonic fluids (0.9% NaCl, LR, D5W in the bag) stay in the vessels. Hypotonic fluids (0.45% and 0.225% NaCl) move water into cells. Hypertonic fluids (3% NaCl, D10W, D5NS, D5LR) pull water out of cells into the vessels. Isotonic stays, hypotonic goes in, hypertonic pulls out.
questions.strategy: Compare each solution with the body's own concentration.

questions.stem: A piggyback of 50 mL is to infuse over 30 minutes by gravity with a 10 gtt/mL set. What is the drip rate?

options.text: 167 gtt/min
options.rationale: Near miss concept This forgets to divide by minutes correctly.

options.text: 100 gtt/min
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is the pump rate in mL/hr, not drops per minute.

options.text: 5 gtt/min
options.rationale: Near miss concept This multiplies and divides in the wrong order.

options.text: 17 gtt/min
options.rationale: gtt/min = volume × drop factor ÷ minutes = 50 × 10 ÷ 30 = 16.7, rounded to 17 gtt/min.

questions.takeaway: Gravity: volume × drop factor ÷ minutes.
questions.strategy: Convert time to minutes for gravity math.

questions.stem: Select all sites the nurse should avoid when starting a peripheral IV.

options.text: A distal forearm vein in the nondominant arm
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Starting distal in the nondominant arm is correct.

options.text: The arm on the side of a mastectomy
options.rationale: Avoid the mastectomy or lymph node removal side, an AV fistula arm, a paralyzed limb, sites below a previous infiltration or phlebitis, the antecubital fossa for short IVs and legs in adults. Start distal and move proximal.

options.text: A paralyzed limb
options.rationale: Avoid the mastectomy or lymph node removal side, an AV fistula arm, a paralyzed limb, sites below a previous infiltration or phlebitis, the antecubital fossa for short IVs and legs in adults. Start distal and move proximal.

options.text: An arm with a dialysis fistula
options.rationale: Avoid the mastectomy or lymph node removal side, an AV fistula arm, a paralyzed limb, sites below a previous infiltration or phlebitis, the antecubital fossa for short IVs and legs in adults. Start distal and move proximal.

options.text: A site below a previous infiltration
options.rationale: Avoid the mastectomy or lymph node removal side, an AV fistula arm, a paralyzed limb, sites below a previous infiltration or phlebitis, the antecubital fossa for short IVs and legs in adults. Start distal and move proximal.

options.text: A straight forearm cephalic vein
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Soft, straight forearm veins are preferred.

questions.takeaway: Start distal, move proximal.
questions.strategy: Eliminate any site with impaired flow, sensation or a fragile vein downstream.

questions.stem: Select all actions the nurse takes before picking up a unit of packed red blood cells.

options.text: Insert or confirm an 18 to 20 gauge IV
options.rationale: Before pickup: consent, type and crossmatch, an 18 to 20 gauge IV and filtered Y tubing primed with 0.9% NaCl only. Baseline vital signs are taken before starting.

options.text: Prime the tubing with lactated Ringer solution
options.rationale: Near miss concept The calcium in LR clots the unit.

options.text: Prime filtered Y tubing with 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Before pickup: consent, type and crossmatch, an 18 to 20 gauge IV and filtered Y tubing primed with 0.9% NaCl only. Baseline vital signs are taken before starting.

options.text: Prime the tubing with D5W
options.rationale: Near miss concept D5W hemolyzes red cells.

options.text: Confirm signed consent
options.rationale: Before pickup: consent, type and crossmatch, an 18 to 20 gauge IV and filtered Y tubing primed with 0.9% NaCl only. Baseline vital signs are taken before starting.

options.text: Confirm the type and crossmatch
options.rationale: Before pickup: consent, type and crossmatch, an 18 to 20 gauge IV and filtered Y tubing primed with 0.9% NaCl only. Baseline vital signs are taken before starting.

questions.takeaway: 0.9% sodium chloride is the only fluid with blood.
questions.strategy: Eliminate any fluid other than normal saline.

questions.stem: Before accessing a central line, how long should the nurse scrub the needleless connector?

options.text: At least 15 seconds
options.rationale: The needleless connector is scrubbed for at least 15 seconds before every access.

options.text: A quick wipe of 2 seconds
options.rationale: Near miss concept A quick wipe does not disinfect the connector.

options.text: 30 seconds with chlorhexidine, then blot dry
options.rationale: Near miss concept The connector scrub is at least 15 seconds and is not blotted.

options.text: No scrub if the cap is new
options.rationale: Near miss concept Every access needs a scrub.

questions.takeaway: Scrub the hub for at least 15 seconds.
questions.strategy: Recall the time for the hub scrub.

questions.stem: Select all elements of the central line infection prevention bundle.

options.text: Giving prophylactic antibiotics while the line is in place
options.rationale: Near miss concept Antibiotics are not part of the bundle and drive resistance.

options.text: Maximal sterile barriers at insertion
options.rationale: The bundle is hand hygiene, maximal sterile barriers at insertion (cap, mask, sterile gown, gloves, full body drape), chlorhexidine prep, the best site (subclavian preferred, femoral highest risk) and daily review with prompt removal.

options.text: Reviewing the need for the line every day
options.rationale: The bundle is hand hygiene, maximal sterile barriers at insertion (cap, mask, sterile gown, gloves, full body drape), chlorhexidine prep, the best site (subclavian preferred, femoral highest risk) and daily review with prompt removal.

options.text: Hand hygiene
options.rationale: The bundle is hand hygiene, maximal sterile barriers at insertion (cap, mask, sterile gown, gloves, full body drape), chlorhexidine prep, the best site (subclavian preferred, femoral highest risk) and daily review with prompt removal.

options.text: Replacing the central line every 72 hours
options.rationale: Near miss concept Routine replacement is not part of the bundle; daily review and prompt removal are.

options.text: Chlorhexidine skin prep
options.rationale: The bundle is hand hygiene, maximal sterile barriers at insertion (cap, mask, sterile gown, gloves, full body drape), chlorhexidine prep, the best site (subclavian preferred, femoral highest risk) and daily review with prompt removal.

options.text: Avoiding the femoral site when possible
options.rationale: The bundle is hand hygiene, maximal sterile barriers at insertion (cap, mask, sterile gown, gloves, full body drape), chlorhexidine prep, the best site (subclavian preferred, femoral highest risk) and daily review with prompt removal.

questions.takeaway: The dropped step is daily review and removal.
questions.strategy: Keep elements that prevent organisms entering or shorten line days.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches a patient going home with a PICC. Select all correct instructions.

options.text: Do not allow blood pressure readings on the PICC arm
options.rationale: PICC teaching: keep the dressing clean, dry and intact, no swimming or baths, shower with a cover, no BP cuff or sticks on that arm, lift no more than 10 lb, do not use it if flushing meets resistance and seek care for signs of infection, clot or leaking.

options.text: Shower with a waterproof cover
options.rationale: PICC teaching: keep the dressing clean, dry and intact, no swimming or baths, shower with a cover, no BP cuff or sticks on that arm, lift no more than 10 lb, do not use it if flushing meets resistance and seek care for signs of infection, clot or leaking.

options.text: Seek care for a fever above 38 °C or chills
options.rationale: PICC teaching: keep the dressing clean, dry and intact, no swimming or baths, shower with a cover, no BP cuff or sticks on that arm, lift no more than 10 lb, do not use it if flushing meets resistance and seek care for signs of infection, clot or leaking.

options.text: Do not lift more than 10 lb with that arm
options.rationale: PICC teaching: keep the dressing clean, dry and intact, no swimming or baths, shower with a cover, no BP cuff or sticks on that arm, lift no more than 10 lb, do not use it if flushing meets resistance and seek care for signs of infection, clot or leaking.

options.text: Swimming is fine once the site heals
options.rationale: Near miss concept No swimming or baths with a PICC.

options.text: Force the flush if it meets resistance
options.rationale: Near miss concept Resistance means do not use it and call.

questions.takeaway: No swimming, no BP on that arm, no forcing a flush.
questions.strategy: Keep instructions that protect the line from infection and damage.

questions.stem: Which task can the nurse assign to assistive personnel during a blood transfusion?

options.text: Starting the transfusion
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Only the RN starts blood.

options.text: Staying with the patient for the first 15 minutes to watch for a reaction
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Watching for and interpreting a reaction stays with the RN.

options.text: Assessing a new complaint of back pain
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Assessment stays with the RN.

options.text: Taking and reporting vital signs
options.rationale: During a transfusion, assistive personnel only take and report vital signs. Starting, staying the first 15 minutes, interpreting and assessing stay with the RN.

questions.takeaway: UAP take vital signs; the RN does everything that needs judgment.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the task needs assessment or interpretation.

questions.stem: After stopping a transfusion for a suspected reaction, how should the nurse keep the vein open?

options.text: Hang new tubing with 0.9% sodium chloride.
options.rationale: The vein is kept open with new tubing and 0.9% NaCl, never by flushing the blood tubing.

options.text: Remove the IV.
options.rationale: Near miss concept IV access is needed to treat the reaction.

options.text: Hang D5W through the blood tubing.
options.rationale: Near miss concept D5W hemolyzes red cells and the tubing still holds blood.

options.text: Flush the existing blood tubing with saline.
options.rationale: Near miss concept The tubing still holds blood that would be pushed in.

questions.takeaway: New tubing, never flush the blood tubing.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the action could push more donor blood in.

questions.stem: Which catheter gauge is most appropriate for a blood transfusion in an adult?

options.text: 24 gauge
options.rationale: Near miss concept 22 to 24 gauge is for fragile veins and children; it is too small for routine blood in an adult.

options.text: 18 or 20 gauge
options.rationale: Blood products use 18 to 20 gauge. 14 to 16 is for trauma, 20 for standard adult infusions and 22 to 24 for older adults, children and fragile veins. A bigger number means a smaller catheter.

options.text: 14 gauge for every transfusion
options.rationale: Absolute language 14 to 16 gauge is for trauma and rapid resuscitation.

options.text: 26 gauge
options.rationale: Near miss concept Too small for blood.

questions.takeaway: A bigger gauge number means a smaller catheter.
questions.strategy: Match the gauge to the purpose.

questions.stem: Place the steps for giving a unit of packed red blood cells in order.

options.text: Recheck vital signs after 15 minutes
Stay with the patient for the first 15 minutes
Perform a two nurse check at the bedside
Start the transfusion slowly
Take baseline vital signs

questions.takeaway: Baseline vital signs come first, then the two nurse bedside check of ID band, label, ABO and Rh, unit number and expiration. The transfusion starts slowly, the nurse stays for 15 minutes because most severe reactions start early, then rechecks vital signs. You stay the first 15 minutes.
questions.strategy: Baseline first, check before spiking, and stay through the risky window.

questions.stem: For each task, indicate who may perform it.

rows.text: Report that the patient says the IV site hurts
Start a unit of blood
Perform the first site assessment on a new IV
Adjust the pump rate
Hang a bag of fluid that is not high alert
Flush an established peripheral line

questions.takeaway: The RN does first site assessments, starts blood, gives high alert IV drugs, interprets and teaches. An LPN may monitor sites, flush established lines and hang fluids that are not high alert, per state. UAP take vital signs and report what they see and hear but never touch the rate, pump or line. UAP report; they never touch the rate, pump or line.
questions.strategy: Decide whether each task needs judgment, a skill or only observation.

questions.stem: An order reads 1,000 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride over 8 hours by pump. What rate should the nurse set?

options.text: 125 mL/hr
options.rationale: Pump rate = total volume ÷ hours = 1,000 ÷ 8 = 125 mL/hr.

options.text: 150 mL/hr
options.rationale: Near miss concept That would finish in under 7 hours.

options.text: 31 mL/hr
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is the gravity drip rate in gtt/min with a 15 gtt/mL set.

options.text: 100 mL/hr
options.rationale: Near miss concept That would take 10 hours.

questions.takeaway: Pump: mL ÷ hours.
questions.strategy: Divide volume by hours.

questions.stem: An older adult with heart failure is receiving 0.9% sodium chloride at 125 mL/hr. Select all findings that suggest fluid overload.

options.text: Dyspnea
options.rationale: Isotonic fluids stay in the vessels, so overload shows as crackles, dyspnea, JVD, a bounding pulse and rising blood pressure and weight. Heart or kidney failure and older age raise the risk. The nurse slows the rate, sits the patient up, gives oxygen as ordered and notifies.

options.text: Urine specific gravity of 1.032
options.rationale: Near miss concept Concentrated urine suggests a deficit.

options.text: Jugular venous distention
options.rationale: Isotonic fluids stay in the vessels, so overload shows as crackles, dyspnea, JVD, a bounding pulse and rising blood pressure and weight. Heart or kidney failure and older age raise the risk. The nurse slows the rate, sits the patient up, gives oxygen as ordered and notifies.

options.text: Crackles in both lung bases
options.rationale: Isotonic fluids stay in the vessels, so overload shows as crackles, dyspnea, JVD, a bounding pulse and rising blood pressure and weight. Heart or kidney failure and older age raise the risk. The nurse slows the rate, sits the patient up, gives oxygen as ordered and notifies.

options.text: Weight gain of 1.5 kg since yesterday
options.rationale: Isotonic fluids stay in the vessels, so overload shows as crackles, dyspnea, JVD, a bounding pulse and rising blood pressure and weight. Heart or kidney failure and older age raise the risk. The nurse slows the rate, sits the patient up, gives oxygen as ordered and notifies.

options.text: Dry mucous membranes
options.rationale: Near miss concept This suggests a fluid deficit.

options.text: Bounding pulse
options.rationale: Isotonic fluids stay in the vessels, so overload shows as crackles, dyspnea, JVD, a bounding pulse and rising blood pressure and weight. Heart or kidney failure and older age raise the risk. The nurse slows the rate, sits the patient up, gives oxygen as ordered and notifies.

questions.takeaway: Isotonic fluid stays in the vessels, so watch for overload.
questions.strategy: Keep findings that show too much volume.

questions.stem: A nurse is starting an IV on an 88 year old with fragile, rolling veins. Select all appropriate actions.

options.text: Apply the tourniquet tightly so the vein stands out
options.rationale: Near miss concept A tight tourniquet can burst a fragile vein.

options.text: Use a loose tourniquet or none
options.rationale: For older adults: the smallest gauge that works (22 to 24), a loose or no tourniquet, gentle traction and no dorsal hand veins. Rates are slower because of less heart and kidney reserve, and new confusion, dyspnea or crackles may be the first sign of overload.

options.text: Apply gentle traction to stabilize the vein
options.rationale: For older adults: the smallest gauge that works (22 to 24), a loose or no tourniquet, gentle traction and no dorsal hand veins. Rates are slower because of less heart and kidney reserve, and new confusion, dyspnea or crackles may be the first sign of overload.

options.text: Use a dorsal hand vein because it is easy to see
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dorsal hand veins are avoided in older adults.

options.text: Use a 22 to 24 gauge catheter
options.rationale: For older adults: the smallest gauge that works (22 to 24), a loose or no tourniquet, gentle traction and no dorsal hand veins. Rates are slower because of less heart and kidney reserve, and new confusion, dyspnea or crackles may be the first sign of overload.

options.text: Expect a slower infusion rate
options.rationale: For older adults: the smallest gauge that works (22 to 24), a loose or no tourniquet, gentle traction and no dorsal hand veins. Rates are slower because of less heart and kidney reserve, and new confusion, dyspnea or crackles may be the first sign of overload.

questions.takeaway: Smallest gauge, loose tourniquet, slower rate.
questions.strategy: Keep actions that protect fragile veins and limited reserve.

questions.stem: An older adult with heart failure receiving a second unit of packed red blood cells develops dyspnea and crackles. The blood pressure has risen from 132/78 to 158/90 mm Hg. What is the most likely problem?

options.text: Allergic reaction
options.rationale: Near miss concept An allergic reaction shows hives or itching.

options.text: Pneumonia
options.rationale: Near miss concept The timing with the transfusion points to overload.

options.text: Hemolytic transfusion reaction
options.rationale: Near miss concept A hemolytic reaction usually drops the blood pressure.

options.text: Circulatory overload
options.rationale: Dyspnea, crackles and a rising blood pressure in an older adult or a patient with heart failure suggest circulatory overload. The nurse slows or stops, sits the patient upright, notifies and expects a diuretic.

questions.takeaway: Rising BP with crackles during a transfusion means overload.
questions.strategy: Use the direction of the blood pressure to separate overload from a hemolytic reaction.

questions.stem: A patient asks why an antibiotic given by IV works faster than the same drug taken by mouth. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: Parenteral means into a vein, so every infusion uses a venous catheter
options.rationale: Absolute language Parenteral means outside the gut, not only into a vein. The routes include intravenous, intra arterial, subcutaneous, intraosseous and intraspinal, so the word every makes this false.

options.text: The liver changes the drug first, which makes it stronger before it acts
options.rationale: Near miss concept First pass metabolism is the liver processing a swallowed drug before it reaches the body. Infusion skips that step, which is why the effect is immediate. This option has it backward.

options.text: It enters the blood directly, skipping gut absorption and first pass metabolism
options.rationale: Parenteral infusion therapy is giving fluids, drugs, blood products or nutrients directly into the vascular system, bypassing the gastrointestinal tract. The test question is: does the drug have to be absorbed from the gut and pass through the liver first? By mouth, yes. By infusion, no. That is why the key is right: the drug skips gut absorption and first pass metabolism (the liver breaking down part of a swallowed dose), so it has an immediate systemic effect. The vein option fails because parenteral routes also include artery, bone marrow, subcutaneous tissue and the spinal spaces. The liver option reverses first pass metabolism. The clean technique option reverses the safety logic: with no gut barrier, strict asepsis is required.

options.text: Clean technique is enough, since the drug never passes through the gut
options.rationale: Near miss concept Skipping the gut removes a barrier, it does not add one. Organisms on the skin or equipment go straight into the blood, so infusion needs strict aseptic technique, not clean technique.

questions.takeaway: Infusion skips the gut and the liver's first pass, so the effect is immediate and asepsis must be strict.
questions.strategy: The word every in the vein option is the detail that rules it out, because parenteral routes include bone, artery, skin and spine. Then ask which option names what is skipped.

questions.topic: time limits for infusion equipment and dressings
questions.stem: A nurse checks the infusion equipment for several patients. For each item, indicate the time limit the nurse follows unless the item is wet, soiled or damaged first.
questions.objective: time limits for infusion equipment and dressings

rows.text: A bag of IV fluid that has been spiked
A primary administration set on a continuous infusion
A gauze dressing over a short peripheral catheter
A transparent dressing over a short peripheral catheter
A PICC dressing for a patient at home

questions.takeaway: Spiked bag, 24 hours: once the spike enters the port, the sterile seal is broken, so the bag hangs no longer than 24 hours. The test question is whether the sterile system has been opened. Primary administration set, 96 hours: tubing is changed every 96 hours or per policy, so the set outlasts several bags. Gauze dressing, 48 hours: gauze hides the site and holds moisture, so it is changed every 2 days. Transparent dressing, up to 7 days: the site can be seen through it, so it can stay longer, changed every 7 days. PICC dressing at home, up to 7 days: the patient is taught to change it every 5 to 7 days or sooner if wet or soiled. Two rows share the 7 day column, so the column cannot be filled one row at a time. Spiked bag 24 hours, tubing 96 hours, gauze 2 days, transparent dressing 7 days, and any wet or loose dressing now.
questions.strategy: Sort by what the item does. The detail that separates the two dressings is whether the site can be seen through it: gauze 2 days, transparent 7 days. Do not let the 24 hour bag pull the tubing into the same column.

questions.stem: For each statement, indicate the central venous device it describes.

rows.text: The patient can swim and bathe with no external catheter to protect
Needs a flush once a month when it is not being used
A cuff under the skin anchors the line and lowers infection risk
An external catheter that needs daily care for months at home
Placed in the internal jugular vein for a few days in intensive care

questions.takeaway: Swim and bathe freely, implanted port: a port is a reservoir placed totally under the skin. The test question is whether anything sticks out of the skin. Nothing does, so water is not a problem. Monthly flush, implanted port: a port sits unused between intermittent treatments such as chemotherapy, so it needs a flush monthly when not in use. Cuff anchors the line, tunneled catheter: a tunneled line (for example a Hickman or Broviac) runs under the skin before entering the vein, and a Dacron cuff in the tunnel holds it and blocks organisms. Daily care for months, tunneled catheter: the tunneled line is long term but still has an external catheter, which needs daily care. Internal jugular for a few days in intensive care, nontunneled catheter: a nontunneled line goes straight through the skin into the subclavian, internal jugular or femoral vein for short term acute care, and it carries the highest infection risk of these devices. Port: nothing outside, swim freely, flush monthly. Tunneled: cuff, external line, daily care. Nontunneled: short term, highest risk.
questions.strategy: Ask two questions of each row: is any catheter outside the skin, and how long will it stay? The detail that separates port from tunneled line is the external catheter.

questions.stem: Both a midline catheter and a PICC are inserted into a basilic vein in the upper arm. Why may total parenteral nutrition run through the PICC but not through the midline?

options.text: The PICC tip ends in the superior vena cava; the midline tip ends below the axilla
options.rationale: Central access means the catheter tip sits in a large central vessel near the heart, where high blood flow dilutes concentrated fluids. The test question is: where does the tip end, not where was it inserted? A PICC is inserted in the arm but its tip rests in the lower superior vena cava, so it is a central line and can carry total parenteral nutrition, vesicants and solutions above 900 mOsm/L. A midline tip ends below the axilla in a peripheral vein, so it is limited to non vesicant drugs under 600 mOsm/L and is never used for TPN or continuous vasopressors. The vein option fails because the stem puts both in the basilic vein. The dwell time option is false, since a midline lasts up to 4 weeks. The lumen option is false, since a PICC can be single lumen.

options.text: The PICC goes into a large deep vein, while the midline uses a small surface vein
options.rationale: Near miss concept The stem says both enter the basilic vein. Insertion vein does not decide central versus peripheral access; tip location does.

options.text: The midline can stay in only a few days, too short for a course of nutrition
options.rationale: Near miss concept A midline can dwell up to 4 weeks, longer than a short peripheral IV. Dwell time is not what bars it from nutrition.

options.text: The midline has only a single lumen, while a PICC always has several lumens
options.rationale: Absolute language A PICC may be single or multi lumen. Lumen count does not make a line central.

questions.takeaway: Tip location, not insertion site, makes a line central. A PICC is central; a midline is not.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out the vein size option is that the stem places both catheters in the same basilic vein. With insertion held equal, only the tip is left.

questions.stem: A catheter sits in a vein just above the wrist. The tape is loose, and the catheter slides each time the wrist bends. The fluid is 0.9% sodium chloride. The site was prepped with chlorhexidine per protocol. Now the vein is red, warm and tender, with no drainage. Which explanation fits best?

options.text: Chemical phlebitis from an irritating solution
options.rationale: Near miss concept Chemical phlebitis comes from an irritating solution. 0.9% sodium chloride is isotonic and not irritating, so the cause lies elsewhere.

options.text: Mechanical phlebitis from catheter movement in the vein
options.rationale: Phlebitis is inflammation of the vein wall: pain, redness, warmth, a streak along the vein and sometimes a palpable cord. It has three types, named by cause. The test question is: what irritated the vein? Mechanical phlebitis comes from the catheter moving and rubbing the vein. Chemical phlebitis comes from an irritating solution. Bacterial phlebitis comes from poor asepsis. Here the catheter is loose and slides with every wrist bend, so the cause is mechanical. The solution is isotonic saline, which rules out chemical. The correct prep with no drainage argues against bacterial. Warmth and redness rule out infiltration, which is cool and pale. The nurse still stops the infusion, removes the catheter, applies a warm moist compress, notifies the provider and documents the grade.

options.text: Bacterial phlebitis from a break in aseptic technique
options.rationale: Near miss concept Bacterial phlebitis comes from poor asepsis. The stem documents a correct chlorhexidine prep and shows no drainage, so there is no evidence of infection.

options.text: Infiltration from fluid leaking into the tissue
options.rationale: Near miss concept Infiltration is fluid in the tissue and feels cool and pale. This site is warm and red along the vein, which is inflammation of the vein wall.

questions.takeaway: Name phlebitis by its cause: movement is mechanical, solution is chemical, poor asepsis is bacterial.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out chemical is the isotonic saline, and the detail that rules out bacterial is the correct prep with no drainage. What remains is the loose, sliding catheter.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence: A nurse reviews IV fluid orders. For a patient with a low blood glucose who needs dextrose by vein, the nurse expects [[1]]. For a patient with diabetic ketoacidosis who has finished initial fluid resuscitation, the next fluid may be [[2]]. The nurse questions any hypotonic solution for a patient with [[3]].

options.text: 10% dextrose in water
0.45% sodium chloride
lactated Ringer solution
0.45% sodium chloride
3% sodium chloride
5% dextrose in 0.9% sodium chloride
hypotension and third spacing
hypertonic dehydration
cellular dehydration

questions.takeaway: Tonicity is how a solution's concentration compares with plasma, which decides which way water moves. [1] 10% dextrose in water: a hypertonic solution used for hypoglycemia because it supplies concentrated dextrose. 0.45% sodium chloride and lactated Ringer solution contain no dextrose, so they do not treat a low glucose. [2] 0.45% sodium chloride: a hypotonic solution that moves water into cells. It is used in diabetic ketoacidosis after initial fluid resuscitation, when the cells are dehydrated. 3% sodium chloride is hypertonic and pulls water out of cells, the opposite of the goal. 5% dextrose in 0.9% sodium chloride is also hypertonic. [3] hypotension and third spacing: hypotonic fluid leaves the vessels and moves into cells, so it worsens a low blood pressure and fluid already pooling outside the vessels. Hypertonic dehydration and cellular dehydration are the indications for hypotonic fluid, not reasons to question it.
