Hypotonic fluid hydrates cells and leaves the vessels; hypertonic fluid pulls water out of cells into the vessels.
questions.strategy: For each blank ask which way water must move. The detail in blank 2 is after initial resuscitation: the vessels are filled, so now the cells need water.

questions.stem: A nurse plans to use a near infrared vein finder for a patient with swollen, edematous arms. Which statement about this device is accurate?

options.text: It confirms the vein is patent before a deep vein is cannulated
options.rationale: Near miss concept Confirming patency of a deep vein in real time is what ultrasound does. Near infrared light shows only veins just under the skin.

options.text: It uses low dose radiation, so repeated use should be limited
options.rationale: Near miss concept Near infrared light is not radiation, so the device is safe for repeated use. The worry about dose belongs to x ray, not this device.

options.text: It is required before placing a catheter in the brachial vein
options.rationale: Near miss concept Ultrasound, not infrared, is required for deep veins such as the basilic and brachial veins. Infrared cannot see that deep.

options.text: It maps surface veins but does not replace the nurse's assessment
options.rationale: A near infrared vein finder shines light on the skin and projects a real time map of the subcutaneous veins onto the surface. The test question is: is the vein close to the skin, or deep? Infrared is for surface veins in patients whose veins are hard to see, such as pediatric, obese, dark skinned, edematous or chemotherapy patients. It uses no radiation and reduces needle sticks, but it does not replace palpation and clinical assessment. Ultrasound is the tool that shows deep veins, arteries and nerves, confirms patency and is required for deep veins such as the basilic and brachial. Both deep vein options describe ultrasound. The radiation option is false.

questions.takeaway: Infrared shows surface veins and helps; ultrasound sees deep veins and is required for them. Neither replaces your assessment.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out the deep vein options is near infrared in the stem: light reaches only veins under the skin.

questions.stem: A nurse is unsure whether two ordered IV drugs can share one line. The nurse also wonders if a new solution is too concentrated for a short peripheral catheter. Whose core role covers both questions?

options.text: The infusion pharmacist
options.rationale: The infusion team splits the work by expertise. The test question for each role is: what does this person check? The infusion pharmacist reviews orders for compatibility, osmolarity (how concentrated a solution is) and dosing, prepares sterile mixtures and advises on drug and solution stability. Both questions in the stem, sharing a line and concentration for a peripheral vein, are compatibility and osmolarity. The vascular access specialist is the insertion expert. The IV therapy nurse is the site and complication expert. The provider writes and changes the order but is not the one who reviews it for compatibility.

options.text: The vascular access specialist
options.rationale: Near miss concept The vascular access specialist places catheters and consults on hard to access patients. Drug compatibility and solution concentration are not that role's focus.

options.text: The IV therapy nurse
options.rationale: Near miss concept The IV therapy nurse monitors sites, manages complications and teaches. That nurse follows infusion standards but does not review orders for compatibility and osmolarity.

options.text: The prescribing provider
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question The provider writes the order and can change it, but checking drug to drug compatibility and osmolarity is the pharmacist's review of that order.

questions.takeaway: Compatibility and osmolarity questions go to the infusion pharmacist.
questions.strategy: The detail that tips it is that both questions are about the solution, not the vein or the insertion. Match the question to the person who reviews that part.

questions.stem: Fifteen minutes into a transfusion a patient develops fever, chills, flank pain and dark urine. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Stop the transfusion; keep the vein open with saline on new tubing
options.rationale: Fever, chills, flank pain and dark urine is an acute hemolytic reaction, the one that kills. Stop the blood, keep the vein open with saline through fresh tubing so you are not pushing the remaining blood in the old line, then notify the provider and the blood bank and send the unit and samples back.

options.text: Stop the transfusion and remove the intravenous catheter at once to stop all exposure
options.rationale: Near miss concept Stops the blood and discards the line you need for fluids and drugs.

options.text: Slow the transfusion rate and give the ordered antipyretic now
options.rationale: Near miss concept Treats it as a mild febrile reaction while hemolysis continues.

options.text: Continue the transfusion and notify the provider of the change
options.rationale: Near miss concept Every additional milliliter makes the hemolysis worse.

questions.takeaway: Stop the blood, keep the line. You need that access more than ever now.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options keep the blood going. One throws away the access.

questions.stem: While the nurse is advancing an intravenous catheter the patient cries out with a shooting, burning pain and says her hand feels like pins and needles. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Continue, then apply a warm compress afterward for the pain
options.rationale: Near miss concept Treats a neurologic injury as if it were soreness.

options.text: Advance the catheter the rest of the way quickly to finish
options.rationale: Near miss concept Speed does not reduce nerve damage; it adds to it.

options.text: Stop, remove the catheter, and check nerve function in the hand
options.rationale: Shooting or burning pain with numbness or tingling during insertion is nerve contact, and continuing can leave a permanent deficit. Stop, remove, assess sensation and movement, document and report. This is one of the few times you abandon the attempt entirely rather than adjusting.

options.text: Withdraw slightly and redirect the catheter toward the vein
options.rationale: Near miss concept Redirecting around a nerve you have already touched risks touching it again.

questions.takeaway: Pins and needles during insertion means the needle is on a nerve. Stop.
questions.strategy: Every wrong option keeps the needle moving in tissue that is already telling you to stop.

questions.stem: Twenty minutes into a unit of packed red cells a patient develops a temperature rise of 1.2 degrees Celsius with chills, no back pain, normal blood pressure and clear urine. What is the most likely reaction, and what should the nurse do?

options.text: An allergic reaction; slow the infusion and give an antihistamine
options.rationale: Near miss concept Allergic reactions are urticarial; slowing rather than stopping is also wrong here.

options.text: An acute hemolytic reaction; stop the transfusion and send the unit and samples to the blood bank
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would include flank or back pain, hypotension and dark urine; the action is nearly identical, which is why stopping comes first.

options.text: An expected response to the transfusion; continue and monitor
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A fever during a transfusion is never dismissed as expected.

options.text: A febrile nonhemolytic reaction; stop the transfusion, assess, and notify the provider
options.rationale: Fever and chills without flank pain, hypotension or hemoglobinuria fits a febrile nonhemolytic reaction, which is the most common type and is caused by recipient antibodies to donor white cells. The key point is that you cannot tell it apart from the start of a hemolytic reaction at the bedside, so the transfusion stops either way and the workup follows. Nothing about a fever during a transfusion is expected.

questions.takeaway: Stop first, classify second. A fever and a hemolytic reaction look identical in the first minutes.
questions.strategy: The hemolytic option is wrong only because the specific findings are absent, and the action it names is nearly the same.

questions.stem: Thirty minutes into an antibiotic infusion a patient develops flushing, itching, a tight throat and a blood pressure of 82/48. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Stop the infusion, call for emergency help, and support the airway
options.rationale: Throat tightness with hypotension is anaphylaxis, and the first two actions are stopping the antigen and getting help, with the airway as the priority throughout. Epinephrine follows immediately per protocol. Slowing the infusion keeps the allergen going in, and antihistamines treat the rash while the airway closes.

options.text: Slow the infusion and give the ordered antihistamine by mouth
options.rationale: Near miss concept Keeps the antigen infusing and treats the least dangerous symptom.

options.text: Change the tubing and restart the antibiotic at a slower rate
options.rationale: Near miss concept Re-exposes a patient who is already reacting.

options.text: Place the patient flat with legs raised and keep the drip running
options.rationale: Near miss concept Positioning for hypotension, with the airway and the drug ignored.

questions.takeaway: Throat tightness plus hypotension is anaphylaxis. Stop the drug, call, airway, epinephrine.
questions.strategy: Slowing an infusion is right for speed shock and wrong for anaphylaxis, which is the discrimination here.

questions.stem: A patient with a central line develops fever, chills and hypotension with no other apparent source. What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Blood cultures from two sites, IV antibiotics, possible line removal
options.rationale: Two sets of cultures, then antibiotics, same as any sepsis workup. Pulling the line before culturing throws away evidence and the access at once. The prevention bundle is what actually matters here: hand hygiene, maximal barriers at insertion, chlorhexidine prep, subclavian over femoral where possible, and a daily review of whether the line is still needed.

options.text: Flushing the catheter with heparin and continuing to monitor closely
options.rationale: Near miss concept Treats a mechanical problem in a patient who is septic.

options.text: Removing the catheter immediately, before any cultures are drawn
options.rationale: Correct but premature Loses both the organism and the access.

options.text: Starting antibiotics through the central line and holding cultures
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cultures come before antibiotics, every time.

questions.takeaway: Every extra day a line stays in raises the infection risk. Ask daily whether it is still needed.
questions.strategy: One option discards the line, one discards the cultures.

questions.stem: During a central line dressing change the patient suddenly becomes short of breath, reports chest pain and drops her blood pressure. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and apply oxygen
options.rationale: Near miss concept Correct for almost every other cause of sudden dyspnea. Here it lets the air rise out of the right ventricle into the pulmonary artery and lock the outflow.

options.text: Start a rapid fluid bolus through the same line
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pushes more air down the line you should have clamped.

options.text: Clamp the catheter; position left side, head down
options.rationale: Sudden dyspnea, chest pain and hypotension during a line manipulation is air embolism. Clamping stops more air entering. Left lateral Trendelenburg traps the air in the right atrium where it cannot be pumped into the pulmonary circulation. Then 100 percent oxygen and a rapid response.

options.text: Remove the catheter and apply firm pressure
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pulling the line open to air is how more air gets in.

questions.takeaway: Clamp, roll left, head down, oxygen. The position is the treatment.
questions.strategy: The instinct to sit a breathless patient up is wrong here, and it is the one thing that kills them.

questions.topic: a central line with a problem
questions.stem: A patient's PICC will not flush and there is swelling in that arm with discomfort along the upper arm. Select all of the appropriate nursing actions.
questions.objective: a central line with a problem

options.text: Flush with a larger syringe to generate enough pressure to clear it
options.rationale: Near miss concept Forcing any flush risks embolizing a clot or rupturing the catheter.

options.text: Apply a warm compress and attempt the flush again in an hour
options.rationale: Near miss concept Delays evaluation of a possible thrombosis and ends in another forced flush.

options.text: Stop attempting to flush and do not force it
options.rationale: Resistance plus a swollen painful arm is catheter related thrombosis until proven otherwise. Forcing a flush can dislodge a clot into the central circulation or rupture the catheter, and a larger syringe generates less pressure per unit of force, not more, which is a common misunderstanding. Assess both arms, stop using the line and escalate.

options.text: Notify the provider, because thrombosis is a possibility
options.rationale: Resistance plus a swollen painful arm is catheter related thrombosis until proven otherwise. Forcing a flush can dislodge a clot into the central circulation or rupture the catheter, and a larger syringe generates less pressure per unit of force, not more, which is a common misunderstanding. Assess both arms, stop using the line and escalate.

options.text: Avoid using that line until it has been evaluated
options.rationale: Resistance plus a swollen painful arm is catheter related thrombosis until proven otherwise. Forcing a flush can dislodge a clot into the central circulation or rupture the catheter, and a larger syringe generates less pressure per unit of force, not more, which is a common misunderstanding. Assess both arms, stop using the line and escalate.

options.text: Assess and compare both arms for circumference, color and temperature
options.rationale: Resistance plus a swollen painful arm is catheter related thrombosis until proven otherwise. Forcing a flush can dislodge a clot into the central circulation or rupture the catheter, and a larger syringe generates less pressure per unit of force, not more, which is a common misunderstanding. Assess both arms, stop using the line and escalate.

questions.takeaway: Never force a flush. The resistance is information, not an obstacle.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options apply more force or more time to a line that should not be used at all.

questions.stem: A patient with a head injury and rising intracranial pressure has an order for 0.45 percent sodium chloride. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Question it; a hypotonic fluid drives water into brain cells
options.rationale: Hypotonic fluid moves water into cells by osmosis, and the brain is the one organ with no room to swell. Hypotonic solutions are contraindicated in head trauma, raised intracranial pressure, third spacing and hypotension. Slowing the rate does not change the direction water moves; it only slows the harm.

options.text: Give it, because the patient needs free water replacement
options.rationale: Near miss concept Free water is exactly what this patient cannot tolerate.

options.text: Give it and monitor the serum sodium every 4 hours
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Monitors the consequence instead of avoiding it.

options.text: Give it at a slower rate to reduce any risk of harm
options.rationale: Near miss concept Slows the shift without preventing it.

questions.takeaway: Hypotonic fluid in a head injury swells the brain. Rate does not fix direction.
questions.strategy: Three options give the fluid with a safeguard attached. None of the safeguards addresses osmosis.

questions.stem: A patient needs a peripheral intravenous line. She has had a left mastectomy with node dissection, a right arm arteriovenous fistula, and a healing infiltration in the right forearm from a line placed before the fistula was created. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Use the left forearm, since the mastectomy was years ago
options.rationale: Near miss concept Lymphatic compromise after node dissection does not expire.

options.text: Use the right hand, distal to the healing infiltration site
options.rationale: Near miss concept Distal to an infiltration is specifically avoided, and the fistula arm is out entirely.

options.text: Use a vein in the lower leg or foot as the next option
options.rationale: Near miss concept Avoided in adults because of thrombosis risk, and it needs an order.

options.text: Contact the provider or vascular access team for a new route
options.rationale: The left arm is out because of lymphatic compromise, the right arm is out because of the fistula, and you never go distal to a previous infiltration because the vein above it is damaged and the fluid will leak again. Lower extremities are avoided in adults. When every usual option is contraindicated, the answer is to escalate for a different kind of access, not to pick the least bad site.

questions.takeaway: When every site is contraindicated, the answer is a different device, not a worse site.
questions.strategy: This is the item where recognizing that you should not proceed is the competence being tested.

questions.stem: An 82 year old with heart failure is receiving 0.9 percent sodium chloride at 150 mL per hour. Four hours later the patient is coughing, short of breath, has crackles in both bases, distended neck veins, a blood pressure of 168/94 and an SpO2 that has fallen from 95 percent to 89 percent. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Apply oxygen and recheck the SpO2 in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Correct but premature Oxygen is on the list, but supporting breathing while the fluid keeps pouring in leaves the cause running.

options.text: Stop the infusion and remove the catheter
options.rationale: Near miss concept Removing the catheter is the move for a bad site, not for overload; the line is still needed for ordered drugs such as a diuretic.

options.text: Switch the fluid to 0.45 percent sodium chloride at the same rate
options.rationale: Near miss concept Changing the tonicity does not change the volume; the problem is too much fluid, not the wrong kind.

options.text: Slow the infusion and sit the patient upright
options.rationale: Isotonic fluid stays in the vessels, which is exactly why it overloads a weak heart. Crackles, dyspnea, cough, high blood pressure, distended neck veins and a falling SpO2 are circulatory overload. The sheet's order is slow the IV, sit upright, give oxygen, take vital signs and notify; a diuretic follows as ordered.

questions.takeaway: Overload: turn the source down first, then support the breathing.
questions.strategy: Ask what is causing the finding. The answer that addresses the cause beats the answer that treats the symptom.

questions.topic: D5W is not a volume expander
questions.stem: A patient with a falling blood pressure after blood loss has four fluid orders written by different providers. Which order should the nurse question?
questions.objective: D5W is not a volume expander

options.text: 5 percent dextrose in water bolus to restore volume
options.rationale: D5W is isotonic in the bag, which makes it look like a safe volume choice. Once the dextrose is used, what is left is free water, which acts hypotonic: it moves out of the vessels into cells, so the blood pressure does not recover. The same reason keeps D5W away from a patient with increased ICP.

options.text: 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus
options.rationale: Near miss concept Normal saline is isotonic and stays in the vessels, which is what a hypotensive patient needs.

options.text: Lactated Ringer solution bolus
options.rationale: Near miss concept Lactated Ringer is isotonic on the slide's list and expands volume.

options.text: 0.9 percent sodium chloride primed through a blood set for an ordered transfusion
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Normal saline is the only fluid that runs with blood, so this order is correct as written.

questions.takeaway: D5W is isotonic in the bag and hypotonic in the body.
questions.strategy: When every option is isotonic on paper, ask what the fluid becomes after the body acts on it.

questions.stem: A nurse receives the order "D5W to keep vein open" for a patient with a new peripheral line. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Hang it at the unit's usual keep vein open rate
options.rationale: Institution as rationale A unit habit is not an order; the rate must come from the prescriber.

options.text: Hang it at 125 mL per hour until the provider rounds
options.rationale: Correct but premature Any rate you choose is your prescription, not the provider's.

options.text: Hang it and document that the order had no rate
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Charting the problem does not fix it; the fluid is already running at a rate nobody ordered.

options.text: Clarify the rate with the provider before hanging the fluid
options.rationale: A complete IV order names the fluid, the rate and any additives. "Keep vein open" is not a rate. An order missing a component is not ready to hang, so you clarify first.

questions.takeaway: Fluid, rate, additives. Missing one means clarify before you hang.
questions.strategy: When the order is incomplete, every option that starts the infusion is wrong.

questions.stem: A PICC was just inserted and the provider asks the nurse to start the patient's total parenteral nutrition through it. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Flush the line with a 10 mL syringe and start the infusion at the ordered rate
options.rationale: Correct but premature The right syringe size, but the tip location is still unknown.

options.text: Check for a blood return and then start the infusion
options.rationale: Near miss concept A blood return shows the catheter is in a vein, not that the tip is central.

options.text: Start the infusion at half rate until the line is confirmed
options.rationale: Near miss concept A lower rate does not make TPN safe in a vein that cannot dilute it.

options.text: Confirm by chest x ray that the tip is in the lower vena cava
options.rationale: The tip, not the insertion site, makes a line central. A central line is not used until a chest x ray confirms the tip at the cavoatrial junction, in the lower superior vena cava, where high blood flow dilutes concentrated solutions such as TPN.

questions.takeaway: No x ray, no infusion.
questions.strategy: Blood return is the near miss. It confirms a vein, not a location.

questions.stem: A nurse finds a peripheral site that is cool, pale and swollen, with the skin taut, the infusion running slowly and no blood return. The fluid is 0.9 percent sodium chloride. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Stop the infusion
options.rationale: Cool, pale, swollen and taut with a slowed rate is infiltration of a nonvesicant. Stop the infusion first, then remove the catheter, elevate the arm, grade it 0 to 4, document and restart in the other arm or higher on the same arm.

options.text: Slow the rate and recheck the site in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Correct but premature Watching while fluid keeps going into the tissue lets the injury grow.

options.text: Apply a warm moist compress
options.rationale: Near miss concept A warm moist compress is the treatment for phlebitis, the warm red site.

options.text: Flush the catheter to restore flow
options.rationale: Near miss concept Flushing pushes more fluid into the tissue that is already swelling.

questions.takeaway: Cool and pale is infiltration. Stop first.
questions.strategy: When a site looks wrong, the first action is always stop. Sort out which complication after.

questions.stem: A patient's chemotherapy infusion stops dripping and the patient reports burning at a forearm site that is now cool, pale and swollen. After stopping the infusion, what should the nurse do next?

options.text: Remove the catheter right away and elevate the arm
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is the sequence for infiltration of a nonvesicant; pulling the catheter loses the chance to draw back the drug and give an antidote through it.

options.text: Flush the catheter with 0.9 percent sodium chloride to dilute the drug
options.rationale: Near miss concept Flushing drives more vesicant into the tissue.

options.text: Disconnect the tubing and aspirate through the catheter before it is removed
options.rationale: The site looks like infiltration, but a vesicant was running, so this is extravasation. Stop, disconnect, aspirate through the catheter and leave it in for an antidote per policy, apply a cold compress for most drugs and notify. Blisters and necrosis come late, so the early look is deceptively mild.

options.text: Apply a warm compress and grade the site
options.rationale: Near miss concept Most vesicants call for a cold compress, and grading comes after the drug is managed.

questions.takeaway: Same look as infiltration; a vesicant makes it extravasation, and the catheter stays in to aspirate.
questions.strategy: Ask what was running. The drug, not the site, decides the name and the next step.

questions.stem: While removing a peripheral catheter, the nurse sees that the tip is jagged and part of it is missing. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Document that the catheter was removed with the tip not intact
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Documentation matters, but a fragment heading to the heart comes first.

options.text: Apply pressure over the site and an occlusive dressing
options.rationale: Correct but premature Site care does nothing about the piece already moving in the vein.

options.text: Massage the arm toward the site to bring the fragment out
options.rationale: Near miss concept Manipulating the arm can move the fragment further.

options.text: Apply a tourniquet high on the limb
options.rationale: A cut or missing tip means a piece of catheter is loose in the vein and can travel to the heart and cause arrest. A tourniquet high on the limb holds it in place; then notify the provider at once and keep the removed piece. This is why you always check that the tip came out intact.

questions.takeaway: Missing tip: tourniquet high, notify, keep the piece.
questions.strategy: Stop the thing that is moving before you care for the site or chart.

questions.stem: Ten minutes into a unit of packed red blood cells, the patient has chills and low back pain. The heart rate has risen from 82 to 110/min and the blood pressure has fallen from 128/76 to 100/60 mm Hg. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Slow the transfusion rate.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Any more donor blood worsens the reaction.

options.text: Stop the transfusion.
options.rationale: Chills, back pain, tachycardia and a falling blood pressure early in a unit suggest an acute transfusion reaction. The nurse stops the blood first, keeps the vein open with new tubing and 0.9% NaCl, stays, notifies the provider and blood bank and returns the bag and tubing.

options.text: Give acetaminophen and continue.
options.rationale: Near miss concept This masks the reaction while more blood enters.

options.text: Flush the blood tubing with saline.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Flushing pushes the blood left in the tubing into the patient.

questions.takeaway: Stop the blood first.
questions.strategy: When harm is flowing in, stop the flow before anything else.

questions.stem: A patient's IV site is warm, red and tender with a red streak along the vein. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Flush the IV to clear the vein and continue.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Flushing an inflamed vein worsens it.

options.text: Stop, remove it, apply warm compress, notify.
options.rationale: Phlebitis is warm, red and painful with a red streak or cord. Stop, remove, apply a warm moist compress, notify and grade it.

options.text: Elevate the arm and recheck it in an hour.
options.rationale: Near miss concept The catheter is removed now.

options.text: Apply a cold compress and keep it running.
options.rationale: Near miss concept The IV is removed, and phlebitis gets a warm compress.

questions.takeaway: Phlebitis: warm compress.
questions.strategy: Match the compress to the problem.

questions.stem: A patient with a head injury has a sodium level of 132 mEq/L. Which IV solution order should the nurse question?

options.text: Lactated Ringer solution
options.rationale: Near miss concept LR is isotonic.

options.text: 0.45% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Hypotonic fluids move water into cells, including brain cells, which worsens cerebral edema. They are never used with increased ICP or head injury.

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Near miss concept Isotonic saline does not move water into brain cells.

options.text: 3% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hypertonic saline pulls water out of cells and is used for severe hyponatremia or cerebral edema.

questions.takeaway: Never hypotonic fluid with a head injury.
questions.strategy: Ask which direction each fluid moves water, and which way the brain cannot tolerate.

questions.stem: A patient with a central line suddenly has dyspnea, chest pain and a low blood pressure after the tubing disconnected. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Remove the central line and apply pressure.
options.rationale: Near miss concept The line is clamped first.

options.text: Flush the line with saline to clear any air.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Flushing could push more air in.

options.text: Clamp it; turn to the left side, head down.
options.rationale: For air embolism: clamp, left side, head down, 100% oxygen and call the rapid response team. Left side, head down traps air in the right atrium.

options.text: Sit the patient upright to ease breathing.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Upright lets air travel. Left side, head down traps it in the right atrium.

questions.takeaway: Clamp, left side, head down.
questions.strategy: Stop more air entering, then trap the air already in.

questions.stem: During IV insertion, the patient reports a sudden shooting pain and tingling down the arm. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Pull back slightly and try again in the same spot.
options.rationale: Near miss concept The catheter is removed.

options.text: Advance the catheter quickly to finish.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Continuing can worsen a nerve injury.

options.text: Stop and remove the catheter at once.
options.rationale: Shooting pain, burning, numbness or tingling during insertion means possible nerve injury. Stop and remove at once, check sensation and movement and report.

options.text: Reassure the patient that this is normal.
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Shooting pain and tingling signal nerve injury.

questions.takeaway: Nerve pain on insertion: stop and remove.
questions.strategy: When the patient reports nerve symptoms, stop immediately.

questions.topic: hemodialysis catheter is not for routine access
questions.stem: A patient with kidney failure has a tunneled hemodialysis catheter in the right chest. The peripheral IV in the left forearm infiltrated and was removed. An IV antibiotic is due now, and morning labs are ordered. The patient says, "Just use my chest line. It is easier." What should the nurse do?
questions.objective: hemodialysis catheter is not for routine access

options.text: Scrub the hub for 15 seconds, then draw labs and give the drug through it
options.rationale: Correct but premature Scrubbing the hub is the right technique for a line you are allowed to use. This is a hemodialysis catheter, which is never used for routine infusion or blood draws.

options.text: Give the antibiotic through the chest line and draw labs by venipuncture
options.rationale: Near miss concept Moving the labs off the catheter fixes half the problem. A routine antibiotic through a dialysis catheter is still off limits.

options.text: Leave the dialysis line alone and arrange new access with the access team
options.rationale: A hemodialysis catheter is a large bore line (about 11 to 14 Fr) built for rapid blood withdrawal and return during dialysis. The test question is: is this line dedicated to one purpose? Yes. It is never used for routine IV infusion or blood draws and is managed only by dialysis trained staff per policy, because the line is reserved for dialysis. So the nurse leaves it alone and gets new access, such as a new peripheral line placed by the vascular access team, so the antibiotic can be given on time. The hub scrub option uses good technique on a forbidden device. The split option still runs the drug through it. The hold option delays a due drug and misreads the dialysis staff's role.

options.text: Hold the antibiotic until dialysis, then ask the dialysis staff to give it
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Dialysis staff manage the catheter for dialysis, not for routine drugs. Holding a due antibiotic for hours delays treatment the patient needs now.

questions.takeaway: A hemodialysis catheter is for dialysis only: no routine drugs, no blood draws.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out the hub scrub option is the word hemodialysis. Correct technique on the wrong device is still wrong.

questions.stem: A patient who does continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis at home is admitted. The fluid drained from the last exchange is cloudy. The patient reports diffuse abdominal pain. Temperature is 38.6 °C. Respirations are 18/min and unlabored. The catheter exit site is clean and dry. Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition they address, and 2 parameters to monitor.

options.text: Report the cloudy effluent, pain and fever to the provider
Use strict aseptic technique for every exchange and connection
Instill the next bag of dialysate cold to ease the abdominal pain
Raise the head of the bed to ease breathing from abdominal pressure
Peritonitis
Respiratory compromise from abdominal pressure
Exit site infection
An expected effect of a long dwell
Clarity of the drained fluid
Temperature
Respiratory rate and effort
Appearance of the exit site

questions.takeaway: Condition, peritonitis: peritonitis is infection of the lining of the abdominal cavity. The test question is whether the drained fluid is cloudy with pain and fever. All three are present, and cloudy effluent is the classic sign. Respiratory compromise fails because respirations are 18/min and unlabored. Exit site infection fails because the site is clean and dry. A long dwell does not make effluent cloudy or cause fever, so this is not expected. Action, report to the provider: cloudy fluid with fever is a new infection that needs treatment, which the nurse cannot start alone. Action, strict aseptic technique: every exchange opens a path into the peritoneum, so asepsis prevents more organisms entering. Cold dialysate fails because dialysate is warmed to body temperature to reduce discomfort; cold fluid adds pain. Raising the head of the bed is a good action for pressure on the lungs, but breathing is normal right now, so it is the right move at the wrong moment. Parameter, clarity of drained fluid: fluid that clears shows the infection is responding. Parameter, temperature: falling fever tracks the same thing. Respiratory rate and the exit site are normal and do not track this problem. In peritoneal dialysis, cloudy effluent with pain or fever means peritonitis until proven otherwise. Report it and keep every exchange aseptic.
questions.strategy: The details that rule out the near misses are planted: unlabored respirations rule out respiratory compromise and the clean exit site rules out exit site infection. That leaves the cloudy fluid.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews findings for several patients receiving infusions by different routes. For each finding, indicate whether it is expected or must be reported promptly.

rows.text: Epidural opioid infusion for cancer pain: respirations 8/min and hard to rouse
Intra arterial thrombolytic through a groin catheter: foot on that side cool and pale with a faint pulse
Intraosseous line placed during a resuscitation 30 hours ago, still infusing
Midline catheter in place 3 weeks for antibiotics: site clean, dry and without redness
Peritoneal dialysis exchange: drained fluid clear, outflow close to inflow volume

questions.takeaway: Epidural opioid, report: intraspinal infusion puts the drug into the epidural or intrathecal space, and a key risk is respiratory depression. The test question is whether breathing and neuro status are safe. A rate of 8/min with a patient hard to rouse is not. Intra arterial thrombolytic, report: an arterial catheter can cause bleeding, arterial spasm and limb ischemia. A cool, pale foot with a faint pulse on the catheter side is ischemia. Intraosseous line at 30 hours, report: IO access goes into the bone marrow cavity for emergencies and is limited to 24 hours, so other access is overdue. Midline at 3 weeks, expected: a midline can dwell up to 4 weeks, and a clean, dry site without redness shows no complication. Peritoneal dialysis, expected: cloudy fluid is the warning sign of peritonitis, so clear fluid is normal, and outflow close to inflow shows a balanced exchange. Know each route's danger sign: epidural, slow breathing; arterial, a cold limb; IO, past 24 hours; peritoneal, cloudy fluid.
questions.strategy: For each row, ask what can go wrong with that route and whether the finding is it. The detail in the IO row is the time: 30 hours is past the 24 hour limit even though the line still works.

questions.stem: Four patients have no usable vein, and each has an order for subcutaneous fluid (hypodermoclysis). For which patient should the nurse question the order?

options.text: A patient in hospice with mild dehydration and poor oral intake
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Mild dehydration in a hospice patient is the main use of hypodermoclysis. This order fits.

options.text: A patient with severe dehydration, BP 78/44 mm Hg, pulse 126/min
options.rationale: Hypodermoclysis is fluid infused into the subcutaneous tissue, usually the abdomen, thighs or scapula, at a maximum of about 1 mL/min. Hyaluronidase may help absorption. It is used for mild to moderate dehydration in older or palliative patients. The test question is: can the patient wait for slow absorption from tissue? A patient with severe dehydration, a blood pressure of 78/44 mm Hg and a pulse of 126/min is in shock. At 1 mL/min the fluid cannot restore volume fast enough, so the route is contraindicated and the nurse questions it and seeks faster vascular access. The other three patients have mild to moderate dehydration and are the patients this route is designed for.

options.text: An older adult with moderate dehydration after days of poor intake
options.rationale: Near miss concept Moderate dehydration in an older adult is within the range hypodermoclysis treats. The word moderate keeps this one safe.

options.text: A patient in palliative care who drinks only small sips each day
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Poor intake in palliative care is a common reason for subcutaneous fluid. Nothing here makes the slow route unsafe.

questions.takeaway: Subcutaneous fluid is slow: fine for mild to moderate dehydration, never for severe dehydration or shock.
questions.strategy: The detail that decides it is the blood pressure and pulse in one option: they show shock, which a 1 mL/min route cannot fix.

questions.stem: As the nurse threads a catheter into a forearm vein, a firm, bruised swelling forms quickly at the site. There is no blood return. The patient reports tenderness but no tingling, numbness or shooting pain. The nurse removes the catheter. What should the nurse do next?

options.text: Apply gentle pressure, then watch the site for any enlargement
options.rationale: A hematoma is blood leaking into the tissue at the insertion site, seen as bruising, swelling and tenderness. The test question is: is the swelling blood at the puncture, or a nerve or fluid problem? Rapid bruised swelling during threading is blood. The response is gentle pressure, no new catheter in the same site, and watching for expansion, since a growing hematoma means ongoing bleeding. Restarting in the same vein ignores the rule to avoid that site. A tight wrap is too much force on injured tissue. Nerve assessment fits nerve injury, which the stem rules out by stating no tingling, numbness or shooting pain.

options.text: Start a new catheter in the same vein just above the swelling
options.rationale: Correct but premature The patient does still need access, but not in this vein now. A hematoma site is not recannulated; choose another site later.

options.text: Apply firm pressure and a tight wrap to keep the swelling down
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pressure is right, but gentle. A tight wrap over fragile, bruised tissue can add injury and hide whether the swelling is growing.

options.text: Assess nerve function in the hand before doing anything else
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nerve assessment is the response to burning, shooting pain or tingling. The stem rules these out, so this is not the priority.

questions.takeaway: Hematoma: gentle pressure, a different site, and watch for growth.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out the nerve option is no tingling, numbness or shooting pain. The trap is restarting in the same vein, a needed action at the wrong place.

questions.stem: A patient arrives after a crash with heavy bleeding and a falling blood pressure. The type and crossmatch has been drawn, but results are not back. The provider orders red blood cells now. Which unit does the nurse expect the blood bank to send?

options.text: Type O positive packed red blood cells
options.rationale: Near miss concept Type O has no A or B antigens, but positive carries the Rh factor. Without knowing the patient's Rh type, O negative is the safe universal choice.

options.text: Type AB negative packed red blood cells
options.rationale: Near miss concept AB red cells carry both A and B antigens, so they would react with most recipients. AB is not the universal donor for red cells.

options.text: Fresh frozen plasma until the type is known
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Plasma replaces clotting factors. It does not carry oxygen or replace lost red cells, which is what the order asks for.

options.text: Type O negative packed red blood cells
options.rationale: Compatibility means the donor red cells carry no antigen the patient's blood will attack. The test question is: when the patient's type is unknown, which red cells are safe for everyone? Type O negative is the universal donor for red cells in emergencies, because it has no A, B or Rh antigen. O positive carries Rh, which an Rh negative patient could react to. AB cells carry both A and B. Fresh frozen plasma replaces clotting factors, not red cells. Even in an emergency, two licensed nurses still verify the unit against the patient's ID band before it is hung, because an incompatible transfusion is a life threatening sentinel event.

questions.takeaway: Type unknown and red cells needed now: O negative. The two nurse check still happens.
questions.strategy: The detail that decides it is that the crossmatch results are not back. With no type, only the universal donor is safe, and the word negative separates it from O positive.

questions.stem: A trauma patient with major bleeding needs large volumes of fluid and blood as fast as possible. The nurse finds one large, straight forearm vein. Which catheter should the nurse choose?

options.text: An 18 gauge catheter, because it is preferred for blood products
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question 18 gauge is the preferred size for a routine blood transfusion. This patient needs rapid resuscitation, which calls for a larger bore.

options.text: A 14 to 16 gauge catheter for the widest lumen and fastest flow
options.rationale: Gauge is the catheter size, and a smaller gauge number means a wider lumen and faster flow. The test question is: how fast must fluid go in, and can the vein take it? 14 to 16 gauge is large bore, used for trauma, major surgery and rapid fluid resuscitation. This patient is bleeding heavily and needs volume fast, and the vein is large enough. 18 gauge is preferred for routine blood products without hemolysis, but here speed is the priority. 20 gauge is the standard for routine adult infusions. 22 to 24 gauge protects small, fragile veins in children and older adults, which this patient does not have.

options.text: A 20 gauge catheter, the standard size for most adult infusions
options.rationale: Near miss concept 20 gauge is the standard for general adult infusions. It balances flow with comfort, but it is too slow for major bleeding.

options.text: A 22 gauge catheter to protect the vein for later infusions
options.rationale: Near miss concept 22 to 24 gauge is for small or fragile veins. The stem gives a large, straight vein, so there is no reason to choose a small bore.

questions.takeaway: Smaller gauge number, wider lumen, faster flow. Trauma resuscitation gets 14 to 16 gauge.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out the 18 gauge option is as fast as possible; blood alone would fit 18 gauge, but resuscitation needs large bore. The large, straight vein rules out the small bore.

questions.stem: A patient with dark skin has a surgical incision. Which assessment finding is most reliable for detecting inflammation at the site?

options.text: Bright redness spreading outward from the incision
options.rationale: Near miss concept Redness can be hard to see on dark skin and may look like darker skin instead.

options.text: A rising white blood cell count on the morning labs
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data A systemic lab does not show what is happening at the incision.

options.text: The patient's report that the incision looks fine
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic The patient's view is useful, but the nurse still needs a hands on assessment.

options.text: Warmth and swelling compared with the opposite side
options.rationale: On darker skin, redness may appear as darker skin or be hard to see, so the nurse relies on warmth, swelling, pain and function, comparing with the other side.

questions.takeaway: On darker skin, feel for warmth and swelling instead of looking for redness.
questions.strategy: When one sign is hard to see, choose the assessment you can measure by touch or comparison.

questions.stem: For each situation, indicate the type of immunity it produces.

rows.text: An infant receives antibodies through breast milk
A patient bitten by a bat receives rabies immune globulin
An adult receives the annual influenza vaccine
A patient receives tetanus toxoid after a puncture wound
A child recovers from chickenpox

questions.takeaway: Active means the person made the antibodies, through illness (natural) or a vaccine or toxoid (artificial). Passive means the antibodies came from another source, through the placenta or breast milk (natural) or immune globulin or antitoxin (artificial). Who made the antibodies decides active or passive. Ordinary life versus health care decides natural or artificial.
questions.strategy: Ask two questions per row: whose antibodies, and did health care give them?

questions.stem: Two hours after a burn to the forearm, the area is red, warm and swollen. Which process is responsible for these findings?

options.text: Vessels at the site dilate and leak, so blood and fluid move in.
options.rationale: The vascular stage comes first. Histamine from mast cells and basophils dilates vessels, raising flow (warmth and redness) and letting fluid leak out (swelling and pain from pressure).

options.text: New tissue forms quickly to replace the damaged cells at the injured site.
options.rationale: Correct but premature Repair is the last stage and does not cause early redness or swelling.

options.text: Antibodies made by plasma cells bind to the damaged tissue.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Antibodies belong to adaptive immunity. The early local response is innate and vascular.

options.text: Neutrophils and macrophages cross into the tissue and engulf debris.
options.rationale: Correct but premature That is the cellular stage, which follows the vascular stage. Early redness and swelling come from the vessels.

questions.takeaway: Open the road first: vessels dilate and leak.
questions.strategy: Match the finding to the stage. Redness and swelling are about blood flow, so the answer is the vessels.

questions.stem: Complete the statement about a patient with a red, swollen knee after a fall.
questions.sentence: Inflammation is [[1]], so redness and swelling alone [[2]]. Infection becomes more likely if [[3]] appear.

options.text: a sign that the immune system is failing
always caused by bacteria
a response to any injury or irritant
rule out infection
confirm infection
do not prove infection
bruising and stiffness
warmth and mild pain
pus, spreading redness or fever

questions.takeaway: Inflammation follows any injury, so local redness and swelling do not prove a pathogen is present. Pus, spreading redness and fever tip the picture toward infection. Inflammation can happen without infection.
questions.strategy: Fill each blank from the definition: inflammation is a response, infection is invasion.

questions.stem: Select all patients whose immune response is likely to be weakened.

options.text: A 40 year old who received the influenza vaccine last month
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit A vaccine strengthens immunity against that virus. It is a protective factor.

options.text: A patient taking prednisone for 6 months
options.rationale: Age extremes (immature or aging immune systems), corticosteroids, high glucose (which impairs white cell function) and low protein (shown by low albumin, since antibodies and immune cells are proteins) all weaken defense.

options.text: An 88 year old resident of a long term care facility
options.rationale: Age extremes (immature or aging immune systems), corticosteroids, high glucose (which impairs white cell function) and low protein (shown by low albumin, since antibodies and immune cells are proteins) all weaken defense.

options.text: A 2 month old infant
options.rationale: Age extremes (immature or aging immune systems), corticosteroids, high glucose (which impairs white cell function) and low protein (shown by low albumin, since antibodies and immune cells are proteins) all weaken defense.

options.text: A patient with an albumin of 2.6 g/dL
options.rationale: Age extremes (immature or aging immune systems), corticosteroids, high glucose (which impairs white cell function) and low protein (shown by low albumin, since antibodies and immune cells are proteins) all weaken defense.

options.text: A 35 year old who exercises daily and eats a balanced diet
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Nothing in this description weakens immunity.

options.text: A patient with diabetes and a glucose of 290 mg/dL
options.rationale: Age extremes (immature or aging immune systems), corticosteroids, high glucose (which impairs white cell function) and low protein (shown by low albumin, since antibodies and immune cells are proteins) all weaken defense.

questions.takeaway: Age extremes, steroids, sugar and poor protein all weaken defense.
questions.strategy: For each patient, name a mechanism. If you cannot, it does not belong.

questions.stem: Which laboratory value best indicates that a patient's nutrition may be limiting wound healing and immune defense?

options.text: Albumin of 2.8 g/dL
options.rationale: Immune cells and antibodies are made of protein, and wounds need protein to heal. A low albumin points to poor protein status, which slows defense and repair.

options.text: Hemoglobin of 14.1 g/dL
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data This value is unremarkable and does not reflect protein for healing.

options.text: White blood cell count of 8,400/mm³
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data This count is unremarkable and says nothing about protein status.

options.text: Sodium of 139 mEq/L
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Sodium reflects fluid balance, not nutrition.

questions.takeaway: Antibodies are proteins. Low protein means weak defense.
questions.strategy: Pick the lab that measures the building material the stem asks about.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a student about the local response to a cut on the hand. Select all of the cardinal signs of inflammation.

options.text: Swelling of the hand
options.rationale: The five cardinal signs are warmth, redness, swelling, pain and decreased function. All five are local. Fever, pus and a raised white count are real findings with infection, but they are not cardinal signs.

options.text: Redness around the cut
options.rationale: The five cardinal signs are warmth, redness, swelling, pain and decreased function. All five are local. Fever, pus and a raised white count are real findings with infection, but they are not cardinal signs.

options.text: Decreased use of the hand
options.rationale: The five cardinal signs are warmth, redness, swelling, pain and decreased function. All five are local. Fever, pus and a raised white count are real findings with infection, but they are not cardinal signs.

options.text: Pain at the site
options.rationale: The five cardinal signs are warmth, redness, swelling, pain and decreased function. All five are local. Fever, pus and a raised white count are real findings with infection, but they are not cardinal signs.

options.text: Temperature of 38.6 °C
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fever is a whole body finding. The cardinal signs are all local.

options.text: Purulent drainage from the cut
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pus is a sign of infection, not one of the five cardinal signs of inflammation.

options.text: Warmth at the site
options.rationale: The five cardinal signs are warmth, redness, swelling, pain and decreased function. All five are local. Fever, pus and a raised white count are real findings with infection, but they are not cardinal signs.

questions.takeaway: The cardinal signs are local. Anything systemic is not on the list.
questions.strategy: In a SATA on cardinal signs, cross out anything that happens to the whole body.

questions.stem: Select all nursing actions that support a patient's first line of defense against infection.

options.text: Keeping the skin clean, moisturized and intact
options.rationale: Intact skin and mucous membranes are the first barrier of innate immunity. Anything that keeps them whole stops organisms from entering at all.

options.text: Providing regular mouth care
options.rationale: Intact skin and mucous membranes are the first barrier of innate immunity. Anything that keeps them whole stops organisms from entering at all.

options.text: Giving an antipyretic whenever the temperature rises
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fever is part of the defense, and lowering it does nothing for the barrier.

options.text: Removing tape gently to avoid skin tears
options.rationale: Intact skin and mucous membranes are the first barrier of innate immunity. Anything that keeps them whole stops organisms from entering at all.

options.text: Monitoring the white blood cell count daily
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Monitoring finds a problem but does not strengthen the barrier.

options.text: Turning a bedbound patient on schedule to prevent skin breakdown
options.rationale: Intact skin and mucous membranes are the first barrier of innate immunity. Anything that keeps them whole stops organisms from entering at all.

questions.takeaway: Intact skin is the first line of defense.
questions.strategy: Keep every action that protects skin or mucosa; drop actions that only measure or treat.

questions.stem: For each description, indicate whether it describes innate immunity or adaptive immunity.

rows.text: Memory cells make the second response faster and stronger
Cytotoxic T cells destroy virus infected cells
Plasma cells make antibodies that bind one specific antigen
Neutrophils and macrophages engulf invading organisms
Includes intact skin and mucous membranes as barriers
Responds the same way the tenth time as the first time

questions.takeaway: Innate immunity is present at birth, acts immediately and responds the same way to any threat: barriers, inflammation, neutrophils, macrophages. Adaptive immunity develops after exposure, targets one antigen and keeps memory: B cells make antibodies and T cells kill infected or abnormal cells. Memory and specificity are what make immunity adaptive.
questions.strategy: Look for the words memory, specific or antibody. Any of them puts the row in adaptive.

questions.stem: A patient who received a kidney transplant develops signs of rejection. Which cells are mainly responsible?

options.text: T lymphocytes
options.rationale: Cell mediated immunity is the work of T cells. Helper T cells coordinate the response and cytotoxic T cells kill infected, abnormal or foreign cells. That is why T cells drive transplant rejection, fight viruses inside cells and cancer cells, and are the basis of the tuberculosis skin test.

options.text: B lymphocytes
options.rationale: Near miss concept B cells make antibodies against bacteria and toxins in body fluids. Rejection is driven by cell mediated immunity.

options.text: Neutrophils
options.rationale: Near miss concept Neutrophils are innate first responders to infection, not the cells that recognize a foreign organ.

options.text: Eosinophils
options.rationale: Near miss concept Eosinophils respond to parasites and allergy.

questions.takeaway: Transplant rejection, viruses inside cells, cancer and the TB skin test all point to T cells.
questions.strategy: Sort by where the target lives: in body fluids means B cells, inside or on a cell means T cells.

questions.stem: A patient with pneumonia has a white blood cell count of 16,800/mm³ with a high percentage of bands. How should the nurse interpret the bands?

options.text: The patient is having an allergic reaction to the antibiotic.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Allergy raises eosinophils, not bands.

options.text: The immune system is too weak to make mature white cells.
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit A high count with bands shows a strong, active response. A weak system would show a low count.

options.text: The marrow is releasing immature neutrophils to fight bacteria.
options.rationale: A left shift means more immature neutrophils (bands) in the blood. The marrow releases them early when demand is high, which happens in acute bacterial infection.

options.text: The infection has resolved and the marrow is now recovering.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Bands rise while the infection is active, when the marrow is racing to keep up.

questions.takeaway: Bands mean the marrow is racing to keep up.
questions.strategy: Translate the lab word into what the body is doing, then pick the option that matches.

questions.stem: A patient has an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 48 mm/hr and a raised C reactive protein. What can the nurse conclude?

options.text: The patient has a bacterial infection that needs antibiotics.
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism These markers rise with inflammation from any cause. They do not prove infection.

options.text: The results are expected after any illness and need no further follow up.
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A raised ESR and CRP show active inflammation, which needs to be found and explained.

options.text: Inflammation is present, but the tests do not show where or why.
options.rationale: ESR and CRP are general markers of inflammation. They confirm that inflammation is present and can track whether it is improving, but they cannot name the source.

options.text: The inflammation is located in the joints, as in arthritis.
options.rationale: Near miss concept ESR and CRP are nonspecific. They do not point to a location.

questions.takeaway: ESR and CRP answer whether, not where.
questions.strategy: When a lab is nonspecific, reject any option that names a cause or a site.

questions.stem: A patient has a draining abscess, and the drainage is thick and yellow. The patient asks what the yellow material is. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: It is new tissue being pushed out as the wound heals from below.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Repair tissue stays in the wound. It does not drain.

options.text: It is plasma that leaked out of the vessels when they dilated.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Leaked fluid is clear exudate from the vascular stage. Pus is the product of the cellular stage.

options.text: It is the antibiotic working its way out of the infected area.
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Pus forms whether or not an antibiotic is given. It comes from the body's own white cells.

options.text: It is mostly dead white blood cells and broken down tissue.
options.rationale: In the cellular stage, neutrophils arrive first and then macrophages, crossing the vessel wall and engulfing organisms and debris. Pus is the dead white cells and debris left behind.

questions.takeaway: Pus is dead white cells. It belongs to the cellular stage.
questions.strategy: Ask which stage involves cells. Pus can only come from a stage that recruits white cells.

questions.stem: An 81 year old patient asks why the nurse recommends a shingles vaccine and a pneumococcal vaccine. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: "Everyone your age is required by law to have them."
options.rationale: Institution as rationale A requirement is not a reason. The patient asked why.

options.text: "Immune responses weaken with age, so vaccines help you prepare."
options.rationale: Immunosenescence means weaker responses and fewer new antibodies with age. Keeping vaccines current, including influenza, pneumococcal, shingles and tetanus, offsets that risk.

options.text: "Older adults have no immunity left, so vaccines replace it."
options.rationale: Absolute language Immunity weakens with age but does not disappear. Vaccines strengthen an existing system.

options.text: "These vaccines give immediate protection against any infection."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Vaccines give active immunity against one organism, and it takes weeks to build.

questions.takeaway: Older adults respond more weakly, so vaccines matter more.
questions.strategy: When a patient asks why, choose the option that gives the mechanism.

questions.stem: A nurse sustains a needlestick from a patient with hepatitis B. The nurse never completed the hepatitis B vaccine series. Which product gives immediate protection?

options.text: A hepatitis B antibody titer
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data A titer measures immunity. It does not give any.

options.text: Hepatitis B immune globulin
options.rationale: Immune globulin is ready made antibody, which gives passive immunity: immediate, short term and with no memory. The vaccine is started at the same time so active, long term immunity develops.

options.text: The first dose of hepatitis B vaccine alone
options.rationale: Correct but premature A vaccine produces active immunity, which takes weeks to build. It does not protect right now.

options.text: A broad spectrum antibiotic
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hepatitis B is a virus. Antibiotics do not treat viruses.

questions.takeaway: Needed now means passive. Meant to last means active. Often both are given.
questions.strategy: Read the time frame in the stem. Immediate protection can only come from antibodies made somewhere else.

questions.stem: A patient recovering from a myocardial infarction asks whether the damaged heart muscle will heal back to normal. Which response is accurate?

options.text: "It heals with scar tissue, which holds but does not contract."
options.rationale: In the repair stage, tissue either regenerates (same tissue, full function) or is replaced by scar (a patch with no function). Heart muscle heals by scar, which is why an infarction can leave lasting weakness.

options.text: "Heart muscle regenerates, so it will work normally once healed."
options.rationale: Absolute language Heart muscle does not regenerate. It heals by scar, so function is not fully restored.

options.text: "The muscle will heal completely if you take all your medications."
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Medications protect the rest of the heart but cannot turn scar back into muscle.

options.text: "Healing is the same in every tissue; it depends only on the size."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Some tissue regenerates with full function and some heals by scar. Heart muscle scars.

questions.takeaway: Repair moves toward normal, not always to normal.
questions.strategy: When a stem names an organ that cannot regenerate, any option promising full recovery is wrong.

questions.stem: Select all of the statements that correctly distinguish inflammation from infection.

options.text: A sprained ankle is inflamed without being infected
options.rationale: Inflammation is the response, infection is the cause, and treating them as the same word is why students reach for antibiotics when they see redness. A white count rises with stress, steroids, trauma and tissue injury, not only with infection. Inflammation is the healing process, so suppressing it indiscriminately works against the patient.

options.text: Every infection produces inflammation, but not every inflammation means infection
options.rationale: Inflammation is the response, infection is the cause, and treating them as the same word is why students reach for antibiotics when they see redness. A white count rises with stress, steroids, trauma and tissue injury, not only with infection. Inflammation is the healing process, so suppressing it indiscriminately works against the patient.

options.text: Inflammation is a protective response that can occur without any organism present
options.rationale: Inflammation is the response, infection is the cause, and treating them as the same word is why students reach for antibiotics when they see redness. A white count rises with stress, steroids, trauma and tissue injury, not only with infection. Inflammation is the healing process, so suppressing it indiscriminately works against the patient.

options.text: Infection means an organism has invaded and is multiplying in tissue
options.rationale: Inflammation is the response, infection is the cause, and treating them as the same word is why students reach for antibiotics when they see redness. A white count rises with stress, steroids, trauma and tissue injury, not only with infection. Inflammation is the healing process, so suppressing it indiscriminately works against the patient.

options.text: An elevated white count always means infection
options.rationale: Absolute language Rises with stress, steroids, trauma and tissue injury too.

options.text: Inflammation should be suppressed whenever it is found
options.rationale: Near miss concept It is the healing response; suppression is selective.

questions.takeaway: Inflammation is the response. Infection is one of its causes, and not the only one.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options overread inflammation as pathology.

questions.stem: Place the stages of the inflammatory response in order.

options.text: Tissue repair and replacement
Cellular exudate, as phagocytes arrive and form exudate
Vascular response with vasodilation and increased permeability

questions.takeaway: Vessels dilate and leak first, which is what produces the redness, heat and swelling you can see within minutes. Then the cells arrive and the exudate forms, which is the pus or drainage. Repair comes last and takes the longest. Knowing the sequence tells you whether what you are looking at is on schedule. The cardinal signs are the vascular stage. They are the response working, not an infection by themselves.
questions.strategy: Mild redness and warmth on postoperative day one is stage one. Spreading redness on day five is not.

questions.stem: A nurse is explaining the immune response. Which description reflects innate immunity?

options.text: The production of specific antibodies after exposure to an antigen
options.rationale: Near miss concept Adaptive, humoral immunity.

options.text: The protection a vaccine provides against a particular organism
options.rationale: Near miss concept Vaccines work by training the adaptive system.

options.text: The immediate, nonspecific response using neutrophils, macrophages and inflammation
options.rationale: Innate immunity is the first line: it acts within minutes, does not care what the invader is, and uses inflammation, phagocytosis, complement and natural killer cells. Adaptive immunity is slower, specific and remembers, which is what antibodies, memory cells and vaccines are. In an older adult the innate side weakens too, which is why fever may be absent.

options.text: The long lived memory response that makes a second exposure milder
options.rationale: Near miss concept Memory is the defining feature of adaptive immunity.

questions.takeaway: Innate is fast and generic. Adaptive is slow, specific and remembers.
questions.strategy: Three options all describe specificity or memory, which are the adaptive side.

questions.stem: Which statement about inflammatory markers is accurate?

options.text: CRP rises fast in acute inflammation; ESR tracks slower, ongoing change
options.rationale: Both are nonspecific: they say inflammation is happening somewhere, not what or where. C reactive protein moves fast, which makes it useful for tracking whether something acute is getting better. The sedimentation rate moves slowly and fits chronic disease. Neither one names an organism.

options.text: Both markers identify which organism is causing the infection
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is what a culture does.

options.text: A normal sedimentation rate reliably rules out any inflammation
options.rationale: Absolute language It lags, so an early acute process can have a normal rate.

options.text: C reactive protein rises only in bacterial infection, never in a viral one
options.rationale: Near miss concept It rises in trauma, autoimmune disease and viral illness too.

questions.takeaway: These markers say that something is inflamed, never what.
questions.strategy: Any option that makes a nonspecific marker specific is wrong.

questions.stem: A nurse has taught a patient about receiving tetanus immune globulin and the tetanus vaccine after a dirty puncture wound. Select all statements that show correct understanding.

options.text: The vaccine teaches my body to make its own antibodies.
options.rationale: Tetanus immune globulin gives immediate, short term passive protection. The vaccine (toxoid) triggers the patient's own antibody production and memory, which lasts but takes weeks and needs boosters.

options.text: The vaccine protects me right away, so the immune globulin is just extra.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Active immunity takes days to weeks to build. The immune globulin covers the gap.

options.text: I will need tetanus boosters in the future.
options.rationale: Tetanus immune globulin gives immediate, short term passive protection. The vaccine (toxoid) triggers the patient's own antibody production and memory, which lasts but takes weeks and needs boosters.

options.text: Since both are injections, they work the same way.
options.rationale: Near miss concept The route does not decide the type. Ready made antibodies are passive; a toxoid is active.

options.text: The immune globulin will protect me for the rest of my life.
options.rationale: Absolute language Passive immunity is short term because borrowed antibodies break down and there are no memory cells.

options.text: The immune globulin protects me right away, but only for a few weeks.
options.rationale: Tetanus immune globulin gives immediate, short term passive protection. The vaccine (toxoid) triggers the patient's own antibody production and memory, which lasts but takes weeks and needs boosters.

questions.takeaway: What is in the syringe decides the type of immunity, not the needle.
questions.strategy: Reject any statement that gives passive immunity memory or active immunity speed.

questions.stem: A patient has taken prednisone for rheumatoid arthritis for a year and says, "I feel great, so I am going to stop the prednisone tomorrow." Which response is the priority?

options.text: "Check your blood glucose regularly after you stop the prednisone."
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Glucose monitoring matters while on the drug, but it does not address the danger of stopping abruptly.

options.text: "You may stop it as long as you watch closely for signs of infection."
options.rationale: Near miss concept The danger of stopping suddenly is adrenal insufficiency, not infection.

options.text: "That is a good idea, since prednisone weakens your immune system."
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic It is true that prednisone suppresses immunity, but agreeing to an abrupt stop puts the patient at risk of adrenal crisis.

options.text: "Stopping suddenly is dangerous; your provider must taper the dose."
options.rationale: Long term steroids suppress the adrenal glands, so a sudden stop can cause adrenal insufficiency. The dose must be tapered under the provider's direction.

questions.takeaway: Never stop a long term steroid suddenly.
questions.strategy: When a patient plans to change a medication, the priority answer addresses the danger of the change itself.

questions.stem: A patient who takes prednisone daily had abdominal surgery 4 days ago. Which assessment finding is most concerning?

options.text: A blood glucose of 168 mg/dL before breakfast
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Steroids raise glucose, so a moderately high value is expected and is managed, not the most concerning finding.

options.text: Feeling "off" and eating less, with a temperature of 37.4 °C
options.rationale: Steroids blunt fever, redness and swelling, so infection may show only as a vague change such as malaise or poor intake, with a temperature that looks nearly normal. That change needs further assessment.

options.text: Incision edges approximated with no drainage noted
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit This is a healthy incision.

options.text: Mild incisional pain rated 3 of 10 with movement and coughing
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Mild pain 4 days after surgery is expected.

questions.takeaway: On steroids, a small change carries a big meaning.
questions.strategy: When the body cannot produce the usual signs, choose the subtle new change over the expected abnormal number.

questions.stem: A patient twisted an ankle playing basketball yesterday. The ankle is red, warm and swollen, and the patient limps. The temperature is 36.9 °C and there is no break in the skin. A family member asks the nurse for antibiotics because "it is obviously infected." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Antibiotics are not used for ankles; the provider will decide on anything else."
options.rationale: Institution as rationale This brushes off the family without explaining the difference between inflammation and infection or what to watch for.

options.text: "The redness and swelling confirm infection, so I will ask for an antibiotic."
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Redness and swelling are the cardinal signs of inflammation, which happens with any injury. They do not prove that a pathogen is present.

options.text: "This is inflammation from the injury; I will explain what would suggest infection."
options.rationale: Inflammation is the protective response to any injury, and a sprain with no broken skin and a normal temperature fits it. Infection is a pathogen multiplying. The nurse assesses the five signs, notes the edges, and reports pus, spreading redness or fever.

options.text: "Swelling after a sprain is normal, so there is nothing you need to watch for."
options.rationale: Absolute language It is expected, but spreading redness, pus or a fever would change the picture, so the area still needs follow up.

questions.takeaway: Redness and swelling mean inflammation. They do not mean infection.
questions.strategy: When an option jumps from a local sign to a diagnosis, ask whether a pathogen has actually been shown.

questions.stem: An 84 year old patient who takes prednisone daily has a reddened, draining pressure injury. The white blood cell count is 7,200/mm³ and the temperature is 37.1 °C. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: The prednisone should be stopped so the immune system can respond.
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Steroids must be tapered, never stopped suddenly, and changing them is a provider decision.

options.text: The drainage is from inflammation, so no culture is needed now.
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Drainage from a wound is a sign of infection and should be assessed and reported, not explained away.

options.text: Infection is unlikely because the white count is within normal.
options.rationale: Absolute language Older age and steroids both blunt the white count and fever, so a normal number proves little here.

options.text: A normal count and temperature do not rule out infection here.
options.rationale: Immunosenescence in older adults and corticosteroids both suppress white cell response and fever. Infection can be present with normal numbers, so local signs like drainage carry more weight.

questions.takeaway: A normal count does not rule out infection in an older adult or a patient on steroids.
questions.strategy: When the stem gives a reason the body cannot respond, a normal lab stops being reassuring.

questions.stem: An 86 year old nursing home resident has a white blood cell count of 9,000 and a temperature of 36.8 degrees Celsius. The family reports she has been "not herself" for two days and has stopped eating. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Focus the assessment on her appetite, intake and nutrition
options.rationale: Near miss concept Anorexia is a symptom here, not the problem.

options.text: Attribute the change to adjusting to the unfamiliar setting
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism She is in her own facility, and it explains away a two day change.

options.text: Reassure the family that the normal laboratory results are reassuring for now
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Uses two blunted responses as evidence of health.

options.text: Screen for infection, since older adults often lack the usual signs
options.rationale: Aging blunts every signal this assessment relies on. Neutrophils function less well, the count may not rise, and the fever may never come.
