If someone else is available, they can open the package onto the field, which is the better answer when it exists and is not among these options.

questions.takeaway: Starting over is the cheap option. Proceeding is the expensive one.
questions.strategy: Every other option saves the setup by compromising it.

questions.stem: A patient on contact precautions for vancomycin resistant enterococcus needs physical therapy to maintain mobility before discharge. What should the nurse arrange?

options.text: Therapy in the room, or in the gym with equipment disinfected after
options.rationale: Precautions are designed to let care continue, not to stop it. Contact precautions control transmission through barriers and disinfection, both of which work in a gym. Deferring therapy trades a controllable infection risk for a certain loss of function, and immobility has its own long list of complications.

options.text: Bedside exercises only, done by the nurse until the precautions end
options.rationale: Near miss concept Less effective than the therapy he was referred for, and it is not the nurse's expertise.

options.text: Postpone therapy until the contact precautions are discontinued
options.rationale: Near miss concept Trades a manageable risk for guaranteed deconditioning.

options.text: Therapy in the hallway outside the room to keep the gym uncontaminated
options.rationale: Near miss concept A corridor is a shared space too, and this provides no barrier at all.

questions.takeaway: Isolation restricts the organism, not the care.
questions.strategy: Any option that cancels needed care to satisfy precautions has misunderstood them.

questions.stem: A patient is admitted with fever, night sweats, weight loss and a three week cough. The chest x ray is pending. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Place the patient in contact precautions and reassess after the x ray
options.rationale: Near miss concept Wrong route entirely. This organism travels on air currents.

options.text: Place the patient in airborne precautions now, before the diagnosis is confirmed
options.rationale: Precautions are based on the suspected organism, not the confirmed one, because the whole point is preventing transmission while you find out. That constellation is tuberculosis until proven otherwise: negative pressure room, N95 on everyone entering, surgical mask on the patient if he leaves the room. Waiting for a culture means waiting weeks.

options.text: Use standard precautions until tuberculosis is confirmed by culture
options.rationale: Near miss concept A culture takes weeks; everyone is exposed by then.

options.text: Place the patient in droplet precautions with a surgical mask
options.rationale: Near miss concept Droplets fall within a few feet; tuberculosis stays airborne and needs an N95 and negative pressure.

questions.takeaway: You isolate on suspicion. Confirmation comes far too late to be useful.
questions.strategy: Any option that waits for a result before isolating has already allowed the transmission.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches a patient with an MRSA wound infection who is going home. Select all statements that show understanding.

options.text: Once the wound is covered, I can stop washing my hands so often.
options.rationale: Absolute language MRSA spreads by touch, so frequent hand hygiene continues even with a covered wound.

options.text: I will wash my linens in hot water and dry them on high heat.
options.rationale: MRSA spreads by touch through the wound, drainage and items it touches. Teaching covers hand hygiene, not sharing personal items, hot water laundry, finishing the antibiotic and telling every provider. Colonized patients still spread it.

options.text: If my nose swab is positive but I have no symptoms, I cannot spread it.
options.rationale: Near miss concept A colonized patient with no symptoms can still spread MRSA.

options.text: I will tell my other providers that I have MRSA.
options.rationale: MRSA spreads by touch through the wound, drainage and items it touches. Teaching covers hand hygiene, not sharing personal items, hot water laundry, finishing the antibiotic and telling every provider. Colonized patients still spread it.

options.text: I will not share my towels or razors.
options.rationale: MRSA spreads by touch through the wound, drainage and items it touches. Teaching covers hand hygiene, not sharing personal items, hot water laundry, finishing the antibiotic and telling every provider. Colonized patients still spread it.

options.text: I will take every dose of the antibiotic even after I feel better.
options.rationale: MRSA spreads by touch through the wound, drainage and items it touches. Teaching covers hand hygiene, not sharing personal items, hot water laundry, finishing the antibiotic and telling every provider. Colonized patients still spread it.

questions.takeaway: Colonized is still contagious.
questions.strategy: For each statement, ask whether it stops touch transmission.

questions.stem: A provider orders a blood culture and the first dose of IV ceftriaxone for a patient with suspected sepsis. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Check the white blood cell count before giving the antibiotic.
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question The count does not change the plan, and waiting for it delays treatment.

options.text: Give the antibiotic first so treatment is not delayed.
options.rationale: Correct but premature Cultures drawn after the antibiotic may grow nothing. If the culture can be drawn with no delay, it comes first.

options.text: Hold the antibiotic until the culture results are back.
options.rationale: Absolute language Results take days. Antibiotics for sepsis are due within 1 hour of recognition.

options.text: Draw the blood culture, then give the antibiotic without delay.
options.rationale: Cultures are drawn before the first antibiotic dose so the organism can be identified, but only if that causes no delay. The antibiotic is never held for results.

questions.takeaway: Culture first, then antibiotic, and never hold the antibiotic for results.
questions.strategy: In a sequence question, the step that loses information if done late goes first.

questions.stem: A patient has new watery diarrhea three days after starting clindamycin. The stool test is pending. Which action should the nurse take now?

options.text: Wait for the stool result before starting any precautions.
options.rationale: Correct but premature Precautions begin on suspicion. Waiting allows spread during the delay.

options.text: Start contact precautions; use soap and water for hand hygiene.
options.rationale: New watery diarrhea after antibiotics suggests C. difficile. Contact precautions start on suspicion. Its spores survive alcohol, so hand hygiene uses soap and water with friction for at least 20 seconds, and the room is cleaned with a sporicidal agent such as bleach.

options.text: Use an alcohol based hand rub each time after leaving the room.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores. Soap and water with friction removes them.

options.text: Give the ordered antidiarrheal to control the stools.
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Antidiarrheals can hold the toxin in the bowel and are not given without a provider order.

questions.takeaway: C. difficile: precautions on suspicion, soap and water, bleach for the room.
questions.strategy: When a stem names a spore former, reject anything that depends on alcohol.

questions.stem: An 86 year old resident is newly confused this morning. Temperature is 37.2 °C, the baseline is 36.2 °C, and the urine is cloudy and foul smelling. The nursing assistant says, "No fever, so it is probably just a bad night." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "A one degree rise can be fever at her age, and new confusion needs assessment."
options.rationale: Older adults run lower temperatures, so 37.2 °C against a baseline of 36.2 °C is meaningful. New confusion with cloudy, foul urine points to a urinary tract infection that needs assessment and reporting.

options.text: "You are right; there is no fever, so we will recheck the temperature again in 4 hours."
options.rationale: Absolute language Waiting accepts the idea that no fever means no infection, which is the wrong conclusion for an older adult.

options.text: "Confusion is common in older adults, so we will just reorient her."
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem New confusion is a change, not an expected part of aging.

options.text: "Please give acetaminophen now and we will reassess the confusion later."
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Treating the temperature does nothing for the cause and can mask the next fever.

questions.takeaway: "No fever, so it is not infection" is the wrong answer.
questions.strategy: Compare every number with the patient's own baseline before calling it normal.

chapters.title: Assessment of the Skin, Hair and Nails

questions.stem: A patient points out a mole that has changed over the past few months. Which feature is most concerning?

options.text: It is uniformly dark brown in color
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Uniform color is the reassuring version of C.

options.text: It has been present since childhood
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Longstanding and unchanged is the opposite of concerning.

options.text: It measures about 4 mm across
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Under the 6 mm threshold, and size alone never decides it.

options.text: It has changed over recent months
options.rationale: ABCDE: asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, diameter over 6 mm, and evolving. Evolving is the one that outranks the rest, because a lesion that is changing is doing something now. A small, uniform, long standing mole is reassuring on every other letter.

questions.takeaway: E is the letter that matters most. Change beats size.
questions.strategy: Three options describe a stable, ordinary mole. One describes movement.

questions.stem: Match each lesion to its description.

rows.text: A flat area of color change that you cannot feel
A small solid raised lesion
A small blister containing clear fluid
A raised, edematous, transient area as in hives

questions.takeaway: The vocabulary matters because it is how the next clinician pictures a lesion they cannot see. Flat is a macule, raised and solid is a papule, fluid filled is a vesicle, and a wheal is the transient edematous one. Describing a rash as a rash tells nobody anything. Say what you can feel. Flat, raised, fluid filled, or transient.
questions.strategy: Run your gloved finger over it. If you can feel it, it is not a macule.

questions.stem: How should the nurse assess for an early pressure injury in a patient with darker skin?

options.text: Press firmly and look for blanching under bright lighting
options.rationale: Near miss concept Still relies on visible erythema, which is the limitation here.

options.text: Rely on the Braden score rather than on the skin examination
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome A score predicts risk; it does not find an injury.

options.text: Assume lower risk, since darker skin resists pressure better
options.rationale: Near miss concept False, and the delayed detection makes outcomes worse, not better.

options.text: Compare with nearby skin for color, warmth, bogginess and pain
options.rationale: Erythema is hard or impossible to see in darker skin, which is why pressure injuries in these patients are found later and at higher stages. Use the other senses: temperature difference, a boggy or firm feel, a color that differs from the surrounding skin, and the patient's report of pain. Pain over a bony prominence is an early finding people skip.

questions.takeaway: If you cannot see redness, feel for temperature and bogginess and ask about pain.
questions.strategy: The option about blanching still depends on seeing a color change.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a patient with dark skin for jaundice. Where should the nurse look?

options.text: The palms, especially over calloused areas
options.rationale: Near miss concept Calloused palms look yellow anyway.

options.text: The outer edges of the sclera near the lids
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fat deposits make the outer sclera look yellow without jaundice.

options.text: The skin of the face and the forearms
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sun exposed, pigmented skin hides color change.

options.text: The hard palate and the sclera near the cornea
options.rationale: Color changes show best where pigment is lowest. Jaundice is checked on the hard palate and the sclera nearest the cornea. Cyanosis and pallor are checked on the oral mucosa, lips, conjunctiva, nail beds, palms and soles, and petechiae on the oral mucosa and conjunctiva. The outer sclera and calloused palms look yellow anyway, so neither proves jaundice.

questions.takeaway: Jaundice: hard palate and the sclera next to the cornea.
questions.strategy: Two options are places that look yellow in everyone. Eliminate them first.

questions.topic: skin turgor in the older adult
questions.stem: A nurse is checking skin turgor on an 86 year old. Where should the nurse test it?
questions.objective: skin turgor in the older adult

options.text: On the back of the hand
options.rationale: Near miss concept Lost elastin makes the back of the hand tent even when the patient is hydrated.

options.text: On the forearm, which is easy to reach
options.rationale: Near miss concept The forearm loses elasticity with age too.

options.text: Over the sternum or under the clavicle
options.rationale: Older adults lose elastin, so skin tents even when they are hydrated, which makes the back of the hand misleading. Testing over the abdomen, the radial wrist or under the clavicle gives a more useful result.

options.text: It cannot be tested in older adults
options.rationale: Absolute language Turgor is less reliable with age, but it can still be tested over a site with less elastic loss, such as the sternum or below the clavicle.

questions.takeaway: Older adult turgor: abdomen, wrist or clavicle, not the back of the hand.
questions.strategy: When the site matters, eliminate the one that changes most with age.

questions.stem: A nurse notes clubbing of the fingertips in a patient with long standing lung disease. How should this finding be interpreted?

options.text: An acute sign that the patient is hypoxic at this very moment in time
options.rationale: Near miss concept Clubbing develops over time and does not signal a sudden change.

options.text: A chronic sign of long term low oxygen, not a new event
options.rationale: Clubbing reflects long term low oxygen. It tells you about the patient's history, not about what is happening this hour, so you still assess current oxygenation by looking at the patient: work of breathing, color, mental status and the saturation trend.

options.text: A sign of jaundice from liver involvement in lung disease
options.rationale: Near miss concept Clubbing reflects oxygenation, not bilirubin.

options.text: An expected change of aging seen in most older adults
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Clubbing has a cause and is not part of normal aging.

questions.takeaway: Clubbing is chronic. It does not tell you the patient is worse today.
questions.strategy: Separate chronic signs from acute ones before you decide how urgent a finding is.

questions.stem: During a skin assessment the nurse inspects several pigmented lesions. Select all of the lesions that should be referred.

options.text: A 5 mm mole that has recently started to bleed
options.rationale: ABCDE is asymmetry, border, color, diameter over 6 mm and evolving, and one feature is enough to refer. Evolving includes changing size, shape, color or elevation and new itching, bleeding or crusting. The 5 mm bleeding mole passes D but fails E, which is the letter students drop.

options.text: A 4 mm round, evenly brown mole unchanged for years
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Small, symmetric, one color and unchanged passes every letter.

options.text: A mole whose two halves do not match
options.rationale: ABCDE is asymmetry, border, color, diameter over 6 mm and evolving, and one feature is enough to refer. Evolving includes changing size, shape, color or elevation and new itching, bleeding or crusting. The 5 mm bleeding mole passes D but fails E, which is the letter students drop.

options.text: A lesion with tan, black and red areas within it
options.rationale: ABCDE is asymmetry, border, color, diameter over 6 mm and evolving, and one feature is enough to refer. Evolving includes changing size, shape, color or elevation and new itching, bleeding or crusting. The 5 mm bleeding mole passes D but fails E, which is the letter students drop.

options.text: An 8 mm mole

Evolving includes changing size, shape, color or elevation and new itching, bleeding or crusting. The 5 mm bleeding mole passes D but fails E, which is the letter students drop.

options.text: A 3 mm freckle with a smooth, even border
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Small, even and smooth passes every letter.

questions.takeaway: One letter is enough to refer.
questions.strategy: Check every letter for every lesion; a lesion is cleared only if it passes all five.

questions.stem: Select all of the actions that reflect correct skin assessment technique.

options.text: Take the history before inspecting and palpating
options.rationale: Skin assessment starts with the history: new drugs, products, allergens, nutrition, sun exposure and family history. Then you inspect and palpate with the patient undressed, privacy protected, in bright natural light, including the scalp, nails, mucous membranes and skinfolds, and you repeat it daily during the bath. Temperature is felt with the back of the hand, and the baseline in dark skin is set on skin with little sun exposure.

options.rationale: Near miss concept Temperature is felt with the back of the hand.

Temperature is felt with the back of the hand, and the baseline in dark skin is set on skin with little sun exposure.

Then you inspect and palpate with the patient undressed, privacy protected, in bright natural light, including the scalp, nails, mucous membranes and skinfolds, and you repeat it daily during the bath. options.text: Inspect the scalp, nails, mucous membranes and skinfolds

Then you inspect and palpate with the patient undressed, privacy protected, in bright natural light, including the scalp, nails, mucous membranes and skinfolds, and you repeat it daily during the bath. Temperature is felt with the back of the hand, and the baseline in dark skin is set on skin with little sun exposure.

options.rationale: Near miss concept Skin is checked daily, during the bath.
