questions.strategy: The wrong options swap one detail of technique or shrink how often the skin is checked.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching about the skin before a skin assessment. Match each function to the skin layer that provides it.

rows.text: Makes vitamin D
Prevents loss of body water
Changes blood flow to help control body temperature
Gives the skin strength and elasticity
Stores fat that insulates for warmth
Contains pressure receptors

questions.takeaway: The epidermis is the outer barrier. It makes vitamin D and keeps body water in, so a patient who loses a large area of epidermis is at risk for dehydration and infection. The dermis is the working layer under it. It holds blood vessels that open and close to release or keep heat, and its fibers give the skin strength and elasticity, and it supports wound healing. Subcutaneous tissue is the deepest layer. It stores fat that cushions and insulates, and it holds the pressure receptors. The dermis holds the nerves for pain, touch and temperature, so the pressure row is the one that belongs deeper. Epidermis is the barrier, dermis is strength and blood flow, subcutaneous tissue is fat, cushion and pressure sense.
questions.strategy: Ask what the layer is made of. Barrier cells, then vessels and fibers, then fat. The detail that rules out dermis for the pressure row is that the dermis senses pain, touch and temperature, while pressure receptors sit in the fat layer.

questions.stem: A nurse is describing skin lesions on several patients. Classify each finding as a primary or a secondary lesion.

rows.text: A flat, tan area 3 cm across with no change in texture
A raised, firm lump about 2 cm wide and deep
A small blister filled with cloudy fluid
Dried yellow serum covering blisters that broke
Thick, leathery skin with deep lines after months of scratching
A thin, shiny, paper like area with lost skin markings

questions.takeaway: A primary lesion is the first change the skin shows. A secondary lesion is what forms later, when a primary lesion breaks, dries or is rubbed, or when the skin changes over time. The flat tan area over 1 cm is a patch, a primary lesion. The firm raised lump over 1 cm wide and deep is a nodule, also primary. A blister with cloudy fluid is a pustule, primary. Dried serum over broken blisters is a crust, secondary, because it needed the blisters to break first. Thick skin with deep lines from long scratching is lichenification, secondary, because it comes from chronic rubbing. Thin, shiny, paper like skin with lost markings is atrophy, secondary. Primary is the first change. Secondary needs something to happen to the skin first.
questions.strategy: Look for a history word in each row. The details that rule out primary are "blisters that broke" and "after months of scratching", which tell you the lesion came from an earlier change. Atrophy is secondary because it is a later change in skin that was once normal, such as aging or stretching.

questions.stem: Several blisters on a patient's arm broke two days ago. The nurse now sees moist, shallow, red areas that are wider than a crack. The top layer of skin is gone, but the loss does not reach the dermis. Which term should the nurse document?

options.text: Ulcer
options.rationale: Near miss concept An ulcer goes below the epidermis into the dermis, and here the loss stops before the dermis.

options.text: Erosion
options.rationale: An erosion is a loss of the epidermis only, wider than a fissure, and it often follows broken vesicles, bullae or pustules. The test is depth: if the loss stays in the epidermis, it is an erosion. This patient's loss does not reach the dermis and follows broken blisters, so it is an erosion. An ulcer is deeper, reaching the dermis and sometimes fat. A fissure is a linear crack. A crust is dried serum or pus over a lesion, which a moist area is not.

options.text: Fissure
options.rationale: Near miss concept A fissure is a narrow linear crack, and these areas are wider than a crack.

options.text: Crust
options.rationale: Near miss concept A crust is dried serum or pus, and these areas are moist.

questions.takeaway: Depth decides it. Epidermis only is an erosion. Into the dermis is an ulcer.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out ulcer is "does not reach the dermis". The word "moist" rules out crust and "wider than a crack" rules out fissure.

questions.stem: A nurse inspects the nails of several patients. Match each nail finding to the condition it is most linked to.

rows.text: Nail angle straightened to 180 degrees with a spongy base
Nail angle greater than 180 degrees with drumstick fingertips
Flattened, smoother nail plate
Concave, scooped nail plate
Horizontal grooves about 1 mm deep across all nails
Many small pits in the fingernails

questions.takeaway: A normal nail meets the proximal fold at about 160 degrees with a firm base. Early clubbing straightens that angle to 180 degrees and the base feels spongy. Late clubbing goes past 180 degrees with drumstick fingertips. Both reflect hypoxia, low oxygen that is longer lasting in late clubbing, as in COPD, lung cancer or chronic heart disease. Early koilonychia, or spoon nail, is a flattened, smoother plate linked to iron deficiency. Late koilonychia is a concave plate, and it is linked to psoriasis, chemical irritants or a developmental cause, not iron. Beau's lines are 1 mm horizontal grooves on all nails, left by a pause in growth during acute severe illness, long fever or severe malnutrition. Pitting is many small pits, linked to psoriasis and alopecia areata. Clubbing means oxygen, early spoon nail means iron, grooves on all nails mean a past acute illness, pits mean psoriasis.
questions.strategy: Spoon nails split by stage. The detail that rules out iron deficiency for the scooped nail is that it is concave, which is the late form linked to psoriasis.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence: A nurse is assessing a patient with very dark skin tone. Pallor is best checked in the [[1]], where it looks [[2]]. Inflammation often makes the area look [[3]] than nearby skin. Dark lengthwise bands in several nails are [[4]].

options.text: mucous membranes
forearm skin
calloused palms
skin of the face
ash gray
bright red
deep blue
yellow orange
darker
lighter
redder
bluer
a common expected finding
a sign of iron deficiency
a sign of long term low oxygen
a sign of acute illness

questions.takeaway: [1] mucous membranes: Color change is easiest to see where pigment is lowest. Forearm and face skin carry sun tanning, and calloused palms can look yellow anyway, so the mucous membranes are inspected, in ambient or halogen light. [2] ash gray: In very dark brown or black skin, pallor looks ash gray. Brown skin may look yellow brown instead. Bright red, deep blue and yellow orange describe other color changes. [3] darker: In dark skin, inflammation and irritation often show as hyperpigmentation, so the area looks darker, not redder. Looking for red is the reason inflammation is missed. [4] a common expected finding: Melanonychia, dark bands in the nail, is seen in about 75 percent of people with dark skin. It is not a sign of iron deficiency, low oxygen or acute illness, which change nail shape instead. In dark skin, look at mucous membranes for color, expect inflammation to look darker, and expect dark nail bands.
questions.strategy: Each wrong choice assumes dark skin shows color the way light skin does. The detail that rules out "redder" is that dark skin shows inflammation as hyperpigmentation.

questions.stem: A nurse sets a patient's baseline skin tone on the inner upper arm instead of the back of the forearm. Why is the inner arm the better site?

options.text: The inner arm has more melanocytes, so color change shows more clearly
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism The site is chosen for less sun exposure, not for more pigment cells.

options.text: The forearm has a thicker dermis, which hides changes in blood flow
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dermal thickness is not the reason. The difference between the sites is UV exposure.

options.text: Forearm color is set by genes, while inner arm color changes with the seasons
options.rationale: Near miss concept This reverses the two types. Sun exposed skin carries the changing, UV driven pigment.

options.text: Forearm color includes tanning from UV light, while the inner arm shows inherited tone
options.rationale: Everyone has two types of pigment. Constitutive pigmentation is the tone set by genes. Facultative pigmentation is added by UV light and the environment, like a tan. The test is whether the site gets sun. The back of the forearm gets sun, so its color mixes both types. The inner upper arm gets little sun, so it shows the inherited baseline. That is why skin tone is assessed on areas less exposed to UV light. More melanocytes and a thicker dermis are not the reason.

questions.takeaway: Set baseline tone where the sun does not reach. Sun exposed skin adds facultative pigment.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out the reversed option is that the forearm is the site that gets sun, so its color is the one that changes.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing the skin of a 78 year old. Select all of the findings the nurse should report.

options.text: Petechiae below the nipple line
options.rationale: Aging changes the skin in predictable ways, so the question is whether a finding is new and dangerous or simply old. Petechiae below the nipple line can mean disseminated intravascular coagulation and are reported now. Any ABCDE feature, such as a notched border, is reported and referred. Sudden patchy hair loss is reported. Thin dry skin, cherry hemangiomas, thick ridged toenails and gray hair are expected.

options.text: Cherry hemangiomas on the trunk
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Cherry hemangiomas are an expected change of aging.

options.text: Sudden patchy hair loss
options.rationale: Aging changes the skin in predictable ways, so the question is whether a finding is new and dangerous or simply old. Petechiae below the nipple line can mean disseminated intravascular coagulation and are reported now. Any ABCDE feature, such as a notched border, is reported and referred. Sudden patchy hair loss is reported. Thin dry skin, cherry hemangiomas, thick ridged toenails and gray hair are expected.

options.text: Thick, ridged toenails
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Thick, ridged toenails are expected in an older adult.

options.text: A pigmented lesion with a notched border
options.rationale: Aging changes the skin in predictable ways, so the question is whether a finding is new and dangerous or simply old. Petechiae below the nipple line can mean disseminated intravascular coagulation and are reported now. Any ABCDE feature, such as a notched border, is reported and referred. Sudden patchy hair loss is reported. Thin dry skin, cherry hemangiomas, thick ridged toenails and gray hair are expected.

options.text: Gray hair
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Gray hair is expected.

questions.takeaway: Report the new and dangerous. Leave the expected aging findings unselected.
questions.strategy: Sort each option into old and expected or new and dangerous.

questions.topic: hair and nail findings to report
questions.stem: A patient with dark skin tone is admitted with fatigue that has lasted several weeks. The patient started a hormone drug two months ago. The nurse inspects the hair and nails. Select all of the findings the nurse should report for follow up.
questions.objective: hair and nail findings to report

options.text: Dark lengthwise bands on several nails that the patient says were always there
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Long standing melanonychia is common and expected in dark skin tone.

options.text: Flattened, smooth, spoon shaped fingernails
options.rationale: The question for each finding is whether it is a normal variation or a change that has a cause. Spoon shaped, flattened nails are early koilonychia, linked to iron deficiency, which fits weeks of fatigue, so report it. New coarse hair on the face and chest is hirsutism, excess body hair from a hormone imbalance or a drug side effect, and its timing after the new drug makes it reportable. Many small pits are nail pitting, linked to psoriasis and alopecia areata. A 180 degree angle with a spongy base is early clubbing, linked to low oxygen and lung cancer. Dark bands that were always there are melanonychia, seen in about 75 percent of people with dark skin. A 160 degree angle is normal.

options.text: New coarse hair on the face and chest since the hormone drug began
options.rationale: The question for each finding is whether it is a normal variation or a change that has a cause. Spoon shaped, flattened nails are early koilonychia, linked to iron deficiency, which fits weeks of fatigue, so report it. New coarse hair on the face and chest is hirsutism, excess body hair from a hormone imbalance or a drug side effect, and its timing after the new drug makes it reportable. Many small pits are nail pitting, linked to psoriasis and alopecia areata. A 180 degree angle with a spongy base is early clubbing, linked to low oxygen and lung cancer. Dark bands that were always there are melanonychia, seen in about 75 percent of people with dark skin. A 160 degree angle is normal.

options.text: A 160 degree angle where the nail plate meets the proximal fold
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem 160 degrees is the normal nail angle.

options.text: Many small pits in the fingernails
options.rationale: The question for each finding is whether it is a normal variation or a change that has a cause. Spoon shaped, flattened nails are early koilonychia, linked to iron deficiency, which fits weeks of fatigue, so report it. New coarse hair on the face and chest is hirsutism, excess body hair from a hormone imbalance or a drug side effect, and its timing after the new drug makes it reportable. Many small pits are nail pitting, linked to psoriasis and alopecia areata. A 180 degree angle with a spongy base is early clubbing, linked to low oxygen and lung cancer. Dark bands that were always there are melanonychia, seen in about 75 percent of people with dark skin. A 160 degree angle is normal.

options.text: A 180 degree nail angle with a spongy feel at the base
options.rationale: The question for each finding is whether it is a normal variation or a change that has a cause. Spoon shaped, flattened nails are early koilonychia, linked to iron deficiency, which fits weeks of fatigue, so report it. New coarse hair on the face and chest is hirsutism, excess body hair from a hormone imbalance or a drug side effect, and its timing after the new drug makes it reportable. Many small pits are nail pitting, linked to psoriasis and alopecia areata. A 180 degree angle with a spongy base is early clubbing, linked to low oxygen and lung cancer. Dark bands that were always there are melanonychia, seen in about 75 percent of people with dark skin. A 160 degree angle is normal.

questions.takeaway: Report nail shape changes and new hair growth after a new drug. Expected variation in dark skin is not a problem.
questions.strategy: Sort normal from caused. The detail that clears the dark bands is "always there" in a patient with dark skin tone, and the detail that flags the hair growth is that it began after the new drug.

questions.topic: skin change after a new drug
questions.stem: A patient admitted with pneumonia started a new IV antibiotic yesterday. Today the nurse finds raised, pale red, itchy areas on the trunk. Each area fades within hours and new ones appear elsewhere. Breathing is unlabored and the lips and tongue are not swollen. What should the nurse do?
questions.objective: skin change after a new drug

options.text: Report the rash and note that it began the day after the new antibiotic
options.rationale: Raised, itchy areas that fade within hours and move are wheals, which are transient swelling in the dermis, as in urticaria. A key part of skin assessment is asking whether the skin changed after a new drug was started. Here the timing points straight at the antibiotic, so the nurse reports the rash and its timing to the provider. Breathing is unlabored with no lip or tongue swelling, so this is not an airway emergency, but it still needs the drug reviewed. Cool cloths and lotion may help comfort, but they come after the report. Calling it vesicular is the wrong term, because vesicles hold clear fluid, and charting it does not act on it.

options.text: Apply cool cloths to the trunk and recheck the skin at the end of the shift
options.rationale: Correct but premature Comfort can come later. Waiting a shift delays the link to the drug.

options.text: Document a vesicular rash on the trunk and continue to monitor it
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting The lesions are wheals, not fluid filled vesicles, and charting alone does not get the drug reviewed.

options.text: Apply a fragrance free lotion and remind the patient not to scratch
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic It treats the itch and ignores the likely cause.

questions.takeaway: A new rash after a new drug is reported with its timing.
questions.strategy: The detail that tips the question is "started a new IV antibiotic yesterday". The detail that rules out vesicular is that each area fades within hours, which is a wheal.

questions.stem: A patient who works outdoors as a lifeguard has a parent who had melanoma. The patient asks what to do at home to keep the skin, hair and nails healthy. Select all of the teaching the nurse should include.

options.text: Examine all of the skin, including the scalp and soles, every month
options.rationale: Health promotion teaching for the skin has a few parts. Adults examine all of the skin every month, using ABCDE: asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, diameter over 6 mm and evolving. The check covers new lesions and changes in existing ones. Sunscreen and less time in UV light lower risk, which matters for someone with daily sun exposure and a family history of melanoma. Bathing, shampooing and keeping nails clean and trimmed protect skin, hair and nails. Checking only old moles misses new lesions, and a yearly check is less often than the monthly exam that is taught.

options.text: Check both new spots and old moles for the ABCDE features
options.rationale: Health promotion teaching for the skin has a few parts. Adults examine all of the skin every month, using ABCDE: asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, diameter over 6 mm and evolving. The check covers new lesions and changes in existing ones. Sunscreen and less time in UV light lower risk, which matters for someone with daily sun exposure and a family history of melanoma. Bathing, shampooing and keeping nails clean and trimmed protect skin, hair and nails. Checking only old moles misses new lesions, and a yearly check is less often than the monthly exam that is taught.

options.text: Use sunscreen and cut down time in direct UV light
options.rationale: Health promotion teaching for the skin has a few parts. Adults examine all of the skin every month, using ABCDE: asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, diameter over 6 mm and evolving. The check covers new lesions and changes in existing ones. Sunscreen and less time in UV light lower risk, which matters for someone with daily sun exposure and a family history of melanoma. Bathing, shampooing and keeping nails clean and trimmed protect skin, hair and nails. Checking only old moles misses new lesions, and a yearly check is less often than the monthly exam that is taught.

options.text: Bathe, shampoo and keep the fingernails clean and trimmed
options.rationale: Health promotion teaching for the skin has a few parts. Adults examine all of the skin every month, using ABCDE: asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, diameter over 6 mm and evolving. The check covers new lesions and changes in existing ones. Sunscreen and less time in UV light lower risk, which matters for someone with daily sun exposure and a family history of melanoma. Bathing, shampooing and keeping nails clean and trimmed protect skin, hair and nails. Checking only old moles misses new lesions, and a yearly check is less often than the monthly exam that is taught.

options.text: Check only moles you already have, since new spots are low risk
options.rationale: Near miss concept The self exam looks for new lesions as well as changes in old ones.

options.text: Do a full skin check once a year, since monthly checks add little
options.rationale: Near miss concept The self exam is monthly, so a changing lesion is found sooner.

questions.takeaway: Monthly whole body self exam with ABCDE, new and old spots, plus sunscreen and basic hygiene.
questions.strategy: The wrong options shrink the self exam, by place or by time. The family history of melanoma and the outdoor job are the details that make full, monthly checks and sun protection matter here.

questions.stem: A patient with very dark skin tone has a platelet count well below normal. The nurse wants to check for petechiae, which are tiny red or purple spots from bleeding under the skin. Which approach is best?

options.text: Inspect the legs and trunk under bright overhead light
options.rationale: Near miss concept Petechiae are often not visible on darkly pigmented skin, even with good light.

options.text: Press on the skin and watch for spots that do not blanch
options.rationale: Near miss concept This still depends on seeing a color change on dark skin.

options.text: Inspect the oral mucosa and the conjunctiva for tiny spots
options.rationale: Petechiae are often not visible on darkly pigmented skin. The test is where pigment is lowest. For petechiae, that is the oral mucosa and the conjunctiva, so the nurse inspects there. A low platelet count makes bleeding under the skin a real risk, so the check matters. Bright light on the legs and trunk and pressing for blanching both still rely on seeing color in dark skin. Palms and soles are where a bluish tinge of cyanosis may show, so they are a near miss.

options.text: Inspect the palms and soles, where the skin is lighter
options.rationale: Near miss concept Palms and soles are used for cyanosis. Petechiae are checked in the mouth and eyes.

questions.takeaway: Petechiae in dark skin: look in the mouth and the conjunctiva.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out skin based options is "very dark skin tone". The detail that rules out palms and soles is that they are the sites for cyanosis, not petechiae.

chapters.title: Managing Patient Care: Delegation, Teamwork, Handoff

questions.stem: A charge nurse is assigning work on a medical unit. Select all of the tasks that may be delegated to assistive personnel.

options.text: Reinforcing the discharge teaching the nurse already provided about a low sodium diet
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reinforcement is within LPN scope. Assistive personnel do not teach at all.

options.text: Recording the intake and output totals for a patient on a strict fluid restriction
options.rationale: Assistive personnel may collect and record data on stable patients and carry out routine physical care. They may not interpret the data, teach, or decide to hold a medication. Reinforcing teaching belongs to the LPN, not to assistive personnel, and the hold decision is nursing judgment.

options.text: Repositioning a patient every two hours per the established turning schedule
options.rationale: Assistive personnel may collect and record data on stable patients and carry out routine physical care. They may not interpret the data, teach, or decide to hold a medication. Reinforcing teaching belongs to the LPN, not to assistive personnel, and the hold decision is nursing judgment.

options.text: Obtaining vital signs on a patient admitted four hours ago with stable readings
options.rationale: Assistive personnel may collect and record data on stable patients and carry out routine physical care. They may not interpret the data, teach, or decide to hold a medication. Reinforcing teaching belongs to the LPN, not to assistive personnel, and the hold decision is nursing judgment.

options.text: Ambulating a stable patient in the hallway for the second time today
options.rationale: Assistive personnel may collect and record data on stable patients and carry out routine physical care. They may not interpret the data, teach, or decide to hold a medication. Reinforcing teaching belongs to the LPN, not to assistive personnel, and the hold decision is nursing judgment.

options.text: Checking a blood pressure before the first dose of a new antihypertensive and deciding whether to hold it
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Taking the pressure is delegable. The decision attached to it is not, and the option bundles the two.

questions.takeaway: Assistive personnel may gather the number. Deciding what the number means never moves.
questions.strategy: Ask of each task: does it require interpretation, teaching or judgment? If yes, it stays with the nurse.

questions.stem: A nurse delegates a bed bath for a stable patient to assistive personnel, gives clear instructions, and asks to be told if the skin looks different. The assistive personnel completes the bath but does not report a new reddened area over the sacrum. The area is found the next shift. Which statement most accurately describes the nurse's position?

options.text: The assistive personnel is accountable because the instruction to report skin changes was given and understood
options.rationale: Near miss concept Right directions were met. Meeting one right does not move accountability.

options.text: The nurse is not accountable because the task was within the scope of assistive personnel
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Scope governs whether you may delegate, not who owns the result.

options.text: Accountability is shared equally because the task was appropriate and the directions were clear
options.rationale: Near miss concept Appealing and wrong. Supervision and evaluation are the nurse's.

options.text: The nurse remains accountable for the outcome because accountability does not transfer with the task
options.rationale: Of the four elements of professional decision making, accountability is the one that stays with the nurse. The task moved; ownership of the result did not. This is also why right supervision is one of the five rights rather than a courtesy.

questions.takeaway: You delegate the task, never the accountability.
questions.strategy: This rule is usually tested as a flatly worded item. The correct option will be the one that keeps the outcome with the RN.

questions.stem: A nurse notices that handoffs on her unit routinely omit pending results, and errors follow. Which TeamSTEPPS pillar does the proposed standardized handoff tool most directly strengthen?

options.text: Team leadership
options.rationale: Near miss concept Organizes the team and assigns the work.

options.text: Communication
options.rationale: TeamSTEPPS rests on four pillars: communication, team leadership, situation monitoring and mutual support. A structured handoff tool is a communication intervention. Situation monitoring is watching the patient and each other; mutual support is backing a colleague up, including speaking up about a safety concern.

options.text: Mutual support
options.rationale: Near miss concept Backing each other up, including speaking up.

options.text: Situation monitoring
options.rationale: Near miss concept Scanning the patient and the team for change.

questions.takeaway: Four pillars: communication, leadership, situation monitoring, mutual support.
questions.strategy: Match the intervention to the pillar it changes, not to the pillar that sounds most important.

questions.stem: A nurse delegates a bed bath to an assistive personnel. The assistive personnel skips repositioning afterward and the patient's heels redden. Which element of professional practice explains why the nurse remains answerable for the outcome?

options.text: Accountability
options.rationale: Responsibility is the duty itself, autonomy is the freedom to make independent choices within your scope, and authority is the legal power to act, including questioning an order. Accountability is ownership of the outcome, and it does not transfer with the task. That is also why right supervision is one of the five rights of delegation rather than a courtesy.

options.text: Responsibility
options.rationale: Near miss concept The duty to perform, which was the part delegated.

options.text: Autonomy
options.rationale: Near miss concept Freedom to choose within scope, not ownership of a result.

options.text: Authority
options.rationale: Near miss concept The power to act, which is what let her delegate in the first place.

questions.takeaway: You can delegate the task. You keep the outcome.
questions.strategy: Four similar sounding terms means a definition item. Ask which one survives after the task has already been handed off.

questions.stem: A nurse is giving a handoff report using SBAR. Select all of the items that belong in it.

options.text: The pending results and what to do with them
options.rationale: A handoff transfers responsibility, so it carries identity, situation, what changed, what is pending and what the next nurse should worry about. Opinions about a family bias the care before the next nurse has met them. Repeating the previous shift's assessment as current is how a finding nobody assessed survives for days.

options.text: The nurse's opinion of the patient's family
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Prejudices the next nurse before she has met them.

options.text: The specific concern and what the receiving nurse should watch for
options.rationale: A handoff transfers responsibility, so it carries identity, situation, what changed, what is pending and what the next nurse should worry about. Opinions about a family bias the care before the next nurse has met them. Repeating the previous shift's assessment as current is how a finding nobody assessed survives for days.

options.text: The changes in condition during the shift and the response to interventions
options.rationale: A handoff transfers responsibility, so it carries identity, situation, what changed, what is pending and what the next nurse should worry about. Opinions about a family bias the care before the next nurse has met them. Repeating the previous shift's assessment as current is how a finding nobody assessed survives for days.

options.text: The patient's name, age and admitting diagnosis
options.rationale: A handoff transfers responsibility, so it carries identity, situation, what changed, what is pending and what the next nurse should worry about. Opinions about a family bias the care before the next nurse has met them. Repeating the previous shift's assessment as current is how a finding nobody assessed survives for days.

options.text: A copy forward of the previous shift's assessment
options.rationale: Near miss concept Report what you assessed; stale findings presented as current are dangerous.

questions.takeaway: End the handoff with what to watch for. That is the part that changes what the next nurse does.
questions.strategy: Two options pass along something that is either unverified or not yours to pass along.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to call a provider about a patient whose urine output has fallen. Select all of the items that belong in the recommendation portion of the report.

options.text: A request that the provider come to assess the patient now
options.rationale: The recommendation is what you want done. The nurse's own conclusion is the assessment, the totals are the situation and background data, and the admitting history is background.

options.text: A request for parameters on when to call again
options.rationale: The recommendation is what you want done. The nurse's own conclusion is the assessment, the totals are the situation and background data, and the admitting history is background.

options.text: The patient's intake and output totals for the past eight hours
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data True, necessary, and part of situation and background.

options.text: A request for an order to give a fluid bolus
options.rationale: The recommendation is what you want done. The nurse's own conclusion is the assessment, the totals are the situation and background data, and the admitting history is background.

options.text: The patient's admitting diagnosis and surgical history
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Background. Correct information in the wrong letter.

options.text: A statement that the nurse believes the patient is hypovolemic
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is the A. It is required, but it is not the R.

questions.takeaway: The R is the step students drop. Without it the call ends with nothing decided.
questions.strategy: Every correct option here is a request. If it is a fact rather than an ask, it belongs in an earlier letter.

questions.stem: A nurse coordinates a patient's transition from the hospital to a rehabilitation facility and then to home, arranging equipment, follow up appointments and home health across all three settings. This describes which nursing care delivery model?

options.text: Team nursing
options.rationale: Near miss concept Divides work among staff on one unit. It does not follow the patient out the door.

options.text: Patient and family centered care
options.rationale: Near miss concept A philosophy of partnership, not a coordination structure.

options.text: Primary nursing
options.rationale: Near miss concept One nurse following the patient, but within a setting.

options.text: Case management
options.rationale: Case management is defined by coordination across settings. Primary nursing is one RN following a patient through a single episode of care and is rare now because of cost. Team nursing is a group led by an RN inside one unit.

questions.takeaway: Case management crosses settings. Coordination inside one unit is not case management.
questions.strategy: Look for the word that names more than one place of care.

questions.stem: A nurse, a pharmacist and a physical therapist meet with a patient and her daughter to build one discharge plan rather than three. Which best describes this?

options.text: Team nursing, in which a registered nurse leads a group of caregivers
options.rationale: Near miss concept Organizes nurses, not disciplines. No pharmacist in it.

options.text: Case management, in which one nurse coordinates care across settings
options.rationale: Near miss concept Close, and it is one nurse coordinating rather than a team deciding.

options.text: Interprofessional collaboration, with the patient and family as partners rather than recipients
options.rationale: Interprofessional practice means several disciplines building one plan together, with the patient and family in the room as partners. The other three are nursing care delivery models, which describe how nursing work is organized rather than how disciplines work together.

options.text: Primary nursing, in which one nurse holds the patient's care from admission to discharge
options.rationale: Near miss concept One nurse, start to finish. Still one discipline.

questions.takeaway: Care delivery models organize nurses. Interprofessional collaboration organizes disciplines.
questions.strategy: Three options here are models from the same card. Check whether the stem is describing nursing structure or team structure.

questions.stem: A charge nurse plans the assignment for a shift with one registered nurse, one licensed practical nurse, and one assistive personnel. For each task, indicate whether it may be delegated to assistive personnel or must be retained by a licensed nurse.
columns: Must be retained by a licensed nurse

rows.text: Recording intake and output for a stable patient
Teaching a newly diagnosed patient how to inject insulin
rows.answer: Must be retained by a licensed nurse

rows.text: Taking vital signs on a patient whose condition has not changed
Assessing a patient who has become newly short of breath
rows.answer: Must be retained by a licensed nurse

rows.text: Assisting a patient who ambulates independently to the bathroom
Evaluating whether a patient met his mobility outcome
rows.answer: Must be retained by a licensed nurse

answer.r2: Must be retained by a licensed nurse
answer.r4: Must be retained by a licensed nurse
answer.r6: Must be retained by a licensed nurse

questions.takeaway: Recording intake and output for a stable patient: A routine measurement task on a stable patient, and it requires no clinical judgment to perform. Teaching a newly diagnosed patient how to inject insulin: Patient education requires assessment of readiness and understanding, and it cannot be delegated. Taking vital signs on a patient whose condition has not changed: Right circumstance is satisfied: the patient is stable. The nurse still interprets what comes back. Assessing a patient who has become newly short of breath: Assessment of an unstable patient. Neither the task nor the circumstance permits delegation. Assisting a patient who ambulates independently to the bathroom: Routine assistance for a patient whose mobility status is known and stable. Evaluating whether a patient met his mobility outcome: Evaluation is a step of the nursing process and stays with the nurse, even when the walking itself was assisted by someone else. Assessment, teaching, evaluation, and unstable patients stay with the nurse. Routine tasks on stable patients may be delegated.
questions.strategy: Two things decide it: what the task requires, and how stable the patient is. A delegable task on an unstable patient is no longer delegable.

questions.stem: A charge nurse considers delegating a task to assistive personnel. Which questions must she answer before doing so? Select all that apply.

options.text: Is this task appropriate to delegate
options.rationale: Right task, and it is the first question because nothing else matters if the answer is no. Right circumstance. A delegable task on an unstable patient is not delegable. Right person, and qualified and competent are two separate checks. Right directions and communication. Right supervision and evaluation, which is the one people treat as optional.

options.text: Is the patient's condition stable and appropriate for delegation
options.rationale: Right task, and it is the first question because nothing else matters if the answer is no. Right circumstance. A delegable task on an unstable patient is not delegable. Right person, and qualified and competent are two separate checks. Right directions and communication. Right supervision and evaluation, which is the one people treat as optional.

options.text: Is this person competent and qualified to perform it
options.rationale: Right task, and it is the first question because nothing else matters if the answer is no. Right circumstance. A delegable task on an unstable patient is not delegable. Right person, and qualified and competent are two separate checks. Right directions and communication. Right supervision and evaluation, which is the one people treat as optional.

options.text: Have I given clear instructions, expectations, and when to report back
options.rationale: Right task, and it is the first question because nothing else matters if the answer is no. Right circumstance. A delegable task on an unstable patient is not delegable. Right person, and qualified and competent are two separate checks. Right directions and communication. Right supervision and evaluation, which is the one people treat as optional.

options.text: Will I monitor the outcome and follow up
options.rationale: Right task, and it is the first question because nothing else matters if the answer is no. Right circumstance. A delegable task on an unstable patient is not delegable. Right person, and qualified and competent are two separate checks. Right directions and communication. Right supervision and evaluation, which is the one people treat as optional.

options.text: Does the patient agree to the task being performed by assistive personnel
options.rationale: Near miss concept Consent concerns whether care happens, not who may lawfully perform it. It is not among the five rights.

questions.takeaway: Five rights of delegation: right task, right circumstance, right person, right directions and communication, right supervision and evaluation.
questions.strategy: One distractor names something reasonable that is not one of the five.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence: A nurse is worried about a patient whose condition is changing. Reporting the situation, background, assessment and recommendation to the provider uses [[1]]. Saying "I am concerned, I am uncomfortable, this is a safety issue" uses [[2]]. Communication, team leadership, situation monitoring and mutual support are the pillars of [[3]]. Her legal power to call the provider and question an order is [[4]].

options.text: SBAR
CUS
TeamSTEPPS
the five rights
CUS
SBAR
TeamSTEPPS
shared governance
TeamSTEPPS
the interprofessional competencies
the Magnet standards
the decision-making framework
authority
autonomy
responsibility
accountability

questions.takeaway: [1] SBAR: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. A structure for handing over information. [2] CUS: Concerned, Uncomfortable, Safety issue. Graded language for escalating when the first report did not work. [3] TeamSTEPPS: Its four pillars: communication, team leadership, situation monitoring, mutual support. [4] authority: The legal power to act, including calling a provider and questioning an order. SBAR reports. CUS escalates. TeamSTEPPS has four pillars. Authority is the legal power to act; autonomy is the freedom to choose.
questions.strategy: Two pairs of four get confused: TeamSTEPPS pillars against the interprofessional competencies, and authority against autonomy.

questions.stem: A nurse questions an order for a dose she believes is unsafe, contacts the prescriber, and documents the conversation. Which elements of the decision-making framework does this demonstrate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Authority, the legal power to call a provider and question an order
options.rationale: Her slide gives this as the example of authority, almost word for word. Deciding the dose looked wrong and acting on that judgment is autonomy. She answers for the decision to question it, and she would have answered for giving it. Safe medication administration is among her duties, and questioning an unsafe order is part of performing it.

options.text: Autonomy, the freedom to make an independent judgment within her scope
options.rationale: Her slide gives this as the example of authority, almost word for word. Deciding the dose looked wrong and acting on that judgment is autonomy. She answers for the decision to question it, and she would have answered for giving it. Safe medication administration is among her duties, and questioning an unsafe order is part of performing it.

options.text: Accountability, owning the outcome of what she does
options.rationale: Her slide gives this as the example of authority, almost word for word. Deciding the dose looked wrong and acting on that judgment is autonomy. She answers for the decision to question it, and she would have answered for giving it. Safe medication administration is among her duties, and questioning an unsafe order is part of performing it.

options.text: Responsibility, carrying out her job duties
options.rationale: Her slide gives this as the example of authority, almost word for word. Deciding the dose looked wrong and acting on that judgment is autonomy. She answers for the decision to question it, and she would have answered for giving it. Safe medication administration is among her duties, and questioning an unsafe order is part of performing it.

options.text: Delegation, transferring the task to someone more senior
options.rationale: Near miss concept She did not hand the problem to anyone. She acted on it herself.

questions.takeaway: The four elements are not alternatives. A single nursing action usually involves all of them at once.
questions.strategy: The distractor describes handing the problem on. Ask whether she transferred anything.

questions.stem: A hospital applies for Magnet recognition. Which standards must it demonstrate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Shared decision-making
options.rationale: Named first, and it connects to shared governance and decentralization. Named, and it reflects how a unit is led affecting outcomes and burnout. Named among the six standards. Named, and it is measured through nursing-sensitive outcomes. Named, and it reflects nurse satisfaction and moral distress.

options.text: Leadership
options.rationale: Named first, and it connects to shared governance and decentralization. Named, and it reflects how a unit is led affecting outcomes and burnout. Named among the six standards. Named, and it is measured through nursing-sensitive outcomes. Named, and it reflects nurse satisfaction and moral distress.

options.text: Safety
options.rationale: Named first, and it connects to shared governance and decentralization. Named, and it reflects how a unit is led affecting outcomes and burnout. Named among the six standards. Named, and it is measured through nursing-sensitive outcomes. Named, and it reflects nurse satisfaction and moral distress.

options.text: Quality
options.rationale: Named first, and it connects to shared governance and decentralization. Named, and it reflects how a unit is led affecting outcomes and burnout. Named among the six standards. Named, and it is measured through nursing-sensitive outcomes. Named, and it reflects nurse satisfaction and moral distress.

options.text: Well-being
options.rationale: Named first, and it connects to shared governance and decentralization. Named, and it reflects how a unit is led affecting outcomes and burnout. Named among the six standards. Named, and it is measured through nursing-sensitive outcomes. Named, and it reflects nurse satisfaction and moral distress.

options.text: Cost containment per patient day
options.rationale: Near miss concept A real organizational concern and not among the Magnet standards. The standards concern how nursing is practised and supported.

questions.takeaway: Magnet standards: shared decision-making, leadership, safety, quality, well-being, and professional development.
questions.strategy: One distractor names a legitimate hospital priority that is not one of the six.

questions.stem: A unit adopts a Professional Practice Model built around patient- and family-centered care. Which set of elements defines it?

options.text: Communication, team leadership, situation monitoring, and mutual support
options.rationale: Near miss concept The TeamSTEPPS pillars, which concern how the team works rather than how patients are engaged.

options.text: Respect and dignity, information sharing, participation, and collaboration
options.rationale: Her four core elements of patient- and family-centered care within the practice model.

options.text: Values and ethics, roles and responsibilities, communication, and teamwork
options.rationale: Near miss concept The four interprofessional competencies.

options.text: Responsibility, autonomy, authority, and accountability
options.rationale: Near miss concept The decision-making framework.

questions.takeaway: Patient- and family-centered care: respect and dignity, information sharing, participation, collaboration. The practice model drives the nursing care delivery model.
questions.strategy: All four options are real sets of four from this chapter. Ask which set is about patients rather than about staff.

questions.stem: A nurse executive introduces a program inviting staff nurses to propose and trial changes to unit practice, with protected time to do so. Which characteristic of an empowered nursing team does this support?

options.text: Compliance with regulatory standards for nursing practice
options.rationale: Near miss concept Regulation sets a floor. Empowerment is about what happens above it.

options.text: Standardization of nursing care across the organization
options.rationale: Near miss concept The opposite direction. This program invites variation in order to test improvements.

options.text: Clear separation between management and clinical decision-making
options.rationale: Near miss concept Decentralization and shared governance blur that line deliberately.

options.text: An environment that supports risk-taking, innovation, and professional growth
options.rationale: Named directly as what empowering environments do, and protected time is what turns the invitation into something real.

questions.takeaway: Empowering environments support risk-taking, innovation, and professional growth. A culture of autonomy, quality and collaboration raises satisfaction and lowers moral distress.
questions.strategy: Two distractors describe control rather than empowerment. Ask what protected time to trial a change actually enables.

questions.stem: A nurse asks what shared governance means in practice on her unit. Which example fits?

options.text: The nurse manager consults staff before announcing a decision
options.rationale: Near miss concept Consultation is better than none and it keeps the decision in one place. Governance means staff hold part of it.

options.text: Staff nurses are surveyed annually about their satisfaction
options.rationale: Near miss concept Collects views without giving anyone a decision to make.

options.text: Staff nurses sit on a council that decides how care is delivered on the unit
options.rationale: Decentralization and shared governance mean decisions move toward the people doing the work.

options.text: Policies are written by a central committee and applied to every unit
options.rationale: Near miss concept Centralization, which is what shared governance moves away from.

questions.takeaway: Decentralization and shared governance move decision-making toward the staff who deliver the care.
questions.strategy: Two distractors gather opinions without transferring any decision. Ask who actually decides in each.

questions.stem: A nurse participates in interprofessional rounds with a physician, a pharmacist, a physical therapist and a social worker. Which interprofessional competencies are being exercised? Select all that apply.

options.text: Values and ethics for interprofessional practice
options.rationale: Named, and it underlies mutual respect between disciplines. Named, and rounds only work if everyone knows what each discipline contributes. Named, and it is the visible activity of a round. Named, and it is what turns four disciplines into one plan.

options.text: Roles and responsibilities
options.rationale: Named, and it underlies mutual respect between disciplines. Named, and rounds only work if everyone knows what each discipline contributes. Named, and it is the visible activity of a round. Named, and it is what turns four disciplines into one plan.

options.text: Interprofessional communication
options.rationale: Named, and it underlies mutual respect between disciplines. Named, and rounds only work if everyone knows what each discipline contributes. Named, and it is the visible activity of a round. Named, and it is what turns four disciplines into one plan.

options.text: Teams and teamwork
options.rationale: Named, and it underlies mutual respect between disciplines. Named, and rounds only work if everyone knows what each discipline contributes. Named, and it is the visible activity of a round. Named, and it is what turns four disciplines into one plan.

options.text: Delegation of tasks across disciplines
options.rationale: Near miss concept Delegation operates within nursing to appropriate personnel. Coordinating with other disciplines is collaboration rather than delegation.

questions.takeaway: Four interprofessional competencies: values and ethics, roles and responsibilities, communication, and teams and teamwork.
questions.strategy: One distractor applies a nursing-specific concept to interdisciplinary work.

questions.stem: A preceptor listens to a new graduate describe her understanding of delegation. Which statement requires correction?

options.text: "Once I delegate a task, the person performing it becomes accountable for the outcome."
options.rationale: Accountability stays with the delegating nurse. The task transfers and the answerability does not.

options.text: "A task that is usually delegable may not be, if the patient is unstable."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Accurate, and it is right circumstance.

options.text: "I need to tell them what to report back and when."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Accurate. Right directions and communication.

options.text: "I cannot delegate assessment, teaching or evaluation."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Accurate. Those require nursing judgment and remain with the nurse.

questions.takeaway: Delegation transfers the task. Accountability for the outcome stays with the nurse who delegated it.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate the rights correctly. The fourth moves accountability with the task.

questions.stem: A charge nurse is making assignments on a busy medical unit with one registered nurse, one licensed practical nurse and one assistive personnel. Select all of the assignments that are appropriate.

options.text: Licensed practical nurse: administering scheduled oral medications to stable patients
options.rationale: The lines that never move are the initial assessment, the nursing diagnosis, the plan, the initial teaching and the evaluation. An LPN can reinforce teaching the nurse has started and give routine medications in most states. Assistive personnel collect data and report it. Evaluating whether a finding needs escalation is interpretation, and interpretation stays with the registered nurse whatever the staffing looks like.

options.text: Licensed practical nurse: reinforcing discharge teaching the registered nurse has already started
options.rationale: The lines that never move are the initial assessment, the nursing diagnosis, the plan, the initial teaching and the evaluation. An LPN can reinforce teaching the nurse has started and give routine medications in most states. Assistive personnel collect data and report it. Evaluating whether a finding needs escalation is interpretation, and interpretation stays with the registered nurse whatever the staffing looks like.

options.text: Licensed practical nurse: the initial admission assessment on a newly arrived patient
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope The initial assessment is the registered nurse's; an LPN may collect data and contribute to it.

options.text: Assistive personnel: hourly rounding and toileting for four stable patients
options.rationale: The lines that never move are the initial assessment, the nursing diagnosis, the plan, the initial teaching and the evaluation. An LPN can reinforce teaching the nurse has started and give routine medications in most states. Assistive personnel collect data and report it. Evaluating whether a finding needs escalation is interpretation, and interpretation stays with the registered nurse whatever the staffing looks like.

options.text: Assistive personnel: evaluating whether a patient's new confusion needs escalation
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope They report the confusion. Deciding what it means is interpretation.

options.text: Assistive personnel: obtaining and reporting vital signs on a stable postoperative patient
options.rationale: The lines that never move are the initial assessment, the nursing diagnosis, the plan, the initial teaching and the evaluation. An LPN can reinforce teaching the nurse has started and give routine medications in most states. Assistive personnel collect data and report it. Evaluating whether a finding needs escalation is interpretation, and interpretation stays with the registered nurse whatever the staffing looks like.

questions.takeaway: Staffing pressure does not move a scope boundary. It only changes what you do first.
questions.strategy: Read the verb and the word initial. Initial assessment and initial teaching are the two that catch people.

questions.stem: A nurse tells assistive personnel to get the vital signs on the patient in room 12 and walks away. The readings are taken an hour later and the patient's blood pressure has fallen to 86/50 without anyone reporting it. Which right of delegation was not met?

options.text: Right task
options.rationale: Near miss concept Vital signs on a stable patient are appropriate to delegate. The task itself was fine.

options.text: Right directions and communication
options.rationale: Clear instructions, expectations, and when to report back. She gave a task and no parameters, so nobody knew 86/50 needed reporting.

options.text: Right person
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nothing suggests the assistive personnel were unqualified to take a blood pressure.

options.text: Right circumstance
options.rationale: Near miss concept The patient was stable when the task was assigned. What followed came from the missing instructions, not from the circumstance.

questions.takeaway: Five rights: right task, right circumstance, right person, right directions and communication, right supervision and evaluation.
questions.strategy: Three of the five were satisfied. Ask what the assistive personnel would have needed to know to act differently.

questions.stem: A nurse delegates a bed bath to assistive personnel. During the bath the patient's oxygen tubing is dislodged and not replaced, and his saturation falls. Who is accountable?

options.text: The assistive personnel, because the omission occurred during their care
options.rationale: Near miss concept They answer for their own performance. That does not remove the nurse's accountability for the outcome.

options.text: Both equally, since the task was shared
options.rationale: Near miss concept Accountability is not divided into halves. Each answers fully for their own part, and the nurse answers for the outcome.

options.text: The charge nurse, who made the assignment
options.rationale: Near miss concept The charge nurse answers for the assignment. The nurse who delegated this task answers for this outcome.

options.text: The nurse, because accountability for the outcome remains with her even when she delegates
options.rationale: Her slide states this directly. The task moves; the accountability does not.

questions.takeaway: Accountability means you own the outcome of what you do, even if you delegate it. The task transfers; the accountability does not.
questions.strategy: Two distractors move accountability elsewhere. One splits it. Ask what delegation actually transfers.

questions.stem: A nurse reports a patient's falling blood pressure and rising pulse to the provider using a structured format. He says to continue monitoring. Two hours later the pressure has fallen further and she calls again. Which tool should she use now?

options.text: SBAR, to repeat the report in a clearer structure
options.rationale: Near miss concept She already reported it using a structure. Repeating the same tool that did not work is unlikely to change the outcome.

options.text: TeamSTEPPS situation monitoring, to continue observing the patient
options.rationale: Near miss concept Situation monitoring is what produced her concern. It does not communicate it to anyone.

options.text: CUS, stating that she is concerned, uncomfortable, and that this is a safety issue
options.rationale: CUS exists for the moment when reporting has not produced a response. The graded language makes the concern impossible to file away.

options.text: The chain of command, going directly to the nursing supervisor
options.rationale: Near miss concept Appropriate if CUS fails, and escalating past the provider before using the graded language skips a step that often works.

questions.takeaway: SBAR hands over information. CUS escalates when the handover has not produced a response.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is repeating SBAR. Ask what changed between the first call and the second.

questions.stem: A nurse notices a colleague about to give a medication to the wrong patient and says nothing, assuming the colleague has checked. Which TeamSTEPPS pillar was not applied?

options.text: Communication
options.rationale: Near miss concept Involved in the sense that she said nothing, and the pillar that names watching out for a colleague is mutual support.

options.text: Mutual support
options.rationale: Mutual support means team members watch out for each other and speak up. Assuming someone else has checked is how errors reach patients.

options.text: Situation monitoring
options.rationale: Near miss concept She did monitor the situation. She saw it. What failed was acting on what she saw.

options.text: Team leadership
options.rationale: Near miss concept Concerns how the team is directed and coordinated, rather than one member covering another.

questions.takeaway: TeamSTEPPS pillars: communication, team leadership, situation monitoring, mutual support.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is situation monitoring, and the stem tells you she noticed. Noticing was not the failure.

questions.stem: A nurse decides that a patient's scheduled bath can wait because he is exhausted after physiotherapy. She makes the decision herself without consulting anyone. Which element of the decision-making framework is she exercising?

options.text: Authority, her legal power to act
options.rationale: Near miss concept The near-miss. Authority is the power to act, such as calling a provider and questioning an order. Autonomy is choosing what to do within scope.

options.text: Responsibility, her assigned job duties
options.rationale: Near miss concept Responsibility is what she is supposed to do. The bath is one of those duties; deciding when is autonomy.

options.text: Accountability, owning the outcome
options.rationale: Near miss concept She will own this decision, and accountability describes answering for it rather than making it.

options.text: Autonomy, her freedom to make independent choices within her scope
options.rationale: Timing routine care is squarely within nursing judgment, and she made the call herself.

questions.takeaway: Responsibility is what you are supposed to do. Autonomy is your freedom to choose within scope. Authority is your legal power to act. Accountability is owning the outcome.
questions.strategy: All four elements are present in any nursing decision. Ask which one names the act of deciding.

questions.stem: A new graduate says she does not see herself as a leader because she manages no one. Which response is most accurate?

options.text: Leading her own patient care requires clinical judgment, priority setting, time management, delegation, and team communication
options.rationale: Her slide lists these as ground-level skills every nurse needs. Leadership is framed as practical rather than positional.

options.text: Leadership skills develop naturally with clinical experience
options.rationale: Near miss concept They are described as learnable and practical, which implies they are taught and practised rather than absorbed.

options.text: Leadership becomes relevant once she moves into a management role
options.rationale: Near miss concept The slide states the opposite: this is not just a management-track skill.

options.text: Her focus should remain on clinical skills until she is more experienced
options.rationale: Near miss concept Separates clinical work from leading it, when prioritizing and delegating are part of the clinical work itself.

questions.takeaway: Leadership skills are learnable and practical: clinical judgment, priority setting, time management, delegation, and team communication.
questions.strategy: Three distractors defer leadership to later, to a role, or to experience. Ask what she does on her own assignment today.

questions.stem: A patient is discharged from hospital to a rehabilitation facility and then home, with one person coordinating across all three settings. Which nursing care delivery model is in use?

options.text: Case management
options.rationale: Someone coordinates care across multiple settings, which is her definition of the model.

options.text: Primary nursing
options.rationale: Near miss concept One registered nurse follows a patient throughout, and it operates within a setting rather than across several. Her slide notes it is rare today because it is expensive.

options.text: Team nursing
options.rationale: Near miss concept A group led by a registered nurse working together on one unit.

options.text: Patient- and family-centered care
options.rationale: Near miss concept Treats the patient and family as partners. It describes the relationship rather than how care is organized across settings.

questions.takeaway: Team nursing is a group led by an RN. Primary nursing is one RN following a patient through. Case management coordinates across settings. Patient- and family-centered care treats them as partners.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is primary nursing, which also involves one person following a patient. The difference is whether it crosses settings.

questions.stem: 0730: Charge nurse reviewing the shift. Unit has four registered nurses, one licensed practical nurse, and two assistive personnel for 28 patients. One registered nurse is orienting on her second shift. Three patients are scheduled for transfer to a step-down unit today. A patient in room 14 was admitted overnight with chest pain and has not yet been assessed this shift. The assistive personnel were told to 'do the vitals' with no reporting parameters given. A newly admitted patient in room 22 needs discharge teaching for a new insulin regimen, and this has been assigned to an assistive personnel. Two patients are stable and awaiting routine morning care. Select all of the findings that the charge nurse must address before the shift proceeds.

options.text: A registered nurse orienting on her second shift
options.rationale: Right person applies to assignments as well as to delegation. A nurse two shifts in needs an assignment matched to her competence and support. An unassessed patient with a cardiac presentation. Nobody currently knows his status. Right directions and communication. Without parameters, an abnormal reading may sit unreported. Patient education cannot be delegated. This fails right task before any other consideration.

options.text: A patient admitted overnight with chest pain, not yet assessed this shift
options.rationale: Right person applies to assignments as well as to delegation. A nurse two shifts in needs an assignment matched to her competence and support. An unassessed patient with a cardiac presentation. Nobody currently knows his status. Right directions and communication. Without parameters, an abnormal reading may sit unreported. Patient education cannot be delegated. This fails right task before any other consideration.

options.text: Assistive personnel told to 'do the vitals' with no reporting parameters
options.rationale: Right person applies to assignments as well as to delegation. A nurse two shifts in needs an assignment matched to her competence and support. Patient education cannot be delegated. This fails right task before any other consideration.

questions.stem: A nurse presses on a reddened area over a patient's sacrum and the redness disappears, then returns when pressure is released. How should this be documented?

options.text: Stage 2 pressure injury
options.rationale: Near miss concept Requires partial thickness skin loss.

options.text: Stage 1 pressure injury
options.rationale: Near miss concept Requires nonblanchable redness; this blanched.

options.text: Deep tissue pressure injury
options.rationale: Near miss concept Maroon or purple discoloration or a blood filled blister.

options.text: Blanchable erythema
options.rationale: Blanching means the capillaries are intact and refilling, which is the body sending extra blood to a spot that was compressed. It is a warning to offload, not an injury. questions.takeaway: Blanchable is the warning. Nonblanchable is the injury.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses a wound and documents thick, opaque, yellow green drainage with an odor. How should this drainage be classified?

options.text: Serosanguineous

options.text: Sanguineous
options.rationale: Near miss concept Frankly bloody, which suggests fresh bleeding.

options.text: Purulent

options.text: Serous
options.rationale: Near miss concept Thin, clear and watery, which is expected in early healing.

questions.takeaway: Thick, opaque and smelly is purulent. The adjective is the finding.

questions.stem: Which wound description is documented correctly?

options.text: Sacral wound looking better than yesterday, healing well, a small amount of drainage, dressing changed and patient comfortable
options.rationale: Near miss concept An interpretation with no measurements to support it.

options.text: Sacral wound 4 by 3 by 1 cm, 70% red granulation, 30% yellow slough, moderate serosanguineous drainage, periwound intact
options.rationale: Documentation has to let the next nurse tell whether the wound changed. That takes measurements in centifeet, the percentage of each tissue type, the amount and character of drainage, and the periwound skin. Better, improving and a lot are comparisons to something nobody else can see.

options.text: Sacral wound improving with the current plan, dressing changed per order, patient tolerated well, will continue to monitor
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome Records that care happened rather than what the wound looks like.

options.text: Large sacral pressure sore with a lot of yellow tissue and some fluid in the base, edges look okay, new dressing applied
options.rationale: Near miss concept Large and a lot are not measurements, and sore is not the terminology.

questions.takeaway: If the next nurse cannot tell from your note whether it got worse, the note did not work.
questions.strategy: Three options evaluate the wound. Only one describes it.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses a heel with intact skin and a deep maroon purple discoloration that is boggy and painful. How should this be documented?

options.text: Stage 1 pressure injury
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nonblanchable redness over intact skin, not maroon or purple discoloration.

options.text: Deep tissue pressure injury
options.rationale: Deep tissue injury is intact or blister covered skin with persistent maroon or purple discoloration, often boggy and painful, and it can evolve rapidly into a deep wound because the damage started at the bone and worked outward. Stage 1 is nonblanchable redness, not maroon. Unstageable means slough or eschar is hiding the base.

options.text: Stage 3 pressure injury
options.rationale: Near miss concept Full thickness loss with visible adipose, which means the skin is open.

options.text: Unstageable pressure injury
options.rationale: Near miss concept Requires slough or eschar obscuring the wound base, and this skin is intact.

questions.takeaway: Maroon over intact skin is damage that started underneath.
questions.strategy: Three of these require either red skin, broken skin or a covered base. Read what the skin is doing.

questions.stem: Select all of the elements the nurse documents in a wound assessment.

options.text: A judgment about which staff member failed to turn the patient
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Not a nursing determination and damaging in the legal record.

options.text: The appearance of the wound bed and the percentage of each tissue type
options.rationale: You document what the next nurse can compare against: measurements, drainage, tissue type and the surrounding skin. Improving is a conclusion, not an observation, and without the numbers behind it there is nothing to compare. Assigning fault is not a nursing determination and does not belong in the record.

options.text: The type and amount of drainage and any odor
options.rationale: You document what the next nurse can compare against: measurements, drainage, tissue type and the surrounding skin. options.text: The condition of the surrounding skin and wound edges
options.rationale: You document what the next nurse can compare against: measurements, drainage, tissue type and the surrounding skin. Improving is a conclusion, not an observation, and without the numbers behind it there is nothing to compare. Assigning fault is not a nursing determination and does not belong in the record.

options.text: Whether the wound is improving, as a single overall impression
options.rationale: Near miss concept A conclusion; document the measurements that support it.

questions.takeaway: Measure it. Improving is an opinion; 3 by 2 by 0.5 centimeters is evidence.
questions.strategy: One wrong option records a conclusion instead of data; the other records blame.

questions.strategy: Both wrong options keep the attention on the dressing or on the patient's character.

questions.stem: Select all of the measures that belong in a pressure injury prevention bundle.

options.text: Reposition on a schedule and offload the heels
options.rationale: Prevention is pressure, moisture, nutrition and shear. Keep the head of the bed at 30 degrees or lower when the patient's condition allows, because sitting higher slides the skin against the sheets while the skeleton stays put, which is shear. Massaging a reddened prominence damages the compromised tissue underneath.

options.text: Use lift sheets to reduce friction and shear
options.rationale: Prevention is pressure, moisture, nutrition and shear. Keep the head of the bed at 30 degrees or lower when the patient's condition allows, because sitting higher slides the skin against the sheets while the skeleton stays put, which is shear. Massaging a reddened prominence damages the compromised tissue underneath.

options.text: Manage moisture with barrier products and prompt incontinence care
options.rationale: Prevention is pressure, moisture, nutrition and shear. options.rationale: Near miss concept Discredited. It damages tissue that is already injured.
