Keep the head of the bed at 30 degrees or lower when the patient's condition allows, because sitting higher slides the skin against the sheets while the skeleton stays put, which is shear. Massaging a reddened prominence damages the compromised tissue underneath.

options.text: Keep the head of the bed above 45 degrees at all times
options.rationale: Near miss concept Thirty degrees or lower where the condition allows; higher creates shear at the sacrum.

questions.takeaway: Shear is what happens when the skin stays and the bones move, and a high head of bed causes it.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options are old teaching that is now known to cause the injury it was meant to prevent.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses a sacral wound with full thickness skin loss, visible subcutaneous fat, no visible bone or tendon, and slough covering about 30 percent of the base. How should this be staged?

options.text: Deep tissue pressure injury, since the base of the wound is not fully visible
options.rationale: Near miss concept That category requires intact skin or a blood filled blister.

options.text: Unstageable, because slough is present anywhere in the base
options.rationale: Near miss concept Unstageable requires the base to be obscured; most of this base is visible.

options.text: Stage 4, because full thickness loss implies deep involvement
options.rationale: Near miss concept Stage 4 requires visible bone, tendon or muscle, which the stem excludes.

options.text: Stage 3, because fat is the deepest tissue visible in the base
options.rationale: Unstageable means the base is obscured so the depth cannot be determined. Here 70 percent is visible and shows fat without bone, tendon or muscle, which is stage 3. Partial slough does not make a wound unstageable; total obscuring does. Stage 4 requires visible bone, tendon or muscle, and deep tissue injury requires intact or blister covered skin.

questions.takeaway: Some slough does not make it unstageable. Ask whether you can see the deepest tissue.
questions.strategy: Stage by the deepest tissue you can actually see, not by how bad the wound looks.

questions.stem: A chronic wound has rolled, thickened edges and has not changed size in three weeks despite appropriate dressings. Which element of the TIME framework does this finding point to?

options.text: Edge, meaning the wound has stalled and may need debridement
options.rationale: TIME is tissue, infection or inflammation, moisture, edge. Rolled edges, called epibole, mean the epithelium has curled under instead of migrating across, and a wound that has not changed in three weeks is stalled. The answer is usually debridement of the edge or an advanced therapy, not another week of the same dressing.

options.text: Infection, meaning systemic antibiotics should be started now
options.rationale: Near miss concept Possible in a stalled wound, and nothing in the stem points to it.

options.text: Moisture, meaning the current dressing is keeping it too wet
options.rationale: Near miss concept Too wet shows up as macerated, white periwound skin.

options.text: Tissue, meaning the granulation in the base is now healthy
options.rationale: Near miss concept Healthy granulation would be good news and would not explain three weeks of no change.

questions.takeaway: Rolled edges mean the skin stopped trying to cross. That wound needs something different.
questions.strategy: The stem describes the edge specifically, so an option about the wound bed or the dressing is answering a different question.

questions.stem: A patient's Braden score is 12. What does this tell the nurse?

options.text: That a pressure injury is already present
options.rationale: Near miss concept Braden predicts risk; it does not detect an existing injury.

options.text: High risk for pressure injury, requiring an individualized prevention plan
options.rationale: Braden runs 6 to 23 and lower is worse, which is the opposite of most scales and the reason students misread it. It scores sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition, and friction and shear. The subscale that is lowest tells you where to aim, which is what turns a number into a plan.

options.text: That the patient needs a wound care consultation before any prevention measures
options.rationale: Correct but premature Prevention starts immediately; a consult does not gate it.

options.text: Low risk, since the scale runs to 23
options.rationale: Near miss concept The direction is inverted; 23 is the best score and 12 is high risk.

questions.takeaway: On Braden, low is bad. Most scales run the other way.
questions.strategy: The score drives prevention now; it does not wait for a consultation.

questions.stem: A patient slides down in bed while the head of the bed is at 45 degrees. What is the main mechanism injuring the sacral tissue?

options.text: Shear, as skin stays on the sheet while deeper tissue slides
options.rationale: Friction is surface rubbing and it damages the epidermis. Shear is deeper and worse: the skin grips the sheet while the skeleton slides down inside, which stretches and tears the small vessels feeding the tissue in between. That is why the damage shows up as a deep injury under skin that still looks intact, and why the head of the bed stays at 30 degrees or less.

options.text: Pressure alone, from the weight of the body over the sacrum
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pressure contributes; the sliding is what makes this shear.

options.text: Moisture, from perspiration trapped beneath the sacral area
options.rationale: Near miss concept Moisture softens the skin and lowers its tolerance, and it is not the mechanical force described.

options.text: Friction, as the surface of the skin rubs against the sheet
options.rationale: Near miss concept Friction is present and it damages the surface; the deep injury here is shear.

questions.takeaway: Shear injures from the inside. That is why a high head of bed is dangerous.
questions.strategy: Friction and shear sound interchangeable and are not. One is surface, one is deep.

questions.stem: A nurse finds an intact blister filled with clear fluid over a patient's heel. The surrounding skin has no purple or maroon discoloration. How should this be documented?

options.text: Stage 2 pressure injury
options.rationale: Stage 2 is partial thickness loss: pink, moist dermis or a clear, serum filled blister, with no fat, slough or eschar. The fluid in the blister is what separates it from a deep tissue injury. Clear fluid means the damage is in the upper layers; blood in the blister or purple and maroon skin means the damage started deep at the bone and is working outward.

options.text: Deep tissue pressure injury
options.rationale: Near miss concept A deep tissue injury is a blood filled blister or persistent purple or maroon skin.

options.text: Stage 1 pressure injury
options.rationale: Near miss concept Stage 1 is intact skin with nonblanchable redness and no blister.

options.text: Unstageable pressure injury
options.rationale: Near miss concept Unstageable means slough or eschar hides the base.

questions.takeaway: Clear blister is stage 2. Blood filled blister is deep tissue injury.
questions.strategy: Look at what is inside the blister before you choose between stage 2 and deep tissue injury.

questions.stem: Select all of the pressure injuries the nurse should document as unstageable.

A device injury on a mucous membrane is always unstageable, because mucosa does not have the skin layers the stages are built on.

options.rationale: Near miss concept Exposed or palpable bone is stage 4.

options.text: A shallow open area with a pink, moist dermal base
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pink, moist dermis is stage 2.

questions.takeaway: Hidden base or mucous membrane means unstageable.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses a sacral pressure injury and can palpate bone at the base of the wound. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: Stage 3, because full thickness loss with fat is present
options.rationale: Near miss concept Stage 3 stops at fat; palpable bone moves it to stage 4.

options.text: Stage 4, and the nurse should be alert for osteomyelitis
options.rationale: Stage 4 is full thickness loss with exposed or palpable bone, tendon, muscle, fascia or cartilage. Bone that can be felt counts even if it cannot be seen. A wound that reaches bone is a direct route to bone infection, so the nurse watches for osteomyelitis.

options.rationale: Near miss concept Palpable bone counts, and unstageable means the base is hidden.

options.text: Deep tissue pressure injury, because the damage started at the bone
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism A deep tissue injury has intact or blistered skin, not an open wound to bone.

questions.takeaway: Felt bone is stage 4, and stage 4 means think osteomyelitis.
questions.strategy: Stage by the deepest tissue you can see or feel.

questions.strategy: An option that limits where you look with the word only is the one to drop.

questions.stem: A nurse is turning a patient at high risk for pressure injury onto the left side. Which position best protects the skin?

options.text: A full 90 degree side lying position so the sacrum is completely off the bed
options.rationale: Near miss concept Takes the pressure off the sacrum by putting all of it on the hip.

options.text: Side lying with the head of the bed raised to 45 degrees
options.rationale: Near miss concept A head of bed above 30 degrees slides the patient down and causes shear.

options.text: A 30 degree side tilt supported with pillows, with the heels floated
options.rationale: A 30 degree tilt moves weight off the sacrum without loading it all onto the hip, which is what a full 90 degree side lie does. Floating the heels offloads the site most often forgotten. Keeping the head of the bed at 30 degrees or less prevents the slide that causes shear.

options.text: A donut cushion under the hip to relieve pressure
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Donut cushions crush capillaries around the ring.

questions.takeaway: Tilt 30, not 90.
questions.strategy: Both the 90 degree turn and the donut relieve one spot by loading another.

questions.stem: Select all of the pressure injury tasks the nurse can delegate to assistive personnel.

options.text: Turning and repositioning the patient
options.rationale: The assistive personnel can turn, bathe, apply barrier cream and report red areas. Anything that requires judgment about the skin, which is skin assessment, staging and the Braden score, stays with the nurse.

options.text: Staging a new pressure injury
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Staging is assessment and stays with the nurse.

options.text: Bathing and applying barrier cream
options.rationale: The assistive personnel can turn, bathe, apply barrier cream and report red areas. Anything that requires judgment about the skin, which is skin assessment, staging and the Braden score, stays with the nurse.

options.text: Calculating the daily Braden score
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope The Braden score is a nursing assessment.

options.text: Reporting reddened areas to the nurse
options.rationale: The assistive personnel can turn, bathe, apply barrier cream and report red areas. Anything that requires judgment about the skin, which is skin assessment, staging and the Braden score, stays with the nurse.

options.text: Performing the admission skin assessment
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Skin assessment is not delegated.

questions.takeaway: The assistive personnel does the care and reports. The nurse assesses, stages and scores.
questions.strategy: Sort each task by whether it requires a judgment. Judgments are not delegated.

questions.stem: Match each pressure injury to the dressing that fits it best.

rows.text: A stage 3 injury with moderate exudate
A clean, noninfected stage 2 injury on the heel
A pressure injury with signs of infection
A stage 3 injury with a dry wound bed

questions.takeaway: Match the dressing to what the wound bed needs. A clean, noninfected stage 2 needs protecting, and hydrocolloid contours to a heel. A dry bed needs moisture added, which is hydrogel. A wet bed with moderate exudate needs absorbing, which is alginate or foam. An infected injury gets an antimicrobial dressing such as silver or honey. Protect, add moisture, absorb, treat infection.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the bed is clean, dry, wet or infected, and the dressing follows.

questions.stem: Select all of the accurate statements about debridement of pressure injuries.

options.text: Mechanical debridement is appropriate over dry, intact heel eschar with no signs of infection
options.rationale: Near miss concept Mechanical and surgical debridement are wrong over intact eschar without infection.

options.text: Debridement removes dead tissue that feeds bacteria
options.rationale: Dead tissue feeds bacteria, so debridement removes it by autolytic, enzymatic, mechanical or surgical methods. Irrigation and wet to dry are mechanical, and surgical is done by a provider. The exception is dry, hard, attached eschar with no redness or drainage, which is a protective cover; mechanical and surgical debridement are wrong there.

options.text: Debridement is needed only when a wound culture is positive
options.rationale: Near miss concept All open pressure injuries are colonized, so a culture does not decide debridement.

options.text: Surgical debridement is performed by a provider
options.rationale: Dead tissue feeds bacteria, so debridement removes it by autolytic, enzymatic, mechanical or surgical methods. Irrigation and wet to dry are mechanical, and surgical is done by a provider. The exception is dry, hard, attached eschar with no redness or drainage, which is a protective cover; mechanical and surgical debridement are wrong there.

options.text: Every wound containing slough or eschar should be surgically debrided right away
options.rationale: Absolute language Stable heel eschar is left in place as a protective cover.

options.text: Irrigation and wet to dry dressings are forms of mechanical debridement
options.rationale: Dead tissue feeds bacteria, so debridement removes it by autolytic, enzymatic, mechanical or surgical methods. Irrigation and wet to dry are mechanical, and surgical is done by a provider. The exception is dry, hard, attached eschar with no redness or drainage, which is a protective cover; mechanical and surgical debridement are wrong there.

questions.takeaway: Debride dead tissue, except stable eschar.
questions.strategy: Watch for the options that turn a method into a rule for every wound.

questions.stem: Complete the statement about wound healing.
questions.sentence: The [[1]] phase begins around day 4 and lasts 2 to 4 weeks, as granulation tissue fills the wound. Remodeling continues during the [[2]] phase, from about 3 weeks to a year or longer. Serosanguineous drainage from a surgical incision is expected only during the first [[3]].

options.text: inflammatory
proliferative
maturation
inflammatory
proliferative
maturation
48 hours
7 days
2 weeks

questions.takeaway: Healing runs in phases: inflammatory on days 1 to 5, when redness and warmth are expected; proliferative from about day 4 to 2 to 4 weeks, when granulation forms; and maturation from 3 weeks to a year or longer. Serosanguineous drainage is normal only in the first 48 hours, and a sudden increase in it often comes before dehiscence. Granulation is proliferative. Serosanguineous drainage past 48 hours is no longer routine.
questions.strategy: Know the order and the rough timing; a finding outside its expected window is the one to report.

questions.stem: A pressure injury is left open and heals as granulation tissue gradually fills it from the base. How is this type of healing described?

options.text: Healing by second intention
options.rationale: First intention means the wound edges are brought together and closed. Second intention means the wound is left open and fills in with granulation tissue. Most pressure injuries heal by second intention, which is why they take longer.

options.text: Healing by first intention
options.rationale: Near miss concept First intention means the edges are closed, as in a sutured incision.

options.text: Dehiscence
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dehiscence is a closed incision splitting open.

options.text: The inflammatory phase of healing
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Granulation belongs to the proliferative phase, and this names a phase rather than the type of healing.

questions.takeaway: Edges closed is first intention. Filling with granulation is second.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the edges were brought together.

questions.stem: Six weeks ago a sacral pressure injury was documented as stage 4 with exposed bone. Today it is shallow, the bone is covered and the base is filled with red granulation tissue. How should the nurse document the wound?

options.text: Stage 2 pressure injury, because it is now shallow
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reverse staging; a shallow healing wound is not partial thickness loss.

options.text: Stage 3 pressure injury, because bone is no longer visible
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reverse staging; the stage records how deep the injury went.

options.text: Resolved pressure injury, because granulation fills the base
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome Granulation is healing in progress, not a closed wound.

options.text: Healing stage 4 pressure injury
options.rationale: You stage by the deepest tissue the injury reached, and you never reverse stage. A stage 4 that is filling in with granulation is a healing stage 4, not a stage 3 or a stage 2. Granulation is the work of the proliferative phase, so the wound is improving, but it is still the same injury and it is documented as one.

questions.takeaway: A healing stage 4 is a healing stage 4.
questions.strategy: If an option renames a healing wound with a lower stage number, eliminate it.

questions.topic: how negative pressure wound therapy works
questions.stem: A patient asks how the wound VAC on a leg wound helps it heal. Which explanation is accurate?
questions.objective: how negative pressure wound therapy works

options.text: The suction sterilizes the wound so no infection can develop
options.rationale: Absolute language No dressing makes infection impossible.

options.text: The suction boosts blood flow, cuts swelling and builds granulation
options.rationale: Negative pressure wound therapy applies suction to the wound. That suction increases blood flow, cuts edema and builds granulation tissue, which is the tissue that fills a wound healing from the base.

options.text: The suction dries the wound bed so that a protective scab forms
options.rationale: Near miss concept The goal is granulation, not a dry scab.

options.text: The suction removes dead tissue the way surgical debridement does
options.rationale: Near miss concept Debridement is a separate treatment.

questions.takeaway: More blood flow, less edema, more granulation.
questions.strategy: Choose the option that names what the suction does to the tissue, not a promise about outcome.

questions.stem: A provider orders autolytic debridement for a pressure injury covered with slough. The patient's partner asks what this involves. Which response is accurate?

options.text: The provider cuts away the dead tissue at the bedside or in surgery
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is surgical debridement.

options.text: Irrigation or wet to dry dressings pull the dead tissue away
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is mechanical debridement.

options.text: A moist dressing lets the body's own enzymes break down the dead tissue
options.rationale: Debridement removes dead tissue that feeds bacteria. Autolytic debridement uses the body's own enzymes under a moist dressing. The other methods are enzymatic, mechanical such as irrigation or wet to dry, and surgical, which is done by a provider.

options.text: The wound is left open to air so the dead tissue dries and falls off
options.rationale: Near miss concept Autolytic debridement depends on keeping the wound moist.

questions.takeaway: Autolytic means the body does it, under a moist dressing.
questions.strategy: Auto means self. Match each method to who or what removes the tissue.

questions.stem: A patient with incontinence and poor oral intake has Braden moisture and nutrition subscales of 2 each. Select all of the interventions the nurse should include in the plan.

options.text: Check briefs every 2 hours
options.rationale: Moisture breaks down skin, so briefs are checked every 2 hours and the skin is cleaned promptly, patted dry and protected with barrier cream. Tissue needs fuel to resist pressure and to heal, so the plan includes fluids of 2000 to 3000 mL a day, protein and calories, and a dietitian consult.

options.text: Limit fluids to reduce the number of incontinent episodes
options.rationale: Near miss concept Tissue needs fluid to resist breakdown and heal; restricting it works against the nutrition goal.

options.text: Clean promptly after each episode and pat the skin dry
options.rationale: Moisture breaks down skin, so briefs are checked every 2 hours and the skin is cleaned promptly, patted dry and protected with barrier cream. Tissue needs fuel to resist pressure and to heal, so the plan includes fluids of 2000 to 3000 mL a day, protein and calories, and a dietitian consult.

options.text: Apply a barrier cream
options.rationale: Moisture breaks down skin, so briefs are checked every 2 hours and the skin is cleaned promptly, patted dry and protected with barrier cream. Tissue needs fuel to resist pressure and to heal, so the plan includes fluids of 2000 to 3000 mL a day, protein and calories, and a dietitian consult.

options.text: Rub the skin briskly to dry it after cleaning
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Rubbing adds friction; pat the skin dry.

options.text: Request a registered dietitian nutritionist consult
options.rationale: Moisture breaks down skin, so briefs are checked every 2 hours and the skin is cleaned promptly, patted dry and protected with barrier cream. Tissue needs fuel to resist pressure and to heal, so the plan includes fluids of 2000 to 3000 mL a day, protein and calories, and a dietitian consult.

options.text: Encourage fluids of 2000 to 3000 mL a day with adequate protein and calories
options.rationale: Moisture breaks down skin, so briefs are checked every 2 hours and the skin is cleaned promptly, patted dry and protected with barrier cream. Tissue needs fuel to resist pressure and to heal, so the plan includes fluids of 2000 to 3000 mL a day, protein and calories, and a dietitian consult.

questions.takeaway: Low moisture subscale: toileting, cleaning and barrier. Low nutrition subscale: fluids, protein and a dietitian.
questions.strategy: Match each intervention to the subscale it fixes, and drop the ones that add friction or take away fuel.

questions.topic: healing by first, second and third intention
questions.stem: For each wound, indicate how it is expected to heal.
questions.objective: healing by first, second and third intention

rows.text: A clean surgical incision closed with staples
A stage 3 sacral pressure injury filling in with granulation tissue
A contaminated abdominal wound left open for several days, then closed once no infection appears
A venous leg ulcer left open to heal from the inside out
A clean laceration with the edges brought together by sutures

questions.takeaway: First intention means the wound edges are brought together, usually with sutures or staples, so there is little tissue loss, no dead space and only a thin scar. Ask: are the edges touching? The stapled incision and the sutured laceration both are, so both heal by first intention. Second intention means the wound is left open and fills from the base with granulation tissue, then contracts, so healing is slower and the scar is larger. Ask: is an open cavity filling in on its own? The stage 3 pressure injury and the venous ulcer are open cavities, so both heal by second intention. Third intention, also called delayed primary closure, means a wound that might be infected is left open for several days and is closed only after the infection risk clears. Ask: was closure planned but held back? The contaminated abdominal wound fits that pattern exactly. Edges together is first intention, open and filling in is second, open then closed later is third.
questions.strategy: Sort by what happens to the edges. The detail that rules out second intention for the abdominal wound is that it is closed once no infection appears, which marks a delayed closure.

questions.stem: Complete the statement about measuring and documenting a pressure injury.
questions.sentence: The nurse measures length, width and depth in [[1]]. To find depth, the nurse gently places a cotton tipped applicator in the deepest part of the wound and marks it where it meets [[2]]. Tunneling is located with the clock method, in which [[3]] is at 12:00. Skin that has separated from the tissue at the wound edges is documented as [[4]].

options.text: centimeters or millimeters
inches
finger widths
the skin level
the wound edge
the wound bed
the patient's head
the patient's feet
the nurse's side of the bed
undermining
tunneling
cellulitis

questions.takeaway: Blank 1: wounds are measured length by width by depth in centimeters or millimeters so every nurse records the same unit and change over time can be tracked. Inches and finger widths are not the standard and finger widths vary from nurse to nurse. Blank 2: depth is the distance from the deepest point to the level of the surrounding skin, so the applicator is marked where it meets the skin level. Marking at the wound edge is a near miss, because a rolled or raised edge sits above or below the skin and gives a false depth; the wound bed is the starting point, not the reference. Blank 3: in the clock method the patient's head is 12:00 and the feet are 6:00, so the position does not depend on where the nurse stands. Blank 4: undermining is skin separating from the tissue at the wound edges, a shelf under the rim. Tunneling is a channel that runs from the wound into deeper tissue, and cellulitis is inflammation spreading beyond the wound into the surrounding skin. Centimeters or millimeters, depth to skin level, head at 12:00, undermining is a separated edge.
questions.strategy: Every blank asks for the fixed reference point. The detail that rules out tunneling in blank 4 is that the separation is at the wound edges, not a channel into deeper tissue.

questions.topic: classifying SJS and TEN by body surface area
questions.stem: Each patient has a drug triggered skin reaction with epidermal detachment. For each patient, indicate the classification.
questions.objective: classifying SJS and TEN by body surface area

rows.text: Detachment over 6 percent of body surface area
Detachment over 22 percent of body surface area
Detachment over 45 percent of body surface area
Detachment over 15 percent of body surface area
Detachment over 8 percent of body surface area

questions.takeaway: Stevens Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) are the same life threatening drug reaction at different sizes, so they are classified only by the percentage of body surface area involved. Ask: how much of the skin is affected? Less than 10 percent is SJS, which fits 6 percent and 8 percent. From 10 to 30 percent is SJS/TEN overlap, which fits 15 percent and 22 percent. More than 30 percent is TEN, which fits 45 percent. The higher the percentage, the greater the loss of the skin barrier, so fluid loss, temperature instability and infection risk climb, and TEN patients are often cared for in an intensive care or burn unit. Under 10 percent is SJS, 10 to 30 percent is overlap, over 30 percent is TEN.
questions.strategy: Ignore everything but the percentage. The detail that rules out SJS for the 15 percent patient is that it is above the 10 percent line.

questions.stem: A patient has hives after eating shellfish. The skin has raised red plaques that come and go, with no blisters or peeling. Select all of the accurate teaching points.

options.text: Avoid shellfish from now on
options.rationale: Urticaria, or hives, is a rash of white or red raised, swollen papules or plaques caused by exposure to an allergen such as a drug, food, temperature extreme, infection or insect bite. Treatment rests on two steps: remove the trigger and give an antihistamine. Avoiding shellfish removes the trigger, and the antihistamine blocks histamine, the chemical that causes the swelling and itch. Anything that dilates blood vessels makes hives worse, so the test for every other option is: does it widen the vessels? Heat, alcohol and overexertion all do. Lukewarm showers and avoiding alcohol keep vessels from dilating, so both are correct. Hard exercise and heating pads both dilate vessels and worsen the rash.

options.text: Take the prescribed antihistamine as directed
options.rationale: Urticaria, or hives, is a rash of white or red raised, swollen papules or plaques caused by exposure to an allergen such as a drug, food, temperature extreme, infection or insect bite. Treatment rests on two steps: remove the trigger and give an antihistamine. Avoiding shellfish removes the trigger, and the antihistamine blocks histamine, the chemical that causes the swelling and itch. Anything that dilates blood vessels makes hives worse, so the test for every other option is: does it widen the vessels? Heat, alcohol and overexertion all do. Lukewarm showers and avoiding alcohol keep vessels from dilating, so both are correct. Hard exercise and heating pads both dilate vessels and worsen the rash.

options.text: Take lukewarm rather than hot showers until the hives clear
options.rationale: Urticaria, or hives, is a rash of white or red raised, swollen papules or plaques caused by exposure to an allergen such as a drug, food, temperature extreme, infection or insect bite. Treatment rests on two steps: remove the trigger and give an antihistamine. Avoiding shellfish removes the trigger, and the antihistamine blocks histamine, the chemical that causes the swelling and itch. Anything that dilates blood vessels makes hives worse, so the test for every other option is: does it widen the vessels? Heat, alcohol and overexertion all do. Lukewarm showers and avoiding alcohol keep vessels from dilating, so both are correct. Hard exercise and heating pads both dilate vessels and worsen the rash.

options.text: Avoid alcohol until the hives clear
options.rationale: Urticaria, or hives, is a rash of white or red raised, swollen papules or plaques caused by exposure to an allergen such as a drug, food, temperature extreme, infection or insect bite. Treatment rests on two steps: remove the trigger and give an antihistamine. Avoiding shellfish removes the trigger, and the antihistamine blocks histamine, the chemical that causes the swelling and itch. Anything that dilates blood vessels makes hives worse, so the test for every other option is: does it widen the vessels? Heat, alcohol and overexertion all do. Lukewarm showers and avoiding alcohol keep vessels from dilating, so both are correct. Hard exercise and heating pads both dilate vessels and worsen the rash.

options.text: Exercise hard to sweat the allergen out of the skin
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Overexertion dilates blood vessels, which makes hives worse, and sweat also worsens itching. The allergen is not removed by sweating.

options.text: Apply heating pads to the itchiest areas
options.rationale: Near miss concept Warmth sounds soothing, but heat dilates vessels and worsens hives.

questions.takeaway: Remove the trigger, give the antihistamine, and avoid heat, alcohol and overexertion.
questions.strategy: Ask whether each action dilates vessels. The detail that rules out a more serious reaction is that the skin has no blisters or peeling.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the causes of skin cancer with a patient. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Squamous cell carcinoma is linked mainly to an inherited gene
options.rationale: Near miss concept Squamous cell carcinoma is tied to chronic skin damage. Genetic predisposition is named for basal cell carcinoma and melanoma.

options.text: Basal cell carcinoma has no link to ultraviolet light
options.rationale: Absolute language Basal cell carcinoma comes from genetic predisposition plus UV exposure, so no link is false.

options.text: Melanoma can arise from genes, UV, chemicals or a prior lesion
options.rationale: Sun overexposure is the major cause of skin cancer, and each type has its own pattern. Melanoma has the widest list of causes: genetic predisposition, ultraviolet (UV) exposure, chemical carcinogens (substances that cause cancer) and precursor lesions, meaning an existing mole or spot that changes. That makes the melanoma statement correct. Squamous cell carcinoma is linked to chronic skin damage, not mainly to an inherited gene. Basal cell carcinoma comes from genetic predisposition and UV exposure, so saying it has no UV link is false. Actinic keratoses are areas of sun damaged skin, not harmless birthmarks.

options.text: Actinic keratoses are benign birthmarks unrelated to the sun
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Actinic keratoses are sun damaged skin, not birthmarks, and they show the damage that leads to cancer.

questions.takeaway: Sun is the major cause; melanoma adds genes, chemicals and precursor lesions.
questions.strategy: Match each cancer to its cause. The detail that rules out the actinic keratosis option is the phrase unrelated to the sun.

questions.stem: A patient had a basal cell carcinoma removed and asks how to watch for new skin cancer. Select all of the accurate teaching points.

options.text: Check all of your skin once a month
options.rationale: Early detection depends on noticing change. A skin self exam is done monthly, and a body map or photos make it possible to compare a mole with how it looked before. Any new or changing lesion is reported, including a change in color, size or shape, redness or swelling around it, new itching or tenderness, and bleeding, oozing, crusting or scaling. The test for each option is: does it catch change early? Monthly exams, a body map, and reporting new itching or crusting all do. A yearly check is too infrequent, and waiting for growth ignores the other warning changes.

options.text: Keep a body map or photos of your moles
options.rationale: Early detection depends on noticing change. A skin self exam is done monthly, and a body map or photos make it possible to compare a mole with how it looked before. Any new or changing lesion is reported, including a change in color, size or shape, redness or swelling around it, new itching or tenderness, and bleeding, oozing, crusting or scaling. The test for each option is: does it catch change early? Monthly exams, a body map, and reporting new itching or crusting all do. A yearly check is too infrequent, and waiting for growth ignores the other warning changes.

options.text: Report a spot that becomes newly itchy or tender
options.rationale: Early detection depends on noticing change. A skin self exam is done monthly, and a body map or photos make it possible to compare a mole with how it looked before. Any new or changing lesion is reported, including a change in color, size or shape, redness or swelling around it, new itching or tenderness, and bleeding, oozing, crusting or scaling. The test for each option is: does it catch change early? Monthly exams, a body map, and reporting new itching or crusting all do. A yearly check is too infrequent, and waiting for growth ignores the other warning changes.

options.text: Check your skin once a year on your birthday
options.rationale: Near miss concept Self exam is done monthly. A yearly check lets a changing lesion go a long time unseen.

options.text: Report a mole only once it has grown larger
options.rationale: Correct but premature Size is one change, but color, shape, redness, itching, tenderness, bleeding, oozing, crusting and scaling are all reasons to report. Waiting for growth delays detection.

options.text: Report a spot that starts to crust or scale
options.rationale: Early detection depends on noticing change. A skin self exam is done monthly, and a body map or photos make it possible to compare a mole with how it looked before. Any new or changing lesion is reported, including a change in color, size or shape, redness or swelling around it, new itching or tenderness, and bleeding, oozing, crusting or scaling. The test for each option is: does it catch change early? Monthly exams, a body map, and reporting new itching or crusting all do. A yearly check is too infrequent, and waiting for growth ignores the other warning changes.

questions.takeaway: Check monthly, track with a map or photos, and report any change, not just growth.
questions.strategy: Growth is only one of many reportable changes. The detail that rules out the birthday option is the once a year timing.

questions.stem: A patient has a large stage 4 sacral pressure injury. For each task, indicate which team member is responsible.

rows.text: Recommends treatment for this complex, hard to heal wound
Sets protein, calorie, vitamin and fluid goals
Plans strategies to offload pressure and maximize function
Performs surgical debridement
Performs the scheduled dressing changes
Orders the wound treatment
Coordinates care among the team members

questions.takeaway: The wound, ostomy and continence nurse (WOCN) is a registered nurse with advanced training in skin, wound and elimination needs who treats and makes recommendations for complex, chronic or hard to heal wounds. The registered dietitian nutritionist (RDN) plans protein, calories, vitamins and fluids, because severe protein deficiency stops healing. The physical therapist plans therapy to redistribute and offload pressure, maximize function and improve quality of life. The provider orders treatment and performs surgery such as debridement, grafts and flaps, so both ordering and debridement belong in that column. The primary registered nurse coordinates with the team and performs and maintains the scheduled dressing changes, so both of those belong there. Ask for each task: does it need an order or surgery, specialty wound expertise, nutrition planning, mobility planning, or daily bedside coordination? The WOCN recommends, the provider orders and operates, the primary nurse coordinates and does the dressings.
questions.strategy: Separate recommending from ordering. The detail that rules out the WOCN for ordering treatment is that the WOCN makes recommendations while the provider writes the order.

questions.stem: A patient at high risk for pressure injury refuses to be repositioned at night, saying it wakes him and he cannot get back to sleep. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Use a pressure redistributing surface and time turns around sleep
options.rationale: Both risks are real: pressure injury and sleep deprivation, which has its own consequences including delirium and impaired healing. The two hour interval is a convention rather than a law, and a redistributing surface, smaller position changes and clustering the turn with other necessary wakings can satisfy both. Turning a competent adult without consent is not an option, and neither is giving up on prevention.

options.text: Document the refusal and reposition him only when he is awake
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Records a problem and abandons the prevention.

options.text: Reposition him anyway while he sleeps, since his risk is high
options.rationale: Near miss concept Care without consent, and it is the thing he specifically declined.

options.text: Explain that policy requires him to be turned every two hours
options.rationale: Institution as rationale Policy as the reason, with his actual objection unaddressed.

questions.takeaway: Two hourly turning is a convention, not a commandment. The goal is offloading, and there is more than one way.
questions.strategy: The two obvious answers, comply or override, are both wrong.

questions.stem: A patient coughs forcefully four days after abdominal surgery and the nurse sees a loop of bowel protruding through the incision. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Place the patient in high Fowler position and call the provider
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sitting up tightens the abdominal wall against an open incision; supine with knees bent is the position.

options.text: Attempt to gently replace the bowel and apply an abdominal binder
options.rationale: Near miss concept Replacing it contaminates the abdomen and can injure the bowel.

options.text: Cover the area with sterile saline moistened dressings and stay with the patient
options.rationale: Evisceration. Moist sterile cover keeps the bowel from drying, which is what kills it. Stay with the patient, call for help, position supine with knees bent to take tension off the incision, keep them nothing by mouth and prepare for surgery. Never push the bowel back in and never let the dressing dry out.

options.text: Apply a dry sterile dressing and press firmly to hold the wound closed
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dry dressing desiccates the bowel and pressure injures it.

questions.takeaway: Moist, sterile, and your hands stay on the patient while someone else makes the call.
questions.strategy: Two of the wrong options involve pressing or replacing. Neither ever happens.

questions.stem: On day 5 after abdominal surgery a patient reports a feeling that something gave way, and the nurse notes a sudden increase in serosanguineous drainage. The wound edges appear approximated. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Document the drainage and continue the current dressing schedule
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Charts the warning sign and does nothing with it.

options.text: Apply an abdominal binder and encourage walking in the hallway
options.rationale: Near miss concept A binder may be ordered, and ambulation now adds exactly the strain to avoid.

options.text: Reinforce the dressing and reassess the incision and drainage in four hours
options.rationale: Correct but premature Four hours is long enough for evisceration.

options.text: Assess the wound, place in low Fowler, flex knees, notify provider
options.rationale: A sudden increase in serosanguineous drainage plus a feeling of giving way is impending dehiscence, often before anything is visible, and the fascia beneath intact looking skin may already have separated. Position to take tension off the incision, stop any straining, and notify. If it does open, cover with sterile saline moistened dressings and stay with him.

questions.takeaway: That popping sensation plus a drainage change is dehiscence announcing itself before you can see it.
questions.strategy: Three options wait or add abdominal pressure. The patient has just told you the fascia gave.

questions.stem: A patient with peripheral arterial disease has dry, stable, intact black eschar on the heel with no drainage, redness or odor. What is the appropriate action?

options.text: Leave it intact, offload and protect the heel, and monitor it
options.rationale: Dry, stable eschar on an ischemic heel is acting as a biological cover over tissue that cannot heal yet, because there is not enough blood supply to support a wound. Opening it creates an unhealable wound and a route for infection. Protect it, offload it, and watch for the signs that change the plan: drainage, redness, odor, fluctuance or softening.

options.text: Soak the heel daily in warm water to loosen the eschar
options.rationale: Near miss concept Same problem, plus a maceration risk.

options.text: Request sharp debridement to expose the base for staging
options.rationale: Near miss concept Staging is less important than not creating an open ischemic wound.

options.text: Apply a moist dressing so the eschar softens and lifts
options.rationale: Near miss concept Moisture softens it into exactly the open wound you are avoiding.

questions.takeaway: Stable dry eschar on an ischemic heel stays. Opening it makes a wound that cannot close.
questions.strategy: Three options all open or soften a cover that is currently protective.

questions.stem: On day two after surgery a patient's incision has mild redness extending 1 cm from the incision line, slight warmth and scant serosanguineous drainage. The patient is afebrile. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: Early wound infection requiring culture
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would bring purulent drainage, spreading redness and systemic signs.

options.text: An allergic reaction to the suture material
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would be itchy and localized along the suture line, usually without drainage.

options.text: Expected inflammatory response in early healing
options.rationale: The inflammatory phase runs for about the first three days and looks like mild redness, warmth, edema and serosanguineous drainage. Infection is the one that keeps going: spreading redness, increasing pain, purulent drainage, fever and a rising white count. The test is direction, not presence.

options.text: Impending dehiscence
options.rationale: Near miss concept Suggested by a sudden increase in serosanguineous drainage and a feeling of giving way, not by mild redness.

questions.takeaway: Early mild inflammation is the wound working. Spreading and worsening is the wound infected.
questions.strategy: Afebrile with scant serosanguineous drainage on day two is exactly what should be there.

questions.stem: A patient with diabetes and neuropathy has a 2 cm ulcer on the plantar surface of the foot with a thick callus rim, minimal pain, and palpable pedal pulses. What should the nurse prioritize in teaching?

options.text: Elevating the leg on pillows to reduce any swelling
options.rationale: Near miss concept There is no edema described, and elevation does not offload walking.

options.text: Offloading that foot and inspecting both feet daily
options.rationale: A plantar ulcer with a callus rim in a neuropathic foot with good pulses is a pressure wound, and pressure is what has to be removed, which means total offloading rather than less walking. He cannot feel it worsening, so inspection substitutes for sensation. Soaking macerates the skin and raises infection risk, and compression is for venous disease.

options.text: Soaking the foot daily to soften the thick callus
options.rationale: Near miss concept Macerates the skin and raises infection risk; it is specifically taught against.

options.text: Applying compression wraps to speed the healing
options.rationale: Near miss concept Compression is venous therapy; pulses are intact and this is pressure.

questions.takeaway: A neuropathic plantar ulcer is a pressure problem. Offload it completely.
questions.strategy: Three options treat edema or callus. The ulcer is caused by weight, not by either.

questions.stem: A patient who drinks large amounts of carrot juice is worried about liver disease because the palms look orange. The sclerae are white and kidney function is normal. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: Carotenemia from diet, which is harmless
options.rationale: Three yellows, one test: look at the sclera. Yellow sclera is jaundice. White sclera with orange palms is carotenemia from diet, which is harmless. White sclera with sallow skin in kidney failure is uremia. White sclera, orange palms and a carrot heavy diet point to carotenemia.

options.text: Jaundice, because yellow or orange skin reflects a rising bilirubin
options.rationale: Near miss concept Jaundice yellows the sclera, and these are white.

options.text: Uremia, because sallow skin signals kidney failure
options.rationale: Near miss concept Uremia is sallow skin with white sclera in kidney failure; kidney function is normal.

options.text: Expected callus color that needs no further thought
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Calloused palms are yellow, but this ignores the diet and the orange color the patient describes.

questions.takeaway: Check the sclera before you call anything jaundice.
questions.strategy: When the sclera is white, jaundice is off the table.

questions.stem: A patient's Braden total is 14. The friction and shear subscale is scored 1 because the patient slides down in bed and has to be pulled up by staff; moisture and nutrition are each scored 3. Which intervention most directly targets the lowest subscale?

options.text: Start a toileting schedule and apply a moisture barrier cream
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question That is the fix for a low moisture score, and moisture is scored 3.

options.text: Move him with a lift sheet; keep the head of the bed at 30 or less
options.rationale: The Braden score is the start, not the plan. Each low subscale points to its own fix, so you read the subscales, not just the total. Friction and shear is scored 1 to 3, so a 1 is the worst it gets. Friction scrapes the surface when the patient is dragged; shear happens when a high head of bed lets the patient slide while the skin stays put. A lift sheet stops the dragging and a head of bed at 30 degrees or less stops the sliding.

options.text: Request a dietitian consult to improve his protein intake
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question That is the fix for a low nutrition score, which is not the problem here.

options.text: Rescore the Braden in one week to see if the total and the friction subscale improve
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Scoring is not prevention, and the Braden is scored daily, not weekly.

questions.takeaway: Find the lowest subscale and aim the intervention at it.
questions.strategy: When a stem gives you subscale scores, the answer matches the lowest one. The other fixes are right for a different patient.

questions.stem: On admission a patient scores 17 on the Braden Scale. The facility defines at risk as a score of 18 or less. A new graduate says no prevention plan is needed because the commonly cited cutoff is 16. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Agree, because 17 is above the published cutoff of 16
options.rationale: Near miss concept 16 or less is one accepted cutoff, but this facility uses 18 or less.

options.text: Hold prevention measures until a reddened area appears
options.rationale: Most dramatic finding Waits for visible damage when the scale exists to act before it.

options.text: Treat the patient as at risk under facility policy, start prevention measures and rescore daily
options.rationale: The Braden Scale runs 6 to 23 and a lower score means higher risk. The usual at risk line is 16 or less, but facilities may set it at 18 or less, and you work to the threshold your facility uses. A score of 17 here is at risk, so prevention starts now and the score is repeated daily. The scale predicts risk; it does not tell you an injury is already there.

options.text: Request a wound care consultation, because a score under 18 means an injury is probably present
options.rationale: Near miss concept The Braden predicts risk; it does not detect an existing injury.

questions.takeaway: Lower is worse, and the facility's cutoff is the one you chart against.
questions.strategy: When a stem gives you a facility policy and a commonly cited number that disagree, the stem is testing whether you follow the policy that applies to the patient in front of you.

questions.topic: assistive personnel actions that need intervention
questions.stem: A nurse observes an assistive personnel caring for a patient with a Braden score of 11. Select all of the actions that require the nurse to intervene.
questions.objective: assistive personnel actions that need intervention

options.text: Places pillows under the calves so the heels float
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Floating the heels is correct offloading.

options.text: Pulls the patient up in bed by the shoulders without a lift sheet
options.rationale: Dragging without a lift sheet causes friction and shear. A full 90 degree side lie loads the hip. Scrubbing off stable heel eschar removes a protective cover. Each of those needs the nurse to step in. Floating heels, a 30 degree tilt at least every 2 hours, and prompt cleaning with patting dry and barrier cream are exactly what the plan asks for.

options.text: Cleans promptly after incontinence, pats the skin dry and applies barrier cream
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit This is correct moisture care.

options.text: Turns the patient fully onto the side at 90 degrees
options.rationale: Dragging without a lift sheet causes friction and shear. A full 90 degree side lie loads the hip. Scrubbing off stable heel eschar removes a protective cover. Each of those needs the nurse to step in. Floating heels, a 30 degree tilt at least every 2 hours, and prompt cleaning with patting dry and barrier cream are exactly what the plan asks for.

options.text: Turns the patient with a 30 degree tilt at least every 2 hours
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit A 30 degree tilt at least every 2 hours is correct.

options.text: Soaks and scrubs dry, intact black eschar off the heel during the bath
options.rationale: Dragging without a lift sheet causes friction and shear. A full 90 degree side lie loads the hip. Scrubbing off stable heel eschar removes a protective cover. Each of those needs the nurse to step in. Floating heels, a 30 degree tilt at least every 2 hours, and prompt cleaning with patting dry and barrier cream are exactly what the plan asks for.

questions.takeaway: Intervene on dragging, the 90 degree lie and removing eschar. Leave the correct care alone.
questions.strategy: In an intervene question, the correct actions are distractors. Read each one asking whether it harms the skin.

questions.topic: responding to a reported red heel
questions.stem: An assistive personnel reports that a patient's right heel looks red. What should the nurse do?
questions.objective: responding to a reported red heel

options.text: Go to the bedside, assess the heel and do the blanch test herself
options.rationale: The assistive personnel turns, bathes, applies barrier cream and reports red areas. Skin assessment, staging and the Braden score stay with the nurse. When a red area is reported, you go and look, press with a gloved finger and release: if it blanches, relieve pressure and recheck; if it stays red, it is stage 1.

options.text: Ask the assistive personnel whether it blanched and document it
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Assessment cannot be handed to the assistive personnel.

options.text: Ask the assistive personnel to recalculate the Braden score
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope The Braden score stays with the nurse.

options.text: Document a stage 1 pressure injury on the heel based on the report given by the aide
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Staging without assessing, and the redness may blanch.

questions.takeaway: A report from the assistive personnel starts your assessment. It does not replace it.
questions.strategy: Any option that has the nurse document or stage from someone else's report is outside scope.

questions.topic: bleeding on negative pressure wound therapy
questions.stem: A patient receiving an anticoagulant has negative pressure wound therapy on an abdominal wound. The nurse sees bright red blood collecting in the canister. What should the nurse do first?
questions.objective: bleeding on negative pressure wound therapy

options.text: Replace the canister and continue therapy at the same setting
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome Keeps the device running while the patient bleeds.

options.text: Increase the suction to clear blood from the wound bed
options.rationale: Near miss concept More suction pulls more blood from the wound.

options.text: Record the canister output and recheck at the next dressing change
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Charts the bleeding instead of stopping it.

options.text: Stop the suction per policy, apply pressure and notify the provider
options.rationale: Negative pressure therapy increases blood flow to the wound, which is how it builds granulation, and in a patient on an anticoagulant that same suction can draw out active bleeding. Bright red blood in the canister means stop suction per policy, apply pressure and notify the provider.

questions.takeaway: Bright red blood in the canister means stop, press and call.
questions.strategy: When a device is causing harm, the first action stops the device.

questions.stem: A nurse new to the unit plans to swab culture a patient's stage 3 sacral pressure injury because it is an open wound. The wound has not grown, the exudate is unchanged and the patient is afebrile. What should the preceptor explain?

options.text: Culture at every dressing change to track which organisms grow
options.rationale: Absolute language Routine cultures only confirm the colonization every open wound has.

options.text: A culture is needed first before any dressing can be chosen
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dressing choice follows the wound bed: clean, dry, wet or infected.

options.text: A positive swab culture would confirm the wound is infected
options.rationale: Near miss concept Organisms grow from every open pressure injury, infected or not.

options.text: Open wounds are colonized; infection is judged by clinical signs
options.rationale: Every open pressure injury is colonized, so a swab will grow something whether or not the wound is infected. That is why cultures are not routine and infection is judged clinically: spreading redness, a change in exudate, a larger wound and fever. This wound shows none of those.

questions.takeaway: Colonized is not infected. Judge infection at the bedside.
questions.strategy: A test that is always positive cannot tell you anything. Look for the option that uses the clinical signs.

questions.topic: muted inflammation in an infected wound
questions.stem: An 84 year old receiving long term corticosteroids has a stage 3 hip pressure injury. Today the surrounding skin is only faintly pink and slightly warm, the exudate has changed in character and the patient is newly confused. Temperature is 37.3 C. What should the nurse conclude?
questions.objective: muted inflammation in an infected wound

options.text: Infection is unlikely, because the redness is minimal and there is no fever
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data The redness and temperature are accurate, but in this patient they cannot rule out infection.

options.text: Steroids and age blunt inflammation; suspect infection and report it
options.rationale: Older adults and patients on steroids mount less redness and swelling, so a barely pink, warm wound with new confusion can be a real infection. A change in exudate is one of the clinical signs used to judge pressure injury infection. The absence of fever and spreading redness does not reassure you in this patient.

options.text: The new confusion reflects aging and is unrelated to the wound
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism New confusion is a change, and it needs a cause.

options.text: Obtain a swab culture and wait for the result before reporting
options.rationale: Correct but premature Delays the report, and a swab grows organisms from every open pressure injury.

questions.takeaway: Muted inflammation hides infection. New confusion may be the loudest sign you get.
questions.strategy: When the patient is old or on steroids, give more weight to the subtle and behavioral findings.

questions.topic: heel eschar that is no longer stable
questions.stem: A patient's heel eschar has been documented for two weeks as dry, hard and attached. Today it is soft at the edges, with new drainage and redness around it. What should the nurse do?
questions.objective: heel eschar that is no longer stable

options.text: Leave it alone, because heel eschar is always left intact
options.rationale: Absolute language Eschar is left alone only while it is stable.

options.text: Soak the heel to finish loosening the softened eschar
options.rationale: Near miss concept Soaking and scrubbing off eschar is the action the nurse stops an assistive personnel from doing.

options.text: Report it; the eschar is no longer stable and needs a new plan
options.rationale: Dry, hard, attached eschar with no redness or drainage on a poorly perfused heel is a protective cover, so it is left in place and the heel is floated. Softening, drainage, redness or odor means it is no longer stable and may be infected, so you report it and the plan changes.

options.text: Document the change and reassess the heel at the next weekly skin check
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Skin is checked daily, and this change needs a report now.

questions.takeaway: Stable eschar stays. Eschar that softens, drains, reddens or smells gets reported.
questions.strategy: Leave it alone is only right while every stability criterion is still met.

questions.topic: recognizing and responding to toxic epidermal necrolysis
questions.stem: A patient started allopurinol 12 days ago. Today the patient has a temperature of 38.9 C and painful red skin that is blistering and peeling over about 40 percent of the body surface area. The eyes are red and gritty, and heart rate is 118/min. Complete the bow tie.
questions.objective: recognizing and responding to toxic epidermal necrolysis

options.text: Hold the allopurinol and notify the provider
Give the prescribed IV fluids and electrolytes
Give the next allopurinol dose with an antihistamine
Rub barrier cream firmly into the reddened skin
Restrict fluids until the blistering stops
Stevens Johnson syndrome
SJS/TEN overlap
Toxic epidermal necrolysis
Urticaria
Airway and breathing
Urine output and electrolytes
Mole size and border
Braden score
Pupil response

questions.takeaway: Condition: a drug triggered reaction with blistering and peeling is classified by body surface area. Under 10 percent is Stevens Johnson syndrome, 10 to 30 percent is SJS/TEN overlap, and over 30 percent is toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN). At 40 percent this is TEN. Urticaria is raised, swollen plaques on intact skin, with no peeling. Actions: the first step is to stop the drug, and allopurinol is a high risk drug for this reaction; holding it and notifying the provider removes the cause. With so much skin barrier lost, fluid and electrolytes pour out, which is why the heart rate is 118/min, so prescribed IV fluids and electrolytes are part of supportive care. Giving the next dose with an antihistamine keeps the trigger going; an antihistamine fits hives, not TEN. Rubbing cream into detached skin causes more shearing and pain. Restricting fluids worsens the fluid loss. Parameters: supportive care covers airway, fluids and electrolytes, temperature, pain, eyes and infection prevention. Airway and breathing are watched because the reaction can involve the lining of the airway, and urine output with electrolytes shows whether fluid replacement is keeping up. Mole size, the Braden score and pupil response do not track this reaction. Classify by percentage, stop the drug first, then support airway, fluids, temperature, pain, eyes and infection.
questions.strategy: The percentage sets the condition. The detail that rules out SJS/TEN overlap is the 40 percent involvement, and the detail that rules out the antihistamine action is that the skin is peeling, not just raised.

questions.stem: Two hours after the first dose of a new antibiotic, a patient develops itchy, raised red plaques on the trunk. The skin is intact with no blisters, breathing is unlabored and oxygen saturation is 98 percent. The patient asks for a hot shower to ease the itch. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Hold the next dose, report the reaction and give the antihistamine
options.rationale: Urticaria, or hives, is a rash of raised, swollen red or white plaques caused by an allergen, and drugs are a common trigger. Treatment is to remove the trigger and give an antihistamine. Here the new antibiotic is the likely trigger, so the nurse holds the next dose and reports the reaction so the provider can change the drug, and gives the prescribed antihistamine to calm the histamine response. A hot shower feels kind but heat dilates vessels and worsens hives. Giving the antibiotic again, even with an antihistamine, keeps exposing the patient to the trigger. Zinc oxide is a barrier cream for incontinence and pressure injury prevention and does nothing for an allergic rash. Intact skin with no blisters and normal breathing point to hives rather than a life threatening reaction.

options.text: Help the patient into a hot shower and then reassess the rash
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic It meets the request, but heat dilates vessels and makes hives worse.

options.text: Give the next antibiotic dose with the prescribed antihistamine
options.rationale: Correct but premature The antihistamine is right, but giving the drug that caused the hives keeps the trigger in place. The provider must first decide about the antibiotic.

options.text: Apply a zinc oxide barrier cream thickly over the plaques
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Zinc oxide protects skin from moisture and pressure damage. It does not treat an allergic rash.

questions.takeaway: For hives, remove the trigger first, then give the antihistamine, and avoid heat.
questions.strategy: The trap is a correct antihistamine given alongside the trigger. The detail that tips it is the timing, two hours after the first dose of a new drug.

questions.topic: pruritus in a patient with diabetes
questions.stem: A patient with diabetes has dry, itchy skin on both lower legs with scratch marks. The toenails are long and thick, and the fingernails are long and jagged. The patient asks the nurse to trim the toenails so they stop scratching the other leg at night. What should the nurse do?
questions.objective: pruritus in a patient with diabetes

options.text: Trim the toenails straight across during morning care today
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Short nails reduce scratch damage, but toenail cutting in a patient with diabetes is referred to podiatry.

options.text: Teach the patient to trim the toenails at home each week
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic It sounds like promoting independence, but patients with diabetes should avoid cutting their own toenails.

options.text: Encourage warm soaks at bedtime to calm the nightly itch
options.rationale: Near miss concept Soaking dries the skin further and warmth changes blood flow, both of which worsen itching.

options.text: Refer to podiatry for the toenails and file the fingernails short
options.rationale: Pruritus is itching caused when itch specific nerve fibers are stimulated by physical agents or chemicals. It is worsened by dry skin, sweat, stress and changes in blood flow. Nursing care keeps nails short and filed so scratching does less damage, prevents dry skin, and uses antihistamines as prescribed. In diabetes, poor circulation and loss of feeling make a small nick from toenail cutting a serious risk, so these patients avoid cutting their own toenails and are referred to podiatry. That makes the podiatry referral with filed fingernails correct. Trimming the toenails at the bedside or teaching self trimming both ignore the diabetes rule. Warm soaks dry the skin and change blood flow, which feeds the itch.

questions.takeaway: Keep nails short, prevent dry skin, and send toenails in diabetes to podiatry.
questions.strategy: The trap is a useful nail trim done by the wrong person. The detail that rules it out is the diabetes in the first line of the stem.

questions.topic: pressure relief for a patient in a chair
questions.stem: A patient recovering from pneumonia spends most of the day in a chair and can stand with a walker. The Braden score is 15. The nurse finds a donut cushion under the patient and a faint pink area over the coccyx that blanches. What should the nurse do?
questions.objective: pressure relief for a patient in a chair

options.text: Massage the pink area over the coccyx to restore circulation
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Massage sounds like it helps blood flow, but it damages capillaries in stressed tissue.

options.text: Remove the donut and have the patient stand and march 5 steps every hour
options.rationale: Pressure injury prevention reduces pressure in the position the patient is actually in. For a patient sitting in a chair who is able, the plan is to stand and march in place 5 steps every hour so blood returns to the compressed tissue. Donut pillows and massage of reddened areas are never used, because both damage capillaries. The pink area blanches, which means blood still returns when pressed, so it is not yet a pressure injury, but it is a warning that this pressure is too long or too concentrated. Leaving the donut and rechecking later keeps the harm going. Sending a patient who can stand back to bed trades one risk for another, since immobility and bed rest are themselves major risk factors.

options.text: Keep the donut cushion in place and recheck the coccyx at the end of shift
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Donut cushions damage capillaries and concentrate pressure on the ring, so leaving it in place keeps harming the skin.

options.text: Return the patient to bed for the rest of the day and turn every 2 hours
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Turning every 2 hours is right for a patient in bed, but this patient can stand, and bed rest adds immobility, a major risk factor.

questions.takeaway: In a chair: no donuts, no massage, stand and march 5 steps every hour if able.
questions.strategy: Match the intervention to the position. The detail that rules out bed rest is that the patient can stand with a walker.

questions.topic: a changing lesion that has not grown
questions.stem: A patient who works outdoors as a roofer has a mole on the shoulder that is new to the patient's body map photos from last year. This month it has begun to itch and has a small crust. The patient says, "It hasn't gotten any bigger, so I'm not worried." What should the nurse do?
questions.objective: a changing lesion that has not grown

options.text: Agree that a lesion that is not growing is not a concern
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data The size may be unchanged, but itching and crusting are changes that must be reported.

options.text: Suggest a new photo and recheck the mole again next month
options.rationale: Correct but premature Tracking with photos is good practice, but this lesion has already changed, so waiting delays detection.

options.text: Recommend a hat and sunscreen and reassess at the yearly visit
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Sun protection prevents new damage but does not address a lesion that is already changing.

options.text: Explain that new itching and crusting need prompt evaluation
options.rationale: Skin cancer is found early by noticing change. Any new or changing lesion is reported, and change includes not only size, color and shape but also redness or swelling around it, new itching or tenderness, and bleeding, oozing, crusting or scaling. Ask: has this lesion changed? Yes, it is new since last year's photos and has begun to itch and crust, so it needs prompt evaluation even though it has not grown. Agreeing with the patient treats size as the only warning sign. A new photo and a recheck next month are useful tracking tools for a stable mole, not for one that has already changed. Sun protection is correct prevention, especially with outdoor work, but it does nothing about this lesion.

questions.takeaway: Report any new or changing lesion, including itching or crusting, even if it has not grown.
questions.strategy: The trap is good tracking at the wrong moment. The detail that tips it is that the mole is new on the body map and has already started to itch and crust.

questions.stem: Select all of the accurate statements about advance directives.

options.text: A do not resuscitate order means comfort measures only
options.rationale: Near miss concept It limits resuscitation and nothing else.

options.text: A do not resuscitate order addresses resuscitation only and not other treatment
options.rationale: A living will says what; a durable power of attorney says who. A do not resuscitate order covers one event, cardiopulmonary arrest, and the patient still gets antibiotics, surgery, dialysis and everything else unless separately limited. Treating a DNR as comfort care only is a documented source of undertreatment.

options.text: A durable power of attorney for health care names a decision maker
options.rationale: A living will says what; a durable power of attorney says who. A do not resuscitate order covers one event, cardiopulmonary arrest, and the patient still gets antibiotics, surgery, dialysis and everything else unless separately limited. Treating a DNR as comfort care only is a documented source of undertreatment.

options.text: Advance directives can be changed or revoked by the patient at any time
options.rationale: A living will says what; a durable power of attorney says who. A do not resuscitate order covers one event, cardiopulmonary arrest, and the patient still gets antibiotics, surgery, dialysis and everything else unless separately limited. Treating a DNR as comfort care only is a documented source of undertreatment.

options.text: A living will states what treatments a patient wants if unable to speak
options.rationale: A living will says what; a durable power of attorney says who. A do not resuscitate order covers one event, cardiopulmonary arrest, and the patient still gets antibiotics, surgery, dialysis and everything else unless separately limited. Treating a DNR as comfort care only is a documented source of undertreatment.

options.text: A living will names someone to make decisions on the patient's behalf
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is the durable power of attorney; a living will states treatment wishes.

questions.takeaway: A do not resuscitate order is not a do not treat order.
questions.strategy: The two wrong options are the two most common misunderstandings of these documents.

questions.stem: A competent patient refuses a blood transfusion on religious grounds, knowing the risk. The team believes the transfusion would save his life. Which ethical principle supports honoring his refusal?

options.text: Beneficence
options.rationale: Near miss concept The principle pulling the other way; acting on it here would override him.

options.text: Autonomy
options.rationale: Autonomy is the patient's right to decide for himself, and it holds even when the decision looks wrong to everyone else, provided he is competent and informed. The conflict here is real: beneficence pushes toward the transfusion. When principles collide, autonomy governs the competent patient's own body.

options.text: Justice
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fair distribution of resources, which is not the question here.

options.text: Nonmaleficence
options.rationale: Near miss concept Avoid harm, which both sides of this argument claim.

questions.takeaway: A competent refusal is binding. Disagreeing with it does not change that.
questions.strategy: The pull you feel toward beneficence is the item's design.

questions.stem: Place the steps of the ethical decision making process in order.

options.text: Gather the relevant facts and identify who is involved
Recognize that the situation is an ethical dilemma
Act on the chosen course
Examine and clarify your own values on the issue
State the problem in a sentence everyone can agree to
Negotiate a plan with those involved
Evaluate the outcome of the action taken

questions.takeaway: You recognize the dilemma first, because a problem with a clear right answer is not a dilemma and does not need this process. Then facts, then your own values, because a nurse who has not examined her values will smuggle them into the problem statement. Stating the problem in a shared sentence is what makes negotiation possible. Then act, then evaluate. Examining your own values is the step people skip, and it is the one that keeps the process honest.
questions.strategy: A dilemma means two defensible options conflict. A situation with one right answer and an obstacle is not a dilemma; it is moral distress.

questions.stem: Select all of the situations that could constitute an intentional or quasi intentional tort.

options.text: Documenting an assessment finding incorrectly by mistake
options.rationale: Near miss concept An error rather than an intentional act.

options.text: Failing to reassess a patient's pain after an analgesic
options.rationale: Near miss concept Negligence, a breach of the standard, not an intentional act.

options.text: Preventing a competent patient from leaving against medical advice
options.rationale: Both categories require a deliberate act. The intentional torts are assault, the threat, battery, the unconsented contact, and false imprisonment, the confinement. Telling the neighbor is invasion of privacy, which Potter and Perry files separately as a quasi intentional tort: you meant to speak, you did not mean to harm her, and no intent to injure has to be proved. The last two options are negligence, a failure to meet a standard rather than a deliberate act, and that distinction changes both the legal analysis and the response.

options.text: Disclosing a patient's diagnosis to a neighbor
options.rationale: Both categories require a deliberate act. The intentional torts are assault, the threat, battery, the unconsented contact, and false imprisonment, the confinement. Telling the neighbor is invasion of privacy, which Potter and Perry files separately as a quasi intentional tort: you meant to speak, you did not mean to harm her, and no intent to injure has to be proved. The last two options are negligence, a failure to meet a standard rather than a deliberate act, and that distinction changes both the legal analysis and the response.

options.text: Giving an injection to a competent patient who has refused it
options.rationale: Both categories require a deliberate act. The intentional torts are assault, the threat, battery, the unconsented contact, and false imprisonment, the confinement. Telling the neighbor is invasion of privacy, which Potter and Perry files separately as a quasi intentional tort: you meant to speak, you did not mean to harm her, and no intent to injure has to be proved. The last two options are negligence, a failure to meet a standard rather than a deliberate act, and that distinction changes both the legal analysis and the response.

options.text: Threatening to catheterize a patient who refuses, so that he complies
options.rationale: Both categories require a deliberate act. The intentional torts are assault, the threat, battery, the unconsented contact, and false imprisonment, the confinement. Telling the neighbor is invasion of privacy, which Potter and Perry files separately as a quasi intentional tort: you meant to speak, you did not mean to harm her, and no intent to injure has to be proved.
