Hypoxemia is low oxygen in the blood; hypoxia is too little oxygen reaching the tissues, and it can occur with a normal saturation when hemoglobin or blood flow is low. An anemic patient can read 100 percent while carrying too little oxygen, so you treat the patient in front of you.

options.text: The patient has hypoxemia, because the arterial oxygen must be low
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hypoxemia is low oxygen in the blood; the problem here is too little hemoglobin to carry it.

options.text: The oximeter is faulty, since a pale patient cannot read 100 percent
options.rationale: Near miss concept The reading can be true: the little hemoglobin there is fully saturated.

questions.takeaway: A full saturation of too little hemoglobin is still too little oxygen.
questions.strategy: Pair every saturation with the patient. When the number and the patient disagree, believe the patient.

questions.stem: Twenty minutes after a thoracentesis the patient becomes suddenly short of breath, with rapid shallow breathing, a heart rate of 118 and absent breath sounds on the side of the procedure. The dressing is dry. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: A pneumothorax needing immediate assessment and provider notification
options.rationale: Sudden dyspnea after the needle is a pneumothorax until proven otherwise. Rapid shallow breathing, tachycardia and absent breath sounds on that side point to it, and a trachea shifted away with a falling blood pressure would make it a tension pneumothorax. Site soreness and dressing reinforcement are the distractors when one of these findings is on the list.

options.text: Expected soreness at the site that limits deep breathing for a while
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Soreness does not take away breath sounds on one side.

options.text: Bleeding at the puncture site that requires reinforcing the dressing
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question The dressing is dry, and the findings are in the chest, not at the site.

options.text: Anxiety after the procedure that should settle with calm reassurance
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Reassurance does not treat air in the pleural space.

questions.takeaway: After a chest needle, new dyspnea with absent sounds on that side is air.
questions.strategy: Do not pick the site care option when the findings are respiratory.

questions.stem: A patient was admitted with loud expiratory wheezes and a respiratory rate of 32 breaths per minute. One hour later, the wheezes can no longer be heard and breath sounds are faint throughout. The patient is drowsy and can say only one or two words. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Document that the wheezing has resolved and continue the plan
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting The wheezes stopped because air stopped moving, not because the airways opened.

options.text: Call for emergency help now, since airflow has nearly stopped
options.rationale: Wheezes are sounds made by air moving through narrowed airways. The test question is: are the airways open, or is air no longer moving? Faint or silent breath sounds, drowsiness and speaking only one or two words point to almost no air moving. Silent breath sounds and confusion are concerning signs that need immediate action, so the nurse calls for help now. Documenting resolution, coaching breathing with a slow recheck, or letting the patient sleep all treat a crisis as improvement.

options.text: Encourage slow deep breaths and recheck lung sounds in one hour
options.rationale: Correct but premature Coaching breathing is reasonable for a stable patient, but a one hour recheck is far too slow for a failing airway.

options.text: Let the patient sleep, since drowsiness shows the distress is easing
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Rest sounds kind, but drowsiness here is a change in mental status, a concerning sign, not recovery.

questions.takeaway: Wheezes that disappear while the patient gets worse mean less air is moving, not that the airways opened.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out improvement is that the patient is drowsy and down to one or two words. A patient who is truly improving talks more, not less.

questions.stem: An older adult is admitted for a hip fracture. A family member says, "Getting winded is just part of getting old." The patient now has to stop to rest while talking. The oxygen saturation is 89 percent on room air, down from 95 percent yesterday. The patient denies feeling short of breath. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Agree that some breathlessness is expected and reassure the family
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Reassuring the family feels supportive, but new shortness of breath is not normal aging.

options.text: Record the patient's report of no dyspnea as the main finding
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data The report is true, but older adults have a blunted hypoxia response, so the objective data must lead.

options.text: Assess the breathing now and report the new change in oxygenation
options.rationale: Aging reduces respiratory reserve, but new or severe shortness of breath is not normal aging. The test question is: is this finding new compared with before? Here, the saturation trend dropped from 95 to 89 percent, and the patient now stops to rest while talking. Dyspnea is subjective, and an older adult's response to hypoxia is blunted, so a denial of breathlessness does not cancel the objective data. The nurse assesses now and reports.

options.text: Plan to recheck the oxygen saturation at the next routine check
options.rationale: Correct but premature Rechecking is reasonable, but a falling saturation trend with new symptoms needs assessment now.

questions.takeaway: Older adults can feel less breathless while getting less oxygen. Follow the trend and the speech, not the denial.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out reassurance is the saturation trend from 95 to 89 percent. That is new, and new is not aging.

questions.stem: A patient is scheduled for a lung biopsy under sedation this morning. The patient takes an anticoagulant daily and reports a rash after a medication in the past but cannot recall which one. Select all of the actions the nurse takes before the procedure.

options.text: Verify that the consent is signed and that the patient followed preparation instructions
options.rationale: Before bronchoscopy, thoracentesis or lung biopsy, the nurse verifies preparation and consent, reviews allergies and bleeding risk, and obtains baseline respiratory findings. The test question for each option is: does it make the procedure safer or give a starting point to compare with? Consent and preparation: confirms the patient agreed and is ready. Allergy history: the unknown rash could involve a drug used during the procedure. Anticoagulant: a biopsy breaks tissue, so bleeding risk must be known before it happens. Baseline: lets the nurse spot pneumothorax, bleeding or worsening distress afterward. A meal goes against preparation for sedation. Holding the anticoagulant without an order is outside the nurse's scope; the nurse reports it so the provider decides.

options.text: Review the allergy history and clarify the medication that caused the rash
options.rationale: Before bronchoscopy, thoracentesis or lung biopsy, the nurse verifies preparation and consent, reviews allergies and bleeding risk, and obtains baseline respiratory findings. The test question for each option is: does it make the procedure safer or give a starting point to compare with? Consent and preparation: confirms the patient agreed and is ready. Allergy history: the unknown rash could involve a drug used during the procedure. Anticoagulant: a biopsy breaks tissue, so bleeding risk must be known before it happens. Baseline: lets the nurse spot pneumothorax, bleeding or worsening distress afterward. A meal goes against preparation for sedation. Holding the anticoagulant without an order is outside the nurse's scope; the nurse reports it so the provider decides.

options.text: Report the daily anticoagulant use and check for bleeding risk before the procedure
options.rationale: Before bronchoscopy, thoracentesis or lung biopsy, the nurse verifies preparation and consent, reviews allergies and bleeding risk, and obtains baseline respiratory findings. The test question for each option is: does it make the procedure safer or give a starting point to compare with? Consent and preparation: confirms the patient agreed and is ready. Allergy history: the unknown rash could involve a drug used during the procedure. Anticoagulant: a biopsy breaks tissue, so bleeding risk must be known before it happens. Baseline: lets the nurse spot pneumothorax, bleeding or worsening distress afterward. A meal goes against preparation for sedation. Holding the anticoagulant without an order is outside the nurse's scope; the nurse reports it so the provider decides.

options.text: Obtain baseline respiratory rate, effort, lung sounds and oxygen saturation
options.rationale: Before bronchoscopy, thoracentesis or lung biopsy, the nurse verifies preparation and consent, reviews allergies and bleeding risk, and obtains baseline respiratory findings. The test question for each option is: does it make the procedure safer or give a starting point to compare with? Consent and preparation: confirms the patient agreed and is ready. Allergy history: the unknown rash could involve a drug used during the procedure. Anticoagulant: a biopsy breaks tissue, so bleeding risk must be known before it happens. Baseline: lets the nurse spot pneumothorax, bleeding or worsening distress afterward. A meal goes against preparation for sedation. Holding the anticoagulant without an order is outside the nurse's scope; the nurse reports it so the provider decides.

options.text: Give a light breakfast so the patient tolerates sedation better
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic It sounds caring, but eating ignores the preparation instructions given before sedation.

options.text: Hold today's anticoagulant dose without an order to lower bleeding risk
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Bleeding risk is real, but stopping a prescribed drug is a provider decision. The nurse reports the anticoagulant use instead.

questions.takeaway: Before an invasive respiratory procedure: consent and preparation, allergies, bleeding risk and a baseline.
questions.strategy: Two details are planted: the daily anticoagulant points to bleeding risk, and the unknown rash points to allergies. Each one maps to a step the nurse must not skip. The tempting wrong move is to act on the bleeding risk alone by holding the drug.

questions.stem: A patient is on a Venturi mask set to a prescribed oxygen concentration. The patient is cold and has pulled a blanket up over the mask and its side ports. The oxygen saturation is still within the target range. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Uncover the side ports and offer another way to keep warm
options.rationale: A Venturi mask gives a controlled oxygen concentration by drawing in room air through side ports. These are called air entrainment ports. The test question is: is the device set up so it can work? Blocked ports change what the patient receives, so the delivered concentration is no longer the prescribed one, even if the reading looks fine right now. The nurse uncovers the ports and meets the comfort need another way. Turning up the flow or changing devices does not fix the setup. Leaving the blanket trades a correct dose for comfort.

options.text: Increase the oxygen flow rate above the setting on the device
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Changing the flow is not the ordered setting and does not fix the blocked ports, which are what keep the concentration controlled.

options.text: Switch to a nonrebreather mask to raise the oxygen delivered
options.rationale: Most dramatic finding Nothing calls for a higher oxygen device; the problem is the setup of the current one.

options.text: Leave the blanket, since the saturation is still in range
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Comfort matters, but blocked ports mean the device no longer delivers the prescribed concentration, whatever the current reading.

questions.takeaway: Keep Venturi air entrainment ports uncovered, or the controlled concentration is lost.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out leaving the blanket is that the ports, not the reading, control the concentration. A normal reading now does not mean the device is working as prescribed.

questions.stem: A patient admitted with COVID-19 is on 2 L per minute of oxygen by nasal cannula. Over 4 hours, the oxygen saturation has fallen from 95 to 90 percent, the respiratory rate has risen from 20 to 28 breaths per minute, and the patient is using neck muscles to breathe. The patient is alert, is drinking well and says, "I just feel tired." Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition they address, and 2 parameters to monitor.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to support ventilation
Report the worsening findings to the provider promptly
Walk the patient in the hall to build activity tolerance
Encourage extra fluids, since hydration supports recovery
Impaired gas exchange with risk for clinical deterioration
Risk for fluid volume deficit
Anxiety related to isolation
Activity intolerance from deconditioning
Oxygen saturation trend
Respiratory rate and effort
Daily intake and output
Pain at rest

questions.takeaway: Actions. Raising the head of the bed: positioning to support ventilation lets the lungs expand. Reporting promptly: worsening findings are escalated, not watched. Walking the patient: mobility is part of care, but exertion now raises oxygen demand in a patient who is already declining. Extra fluids: hydration is supported, but this patient is drinking well, so fluids do not address the change. Condition. Impaired gas exchange with risk for deterioration: the falling saturation and rising rate and effort show oxygen is not reaching the blood well. Risk for fluid volume deficit: ruled out by good intake. Anxiety: nothing in the stem shows it. Activity intolerance: tiredness is real, but the cause is the oxygen problem, not deconditioning. Parameters. Saturation trend and respiratory rate and effort show whether gas exchange is improving. Intake and output fits a fluid problem. Pain at rest does not track this change. In COVID-19, a falling saturation with rising rate and effort is deterioration. Position, escalate and watch the trend.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out the fluid condition is that the patient is drinking well. The detail that rules out walking is the rising respiratory rate.

questions.stem: A patient comes to an urgent care clinic with nausea, diarrhea, fatigue and muscle aches that began yesterday. The patient has no cough yet. A coworker tested positive for COVID-19 three days ago. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Treat this as stomach illness, since COVID-19 starts with a cough
options.rationale: Absolute language Presentation varies, and stomach symptoms can come before any breathing symptoms.

options.text: Rule out COVID-19, since loss of taste or smell is not reported
options.rationale: Near miss concept Loss of taste or smell can occur, but it is now less common, so its absence rules nothing out.

options.text: Send the patient home and test only if breathing problems develop
options.rationale: Correct but premature Watching for breathing problems matters, but waiting delays precautions and diagnosis with a known exposure.

options.text: Start the required precautions and anticipate a COVID-19 test
options.rationale: COVID-19 presentation varies. Gastrointestinal symptoms, meaning nausea, vomiting or diarrhea, may come before respiratory findings. The test question is: do the symptoms plus the exposure make COVID-19 possible? Yes. A close contact tested positive three days ago, and fatigue and muscle aches are common cues. The nurse starts the required infection control precautions and expects an antigen or nucleic acid amplification test, such as PCR. Labeling it a stomach illness, relying on taste and smell, or waiting for breathing symptoms all miss the exposure.

questions.takeaway: In COVID-19, stomach symptoms can come first, and loss of taste or smell is no longer a reliable sign.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out stomach illness is the coworker who tested positive. Assess exposure along with symptoms.

questions.stem: A patient with COVID-19 and impaired gas exchange is on oxygen. The saturation drops from 93 to 87 percent during a bath. It drops again during a dressing change an hour later and again during a linen change after that. Each time it recovers within minutes of rest. Which plan should the nurse use?

options.text: Spread care into many short sessions spaced out across the shift
options.rationale: Near miss concept Many small sessions mean more interruptions and shorter rest, the same pattern already causing repeated drops.

options.text: Group care into planned sessions with rest periods in between
options.rationale: Clustering care means grouping nursing tasks into planned sessions so the patient gets real rest between them. The test question is: does the plan reduce how often oxygen demand spikes? Each activity here pushes oxygen demand up, and the saturation drops each time. Planned sessions with rest in between reduce oxygen demand while care still happens. Spreading care out keeps interrupting rest. Skipping care stops needed hygiene. Rushing ignores the drops.

options.text: Skip hygiene and linen changes until the patient no longer needs oxygen
options.rationale: Absolute language Hygiene and rest are both supported; stopping all care is not the goal.

options.text: Complete all care at once as fast as possible, even if the saturation drops
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome Finishing quickly measures the task, not the patient's oxygenation during it.

questions.takeaway: Cluster care with rest periods to lower oxygen demand in a patient with impaired gas exchange.
questions.strategy: The detail that guides the plan is three separate drops at three separate times: each stand alone task interrupts rest. Grouping tasks leaves longer, uninterrupted rest periods between sessions.

questions.stem: A patient arrives with fever, severe muscle aches and rapid breathing during an outbreak of a new influenza strain. Health officials have not yet confirmed how this strain spreads. Which precautions should the nurse start?

options.text: Standard precautions only, until a test confirms influenza
options.rationale: Correct but premature Standard precautions always apply, but waiting for a test before adding more leaves staff and patients exposed.

options.text: Droplet precautions, since seasonal influenza spreads by droplets
options.rationale: Near miss concept That rule fits seasonal influenza, but the route of this new strain is still unknown.

options.text: Contact and airborne precautions until the route is known
options.rationale: Pandemic influenza is a new strain that can spread globally. Until the specific type is identified and its routes of transmission are known, the patient is placed on contact and airborne precautions, along with early recognition and quarantine. The test question is: is the route of spread known yet? Here it is not. Standard only and droplet only assume the route is known. Contact only leaves out airborne spread.

options.text: Contact precautions only, since hand washing stops the spread
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hand washing is critical, but it does not protect against airborne spread.

questions.takeaway: For a new pandemic influenza strain, use contact and airborne precautions until the route of spread is known.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out droplet precautions is that officials have not confirmed how this strain spreads. Seasonal rules do not transfer to an unknown strain.

questions.stem: A patient is being discharged after treatment for pneumonia. One planned outcome is that the patient attains adequate gas exchange. Which finding best shows that this outcome is met?

options.text: Oxygen saturation stays in the target range on room air while walking
options.rationale: An outcome is a change in the patient that shows the goal was reached. The test question is: does this finding measure the patient's gas exchange directly? A saturation in range on room air during activity does, because walking raises oxygen demand. Completing doses and a correctly timed culture are tasks done, not results. Stating spirometer steps shows knowledge, not oxygenation.

options.text: The patient has taken every scheduled dose of the antibiotic
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome Doses taken show the plan was followed, not that gas exchange is adequate.

options.text: The patient can state the steps for using the incentive spirometer
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Knowing the technique supports a patent airway but does not show gas exchange itself.

options.text: The patient's sputum culture was sent before antibiotics started
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Correct practice, but it describes a diagnostic step, not the patient's current oxygenation.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate an outcome with a finding in the patient, not with a task that was completed.
questions.strategy: The detail that makes the key strong is on room air while walking: oxygenation holds without support and under demand.

questions.stem: A patient is going home on oxygen by nasal cannula. The patient's nose and lips feel dry, and a family member smokes. Select all of the teaching points the nurse includes.

options.text: Keep oxygen away from open flames, and no smoking in the home
options.rationale: Oxygen supports burning, so safety teaching focuses on fire, equipment and skin. The test question for each point is: does it prevent fire, injury or a complication without stopping therapy? Flames and smoking: oxygen is kept away from both, which matters because a family member smokes. Water based product: treats dry mucous membranes without using petroleum products near oxygen. Securing cylinders: prevents falls and damage. Checking skin under tubing and behind the ears: prevents pressure injury. Petroleum jelly: avoided around oxygen equipment. Removing the cannula: stops prescribed therapy.

options.text: Use a water based product, not petroleum jelly, for dry lips and nose
options.rationale: Oxygen supports burning, so safety teaching focuses on fire, equipment and skin. The test question for each point is: does it prevent fire, injury or a complication without stopping therapy? Flames and smoking: oxygen is kept away from both, which matters because a family member smokes. Water based product: treats dry mucous membranes without using petroleum products near oxygen. Securing cylinders: prevents falls and damage. Checking skin under tubing and behind the ears: prevents pressure injury. Petroleum jelly: avoided around oxygen equipment. Removing the cannula: stops prescribed therapy.

options.text: Keep the oxygen cylinders secured upright so they cannot fall
options.rationale: Oxygen supports burning, so safety teaching focuses on fire, equipment and skin. The test question for each point is: does it prevent fire, injury or a complication without stopping therapy? Flames and smoking: oxygen is kept away from both, which matters because a family member smokes. Water based product: treats dry mucous membranes without using petroleum products near oxygen. Securing cylinders: prevents falls and damage. Checking skin under tubing and behind the ears: prevents pressure injury. Petroleum jelly: avoided around oxygen equipment. Removing the cannula: stops prescribed therapy.

options.text: Check the skin behind the ears and under the tubing every day
options.rationale: Oxygen supports burning, so safety teaching focuses on fire, equipment and skin. The test question for each point is: does it prevent fire, injury or a complication without stopping therapy? Flames and smoking: oxygen is kept away from both, which matters because a family member smokes. Water based product: treats dry mucous membranes without using petroleum products near oxygen. Securing cylinders: prevents falls and damage. Checking skin under tubing and behind the ears: prevents pressure injury. Petroleum jelly: avoided around oxygen equipment. Removing the cannula: stops prescribed therapy.

options.text: Apply petroleum jelly inside the nose to protect it from drying
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic It treats the dryness, but petroleum based products are avoided around oxygen equipment.

options.text: Remove the cannula when the nose feels dry until it feels better
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question It ends the discomfort but stops the prescribed oxygen; dryness is handled with oral and nasal care instead.

questions.takeaway: Home oxygen: no flames or smoking, no petroleum products, secure cylinders, check skin under tubing.
questions.strategy: The dry nose and lips are the planted detail that makes petroleum jelly tempting. It soothes dryness but is the product to avoid.

questions.stem: Select all of the nurse responses that are blocks to therapeutic communication.

options.text: "Tell me what a typical day looks like for you."
options.rationale: Near miss concept An open ended invitation.

options.text: "Don't worry, your doctor knows what he is doing."
options.rationale: Giving personal opinions, offering a cliche, asking why and giving false reassurance are all blocks. Why questions sound like information gathering and land as an accusation, so the better version is what got in the way of taking it. Naming an observed feeling and asking an open question are therapeutic.

options.text: "If I were you, I would have the surgery."
options.rationale: Giving personal opinions, offering a cliche, asking why and giving false reassurance are all blocks. Why questions sound like information gathering and land as an accusation, so the better version is what got in the way of taking it. Naming an observed feeling and asking an open question are therapeutic.

options.text: "Everything happens for a reason."
options.rationale: Giving personal opinions, offering a cliche, asking why and giving false reassurance are all blocks. Why questions sound like information gathering and land as an accusation, so the better version is what got in the way of taking it. Naming an observed feeling and asking an open question are therapeutic.

options.text: "Why did you stop taking your medication?"
options.rationale: Giving personal opinions, offering a cliche, asking why and giving false reassurance are all blocks. Why questions sound like information gathering and land as an accusation, so the better version is what got in the way of taking it. Naming an observed feeling and asking an open question are therapeutic.

options.text: "You seem worried about going home."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sharing an observation, which is therapeutic.

questions.takeaway: Why makes the patient defend himself. Ask what instead.
questions.strategy: Scan for opinions, cliches, reassurance and why. Those four cover most of the blocks on an exam.

questions.stem: Select all of the nurse statements that are therapeutic communication techniques.

options.text: "So if I understand you, the pain is worse at night than during the day."
options.rationale: Focusing, restating, sharing an observation and silence are four techniques, and silence is the one students are least comfortable with and patients value most. Claiming to know exactly how someone feels shifts the conversation to you and is almost never true, and generalizing about everyone on the unit is reassurance that dismisses her situation.

options.text: "Everyone on this unit gets through this, you will too."
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Generalized reassurance that minimizes what she is facing.

options.text: "I know exactly how you feel, I went through this myself."
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Shifts the focus to the nurse and claims an equivalence she cannot know.

options.text: "You seem uncomfortable when we talk about your wife."
options.rationale: Focusing, restating, sharing an observation and silence are four techniques, and silence is the one students are least comfortable with and patients value most. Claiming to know exactly how someone feels shifts the conversation to you and is almost never true, and generalizing about everyone on the unit is reassurance that dismisses her situation.

options.text: "You mentioned you are worried about going home. Tell me more about that."
options.rationale: Focusing, restating, sharing an observation and silence are four techniques, and silence is the one students are least comfortable with and patients value most. Claiming to know exactly how someone feels shifts the conversation to you and is almost never true, and generalizing about everyone on the unit is reassurance that dismisses her situation.

options.text: Sitting quietly with the patient after she begins to cry
options.rationale: Focusing, restating, sharing an observation and silence are four techniques, and silence is the one students are least comfortable with and patients value most. Claiming to know exactly how someone feels shifts the conversation to you and is almost never true, and generalizing about everyone on the unit is reassurance that dismisses her situation.

questions.takeaway: Silence is a technique. Sitting there without filling the gap takes practice.
questions.strategy: The two blocks here are the two that come most naturally when you want to help.

questions.stem: A nurse talks with a patient who has just been told his cancer has returned. For each nurse response, indicate whether it is a therapeutic technique or a communication block.

rows.text: "You don't feel confident that you can manage this."
"Why didn't you come in sooner?"
"I am here with you. Let me sit down."
"My mother went through this and she was fine."
"So what worries you most is what this means for your work."
"If I were you, I would start the treatment right away."

questions.takeaway: "You don't feel confident that you can manage this.": Reflection. It directs his attention back to his own feelings and thoughts. "Why didn't you come in sooner?": Asking why puts him on the defensive and implies he did something wrong. "I am here with you. Let me sit down.": Offering self. It demonstrates presence and reduces the sense of being alone with it. "My mother went through this and she was fine.": Changing the subject to herself, and it also carries false reassurance. "So what worries you most is what this means for your work.": Restating. It repeats his main idea in different words, which shows listening and verifies understanding. "If I were you, I would start the treatment right away.": Unsolicited advice. It substitutes her judgment for his decision. Therapeutic: clarification, restating, reflection, silence, offering self, giving information. Blocks: false reassurance, unsolicited advice, asking why, changing the subject, minimizing, judging, stereotyping, approving, defending, leading questions.
questions.strategy: Every block here is well-intentioned. Ask whether the response keeps him talking or shuts the conversation down.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence: A nurse reviews the communication process with a student. The person who initiates the communication and encodes the message is the [[1]]. The route the message travels, whether spoken, written or electronic, is the [[2]]. The response that tells the sender the message was received is the [[3]]. Repeating a patient's main idea in different words is [[4]].

options.text: sender
receiver
channel
context
channel
message
feedback
context
feedback
decoding
channel
congruence
restating
reflection
clarification
giving information

questions.takeaway: [1] sender: Initiates the communication and encodes the message. [2] channel: Speech, writing, a phone or a screen. The route rather than the content. [3] feedback: What tells the sender whether the message arrived and how it was understood. [4] restating: Repeats the main idea using different words, which demonstrates listening and verifies understanding. Six components: sender, message, channel, receiver, feedback, context. Restating repeats the idea; reflection names the feeling.
questions.strategy: Two near-miss pairs: message against channel, and restating against reflection. Content against route, and idea against feeling.

questions.stem: A nurse begins a relationship with a newly admitted patient. Which actions establish a therapeutic relationship? Select all that apply.

options.text: Introduce herself and explain her role
options.rationale: Named first. He needs to know who is in the room and why. Named, and it means asking rather than assuming what he wants to be called. Named, and it determines what he is willing to say. Named, and it protects the relationship from becoming something else. Named, and small promises kept are what make larger assurances believable.

options.text: Address the patient properly

Named, and it determines what he is willing to say. Named, and it protects the relationship from becoming something else. Named, and small promises kept are what make larger assurances believable.

options.text: Share a personal experience to build rapport
options.rationale: Near miss concept Moves the focus to the nurse. Changing the subject to yourself is among the named blocks.

questions.takeaway: Therapeutic communication: introduce yourself, explain your role, address the patient properly, maintain privacy, demonstrate respect, maintain boundaries, be present and attentive, follow through.
questions.strategy: One distractor sounds warm and moves the conversation to the nurse.

questions.stem: A preceptor listens to a new graduate discuss communication. Which statement requires correction?

options.text: "My nonverbal behavior may communicate more than my words."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Accurate, and it is her note on nonverbal communication.

options.text: "If the patient says he has no questions, I can record that he understood the teaching."
options.rationale: Assuming understanding is a named error. No questions may mean he does not know what to ask, or does not want to appear slow.

options.text: "Silence is a technique, not a gap I need to fill."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Accurate, and she notes that nurses find it uncomfortable because they feel they should be doing something.

options.text: "Therapeutic communication is purposeful rather than just being nice."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Accurate, and it is her framing.

questions.takeaway: Assuming understanding is a named error. Silence is a technique. Nonverbal behavior often says more than words.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate her slides correctly. The fourth treats an absence of questions as proof of comprehension.

questions.stem: A patient newly diagnosed with diabetes says, "I do not think I can ever learn to give myself a shot." Which response by the nurse is therapeutic?

options.text: "I will show you how simple it is, and then you will feel better about it."
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Calling it simple contradicts the patient and moves to teaching before the fear is addressed.

options.text: "Many people feel that way at first, and almost everyone learns it."
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic False reassurance. It tells the patient the feeling is not worth discussing.

options.text: "Your spouse could give the injections if you are not able to."
options.rationale: Correct but premature Removes the patient's independence before assessing whether it is needed.

options.text: "Why do you think you cannot learn it?"
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Asking why demands that the patient defend a feeling.

options.text: "You do not feel confident that you can manage the injections."
options.rationale: Reflection names the feeling underneath the statement and leaves the conversation open. The other four all close it: reassurance dismisses, why demands justification, the demonstration overrides the stated fear, and handing the task to a spouse solves a problem the patient has not agreed to give up.

questions.takeaway: Test any response by asking whether it makes the NEXT thing the patient says easier or harder.
questions.strategy: Three of these sound kind. Kind is not the standard; open is.

questions.stem: A patient who is newly widowed says, "I do not see the point in going home to an empty house." Select all of the nurse responses that are nontherapeutic.

options.text: "Why would you say something like that?"
options.rationale: False reassurance, a why question, shifting to the nurse's own story and a minimizing at least are four distinct blocks. The statement also needs a second look: no point in going home is worth exploring directly rather than smoothing over, which is another reason the reassuring answers are wrong. An open invitation and a reflection of what he said are therapeutic.

options.text: "At least you had many years together."
options.rationale: False reassurance, a why question, shifting to the nurse's own story and a minimizing at least are four distinct blocks. The statement also needs a second look: no point in going home is worth exploring directly rather than smoothing over, which is another reason the reassuring answers are wrong. An open invitation and a reflection of what he said are therapeutic.

options.text: "You will feel better once you are back in your own surroundings."
options.rationale: False reassurance, a why question, shifting to the nurse's own story and a minimizing at least are four distinct blocks. The statement also needs a second look: no point in going home is worth exploring directly rather than smoothing over, which is another reason the reassuring answers are wrong. An open invitation and a reflection of what he said are therapeutic.

options.text: "My mother went through the same thing and she got through it."
options.rationale: False reassurance, a why question, shifting to the nurse's own story and a minimizing at least are four distinct blocks. The statement also needs a second look: no point in going home is worth exploring directly rather than smoothing over, which is another reason the reassuring answers are wrong. An open invitation and a reflection of what he said are therapeutic.

options.text: "That sounds like a very empty place to be returning to."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reflection, which shows him he was heard.

options.text: "Tell me what going home feels like to you."
options.rationale: Near miss concept An open invitation, which is exactly right here.

questions.takeaway: At least is almost always the start of a block. So is a story about your family.
questions.strategy: Read the statement for risk as well as for sadness, then look at which responses close it down.

questions.stem: A patient scheduled for surgery tomorrow says, "I do not think I am going to make it through this." Which response is most therapeutic?

options.text: "Your surgeon is excellent and this procedure has a very high success rate."
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic False reassurance; it answers a fear with statistics.

options.text: "What makes you say that? Have you had a bad experience with surgery before?"
options.rationale: Near miss concept Opens with a why and then supplies his answer for him.

options.text: "Try not to think that way. You need to stay positive for your recovery."
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Dismisses the feeling and assigns him a mood.

options.text: "Tell me more about what you are thinking."
options.rationale: An open invitation keeps the patient talking and lets him say what he actually means, which could be fear, a premonition, unfinished business or a wish to decline surgery. Reassurance ends the conversation, telling him to stay positive dismisses the feeling, and a stacked double question steers him.

questions.takeaway: When a patient opens a door, walk through it. Do not close it with comfort.
questions.strategy: False reassurance is the single most common wrong answer in communication items because it sounds caring.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of assault becomes rigid when told she needs a pelvic examination. Which nursing action best reflects trauma informed care?

options.text: Reassure her that the examination is routine and will be over quickly
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Minimizes her reaction and gives her no control.

options.text: Ask her to describe the assault so the team understands her reaction
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sounds thorough and asks her to relive it for the team's benefit.

options.text: Document the history carefully and ask the provider to begin the examination as promptly as possible
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Charts the history and speeds up the thing she is braced against.

options.text: Explain each step beforehand and tell her she can stop at any point
options.rationale: Trauma informed care rests on safety, trust, choice, collaboration, empowerment and respect. Giving the patient the information and the power to stop restores the control that trauma took away. The point is not to retrieve the story; it is to run the care so it does not reenact the loss of control.

questions.takeaway: Trauma informed care gives control back. It does not collect the history.
questions.strategy: An option that asks the patient to recount the trauma is almost always wrong unless she offers it.

questions.stem: A patient says, "If this comes back again I am not doing chemo. I would rather have six good months." His wife, sitting beside him, says, "Do not talk like that." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: “Those are big thoughts. Would you like to talk about them together?”
options.rationale: Two people in the room need something different, and he has just said something that took courage. Validating it keeps the door open, and offering the choice of audience lets him decide whether he can say the rest in front of her. Reassurance, deferral and a lecture on rights all end the conversation, the last one by turning a human moment into a legal one.

options.text: “Your wife is right; there is still a lot of reason to stay hopeful.”
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Takes a side and tells him his thinking is wrong.

options.text: “Let us wait to see what the next scan shows before deciding anything.”
options.rationale: Correct but premature Defers the one conversation he is ready to have.

options.text: “You have every right to refuse any treatment that you do not want.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Accurate and it converts an emotional disclosure into a procedural one.

questions.takeaway: When two people need opposite things, give the patient the choice of who is in the room.
questions.strategy: The legally correct option is the subtlest trap here: true, and it answers a feeling with a right.

questions.stem: A nurse tells a patient she is listening while she continues to type and does not look up. The room is quiet and there are no interruptions. He stops mid-sentence and says it can wait. Which term describes what happened?

options.text: Ineffective feedback, because she did not respond to his message
options.rationale: Near miss concept Feedback is the response coming back. She did respond, and the problem is that her two responses contradicted each other.

options.text: A channel problem, since the message was spoken rather than written
options.rationale: Near miss concept The channel is the route a message travels. The spoken channel worked and he heard her clearly.

options.text: Environmental interference from competing demands on her attention
options.rationale: Near miss concept The environment is everything outside the two of them. The stem rules out noise and interruptions, and her typing comes from her rather than from the room.

options.text: Incongruent communication, where the verbal and nonverbal messages conflict
options.rationale: Congruence is whether words and body say the same thing. He received both and believed the behavior, which is why he withdrew rather than repeating himself.

questions.takeaway: Four different failures: the channel is whether words arrive, feedback is whether a response comes back, the environment is disruption from outside, congruence is whether words and body agree.
questions.strategy: When two options both look true, check which one explains his reaction. Interference stops a message arriving; he received it and withdrew.

questions.stem: A patient with newly diagnosed heart failure says he does not understand any of it and that everyone uses words he does not know. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Ask what he does understand so far, to find where the gap begins
options.rationale: You cannot pitch an explanation without knowing where to start. Assessing before teaching applies here as it does everywhere else.

options.text: Explain heart failure again using plain language
options.rationale: Near miss concept The right eventual move, and starting there means guessing which part lost him.

options.text: Provide written material he can read at his own pace
options.rationale: Correct but premature Useful once you know his reading level and where the gap is. Handing over paper before assessing repeats the problem in a new format.

options.text: Reassure him that it will make more sense over time
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic False reassurance, and it closes the opening he has just given you.

questions.takeaway: Assess before teaching. Excessive medical jargon is the named barrier, and plain language is the remedy once you know where to begin.
questions.strategy: Two distractors deliver the teaching correctly and too early. One closes the conversation.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to talk with a patient about a difficult diagnosis. Which environmental factors should she consider? Select all that apply.

options.text: Noise in the room and corridor
options.rationale: Named, and it forces both people to work harder to be understood. Named, and it determines what he is willing to say. Named, and an audience changes what gets disclosed. Named, and standing over someone communicates before anyone speaks. Named, and a conversation started without time for it is worse than one deferred.

options.text: Privacy from other patients and visitors

Named, and standing over someone communicates before anyone speaks. Named, and a conversation started without time for it is worse than one deferred.

options.text: How she and the patient are positioned
options.rationale: Named, and it forces both people to work harder to be understood. Named, and it determines what he is willing to say. Named, and an audience changes what gets disclosed. Named, and standing over someone communicates before anyone speaks. Named, and a conversation started without time for it is worse than one deferred.

options.text: The time available for the conversation
options.rationale: Named, and it forces both people to work harder to be understood. Named, and it determines what he is willing to say. Named, and an audience changes what gets disclosed. Named, and standing over someone communicates before anyone speaks. Named, and a conversation started without time for it is worse than one deferred.

options.text: The patient's level of education
options.rationale: Near miss concept A genuine factor influencing communication and it is not environmental. The environment is what surrounds the exchange.

questions.takeaway: Environment: noise, privacy, lighting, temperature, number of people present, positioning, and time available.
questions.strategy: One distractor names a real factor from the other list. Environment is what is around the conversation, not what either person brings to it.

questions.stem: A patient stops talking and looks out of the window after describing his symptoms. The nurse waits without speaking. Which technique is she using and why?

options.text: Silence, which gives him time to think and allows emotions to surface
options.rationale: Named as a therapeutic technique. It feels uncomfortable because nurses feel they are supposed to be doing something.

options.text: Clarification, to allow him to correct what he has said
options.rationale: Near miss concept Clarification asks a question when a statement is unclear or incomplete. She has asked nothing.

options.text: Reflection, to direct him back to his feelings
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reflection names the feeling out loud. Silence makes room for it without naming it.

options.text: Offering self, to demonstrate presence
options.rationale: Near miss concept The near-miss. Offering self involves saying something like I am here with you. Silence is presence without words.

questions.takeaway: Silence gives the patient time to think, allows emotions to surface, and encourages communication. It is a technique rather than an absence of one.
questions.strategy: Three distractors require the nurse to say something. She has said nothing.

questions.stem: A patient says he does not know whether he can manage his insulin at home. Which response is reflection?

options.text: "So you are unsure about the insulin injections specifically."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Restating. It repeats his idea in different words rather than naming the feeling underneath it.

options.text: "Can you tell me more about which part concerns you?"
options.rationale: Near miss concept Clarification. It asks a question to make an incomplete statement clearer.

options.text: "You are not feeling confident that you can manage this."
options.rationale: Reflection directs his attention back to his own feeling, which is her exact example.

options.text: "Most people find it easier after the first week."
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic False reassurance, and it is a block rather than a technique.

questions.takeaway: Reflection directs attention back to feelings, thoughts and ideas. Restating repeats the content.
questions.strategy: Restating and reflection are the pair that gets confused. One returns the idea, the other returns the feeling.

questions.stem: A nurse notices a patient's condition has changed but mentions it vaguely to the provider without giving the specific findings. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: It is acceptable, since the change was communicated in some form
options.rationale: Near miss concept Mentioning is not communicating. The findings are what let someone else act.

options.text: This is a safety concern, because professional communication supports safety and clinical decision-making
options.rationale: Her slide names safety and clinical decision-making among what professional communication supports. A provider cannot act on information he did not receive.

options.text: The responsibility passes to the provider once he has been told something
options.rationale: Near miss concept She remains accountable for communicating clearly enough to be acted on.

options.text: The written record makes verbal communication less important
options.rationale: Near miss concept The record documents; it does not alert anyone in time.

questions.takeaway: Professional communication supports continuity, safety, collaboration and clinical decision-making. Miscommunication causes errors.
questions.strategy: Two distractors treat partial communication as sufficient. Ask whether the provider can act on what he received.

questions.stem: A nurse tells a frightened preoperative patient not to worry because the surgeon is excellent. Which block is this?

options.text: Minimizing feelings
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic The near-miss, and both are present. Minimizing dismisses the feeling as unimportant; false reassurance replaces it with a promise.

options.text: Changing the subject
options.rationale: Near miss concept She stayed on the topic. She answered it with a promise instead of an exploration.

options.text: Defending
options.rationale: Near miss concept Defending protects a person or the institution from criticism. Nobody has been criticized.

options.text: False reassurance
options.rationale: It promises an outcome nobody can guarantee, and it tells him the subject is closed.

questions.takeaway: Blocks: false reassurance, unsolicited advice, asking why, changing the subject, minimizing feelings, judging, stereotyping, approving and disapproving, defending, leading questions.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is minimizing, and both elements are arguably present. The promise about the outcome is the defining feature.

questions.stem: 1100: Nurse enters to discuss discharge medications with a 68-year-old. Television is on at volume. His daughter and two grandchildren are visiting. He is due to leave for a scan in ten minutes. He reports pain of 7 of 10 and has not had analgesia since 0600. He wears bilateral hearing aids, both in place. He is alert and oriented. The curtain is open and the adjacent bed is occupied. He speaks English fluently and reads without difficulty. Select all of the findings that should make the nurse defer or change this conversation.

options.rationale: Noise is a named environmental factor, and it is the easiest of these to fix. The number of people present is named, and young children in the room affect what anyone will raise. Time available is named. Starting a discharge medication discussion with ten minutes is worse than deferring it. Health status, specifically pain, is a named factor influencing communication. Nobody learns well at 7 of 10. Privacy is named, and medication discussions disclose diagnoses.

options.text: Wears bilateral hearing aids, both in place
options.rationale: Near miss concept A potential barrier that is already managed. Aids in place is the reassuring detail.

options.text: Alert and oriented
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cognitive ability is a named factor and here it is intact, which removes it as a barrier.

options.text: Speaks English fluently and reads without difficulty
options.rationale: Near miss concept Language and literacy are both potential barriers, and both are ruled out by this finding.

questions.takeaway: Factors influencing communication: developmental level, culture, language, health status, emotional state, cognitive ability, environment, previous experience, personal perceptions.
questions.strategy: Three findings are barriers that are already resolved or absent. They are there to be left alone, and each one tells you something useful.

questions.stem: A nurse asks a patient whether the pain is worse today. He answers yes and says nothing further. Which change would improve the exchange?

options.text: Ask an open-ended question about how the pain has been
options.rationale: Open-ended questions encourage communication. A closed question produced exactly what it invited.

options.text: Ask whether the pain is sharp or dull
options.rationale: Near miss concept Another closed question. It narrows further rather than opening.

options.text: Ask why he did not mention it sooner
options.rationale: Near miss concept Asking why is a named block and it puts him on the defensive.

options.text: Tell him the analgesia will be due shortly
options.rationale: Near miss concept Moves to a solution before the assessment is complete.

questions.takeaway: Questions that encourage communication are open-ended. Closed questions have a place and they produce short answers.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is another closed question dressed as a follow-up. Ask which option cannot be answered in one word.

questions.stem: A nurse is told a patient from a particular cultural background will avoid eye contact and will want family present for decisions. Which approach is appropriate?

options.text: Plan the encounter around the described pattern
options.rationale: Near miss concept Applies a group generalization to an individual, which is how cultural knowledge becomes stereotyping.

options.text: Avoid eye contact throughout to show respect
options.rationale: Near miss concept Adopts the assumption as a rule. He may find it disconcerting.

options.text: Treat this as something to ask about rather than something to assume
options.rationale: Not all people from a particular culture communicate the same way, which is her opening line on the topic.

options.text: Ask the family what he would prefer
options.rationale: Near miss concept Asks about him without asking him. He is the person who knows.

questions.takeaway: Not all people from a particular culture communicate the same way. Cultural knowledge tells you what to ask about, not what to assume.
questions.strategy: Two distractors act on the generalization. One asks the wrong person.

questions.stem: A nurse gives information to a patient about a new medication. Which characteristics should that information have? Select all that apply.

options.text: Accurate
options.rationale: Named, and information that turns out to be wrong damages more than it helped. Named, and it means relevant to him rather than comprehensive. Named, and information he cannot use has not been given. Named among effective verbal communication, and jargon is the named barrier.

options.text: Appropriate to the patient's needs
options.rationale: Named, and information that turns out to be wrong damages more than it helped. Named, and it means relevant to him rather than comprehensive. Named, and information he cannot use has not been given. Named among effective verbal communication, and jargon is the named barrier.

options.text: Understandable
options.rationale: Named, and information that turns out to be wrong damages more than it helped. Named, and it means relevant to him rather than comprehensive. Named, and information he cannot use has not been given. Named among effective verbal communication, and jargon is the named barrier.

options.text: Delivered in language free of excessive medical jargon
options.rationale: Named, and information that turns out to be wrong damages more than it helped. Named, and it means relevant to him rather than comprehensive. Named, and information he cannot use has not been given. Named among effective verbal communication, and jargon is the named barrier.

options.text: Comprehensive enough to cover every possible side effect
options.rationale: Near miss concept Overloading with information is a named thing to avoid, and an exhaustive list is unusable at home.

questions.takeaway: Giving information: accurate, appropriate to the patient's needs, understandable. It decreases uncertainty and supports decision making.
questions.strategy: One distractor mistakes completeness for quality. Overloading is a named error.

questions.stem: A nurse sits at eye level, does not interrupt, repeats key phrases, and watches the patient's facial expression while he speaks. Which does this describe?

options.text: Therapeutic silence
options.rationale: Near miss concept Silence is waiting without speaking. She is repeating phrases and responding.

options.text: Clarification
options.rationale: Near miss concept One technique within the exchange rather than the whole approach described.

options.text: Active listening
options.rationale: Paying attention, appropriate eye contact and body language, allowing him to speak, being mindful of interruptions, clarifying, and attending to nonverbal cues.

options.text: Offering self
options.rationale: Near miss concept Offering self means making yourself available: I am here with you. This describes how she listens.

questions.takeaway: Active listening: pay attention, appropriate eye contact and body language, allow the patient to speak, mind interruptions, clarify and repeat phrases, reflect and validate, attend to nonverbal cues.
questions.strategy: Three distractors name a single technique. The stem describes several behaviors together.

questions.stem: A patient with expressive difficulty after a stroke struggles to find a word and the nurse finishes his sentence for him. Which problem does this create?

options.text: Interrupting, which is a named barrier and removes the time he needs
options.rationale: Being mindful of interruptions is part of active listening. For a patient with expressive difficulty, the time is the intervention.

options.text: Minimizing feelings, because his difficulty is dismissed
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Nothing about his feelings is addressed or dismissed. The problem is the time taken from him.

options.text: Giving unsolicited advice about how to communicate
options.rationale: Near miss concept She supplied a word rather than advice.

options.text: Leading, because she directed his answer
options.rationale: Near miss concept The near-miss. She supplied a word he may or may not have wanted, and the core failure is that she did not let him finish.

questions.takeaway: Be mindful of interruptions. For a patient with expressive difficulty, allowing time is the intervention.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is leading, and supplying a word does steer him. What the technique names is the interruption.

questions.stem: A nurse explains a procedure quickly, uses several abbreviations, and asks at the end whether the patient has any questions. He says no. Which error has she made?

options.text: Failing to obtain informed consent for the procedure
options.rationale: Near miss concept Consent is a separate process and is not what the stem describes.

options.text: Using a closed-ended question to end the conversation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Any questions is closed, and the deeper error is treating the answer as proof of comprehension.

options.text: Providing information that was not accurate
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nothing suggests the content was wrong. The problem is whether it landed.

options.text: Assuming understanding, which her slide names among the things to avoid
options.rationale: No questions is not evidence of understanding. Talking too fast, jargon, overloading and assuming understanding are all named together.

questions.takeaway: Avoid excessive medical jargon, talking too fast, overloading with information, and assuming understanding.
questions.strategy: One distractor names a real weakness in her closing question. Ask what she concluded from his answer.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old admitted with pneumonia has become withdrawn. He answers in single words, has not touched his meals, and turns toward the window when staff enter. His oxygen saturation is 95% and his pain is 2 of 10. His wife died three weeks ago. The unit is busy and the nurse has been documenting at the bedside computer while talking to him. Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem they address, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Sit down at eye level, stop documenting, and give him her full attention
Use reflection to name what he may be feeling, then allow silence
Reassure him that he will feel better once the pneumonia clears
Ask him why he is not eating
Withdrawal with a recent bereavement, and no one has been fully present with him
Hypoxia contributing to altered behavior
Uncontrolled pain limiting his willingness to talk
Cognitive impairment affecting his ability to converse
Whether he begins to say more than single words
Whether he raises his wife or his situation without being prompted
Whether his oxygen saturation remains above 92%
Whether he finishes his next meal

questions.takeaway: His emotional state is a named factor influencing communication, and the nurse's own incongruent behavior is part of why nothing has been said. Her own congruence example in reverse. Documenting while talking tells him she is not available, whatever she says. Reflection directs him back to his own feelings, and silence gives the time for them to surface. The behavior that defined the problem, measured directly. Measures whether the relationship has become one he can use, which is what the actions aimed at. Emotional state is a factor influencing communication. When the clinical numbers are reassuring, the withdrawal is telling you something the numbers cannot.
questions.strategy: Two condition distractors are ruled out by values in the stem. The saturation and the pain score are placed there to eliminate the easy explanations.

questions.stem: A nurse says to a patient, "You didn't take your medication again, did you?" Which two blocks does this combine?

options.text: Clarification and restating
options.rationale: Near miss concept Both are therapeutic techniques, and neither is present here.

options.text: A leading question and judging
options.rationale: The phrasing directs him to a particular answer, and again carries a verdict about him before he has spoken.

options.text: False reassurance and defending
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Nothing is being promised, and nobody is being defended.

options.text: Changing the subject and stereotyping
options.rationale: Near miss concept The subject has not changed, and no group generalization is made.

questions.takeaway: Blocks include leading questions and judging. A single sentence can carry more than one.
questions.strategy: Two options list therapeutic techniques or blocks that are simply not present. Read the sentence for what it does to him.

questions.stem: Select all of the measures that improve teaching effectiveness with an older adult.

options.text: Teach in short sessions rather than one long one
options.rationale: Short sessions, a quiet room, confirmation and reinforcement. The two wrong options are the two reflexes to resist: cramming everything into discharge day is the moment of lowest retention and highest anxiety, and assuming hearing loss and shouting at everyone over 75 is both inaccurate and undignified. Assess the individual.

options.text: Speak loudly throughout, since hearing loss is common at this age
options.rationale: Near miss concept Assumes a deficit, and shouting raises pitch into the range most often lost.

options.text: Teach everything at once on the day of discharge to keep it fresh
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome Completes the requirement at the point of worst retention.

options.text: Reduce background noise and face the patient directly
options.rationale: Short sessions, a quiet room, confirmation and reinforcement. The two wrong options are the two reflexes to resist: cramming everything into discharge day is the moment of lowest retention and highest anxiety, and assuming hearing loss and shouting at everyone over 75 is both inaccurate and undignified. Assess the individual.

options.text: Use teach back and return demonstration to confirm learning
options.rationale: Short sessions, a quiet room, confirmation and reinforcement. The two wrong options are the two reflexes to resist: cramming everything into discharge day is the moment of lowest retention and highest anxiety, and assuming hearing loss and shouting at everyone over 75 is both inaccurate and undignified. Assess the individual.

options.text: Provide large print written material to reinforce the session
options.rationale: Short sessions, a quiet room, confirmation and reinforcement. The two wrong options are the two reflexes to resist: cramming everything into discharge day is the moment of lowest retention and highest anxiety, and assuming hearing loss and shouting at everyone over 75 is both inaccurate and undignified. Assess the individual.

questions.takeaway: Teach back is the only way you find out whether the teaching worked.
questions.strategy: Do not assume a deficit on the basis of age. Assess, then adapt.

questions.stem: Classify each patient teaching outcome by learning domain.

rows.text: The patient will draw up and inject the correct insulin dose
The patient will state three signs of hypoglycemia
The patient will explain why the insulin dose changes with activity
The patient will express willingness to test glucose before meals

questions.takeaway: Cognitive is knowing, affective is valuing and attitude, psychomotor is doing with the hands. The teaching method follows the domain: you lecture or discuss for cognitive, explore feelings and model for affective, and demonstrate with a return demonstration for psychomotor. The domain picks the method, and the method picks how you evaluate.
questions.strategy: Read the verb. State and explain are cognitive, inject and demonstrate are psychomotor, express willingness and accept are affective.

questions.stem: A nurse is writing outcomes for a patient learning to care for a new colostomy. Select all of the outcomes that are correctly written.

options.text: The patient will state three signs of skin breakdown around the stoma by the second teaching session
options.rationale: A correctly written outcome describes what the PATIENT will do, observably, by a deadline. Understand and feel comfortable cannot be measured. The option in which the nurse teaches pouch care describes a nursing intervention rather than a patient outcome.

options.text: The patient will demonstrate emptying the pouch independently before discharge
options.rationale: A correctly written outcome describes what the PATIENT will do, observably, by a deadline. Understand and feel comfortable cannot be measured. The option in which the nurse teaches pouch care describes a nursing intervention rather than a patient outcome.

options.text: The patient will understand the importance of proper pouch fit
options.rationale: Near miss concept Understanding is the goal of teaching and the wrong verb for an outcome.

options.text: The patient will feel comfortable with the ostomy by discharge
options.rationale: Near miss concept Has a deadline, which makes it look correct, but feeling is not observable.

options.text: The nurse will teach pouch care using a return demonstration
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome What the nurse did, offered as what the patient achieved.

options.text: The patient will measure the stoma and cut the barrier to fit on two consecutive changes
options.rationale: A correctly written outcome describes what the PATIENT will do, observably, by a deadline. Understand and feel comfortable cannot be measured. The option in which the nurse teaches pouch care describes a nursing intervention rather than a patient outcome.

questions.takeaway: An outcome that cannot be observed cannot be evaluated.
questions.strategy: Scan the verb first. If you cannot watch it happen, it is not an outcome.

questions.stem: A nurse writes learning objectives for a patient newly diagnosed with diabetes. For each objective, indicate which learning domain it belongs to.

rows.text: The patient will name three signs of hypoglycemia
The patient will draw up and inject the correct insulin dose
The patient will express his concerns about injecting himself
The patient will decide what to do when his glucose reads 58 mg/dL
The patient will demonstrate rotating his injection sites
The patient will state that managing his diabetes is worth the effort

questions.takeaway: The patient will name three signs of hypoglycemia: Knowledge and recall. The cognitive domain covers knowing, understanding and problem solving. The patient will draw up and inject the correct insulin dose: A physical skill, demonstrated. Psychomotor covers physical skills and demonstration of procedures. The patient will express his concerns about injecting himself: Feelings and attitudes. The affective domain covers feelings, values and motivation. The patient will decide what to do when his glucose reads 58 mg/dL: Problem solving, which sits in the cognitive domain alongside knowledge. The patient will demonstrate rotating his injection sites: Another physical skill performed and observed. The patient will state that managing his diabetes is worth the effort: A value and a motivation rather than a fact or a skill. Cognitive is knowing. Psychomotor is doing. Affective is valuing. The domain determines how the outcome is evaluated.
questions.strategy: Problem solving sits in cognitive rather than forming a domain of its own. Deciding what to do is still knowing.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence: A nurse plans education for a patient going home with a new wound. What the nurse does to facilitate learning is [[1]]. A change in knowledge, behavior, skill or understanding is [[2]]. Watching the patient perform the dressing change himself is [[3]]. A patient's ability to obtain, understand and use health information is [[4]].

options.text: teaching
learning
evaluation
health literacy
learning
teaching
readiness
reinforcement
return demonstration
demonstration
teach-back
hands-on practice
health literacy
readiness to learn
cognitive ability
the affective domain

questions.takeaway: [1] teaching: Her definition: what the nurse does to facilitate learning. [2] learning: Her definition, and it is measured by change rather than by exposure. [3] return demonstration: The patient performs the skill back. It evaluates a psychomotor objective directly. [4] health literacy: Affects the ability to obtain, understand and use information, make decisions, and follow instructions. Teaching is what the nurse does. Learning is the change in the patient. Demonstration is the nurse showing; return demonstration is the patient doing.
questions.strategy: Two near-miss pairs: teaching against learning, and demonstration against return demonstration. In both, the question is who is acting.

questions.stem: A nurse documents a teaching session about a new anticoagulant. Which elements belong in the entry? Select all that apply.

options.text: What was taught
options.rationale: Named first, and it tells the next nurse what has been covered. Named, and it matters because a video and a return demonstration are not equivalent. Named, and it is the part that distinguishes teaching from learning. Named, and demonstrated is the operative word. Named, and unanswered questions are the reason for the next session.

options.text: The teaching method used
options.rationale: Named first, and it tells the next nurse what has been covered. Named, and it matters because a video and a return demonstration are not equivalent. Named, and it is the part that distinguishes teaching from learning. Named, and demonstrated is the operative word. Named, and unanswered questions are the reason for the next session.

options.text: The patient's response
options.rationale: Named first, and it tells the next nurse what has been covered. Named, and it matters because a video and a return demonstration are not equivalent. Named, and it is the part that distinguishes teaching from learning. Named, and demonstrated is the operative word. Named, and unanswered questions are the reason for the next session.

options.text: The level of understanding demonstrated
options.rationale: Named first, and it tells the next nurse what has been covered. Named, and it matters because a video and a return demonstration are not equivalent. Named, and it is the part that distinguishes teaching from learning. Named, and demonstrated is the operative word. Named, and unanswered questions are the reason for the next session.

options.text: Any questions or concerns raised
options.rationale: Named first, and it tells the next nurse what has been covered. Named, and it matters because a video and a return demonstration are not equivalent. Named, and it is the part that distinguishes teaching from learning. Named, and demonstrated is the operative word. Named, and unanswered questions are the reason for the next session.

options.text: The amount of time the session took
options.rationale: Near miss concept Not among the named elements. Duration says nothing about whether learning occurred.

questions.takeaway: Document what was taught, the method, the patient or caregiver response, level of understanding, demonstrated skills, questions and concerns, and any additional teaching needed.
questions.strategy: One distractor records effort rather than outcome. Ask what the next nurse needs to know.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked whether patient education can be assigned to assistive personnel during a busy shift. Which response is accurate?

options.text: It may be delegated if the assistive personnel is familiar with the content
options.rationale: Near miss concept Familiarity with content does not confer the scope to assess or evaluate learning.

options.text: Patient education is within the nurse's scope and cannot be delegated
options.rationale: Her slide states this directly. Teaching requires assessment of learning needs and evaluation of learning, neither of which is delegable.

options.text: It may be delegated provided the nurse documents the education afterwards
options.rationale: Near miss concept Documenting something you did not do is a separate problem on top of the delegation error.

options.text: It may be delegated for routine topics such as diet
options.rationale: Near miss concept The topic does not change the scope. Reinforcing a message is different from teaching.

questions.takeaway: Patient education is in the nurse's scope of practice and is not something that can be delegated.
questions.strategy: Three distractors offer conditions under which it becomes acceptable. There are none.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the sequence that effective patient education follows. Which order is correct?

options.text: Assess, communicate, teach, practice, evaluate, reinforce
options.rationale: Her stated sequence. Assessment opens it and reinforcement closes it.

options.text: Teach, assess, practice, evaluate, communicate, reinforce
options.rationale: Correct but premature Places teaching before assessment, which is the error the whole chapter is built against.

options.text: Assess, teach, evaluate, communicate, practice, reinforce
options.rationale: Near miss concept Places evaluation before practice, so the skill is assessed before it has been built.

options.text: Communicate, teach, assess, reinforce, practice, evaluate
options.rationale: Near miss concept Assessment third and evaluation last with practice after reinforcement. The sequence is scrambled.

questions.takeaway: Assess, communicate, teach, practice, evaluate, reinforce. Effective education depends on effective communication.
questions.strategy: Two things anchor the sequence: assessment comes first, and practice comes before evaluation.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews her own documentation of a teaching session with a colleague. Which entry requires correction?

options.text: "Patient education is in my scope and I cannot delegate it."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Accurate, and it is stated directly on her slide.

options.text: "Teaching is what I do; learning is the change in the patient."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Accurate, and the distinction is why evaluation exists.

options.text: "A 20-year-old with diabetes needs different teaching from a 74-year-old."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Accurate, and it is her own example of individualization.
