options.text: "Patient nodded and stated he understood; learning objectives met."
options.rationale: Never assume a patient understands because they nod. Learning is a change that has to be evaluated, not inferred.

questions.takeaway: Never assume understanding from a nod. Teaching is what the nurse does; learning is the change that has to be demonstrated.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate her slides correctly. The fourth treats a nod as evaluation.

questions.stem: A nurse finishes teaching a patient about a new anticoagulant. Which action best evaluates learning?

options.text: Document that teaching was completed and the patient verbalized understanding
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome Task completion recorded as a patient outcome.

options.text: Give written material and ask the patient to read all of it carefully at home before his discharge appointment
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome Material delivered is not learning achieved.

options.text: Ask the patient to explain in his own words what to do if he misses a dose
options.rationale: Teach back requires the patient to explain or demonstrate, and it places responsibility on the teacher rather than the learner. Asking whether someone understands produces a nod, which is not evidence of anything.

options.text: Ask the patient whether he understands everything that was taught to him
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic The classic yes or no question that produces a nod.

options.text: Ask the patient whether he has any more questions about the new medication
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Useful and insufficient. Silence here means nothing.

questions.takeaway: A nod is not understanding, and documenting that teaching occurred is not evidence of learning.
questions.strategy: The right answer makes the patient produce something. The wrong ones make the nurse feel finished.

questions.stem: A patient diagnosed with diabetes two hours ago is tearful and says she cannot take any of this in. Insulin teaching is scheduled for today and discharge is planned for tomorrow. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Postpone all teaching until she is emotionally ready
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Sends her home unable to recognize hypoglycemia.

options.text: Proceed with the full teaching plan as scheduled
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome Completes the teaching requirement and teaches nothing.

options.text: Give her the written materials and the video to review on her own
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome Distributes information with no verification and no support.

options.text: Teach only the survival skills she needs before discharge and schedule the rest
options.rationale: Anxiety at this level blocks learning, and a patient in crisis cannot absorb a full regimen. But she cannot leave without survival skills either: recognizing and treating hypoglycemia, giving the insulin, and knowing who to call. You teach that much, confirm it with teach back, and build the rest over follow up. Postponing everything and handing over a packet both leave her unsafe at home.

questions.takeaway: High anxiety blocks learning, and survival skills are not optional. Teach the short list.
questions.strategy: The two extremes, everything and nothing, are both wrong. The middle is the answer.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to teach a newly diagnosed patient about his insulin. He reports pain of 8 of 10, his roommate's television is on, and his daughter is due in ten minutes. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Teach now and repeat the session before discharge
options.rationale: Near miss concept Two ineffective sessions rather than one effective one, and the first may leave him thinking he has already been taught.

options.text: Give him written material and review it later
options.rationale: Near miss concept Written material is a strategy, not a substitute for assessing readiness. He is unlikely to read it at 8 of 10.

options.text: Address the pain and the distractions, then teach when he is ready
options.rationale: Readiness asks whether pain is controlled, whether he is free from distractions, and whether he is interested. Teaching through 8 of 10 pain wastes the session.

options.text: Teach the daughter instead when she arrives
options.rationale: Near miss concept Family involvement is appropriate when he wants it and when they will provide the care. It is not a workaround for his pain.

questions.takeaway: Readiness to learn: is pain controlled, is he free from distractions, is he interested. Assess readiness before teaching.
questions.strategy: Three options proceed in some form. Ask what he is likely to retain at 8 of 10 with a television on.

questions.stem: A nurse writes the objective that a patient will understand his new anticoagulant. Which revision is better?

options.text: The patient will state three foods to limit and two signs of bleeding before discharge
options.rationale: Observable, measurable and time-bound. Understand cannot be seen, and her slide gives exactly this contrast.

options.text: The nurse will teach the patient about his anticoagulant before discharge
options.rationale: Near miss concept Describes what the nurse does. A learning objective describes what the patient will be able to do.

options.text: The patient will feel confident managing his anticoagulant at home
options.rationale: Near miss concept Confidence is no more observable than understanding. It replaces one unmeasurable verb with another.

options.text: The patient will comprehend the importance of consistent dosing
options.rationale: Near miss concept Comprehend is understand in different clothing.

questions.takeaway: Learning objectives describe what the patient will be able to do after teaching, and they must be evaluable.
questions.strategy: Two distractors swap one unobservable verb for another. One changes the subject to the nurse.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to teach a patient before discharge. Which assessments belong to the period before teaching begins? Select all that apply.

options.text: What the patient already knows
options.rationale: Named first. You cannot pitch a session without knowing where to start. Named, and barriers include pain, distraction, language and literacy. Named, and it covers cognitive and physical ability. Named under readiness. Named under readiness, and a patient who is not interested will not retain it.

options.text: Whether any barriers are present
options.rationale: Named first. You cannot pitch a session without knowing where to start. Named, and barriers include pain, distraction, language and literacy. Named, and it covers cognitive and physical ability. Named under readiness. Named under readiness, and a patient who is not interested will not retain it.

options.text: The patient's ability to learn
options.rationale: Named first. You cannot pitch a session without knowing where to start. Named, and barriers include pain, distraction, language and literacy. Named, and it covers cognitive and physical ability. Named under readiness. Named under readiness, and a patient who is not interested will not retain it.

options.text: Whether his pain is controlled
options.rationale: Named first. You cannot pitch a session without knowing where to start. Named, and barriers include pain, distraction, language and literacy. Named, and it covers cognitive and physical ability. Named under readiness. Named under readiness, and a patient who is not interested will not retain it.

options.text: Whether he is interested
options.rationale: Named first. You cannot pitch a session without knowing where to start. Named, and barriers include pain, distraction, language and literacy. Named, and it covers cognitive and physical ability. Named under readiness. Named under readiness, and a patient who is not interested will not retain it.

options.text: Whether the teaching was effective
options.rationale: Near miss concept Evaluation comes after teaching. It cannot be assessed before anything has been taught.

questions.takeaway: Before teaching: assess what he knows, what barriers exist, and his ability to learn. Assess readiness: pain controlled, free from distractions, interested.
questions.strategy: One distractor belongs to the end of the process. Place yourself in time before choosing.

questions.stem: A nurse tells a visiting daughter that her mother has hypertension exacerbated by failure to take her diuretic, that her systolic has been over 180, and that she is NPO pending an echocardiogram and an EKG. She then charts that the family was updated on the plan of care. Which problem does this create?

options.text: The nurse breached confidentiality by discussing the mother's care
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nothing suggests the daughter is not an appropriate person to speak with.

options.text: The jargon means the daughter may not have understood, so the chart entry may be inaccurate
options.rationale: Documenting that a family was updated records what the nurse said, not what they received. The entry is only true if the information landed.

options.text: The information given was clinically inaccurate
options.rationale: Near miss concept The content is accurate. The problem is that it was unusable.

options.text: The nurse should have waited for the provider to give this information
options.rationale: Near miss concept Explaining the plan of care is squarely nursing work. The failure is in how it was explained.

questions.takeaway: Avoid medical jargon. Never assume a patient or family understood, and documenting that you updated someone records your action rather than their understanding.
questions.strategy: One distractor questions the accuracy of the content. Ask what the daughter can now do with what she was told.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches a patient to use a new inhaler, then asks whether he understood. He nods and says yes. Which action should follow?

options.text: Ask him to use the inhaler while she watches
options.rationale: A psychomotor skill is evaluated by watching it performed. Never assume a patient understands because they nod.

options.text: Provide written instructions to reinforce the teaching
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reinforcement is a legitimate later step, and it does not tell you whether he can use the device.

options.text: Ask whether he has any questions about the inhaler
options.rationale: Near miss concept Another closed question, and no questions is not evidence of competence.

options.text: Document that the patient verbalized understanding
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Records the nod as evidence. Her slide names this assumption explicitly.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate learning by the method the objective requires. A physical skill is evaluated by demonstration, not by a nod.
questions.strategy: Three options accept a verbal answer as proof of a physical skill.

questions.stem: A patient with a new abdominal wound cannot reach the site to change his own dressing. He lives with his son, who will perform the care. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Teach the patient thoroughly, since the education is for him
options.rationale: Near miss concept He cannot physically perform it. Teaching the person who cannot do the task leaves the person who will untrained.

options.text: Provide written instructions for the son to follow
options.rationale: Near miss concept Written material supports a skill. It does not establish that he can perform it.

options.text: Arrange home health so that nobody at home needs to be taught
options.rationale: Near miss concept May be appropriate and it does not remove the need for someone in the house to recognize problems.

options.text: Teach the son and confirm by return demonstration that he can perform it
options.rationale: Teaching should include the caregiver who will actually perform the care, and the confirmation is what makes it safe.

questions.takeaway: Ask who will provide care after discharge, who needs to learn the skill, whether the patient wants family involved, and whether the caregiver is an appropriate learner. Confirm by demonstration.
questions.strategy: One distractor keeps the teaching with the patient on principle. Ask who will be holding the dressing.

questions.stem: A nurse uses the same standardized diabetes teaching packet for a 20-year-old university student and a 74-year-old who lives alone. Which principle has she overlooked?

options.text: The younger patient requires less teaching than the older patient
options.rationale: Near miss concept Assumes from age in the other direction, which is the same error.

options.text: Written materials are inappropriate for older adults
options.rationale: Near miss concept Age does not determine whether written material works. Assessment does.

options.text: Diabetes teaching should always be delivered over multiple sessions
options.rationale: Near miss concept The number of sessions is not the principle at issue.

options.text: Teaching must be individualized rather than one size fits all
options.rationale: Her own example. The two patients differ in ability, resources, routine and what they need to manage.

questions.takeaway: Avoid one size fits all. Assess the individual, identify specific needs, match teaching to ability, use appropriate resources, and adapt the method.
questions.strategy: Two distractors make a new assumption based on age. That is the same error the question is about.

questions.stem: 1400: Nurse prepares discharge teaching for a 79-year-old going home with a new anticoagulant and a wound requiring daily dressing changes. Patient reports pain of 3 of 10, controlled with acetaminophen. States he left his reading glasses at home. Says he stopped school at 14 and finds forms difficult. His wife, who will do the dressings, is present and attentive. He is alert and oriented. The room is quiet. He asks three specific questions about the medication. He has no prior experience of wound care. Select all of the findings that should change how the nurse delivers this teaching.

options.text: Left his reading glasses at home
options.rationale: A physical barrier to written material, and it is fixable within the session by using verbal and demonstrated methods. Points to limited health literacy, which affects obtaining, understanding and using the information. She is the person who will perform the skill, so she is the person who must demonstrate it back. What he already knows is the first thing you assess, and starting from nothing changes the pace and the method.

options.text: Stopped school at 14 and finds forms difficult
options.rationale: A physical barrier to written material, and it is fixable within the session by using verbal and demonstrated methods. Points to limited health literacy, which affects obtaining, understanding and using the information. She is the person who will perform the skill, so she is the person who must demonstrate it back. What he already knows is the first thing you assess, and starting from nothing changes the pace and the method.

options.text: His wife will do the dressings and is present
options.rationale: A physical barrier to written material, and it is fixable within the session by using verbal and demonstrated methods. Points to limited health literacy, which affects obtaining, understanding and using the information. She is the person who will perform the skill, so she is the person who must demonstrate it back. What he already knows is the first thing you assess, and starting from nothing changes the pace and the method.

options.text: No prior experience of wound care
options.rationale: A physical barrier to written material, and it is fixable within the session by using verbal and demonstrated methods. Points to limited health literacy, which affects obtaining, understanding and using the information. She is the person who will perform the skill, so she is the person who must demonstrate it back. What he already knows is the first thing you assess, and starting from nothing changes the pace and the method.

options.text: Pain of 3 of 10, controlled with acetaminophen
options.rationale: Near miss concept Controlled pain. Readiness on this count is satisfied, which is why it is here.

options.text: Alert and oriented
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cognitive ability intact, removing it as a barrier.

options.text: The room is quiet
options.rationale: Near miss concept Free from distractions, which is one of the readiness criteria met.

options.text: Asks three specific questions about the medication
options.rationale: Near miss concept Evidence of interest, and interest is the third readiness criterion. A strength rather than a barrier.

questions.takeaway: Four findings change the method: no glasses, limited literacy, a caregiver who will do the skill, and no prior experience. Four confirm he is ready.
questions.strategy: Every readiness criterion is met here and stated explicitly. The findings that matter are about how to teach, not whether to.

questions.stem: A nurse wants to teach a patient how to use a walker safely. Which teaching strategy best matches the objective?

options.text: A video showing correct walker technique
options.rationale: Near miss concept Better than text and still passive. Watching is not doing.

options.text: Written instructions with diagrams for reference at home
options.rationale: Near miss concept Useful as reinforcement. Nobody learns to walk with a device from a page.

options.text: Demonstration followed by hands-on practice and return demonstration
options.rationale: Demonstration is useful for psychomotor skills, and practice with return demonstration is how the skill is built and confirmed.

options.text: A discussion about the importance of using the walker correctly
options.rationale: Near miss concept Discussion suits cognitive and affective objectives. It does not build a physical skill.

questions.takeaway: Match the teaching strategy to the learning goal. Demonstration is useful for psychomotor skills.
questions.strategy: Two distractors are strategies that would support the learning without producing it. Ask what the objective requires him to do.

questions.stem: A patient with newly diagnosed heart failure says he does not see the point of weighing himself daily because it will not change anything. Which learning domain should the nurse address first?

options.text: Cognitive, by explaining how daily weights detect fluid retention
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reasonable teaching and it addresses knowledge he may already have. He has not said he does not understand.

options.text: All three simultaneously, to be thorough
options.rationale: Near miss concept Spreads effort across two domains where there is no gap, and misses that his objection is about meaning.

options.text: Affective, because his attitude and motivation are the obstacle
options.rationale: He is not lacking the knowledge or the skill. Feelings, attitudes, values and motivation sit in the affective domain.

options.text: Psychomotor, by demonstrating correct use of the scale
options.rationale: Near miss concept Weighing is not the skill gap. He knows how to stand on a scale.

questions.takeaway: Cognitive is knowing, psychomotor is doing, affective is valuing. Address the domain where the gap actually is.
questions.strategy: One distractor is correct teaching aimed at a gap he has not shown. Ask what he actually said.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares discharge teaching for a patient going home after surgery. Which topics belong in it? Select all that apply.

options.text: Medications and how to take them
options.rationale: Named first among discharge education topics. Named, and confirming them is part of the plan rather than an afterthought. Both named, and both are where patients improvise if not told. Named, and it is the topic most often requiring return demonstration. Named, and it is the topic that prevents the readmission.

options.text: Follow-up appointments
options.rationale: Named first among discharge education topics. Named, and confirming them is part of the plan rather than an afterthought. Both named, and both are where patients improvise if not told. Named, and it is the topic most often requiring return demonstration. Named, and it is the topic that prevents the readmission.

options.text: Activity and diet restrictions
options.rationale: Named first among discharge education topics. Named, and confirming them is part of the plan rather than an afterthought. Both named, and both are where patients improvise if not told. Named, and it is the topic most often requiring return demonstration. Named, and it is the topic that prevents the readmission.

options.text: Wound care
options.rationale: Named first among discharge education topics. Named, and confirming them is part of the plan rather than an afterthought. Both named, and both are where patients improvise if not told. Named, and it is the topic most often requiring return demonstration. Named, and it is the topic that prevents the readmission.

options.text: Warning signs and when and how to seek help
options.rationale: Named first among discharge education topics. Named, and confirming them is part of the plan rather than an afterthought. Both named, and both are where patients improvise if not told. Named, and it is the topic most often requiring return demonstration. Named, and it is the topic that prevents the readmission.

options.text: The names of the staff who provided his care
options.rationale: Near miss concept Courteous and not part of discharge education. Nothing about it affects his safety at home.

questions.takeaway: Discharge education: medications, follow-up appointments, activity, diet, wound care, warning signs, when and how to seek help, equipment, and self-management.
questions.strategy: One distractor is pleasant and changes nothing about how he manages at home.

questions.stem: A nurse completes a teaching session and moves on to her next patient without checking what the patient took from it. Which error has she made?

options.text: Failing to individualize the teaching
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nothing in the stem suggests the content was generic. The omission is at the end, not the start.

options.text: Teaching without evaluating learning
options.rationale: Her slide names this directly. Teaching and learning are separate things, and only evaluation tells you whether the second happened.

options.text: Failing to identify barriers before teaching
options.rationale: Near miss concept An error that happens before teaching. Hers happened after.

options.text: Failing to document the session
options.rationale: Near miss concept Documentation matters and it is a separate step. She could document accurately and still not know whether he learned.

questions.takeaway: Avoid teaching without evaluation of learning. Evaluation may be verbal explanation, demonstration, observation, or asking questions.
questions.strategy: Three distractors name real errors that occur at other points in the process. Place the omission in time.

questions.stem: A nurse explains that a patient should ambulate three times daily, watch for edema, and remain NPO after midnight. Which change would most improve this?

options.text: Replace the clinical terms with words the patient uses
options.rationale: Ambulate, edema and NPO are all on her list of commonly used jargon. None of them means anything to most patients.

options.text: Repeat the instructions a second time before leaving
options.rationale: Near miss concept Repeating words he does not understand produces the same result twice.

options.text: Provide the instructions in writing as well
options.rationale: Near miss concept The same jargon in a different format.

options.text: Ask whether he has any questions about the instructions
options.rationale: Near miss concept He cannot form a question about terms he did not follow, and no questions would then be recorded as understanding.

questions.takeaway: Avoid medical jargon. Ambulate, edema, NPO, dyspnea, hypertension, PRN, EDD and SBA are all named as commonly used and commonly misunderstood.
questions.strategy: Three distractors deliver the same words again in a different way. Ask what he did not understand the first time.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old is readmitted with heart failure three weeks after discharge. He was taught about daily weights, fluid restriction and his diuretic before he left. He can recite the instructions accurately when asked. He says he has been taking the diuretic in the evening because mornings are rushed, and that he has not been weighing himself because he does not own scales. His discharge record documents that he verbalized understanding of all topics. Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem they address, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Establish what he can actually do at home, including what equipment he has
Work out a medication timing and monitoring plan that fits his mornings
Repeat the discharge teaching on all three topics before he leaves
Document that he verbalized understanding of the corrected instructions
Teaching was delivered and learning was never evaluated against his actual circumstances
Knowledge deficit regarding heart failure self-management
Nonadherence with the prescribed regimen
Low health literacy affecting his understanding of the instructions
Whether he is recording daily weights using equipment he now has
Whether he is readmitted within 30 days
Whether he can state three signs of fluid overload
Whether the discharge teaching was documented completely

questions.takeaway: He knows the content and cannot apply it. Nobody checked whether the plan was executable in his house. Assessment before teaching. Nobody established that he owned scales, and the plan assumed he did. Individualizing rather than repeating a generic plan. The evening dosing has a reason, and the reason can be worked with. Measures whether the practical barrier was actually removed, rather than whether he was told again. The outcome the whole intervention exists to prevent, and the pattern that brought him back. Verbalized understanding is not learning. Evaluate whether the plan can be executed in the patient's actual circumstances.
questions.strategy: The stem rules out knowledge and literacy explicitly by telling you he can recite the instructions. Two evaluation distractors test knowledge or paperwork.

questions.stem: Select all of the measures that reduce a hospitalized patient's risk of pneumonia.

options.text: Elevate the head of the bed for anyone receiving tube feeding
options.rationale: Most hospital pneumonia starts as aspiration of mouth organisms, which is why oral care is a pneumonia intervention and not a comfort measure. Head of bed up, moving, breathing deeply and vaccinated covers the rest. Lying flat invites aspiration, and routine suctioning when nothing is there traumatizes the mucosa and introduces organisms.

options.text: Perform oral care at least twice daily
options.rationale: Most hospital pneumonia starts as aspiration of mouth organisms, which is why oral care is a pneumonia intervention and not a comfort measure. Head of bed up, moving, breathing deeply and vaccinated covers the rest. Lying flat invites aspiration, and routine suctioning when nothing is there traumatizes the mucosa and introduces organisms.

options.text: Suction routinely every two hours whether or not secretions are present
options.rationale: Near miss concept Suction for a reason; routine suctioning injures the airway.

options.text: Encourage coughing, deep breathing and early ambulation
options.rationale: Most hospital pneumonia starts as aspiration of mouth organisms, which is why oral care is a pneumonia intervention and not a comfort measure. Head of bed up, moving, breathing deeply and vaccinated covers the rest. Lying flat invites aspiration, and routine suctioning when nothing is there traumatizes the mucosa and introduces organisms.

options.text: Keep the patient supine to conserve energy
options.rationale: Near miss concept Flat is the aspiration position.

options.text: Ensure pneumococcal and influenza vaccination where indicated
options.rationale: Most hospital pneumonia starts as aspiration of mouth organisms, which is why oral care is a pneumonia intervention and not a comfort measure. Head of bed up, moving, breathing deeply and vaccinated covers the rest. Lying flat invites aspiration, and routine suctioning when nothing is there traumatizes the mucosa and introduces organisms.

questions.takeaway: Oral care prevents pneumonia. It is the intervention most often treated as optional.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options are things that used to be done routinely and cause the problem.

questions.stem: Classify each case of pneumonia.

rows.text: New infiltrate on day 4 of mechanical ventilation
New infiltrate on day 5 of a hospital stay in a patient who is not intubated
Symptoms began at home three days before admission
A nursing home resident admitted with a cough that began at the facility

questions.takeaway: The category is set by where the infection was acquired and when it appeared. Hospital acquired means onset 48 hours or more after admission in a patient who was not incubating it on arrival. Ventilator associated means 48 hours or more after intubation. The split matters because the likely organisms and the antibiotic choice differ. Long term care residents count as community acquired, which surprises people.
questions.strategy: Ask where the patient was 48 hours before the symptoms started.

questions.stem: Select all of the accurate statements the nurse can make about influenza prevention.

options.text: A person can still get influenza after vaccination, usually with milder illness
options.rationale: The inactivated vaccine cannot cause influenza; post vaccination aches are an immune response, not infection. Health care workers are vaccinated to protect patients as much as themselves, which is the argument that answers the young and healthy objection. Breakthrough illness happens and is typically milder.

options.text: Hand hygiene and respiratory etiquette reduce transmission
options.rationale: The inactivated vaccine cannot cause influenza; post vaccination aches are an immune response, not infection. Health care workers are vaccinated to protect patients as much as themselves, which is the argument that answers the young and healthy objection. Breakthrough illness happens and is typically milder.

options.text: Vaccination is unnecessary for health care workers who are young and healthy
options.rationale: Near miss concept Ignores transmission to patients.

options.text: Annual vaccination is recommended for everyone 6 months and older with rare exceptions
options.rationale: The inactivated vaccine cannot cause influenza; post vaccination aches are an immune response, not infection. Health care workers are vaccinated to protect patients as much as themselves, which is the argument that answers the young and healthy objection. Breakthrough illness happens and is typically milder.

options.text: The vaccine is reformulated each year because the virus changes
options.rationale: The inactivated vaccine cannot cause influenza; post vaccination aches are an immune response, not infection. Health care workers are vaccinated to protect patients as much as themselves, which is the argument that answers the young and healthy objection. Breakthrough illness happens and is typically milder.

options.text: The vaccine causes influenza in some people
options.rationale: Near miss concept The most common misconception; the inactivated vaccine contains no live virus.

questions.takeaway: The vaccine cannot give you the flu. That sentence answers the most common patient objection.
questions.strategy: Two options here are the beliefs the teaching is meant to correct.

questions.stem: A patient recovering from influenza felt better for two days and now has a new fever of 102.2 F, a productive cough with thick yellow sputum and sharp pain on deep inspiration. What does this pattern suggest?

options.text: An expected part of influenza recovery
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Normalizes a new complication.

options.text: A relapse of the influenza infection
options.rationale: Near miss concept Influenza does not typically relapse with purulent sputum.

options.text: Secondary bacterial pneumonia
options.rationale: Improvement followed by a new fever, purulent sputum and pleuritic chest pain is the classic pattern of a bacterial pneumonia superimposed on influenza. The period of improvement is what distinguishes it from a continuing viral course.

options.text: Pulmonary embolism
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pleuritic pain fits, but fever and purulent sputum do not.

questions.takeaway: Better, then worse, is the sequence that names this complication.
questions.strategy: Watch for a stem that includes an interval of improvement. That detail is never decorative.

questions.stem: An 83 year old is admitted with suspected pneumonia. Select all of the findings consistent with this diagnosis in an older adult.

options.text: A respiratory rate of 26
options.rationale: In an older adult, pneumonia often presents as delirium, functional decline and a low grade or absent fever, because the febrile response is blunted. A near normal temperature is consistent with the diagnosis rather than evidence against it.

options.text: Absence of fever, which rules out an infectious process
options.rationale: Absolute language Uses a blunted response as proof of no infection.

options.text: A temperature of 99.1 F
options.rationale: In an older adult, pneumonia often presents as delirium, functional decline and a low grade or absent fever, because the febrile response is blunted. A near normal temperature is consistent with the diagnosis rather than evidence against it.

options.text: New confusion over the past 24 hours
options.rationale: In an older adult, pneumonia often presents as delirium, functional decline and a low grade or absent fever, because the febrile response is blunted. A near normal temperature is consistent with the diagnosis rather than evidence against it.

options.text: A productive cough with rust colored sputum
options.rationale: In an older adult, pneumonia often presents as delirium, functional decline and a low grade or absent fever, because the febrile response is blunted. A near normal temperature is consistent with the diagnosis rather than evidence against it.

options.text: Decreased appetite and generalized weakness
options.rationale: In an older adult, pneumonia often presents as delirium, functional decline and a low grade or absent fever, because the febrile response is blunted. A near normal temperature is consistent with the diagnosis rather than evidence against it.

questions.takeaway: Treat a sudden functional or mental change in an older adult as the infection sign.
questions.strategy: The option that uses a normal finding to RULE OUT a diagnosis is almost always the wrong one.

questions.stem: A patient admitted with pneumonia has been stable. Select all of the findings that indicate deterioration requiring escalation.

options.text: Inability to speak a full sentence without pausing
options.rationale: Mental status change, a rising respiratory rate, a rising lactate and increasing work of breathing are the four that say this is becoming sepsis or respiratory failure. A falling temperature on treatment is improvement, and purulent sputum is expected in pneumonia and is not itself a deterioration.

options.text: A productive cough with thick yellow sputum
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Expected in bacterial pneumonia; it is not a change.

options.text: A temperature that has fallen from 38.9 to 38.1
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Moving toward normal on treatment.

options.text: A lactate that has risen from 1.4 to 3.2
options.rationale: Mental status change, a rising respiratory rate, a rising lactate and increasing work of breathing are the four that say this is becoming sepsis or respiratory failure. A falling temperature on treatment is improvement, and purulent sputum is expected in pneumonia and is not itself a deterioration.

options.text: A respiratory rate that has risen from 20 to 30
options.rationale: Mental status change, a rising respiratory rate, a rising lactate and increasing work of breathing are the four that say this is becoming sepsis or respiratory failure. A falling temperature on treatment is improvement, and purulent sputum is expected in pneumonia and is not itself a deterioration.

options.text: New confusion in an otherwise alert patient
options.rationale: Mental status change, a rising respiratory rate, a rising lactate and increasing work of breathing are the four that say this is becoming sepsis or respiratory failure. A falling temperature on treatment is improvement, and purulent sputum is expected in pneumonia and is not itself a deterioration.

questions.takeaway: Confusion and respiratory rate are the two earliest signs, and both get missed because neither has an alarm.
questions.strategy: Two options are findings moving in the right direction or findings that were always going to be there.

questions.topic: influenza in a high risk patient
questions.stem: A pregnant patient at 30 weeks presents with abrupt fever, myalgias and headache that began about 36 hours ago. Influenza is circulating in the community. What should the nurse anticipate?
questions.objective: influenza in a high risk patient

options.text: Antiviral treatment now, since pregnancy is high risk and she is in the window
options.rationale: Pregnancy is one of the highest risk conditions in influenza, with a real risk of severe disease and of complications for the pregnancy. Antivirals are recommended in high risk patients and treatment is started on clinical suspicion rather than waiting for a test, because the benefit falls as the clock runs. Vaccination in pregnancy is also recommended and protects the infant.

options.text: Waiting for a confirmatory influenza test result before any treatment decision
options.rationale: Correct but premature Benefit declines hourly; treatment starts on suspicion.

options.text: Treatment only if she later develops respiratory distress or a low oxygen saturation reading
options.rationale: Correct but premature That is the outcome treatment is meant to prevent.

options.text: Supportive care only, since antiviral medications are unsafe during pregnancy
options.rationale: Near miss concept They are recommended in pregnancy, which is a high risk condition.

questions.takeaway: High risk plus clinical suspicion equals treat now. Do not wait for the swab.
questions.strategy: The contraindication option is false and is believed widely enough to be worth knowing.

questions.stem: A patient calls the clinic reporting that severe headache, body aches, fever and chills began abruptly about 30 hours ago. Which information is most important for the nurse to obtain and act on?

options.text: The exact time symptoms began, since antivirals work best within 48 hours
options.rationale: The abrupt onset of severe headache, myalgias, fever and chills is influenza, and the benefit of an antiviral falls off as the clock runs. At about 30 hours this patient is well inside the window, which makes confirming and documenting the onset a time critical clinical question rather than history taking. Treatment beyond 48 hours is still given to hospitalized, severe or high risk patients, so the window narrows the benefit rather than closing the door.

options.text: Whether the patient has received the pneumococcal vaccine in the past
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Relevant to prevention and to later risk, not to this decision today.

options.text: Whether anyone else in the household has the same symptoms right now
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Useful epidemiology that does not change this patient's treatment window.

options.text: The patient's usual temperature pattern and the antipyretic preferred
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Comfort information while a treatment window closes.

questions.takeaway: Rapid onset is the tell for influenza, and the clock is part of the assessment.
questions.strategy: When a treatment has a time window, the stem will give you a time. Use it.

questions.stem: A nurse discovers a small fire in a patient's trash can. In what order should she act?

options.text: Extinguish the fire, rescue the patient, activate the alarm, confine it
options.rationale: Near miss concept Puts the nurse alone against a fire with a patient still in it.

options.text: Confine the fire, rescue the patient, activate the alarm, extinguish it
options.rationale: Near miss concept Closes the door on a patient who is still in the room.

options.text: Activate the alarm, rescue the patient, extinguish the fire, confine it
options.rationale: Near miss concept Alarm before rescue, and confining after extinguishing does nothing.

options.text: Rescue the patient, activate the alarm, confine the fire, extinguish it
options.rationale: RACE: rescue, alarm, confine, extinguish. People first, always. Confining means closing doors and windows to starve the fire of air while help comes. Extinguishing is last because a nurse with a fire extinguisher is not the plan, she is the stopgap.

questions.takeaway: RACE. The patient comes out before the alarm goes in.
questions.strategy: Every wrong option here puts the fire ahead of the person.

questions.stem: After a patient fall, the unit holds a post fall huddle. What is its purpose?

options.text: To learn what happened and what in the plan or setting must change
options.rationale: The huddle asks four questions: what happened, what contributed, were the interventions actually in place, and what needs to change. It happens soon after the fall while details are fresh. Looking for a person to blame ends the usefulness of it, because the next person stops reporting.

options.text: To decide whether the patient should now be placed in restraints overnight for safety
options.rationale: Near miss concept Restraints are never routine fall prevention.

options.text: To complete the occurrence report together as a whole team
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting The report is an individual quality document, not the point of the huddle.

options.text: To identify which staff member was responsible for the lapse
options.rationale: Near miss concept Blame is the thing a safety culture is built to avoid.

questions.takeaway: The huddle looks at the system. Finding a culprit kills the reporting it depends on.
questions.strategy: A restraint is not a fall prevention measure, which rules out one option on principle.

questions.stem: Which reason for applying a restraint is never acceptable?

options.text: The patient is swinging at staff during a delirium episode
options.rationale: Near miss concept Danger to others, which is an accepted indication.

options.text: The unit is short staffed tonight
options.rationale: Restraints are never used for staff convenience, as punishment, or as routine fall prevention. The acceptable reasons are immediate harm the patient cannot control: interference with critical treatment, danger to self or others. Staffing is a system problem, and solving it with restraints is how facilities lose accreditation and patients get hurt.

options.text: The patient is pulling at a central line
options.rationale: Near miss concept A legitimate reason once alternatives have failed.

options.text: The patient keeps removing a tracheostomy tube
options.rationale: Near miss concept Interference with critical treatment, which is accepted.

questions.takeaway: Convenience, punishment and routine fall prevention are the three that are never allowed.
questions.strategy: Three options describe immediate physical danger. One describes the unit's problem, not the patient's.

questions.stem: A patient is in bilateral soft wrist restraints. Select all of the assessments the nurse must perform on an ongoing basis.

options.text: Hydration, elimination and comfort
options.rationale: A restrained patient cannot meet his own needs, so you meet them: skin, circulation, movement, food, fluid, toileting, comfort and mental status. Every check also asks whether the restraint is still necessary, because the standard is to remove it at the earliest possible moment.

options.text: Skin integrity under and around the restraint
options.rationale: A restrained patient cannot meet his own needs, so you meet them: skin, circulation, movement, food, fluid, toileting, comfort and mental status. Every check also asks whether the restraint is still necessary, because the standard is to remove it at the earliest possible moment.

options.text: Range of motion and repositioning
options.rationale: A restrained patient cannot meet his own needs, so you meet them: skin, circulation, movement, food, fluid, toileting, comfort and mental status. Every check also asks whether the restraint is still necessary, because the standard is to remove it at the earliest possible moment.

options.text: Whether the restraint can be discontinued
options.rationale: A restrained patient cannot meet his own needs, so you meet them: skin, circulation, movement, food, fluid, toileting, comfort and mental status. Every check also asks whether the restraint is still necessary, because the standard is to remove it at the earliest possible moment.

options.text: Circulation distal to the restraint
options.rationale: A restrained patient cannot meet his own needs, so you meet them: skin, circulation, movement, food, fluid, toileting, comfort and mental status. Every check also asks whether the restraint is still necessary, because the standard is to remove it at the earliest possible moment.

options.text: The patient's willingness to agree to the restraint before each check
options.rationale: Near miss concept Consent is not the mechanism here. The patient is informed and the family notified, and the authority is the order and the ongoing need.

questions.takeaway: You are not checking the restraint. You are checking the person inside it.
questions.strategy: The option that mentions consent is the trap. Restraints are ordered, not negotiated at each check.

questions.stem: Select all of the universal fall precautions that apply to every patient.

options.text: Provide nonslip, well fitting footwear
options.rationale: Universal precautions apply to everyone regardless of score, and they are mostly environmental. Note the demonstration: having the patient show you they can work the call light is different from telling them where it is. Keeping people in bed is not a universal precaution, it is a restriction that produces the weakness causing the next fall.

options.text: Keep the bed in low position with the brakes locked
options.rationale: Universal precautions apply to everyone regardless of score, and they are mostly environmental. Note the demonstration: having the patient show you they can work the call light is different from telling them where it is. Keeping people in bed is not a universal precaution, it is a restriction that produces the weakness causing the next fall.

options.text: Keep the patient in bed unless a staff member is present
options.rationale: Near miss concept Immobility worsens weakness, and the goal is safe mobility.

options.text: Clean up spills promptly and keep the area uncluttered
options.rationale: Universal precautions apply to everyone regardless of score, and they are mostly environmental. Note the demonstration: having the patient show you they can work the call light is different from telling them where it is. Keeping people in bed is not a universal precaution, it is a restriction that produces the weakness causing the next fall.

options.text: Keep the call light and personal items within reach
options.rationale: Universal precautions apply to everyone regardless of score, and they are mostly environmental. Note the demonstration: having the patient show you they can work the call light is different from telling them where it is. Keeping people in bed is not a universal precaution, it is a restriction that produces the weakness causing the next fall.

options.text: Orient the patient to the room and have them demonstrate the call light
options.rationale: Universal precautions apply to everyone regardless of score, and they are mostly environmental. Note the demonstration: having the patient show you they can work the call light is different from telling them where it is. Keeping people in bed is not a universal precaution, it is a restriction that produces the weakness causing the next fall.

questions.takeaway: Have them show you the call light. Telling them is not the same as knowing they can use it.
questions.strategy: The wrong option is the one that trades function for stillness.

questions.stem: Select all of the elements the nurse documents after a patient fall.

options.text: The interventions performed and the patient's response
options.rationale: The chart holds findings, quotations, notifications, actions and responses. Fault is not a nursing determination and asserting it in the legal record is both unsupportable and damaging. The occurrence report is a separate quality document and referencing it in the chart can make it discoverable, which is why it is never mentioned.

options.text: The patient's own account of what happened, in quotation
options.rationale: The chart holds findings, quotations, notifications, actions and responses. Fault is not a nursing determination and asserting it in the legal record is both unsupportable and damaging. The occurrence report is a separate quality document and referencing it in the chart can make it discoverable, which is why it is never mentioned.

options.text: A conclusion about which staff member was at fault
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Not a nursing determination and damaging in the legal record.

options.text: A reference to the occurrence report in the medical record
options.rationale: Near miss concept Keeps the quality document separate; mentioning it can expose it.

options.text: The time the provider was notified and what was reported
options.rationale: The chart holds findings, quotations, notifications, actions and responses. Fault is not a nursing determination and asserting it in the legal record is both unsupportable and damaging. The occurrence report is a separate quality document and referencing it in the chart can make it discoverable, which is why it is never mentioned.

options.text: The objective findings of the post fall assessment
options.rationale: The chart holds findings, quotations, notifications, actions and responses. Fault is not a nursing determination and asserting it in the legal record is both unsupportable and damaging. The occurrence report is a separate quality document and referencing it in the chart can make it discoverable, which is why it is never mentioned.

questions.takeaway: Never reference the occurrence report in the chart, and never assign fault.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options put something in the legal record that does not belong there.

questions.stem: Which fall prevention activity may the nurse delegate to assistive personnel?

options.text: Assessing the patient's fall risk on admission to the unit
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Assessment is never delegated, scored tool or not.

options.text: Choosing which fall prevention measures this patient needs
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope That is planning, which follows from the nurse's assessment.

options.text: Judging whether the fall prevention plan has been effective
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Evaluation closes the nursing process and stays with the nurse.

options.text: Toileting the patient every 2 hours on a set schedule
options.rationale: Assistive personnel carry out the plan: scheduled toileting, keeping the environment safe, assisting with mobility as the plan directs, and reporting what they see. Building the plan, scoring the risk and judging whether it worked are all nursing judgment.

questions.takeaway: They can do the rounding. They cannot decide that rounding is the answer.
questions.strategy: Assess, determine, evaluate. Three verbs that never move.

questions.stem: A nurse realizes she gave a scheduled medication an hour late. The patient is unharmed. What reflects a culture of safety?

options.text: Report the error so the system factors behind it can be examined
options.rationale: A culture of safety is blame free and learns from events, which only works if people report near misses and no harm errors. Those are the free lessons: the same system pressure that made this dose late will eventually make a dose wrong. Framing it as a personal failing is exactly what stops the next person from reporting.

options.text: Record it in the occurrence report as a personal lapse in attention
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reporting is right, and blaming the individual is the thing a safety culture is built to avoid.

options.text: Document the time given and say nothing, since there was no harm
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Charts the fact and loses the lesson.

options.text: Report it only if the charge nurse noticed the delay
options.rationale: Near miss concept Makes reporting contingent on being observed.

questions.takeaway: No harm is the best time to report, not a reason to skip it.
questions.strategy: Any option that makes reporting conditional on harm or on being caught is wrong.

questions.stem: Select all of the complications a restrained patient is at risk for.

options.text: Improved orientation from the enforced rest
options.rationale: Near miss concept Restraint worsens delirium rather than settling it.

options.text: Injury sustained while trying to escape the restraint
options.rationale: Restraints cause the harms they are meant to prevent. Patients fight them, which worsens agitation and delirium, and the serious injuries in restrained patients usually happen during escape attempts rather than during quiet compliance. Immobility costs strength and joint range within days.

options.text: Increased agitation and worsening confusion
options.rationale: Restraints cause the harms they are meant to prevent. Patients fight them, which worsens agitation and delirium, and the serious injuries in restrained patients usually happen during escape attempts rather than during quiet compliance. Immobility costs strength and joint range within days.

options.text: Reduced risk of aspiration
options.rationale: Near miss concept A supine restrained patient is at higher aspiration risk, not lower.

options.text: Skin breakdown and neurovascular injury at the restraint site
options.rationale: Restraints cause the harms they are meant to prevent. Patients fight them, which worsens agitation and delirium, and the serious injuries in restrained patients usually happen during escape attempts rather than during quiet compliance. Immobility costs strength and joint range within days.

options.text: Loss of muscle strength and joint mobility
options.rationale: Restraints cause the harms they are meant to prevent. Patients fight them, which worsens agitation and delirium, and the serious injuries in restrained patients usually happen during escape attempts rather than during quiet compliance. Immobility costs strength and joint range within days.

questions.takeaway: Most restraint injuries happen while the patient is trying to get out.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options claim a benefit from immobilization. There is none.

questions.stem: Classify each intervention.

rows.text: An antipsychotic given to quiet a patient who is agitated, with no psychiatric indication
A bed alarm that sounds when the patient sits up
Confining a patient alone in a room he cannot leave
All four side rails raised on a confused patient who tries to climb out

questions.takeaway: A restraint is anything that restricts movement and the patient cannot remove. Four raised rails qualify. A drug given to control behavior rather than to treat a diagnosed condition is a chemical restraint and carries the same rules. An alarm signals but does not restrict, so it is an alternative rather than a restraint. The test is whether the patient can get out of it, not whether it looks like a restraint.
questions.strategy: Ask two questions: does it restrict movement, and can the patient remove it?

questions.stem: Select all of the fall risk factors that are extrinsic, meaning they live in the environment or the process rather than in the patient.

options.text: Nonslip footwear not available
options.rationale: Extrinsic factors live in the room and the process: clutter, lighting, bed height, footwear, missing equipment, nobody available to help. They are usually fixed in about a minute, which is why they are the first thing to check. Intrinsic factors live in the patient: weakness, dizziness, gait, confusion, sensory change, urgency, medication effects.

options.text: Urinary urgency and frequency
options.rationale: Near miss concept Intrinsic, and it is the one that sends people to the bathroom alone at night.

options.text: Lower extremity weakness
options.rationale: Near miss concept Intrinsic. It lives in the patient and takes an intervention, not a tidy up.

options.text: A bed left in the high position
options.rationale: Extrinsic factors live in the room and the process: clutter, lighting, bed height, footwear, missing equipment, nobody available to help. They are usually fixed in about a minute, which is why they are the first thing to check. Intrinsic factors live in the patient: weakness, dizziness, gait, confusion, sensory change, urgency, medication effects.

options.text: Poor lighting in the room
options.rationale: Extrinsic factors live in the room and the process: clutter, lighting, bed height, footwear, missing equipment, nobody available to help. They are usually fixed in about a minute, which is why they are the first thing to check. Intrinsic factors live in the patient: weakness, dizziness, gait, confusion, sensory change, urgency, medication effects.

options.text: Clutter in the walking path
options.rationale: Extrinsic factors live in the room and the process: clutter, lighting, bed height, footwear, missing equipment, nobody available to help. They are usually fixed in about a minute, which is why they are the first thing to check. Intrinsic factors live in the patient: weakness, dizziness, gait, confusion, sensory change, urgency, medication effects.

questions.takeaway: Extrinsic risks get fixed. Intrinsic risks get a nursing intervention.
questions.strategy: Ask where you would go to fix it. If the fix is in the room, it is extrinsic.

questions.topic: safety with equipment and the environment
questions.stem: Select all of the nursing actions that reduce environmental risk on the unit.
questions.objective: safety with equipment and the environment

options.text: Know the location of the nearest fire extinguisher, alarm and oxygen shutoff
options.rationale: Knowing where the oxygen shutoff is matters because a fire in an oxygen enriched room behaves very differently. Extension cords are a fire and trip hazard and are not permitted for patient care equipment, and a propped fire door defeats the compartmentalization that keeps a fire in one place, which is the confine step of RACE.

options.text: Use an extension cord to reach a distant outlet for a patient's device
options.rationale: Near miss concept A fire and trip hazard, and not permitted for patient care equipment.

options.text: Prop a fire door open to make transport easier
options.rationale: Near miss concept Defeats the compartmentalization that confines a fire.

options.text: Remove damaged electrical equipment from service and report it
options.rationale: Knowing where the oxygen shutoff is matters because a fire in an oxygen enriched room behaves very differently. Extension cords are a fire and trip hazard and are not permitted for patient care equipment, and a propped fire door defeats the compartmentalization that keeps a fire in one place, which is the confine step of RACE.

options.text: Keep corridors and patient rooms free of clutter
options.rationale: Knowing where the oxygen shutoff is matters because a fire in an oxygen enriched room behaves very differently. Extension cords are a fire and trip hazard and are not permitted for patient care equipment, and a propped fire door defeats the compartmentalization that keeps a fire in one place, which is the confine step of RACE.

options.text: Clean spills promptly and use wet floor signage
options.rationale: Knowing where the oxygen shutoff is matters because a fire in an oxygen enriched room behaves very differently. Extension cords are a fire and trip hazard and are not permitted for patient care equipment, and a propped fire door defeats the compartmentalization that keeps a fire in one place, which is the confine step of RACE.

questions.takeaway: Find the oxygen shutoff on your unit. You will not have time to look during a fire.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options are convenience shortcuts that defeat a fire safety system.

questions.stem: Select all of the restraint alternatives the nurse should try first.

options.text: Involve family in sitting with the patient
options.rationale: Before a restraint you ask why the behavior is happening. Pain, a full bladder, hunger, thirst, fear, delirium, a new medication, too much stimulation and an unfamiliar environment all produce the agitation that gets treated with restraints. Fix the cause and the behavior often goes with it.

options.text: Raise all four side rails so the patient cannot get out
options.rationale: Near miss concept Four raised rails is a physical restraint, not an alternative to one.

options.text: Address unmet needs such as pain, hunger and toileting
options.rationale: Before a restraint you ask why the behavior is happening. Pain, a full bladder, hunger, thirst, fear, delirium, a new medication, too much stimulation and an unfamiliar environment all produce the agitation that gets treated with restraints. Fix the cause and the behavior often goes with it.

options.text: Reduce excess noise and stimulation
options.rationale: Before a restraint you ask why the behavior is happening. Pain, a full bladder, hunger, thirst, fear, delirium, a new medication, too much stimulation and an unfamiliar environment all produce the agitation that gets treated with restraints. Fix the cause and the behavior often goes with it.

options.text: Provide diversional activity and familiar objects
options.rationale: Before a restraint you ask why the behavior is happening. Pain, a full bladder, hunger, thirst, fear, delirium, a new medication, too much stimulation and an unfamiliar environment all produce the agitation that gets treated with restraints. Fix the cause and the behavior often goes with it.

options.text: Move the patient closer to the nursing station for observation
options.rationale: Before a restraint you ask why the behavior is happening. Pain, a full bladder, hunger, thirst, fear, delirium, a new medication, too much stimulation and an unfamiliar environment all produce the agitation that gets treated with restraints. Fix the cause and the behavior often goes with it.

questions.takeaway: Agitation is a symptom. Look for what it is a symptom of.
questions.strategy: The one wrong option is itself a restraint, which is what you were trying to avoid.

questions.topic: safety for the patient with a seizure history
questions.stem: A patient with a history of generalized seizures is admitted. Which precautions should the nurse put in place?
questions.objective: safety for the patient with a seizure history

options.text: Padded rails, low bed, suction and oxygen ready, call light in reach
options.rationale: Seizure precautions are about limiting injury during an event you cannot prevent: padding, a low bed, suction and oxygen ready, and a way to call for help. Nothing goes in the mouth during a seizure, so an airway taped to the bed is an invitation to do the wrong thing. Restraints during a convulsion cause fractures, and four raised rails is itself a restraint.

options.text: Soft wrist restraints at night in case a seizure occurs while asleep
options.rationale: Near miss concept Restraining a convulsing limb causes fractures, and this is prophylactic restraint.

options.text: Strict bedrest with all four side rails raised throughout the stay
options.rationale: Near miss concept Four raised rails is a restraint and patients climb over them.

options.text: An oral airway taped to the bed to insert during the next seizure
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nothing is inserted during a seizure; it breaks teeth and obstructs.

questions.takeaway: Nothing in the mouth, nothing holding the limbs. Pad, lower, and have suction ready.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options are practices that were taught for decades and cause injury.

questions.stem: Two patients have identical high fall risk scores. One falls because of urinary urgency and the other because of new confusion. What does this tell the nurse about the care plan?

options.text: The scores should be recalculated, since two risks cannot match
options.rationale: Near miss concept Two patients absolutely can score the same for different reasons; that is the whole point.

options.text: Both patients need the identical standard high risk protocol
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome Applies a checklist and leaves both actual causes untouched.

options.text: Each plan must target that patient's own reason for falling
options.rationale: A score tells you that someone is at risk. It does not tell you why, and the why is what you treat. Urgency gets scheduled toileting every one to two hours. Confusion gets frequent reorientation and familiar cues. Medication dizziness gets a pharmacy review and a timing change. Visual impairment gets light and glasses within reach.

options.text: Both patients should stay in bed until their scores improve
options.rationale: Near miss concept Immobility worsens the weakness that drives the next fall.

questions.takeaway: Score the risk, then treat the reason. A high score with a generic plan prevents nothing.
questions.strategy: Any option that applies one protocol to every high scoring patient misses the point of the assessment.

questions.stem: A nurse notices a frayed cord on a patient's personal heating pad. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Remove the device from use and report it to engineering
options.rationale: Damaged electrical equipment comes out of service, full stop. Hospitals carry oxygen, which turns an electrical spark into a fire, and patients with impaired sensation cannot feel a device overheating. The same logic applies to chemical exposures: remove the hazard, then report it, and consult the safety data sheet for a spill.

options.text: Tape the cord and allow continued use with monitoring
options.rationale: Near miss concept An improvised repair on equipment nobody has inspected.

options.text: Document the finding and tell the patient to be careful
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Transfers the hazard to the patient.

options.text: Allow use only while the nurse is in the room
options.rationale: Near miss concept Supervision does not make faulty wiring safe.

questions.takeaway: A damaged device gets removed, not supervised.
questions.strategy: Every wrong option keeps a known hazard in the room with a mitigation attached.

questions.stem: A nurse needs to move a patient who cannot bear weight from the bed to a chair. What should she do?

options.text: Use a gait belt and lift under the patient's arms with a second nurse
options.rationale: Near miss concept Under the arms risks shoulder injury, and a gait belt is for a patient who can bear weight.

options.text: Have the patient hold around her neck while she lifts
options.rationale: Near miss concept Puts the nurse's cervical spine at risk and offers no control.

options.text: Use a mechanical lift with the number of staff the device requires
options.rationale: Safe patient handling means equipment does the lifting, because good body mechanics do not make a human lift safe at these weights. Nurses injure their backs doing it correctly. Lifting under the arms can dislocate a shoulder or damage the brachial plexus, and a patient holding your neck can pull you both down.

options.text: Lift with her knees bent and her back straight, alone
options.rationale: Near miss concept Technique does not protect a spine under that load.

questions.takeaway: Body mechanics do not make a manual lift safe. Equipment does.
questions.strategy: The option that mentions correct body mechanics is the trap.

questions.topic: a fall that should not have happened
questions.stem: A patient at high fall risk fell while walking to the bathroom unassisted at 0300. Select all of the factors the post fall huddle should examine.
questions.objective: a fall that should not have happened

options.text: Which staff member was assigned to the patient at the time
options.rationale: Near miss concept Blame ends the inquiry and stops the next report.

options.text: Whether the call light was within reach and the patient could use it
options.rationale: The huddle asks what happened, what contributed, whether the interventions were actually in place, and what needs to change. Three of those are environmental and process questions and one is pharmacologic, which is the one most often missed because the drug was given hours earlier. Identifying the assigned staff member turns the huddle into a disciplinary process, and a restraint is never routine fall prevention.

options.text: Whether a toileting schedule was in place and followed
options.rationale: The huddle asks what happened, what contributed, whether the interventions were actually in place, and what needs to change. Three of those are environmental and process questions and one is pharmacologic, which is the one most often missed because the drug was given hours earlier. Identifying the assigned staff member turns the huddle into a disciplinary process, and a restraint is never routine fall prevention.

options.text: Whether a new medication given that evening contributed
options.rationale: The huddle asks what happened, what contributed, whether the interventions were actually in place, and what needs to change. Three of those are environmental and process questions and one is pharmacologic, which is the one most often missed because the drug was given hours earlier. Identifying the assigned staff member turns the huddle into a disciplinary process, and a restraint is never routine fall prevention.

options.text: Whether the bed was in low position with the brakes locked
options.rationale: The huddle asks what happened, what contributed, whether the interventions were actually in place, and what needs to change. Three of those are environmental and process questions and one is pharmacologic, which is the one most often missed because the drug was given hours earlier. Identifying the assigned staff member turns the huddle into a disciplinary process, and a restraint is never routine fall prevention.

options.text: Whether the patient should now be restrained at night
options.rationale: Near miss concept Restraints are explicitly not routine fall prevention.

questions.takeaway: Ask whether the plan was in place, not who was on. The first question finds the cause.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options are instincts that feel like accountability and prevent the next review.

questions.stem: A small fire has started in a wastebasket in a patient room. The patient has been moved out, the alarm is sounding, and the door is closed. The nurse picks up the extinguisher and pulls the pin. Where should the nurse aim?

options.text: At the top of the flames, where the fire is tallest
options.rationale: Most dramatic finding The flames are what draw the eye, but the fuel burns at the base, which is where PASS directs the spray.

options.text: At the center of the flames, holding the stream still
options.rationale: Near miss concept PASS ends with sweep, side to side across the base; a fixed stream at the middle misses the fuel.

options.text: At the base of the fire, sweeping side to side
options.rationale: PASS is the E of RACE for a small, contained fire: pull the pin, aim at the base, squeeze the handle, sweep side to side across the base. The fuel is at the base, so that is where the agent has to land.

options.text: At the ceiling above the fire to cool the smoke
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Smoke is handled by containment, closing doors; the extinguisher is for the burning material itself.

questions.takeaway: Aim low, at the base, and sweep.
questions.strategy: Recall the A of PASS. Any option aimed at the flames rather than the base is the trap.

questions.stem: A provider has ordered soft wrist restraints for a patient who keeps pulling at an endotracheal tube after alternatives failed. Select all of the actions that reflect correct application.

options.text: Pad the bony prominences under the device
options.rationale: Padding protects the skin under the device. Two fingers keeps it snug enough to hold and loose enough for circulation. A quick release knot lets you free the patient fast in an emergency. The strap goes to the bed frame, never the side rail. The order is time limited and never PRN.

options.text: Secure the strap to the side rail so it is easy to reach
options.rationale: Near miss concept Moving the side rail tightens the strap and can injure the wrist; the strap goes to the bed frame.

options.text: Use a quick release knot
options.rationale: Padding protects the skin under the device. Two fingers keeps it snug enough to hold and loose enough for circulation. A quick release knot lets you free the patient fast in an emergency. The strap goes to the bed frame, never the side rail. The order is time limited and never PRN.

options.text: Check that two fingers fit between the restraint and the wrist
options.rationale: Padding protects the skin under the device. Two fingers keeps it snug enough to hold and loose enough for circulation. A quick release knot lets you free the patient fast in an emergency. The strap goes to the bed frame, never the side rail. The order is time limited and never PRN.

options.text: Tie the strap to the movable part of the bed frame
options.rationale: Padding protects the skin under the device. Two fingers keeps it snug enough to hold and loose enough for circulation. A quick release knot lets you free the patient fast in an emergency. The strap goes to the bed frame, never the side rail. The order is time limited and never PRN.

options.text: Ask the provider to write the order as needed for the rest of the stay
options.rationale: Near miss concept A restraint order is time limited and never PRN, because the need has to be reassessed, not assumed.

questions.takeaway: Bed frame, quick release, two fingers, padded, time limited.
questions.strategy: The side rail and the PRN order both sound convenient; convenience is the signal that they are wrong.

questions.stem: A patient walking to the bathroom begins to have a generalized seizure. Select all of the actions the nurse should take during and after the seizure.

options.text: Guide the patient to the floor
options.rationale: During a seizure you protect the patient from injury and keep the airway open: guide a standing patient to the floor, turn to the side, protect the head, loosen tight clothing, clear the area, and time it. Afterward the patient stays side lying so secretions drain, you suction if needed, check airway and breathing, and reorient. Documentation covers onset, duration, the body parts involved, and the postictal state.

options.text: Loosen tight clothing and move nearby furniture away
options.rationale: During a seizure you protect the patient from injury and keep the airway open: guide a standing patient to the floor, turn to the side, protect the head, loosen tight clothing, clear the area, and time it. Afterward the patient stays side lying so secretions drain, you suction if needed, check airway and breathing, and reorient. Documentation covers onset, duration, the body parts involved, and the postictal state.

options.text: Hold the arms and legs still to prevent injury
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Restraining the limbs during a seizure causes injury rather than preventing it.

options.text: Insert an oral airway once the jaw relaxes
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Nothing goes in the mouth; an airway or tongue blade breaks teeth, injures the nurse, and can block the airway.

options.text: Note the time the seizure starts and how long it lasts
options.rationale: During a seizure you protect the patient from injury and keep the airway open: guide a standing patient to the floor, turn to the side, protect the head, loosen tight clothing, clear the area, and time it. Afterward the patient stays side lying so secretions drain, you suction if needed, check airway and breathing, and reorient. Documentation covers onset, duration, the body parts involved, and the postictal state.

options.text: Keep the patient side lying afterward and reorient
options.rationale: During a seizure you protect the patient from injury and keep the airway open: guide a standing patient to the floor, turn to the side, protect the head, loosen tight clothing, clear the area, and time it. Afterward the patient stays side lying so secretions drain, you suction if needed, check airway and breathing, and reorient. Documentation covers onset, duration, the body parts involved, and the postictal state.

options.text: Document the body parts involved and the postictal state
options.rationale: During a seizure you protect the patient from injury and keep the airway open: guide a standing patient to the floor, turn to the side, protect the head, loosen tight clothing, clear the area, and time it. Afterward the patient stays side lying so secretions drain, you suction if needed, check airway and breathing, and reorient. Documentation covers onset, duration, the body parts involved, and the postictal state.

questions.takeaway: Protect, side lying, time it; nothing in the mouth, nothing holding the limbs.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options feel protective. On seizure items, the options that sound most caring are the ones that cause injury.

questions.stem: A bottle of an unfamiliar cleaning solution has spilled on the floor of a patient's room. What should the nurse check to learn how to clean it up safely?

options.text: The manufacturer's label for the active ingredient only
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Knowing the ingredient does not tell you the hazards, PPE, cleanup, and first aid you need now.

options.text: The patient's allergy list
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Allergies matter for the patient, but they do not tell you how to handle the chemical.

options.text: The unit's housekeeping schedule
options.rationale: Institution as rationale A schedule does not supply hazard or cleanup information for this chemical.
