options.text: The safety data sheet for the product
options.rationale: For an unfamiliar chemical or spill, the SDS lists the hazards, the PPE to wear, how to clean up the spill, and first aid for exposure.

questions.takeaway: Unfamiliar chemical: check the SDS.
questions.strategy: Pick the source that answers all four needs at once: hazard, PPE, cleanup, first aid.

questions.stem: During a fire on a medical unit, patients in the room have been rescued and the alarm has been activated. The fire is too large to extinguish. Which action is correct?

options.text: Evacuate patients down the stairwell to the ground floor first
options.rationale: Near miss concept Evacuation moves horizontally first, to a safe area on the same floor, before moving between floors.

options.text: Prop the fire doors open so staff can move patients quickly
options.rationale: Near miss concept Open doors let smoke spread down the hall; containment means closing doors and windows.

options.text: Close doors, shut off oxygen if safe, and move patients horizontally
options.rationale: After rescue and alarm comes contain: close doors and windows and turn oxygen off if safe. When a fire cannot be extinguished, the E of RACE becomes evacuate, horizontally first.

options.text: Keep oxygen flowing to all patients until each one has been moved
options.rationale: Near miss concept Oxygen feeds a fire, so it is turned off if safe as part of containment.

questions.takeaway: Contain, then evacuate sideways before downward.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option breaks one piece of containment or evacuation; check every part of the correct option against RACE.

questions.stem: Which finding would be classified as a never event?

options.text: A readmission within 30 days for heart failure exacerbation
options.rationale: Near miss concept A quality and reimbursement measure, not a never event.

options.text: A stage 4 pressure injury that developed during the hospital stay
options.rationale: Never events, formally the serious reportable events, are preventable occurrences that should not happen in a hospital at all: wrong site surgery, a retained foreign object, an incompatible blood transfusion, and a hospital acquired stage 3 or 4 pressure injury. The test is preventability plus should never happen, not how sick the outcome makes the patient.

options.text: A patient who falls while ambulating with a gait belt and two staff members
options.rationale: Near miss concept A fall with appropriate precautions in place is an adverse event, not a never event.

options.text: Ventilator associated pneumonia in a patient intubated for six days
options.rationale: Near miss concept A health care associated infection. Serious, largely preventable, and not on the serious reportable events list.

questions.takeaway: Hospital acquired and stage 3 or 4 is the combination that makes a pressure injury a never event.
questions.strategy: Not every bad outcome is a never event. Look for preventable plus should never happen.

questions.stem: A patient develops a stage 3 pressure injury on day 6 of admission. The nurse reviews the record and finds a Braden score of 11 documented on admission, with no turning schedule and no support surface ordered. What does this represent?

options.text: A preventable harm to report so the system failure can be examined
options.rationale: A hospital acquired stage 3 or 4 pressure injury is on the serious reportable events list because it is preventable, and the record shows exactly how it was not prevented: the risk was identified and nothing followed from it. The useful question is why a score of 11 did not trigger a protocol, which is a system question. Naming one nurse ends the inquiry before it finds that answer.

options.text: An unavoidable complication of the patient's limited mobility on admission
options.rationale: Near miss concept Some injuries are genuinely unavoidable; one with an identified risk and no interventions is not.

options.text: A documentation gap rather than an actual gap in the care that was given
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting The missing turning schedule is missing care, not just missing charting.

options.text: An individual performance problem to address with the admitting nurse only
options.rationale: Near miss concept Ends the investigation at a person rather than at the process.

questions.takeaway: A risk score that triggers nothing is a system failure, not a charting failure.
questions.strategy: The option that blames an individual feels like accountability and prevents the next one.

questions.stem: A nurse notices that the same principle appears in fall prevention, restraint use, infection control and discharge teaching: the intervention chosen should accomplish the goal with the least interference in the patient's functioning. Which principle is this?

options.text: Patient centered care
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism True of all of it and not this specific rule.

options.text: Beneficence
options.rationale: Near miss concept The broader ethical principle underneath it, not the rule being described.

options.text: Least restrictive intervention
options.rationale: Least restrictive intervention is the thread: a bed alarm before a rail, a sitter before a restraint, a contact precaution before isolation of the person. It appears wherever a safety measure can also take something away from the patient, and exam items are built on it.

options.text: Standard precautions
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data One application, not the principle.

questions.takeaway: Choose the smallest intervention that achieves the goal.
questions.strategy: A question that lists several unrelated contexts is asking you to name the thread, not the context.

questions.topic: individual versus health care environment risk
questions.stem: Classify each risk for injury. An individual risk factor is one the patient brings. A health care environment risk comes from care itself or from the care setting.
questions.objective: individual versus health care environment risk

rows.text: A patient with hearing loss cannot follow spoken teaching about the call light
A patient cannot afford grab bars or a raised toilet seat at home
A patient believes falls only happen to frail people and declines help
An infusion pump malfunctions and runs a fluid at the wrong rate
A patient breathes fumes from a strong cleaning product used in the room
A patient develops a hematoma where a central line was inserted

questions.takeaway: The deciding question is where the risk comes from: would it still exist if the patient were at home and nobody were giving care? Hearing loss is a sensory and communication impairment the patient brings, so it is individual. Not being able to afford safety equipment is an economic resource problem, also individual. Believing falls only happen to other people is a lack of safety awareness, which lives in the patient. A pump that runs at the wrong rate is equipment related injury, a risk created by the care setting. Fumes from a cleaning product are chemical exposure, also from the setting. A hematoma at a line insertion site is procedure related injury: the procedure caused it, so it belongs to the health care environment. Individual risks travel with the patient; health care environment risks are created by the procedures, equipment, chemicals and hazards of care.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the risk would exist if no care were being given. The detail that sorts the hematoma is that the procedure created it, so it is not a patient trait even though it shows up on the patient's body.

questions.stem: The safety competency for nurses means reducing risk of harm through both system effectiveness and individual performance. Match each nursing action to the skill it shows.

rows.text: Scans the patient's wristband and the medication barcode before every dose
Follows a printed checklist during every central line dressing change
Tells the charge nurse that a bathroom floor tile is loose and lifting
Explains to the family why the bed alarm must stay on overnight
Joins a team review of a wrong dose event to redesign the order screen

questions.takeaway: Reducing reliance on memory means using technology or a standard tool so that safety does not depend on what a tired nurse recalls. Barcode scanning lets the system check the patient and the drug, and a printed checklist makes each step visible. Communicating hazards means telling the people who can act about a risk you see. A lifting tile goes to the charge nurse, and the reason for a bed alarm goes to the family, because the skill includes patients and families, not only staff. Analyzing errors and designing improvements means looking at why an error happened and changing the system, which is what a review that redesigns the order screen does. A safe nurse leans on tools instead of memory, speaks up about hazards to staff and families, and helps fix the system after an error.
questions.strategy: Ask what each action produces: a check that does not depend on memory, a message to someone who can act, or a change to the system. The detail that places the family row is that hazard communication includes patients and families, not only the team.

questions.topic: matching the intervention to the fall risk factor
questions.stem: Each patient below already has universal fall precautions in place. Choose the added intervention that targets each patient's own reason for falling.
questions.objective: matching the intervention to the fall risk factor
columns: Better lighting and glasses within reach

rows.text: Has cataracts and misjudged the distance to the chair this morning
rows.answer: Better lighting and glasses within reach

rows.text: Left reading glasses in a bag across the room and squints at the call light
rows.answer: Better lighting and glasses within reach

rows.text: Takes a diuretic and hurries to the bathroom several times each night
Has a urinary tract infection with a sudden urge to void many times a day
Feels the knees buckle on standing after six days in bed after surgery

answer.r1: Better lighting and glasses within reach
answer.r2: Better lighting and glasses within reach

questions.takeaway: Poor vision causes falls because the patient misjudges the room, so the fix is to make the room easier to see: good lighting and glasses where the patient can reach them. That fits both the patient with cataracts and the patient whose glasses are across the room. Urgency and frequency cause falls because the patient rushes to the bathroom, so scheduled toileting every 1 to 2 hours removes the rush. That fits both the diuretic and the infection. Weakness causes falls because reduced strength impairs balance, so the fix is hands on help with transfers and walking, not more time in bed. Reorientation answers confusion, and no patient here is confused, so that column is not used. Name why the patient would fall, then pick the intervention aimed at that reason.
questions.strategy: For each row ask what would happen in the moment of the fall: misjudging, rushing or buckling. The detail that rules out reorientation is that none of these patients is described as disoriented.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence: A fall in the hospital can cause serious injury, and it [[1]]. A fall that happens during a hospital stay is [[2]] by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. Even a fall that causes no injury can [[3]].

options.text: increases the length of stay
is an expected part of aging
leaves the plan of care unchanged
matters only when a bone breaks
not reimbursable
fully reimbursed
reimbursed only with an injury
reimbursed if documented
reduce the patient's confidence and independence
make the patient more careful and safer
be left out of the medical record
be handled without telling the provider

questions.takeaway: [1] increases the length of stay: an injury from a fall adds treatment and recovery time, so the patient stays longer. It is not an expected part of aging, it does change the plan, and harm is not limited to fractures. [2] not reimbursable: the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services treat a fall during a stay as preventable and do not pay for the care it causes, whether or not it is documented. [3] reduce the patient's confidence and independence: a patient who has fallen often becomes afraid to move, which leads to less activity and more weakness. Fear does not make a patient safer. Every fall is documented and the provider is notified, even with no injury. A fall costs the patient time, independence and confidence, and costs the hospital money that will not be paid back.
questions.strategy: Read each blank as a consequence. The detail that rules out the near miss in blank 3 is the phrase no injury: a fall without harm still changes how the patient moves afterward.

questions.topic: team roles in individualized fall prevention
questions.stem: A patient's fall risk comes from dizziness after each dose of a newly started medication. The nurse plans to monitor symptoms and assist with mobility. Which team member does the nurse work with to adjust when the dose is given?
questions.objective: team roles in individualized fall prevention

options.text: The physical therapist
options.rationale: Near miss concept Physical therapy is the partner for weakness, building strength and safe movement. It does not decide medication timing, which is the cause named here.

options.text: The assistive personnel
options.rationale: Near miss concept Assistive personnel help with mobility, toileting and lighting under the plan. Adjusting dose timing is a medication decision outside that role.

options.text: The pharmacist
options.rationale: Medication dizziness causes falls because side effects impair balance and coordination. The targeted plan is to monitor symptoms, adjust the timing of the dose, and assist with mobility. The pharmacist works with the nurse on timing, for example moving a dose so the peak effect does not come when the patient is likely to get up. Each other team member matches a different risk: physical therapy for weakness, assistive personnel for help with toileting and moving, and family for confusion.

options.text: A family caregiver
options.rationale: Near miss concept Family is the key partner when confusion is the cause, through reorientation and presence. Family cannot change when a dose is given.

questions.takeaway: Medication dizziness is solved with the pharmacist; weakness with physical therapy; confusion with family.
questions.strategy: Find the cause in the stem, then the person who can change that cause. The detail that rules out the near misses is the phrase adjust when the dose is given, which only a medication expert can address.

questions.stem: A patient can sit unsupported and bears some weight on both legs but cannot stand without help. Which equipment does the nurse use for the transfer from bed to chair?

options.text: A full body mechanical lift
options.rationale: Near miss concept The full body lift is for a patient who cannot sit unsupported; this patient can.

options.text: Standing equipment
options.rationale: Match the equipment to what the patient can do. Cannot sit unsupported: full body mechanical lift and enough staff. Bears some weight but cannot stand alone: standing equipment. Walks steadily: gait belt or standby help. Body mechanics still apply to every move, but they do not replace the equipment.

options.text: A gait belt with standby help
options.rationale: Near miss concept A gait belt or standby help is for a patient who walks steadily; this patient cannot stand alone.

options.text: Proper body mechanics with one other nurse lifting
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Manual lifting of a dependent adult exceeds what a spine can safely tolerate, however good the posture.

questions.takeaway: The patient's ability picks the equipment.
questions.strategy: Locate the patient on the ladder: sit, bear weight, walk. The two neighboring rungs are the near misses.

questions.stem: An assistive personnel reports that a patient was found sitting on the floor. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Have the assistive personnel take vital signs and report back
options.rationale: Correct but premature Delegable data collection, and it is not an injury assessment.

options.text: Ask the assistive personnel to help the patient back into bed right away
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Moves a possibly injured patient on an unlicensed assessment.

options.text: Go to the patient and assess for injury before anyone moves her
options.rationale: Assessment after a fall is the nurse's, and it happens before the patient is moved. Assistive personnel can stay with her and call for help; they cannot determine whether she is injured. Vital signs are useful and do not rule out a fracture or a head injury.

options.text: Start the occurrence report using the details reported so far
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Paperwork while the patient is on the floor.

questions.takeaway: The nurse goes to the patient. The assessment is not delegable and it comes before moving her.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options move or measure the patient before anyone has looked at her.

questions.stem: A nurse caring for an older adult at high fall risk plans to keep the patient in bed for the entire shift. How should the charge nurse respond?

options.text: The plan is appropriate as long as a bed alarm is also in place
options.rationale: Near miss concept An alarm tells you someone is already getting up. It does not make bedrest therapeutic.

options.text: Bedrest worsens the weakness behind falls; plan assisted mobility
options.rationale: Fall prevention is not keeping people in bed. Bedrest costs muscle mass within days, and a weaker patient falls harder when they finally do get up. The goal is safe movement: scheduled toileting, assistance with transfers, the right footwear, a bed in low position.

options.text: The plan is appropriate, because the fall risk score is high
options.rationale: Near miss concept A score tells you to individualize, not to immobilize.

options.text: The plan should add all four side rails for additional safety
options.rationale: Near miss concept Four raised rails is a restraint, and patients climb over them and fall farther.

questions.takeaway: The goal is safe mobility, not immobility.
questions.strategy: Any option that trades function for stillness is the wrong kind of safety.

questions.stem: A patient recovering from a stroke is at high fall risk and also at high risk for pressure injury and deconditioning. The family asks that she be kept in bed so she does not fall. What should the nurse explain?

options.text: A bed alarm will let her stay in bed safely for the whole stay
options.rationale: Near miss concept An alarm detects; it does not prevent, and it does not address deconditioning.

options.text: Bedrest is the safest option while her fall risk score stays high
options.rationale: Near miss concept Safest against one risk and worst against four others.

options.text: The family's preference decides the activity plan for her care
options.rationale: Near miss concept Family input matters and does not override a plan built on her clinical needs.

options.text: Bedrest trades one risk for several; plan assisted mobility
options.rationale: Every safety intervention has a cost, and the nursing skill is naming the trade. Bedrest prevents falls and produces pressure injury, deconditioning, pneumonia, clots and constipation, and the weakness it causes makes the eventual fall worse. The answer is mobility with safeguards: assistance, scheduled toileting, footwear, a low bed, therapy involvement.

questions.takeaway: Safety is not stillness. Name the trade out loud for the family.
questions.strategy: A bed alarm tells you someone is already getting up. It does not make bedrest therapeutic.

questions.stem: A patient begins having a generalized tonic clonic seizure in bed. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Move the patient to the floor to prevent a fall from the bed
options.rationale: Near miss concept Lifting someone mid seizure injures both of you. Lower the bed and pad instead.

options.text: Turn the patient to the side, protect the head and time the seizure
options.rationale: Side lying lets secretions drain and keeps the tongue forward. You protect the head, clear what is nearby, loosen anything tight and time it. You do not put anything in the mouth and you do not hold the limbs down, because both cause injury without shortening the seizure.

options.text: Insert a padded tongue blade to protect the airway
options.rationale: Near miss concept Breaks teeth and can obstruct the airway it is supposed to protect.

options.text: Restrain the extremities to prevent injury from the movements
options.rationale: Near miss concept Holding a convulsing limb is how fractures and dislocations happen.

questions.takeaway: Nothing in the mouth. Nothing holding the arms. Side lying and a clock.
questions.strategy: Two of the wrong options are old practice that is still taught by families and television.

questions.topic: restraint as a last resort in practice
questions.stem: A delirious patient has pulled out two intravenous lines and is trying to climb over the rail. A sitter is unavailable, the family cannot come in, and reorientation has not worked. The patient needs intravenous antibiotics for sepsis. What should the nurse do?
questions.objective: restraint as a last resort in practice

options.text: Ask the provider for a sedative instead, so restraints are avoided
options.rationale: Near miss concept A drug given to control behavior is a chemical restraint with the same rules.

options.text: Apply restraints now and obtain the order at the end of the shift
options.rationale: Near miss concept An emergency application is followed by an order promptly, not hours later.

options.text: Get an order for the least restrictive restraint; document and reassess
options.rationale: This is the situation restraints exist for: interference with treatment that cannot be safely interrupted, after alternatives have genuinely been tried and failed, with the failure documented. The least restrictive option that protects the line, an order, ongoing monitoring, and removal at the earliest point. A sedative ordered to control the behavior is a chemical restraint, so it is not a way around the decision.

options.text: Keep trying alternatives, since restraints are never used for confusion
options.rationale: Absolute language They have failed, and interference with critical treatment is an accepted indication.

questions.takeaway: Document which alternatives failed. That record is what makes the restraint defensible.
questions.strategy: The option that calls restraints never appropriate is absolute, and the sedative option is a restraint wearing a different name.

questions.stem: A patient at high fall risk says, "I have been walking on my own for 80 years, I do not need help to the bathroom." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ask his daughter to convince him to use the call light
options.rationale: Near miss concept Outsources a conversation that is yours, and he may resent it.

options.text: Tell him hospital policy requires staff assistance for all patients at risk of falling
options.rationale: Institution as rationale Policy as the reason gives him nothing to agree with.

options.text: Document that the patient refuses all fall precautions
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Records a disagreement instead of resolving it.

options.text: Explain why his risk is higher now and agree on a plan together
options.rationale: He is not being difficult; he is reasoning from a lifetime of evidence that he can walk. What he does not know is what changed: the new medication, the illness, the unfamiliar room, the line he is attached to. Name those and negotiate something he will actually do, because a plan he has not agreed to is a plan that fails at 2 in the morning.

questions.takeaway: Tell him what changed. He already knows he can walk.
questions.strategy: Policy and family pressure both skip the step where he understands the reason.

questions.stem: A nurse enters a room and finds a patient on the floor beside the bed. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Complete an occurrence report before the details are forgotten
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting The report happens, and after the patient is safe.

options.text: Stay with the patient and call for assistance
options.rationale: You do not leave a patient on the floor and you do not lift them until you know what is broken. Call for help, stay, assess for injury, then move with enough hands. Notify the provider, follow policy, reassess the prevention plan, document the event and complete the occurrence report. The report is a separate quality document and is never charted as part of the note.

options.text: Help the patient back into bed and then assess for injury
options.rationale: Correct but premature Moves a possibly fractured patient before anyone has looked.

options.text: Check the bed alarm to determine why it did not sound
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question That belongs in the post fall huddle, not to the patient on the floor.

questions.takeaway: Stay. Assess. Then move. Lifting first is how a hip fracture becomes a displaced hip fracture.
questions.strategy: Every other option takes you away from the patient or moves them before you know what is wrong.

questions.stem: A confused patient keeps pulling at his nasogastric tube. The nurse has reoriented him, moved him near the station and asked family to sit with him, and he is still pulling. What should the nurse do next?

options.text: Give a sedative to settle him before he dislodges the tube
options.rationale: Near miss concept A drug given to control behavior is a chemical restraint, not a way around the restraint rules.

options.text: Keep trying alternatives only, since restraints are never used to protect any tube
options.rationale: Absolute language They have already failed, and never is wrong: interference with critical treatment is one of the accepted reasons.

options.text: Get an order for the least restrictive restraint to protect the tube
options.rationale: Restraints come after alternatives have been tried and failed, and interfering with a treatment that cannot be safely interrupted is a legitimate reason. The order comes first except in an emergency. A sedative given to control behavior rather than to treat a condition is a chemical restraint and carries the same rules.

options.text: Apply soft wrist restraints now and get the order afterward
options.rationale: Near miss concept Right restraint, wrong order of operations. Applying first is for an emergency you are already in.

questions.takeaway: Alternatives first, then the least restrictive option, with an order.
questions.strategy: The question is not whether restraints are allowed. It is whether you have exhausted what comes before them.

questions.stem: A charge nurse assigns a newly licensed nurse four patients, including one receiving a continuous insulin infusion and one on a titrated vasoactive drip. The new nurse has not been oriented to titrated drips. What should she do?

options.text: Accept it and document that she raised a concern about it
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Records the concern and keeps the unsafe assignment.

options.text: Accept it, since refusing could be considered patient abandonment
options.rationale: Near miss concept Abandonment applies after you accept the patients, not to raising a competence gap.

options.text: Accept it and ask a colleague to keep an eye on the drip for her
options.rationale: Near miss concept An informal arrangement with no accountability, and the colleague has her own patients.

options.text: Tell the charge nurse she lacks orientation and ask for a change
options.rationale: Accepting an assignment you are not competent to perform is accepting the liability for it, and competence is part of scope. Raising it before the shift is neither refusal nor abandonment: abandonment is leaving patients you have already accepted. The constructive version names the specific gap and proposes a change, which is also what makes it fixable.

questions.takeaway: Competence is part of scope. Raising a gap before you accept is not abandonment.
questions.strategy: Two options accept the assignment with a workaround, which leaves her accountable for care she cannot provide.

questions.topic: targeting the cause of fall risk
questions.stem: An older adult started a new antihypertensive yesterday and reports feeling lightheaded each time when getting out of bed. Universal fall precautions are in place. Which added intervention best addresses this patient's fall risk?
questions.objective: targeting the cause of fall risk

options.text: Teach slow position changes and assist each time she gets up
options.rationale: Medication dizziness causes falls through an orthostatic drop or sedation, so the layer you add is slow position changes, assisted mobility, and a conversation with the pharmacist and provider about timing. Universal precautions apply to everyone; the added layer has to answer the cause named in the stem.

options.text: Place the call light within easy reach on the unaffected side
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Always true and already part of universal precautions, but it does not answer the dizziness that is causing this risk.

options.text: Set up scheduled toileting rounds every 1 to 2 hours
options.rationale: Near miss concept Scheduled toileting answers urgency or frequency, not a medication related drop on standing.

options.text: Keep the patient in bed until the new medication is stopped
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fall prevention means safe mobility, not bed rest; immobility worsens the weakness behind fall risk.

questions.takeaway: Answer the cause in the stem.
questions.strategy: Find the reason this patient is at risk, then pick the intervention that matches it. The universal precaution is the tempting distractor.

questions.stem: An assistive personnel applied a patient's ordered wrist restraint and tied it to the side rail. An hour later the assistive personnel reports that the fingers on that hand look pale and feel cool, while the other hand is pink and warm. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ask the assistive personnel to retie the strap to the bed frame and recheck in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Evaluating circulation and skin stays with the RN; a cool, pale hand is not a finding to hand back for a recheck.

options.text: Document the finding and the correction in the restraint flow sheet
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Charting comes after the patient's circulation has been assessed and the restraint corrected.

options.text: Have the assistive personnel offer fluids and toileting, then reassess at the next scheduled check
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Fluids and toileting are part of restraint care, but they do not address a hand that may be losing circulation.

options.text: Go to the bedside, assess circulation below the restraint, and secure the strap to the bed frame
options.rationale: Cool, pale fingers below a wrist restraint, with a pink, warm hand on the other side, is a circulation finding. The UAP may help apply a restraint and report changes, but the RN assesses the need and evaluates circulation and skin. The side rail tie is a second problem: moving the rail tightens the strap, so it must go to the bed frame.

questions.takeaway: A UAP report of a cool limb sends you to the bedside.
questions.strategy: Two problems sit in this stem. The one that can harm the patient now, circulation, is the priority, and it belongs to the RN.

questions.stem: The daughter of an older adult at high fall risk asks the nurse to put a vest restraint on the patient at night so the patient cannot get out of bed. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: “I will ask the provider for a vest order, since the fall risk score is high.”
options.rationale: Correct but premature Restraints are never used for routine fall prevention, so an order is not the next step at all.

options.text: “Restraints raise injury risk; let us use an alarm, toileting and a closer room.”
options.rationale: Restraints are never used for staff convenience, punishment, wandering, or routine fall prevention. They raise injury risk through escape attempts, agitation, and lost mobility. The answer for a high fall risk patient is an alternative that meets the need: a bed alarm, scheduled toileting, or closer observation.

options.text: “We can raise all four side rails instead, since rails are not a restraint.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept All four side rails up is a restraint, and a confused patient climbs over them and falls from higher.

options.text: “Hospital policy does not allow restraints, so there is nothing more to add.”
options.rationale: Institution as rationale Policy is not the reason, and the answer leaves the real risk unaddressed when alternatives exist.

questions.takeaway: A vest for fall risk is wrong every time.
questions.strategy: The family's worry is real, so the right response honors it with an alternative rather than refusing or complying.

questions.stem: A nurse hears a cry and finds a patient slumped against a bedside lamp, with a hand still touching the lamp's metal base. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Turn off the power to the lamp
options.rationale: When a patient receives a shock, you turn off the power before you touch the patient, then assess. Damaged equipment is taken out of service, labeled, and reported once the emergency is handled.

options.text: Pull the patient's hand away from the lamp
options.rationale: Correct but premature Touching the patient while the current is live can pass the shock to the nurse; the power goes off first.

options.text: Assess the patient's airway, breathing, and pulse
options.rationale: Correct but premature Assessment is the next step, after the power is off and it is safe to touch the patient.

options.text: Label the lamp as defective and report it to engineering
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Taking damaged equipment out of service is right, but it comes after the patient is safe.

questions.takeaway: Power off, then touch, then assess.
questions.strategy: Assessment usually comes first, but not when the scene itself is still dangerous to the rescuer.

questions.stem: A patient lives alone, walks without an aid, and manages all self care at home. The patient is admitted to an unfamiliar unit with pneumonia. The patient has an intravenous line and oxygen tubing and received a new sleep medication last night. Vital signs were taken every 4 hours overnight. Select all of the factors that raise this patient's risk of injury now that the patient is in the hospital.

options.text: The intravenous line and oxygen tubing
options.rationale: Hospitalization raises injury risk even in a patient who is fully independent at home. Tubes, lines and equipment are trip and tangle hazards whenever the patient moves. A new medication, especially a sleep medication, can cause drowsiness and poor balance. Broken sleep from overnight vital signs causes fatigue and can cloud thinking. An unfamiliar room and changed routine mean the patient does not know where the bathroom, light or furniture are. Acute illness itself lowers strength and oxygen reserve. Living alone and walking without an aid describe what the patient could do before admission; they are strengths and the baseline the nurse works to keep.

options.text: The new sleep medication given last night
options.rationale: Hospitalization raises injury risk even in a patient who is fully independent at home. Tubes, lines and equipment are trip and tangle hazards whenever the patient moves. A new medication, especially a sleep medication, can cause drowsiness and poor balance. Broken sleep from overnight vital signs causes fatigue and can cloud thinking. An unfamiliar room and changed routine mean the patient does not know where the bathroom, light or furniture are. Acute illness itself lowers strength and oxygen reserve. Living alone and walking without an aid describe what the patient could do before admission; they are strengths and the baseline the nurse works to keep.

options.text: Sleep broken by vital signs every 4 hours
options.rationale: Hospitalization raises injury risk even in a patient who is fully independent at home. Tubes, lines and equipment are trip and tangle hazards whenever the patient moves. A new medication, especially a sleep medication, can cause drowsiness and poor balance. Broken sleep from overnight vital signs causes fatigue and can cloud thinking. An unfamiliar room and changed routine mean the patient does not know where the bathroom, light or furniture are. Acute illness itself lowers strength and oxygen reserve. Living alone and walking without an aid describe what the patient could do before admission; they are strengths and the baseline the nurse works to keep.

options.text: Being in an unfamiliar room on a new routine
options.rationale: Hospitalization raises injury risk even in a patient who is fully independent at home. Tubes, lines and equipment are trip and tangle hazards whenever the patient moves. A new medication, especially a sleep medication, can cause drowsiness and poor balance. Broken sleep from overnight vital signs causes fatigue and can cloud thinking. An unfamiliar room and changed routine mean the patient does not know where the bathroom, light or furniture are. Acute illness itself lowers strength and oxygen reserve. Living alone and walking without an aid describe what the patient could do before admission; they are strengths and the baseline the nurse works to keep.

options.text: The acute infection that led to admission
options.rationale: Hospitalization raises injury risk even in a patient who is fully independent at home. Tubes, lines and equipment are trip and tangle hazards whenever the patient moves. A new medication, especially a sleep medication, can cause drowsiness and poor balance. Broken sleep from overnight vital signs causes fatigue and can cloud thinking. An unfamiliar room and changed routine mean the patient does not know where the bathroom, light or furniture are. Acute illness itself lowers strength and oxygen reserve. Living alone and walking without an aid describe what the patient could do before admission; they are strengths and the baseline the nurse works to keep.

options.text: Living alone before admission
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Living alone shows the patient has managed safely without help. It does not create a new risk inside the hospital, where staff are present.

options.text: Walking without an aid at home
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Walking without an aid is the patient's normal ability. It is the baseline the plan protects, not a source of risk.

questions.takeaway: A hospital stay adds new risks to a patient who was safe at home: equipment, new drugs, lost sleep, a strange room and acute illness.
questions.strategy: Sort each option into before admission or since admission. The detail that rules out the last two options is the phrase at home: those describe the baseline, not a new risk.

questions.stem: A patient admitted with heart failure started a diuretic today. The patient says, “At home I get up once a night to use the bathroom. I turn on a night light and hold the dresser on the way.” The nurse is building a safety plan with the patient. Which question should the nurse ask next?

options.text: “Would you like the bed alarm turned on before you sleep tonight?”
options.rationale: Correct but premature A bed alarm may end up in the plan, but choosing it now skips finding out what has changed. The plan has to fit the new limitation first.

options.text: “What feels different now about getting up than it does at home?”
options.rationale: Seeing safety through the patient's eyes means learning what the patient believes is safe, what the routines and normal abilities are at home, and what limitations are new. The patient has already described the home routine and the strategies that work there: a night light and something to hold. The missing piece is what is new. A diuretic started today will likely mean more trips to the bathroom and more urgency, which is a new fall risk the home routine was not built for. Asking what feels different invites the patient to name it, and the plan can then build on what already works at home.

options.text: “Do you know hospital policy says you must call for help to get up?”
options.rationale: Institution as rationale Quoting policy gives the patient a rule instead of a reason. It does not explore the patient's view of safety or what is new.

options.text: “Could a family member stay overnight to keep an eye on you?”
options.rationale: Correct but premature Involving family is part of safety planning, but asking for a sitter before knowing the new risk jumps to an intervention.

questions.takeaway: Learn the home routine and abilities, then find what is new; the plan bridges the two.
questions.strategy: Ask which part of the patient's picture is still missing. The detail that points to the key is that the patient has already described home habits, and the diuretic started today is the new limitation no one has asked about.

questions.topic: scoring a fall risk assessment tool
questions.stem: A nurse uses a fall risk tool. Recent falls: none in 12 months scores 2, one or more 3 to 12 months ago scores 4, one or more in the last 3 months scores 6, one or more in the last 3 months while an inpatient scores 8. Risk medications: none 1, one 2, two 3, more than two 4. Psychological: none 1, mild 2, moderate 3, severe 4. Mental test score: 9 to 10 scores 1, 7 to 8 scores 2, 5 to 6 scores 3, 4 or less scores 4. A total of 5 to 11 is low risk, 12 to 15 medium, and 16 to 20 high. The patient fell at home 6 weeks ago. Current medications are a diuretic, an antihypertensive and a hypnotic. The nurse rates the patient's depression as moderate. The mental test score is 8. What is the total score and risk level?
questions.objective: scoring a fall risk assessment tool

options.text: 15, medium risk
options.rationale: Score each item against its band. A fall at home 6 weeks ago is in the last 3 months but not as an inpatient, so it scores 6. Three listed risk medications are more than two, so they score 4. Moderate depression scores 3. A mental test score of 8 is mild impairment and scores 2. The total is 6 plus 4 plus 3 plus 2, which is 15, the top of the medium band. Each wrong total comes from one misread band. The score tells the nurse how much risk there is, but the plan still has to target the reasons: here the medications and the recent fall.

options.text: 17, high risk
options.rationale: Near miss concept This scores the fall as 8, but that band is for a fall while an inpatient. This fall happened at home, so it scores 6.

options.text: 14, medium risk
options.rationale: Near miss concept This scores the medications as two. A diuretic, an antihypertensive and a hypnotic are three, which is more than two and scores 4.

options.text: 11, low risk
options.rationale: Near miss concept This scores the fall as none in 12 months. A fall 6 weeks ago is within the last 3 months and scores 6.

questions.takeaway: Score every item by its exact band; one misread band can move a patient into the wrong risk level.
questions.strategy: Check the two easy misreads first. The detail that rules out 17 is the word home, and the detail that rules out 14 is that three medications are more than two.

questions.topic: assessing the cause of behavior before a restraint
questions.stem: A patient two days after shoulder surgery was calm this morning. Tonight the patient is restless, pulls at the intravenous line, and keeps pressing on the lower abdomen. The last void was 7 hours ago. Reorientation calms the patient for only a few minutes. What should the nurse do next?
questions.objective: assessing the cause of behavior before a restraint

options.text: Ask the provider for an order for soft wrist restraints
options.rationale: Correct but premature A restraint is a last resort after the cause is found and alternatives fail. The cause here has not been assessed yet.

options.text: Ask a family member to come and sit at the bedside
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Family presence is a good restraint alternative, but it will not relieve a full bladder, so the restlessness will continue.

options.text: Move the patient to a room near the nursing station
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Closer observation helps the nurse watch the patient, but it does not treat the unmet need that is driving the behavior.

options.text: Check the bladder for distention and help the patient void
options.rationale: Before using a restraint, the nurse asks why the patient is behaving this way. Common causes are pain, toileting needs, hunger, thirst, delirium, medication effects, fear, too much stimulation and an unfamiliar setting. Here the cues fit together: a new change in behavior, pressing on the lower abdomen, and no void for 7 hours. That points to urinary retention. Checking the bladder and helping the patient void treats the cause. Restraints, family presence and a room near the station all handle the behavior without fixing the need behind it.

questions.takeaway: Agitation is a symptom; find and treat the unmet need before restraining the patient.
questions.strategy: Look for the cue cluster that explains the behavior. The detail that rules out the alternatives is no void for 7 hours plus pressing on the lower abdomen, which names a need that only a bladder check addresses.

questions.topic: removing a restraint as early as possible
questions.stem: A patient was placed in soft wrist restraints yesterday for pulling at an endotracheal tube. The tube was removed this morning. The patient is now calm, oriented, and follows commands. The restraint order stays active until this evening. What should the nurse do?
questions.objective: removing a restraint as early as possible

options.text: Keep the restraints on until the order ends this evening
options.rationale: Institution as rationale An active order allows a restraint; it does not require one. The order end time is not a reason to keep restricting a patient who no longer needs it.

options.text: Keep them on tonight, since the patient is at high fall risk
options.rationale: Near miss concept Restraints are never used for routine fall prevention. Fall risk is handled with fall precautions, not by tying the patient down.

options.text: Remove the restraints now and keep monitoring the patient
options.rationale: Restraints are used only to prevent immediate harm when a patient cannot safely control their actions. The nurse keeps reassessing the need and removes the restraint as early as possible. The reason for this restraint was protecting the endotracheal tube, and the tube is gone. The patient is also calm, oriented and following commands, so the patient can now control their actions. The nurse removes the restraints now, follows facility policy for discontinuing them, and keeps monitoring.

options.text: Document that the patient is calm and continue restraint checks
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Recording that the patient is calm is accurate, but it leaves the patient restrained after the reason is gone.

questions.takeaway: When the reason for a restraint is gone, the restraint comes off; the order is a ceiling, not a schedule.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the reason for the restraint still exists. The detail that rules out keeping it is that the tube it protected was removed this morning.

questions.topic: individualized fall prevention for new confusion
questions.stem: A patient admitted with cellulitis of the arm was oriented this morning. At 2200 the patient is disoriented to place, says, “I need to go home and feed the dog,” and has tried to stand alone twice. The patient voided 30 minutes ago. Lying and standing blood pressures are stable, and the patient walked steadily with the nurse at supper. The family went home for the night. Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition they address, and 2 parameters to monitor.
questions.objective: individualized fall prevention for new confusion

options.text: Reorient the patient often and place familiar items in view
Call the family to talk with the patient or come to sit
Ask the provider for an order for a vest restraint
Start scheduled toileting every 1 to 2 hours overnight
Raise all four side rails so the patient cannot climb out
Confusion leading to unsafe attempts to get up
Urgency driving rushed trips to the bathroom
Medication dizziness affecting balance
Weakness that impairs balance on standing
Number of attempts to stand without help
Orientation to person, place and time
Fall risk score recalculated each shift
Hours spent in bed overnight
Amount of urine voided overnight

questions.takeaway: Condition: the new disorientation and the wish to go home explain the attempts to stand, so confusion leading to unsafe attempts to get up is the problem. Urgency is ruled out because the patient voided 30 minutes ago. Medication dizziness is ruled out by stable lying and standing pressures. Weakness is ruled out by the steady walk at supper. Actions: confusion is treated with frequent reorientation and familiar cues, and family presence is the partner the plan names for confusion, so calling the family fits. A vest restraint is never used for routine fall prevention and can increase agitation. Raising all four rails is itself a restraint and invites a climb over the rails. Scheduled toileting answers urgency, which this patient does not have. Parameters: the number of attempts to stand alone shows whether the unsafe behavior is decreasing, and orientation shows whether the confusion itself is improving. A recalculated score does not show whether these actions worked. Hours in bed would reward keeping the patient still, which is not the goal. Urine output tracks a problem the patient does not have. Treat confusion driven fall risk with reorientation and family, and judge success by fewer unsafe attempts and better orientation.
questions.strategy: Rule out each cause with its planted cue: the void 30 minutes ago, the stable standing pressure and the steady walk at supper leave confusion as the only cause.

questions.stem: A nurse presses over the tibia and leaves an indentation about 5 mm deep that is still visible more than a minute later. How should this be documented?

options.text: 1 plus pitting edema
options.rationale: Near miss concept 2 mm or less, and it springs back immediately rather than lasting a minute.

options.text: 4 plus pitting edema
options.rationale: Near miss concept 6 to 8 mm, with the dent lasting 2 to 5 minutes.

options.text: 3 plus pitting edema
options.rationale: The scale runs by depth and by how long the dent lasts. 1 plus is 2 mm or less and springs back right away. 2 plus is 2 to 4 mm and takes 10 to 15 seconds. 3 plus is 4 to 6 mm and stays more than a minute. 4 plus is 6 to 8 mm and can last 2 to 5 minutes. Grading matters because it is how you track whether the diuretic is working.

options.text: 2 plus pitting edema
options.rationale: Near miss concept 2 to 4 mm with a 10 to 15 second rebound, which is much faster than this.

questions.takeaway: The rebound time separates the grades more reliably than the depth does.
questions.strategy: Read both numbers. If a stem gives depth and duration, they should point to the same grade.

questions.stem: Select all of the bedside findings that indicate inadequate tissue perfusion.

options.text: New confusion or restlessness
options.rationale: You assess perfusion at the bedside with the brain, the skin and the kidneys, which is why those three keep appearing together. All three are more useful than the blood pressure, because a patient can compensate and hold a pressure while perfusion is already failing. The last two options describe a patient who is perfusing well.

options.text: Capillary refill longer than 3 seconds
options.rationale: You assess perfusion at the bedside with the brain, the skin and the kidneys, which is why those three keep appearing together. All three are more useful than the blood pressure, because a patient can compensate and hold a pressure while perfusion is already failing. The last two options describe a patient who is perfusing well.

options.text: Warm, dry skin with brisk capillary refill
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Evidence of good peripheral perfusion.

options.text: Urine output under 0.5 mL per kilogram per hour
options.rationale: You assess perfusion at the bedside with the brain, the skin and the kidneys, which is why those three keep appearing together. All three are more useful than the blood pressure, because a patient can compensate and hold a pressure while perfusion is already failing. The last two options describe a patient who is perfusing well.

options.text: A blood pressure of 118/72 in a patient whose baseline is 116/70
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data At baseline, and pressure is the last thing to fail anyway.

options.text: Cool, mottled extremities
options.rationale: You assess perfusion at the bedside with the brain, the skin and the kidneys, which is why those three keep appearing together. All three are more useful than the blood pressure, because a patient can compensate and hold a pressure while perfusion is already failing. The last two options describe a patient who is perfusing well.

questions.takeaway: Brain, skin, urine. All three tell you more than the blood pressure does.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options are normal findings, one of them a pressure at the patient's own baseline.

questions.stem: A nurse auscultating a patient with heart failure hears an extra low pitched sound just after S2, giving a gallop rhythm. What does this most likely represent?

options.text: A systolic murmur from turbulent flow across a stiff valve
options.rationale: Near miss concept A murmur is a whooshing sound across a period, not a discrete extra sound.

options.text: An S4, reflecting a stiff ventricle resisting atrial filling
options.rationale: Near miss concept Correct description of S4, and S4 lands just before S1, not after S2.

options.text: An S3, suggesting volume overload and ventricular failure
options.rationale: S3 comes right after S2, in early diastole, when blood rushes into a dilated ventricle that is already volume loaded with high filling pressures. In an adult it is a classic sign of fluid overload and failure. S4 comes just before S1, from the atrium pushing against a stiff, noncompliant ventricle, and is linked to hypertension and hypertrophy.

options.text: A pericardial friction rub from inflamed pericardial layers
options.rationale: Near miss concept Scratchy and triphasic, and it does not produce a gallop.

questions.takeaway: S3 follows S2 and means volume. S4 precedes S1 and means stiffness.
questions.strategy: The timing in the stem is the whole answer: just after S2.

questions.stem: A patient presents with chest pressure that began 90 minutes ago. The initial troponin is within normal limits. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: It points to stable angina rather than an acute coronary syndrome
options.rationale: Near miss concept Stable angina is defined by a predictable exertional pattern, not by one lab.

options.text: It rules out myocardial injury, so the patient can be reassured
options.rationale: Absolute language Treats a single value as definitive.

options.text: One normal value does not rule out infarction; serial levels are needed
options.rationale: Troponin takes time to rise after injury begins, so a level drawn early can be normal in a patient who is actively infarcting. That is why troponins are drawn in series. The timing in the stem, 90 minutes, is the clue.

options.text: It should be repeated only if the chest pressure comes back later
options.rationale: Near miss concept Makes serial testing conditional on symptoms rather than on protocol.

questions.takeaway: One normal troponin is a snapshot taken early, not a negative result.
questions.strategy: Any lab question that gives you the time since symptom onset is asking about the timing of the marker.

questions.stem: Which patient is most likely to have an S4 heart sound?

options.text: A patient in atrial fibrillation
options.rationale: Near miss concept An S4 comes from the atria contracting. In atrial fibrillation there is no organized atrial contraction, so there is no S4.

options.text: A patient with long standing hypertension
options.rationale: An S4 is the atria pushing blood into a stiff ventricle just before S1. Hypertension, MI and aging stiffen the ventricle. It is absent in atrial fibrillation.

options.text: A patient with mild dehydration
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dehydration does not stiffen the ventricle.

options.text: A healthy 19 year old athlete
options.rationale: Near miss concept An S3 can be normal in young people. An S4 suggests a stiff ventricle.

questions.takeaway: S4 means a stiff ventricle and needs an atrial kick.
questions.strategy: Ask what the sound needs to happen. An S4 needs organized atrial contraction.

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it suggests peripheral arterial disease or venous insufficiency.

rows.text: Aching and heaviness that improve with the legs elevated
A shallow ulcer at the medial ankle with heavy drainage
Calf cramping when walking that eases with rest
Shiny, hairless skin with thick toenails
Brown discoloration and edema of the lower legs
Pain that improves with the legs dangling

questions.takeaway: Arterial disease is poor flow in: claudication, pale shiny hairless skin, weak pulses, painful ulcers on the toes, relief with the legs down. Venous insufficiency is poor flow out: edema, brown skin, aching that improves with elevation, shallow draining ulcers at the medial ankle. Arterial: dangle the legs. Venous: elevate them.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the problem is getting blood in or getting blood out.

questions.stem: Which statement about the pulmonary vessels is accurate?

options.text: The pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood to the left atrium.
options.rationale: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins carry it toward the heart. The pulmonary vessels are the exception for oxygen: pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the lungs and pulmonary veins bring oxygenated blood to the left atrium.

options.text: The pulmonary arteries carry blood from the lungs toward the heart.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Arteries carry blood away from the heart, including the pulmonary arteries.

options.text: The pulmonary veins carry deoxygenated blood to the right atrium.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Deoxygenated blood returns to the right atrium through the vena cavae.

options.text: The pulmonary arteries carry oxygenated blood to the lungs.
options.rationale: Near miss concept The pulmonary arteries leave the right ventricle carrying deoxygenated blood to pick up oxygen.

questions.takeaway: Artery and vein describe direction, not oxygen.
questions.strategy: Define the vessel by direction first, then ask where the blood is coming from.

questions.stem: For each heart sound finding, indicate what it most likely represents.

rows.text: A scratchy sound that continues when the patient holds the breath
A new systolic murmur radiating to the left axilla after a myocardial infarction
S3 in a healthy 22 year old
S3 in a 78 year old with heart failure
S1 loudest at the apex
S2 loudest at the base

questions.takeaway: S1 (mitral and tricuspid closing) is loudest at the apex and S2 (aortic and pulmonic closing) at the base. An S3 is normal in children and young adults but signals heart failure or overload in older adults. A new murmur after an MI may mean papillary muscle rupture, and a rub that continues during breath holding is pericardial. The same sound can be normal at 22 and an emergency at 78.
questions.strategy: Read the age and the history in every row before deciding.

questions.stem: A patient is scheduled for an exercise stress test tomorrow morning. Select all correct instructions.

options.text: Do not eat or drink anything after midnight
options.rationale: Near miss concept An exercise test needs only a light meal up to 2 hours before. NPO applies to a drug stress test.

options.text: Take a hot shower right after the test to relax
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hot showers are avoided for 1 to 2 hours after because vasodilation can drop the blood pressure.

options.text: Wear comfortable walking shoes
options.rationale: Before a stress test: consent, rest the night before, a light meal up to 2 hours before, no caffeine, smoking or alcohol that day, a beta or calcium channel blocker held if ordered, and walking shoes.

options.text: Avoid caffeine on the day of the test
options.rationale: Before a stress test: consent, rest the night before, a light meal up to 2 hours before, no caffeine, smoking or alcohol that day, a beta or calcium channel blocker held if ordered, and walking shoes.

options.text: Do not smoke on the day of the test
options.rationale: Before a stress test: consent, rest the night before, a light meal up to 2 hours before, no caffeine, smoking or alcohol that day, a beta or calcium channel blocker held if ordered, and walking shoes.

options.text: Eat only a light meal up to 2 hours before
options.rationale: Before a stress test: consent, rest the night before, a light meal up to 2 hours before, no caffeine, smoking or alcohol that day, a beta or calcium channel blocker held if ordered, and walking shoes.

questions.takeaway: Exercise stress test: light meal, no caffeine, no smoking.
questions.strategy: Separate the exercise test from the drug test, which has NPO rules.

questions.stem: A nurse is applying a 5 lead cardiac monitor. Select all correct actions.

options.text: Place the red electrode on the right lower chest
options.rationale: Near miss concept Red goes on the left lower chest; green goes on the right lower chest.

options.text: Place the black electrode below the left clavicle
options.rationale: White on the right below the clavicle, black on the left below the clavicle, red on the left lower chest, green on the right lower chest, brown on the chest. Clip hair because shaving nicks raise infection risk, clean and dry the skin, avoid bone, change electrodes at least every 24 hours and keep alarms on with limits set to the patient.

options.text: Place electrodes over the sternum and ribs so they stay flat
options.rationale: Near miss concept Electrodes go on flat skin, not over bone.

options.text: Clip chest hair instead of shaving it
options.rationale: White on the right below the clavicle, black on the left below the clavicle, red on the left lower chest, green on the right lower chest, brown on the chest. Clip hair because shaving nicks raise infection risk, clean and dry the skin, avoid bone, change electrodes at least every 24 hours and keep alarms on with limits set to the patient.

options.text: Clean the skin with soap and water and dry it well
options.rationale: White on the right below the clavicle, black on the left below the clavicle, red on the left lower chest, green on the right lower chest, brown on the chest. Clip hair because shaving nicks raise infection risk, clean and dry the skin, avoid bone, change electrodes at least every 24 hours and keep alarms on with limits set to the patient.

options.text: Set the alarm limits for this patient
options.rationale: White on the right below the clavicle, black on the left below the clavicle, red on the left lower chest, green on the right lower chest, brown on the chest. Clip hair because shaving nicks raise infection risk, clean and dry the skin, avoid bone, change electrodes at least every 24 hours and keep alarms on with limits set to the patient.

options.text: Place the white electrode below the right clavicle
options.rationale: White on the right below the clavicle, black on the left below the clavicle, red on the left lower chest, green on the right lower chest, brown on the chest. Clip hair because shaving nicks raise infection risk, clean and dry the skin, avoid bone, change electrodes at least every 24 hours and keep alarms on with limits set to the patient.

questions.takeaway: White on the right, smoke over fire, snow over grass.
questions.strategy: Check every placement against the memory trick, then check the skin prep.

questions.stem: Place the structures in the order blood passes through them, starting from the body.

options.text: Right ventricle
Pulmonic valve
Lungs
Left atrium
Mitral valve
Left ventricle
Tricuspid valve
Right atrium

questions.takeaway: Blood returns from the body through the vena cavae to the right atrium, crosses the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle, leaves through the pulmonic valve to the lungs, returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, crosses the mitral valve to the left ventricle, and leaves through the aortic valve to the aorta. Right side to the lungs, left side to the body; each chamber has a valve on the way out.
questions.strategy: Alternate chamber and valve: atrium, AV valve, ventricle, semilunar valve.

questions.stem: A patient with new hypertension is having a history taken. Select all over the counter products or substances the nurse should ask about because they can raise blood pressure.

options.text: A daily multivitamin
options.rationale: Near miss concept A standard multivitamin does not raise blood pressure.

options.text: Acetaminophen
options.rationale: Near miss concept Acetaminophen does not raise blood pressure or hold fluid the way NSAIDs do.

options.text: Cocaine
options.rationale: Decongestants, diet pills, energy drinks, caffeine, cocaine and other stimulants raise blood pressure and heart rate. NSAIDs raise blood pressure, hold fluid and worsen heart failure.

options.text: Pseudoephedrine decongestants
options.rationale: Decongestants, diet pills, energy drinks, caffeine, cocaine and other stimulants raise blood pressure and heart rate. NSAIDs raise blood pressure, hold fluid and worsen heart failure.

options.text: Diet pills
options.rationale: Decongestants, diet pills, energy drinks, caffeine, cocaine and other stimulants raise blood pressure and heart rate. NSAIDs raise blood pressure, hold fluid and worsen heart failure.

options.text: Ibuprofen
options.rationale: Decongestants, diet pills, energy drinks, caffeine, cocaine and other stimulants raise blood pressure and heart rate. NSAIDs raise blood pressure, hold fluid and worsen heart failure.

options.text: Energy drinks
options.rationale: Decongestants, diet pills, energy drinks, caffeine, cocaine and other stimulants raise blood pressure and heart rate. NSAIDs raise blood pressure, hold fluid and worsen heart failure.

questions.takeaway: Always ask about over the counter drugs.
questions.strategy: Sort each item by mechanism: stimulant, fluid retention or neither.

questions.stem: The nurse palpates the point of maximal impulse at the 6th intercostal space, lateral to the midclavicular line. What does this suggest?

options.text: Right ventricular failure
options.rationale: Near miss concept The PMI reflects the left ventricle at the apex.

options.text: Dehydration
options.rationale: Near miss concept Volume status does not move the PMI.

options.text: An enlarged left ventricle
options.rationale: The PMI is normally at the left 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line. A PMI shifted left and down suggests the left ventricle has enlarged, as in heart failure.

options.text: A normal finding in an older adult
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem The PMI normally sits at the 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line. Shifting left and down is not a normal aging change.

questions.takeaway: A PMI shifted left and down means a big left ventricle.
questions.strategy: Compare the location in the stem with the expected landmark.

questions.stem: A nurse is auscultating the heart. Select all correct techniques.

options.text: Listen through the gown to keep the patient warm
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fabric muffles and distorts sounds. The stethoscope goes on bare skin.

options.text: Use the bell for S3, S4 and low pitched murmurs
options.rationale: APE to MAN: aortic, pulmonic, Erb point, tricuspid, mitral. The diaphragm picks up high pitched sounds and the bell low pitched ones. The step students drop is the bell at the apex with the patient turned left.

options.text: Use the diaphragm for S1 and S2
options.rationale: APE to MAN: aortic, pulmonic, Erb point, tricuspid, mitral. The diaphragm picks up high pitched sounds and the bell low pitched ones. The step students drop is the bell at the apex with the patient turned left.

options.text: Listen at the mitral area at the 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line
options.rationale: APE to MAN: aortic, pulmonic, Erb point, tricuspid, mitral. The diaphragm picks up high pitched sounds and the bell low pitched ones. The step students drop is the bell at the apex with the patient turned left.

options.text: Listen at the aortic area at the 2nd intercostal space, right sternal border
options.rationale: APE to MAN: aortic, pulmonic, Erb point, tricuspid, mitral. The diaphragm picks up high pitched sounds and the bell low pitched ones. The step students drop is the bell at the apex with the patient turned left.

options.text: Listen at the tricuspid area at the 2nd intercostal space, left sternal border
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is the pulmonic area. The tricuspid area is at the 4th intercostal space, left lower sternal border.

options.text: Turn the patient to the left side and listen at the apex with the bell
options.rationale: APE to MAN: aortic, pulmonic, Erb point, tricuspid, mitral. The diaphragm picks up high pitched sounds and the bell low pitched ones. The step students drop is the bell at the apex with the patient turned left.

questions.takeaway: APE to MAN, then the bell at the apex with the patient on the left side.
questions.strategy: Check each location against the APE to MAN map.

questions.stem: A patient returns from a cardiac catheterization through the femoral artery. Select all appropriate nursing actions.

options.text: Keep the affected leg straight
options.rationale: After a femoral cath: bed rest for 2 to 6 hours with the leg straight, head of bed 30 degrees or lower, site and distal pulses checked with every vital sign check, and fluids to flush the contrast.

options.text: Help the patient walk to the bathroom in 1 hour
options.rationale: Correct but premature Bed rest for 2 to 6 hours protects the arterial puncture site.

options.text: Encourage fluids
options.rationale: After a femoral cath: bed rest for 2 to 6 hours with the leg straight, head of bed 30 degrees or lower, site and distal pulses checked with every vital sign check, and fluids to flush the contrast.

options.text: Elevate the head of bed to 60 degrees for comfort
options.rationale: Near miss concept Raising the head flexes the hip and puts pressure on the femoral site.

options.text: Check the site and distal pulses with every vital sign check
options.rationale: After a femoral cath: bed rest for 2 to 6 hours with the leg straight, head of bed 30 degrees or lower, site and distal pulses checked with every vital sign check, and fluids to flush the contrast.

options.text: Keep the head of bed at 30 degrees or lower
options.rationale: After a femoral cath: bed rest for 2 to 6 hours with the leg straight, head of bed 30 degrees or lower, site and distal pulses checked with every vital sign check, and fluids to flush the contrast.

questions.takeaway: After a cath, the site and the pulses come before walking.
questions.strategy: Protect the puncture site and watch what is downstream of it.

questions.stem: A patient had a myocardial infarction 5 days ago and has new chest pain today. Which lab best detects a new injury?

options.text: Troponin
options.rationale: Near miss concept Troponin stays raised for 7 to 14 days after the first MI, so a new rise is hard to separate from the old one.

options.text: BNP
options.rationale: Near miss concept BNP shows ventricular stretch, not new muscle injury.

options.text: CK MB
options.rationale: CK MB clears in 2 to 3 days, so it is back to normal by day 5. A new rise points to a new injury such as a reinfarction.

options.text: Lipid panel
options.rationale: Near miss concept Lipids show risk, not injury.

questions.takeaway: CK MB clears fast, so it shows reinfarction.
questions.strategy: When a lab stays raised for days, it cannot show a second event in that window.

questions.stem: A patient with chest pain 1 hour ago has a normal troponin level. Which action should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Discharge the patient because a heart attack has been ruled out.
options.rationale: Absolute language Troponin rises over hours, so it may be normal early in an MI.

options.text: Repeat the troponin in 3 to 6 hours.
options.rationale: Troponin is the preferred, heart specific marker. It rises over hours and stays up for 7 to 14 days, so a normal level early does not rule out an MI and the test is repeated.

options.text: Order a CK MB because troponin is not specific to the heart.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Troponin is heart specific and is the preferred marker.

options.text: Draw a BNP to confirm the heart attack.
options.rationale: Near miss concept BNP reflects a stretched ventricle in heart failure, not heart muscle injury.

questions.takeaway: One normal troponin early does not rule out an MI.
questions.strategy: Consider timing. A marker that rises over hours cannot be trusted minutes after the event.

questions.stem: A patient with coronary artery disease develops chest pain when the heart rate rises to 128/min. Which explanation best accounts for this?

options.text: Coronaries fill in systole, and tachycardia shortens systole.
options.rationale: Near miss concept The coronaries fill during diastole, when the heart muscle relaxes and is not squeezing them shut.

options.text: A fast rate raises pressure, which damages the coronary walls.
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism This does not explain the sudden pain. The problem is less filling time with higher demand.

options.text: Coronaries fill in diastole, and tachycardia shortens diastole.
options.rationale: The coronary arteries fill during diastole. Tachycardia shortens diastole, reducing supply at the same time it raises the heart's demand, which can trigger angina.

options.text: A fast heart rate lowers the oxygen content of arterial blood.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Oxygen content depends on the lungs and hemoglobin, not heart rate.

questions.takeaway: Coronaries fill in diastole, so a fast rate starves the heart.
questions.strategy: Find the option that explains both supply and timing.

questions.stem: The nurse hears a high pitched, scratchy sound at the left sternal border. To tell whether it is a pericardial or pleural friction rub, what should the nurse do?

options.text: Palpate for a thrill over the area.
options.rationale: Near miss concept A thrill is felt with loud murmurs, not friction rubs.

options.text: Ask the patient to hold the breath and listen again.
options.rationale: A pericardial rub continues when the breath is held because the heart keeps beating. A pleural rub stops because the lungs stop moving. A pericardial rub is best heard with the patient leaning forward.

options.text: Count the apical pulse for a full minute.
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question The rate does not tell which layers are rubbing.

options.text: Turn the patient to the left side and listen with the bell.
options.rationale: Near miss concept That position brings out low pitched sounds such as S3 and S4.

questions.takeaway: Hold the breath: a pericardial rub keeps going, a pleural rub stops.
questions.strategy: Pick the action that removes one possible source of the sound.

questions.stem: A patient's blood pressure is 120/60 mm Hg. Which mean arterial pressure is correct?

options.text: 100 mm Hg
options.rationale: Near miss concept This weights the systolic pressure, which is backwards.

options.text: 60 mm Hg
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data This is just the diastolic pressure.

options.text: 90 mm Hg
options.rationale: Near miss concept This is the simple average of the two numbers. MAP counts the diastolic pressure twice.

options.text: 80 mm Hg
options.rationale: MAP = (systolic + 2 × diastolic) ÷ 3 = (120 + 120) ÷ 3 = 80 mm Hg. Diastole counts twice because the heart spends about two thirds of each cycle there.

questions.takeaway: Diastole counts twice in MAP.
questions.strategy: Write the formula before looking at the options.

questions.stem: A patient with peripheral arterial disease has pain in the feet at night. Which position should the nurse suggest?

options.text: Wear compression stockings at night.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Compression reduces flow into an already poorly perfused limb.

options.text: Dangle the legs over the side of the bed.
options.rationale: In arterial disease the problem is getting blood in. Gravity helps, so dangling the legs eases rest pain. Elevation and compression are for venous disease.

options.text: Cross the legs at the knees in bed.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Crossing the legs compresses vessels and reduces flow.

options.text: Raise both legs on two pillows at night in bed.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Elevation helps venous return but makes arterial flow worse.

questions.takeaway: Arterial: let gravity help blood flow in.
questions.strategy: Decide which direction blood needs to go, then pick the position that lets gravity help.

questions.stem: Two nurses count a patient's apical pulse at 118/min and radial pulse at 92/min at the same time. What does this finding mean?

options.text: The radial count was done wrong and should be repeated.
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data A difference between simultaneous counts is a real finding, not an error.

options.text: This is a normal apical to radial difference.
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Apical and radial rates should match.

options.text: The patient has a bounding, strong pulse.
options.rationale: Near miss concept A bounding pulse describes strength, not a difference between sites.

options.text: A pulse deficit of 26; some beats do not perfuse.
options.rationale: Two nurses count apical and radial pulses at the same time for a full minute. Apical minus radial equals the deficit. Any deficit means beats are not reaching the periphery, as in atrial fibrillation.

questions.takeaway: Apical minus radial equals the deficit.
questions.strategy: Subtract, then explain what a beat that is heard but not felt means.
