questions.stem: A patient's BNP has fallen from 1,240 to 380 pg/mL after 3 days of treatment for heart failure. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: The patient's heart failure has now fully resolved.
options.rationale: Absolute language BNP is still high. It is improving, not normal.

options.text: The ventricle is less stretched; treatment is working.
options.rationale: BNP is released when the ventricle is stretched. It is high in heart failure and falls with effective treatment.

options.text: The patient is now dehydrated from the diuretic.
options.rationale: Near miss concept A falling BNP shows less ventricular stretch, not dehydration.

options.text: The value shows the heart muscle has been injured.
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is troponin. BNP reflects stretch.

questions.takeaway: BNP tracks stretch. Falling BNP means treatment is working.
questions.strategy: Read the trend, not the single value.

questions.stem: A patient has a new murmur and a temperature of 38.9 °C. Which condition should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Infective endocarditis
options.rationale: A murmur is turbulent flow through a narrowed or leaky valve. A new murmur with fever suggests endocarditis, where organisms grow on the valve. It is reported.

options.text: Normal aging of the valves
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Aging can cause murmurs, but a new murmur with fever points to infection of the valve.

options.text: Papillary muscle rupture
options.rationale: Near miss concept That causes a new murmur after an MI, not with fever.

options.text: Pericarditis
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pericarditis causes a friction rub, not a murmur.

questions.takeaway: New murmur plus fever means endocarditis.
questions.strategy: Pair the new finding with the other cue in the stem.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a 79 year old patient. Select all findings that are expected age related changes.

options.text: An S3 heart sound with crackles
options.rationale: Near miss concept An S3 in an older adult points to fluid overload, not aging.

options.text: A new murmur with fever
options.rationale: Near miss concept A new murmur with fever suggests endocarditis.

options.text: A blood pressure drop when standing up
options.rationale: With age the arteries stiffen (isolated systolic hypertension, wide pulse pressure), the left ventricle stiffens (S4, less reserve, slower return of the heart rate), and baroreceptors become less sensitive (orthostatic drops). Expected does not mean untreated: high systolic pressure is still treated and falls are prevented.

options.text: An S4 heart sound
options.rationale: With age the arteries stiffen (isolated systolic hypertension, wide pulse pressure), the left ventricle stiffens (S4, less reserve, slower return of the heart rate), and baroreceptors become less sensitive (orthostatic drops). Expected does not mean untreated: high systolic pressure is still treated and falls are prevented.

options.text: A wide pulse pressure with a systolic pressure of 158 mm Hg
options.rationale: With age the arteries stiffen (isolated systolic hypertension, wide pulse pressure), the left ventricle stiffens (S4, less reserve, slower return of the heart rate), and baroreceptors become less sensitive (orthostatic drops). Expected does not mean untreated: high systolic pressure is still treated and falls are prevented.

options.text: Slower return of the heart rate after activity
options.rationale: With age the arteries stiffen (isolated systolic hypertension, wide pulse pressure), the left ventricle stiffens (S4, less reserve, slower return of the heart rate), and baroreceptors become less sensitive (orthostatic drops). Expected does not mean untreated: high systolic pressure is still treated and falls are prevented.

questions.takeaway: Expected with aging still needs a plan.
questions.strategy: For each finding, name the aging change that causes it. If none does, it is not expected.

questions.stem: A patient's blood pressure is 86/48 with a mean arterial pressure of 61. He is drowsy, his skin is cool and clammy, and the urine output has been 15 mL per hour for two hours. What is the nurse's priority action?

options.text: Place the patient in reverse Trendelenburg and reassess in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Near miss concept Wrong position for hypotension, and 30 minutes is too long.

options.text: Initiate a rapid response and establish intravenous access
options.rationale: A mean arterial pressure below about 60 to 65 with altered mental status, cool clammy skin and oliguria means organs are no longer being perfused. Three organ systems are already reporting failure. This is an escalation, not a confirmation exercise.

options.text: Obtain a urine specimen for culture and notify the provider of the low output
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Treats oliguria as an infection question rather than a perfusion one.

options.text: Recheck the blood pressure in the opposite arm to confirm the reading
options.rationale: Correct but premature Confirming a number the clinical picture has already confirmed.

questions.takeaway: Mean arterial pressure, not systolic, is what perfuses organs.
questions.strategy: When three systems are telling you the same thing, stop gathering and start escalating.

questions.stem: A nurse cannot palpate a pedal pulse on a patient four hours after a femoral angiogram. The foot is pale and cool and the patient reports new pain. A Doppler fails to detect a signal. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Notify the provider immediately and keep the limb at the level of the heart and warm
options.rationale: An absent pulse by Doppler is a medical emergency, and vascular surgery may be needed to restore perfusion. The limb is kept neutral and warm. Elevating it reduces arterial inflow, and massage risks dislodging thrombus.

options.text: Document the findings and include them in the next scheduled report
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting A delay the limb cannot afford.

options.text: Elevate the limb above the level of the heart to reduce swelling and recheck in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Near miss concept Correct for venous congestion, harmful in arterial occlusion.

options.text: Apply a warm compress and massage the calf to encourage circulation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Massage is contraindicated whenever thrombus is possible.

questions.takeaway: Absent by Doppler is not a weak pulse. It is an emergency.
questions.strategy: When an option would reduce flow to an already ischemic limb, it is wrong no matter how familiar it sounds.

questions.stem: A patient is 8 hours post operative. Over four hours the heart rate rises from 76 to 112 while the blood pressure moves from 124/76 to 118/74. The nurse recognizes that which statement best describes this pattern?

options.text: The stable blood pressure indicates that cardiac output is being maintained adequately
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Reads the compensation as the reassurance.

options.text: The findings are within expected post operative limits and warrant routine monitoring
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Normalizes a 36 beat trend.

options.text: Tachycardia is defending cardiac output, and a falling pressure would be a late sign
options.rationale: Cardiac output is heart rate times stroke volume. When stroke volume falls, the rate rises to defend output, which is why tachycardia is an early compensation and hypotension is a late one. By the time the pressure drops, compensation has already failed.

options.text: The rising heart rate most likely reflects post operative pain and should be treated as such
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pain does cause tachycardia, which is what makes this the common wrong answer.

questions.takeaway: A normal blood pressure is not reassurance when the heart rate is climbing to produce it.
questions.strategy: Ask what is doing the work to keep the number normal, and what happens when it runs out.

questions.stem: An 82 year old patient takes an antihypertensive and reports feeling dizzy after meals and on standing. Which instruction is most important?

options.text: "Stop the blood pressure medicine on days you feel dizzy."
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Changing the medication is the provider's decision. Stopping it suddenly can cause rebound hypertension.

options.text: "Dizziness is normal at your age, so nothing needs to change."
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem The cause may be expected, but the fall risk needs a plan.

options.text: "Drink a cup of coffee right after each meal to help raise your pressure."
options.rationale: Near miss concept This is not a safe or reliable way to prevent postural drops.

options.text: "Sit on the edge of the bed a moment, then stand up slowly."
options.rationale: Less sensitive baroreceptors make orthostatic and after meal drops common in older adults. Rising slowly and sitting first reduces falls.

questions.takeaway: Rise slowly, sit first.
questions.strategy: Choose the action the patient controls that prevents the fall.

questions.stem: The cardiac monitor shows a flat line for a patient who is sitting up in bed eating breakfast. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Start chest compressions right away
options.rationale: Near miss concept A patient who is sitting up and eating has a perfusing rhythm. Compressions would cause harm.

options.text: Call a code and bring the crash cart
options.rationale: Near miss concept The monitor is not the patient. This is almost certainly a lead problem.

options.text: Look at the patient and check the leads
options.rationale: Treat the patient, not the monitor. A talking, eating patient has a perfusing rhythm, so the nurse assesses the patient and then checks the leads and electrodes.

options.text: Prepare to give intravenous epinephrine
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope There is no arrest to treat.

questions.takeaway: Assess the patient before the equipment.
questions.strategy: When the monitor and the patient disagree, believe the patient.

questions.stem: Two hours after a femoral cardiac catheterization, a patient reports new back pain. The blood pressure is 90/56 mm Hg (it was 132/78), heart rate is 114/min and the groin dressing is dry. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: A retroperitoneal bleed
options.rationale: Back or flank pain with a falling blood pressure and rising heart rate after a femoral puncture suggests bleeding into the retroperitoneal space. A dry dressing does not rule it out. The nurse notifies the provider immediately.

options.text: No bleeding, because the dressing is dry
options.rationale: Absolute language A retroperitoneal bleed is hidden behind the abdomen, so the dressing stays dry.

options.text: A normal reaction to the contrast dye
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Contrast reactions cause itching, hives or wheezing, not back pain with signs of blood loss.

options.text: Muscle strain from lying flat
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Back pain with a falling blood pressure and rising heart rate points to hidden bleeding, not a strain.

questions.takeaway: A dry dressing does not rule out bleeding after a femoral cath.
questions.strategy: When vital signs show blood loss and nothing is visible, look for where blood can hide.

questions.stem: While auscultating a 76 year old patient with heart failure, the nurse hears an extra sound just after S2. Which action should the nurse take next?

options.text: Ask the patient to lean forward and hold the breath.
options.rationale: Near miss concept That position is used to hear a pericardial friction rub, not an S3.

options.text: Listen again with the diaphragm at the base.
options.rationale: Near miss concept An S3 is low pitched and heard best with the bell at the apex with the patient turned left.

options.text: Assess for crackles and weight gain, then report the finding.
options.rationale: An extra sound right after S2 is an S3, blood rushing into an overloaded ventricle. In an older adult with heart failure it suggests fluid overload, so the nurse looks for related cues and reports.

options.text: Document it as a normal finding for the patient's age.
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem An S3 after age 35 suggests a full, overloaded ventricle, not normal aging.

questions.takeaway: S3 in an older adult means fluid overload until proven otherwise.
questions.strategy: When a finding suggests a worsening condition, gather the related cues and report.

questions.stem: A patient has a cool, pale right foot with no pedal pulse and reports numbness that started an hour ago. What is the nurse's priority action?

options.text: Notify the provider immediately.
options.rationale: Pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis and poikilothermia (the 6 Ps) mean acute arterial occlusion. It is an emergency to report now, and the leg is not elevated.

options.text: Elevate the leg on pillows.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Elevation reduces arterial flow further into a limb that is already not getting blood.

options.text: Apply a warm compress to the foot.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Heat raises tissue demand in a limb without blood supply and can burn numb skin.

options.text: Recheck the pulse with a Doppler in 1 hour.
options.rationale: Correct but premature Every minute without flow risks permanent damage. This needs immediate reporting.

questions.takeaway: A cool, pale, pulseless limb is an emergency.
questions.strategy: When blood supply is cut off, the priority is the person who can restore it.

questions.stem: A patient is 6 hours after cardiac surgery. The blood pressure has fallen from 118/74 to 86/70 mm Hg, the neck veins are distended with the head of bed at 45 degrees, and the heart sounds are muffled. The systolic pressure drops 16 mm Hg during inspiration. Complete the bow tie.

options.text: Place the patient flat with the legs raised and recheck in an hour
Increase the IV rate to keep the vein open
Prepare for pericardiocentesis
Notify the provider immediately
Give a diuretic for the distended neck veins
Left sided heart failure
Hypovolemia from bleeding
Pneumothorax
Cardiac tamponade
Daily weight
Urine specific gravity
Heart sounds and neck veins
Blood pressure and pulse pressure
Serum potassium

questions.takeaway: Low blood pressure, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds are the Beck triad, and a systolic drop of more than 10 mm Hg on inspiration is a paradoxical pulse. Fluid in the pericardial sac squeezes the heart so it cannot fill. It is an emergency; the provider drains the sac. Beck triad: low BP, JVD, muffled heart sounds.
questions.strategy: Distended neck veins rule out simple bleeding. Pick the condition that explains every cue.

questions.stem: A patient 4 hours after surgery has a heart rate that has climbed from 84 to 112/min, cool clammy skin and new restlessness. Blood pressure is 118/76 mm Hg. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: Postoperative anxiety, with a normal pressure showing good circulation
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data The pressure is normal because the body is compensating. A falling blood pressure is a late sign.

options.text: Postoperative pain that should be treated now with the ordered analgesic
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Pain can raise the heart rate but does not explain cool clammy skin with restlessness.

options.text: Expected findings after surgery that need routine monitoring only
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A rising heart rate with vasoconstriction is a warning, not the expected course.

options.text: Compensation for low volume; a normal pressure does not mean stable
options.rationale: When volume falls, baroreceptors fire the sympathetic system. The heart rate rises first, vessels constrict (cool, pale skin), the kidneys hold water (low urine) and the patient turns restless. Blood pressure falls late.

questions.takeaway: A rising heart rate, restlessness and falling urine come before the blood pressure drops.
questions.strategy: If blood pressure is the only normal number, ask what the other cues show.

questions.stem: A patient's left calf is swollen, warm, red and tender. The right calf is normal. Which action is correct?

options.text: Keep the patient from massaging the leg; report it.
options.rationale: One sided calf swelling, warmth, redness and pain suggest a deep vein thrombosis. The nurse prevents massage and reports it, because the clot can travel to the lungs.

options.text: Apply compression stockings to both legs right now.
options.rationale: Correct but premature Compression is for prevention. A suspected clot is reported first.

options.text: Massage the calf gently to improve its circulation.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Massage can dislodge a clot, which can travel to the lungs.

options.text: Have the patient walk to see whether the pain eases.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Walking does not test for a clot and delays reporting.

questions.takeaway: Suspected DVT: no massage, report.
questions.strategy: When a finding could break loose and travel, choose the option that keeps it still.

questions.stem: Which assessment provides the most reliable indication that a patient with heart failure is retaining fluid?

options.text: Daily weight on the same scale at the same time
options.rationale: Weight is the most reliable indicator of fluid change because it captures fluid that is not yet visible. Edema lags and requires several liters before it appears, jugular distention is position and observer dependent, and intake and output records miss insensible losses and depend on complete charting.

options.text: The 24 hour intake and output totals for the day
options.rationale: Near miss concept Valuable, and only as complete as the charting.

options.text: The presence and height of jugular venous distention
options.rationale: Near miss concept Useful and highly dependent on position and examiner.

options.text: The depth of pitting edema in both lower legs
options.rationale: Near miss concept Visible, intuitive and late.

questions.takeaway: A gain of about 1 kg, which is 2.2 lb, in 24 hours is a liter of fluid, not fat.
questions.strategy: Reliability questions reward the measure with the fewest ways to be wrong.

questions.stem: Classify each finding by the side of the heart that has failed.

rows.text: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea and frothy sputum
Jugular venous distention with increased abdominal girth
A weight gain of 1.4 kg overnight
Bilateral crackles that do not clear with coughing

questions.takeaway: The left ventricle pumps into the body, so when it fails the backup goes into the lungs: dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, crackles, frothy sputum. The right ventricle pumps into the lungs, so when it fails the backup goes into the systemic veins: neck veins, liver, ascites, dependent edema. Weight gain belongs to both, which is why daily weight is the most reliable single indicator. Left backs up into the lungs, right backs up into the body. Weight catches either one first.
questions.strategy: Trace where the failing ventricle was supposed to send the blood. The backup goes upstream from there.

questions.stem: Select all of the self management instructions for a patient with heart failure.

options.text: Report increasing shortness of breath, new swelling or needing more pillows to sleep
options.rationale: The whole plan turns on one number he measures himself, which is why same time, same scale and after voiding matter. Needing more pillows is orthopnea and he should recognize it by name. Self adjusting a diuretic is prescribing, and 500 mL is far below any prescribed restriction and would cause prerenal injury.

options.text: Weigh yourself at the same time each morning after voiding
options.rationale: The whole plan turns on one number he measures himself, which is why same time, same scale and after voiding matter. Needing more pillows is orthopnea and he should recognize it by name. Self adjusting a diuretic is prescribing, and 500 mL is far below any prescribed restriction and would cause prerenal injury.

options.text: Report a gain of 2 to 3 pounds in a day or 5 in a week
options.rationale: The whole plan turns on one number he measures himself, which is why same time, same scale and after voiding matter. Needing more pillows is orthopnea and he should recognize it by name. Self adjusting a diuretic is prescribing, and 500 mL is far below any prescribed restriction and would cause prerenal injury.

options.text: Restrict all fluids to under 500 mL daily
options.rationale: Near miss concept Far below any usual restriction and enough to cause kidney injury.

options.text: Limit sodium as prescribed and read labels
options.rationale: The whole plan turns on one number he measures himself, which is why same time, same scale and after voiding matter. Needing more pillows is orthopnea and he should recognize it by name. Self adjusting a diuretic is prescribing, and 500 mL is far below any prescribed restriction and would cause prerenal injury.

options.text: Double the diuretic dose on days when the weight is up
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Some patients have a provider authorized sliding scale; self doubling is not it.

questions.takeaway: Teach him the number that makes him pick up the phone. Without it, teaching is just information.
questions.strategy: One wrong option has him prescribing and the other invents a restriction.

questions.stem: A patient reports two weeks of worsening fatigue and shortness of breath climbing stairs. He sleeps on three pillows now, up from one. His weight is up 4 kg. Heart rate 104, blood pressure 148/92, respirations 24, oxygen saturation 92 percent. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Community acquired pneumonia with early sepsis developing
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pneumonia does not explain orthopnea that has progressed from one to three pillows with a 4 kg weight gain, and no fever or sputum is described.

options.text: Anxiety with hyperventilation and air hunger
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Anxiety does not cause weight gain, orthopnea and a low saturation.

options.text: Anemia causing exertional shortness of breath
options.rationale: Near miss concept Anemia can cause exertional dyspnea but not orthopnea with fluid weight gain.

options.text: New or worsening heart failure with congestion
options.rationale: The positional detail is the one that decides it. Needing three pillows instead of one is orthopnea, which is specific to pulmonary congestion: lying flat redistributes fluid into the lungs. Add four kilograms, which is four liters, and a two week course, and this is heart failure. Pneumonia comes on over days with fever and a cough, and anemia does not add weight.

questions.takeaway: Ask how many pillows. The change in that number is one of the most specific histories in cardiology.
questions.strategy: The weight gain is the second clue, and it is the one students skip past looking for a temperature.

questions.stem: Which task related to daily weights can the nurse assign to assistive personnel?

options.text: Deciding whether the weight change needs to be reported
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Interpreting the weight is the nurse's responsibility.

options.text: Teaching the patient when to call the provider about weight gain
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Teaching stays with the nurse.

options.text: Weighing the patient and recording the result
options.rationale: Assistive personnel can weigh and record. The nurse interprets the weight, teaches and reports.

options.text: Adjusting the diuretic based on the weight
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Changing a dose is outside the scope of both assistive personnel and the nurse without an order.

questions.takeaway: Assistive personnel weigh; the nurse interprets.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the task needs judgment. If it does, it stays with the nurse.

questions.stem: Complete the statement about heart failure drugs.
questions.sentence: Beta blockers block the [[1]], ACE inhibitors and ARBs block the [[2]], and diuretics [[3]].

options.text: immune response
renin angiotensin system
sympathetic drive
calcium channels
sympathetic drive
renin angiotensin aldosterone system
strengthen the heart's squeeze
raise the potassium
remove the extra fluid

questions.takeaway: Low output triggers the sympathetic system and RAAS, which add volume and resistance. Beta blockers block sympathetic drive, ACE inhibitors and ARBs block RAAS, and diuretics remove fluid. Each core drug undoes one compensation.
questions.strategy: Match each drug class to the compensation it reverses.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a patient how to weigh at home. Select all correct instructions.

options.text: Weigh only when the ankles look swollen
options.rationale: Near miss concept Edema appears late. Daily weights catch fluid earlier.

options.text: Weigh at the same time each morning
options.rationale: Daily weights are taken at the same time each morning, after voiding and before breakfast, on the same scale and in the same clothing, and logged.

options.text: Use the same scale each day
options.rationale: Daily weights are taken at the same time each morning, after voiding and before breakfast, on the same scale and in the same clothing, and logged.

options.text: Weigh after voiding and before breakfast
options.rationale: Daily weights are taken at the same time each morning, after voiding and before breakfast, on the same scale and in the same clothing, and logged.

options.text: Keep a written log of each weight
options.rationale: Daily weights are taken at the same time each morning, after voiding and before breakfast, on the same scale and in the same clothing, and logged.

options.text: Weigh after breakfast so the reading is consistent
options.rationale: Near miss concept Weighing before breakfast avoids adding food and drink to the reading.

options.text: Wear the same type of clothing
options.rationale: Daily weights are taken at the same time each morning, after voiding and before breakfast, on the same scale and in the same clothing, and logged.

questions.takeaway: Same time, same scale, same clothes.
questions.strategy: Keep every instruction that removes a source of variation.

questions.stem: Select all signs of digoxin toxicity.

options.text: Increased appetite
options.rationale: Near miss concept Toxicity causes anorexia.

options.text: Confusion
options.rationale: Digoxin toxicity causes anorexia, nausea, vomiting, blurred or yellow vision, confusion, bradycardia and new irregular beats.

options.text: Bradycardia
options.rationale: Digoxin toxicity causes anorexia, nausea, vomiting, blurred or yellow vision, confusion, bradycardia and new irregular beats.

options.text: Tachycardia with a strong regular pulse
options.rationale: Near miss concept Digoxin slows the heart. Toxicity brings bradycardia and new irregular beats.

options.text: Anorexia
options.rationale: Digoxin toxicity causes anorexia, nausea, vomiting, blurred or yellow vision, confusion, bradycardia and new irregular beats.

options.text: Nausea and vomiting
options.rationale: Digoxin toxicity causes anorexia, nausea, vomiting, blurred or yellow vision, confusion, bradycardia and new irregular beats.

options.text: Blurred or yellow vision
options.rationale: Digoxin toxicity causes anorexia, nausea, vomiting, blurred or yellow vision, confusion, bradycardia and new irregular beats.

questions.takeaway: Digoxin toxicity: gut, eyes, brain, slow heart.
questions.strategy: Group the signs by system and check each against the drug's action.

questions.stem: Why does a patient with heart failure retain sodium and water?

options.text: The kidneys have been damaged by the diuretic therapy.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Retention starts before any diuretic.

options.text: The patient is eating far too much salt in the diet.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Diet can worsen it, but the body retains sodium even on a restricted diet.

options.text: The liver has stopped making enough albumin to hold fluid.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Low albumin is not the main cause of retention in heart failure.

options.text: Low cardiac output activates RAAS, which holds sodium.
options.rationale: Low output triggers the sympathetic system and RAAS. Both help briefly, then add volume and resistance. Beta blockers block sympathetic drive, ACE inhibitors and ARBs block RAAS, and diuretics remove fluid.

questions.takeaway: Each core drug undoes one of the body's compensations.
questions.strategy: Name the mechanism, then match it to the drug that blocks it.

questions.stem: For each finding in a patient with heart failure, indicate whether it is more typical of left sided or right sided failure.

rows.text: Jugular venous distention
Crackles at the lung bases
Needs three pillows to sleep
Wakes up at night gasping for breath
Swelling of the ankles and sacrum
Enlarged, tender liver

questions.takeaway: Left sided failure backs fluid into the lungs: dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, crackles and pink frothy sputum. Right sided failure backs fluid into the body: JVD, dependent edema, weight gain, ascites and an enlarged liver. Left is Lungs, Right is the Rest.
questions.strategy: Ask where the fluid has backed up to: the lungs or the body.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure starts spironolactone. Which instruction is correct?

options.text: Eat extra bananas and oranges each day.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Spironolactone keeps potassium, so extra potassium can push the level too high.

options.text: Avoid salt substitutes and potassium pills.
options.rationale: Spironolactone blocks aldosterone and keeps potassium. Salt substitutes are potassium chloride, so they and supplements are avoided unless ordered.

options.text: Expect your potassium level to drop.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Spironolactone raises potassium.

options.text: Take it at bedtime to avoid urinating.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Diuretics are taken in the morning to avoid nocturia.

questions.takeaway: Spironolactone keeps potassium.
questions.strategy: Decide which direction the drug moves potassium before reading the options.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure walks in the hallway with the nurse. Select all findings that mean the nurse should stop the activity.

options.text: The patient reports dizziness
options.rationale: Activity stops and is reported for a heart rate rise of more than 20 beats per minute, a systolic drop of more than 20 mm Hg, dyspnea, chest pain, dizziness, a saturation below 90% or fatigue into the next day.

options.text: Systolic pressure falls from 128 to 104 mm Hg
options.rationale: Activity stops and is reported for a heart rate rise of more than 20 beats per minute, a systolic drop of more than 20 mm Hg, dyspnea, chest pain, dizziness, a saturation below 90% or fatigue into the next day.

options.text: Respiratory rate rises from 16 to 20/min
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A small rise in breathing rate with activity is expected.

options.text: SpO2 falls to 88%
options.rationale: Activity stops and is reported for a heart rate rise of more than 20 beats per minute, a systolic drop of more than 20 mm Hg, dyspnea, chest pain, dizziness, a saturation below 90% or fatigue into the next day.

options.text: The patient reports chest pain
options.rationale: Activity stops and is reported for a heart rate rise of more than 20 beats per minute, a systolic drop of more than 20 mm Hg, dyspnea, chest pain, dizziness, a saturation below 90% or fatigue into the next day.

options.text: Heart rate rises from 74 to 102/min
options.rationale: Activity stops and is reported for a heart rate rise of more than 20 beats per minute, a systolic drop of more than 20 mm Hg, dyspnea, chest pain, dizziness, a saturation below 90% or fatigue into the next day.

options.text: Heart rate rises from 74 to 86/min
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A rise of 12 beats per minute is an expected response to walking.

questions.takeaway: A rise of more than 20 beats per minute means stop.
questions.strategy: Calculate each change and compare it with the stop criteria.

questions.stem: A patient with dyspnea has a BNP of 48 pg/mL. What does this suggest?

options.text: The patient is dehydrated and needs IV fluids.
options.rationale: Near miss concept BNP is not a hydration marker.

options.text: The patient has severe, decompensated heart failure that needs aggressive diuresis now.
options.rationale: Near miss concept A BNP below 100 pg/mL argues against heart failure.

options.text: The dyspnea more likely has a lung cause than a cardiac one.
options.rationale: BNP is released by stretched ventricles. A level above 100 pg/mL supports heart failure, and a normal BNP points to a lung cause of dyspnea.

options.text: The patient has had a recent myocardial infarction.
options.rationale: Near miss concept BNP reflects ventricular stretch, not muscle death.

questions.takeaway: BNP separates cardiac from lung dyspnea.
questions.strategy: Compare the value with the threshold, then decide which organ it points to.

questions.stem: A 79 year old patient with long standing hypertension has heart failure symptoms. The ejection fraction is 58%. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: The patient has systolic failure with a weak squeeze.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Systolic failure has an ejection fraction below 40%.

options.text: Heart failure is ruled out, because the fraction is normal.
options.rationale: Absolute language A normal ejection fraction does not rule out heart failure.

options.text: The normal fraction means the symptoms come from the lungs.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Diastolic failure gives the same symptoms as systolic failure.

options.text: A stiff ventricle can cause failure with preserved fraction.
options.rationale: HFpEF (diastolic failure) is a stiff wall that cannot relax to fill, with an ejection fraction of 50% or more, often in older adults with long standing hypertension. HFrEF (systolic failure) is a weak squeeze with an ejection fraction below 40%.

questions.takeaway: A normal ejection fraction does not rule out heart failure.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the problem is squeezing or filling.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure has gained 1.6 kg since yesterday and has new bilateral crackles. His blood pressure is 86/50 and heart rate is 118. The ordered furosemide is due. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the furosemide and start a fluid bolus to support the pressure
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pushes fluid into lungs that are already wet while removing it elsewhere.

options.text: Hold the furosemide and notify the provider about the hypotension
options.rationale: The weight and the crackles say too much fluid, and the pressure and the rate say the circulation is failing to deliver it, which is cardiogenic rather than simply congested. Diuresing a patient at 86/50 can drop the pressure into organ injury. This is the situation where you stop and get help rather than follow the order, and the answer may be an inotrope before any diuretic.

options.text: Give the furosemide, because the weight gain confirms fluid overload
options.rationale: Near miss concept Treats one half of the picture and ignores the half that can kill him.

options.text: Give half of the furosemide dose and then recheck the blood pressure
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Altering a prescribed dose is outside nursing scope.

questions.takeaway: Fluid overload with hypotension is not a diuretic problem. It is a pump problem.
questions.strategy: Half a dose is not a nursing option, and the bolus treats the pressure by worsening the congestion.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure has gained 1.4 kg since yesterday. Select all of the assessment findings that would support left sided failure specifically.

options.text: A cough productive of frothy sputum
options.rationale: Left sided failure backs up into the lungs, producing dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, crackles and frothy sputum. Right sided failure backs up into the body, producing jugular venous distention, dependent edema, hepatomegaly, ascites and increased abdominal girth.

options.text: Crackles in the bilateral lung bases
options.rationale: Left sided failure backs up into the lungs, producing dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, crackles and frothy sputum. Right sided failure backs up into the body, producing jugular venous distention, dependent edema, hepatomegaly, ascites and increased abdominal girth.

options.text: Increased abdominal girth
options.rationale: Near miss concept Right sided. Ascites is the liver and gut congesting.

options.text: Jugular venous distention
options.rationale: Near miss concept Right sided. A real heart failure finding in the wrong chamber.

options.text: Dependent pitting edema of the ankles
options.rationale: Near miss concept Right sided. Blood backs up into the legs, not the lungs.

options.text: Waking at night short of breath and needing to sit up
options.rationale: Left sided failure backs up into the lungs, producing dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, crackles and frothy sputum. Right sided failure backs up into the body, producing jugular venous distention, dependent edema, hepatomegaly, ascites and increased abdominal girth.

questions.takeaway: Left backs up into the lungs. Right backs up into the rest of the body.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding by where the fluid went, not by how serious it sounds.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure says, "I will take my enalapril and my valsartan together every morning." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the patient to take them at different times of day.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Spacing them does not make the combination safe.

options.text: Clarify the order; an ACE inhibitor and ARB are not combined.
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors and ARBs both block RAAS. They are never combined. Sacubitril valsartan is never given within 36 hours of an ACE inhibitor dose.

options.text: Document the statement in the patient's teaching record.
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Documentation does not prevent harm.

options.text: Reinforce that taking both in the morning is correct.
options.rationale: Near miss concept The combination raises the risk of high potassium, low blood pressure and kidney injury.

questions.takeaway: Never an ACE inhibitor and an ARB together.
questions.strategy: Recognize the two drug classes by their endings: pril and sartan.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure weighs 74.2 kg this morning and weighed 72.8 kg yesterday morning. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Report the weight gain to the provider.
options.rationale: One kilogram is about 1 L of fluid. A gain of 2 to 3 lb in a day or 5 lb in a week is reported. Weight shows fluid before edema does.

options.text: Document the weight as stable.
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting A 1.4 kg gain overnight is about 1.4 L of fluid.

options.text: Check the ankles for edema and report only if pitting is present.
options.rationale: Near miss concept An adult can hold 4 to 7 L before pitting appears. Weight is more sensitive.

options.text: Recheck the weight tomorrow before reporting.
options.rationale: Correct but premature A gain of 1.4 kg (about 3 lb) in a day meets the threshold to call now.

questions.takeaway: Weight beats edema.
questions.strategy: Convert the weight change to pounds or liters and compare with the threshold.

questions.stem: A patient taking digoxin reports nausea, poor appetite and seeing yellow halos. The apical pulse is 54/min. Which lab result should the nurse check first?

options.text: Serum potassium
options.rationale: Anorexia, nausea, vomiting, blurred or yellow vision, confusion and bradycardia suggest digoxin toxicity. Low potassium raises toxicity, so the potassium is checked with the digoxin level. The dose is held for an apical pulse below 60.

options.text: Serum sodium
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sodium does not drive digoxin toxicity the way potassium does.

options.text: White blood cell count
options.rationale: Near miss concept The symptoms are toxicity, not infection.

options.text: Hemoglobin
options.rationale: Near miss concept Anemia does not explain these symptoms.

questions.takeaway: Low potassium raises digoxin toxicity.
questions.strategy: When a drug becomes toxic, look for the electrolyte that changes its effect.

questions.stem: A patient is due for IV furosemide. The potassium level is 3.1 mEq/L. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the furosemide and recheck the potassium tomorrow.
options.rationale: Correct but premature Furosemide lowers potassium further, raising the risk of dysrhythmias.

options.text: Hold the dose and notify the provider about the low potassium.
options.rationale: Loop diuretics lower potassium. Low potassium causes weakness, cramps and dysrhythmias and raises digoxin toxicity. A potassium of 3.1 is reported before the dose.

options.text: Give the furosemide quickly to finish before the next lab draw.
options.rationale: Near miss concept IV furosemide is pushed slowly to prevent hearing damage.

options.text: Give the furosemide with a glass of orange juice.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Juice will not correct a potassium of 3.1 quickly enough.

questions.takeaway: Check potassium before furosemide or digoxin.
questions.strategy: Ask what the drug will do to the abnormal lab.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure suddenly has severe dyspnea, crackles throughout both lungs and pink frothy sputum. The blood pressure is 158/92 mm Hg. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Call the rapid response team from the bedside
Position in high Fowler with the legs down
Give IV furosemide after a blood pressure check
Apply oxygen and titrate to an SpO2 above 90%
Reassess SpO2, respiratory rate, crackles and urine output

questions.takeaway: Positioning with the legs down reduces venous return. Oxygen follows, then the nurse calls for help without leaving the room. Prescribed drugs come after a blood pressure check, and the patient is reassessed. Position and oxygen first; the diuretic takes time.
questions.strategy: The quickest actions that change breathing come before drugs that need a line and time.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure asks whether a salt substitute is a good idea. Which response is best?

options.text: Yes, salt substitutes are always safe on a low sodium diet.
options.rationale: Absolute language Salt substitutes are potassium chloride, which can be dangerous with spironolactone, ACE inhibitors or ARBs.

options.text: Use it only on vegetables.
options.rationale: Near miss concept The risk is the potassium, not the food.

options.text: No, you must never use any seasoning.
options.rationale: Absolute language Lemon, herbs and spices are encouraged for flavor.

options.text: Check with your provider first, because salt substitutes contain potassium.
options.rationale: Patients ask before using a salt substitute because it is potassium chloride. Lemon, herbs and spices add flavor without sodium.

questions.takeaway: Salt substitutes are potassium.
questions.strategy: Ask what is actually in the substitute.

questions.stem: A nurse receives report on four patients with heart failure. Which patient should the nurse see first?

options.text: A patient with crackles higher than last shift and new confusion
options.rationale: New or worsening findings outrank stable ones. Crackles climbing and new confusion mean worsening failure and poor perfusion.

options.text: A patient asking the nurse for a copy of the low sodium menu
options.rationale: Near miss concept This is a teaching need, not an urgent one.

options.text: A patient with a potassium of 3.6 mEq/L due for furosemide
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data The potassium is acceptable.

options.text: A patient with 1+ ankle edema that has been present for months
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Stable, long standing edema is not a change.

questions.takeaway: New and worsening beats stable and familiar.
questions.strategy: Rank by change from baseline.

questions.stem: An older adult on IV furosemide twice daily is newly confused. The lungs are clear, weight is down 3 kg in 2 days, blood pressure is 92/56 mm Hg, heart rate is 108/min and the urine is scant and dark. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Worsening heart failure
options.rationale: Near miss concept Worsening failure would bring crackles and weight gain, not clear lungs and weight loss.

options.text: A stroke
options.rationale: Near miss concept The cluster of low weight, low pressure and dark urine points to volume loss.

options.text: Dehydration from overdiuresis
options.rationale: Clear lungs, falling weight, low blood pressure, tachycardia and scant dark urine on a diuretic mean dehydration. The nurse holds the next dose and calls with the full cluster.

options.text: Expected confusion from hospitalization
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem New confusion is a change that needs an explanation.

questions.takeaway: Read the cluster, not the diagnosis label.
questions.strategy: Before assuming the known disease is worse, check whether the cues point the other way.

questions.stem: A nurse uses teach back with a patient going home with heart failure. Select all statements that show understanding.

options.text: I will avoid ibuprofen.
options.rationale: MAWDS: medications as prescribed with no NSAIDs, activity within limits, daily weight, diet with sodium about 2 to 3 g, and symptoms that get a call the same day. The step people drop is the S: calling instead of waiting out a bad week.

options.text: If I feel worse for a few days, I will wait until my next appointment.
options.rationale: Near miss concept New or worse symptoms get a call that day.

options.text: I will call if I need more pillows to breathe at night.
options.rationale: MAWDS: medications as prescribed with no NSAIDs, activity within limits, daily weight, diet with sodium about 2 to 3 g, and symptoms that get a call the same day. The step people drop is the S: calling instead of waiting out a bad week.

options.text: I will read labels for sodium.
options.rationale: MAWDS: medications as prescribed with no NSAIDs, activity within limits, daily weight, diet with sodium about 2 to 3 g, and symptoms that get a call the same day. The step people drop is the S: calling instead of waiting out a bad week.

options.text: I will check my ankles for swelling instead of weighing myself.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Weight shows fluid before ankle swelling does.

options.text: If I gain 3 lb by tomorrow, I will call the clinic.
options.rationale: MAWDS: medications as prescribed with no NSAIDs, activity within limits, daily weight, diet with sodium about 2 to 3 g, and symptoms that get a call the same day. The step people drop is the S: calling instead of waiting out a bad week.

questions.takeaway: The step people drop is symptoms: call the same day.
questions.strategy: Keep statements that act early and drop any that wait.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure starts carvedilol and says, "I feel more tired since I started this pill. Should I stop it?" Which response is best?

options.text: "Do not stop it; tiredness is common early and the dose rises slowly."
options.rationale: Beta blockers in heart failure are started at a very low dose and raised slowly. Patients may feel more tired the first weeks. They are never stopped suddenly.

options.text: "Feeling more tired means your heart failure is getting worse."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fatigue is expected early. Worsening failure would show weight gain or more dyspnea.

options.text: "Take it every other day for now to reduce the tiredness."
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Changing the schedule is not the patient's or nurse's decision.

options.text: "Yes, you should stop it right away if it is making you that tired."
options.rationale: Absolute language Beta blockers are never stopped suddenly.

questions.takeaway: Never stop a beta blocker suddenly.
questions.strategy: Reject any answer that changes the dose without the provider.

questions.stem: A patient in acute pulmonary edema has a blood pressure of 84/50 mm Hg. Which position change is correct?

options.text: Flat with the legs raised to support the blood pressure
options.rationale: Near miss concept Lying flat would worsen the breathing.

options.text: High Fowler with the legs dangling, as for any edema
options.rationale: Absolute language Legs down reduces venous return and would drop a low pressure further.

options.text: Upright without dangling the legs, to protect venous return
options.rationale: The step people drop is the blood pressure check. Legs down is for pulmonary edema when the pressure allows; a low pressure changes the plan. The blood pressure decides.

options.text: Prone, to improve ventilation of the dependent lung areas
options.rationale: Near miss concept Prone is not used for acute pulmonary edema.

questions.takeaway: The blood pressure decides the legs.
questions.strategy: When a standard action has a condition, check whether the stem meets it.

questions.stem: Select all of the lifestyle measures the nurse should teach a patient with newly diagnosed hypertension.

options.text: Aim for regular moderate aerobic activity most days
options.rationale: Hypertension is asymptomatic, which is why both wrong options are the two beliefs that cause patients to stop treatment. A normal reading means the medication is working, not that it is no longer needed, and there are no reliable warning symptoms, which is the entire reason it is called a silent disease.

options.text: Reduce sodium intake and read labels for hidden sodium
options.rationale: Hypertension is asymptomatic, which is why both wrong options are the two beliefs that cause patients to stop treatment. A normal reading means the medication is working, not that it is no longer needed, and there are no reliable warning symptoms, which is the entire reason it is called a silent disease.

options.text: Take the medication even when the blood pressure reads normal
options.rationale: Hypertension is asymptomatic, which is why both wrong options are the two beliefs that cause patients to stop treatment. A normal reading means the medication is working, not that it is no longer needed, and there are no reliable warning symptoms, which is the entire reason it is called a silent disease.

options.text: Limit alcohol and stop tobacco use
options.rationale: Hypertension is asymptomatic, which is why both wrong options are the two beliefs that cause patients to stop treatment. A normal reading means the medication is working, not that it is no longer needed, and there are no reliable warning symptoms, which is the entire reason it is called a silent disease.

options.text: Expect symptoms to warn you when the pressure is dangerously high
options.rationale: Near miss concept There are no reliable warning symptoms, which is the point of monitoring.

options.text: Stop the medication once the pressure is consistently normal
options.rationale: Near miss concept The pressure is normal because of the drug.

questions.takeaway: A normal pressure on medication is the medication working. It is not permission to stop.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options are patient beliefs rather than nursing errors, and they are what the teaching exists to correct.

questions.stem: Select all of the laboratory findings that increase this patient's cardiovascular risk.

options.text: Triglycerides of 310 mg/dL
options.rationale: Low density lipoprotein deposits in the wall, so high is bad. High density lipoprotein carries it away, so low is bad and high is protective. Triglycerides above 150 add risk. High sensitivity C reactive protein reflects vascular inflammation, which is part of how plaque becomes unstable. An undetectable troponin means no current myocardial injury.

options.text: A troponin that is undetectable
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Rules out current injury; it says nothing about long term risk and does not raise it.

options.text: High density lipoprotein of 68 mg/dL
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Protective. A high HDL lowers risk, which is why direction matters more than the word high.

options.text: An elevated high sensitivity C reactive protein
options.rationale: Low density lipoprotein deposits in the wall, so high is bad. High density lipoprotein carries it away, so low is bad and high is protective. Triglycerides above 150 add risk. High sensitivity C reactive protein reflects vascular inflammation, which is part of how plaque becomes unstable. An undetectable troponin means no current myocardial injury.

options.text: Low density lipoprotein of 168 mg/dL
options.rationale: Low density lipoprotein deposits in the wall, so high is bad. High density lipoprotein carries it away, so low is bad and high is protective. Triglycerides above 150 add risk. High sensitivity C reactive protein reflects vascular inflammation, which is part of how plaque becomes unstable. An undetectable troponin means no current myocardial injury.

options.text: High density lipoprotein of 32 mg/dL
options.rationale: Low density lipoprotein deposits in the wall, so high is bad. High density lipoprotein carries it away, so low is bad and high is protective. Triglycerides above 150 add risk. High sensitivity C reactive protein reflects vascular inflammation, which is part of how plaque becomes unstable. An undetectable troponin means no current myocardial injury.

questions.takeaway: The only lipid where a high number is good news is HDL.
questions.strategy: One option is a protective value and one is a normal value. Both are there to see whether you read the direction.

questions.stem: A patient has a lower leg ulcer. The surrounding skin is shiny and hairless, the foot is cool, pedal pulses are difficult to palpate, and the pain is worse when the leg is elevated. What does this indicate, and what is the nursing implication?

options.text: Cellulitis; apply warm compresses and keep the leg elevated
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would be warm, red and spreading, with elevation easing it.

options.text: Venous insufficiency; elevate the limb and apply compression stockings
options.rationale: Near miss concept The right treatment for the opposite problem, and dangerous here.

options.text: Lymphedema; begin manual lymphatic drainage and wrap the leg
options.rationale: Near miss concept Lymphedema is nonpitting swelling without these arterial signs.

options.text: Arterial insufficiency; avoid elevating or compressing the limb
options.rationale: Pain that worsens with elevation is the discriminator: raising the limb makes gravity work against an already inadequate arterial supply. Shiny hairless skin, coolness and absent pulses fit the same picture. Venous ulcers are the opposite, with edema, warmth, and pain relieved by elevation, and they are treated with compression, which in an arterial limb can cause necrosis.

questions.takeaway: Elevation helps a venous leg and hurts an arterial one. Ask what position relieves the pain.
questions.strategy: Compression on the wrong leg is how a limb is lost, so this discrimination matters more than most.

questions.stem: Which statement about primary (essential) hypertension is accurate?

options.text: It can be stopped once the pressure returns to the normal range.
options.rationale: Absolute language A normal reading on treatment means the treatment works. It is not a cure.

options.text: It has no single cause and is usually managed for life.
options.rationale: Primary hypertension is the most common form, has no single cause, cannot be cured and is controlled with lifestyle plus drugs, usually for life. Secondary hypertension has a findable cause that can be treated.

options.text: It is rare compared with secondary hypertension in adults.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Primary hypertension is the most common type.

options.text: It is cured once the underlying cause has been removed.
options.rationale: Near miss concept That describes secondary hypertension.

questions.takeaway: Primary is controlled, not cured.
questions.strategy: Ask whether a cause exists. If none, it cannot be removed.

questions.stem: Complete the statement about potassium and blood pressure medications.
questions.sentence: Hydrochlorothiazide tends to [[1]] potassium, so the patient should [[2]]. Lisinopril tends to [[3]] potassium, so the patient should avoid [[4]].

options.text: raise
not change
lower
limit potassium rich foods
eat more potassium rich foods
stop the drug when the level falls
not change
lower
raise
calcium rich foods
salt substitutes and potassium supplements
all fruits and vegetables

questions.takeaway: Thiazide and loop diuretics lower potassium, so patients eat more potassium. ACE inhibitors, ARBs and spironolactone raise it, so patients limit potassium supplements and salt substitutes. Both extremes cause dysrhythmias. Potassium runs two ways depending on the drug.
questions.strategy: Decide the direction of each drug first, then the advice follows.

questions.stem: A patient takes losartan. Select all instructions that are correct.

options.text: Take a potassium supplement daily
options.rationale: Near miss concept ARBs raise potassium, so supplements are avoided unless ordered.

options.text: Avoid salt substitutes unless they are ordered
options.rationale: ARBs act like ACE inhibitors with less cough. They still raise potassium, can cause angioedema and first dose hypotension, and require monitoring of potassium and creatinine. They are never combined with an ACE inhibitor.

options.text: Rise slowly when standing up
options.rationale: ARBs act like ACE inhibitors with less cough. They still raise potassium, can cause angioedema and first dose hypotension, and require monitoring of potassium and creatinine. They are never combined with an ACE inhibitor.

options.text: Expect potassium and creatinine to be checked
options.rationale: ARBs act like ACE inhibitors with less cough. They still raise potassium, can cause angioedema and first dose hypotension, and require monitoring of potassium and creatinine. They are never combined with an ACE inhibitor.

options.text: Add lisinopril if the pressure stays high
options.rationale: Near miss concept An ACE inhibitor and an ARB are never combined.

options.text: Report swelling of the lips, tongue or throat
options.rationale: ARBs act like ACE inhibitors with less cough. They still raise potassium, can cause angioedema and first dose hypotension, and require monitoring of potassium and creatinine. They are never combined with an ACE inhibitor.

questions.takeaway: ARBs still raise potassium.
questions.strategy: For each instruction, ask which way the drug moves potassium.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing the carotid pulses. Which technique is correct?

options.text: Palpate firmly with the thumb.
options.rationale: Near miss concept The thumb has its own pulse and firm pressure reduces flow.

options.text: Palpate one carotid artery at a time.
options.rationale: Carotid arteries are palpated one at a time, never both, because pressing both can reduce blood flow to the brain.

options.text: Palpate both carotid arteries at the same time to compare.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pressing both at once can reduce blood flow to the brain.

options.text: Massage the carotid to find the pulse.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Massage can stimulate the vagus nerve and slow the heart.

questions.takeaway: One carotid at a time.
questions.strategy: Reject any technique that could cut off blood to the brain.

questions.stem: For each blood pressure reading in an adult, indicate the correct category.

rows.text: 128/82 mm Hg
118/76 mm Hg
136/92 mm Hg
126/78 mm Hg

questions.takeaway: Classify by the higher stage reached by either number. 128/82 is stage 1 because the diastolic is 80 or above. 136/92 is stage 2 because a diastolic of 90 or more is enough. A systolic of 180 or more is crisis range. Either number can push a reading into a higher stage.
questions.strategy: Classify each number separately and take the higher category.

questions.stem: A patient with diabetes starts atenolol. Select all correct teaching points.

options.text: Expect your blood glucose to rise on this drug
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is a thiazide effect.

options.text: Do not stop this drug suddenly
options.rationale: Beta blockers are never stopped suddenly because of rebound hypertension, angina or MI. They mask the tremor and tachycardia of hypoglycemia while sweating remains, so patients with diabetes check their glucose when they feel unwell.

options.text: This drug can hide the shakiness and racing pulse of low blood glucose
options.rationale: Beta blockers are never stopped suddenly because of rebound hypertension, angina or MI. They mask the tremor and tachycardia of hypoglycemia while sweating remains, so patients with diabetes check their glucose when they feel unwell.

options.text: Check your glucose if you feel sweaty or unwell
options.rationale: Beta blockers are never stopped suddenly because of rebound hypertension, angina or MI. They mask the tremor and tachycardia of hypoglycemia while sweating remains, so patients with diabetes check their glucose when they feel unwell.

options.text: Take it only on days your pressure is high
options.rationale: Near miss concept Antihypertensives are taken every day, not as needed.

options.text: Rise slowly when standing up
options.rationale: Beta blockers are never stopped suddenly because of rebound hypertension, angina or MI. They mask the tremor and tachycardia of hypoglycemia while sweating remains, so patients with diabetes check their glucose when they feel unwell.

questions.takeaway: Beta blockers mask the warning signs of low glucose.
questions.strategy: Keep teaching that protects against the drug's two big dangers: stopping it and hiding a low.

questions.stem: A nurse uses a cuff that is too small for a patient's arm. How will this affect the reading?

options.text: The systolic will be high and the diastolic low.
options.rationale: Near miss concept A small cuff raises both readings.

options.text: The reading will be accurate if the arm is at heart level.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Arm position matters, but it does not correct the error from a small cuff.

options.text: The reading will be falsely low.
options.rationale: Near miss concept A cuff that is too large reads falsely low.

options.text: The reading will be falsely high.
options.rationale: A small cuff needs more pressure to compress the artery, so it reads falsely high. Correct technique uses the right cuff size, the patient seated with feet flat, the arm at heart level and at least two readings.

questions.takeaway: Too small a cuff reads too high.
questions.strategy: Picture the cuff squeezing a too large arm: it takes more pressure.

questions.stem: Place the steps in the development of atherosclerosis in order.

options.text: LDL enters the wall and macrophages become foam cells
Collagen covers the fatty streak and narrows the lumen
Injury to the inner lining from hypertension, smoking or high LDL
The fibrous cap ruptures and a clot forms

questions.takeaway: Injury to the lining comes first. LDL enters and is swallowed by macrophages, which become foam cells (the fatty streak). A fibrous cap forms and narrows the lumen. If the cap ruptures, platelets stick and a clot forms in minutes. Slow narrowing causes effort pain. Rupture causes ACS.
questions.strategy: Start with the injury that lets LDL in and end with the event that causes a sudden blockage.

questions.stem: Which food choice best fits a low sodium diet for a patient with hypertension?

options.text: Grilled chicken with fresh vegetables and brown rice
options.rationale: Processed food, canned soup, deli meat and takeout carry most sodium. The optimal goal is below 1,500 mg a day. Fresh, unprocessed foods fit the DASH pattern.

options.text: Canned chicken noodle soup with saltine crackers
options.rationale: Near miss concept Canned soup is one of the highest sodium foods.

options.text: Takeout vegetable fried rice with a side of soy sauce
options.rationale: Near miss concept Restaurant and takeout food carries much of the sodium in the diet.

options.text: A deli turkey sandwich on whole wheat with mustard
options.rationale: Near miss concept Deli meats are processed and high in sodium.

questions.takeaway: Most sodium hides in processed and takeout food.
questions.strategy: Ask which option is made from fresh ingredients.

questions.stem: Select all findings that fit a hypertensive crisis.

options.text: New confusion
options.rationale: Hypertensive crisis is 180/120 mm Hg or higher, often with severe headache, blurred vision, chest pain, dyspnea, confusion or a nosebleed. Stopping drugs is a common trigger.

options.text: Blood pressure 196/124 mm Hg
options.rationale: Hypertensive crisis is 180/120 mm Hg or higher, often with severe headache, blurred vision, chest pain, dyspnea, confusion or a nosebleed. Stopping drugs is a common trigger.

options.text: Chest pain
options.rationale: Hypertensive crisis is 180/120 mm Hg or higher, often with severe headache, blurred vision, chest pain, dyspnea, confusion or a nosebleed. Stopping drugs is a common trigger.

options.text: Blurred vision
options.rationale: Hypertensive crisis is 180/120 mm Hg or higher, often with severe headache, blurred vision, chest pain, dyspnea, confusion or a nosebleed. Stopping drugs is a common trigger.

options.text: Blood pressure 162/98 mm Hg with no symptoms
options.rationale: Near miss concept This is stage 2 hypertension, below the crisis threshold of 180/120.

options.text: Stopped antihypertensives 2 years ago with no change since
options.rationale: Near miss concept Stopping drugs is a common trigger, but a long, stable gap is not itself a crisis finding.

options.text: Severe headache
options.rationale: Hypertensive crisis is 180/120 mm Hg or higher, often with severe headache, blurred vision, chest pain, dyspnea, confusion or a nosebleed. Stopping drugs is a common trigger.

questions.takeaway: Crisis starts at 180/120.
questions.strategy: Compare each pressure with the crisis threshold, then keep the target organ symptoms.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches a patient about the DASH eating plan. Select all foods to emphasize.

options.text: Sweets for energy
options.rationale: Near miss concept DASH is low in sweets.

options.text: Vegetables
options.rationale: DASH emphasizes fruits, vegetables, whole grains and low fat dairy, which are rich in potassium, calcium, magnesium and fiber, and limits saturated fat and sweets.

options.text: Whole grains
options.rationale: DASH emphasizes fruits, vegetables, whole grains and low fat dairy, which are rich in potassium, calcium, magnesium and fiber, and limits saturated fat and sweets.

options.text: Fruits
options.rationale: DASH emphasizes fruits, vegetables, whole grains and low fat dairy, which are rich in potassium, calcium, magnesium and fiber, and limits saturated fat and sweets.

options.text: Low fat dairy
options.rationale: DASH emphasizes fruits, vegetables, whole grains and low fat dairy, which are rich in potassium, calcium, magnesium and fiber, and limits saturated fat and sweets.

options.text: Red meat at most meals
options.rationale: Near miss concept DASH is low in saturated fat and limits red meat.

questions.takeaway: DASH: fruits, vegetables, whole grains, low fat dairy.
questions.strategy: Keep the plant based and low fat foods.

questions.stem: A patient with peripheral arterial disease asks about exercise. Which instruction is correct?

options.text: Avoid walking, because walking brings on the leg pain.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Walking to the point of pain builds collateral circulation.

options.text: Elevate the legs above the heart after each walk.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Elevation reduces arterial flow.

options.text: Walk until pain starts, rest until it eases, then repeat.
options.rationale: For PAD, patients walk to the point of pain, rest and repeat, which builds collateral flow. They stop smoking, keep warm, avoid crossing the legs and keep the legs down rather than raised.

options.text: Push through the pain each time to build up strength.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Walking past the point of pain is not the teaching. Rest relieves the ischemia.

questions.takeaway: PAD: walk to pain, rest, repeat.
questions.strategy: Choose the option that uses the claudication pattern on purpose.

questions.stem: A patient with previously controlled hypertension now has readings of 164/98 mm Hg. Select all medications the nurse should ask about as possible causes.

options.text: Ibuprofen
options.rationale: Decongestants constrict vessels, NSAIDs hold sodium and water, glucocorticoids hold sodium, and stimulants raise heart rate and constrict vessels. All can raise blood pressure.

options.text: Prednisone
options.rationale: Decongestants constrict vessels, NSAIDs hold sodium and water, glucocorticoids hold sodium, and stimulants raise heart rate and constrict vessels. All can raise blood pressure.

options.text: Amphetamines
options.rationale: Decongestants constrict vessels, NSAIDs hold sodium and water, glucocorticoids hold sodium, and stimulants raise heart rate and constrict vessels. All can raise blood pressure.

options.text: Pseudoephedrine
options.rationale: Decongestants constrict vessels, NSAIDs hold sodium and water, glucocorticoids hold sodium, and stimulants raise heart rate and constrict vessels. All can raise blood pressure.

options.text: Acetaminophen
options.rationale: Near miss concept Acetaminophen does not hold sodium and water or constrict vessels.

options.text: Metformin
options.rationale: Near miss concept Metformin does not raise blood pressure.

questions.takeaway: A controlled pressure that rises means look for a new drug.
questions.strategy: For each drug, name how it would raise the pressure.

questions.stem: A patient has a blood pressure of 214/128 mm Hg, a severe headache and blurred vision. A nitroprusside infusion is started. What is the goal for the first hour?

options.text: Lower the systolic pressure by no more than 25%
options.rationale: In a crisis, pressure is lowered gradually: systolic down no more than 25% in the first hour, about 160/100 over the next 2 to 6 hours, then normal over 24 to 48 hours. Blood pressure is checked every 5 to 15 minutes.

options.text: Keep the pressure the same until symptoms improve
options.rationale: Near miss concept A crisis needs controlled lowering, not waiting.

options.text: Lower the pressure to 160/100
options.rationale: Correct but premature That is the target over the next 2 to 6 hours, not the first hour.

options.text: Bring the pressure to below 130/80 as fast as possible
options.rationale: Absolute language Organs used to high pressure need it to stay perfused. Lowering it fast can cause a stroke or MI.

questions.takeaway: Lower it gradually: 25% in the first hour.
questions.strategy: Reject any answer that brings a crisis to normal right away.

questions.stem: A patient's blood pressure is 134/94 mm Hg on two separate visits. How is this classified?

options.text: Stage 1 hypertension
options.rationale: Near miss concept The systolic alone fits stage 1, but a diastolic of 90 or more is stage 2, and the higher stage wins.

options.text: Elevated blood pressure
options.rationale: Near miss concept Elevated requires a diastolic below 80.

options.text: Hypertensive crisis
options.rationale: Most dramatic finding Crisis is 180/120 or higher.

options.text: Stage 2 hypertension
options.rationale: Stage 2 is a systolic of at least 140 or a diastolic of at least 90. "Or" means either number is enough, so 134/94 is stage 2.

questions.takeaway: Do not classify by the systolic alone.
questions.strategy: Find the stage for each number and choose the higher one.

questions.stem: A patient taking amlodipine reports swollen ankles. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: Ankle edema is a common effect of this drug; report it.
options.rationale: Calcium channel blockers dilate vessels, which can cause ankle edema, flushing, headache and dizziness. Verapamil also causes constipation, and grapefruit juice is avoided.

options.text: The swelling is caused by a low serum potassium level.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Calcium channel blockers do not lower potassium.

options.text: The swelling means the drug is not lowering the pressure.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Edema is a side effect of the vessel dilation the drug causes.

options.text: The swelling is an early sign of an allergic reaction to the drug.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Ankle edema is a common vasodilation effect, not an allergy.

questions.takeaway: Calcium channel blockers: ankle edema, flushing, headache.
questions.strategy: Link the side effect to the drug's action on the vessels.

questions.stem: A patient starts hydrochlorothiazide. Which instruction should the nurse include?

options.text: Avoid foods that are high in potassium, such as bananas.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Thiazides lower potassium. Avoiding potassium is the teaching for ACE inhibitors.

options.text: Take it in the morning and eat potassium rich foods.
options.rationale: Thiazides cause loss of potassium and sodium and can raise glucose and uric acid. They are taken in the morning to avoid nocturia, and patients eat potassium rich foods.

options.text: Take it at bedtime so that it works through the night.
options.rationale: Near miss concept A bedtime dose causes nocturia and broken sleep.

options.text: Use a salt substitute to replace the sodium you lose.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Salt substitutes contain potassium and are relevant to drugs that raise potassium, not this teaching.

questions.takeaway: Thiazides lower potassium. Morning dose.
questions.strategy: Match the food advice to the direction the drug moves potassium.

questions.stem: A patient has had poorly controlled hypertension for 15 years. Select all findings that suggest target organ damage.

options.text: Isolated mild ankle edema after a long flight
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dependent swelling after sitting is not organ damage.

options.text: Left ventricular hypertrophy on the ECG
options.rationale: Constant high pressure thickens arterioles and starves the organs: brain (weakness, stroke), heart (LVH, MI, heart failure), kidneys (protein, rising creatinine and BUN), vessels and eyes (retinal changes).

options.text: Retinal changes
options.rationale: Constant high pressure thickens arterioles and starves the organs: brain (weakness, stroke), heart (LVH, MI, heart failure), kidneys (protein, rising creatinine and BUN), vessels and eyes (retinal changes).

options.text: A headache relieved by acetaminophen
options.rationale: Near miss concept Headache does not track pressure and is not a sign of organ damage.

options.text: New weakness on one side
options.rationale: Constant high pressure thickens arterioles and starves the organs: brain (weakness, stroke), heart (LVH, MI, heart failure), kidneys (protein, rising creatinine and BUN), vessels and eyes (retinal changes).

options.text: Rising creatinine
options.rationale: Constant high pressure thickens arterioles and starves the organs: brain (weakness, stroke), heart (LVH, MI, heart failure), kidneys (protein, rising creatinine and BUN), vessels and eyes (retinal changes).

options.text: Protein in the urine
options.rationale: Constant high pressure thickens arterioles and starves the organs: brain (weakness, stroke), heart (LVH, MI, heart failure), kidneys (protein, rising creatinine and BUN), vessels and eyes (retinal changes).

questions.takeaway: Hypertension shows up in the brain, heart, kidneys and eyes.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding by organ. If it does not show organ injury, it is out.

questions.stem: A patient with high blood pressure has a serum potassium of 3.0 mEq/L and is not taking a diuretic. Which cause should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Primary aldosteronism
options.rationale: Aldosterone keeps sodium and excretes potassium. High blood pressure with low potassium and no diuretic points to excess aldosterone, a secondary cause.

options.text: Essential hypertension
options.rationale: Near miss concept Essential hypertension has no single cause and does not explain the low potassium.

options.text: Sleep apnea
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sleep apnea gives loud snoring and daytime sleepiness.

options.text: Pheochromocytoma
options.rationale: Near miss concept That causes episodes of pounding headache, racing pulse and sweating, not low potassium.

questions.takeaway: High blood pressure with low potassium suggests aldosterone.
questions.strategy: When the stem gives a clue beyond the pressure, think secondary hypertension and match the clue.

questions.stem: A patient with known hypertension arrives with a blood pressure of 210/118, a severe headache, blurred vision and new difficulty finding words. What does this presentation indicate?

options.text: Stage 2 hypertension requiring medication adjustment at the next clinic visit
options.rationale: Near miss concept A chronic category applied to an acute emergency.

options.text: Hypertensive urgency requiring oral medication and follow up within 24 hours
options.rationale: Near miss concept Urgency is a high pressure WITHOUT organ damage.

options.text: Hypertensive emergency with evidence of end organ damage
options.rationale: What separates emergency from urgency is not the number, it is evidence that organs are being damaged now. Neurologic deficits, visual changes and severe headache are that evidence. This is a rapid response and intravenous therapy per protocol.

options.text: An expected elevation related to pain and anxiety
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Explains away a neurologic deficit.

questions.takeaway: Hypertension is usually silent. When it speaks, ask which organ is talking.
questions.strategy: Look past the pressure to the organ findings. Those decide the category.

questions.stem: A patient's blood pressure is 212/124. He reports a severe headache and blurred vision. How should the nurse classify and act on this?

options.text: Stage 2 hypertension requiring medication adjustment at the next visit
options.rationale: Near miss concept A chronic category applied to an acute event.

options.text: An expected reading in an anxious patient, requiring a recheck in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Explains away end organ signs.
