options.text: Hypertensive urgency, because the pressure is severely elevated without evidence of acute target organ damage
options.rationale: Near miss concept The correct definition of urgency, and the blurred vision is a retinal sign of acute damage.

options.text: Hypertensive emergency, because end organ signs are present, requiring immediate treatment
options.rationale: What separates emergency from urgency is not the number and not whether the patient feels bad; it is evidence that organs are being damaged right now. Blurred vision points to the retina, and visual change, neurologic deficit, chest pain, pulmonary edema or falling urine output turn a severe reading into an emergency requiring controlled intravenous lowering. Headache alone appears in urgency too, which is why the visual change is the finding that decides this item.

questions.takeaway: The number raises the suspicion. The end organ findings make the diagnosis.
questions.strategy: Look past the pressure to what the pressure is doing.

questions.stem: A patient reports new unilateral calf pain. The calf is warm, swollen and slightly red. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Massage the calf gently to tell whether the pain is muscular
options.rationale: Near miss concept An assessment maneuver that can kill the patient.

options.text: Apply a sequential compression device to the affected leg
options.rationale: Near miss concept A prevention device applied to an existing clot.

options.text: Walk the patient in the hall to see if movement eases the pain
options.rationale: Near miss concept Mobility is usually right, and not here.

options.text: Rest the leg, avoid massaging it, and notify the provider
options.rationale: Unilateral swelling, pain, warmth and color change is a suspected deep vein thrombosis. Do not massage and do not walk the patient until it has been evaluated, because either can dislodge the clot. Watch for sudden dyspnea or pleuritic chest pain, which signal pulmonary embolism. Once anticoagulation is established, prolonged bed rest is no longer recommended and ambulation is encouraged, so the restriction here belongs to the undiagnosed window, not to the treatment.

questions.takeaway: The three wrong answers all move the clot.
questions.strategy: In a suspected thrombus, any option involving pressure or movement of the limb is wrong.

questions.stem: A patient with untreated hypertension says, "I never get headaches, so my pressure must be fine." Which response is best?

options.text: "You should still take your medicine every day just in case."
options.rationale: Institution as rationale This does not correct the misunderstanding.

options.text: "That is a good sign that your pressure is well controlled."
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Agreeing reinforces a dangerous belief. Symptoms do not track blood pressure.

options.text: "Hypertension rarely causes symptoms; only a reading can tell."
options.rationale: Hypertension is usually silent. It damages the brain, heart, kidneys, vessels and eyes without symptoms, so only measurement shows control.

options.text: "Tell me if headaches start so we can check your pressure then."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Waiting for symptoms allows silent damage to the organs.

questions.takeaway: No headache does not mean the pressure is fine.
questions.strategy: Correct the belief first. A response that agrees or waits for symptoms is wrong.

questions.stem: A patient starting lisinopril says, "Now that I am on a pill, I can go back to eating what I want." Which response is best?

options.text: "Your provider will decide whether you still need the diet."
options.rationale: Institution as rationale This defers the teaching that the nurse can give now.

options.text: "You can stop the diet once your pressure is back to normal."
options.rationale: Absolute language A normal pressure on treatment is the goal, not a reason to stop.

options.text: "That is fine as long as you take the pill every single day."
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Lifestyle continues after drugs start. A pill never replaces it.

options.text: "The pill works best with the diet, so those changes continue."
options.rationale: Lifestyle changes are first and always. They continue when drugs start, because the drug and the diet work together.

questions.takeaway: A pill never replaces lifestyle.
questions.strategy: Reject any answer that lets one treatment replace another.

questions.stem: A patient's blood pressure is 132/80 mm Hg lying down and 108/72 mm Hg after 3 minutes of standing. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the scheduled antihypertensive and recheck in an hour.
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question More medication could worsen the drop. The finding is reported first.

options.text: Have the patient walk in the hall to see whether it improves.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Walking raises the fall risk.

options.text: Document the readings as within normal limits for the patient.
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting A systolic drop of 24 meets the definition of orthostatic hypotension.

options.text: Start fall precautions and report the orthostatic hypotension.
options.rationale: A drop of 20 mm Hg systolic or 10 mm Hg diastolic on standing is orthostatic hypotension. The nurse puts fall precautions in place and reports it.

questions.takeaway: A 20 systolic or 10 diastolic drop is orthostatic.
questions.strategy: Subtract, then compare with the threshold.

questions.stem: A patient is due for metoprolol. The apical pulse is 52/min and the blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give half the dose.
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Changing the dose is not within the nurse's scope.

options.text: Hold the dose and notify the provider.
options.rationale: Before a beta blocker, check the apical pulse for a full minute and the blood pressure. Hold and call for a heart rate below 50 to 60 or a systolic below 100.

options.text: Give the dose and recheck the pulse in an hour.
options.rationale: Correct but premature Giving it would slow the heart further.

options.text: Give the dose because the blood pressure is normal.
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data The pulse is the parameter that is out of range. A normal blood pressure does not make it safe.

questions.takeaway: Beta blocker: hold for a low pulse or low systolic pressure.
questions.strategy: Check every hold parameter, not just the one that looks normal.

questions.stem: A patient taking atorvastatin reports muscle aches and dark urine. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Reassure the patient that this is expected with exercise.
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Muscle pain with dark urine on a statin suggests muscle breakdown, not exercise soreness.

options.text: Tell the patient to take the drug with food.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Taking it with food does not address possible muscle breakdown.

options.text: Report the findings to the provider promptly.
options.rationale: Statins can cause muscle breakdown. Muscle pain or weakness with dark urine is reported, and liver enzymes are monitored.

options.text: Teach the patient to drink grapefruit juice.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Grapefruit raises statin levels and is limited.

questions.takeaway: Statin plus muscle pain means report.
questions.strategy: Statin items turn on muscle pain. Choose reporting.

questions.stem: A patient taking lisinopril develops swelling of the lips and tongue. What is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Switch the patient to an ARB at the next scheduled dose.
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Changing drugs is the provider's decision, and the airway comes first.

options.text: Give an antihistamine and recheck the swelling in an hour.
options.rationale: Correct but premature Angioedema threatens the airway. Waiting is unsafe.

options.text: Assess the airway, hold the drug and notify the provider now.
options.rationale: Angioedema of the lips, tongue or throat is an airway emergency. The drug is stopped and the provider notified at once.

options.text: Document it as a common, expected side effect of the drug.
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting A dry cough is common. Angioedema is an emergency.

questions.takeaway: Swelling of the lips or tongue on an ACE inhibitor is an airway emergency.
questions.strategy: When the airway is involved, every other answer waits.

questions.stem: Place the hour 1 sepsis bundle interventions in the order the nurse should carry them out.

options.text: Administer broad spectrum antibiotics
Measure the serum lactate
Begin 30 mL per kg of crystalloid for hypotension or a lactate of 4 or more
Begin vasopressors if hypotension persists, targeting a mean arterial pressure of 65 or higher
Obtain blood cultures

questions.takeaway: Cultures are drawn before antibiotics so the organism can still be identified, but antibiotics are never delayed to obtain them. Fluid follows, and vasopressors are added only if hypotension persists after adequate volume. Cultures before antibiotics, and antibiotics before perfect cultures.
questions.strategy: The bundle is nurse driven. Know the order, because the stem will scramble it.

questions.stem: Four hours into sepsis resuscitation, select all of the findings that indicate the patient is responding.

options.text: Urine output rising from 20 to 55 mL per hour
options.rationale: Perfusion is the outcome, and these four measure it from four directions: the lactate says the tissues are getting oxygen again, the urine output says the kidneys are, the mean arterial pressure is above the 65 target, and capillary refill says the skin is. A rising heart rate means the compensation is still escalating. The white count is not a resuscitation endpoint and moves for many reasons.

options.text: Capillary refill improving from 5 seconds to 2 seconds
options.rationale: Perfusion is the outcome, and these four measure it from four directions: the lactate says the tissues are getting oxygen again, the urine output says the kidneys are, the mean arterial pressure is above the 65 target, and capillary refill says the skin is. A rising heart rate means the compensation is still escalating. The white count is not a resuscitation endpoint and moves for many reasons.

options.text: Heart rate rising from 112 to 128
options.rationale: Near miss concept Moving the wrong way; compensation is increasing, not resolving.

options.text: Lactate falling from 3.6 to 2.1
options.rationale: Perfusion is the outcome, and these four measure it from four directions: the lactate says the tissues are getting oxygen again, the urine output says the kidneys are, the mean arterial pressure is above the 65 target, and capillary refill says the skin is. A rising heart rate means the compensation is still escalating. The white count is not a resuscitation endpoint and moves for many reasons.

options.text: A white blood cell count that has risen from 16,000 to 19,000
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Not a perfusion endpoint and a poor guide to resuscitation.

options.text: Mean arterial pressure rising from 58 to 72
options.rationale: Perfusion is the outcome, and these four measure it from four directions: the lactate says the tissues are getting oxygen again, the urine output says the kidneys are, the mean arterial pressure is above the 65 target, and capillary refill says the skin is. A rising heart rate means the compensation is still escalating. The white count is not a resuscitation endpoint and moves for many reasons.

questions.takeaway: Four perfusion windows: lactate, urine, mean pressure, capillary refill. Watch all four.
questions.strategy: The white count is the trap. It feels like the infection marker and it tells you nothing about perfusion.

questions.stem: Select all of the factors that increase a patient's risk of sepsis.

options.text: Age over 80
options.rationale: Risk comes from a weakened defense, a portal of entry, or both. Age, neutropenia, chronic disease and indwelling devices all qualify, and the devices are the modifiable one. A healed scar is not a portal and an allergy affects which antibiotic is chosen rather than whether infection occurs.

options.text: An indwelling urinary catheter and a central line
options.rationale: Risk comes from a weakened defense, a portal of entry, or both. Age, neutropenia, chronic disease and indwelling devices all qualify, and the devices are the modifiable one. A healed scar is not a portal and an allergy affects which antibiotic is chosen rather than whether infection occurs.

options.text: A documented penicillin allergy
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Affects antibiotic choice, not susceptibility to infection.

options.text: Chronic kidney disease and diabetes
options.rationale: Risk comes from a weakened defense, a portal of entry, or both. Age, neutropenia, chronic disease and indwelling devices all qualify, and the devices are the modifiable one. A healed scar is not a portal and an allergy affects which antibiotic is chosen rather than whether infection occurs.

options.text: Chemotherapy induced neutropenia
options.rationale: Risk comes from a weakened defense, a portal of entry, or both. Age, neutropenia, chronic disease and indwelling devices all qualify, and the devices are the modifiable one. A healed scar is not a portal and an allergy affects which antibiotic is chosen rather than whether infection occurs.

options.text: A well healed surgical scar from five years ago
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Intact skin is a barrier, not a portal.

questions.takeaway: Every indwelling device is a portal. That is the risk factor you can actually remove.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options are history that sounds relevant and changes nothing about risk.

questions.stem: Which statement best defines sepsis?

options.text: An infection that has caused organ dysfunction
options.rationale: Sepsis is infection plus organ dysfunction. Vessels dilate and leak, perfusion falls and organs begin to fail. The source can be anywhere.

options.text: A low blood pressure that does not respond to fluids
options.rationale: Near miss concept That describes septic shock, a later stage.

options.text: A temperature above 38 °C with a high white count
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism These are SIRS criteria, which also occur with trauma, burns or pancreatitis.

options.text: An infection that has spread into the bloodstream
options.rationale: Near miss concept A positive blood culture is not required. Sepsis can come from urine, lungs or a wound, and a negative culture does not rule it out.

questions.takeaway: Sepsis = infection plus organ dysfunction.
questions.strategy: Look for the option that includes both pieces: an infection and an organ in trouble.

questions.stem: Which finding is often the earliest sign of sepsis in an older adult?

options.text: A positive blood culture
options.rationale: Near miss concept Results take days, and a negative culture does not rule sepsis out.

options.text: Systolic blood pressure below 90 mm Hg
options.rationale: Correct but premature Low blood pressure is a late sign. The body compensates for a long time before it falls.

options.text: New confusion or restlessness
options.rationale: The brain is very sensitive to poor perfusion, so a change in mental status is often the earliest cue, especially in older adults. A normal blood pressure does not reassure.

options.text: Mottled, cool extremities
options.rationale: Correct but premature Mottling appears late, in cold septic shock.

questions.takeaway: Mental status changes early. Blood pressure falls late.
questions.strategy: When asked for the earliest sign, eliminate anything that needs the body to stop compensating.

questions.stem: A patient with sepsis has received fluids and antibiotics. Select all findings that show the treatment is working.

options.text: Heart rate rising from 108 to 120/min
options.rationale: Near miss concept A rising heart rate suggests ongoing low volume or worsening shock.

options.text: Capillary refill under 3 seconds
options.rationale: Improvement looks like better perfusion: MAP 65 or higher, urine output at least 0.5 mL/kg/hr (30 mL/hr), falling lactate, mentation back toward baseline and warm skin with brisk capillary refill.

options.text: Urine output 45 mL/hr
options.rationale: Improvement looks like better perfusion: MAP 65 or higher, urine output at least 0.5 mL/kg/hr (30 mL/hr), falling lactate, mentation back toward baseline and warm skin with brisk capillary refill.

options.text: All ordered doses given on time
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome Completing the orders is a task, not an outcome. Perfusion shows whether they worked.

options.text: MAP 70 mm Hg
options.rationale: Improvement looks like better perfusion: MAP 65 or higher, urine output at least 0.5 mL/kg/hr (30 mL/hr), falling lactate, mentation back toward baseline and warm skin with brisk capillary refill.

options.text: Lactate falling from 4.1 to 1.8 mmol/L
options.rationale: Improvement looks like better perfusion: MAP 65 or higher, urine output at least 0.5 mL/kg/hr (30 mL/hr), falling lactate, mentation back toward baseline and warm skin with brisk capillary refill.

options.text: Patient more alert and oriented
options.rationale: Improvement looks like better perfusion: MAP 65 or higher, urine output at least 0.5 mL/kg/hr (30 mL/hr), falling lactate, mentation back toward baseline and warm skin with brisk capillary refill.

questions.takeaway: Urine output is the key marker that perfusion is back.
questions.strategy: Pick findings that show organs working again, not tasks completed.

questions.stem: A nurse recognizes sepsis in a patient whose blood pressure is 84/48 mm Hg and lactate is 4.6 mmol/L. Which order should the nurse expect?

options.text: A continuous norepinephrine infusion before any fluid
options.rationale: Correct but premature A vasopressor is added when the MAP stays below 65 despite adequate fluids. Fluids come first.

options.text: Restricting fluids to protect the lungs
options.rationale: Near miss concept This patient is hypotensive with a high lactate. Volume replacement is the priority.

options.text: A 250 mL bolus of 5% dextrose in water
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dextrose in water does not stay in the vessels. Sepsis calls for a large volume of isotonic crystalloid.

options.text: A rapid IV crystalloid bolus of 30 mL/kg
options.rationale: Low blood pressure or a lactate of 4 mmol/L or more calls for a rapid 30 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid bolus, ideally through two large bore IV lines.

questions.takeaway: Fluids first; pressors only if fluids fail.
questions.strategy: Look for the dose. A specific weight based fluid volume is the bundle answer.

questions.stem: A patient with sepsis has received 30 mL/kg of IV fluid, and the MAP is still 58 mm Hg with a lactate of 3.9 mmol/L. What does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Oral fluids and a recheck of the lactate level tomorrow
options.rationale: Near miss concept This patient is in shock and needs immediate support.

options.text: A diuretic to remove the fluid that has already been given
options.rationale: Near miss concept Removing volume would drop the pressure further.

options.text: Norepinephrine, ideally by central line, and a higher level of care
options.rationale: Septic shock is a MAP below 65 mm Hg despite adequate fluids with a lactate above 2 mmol/L. It needs a vasopressor such as norepinephrine to keep the MAP 65 or higher, ideally through a central line, and a higher level of care.

options.text: A second 30 mL/kg fluid bolus and a recheck in 4 hours
options.rationale: Near miss concept Persistent hypotension despite adequate fluids defines septic shock and calls for a vasopressor, not another wait.

questions.takeaway: Shock is low MAP despite fluids. Pressors are next.
questions.strategy: When the stem says fluids were already given, the next answer is not more of the same.

questions.stem: A patient with a urinary tract infection has a blood pressure of 88/50 mm Hg. What is the mean arterial pressure, and what does it mean?

options.text: About 63 mm Hg, below 65, so the organs are poorly perfused.
options.rationale: MAP = (systolic + 2 × diastolic) ÷ 3 = (88 + 100) ÷ 3 = about 63 mm Hg. Below 65, organs are not perfused.

options.text: About 75 mm Hg, which reflects adequate organ perfusion.
options.rationale: Near miss concept This uses the systolic pressure twice. The formula doubles the diastolic.

options.text: About 69 mm Hg, which reflects adequate organ perfusion.
options.rationale: Near miss concept This adds the pressures and divides by two. MAP counts the diastolic pressure twice because the heart spends more time in diastole.

options.text: About 63 mm Hg, which is expected with an infection like this.
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem The number is right but the meaning is wrong. A MAP below 65 shows poor perfusion and needs action.

questions.takeaway: MAP below 65 means organs are not perfused.
questions.strategy: Do the math, then check that the option interprets the number correctly.

questions.stem: A 68 year old admitted with a urinary tract infection has a temperature of 100.9 F, heart rate 112, respiratory rate 24, blood pressure 118/72 and has become intermittently confused over the past two hours. Urine output has been 20 mL per hour. What is the nurse's interpretation?

options.text: The confusion is most likely related to the unfamiliar environment and the hour
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Sundowning offered instead of a mechanism.

options.text: The normal blood pressure indicates the patient is compensating adequately and can be monitored
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit The exact reasoning error this item is built on.

options.text: This presentation is consistent with sepsis and the sepsis protocol should be initiated
options.rationale: Fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, new confusion and falling urine output in a patient with a known source is sepsis. A normal blood pressure does not rule it out; hypotension is a late finding. A sudden change in mental status is often the earliest sign, and low urine output is a perfusion red flag on its own.

options.text: The findings are consistent with the known urinary tract infection and need no escalation
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Uses the known source to normalize organ dysfunction.

questions.takeaway: Normal blood pressure is not reassurance in sepsis.
questions.strategy: Count the organ systems already reporting. Brain and kidney here is enough.

questions.stem: A patient has a temperature of 38.7, heart rate 118, respirations 26, blood pressure 84/48 and a lactate of 4.2. Blood cultures have been drawn. The antibiotic has arrived and the fluid bolus is ordered. The nurse is alone with the patient. What should she do first?

options.text: Repeat the lactate before giving either
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Measures the problem instead of treating it.

options.text: Start the antibiotic, then begin the fluid bolus
options.rationale: Both belong inside the first hour and the cultures are already drawn, so nothing is waiting on the antibiotic. Mortality rises with every hour antibiotics are delayed, and the antibiotic takes seconds to hang while the bolus runs over much longer. Start the drug, then start the fluid, which is sequencing rather than choosing. Repeating the lactate comes later to judge the response.

options.text: Begin the fluid bolus, then start the antibiotic
options.rationale: Near miss concept Defensible, and it delays the intervention most tied to mortality for the sake of one that takes longer to run anyway.

options.text: Obtain a second set of blood cultures from a different site
options.rationale: Correct but premature Two sets are standard and the first is drawn; this delays the antibiotic.

questions.takeaway: Cultures are drawn, so hang the antibiotic. It takes seconds and the clock is on mortality.
questions.strategy: This is a sequencing question disguised as a choice. Ask which action is quickest to initiate.

questions.stem: A patient with septic shock begins oozing blood from two intravenous sites and from the gums. Petechiae are noted on the chest. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Apply pressure and continue routine care, since oozing is common with multiple sticks
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Normalizes a systemic coagulopathy.

options.text: Notify the provider and anticipate coagulation studies and blood products
options.rationale: Bleeding from multiple sites with petechiae in a patient with septic shock is disseminated intravascular coagulation. The nurse escalates, anticipates coagulation testing and products, and minimizes further punctures.

options.text: Request an order for a heparin flush to maintain line patency
options.rationale: Near miss concept Anticoagulation in an actively bleeding patient.

options.text: Restart both intravenous lines in new sites to reduce the bleeding
options.rationale: Near miss concept Adds two more puncture sites to a patient who is bleeding.

questions.takeaway: Oozing from IV sites in sepsis is a coagulation emergency, not a technique problem.
questions.strategy: When bleeding appears at more than one site at once, think systemic rather than local.

questions.stem: A patient three days after hip surgery has a heart rate of 112, a temperature of 38.4 degrees Celsius, a respiratory rate of 24, a blood pressure of 96/54 and new confusion. The white count is 17,800.

options.text: Hold the next opioid dose and reassess
Reorient the patient and reduce stimulation
Encourage incentive spirometry every hour
Begin the ordered isotonic fluid bolus
Obtain blood cultures before starting antibiotics
Opioid induced delirium
Hypovolemic shock from bleeding
Postoperative atelectasis
Sepsis
Urine output
Mean arterial pressure
Serum lactate
Hemoglobin
Pain score

questions.takeaway: Fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, leukocytosis and new confusion in a postoperative patient is sepsis. Cultures are drawn before antibiotics, because once the antibiotic is in, the organism may never be identified, and fluid resuscitation begins within the first hour. Lactate reflects tissue perfusion and urine output is the cheapest real time perfusion monitor you have. Mean arterial pressure is the resuscitation target, at or above 65, and it is what decides whether a vasopressor is started. Cultures before antibiotics, fluids within the hour, lactate and urine output to track perfusion.
questions.strategy: In a bowtie, settle the condition first from the pattern, then ask which actions and which monitored values belong to THAT condition rather than to the others offered.

questions.stem: A patient with sepsis has received 30 mL per kg of crystalloid. The blood pressure is now 84/44 with a mean arterial pressure of 57, the skin is cool and mottled, and the lactate has risen from 3.1 to 4.6. What does this indicate?

options.text: An improving response, since the skin is no longer warm and flushed
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Misreads the late phase as resolution of the early one.

options.text: An expected fluid shift that should be reassessed in another hour
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Another hour at a mean arterial pressure of 57 is organ injury.

options.text: Fluid overload, so diuresis is needed before any more resuscitation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would further drop an already failing perfusion pressure.

options.text: Septic shock needing vasopressors to keep the MAP at 65 or above
options.rationale: Hypotension persisting after adequate fluid is septic shock by definition. The cool mottled skin is not improvement; it is the body clamping down after the early warm vasodilated phase, and the rising lactate confirms worsening perfusion.

questions.takeaway: Cool skin in sepsis is deterioration, not improvement.
questions.strategy: Read the direction of the lactate. It settles any argument about whether the patient is getting better.

questions.stem: A patient with pneumonia has these findings. Select all that suggest sepsis.

options.text: Urine output 20 mL in the last hour
options.rationale: Each cue is an organ short of oxygen: confusion (brain), fast breathing (compensation for acidosis), tachycardia (low volume), low urine (kidneys) and lactate above 2 (tissues on low oxygen). Hypothermia is a bad sign, not a reassuring one.

options.text: Lactate 3.4 mmol/L
options.rationale: Each cue is an organ short of oxygen: confusion (brain), fast breathing (compensation for acidosis), tachycardia (low volume), low urine (kidneys) and lactate above 2 (tissues on low oxygen). Hypothermia is a bad sign, not a reassuring one.

options.text: Blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data A normal pressure does not rule sepsis out. Low pressure is a late sign, so this value is not a cue for sepsis.

options.text: Temperature 35.8 °C
options.rationale: Each cue is an organ short of oxygen: confusion (brain), fast breathing (compensation for acidosis), tachycardia (low volume), low urine (kidneys) and lactate above 2 (tissues on low oxygen). Hypothermia is a bad sign, not a reassuring one.

options.text: New confusion
options.rationale: Each cue is an organ short of oxygen: confusion (brain), fast breathing (compensation for acidosis), tachycardia (low volume), low urine (kidneys) and lactate above 2 (tissues on low oxygen). Hypothermia is a bad sign, not a reassuring one.

options.text: Respiratory rate 26/min
options.rationale: Each cue is an organ short of oxygen: confusion (brain), fast breathing (compensation for acidosis), tachycardia (low volume), low urine (kidneys) and lactate above 2 (tissues on low oxygen). Hypothermia is a bad sign, not a reassuring one.

options.text: Heart rate 112/min
options.rationale: Each cue is an organ short of oxygen: confusion (brain), fast breathing (compensation for acidosis), tachycardia (low volume), low urine (kidneys) and lactate above 2 (tissues on low oxygen). Hypothermia is a bad sign, not a reassuring one.

questions.takeaway: A low temperature in sepsis is a warning, not good news.
questions.strategy: For each finding, ask which organ it shows is struggling.

questions.stem: A patient's blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. The baseline is 136/84 mm Hg. Heart rate is 104/min and respiratory rate is 22/min. The patient has a new productive cough. How should the nurse interpret the blood pressure?

options.text: It is improved, because the pressure is now lower than before.
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit The patient's baseline was not a problem being treated. The drop reflects falling perfusion.

options.text: It is a warning sign; a 24 point drop with these changes may be sepsis.
options.rationale: Blood pressure falls late in sepsis. A pressure that still looks normal but is well below baseline, together with tachycardia and tachypnea, is an early warning.

options.text: It is reassuring, because the value is within the normal range.
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data A number in the normal range can still be a big change for this patient.

options.text: It is an expected finding with a respiratory infection like this one, so continue to monitor.
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A drop from baseline with a fast heart rate is not an expected part of pneumonia; it shows the body compensating.

questions.takeaway: Compare blood pressure with the patient's baseline, not with the population normal.
questions.strategy: If a stem gives a baseline, the question is about the change.

questions.stem: A nurse finds a patient with new confusion, a heart rate of 118/min and a blood pressure of 86/50 mm Hg, 24 points below baseline. A urinary catheter is in place. Place the nurse's actions in priority order.

options.text: Draw blood cultures as ordered
Call the rapid response team
Give the ordered antibiotic
Reassess airway, breathing, circulation and mentation
Reassess perfusion after the fluids and antibiotic

questions.takeaway: Infection plus organ changes is already in the stem, so the nurse escalates first. Airway, breathing and circulation are reassessed, cultures are drawn before the antibiotic, and the patient is reassessed after treatment because ongoing poor perfusion means escalating again. Escalate, stabilize, culture, treat, reassess.
questions.strategy: The step students drop is the reassessment after treatment. It always comes last.

questions.stem: A patient receiving norepinephrine through a peripheral IV has a cool, pale, swollen area around the site. What is the nurse's first action?

options.text: Slow the infusion rate and keep watching the site.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Any further infusion into the tissue causes more injury.

options.text: Document the finding and continue to monitor it.
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Documentation does not stop the drug from injuring tissue.

options.text: Elevate the arm and recheck the site in 30 minutes.
options.rationale: Correct but premature Elevation may help later, but a vasopressor leaking into tissue causes damage and must be stopped now.

options.text: Stop the infusion at that site and notify the provider.
options.rationale: Vasopressors constrict vessels in the tissue if they leak out, which can cause tissue death. The infusion is stopped at that site and the provider notified. This is why pressors go through a central line when possible.

questions.takeaway: A vasopressor outside the vein is an emergency for the tissue.
questions.strategy: When something harmful is flowing, stop it first. Assessment comes after.

chapters.title: Coronary Artery Disease and Acute Coronary Syndrome

questions.stem: Select all findings that suggest cardiogenic shock in a patient after an MI.

options.text: Temperature of 38.0 °C
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A low grade fever after MI is expected from inflammation.

options.text: Systolic pressure of 84 mm Hg
options.rationale: Cardiogenic shock is the pump failing to perfuse the body: systolic below 90, urine below 30 mL an hour, cold clammy skin, confusion and a rising heart rate.

options.text: New confusion
options.rationale: Cardiogenic shock is the pump failing to perfuse the body: systolic below 90, urine below 30 mL an hour, cold clammy skin, confusion and a rising heart rate.

options.text: Blood pressure 132/80 mm Hg
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit A normal blood pressure does not suggest shock.

options.text: Rising heart rate
options.rationale: Cardiogenic shock is the pump failing to perfuse the body: systolic below 90, urine below 30 mL an hour, cold clammy skin, confusion and a rising heart rate.

options.text: Cold, clammy skin
options.rationale: Cardiogenic shock is the pump failing to perfuse the body: systolic below 90, urine below 30 mL an hour, cold clammy skin, confusion and a rising heart rate.

options.text: Urine output of 18 mL in the last hour
options.rationale: Cardiogenic shock is the pump failing to perfuse the body: systolic below 90, urine below 30 mL an hour, cold clammy skin, confusion and a rising heart rate.

questions.takeaway: Shock is poor perfusion everywhere.
questions.strategy: For each finding, ask whether it shows an organ not getting blood.

questions.stem: For each description, indicate whether it describes ischemia, angina or infarction.

rows.text: Too little oxygen reaching the heart muscle, which is reversible
Heals with scar tissue that does not contract
Death of heart muscle that raises the troponin level
Chest pressure caused by the oxygen shortage

questions.takeaway: Ischemia is the oxygen shortage, which is reversible. Angina is the discomfort ischemia causes. Infarction is muscle death, which is permanent, heals by scar and raises troponin. Ischemia is the shortage, angina is the pain, infarction is the death.
questions.strategy: Ask whether each row describes a cause, a symptom or permanent damage.

questions.stem: A patient with a STEMI cannot reach PCI in time and alteplase is being considered. Select all findings that are contraindications.

options.text: Chest pain that started 2 hours ago
options.rationale: Near miss concept Early presentation makes fibrinolysis useful.

options.text: Suspected aortic dissection
options.rationale: Fibrinolytics are for STEMI when PCI cannot happen in time. They are never given after recent bleeding, a prior brain bleed, a recent stroke or surgery, or a suspected aortic dissection, and the nurse watches neuro status and every site for bleeding.

options.text: Type 2 diabetes
options.rationale: Near miss concept Diabetes is not a contraindication.

options.text: A brain hemorrhage 2 years ago
options.rationale: Fibrinolytics are for STEMI when PCI cannot happen in time. They are never given after recent bleeding, a prior brain bleed, a recent stroke or surgery, or a suspected aortic dissection, and the nurse watches neuro status and every site for bleeding.

options.text: Surgery 1 week ago
options.rationale: Fibrinolytics are for STEMI when PCI cannot happen in time. They are never given after recent bleeding, a prior brain bleed, a recent stroke or surgery, or a suspected aortic dissection, and the nurse watches neuro status and every site for bleeding.

options.text: Active bleeding
options.rationale: Fibrinolytics are for STEMI when PCI cannot happen in time. They are never given after recent bleeding, a prior brain bleed, a recent stroke or surgery, or a suspected aortic dissection, and the nurse watches neuro status and every site for bleeding.

options.text: A stroke 1 month ago
options.rationale: Fibrinolytics are for STEMI when PCI cannot happen in time. They are never given after recent bleeding, a prior brain bleed, a recent stroke or surgery, or a suspected aortic dissection, and the nurse watches neuro status and every site for bleeding.

questions.takeaway: Anything that could bleed catastrophically rules out fibrinolytics.
questions.strategy: For each finding, ask whether dissolving clots would cause a bleed there.

questions.stem: Select all actions the nurse should take before giving sublingual nitroglycerin.

options.text: Have the patient swallow the tablet with water
options.rationale: Near miss concept The tablet dissolves under the tongue.

options.text: Give the dose only if the patient has a headache
options.rationale: Near miss concept Headache is an expected effect, not a requirement.

options.text: Have the patient sit or lie down
options.rationale: Nitroglycerin dilates veins and drops the blood pressure, so the nurse checks it and has the patient sit or lie down. PDE5 inhibitors in the past 24 to 48 hours cause profound hypotension with nitrates.

options.text: Ask about sildenafil, tadalafil or vardenafil in the past 24 to 48 hours
options.rationale: Nitroglycerin dilates veins and drops the blood pressure, so the nurse checks it and has the patient sit or lie down. PDE5 inhibitors in the past 24 to 48 hours cause profound hypotension with nitrates.

options.text: Check the blood pressure
options.rationale: Nitroglycerin dilates veins and drops the blood pressure, so the nurse checks it and has the patient sit or lie down. PDE5 inhibitors in the past 24 to 48 hours cause profound hypotension with nitrates.

questions.takeaway: Check BP and ask about PDE5 drugs before nitroglycerin.
questions.strategy: Each action should protect against the drop in blood pressure.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches a patient after an MI. Select all correct instructions.

options.text: Strain hard during bowel movements to avoid constipation medicine
options.rationale: Near miss concept Straining at stool is avoided because it strains the heart.

options.text: Use acetaminophen instead of ibuprofen for pain
options.rationale: Rehab teaching includes daily walking with pulse checks, stopping for a rise of more than 20 beats per minute, chest pain, dyspnea or dizziness, no heavy lifting early, avoiding straining, avoiding NSAIDs and reporting every chest pain. Sexual activity is usually safe once the patient climbs 2 flights of stairs without symptoms.

options.text: Report every episode of chest pain
options.rationale: Rehab teaching includes daily walking with pulse checks, stopping for a rise of more than 20 beats per minute, chest pain, dyspnea or dizziness, no heavy lifting early, avoiding straining, avoiding NSAIDs and reporting every chest pain. Sexual activity is usually safe once the patient climbs 2 flights of stairs without symptoms.

options.text: Check your pulse before, during and after walking
options.rationale: Rehab teaching includes daily walking with pulse checks, stopping for a rise of more than 20 beats per minute, chest pain, dyspnea or dizziness, no heavy lifting early, avoiding straining, avoiding NSAIDs and reporting every chest pain. Sexual activity is usually safe once the patient climbs 2 flights of stairs without symptoms.

options.text: Sexual activity must wait 6 months
options.rationale: Near miss concept It is usually safe once the patient climbs 2 flights of stairs without symptoms.

options.text: Avoid lifting more than about 15 lb early in recovery
options.rationale: Rehab teaching includes daily walking with pulse checks, stopping for a rise of more than 20 beats per minute, chest pain, dyspnea or dizziness, no heavy lifting early, avoiding straining, avoiding NSAIDs and reporting every chest pain. Sexual activity is usually safe once the patient climbs 2 flights of stairs without symptoms.

options.text: Stop and rest if your heart rate rises more than 20 beats per minute
options.rationale: Rehab teaching includes daily walking with pulse checks, stopping for a rise of more than 20 beats per minute, chest pain, dyspnea or dizziness, no heavy lifting early, avoiding straining, avoiding NSAIDs and reporting every chest pain. Sexual activity is usually safe once the patient climbs 2 flights of stairs without symptoms.

questions.takeaway: Denial delays care, so every chest pain is reported.
questions.strategy: Keep statements that protect the healing heart and catch warning signs.

questions.stem: Which instruction about aspirin for a patient with suspected ACS is correct?

options.text: Chew 325 mg of non enteric coated aspirin.
options.rationale: Aspirin 325 mg is chewed, not enteric coated, as prescribed. It stops platelets clumping on the ruptured plaque.

options.text: Take 81 mg of aspirin with a full meal.
options.rationale: Near miss concept The loading dose is 325 mg, and food would delay it.

options.text: Swallow an enteric coated tablet whole.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Enteric coating delays absorption. Chewing a plain tablet works fastest.

options.text: Wait until the troponin result is back.
options.rationale: Correct but premature Aspirin is given early to stop platelets clumping on the plaque.

questions.takeaway: Chew the aspirin.
questions.strategy: Look for the option that gets the drug working fastest.

questions.stem: Select all patients at higher risk of having an MI without typical chest pain.

options.text: A 30 year old athlete
options.rationale: Near miss concept Younger patients usually present with classic chest pressure.

options.text: A patient with peripheral nerve damage from diabetes
options.rationale: Older adults and patients with diabetes often have atypical symptoms such as fatigue, indigestion, jaw or back pain, dyspnea or confusion. Diabetic nerve damage can make ischemia silent.

options.text: A patient who describes crushing chest pressure radiating to the jaw
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is a classic presentation.

options.text: An 82 year old patient
options.rationale: Older adults and patients with diabetes often have atypical symptoms such as fatigue, indigestion, jaw or back pain, dyspnea or confusion. Diabetic nerve damage can make ischemia silent.

options.text: A patient with long standing diabetes
options.rationale: Older adults and patients with diabetes often have atypical symptoms such as fatigue, indigestion, jaw or back pain, dyspnea or confusion. Diabetic nerve damage can make ischemia silent.

questions.takeaway: The missing chest pain is the trap.
questions.strategy: Look for age and diabetes, which blunt the classic signs.

questions.stem: Which finding separates an NSTEMI from unstable angina?

options.text: Pain that is not relieved by rest
options.rationale: Near miss concept Both can persist with rest.

options.text: A rising troponin level
options.rationale: Unstable angina and NSTEMI can look the same on the ECG and in symptoms. Troponin rises only when muscle dies, so a rise means NSTEMI and no rise means unstable angina.

options.text: ST depression on the ECG
options.rationale: Near miss concept Both can show ST depression.

options.text: Chest pain at rest
options.rationale: Near miss concept Both cause pain at rest.

questions.takeaway: Troponin separates unstable angina from NSTEMI.
questions.strategy: Find the one test that shows muscle death.

questions.stem: A patient with stable angina has chest pain at home. Place the patient's steps in the correct order.

options.text: Take one nitroglycerin tablet and wait 5 minutes
Stop the activity and sit or lie down
Take a second tablet while waiting for help
Call 911 if the pain is not better or is worse

questions.takeaway: The patient stops, takes one tablet and waits 5 minutes. If the pain is not better or is worse, the patient calls 911, then takes a second dose while waiting and a third 5 minutes later. The 911 call comes after the first dose fails.
questions.strategy: Do not wait for all three doses to call for help, and never drive to the hospital.

questions.stem: A patient asks why nitroglycerin causes a headache. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: The headache is an early sign of an allergy to the drug.
options.rationale: Near miss concept It is a common side effect, not an allergy.

options.text: The headache means the dose was too high and must be stopped.
options.rationale: Absolute language Headache is expected and treated with acetaminophen.

options.text: The headache means the drug is not working on the heart.
options.rationale: Near miss concept The headache is an expected effect of vasodilation.

options.text: The drug widens vessels, including those in the head.
options.rationale: Nitroglycerin dilates arteries and veins. The vasodilation causes a headache, which is expected and can be relieved with acetaminophen.

questions.takeaway: Headache with nitroglycerin is expected.
questions.strategy: Explain the side effect through the drug's action.

questions.stem: A patient on a heparin infusion has a PTT of 112 seconds and new gum bleeding. Which antidote should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Vitamin K
options.rationale: Near miss concept Vitamin K reverses warfarin.

options.text: Protamine sulfate
options.rationale: Heparin is monitored with the PTT (goal 1.5 to 2.5 times control) and reversed with protamine. Warfarin uses INR and vitamin K.

options.text: Naloxone
options.rationale: Near miss concept Naloxone reverses opioids.

options.text: Aspirin
options.rationale: Near miss concept Aspirin adds to bleeding.

questions.takeaway: Heparin: PTT and protamine. Warfarin: INR and vitamin K.
questions.strategy: Pair the anticoagulant with its lab and its antidote.

questions.stem: A patient reports chest pressure that began 40 minutes ago, radiating to the left jaw, with nausea and diaphoresis. Select all of the nursing actions that are appropriate immediately.

options.text: Draw a troponin and anticipate serial measurements
options.rationale: Electrocardiogram within ten minutes, access, monitoring and troponins. Oxygen has changed: it is given for hypoxemia rather than routinely, because supplemental oxygen in a patient who is not hypoxemic may cause coronary vasoconstriction and worsen the infarct. And a patient with possible ischemia does not walk anywhere; exertion increases the demand on a muscle that is already starving.

options.text: Establish intravenous access and begin continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Electrocardiogram within ten minutes, access, monitoring and troponins. Oxygen has changed: it is given for hypoxemia rather than routinely, because supplemental oxygen in a patient who is not hypoxemic may cause coronary vasoconstriction and worsen the infarct. And a patient with possible ischemia does not walk anywhere; exertion increases the demand on a muscle that is already starving.

options.text: Have the patient walk to the electrocardiogram machine to save time
options.rationale: Near miss concept Exertion increases myocardial demand; bring the machine to him.

options.text: Obtain a 12 lead electrocardiogram
options.rationale: Electrocardiogram within ten minutes, access, monitoring and troponins. Oxygen has changed: it is given for hypoxemia rather than routinely, because supplemental oxygen in a patient who is not hypoxemic may cause coronary vasoconstriction and worsen the infarct. And a patient with possible ischemia does not walk anywhere; exertion increases the demand on a muscle that is already starving.

options.text: Administer oxygen if the oxygen saturation is below 90 percent
options.rationale: Electrocardiogram within ten minutes, access, monitoring and troponins. Oxygen has changed: it is given for hypoxemia rather than routinely, because supplemental oxygen in a patient who is not hypoxemic may cause coronary vasoconstriction and worsen the infarct. And a patient with possible ischemia does not walk anywhere; exertion increases the demand on a muscle that is already starving.

options.text: Give oxygen at 4 L per minute regardless of the saturation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Former practice. Oxygen in a normoxic patient can worsen the infarct.

questions.takeaway: Oxygen only if the saturation is low. Routine oxygen in acute coronary syndrome is out.
questions.strategy: The routine oxygen option is the one that used to be correct, which is exactly why it is here.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman with type 2 diabetes reports that she has felt unusually tired for two days, is short of breath climbing one flight of stairs, and has an upset stomach she attributes to a meal. She denies chest pain. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Obtain a 12 lead electrocardiogram
options.rationale: Atypical presentation is more common in older adults, in women and in people with diabetes, where neuropathy blunts the warning. Fatigue, exertional dyspnea and epigastric discomfort in this patient is acute coronary syndrome until proven otherwise, and the electrocardiogram comes as fast as possible.

options.text: Reassure her that the absence of chest pain makes a cardiac cause unlikely
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Reassurance built on the exact assumption this population breaks.

options.text: Administer an antacid and reassess the stomach discomfort in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Near miss concept Takes the patient's own explanation at face value.

options.text: Ask her to rate her fatigue and document the findings for the next shift
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Charting a presentation that needs action now.

questions.takeaway: Expecting chest pain in every infarction is one of the most dangerous assumptions in cardiac care.
questions.strategy: When the stem lists diabetes, female sex or advanced age alongside vague symptoms, think atypical presentation.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman with diabetes reports unusual fatigue, mild nausea and a sense of pressure between her shoulder blades. She denies chest pain. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Attribute the fatigue to her diabetes and check a fingerstick glucose
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Explains a new symptom with a known diagnosis.

options.text: Treat this as possible acute coronary syndrome and obtain a 12 lead ECG
options.rationale: Women, older adults and people with diabetes often present without chest pain. Fatigue, nausea, jaw, neck or back discomfort and shortness of breath are the atypical picture, and neuropathy is why diabetes blunts the pain. Denying chest pain does not rule out ischemia; it raises the chance you will miss it.

options.text: Encourage rest in a quiet room and reassess her symptoms in one hour
options.rationale: Correct but premature An hour of ischemia is myocardium.

options.text: Assess for gastrointestinal causes first, since she denies chest pain
options.rationale: Near miss concept Uses the absence of the classic symptom as reassurance.

questions.takeaway: Three groups get atypical presentations: women, older adults, people with diabetes.
questions.strategy: When a stem names one of those three groups and a vague complaint, think heart before you think stomach.

questions.stem: A hospitalized patient reports crushing chest pressure. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Give aspirin 325 mg chewed as prescribed
Give sublingual nitroglycerin if the blood pressure allows
Obtain vital signs and start continuous cardiac monitoring
Stay with the patient and call for help
Recheck blood pressure and pain 5 minutes later
Obtain a 12 lead ECG

questions.takeaway: Airway, breathing and circulation come first with the nurse staying and calling for help. A brief assessment and monitoring follow, then a 12 lead ECG within 10 minutes, IV access, aspirin, nitroglycerin if the pressure allows, and a recheck in 5 minutes. The step people drop is the 5 minute recheck.
questions.strategy: Assessment and the ECG come before drugs, and the recheck closes the loop.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches a patient about nitroglycerin at home. Select all statements that show understanding.

options.text: I will keep the bottle in my car so it is always handy.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Heat and light degrade nitroglycerin.

options.text: I will carry them with me at all times.
options.rationale: Nitroglycerin is stored in its original dark bottle away from heat and light, carried at all times and replaced per the expiration date. Patches go on clean hairless skin, sites rotate, and they come off at night for a nitrate free period that prevents tolerance.

options.text: I will take one before an activity that usually brings on my chest pain.
options.rationale: Nitroglycerin is stored in its original dark bottle away from heat and light, carried at all times and replaced per the expiration date. Patches go on clean hairless skin, sites rotate, and they come off at night for a nitrate free period that prevents tolerance.

options.text: I will keep the tablets in the original dark glass bottle.
options.rationale: Nitroglycerin is stored in its original dark bottle away from heat and light, carried at all times and replaced per the expiration date. Patches go on clean hairless skin, sites rotate, and they come off at night for a nitrate free period that prevents tolerance.

options.text: I will remove my patch at night.
options.rationale: Nitroglycerin is stored in its original dark bottle away from heat and light, carried at all times and replaced per the expiration date. Patches go on clean hairless skin, sites rotate, and they come off at night for a nitrate free period that prevents tolerance.

options.text: I will apply my patch to the same spot every day.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sites are rotated to protect the skin.

questions.takeaway: Nitrate free time at night prevents tolerance.
questions.strategy: Look for statements about protecting the drug and preventing tolerance.

questions.stem: A patient's 12 lead ECG shows ST elevation in two contiguous leads. The first troponin is normal. What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: A stress test scheduled for the next morning
options.rationale: Near miss concept A stress test is never done during an active STEMI.

options.text: Opening the artery by PCI within 90 minutes
options.rationale: ST elevation in two contiguous leads is a STEMI, decided by the ECG. The goal is to open the artery with PCI within 90 minutes. Troponin may be normal early.

options.text: Discharge, since the first troponin is normal
options.rationale: Absolute language One normal troponin never rules out an MI, and ST elevation is diagnostic.

options.text: Waiting for a second troponin before treating
options.rationale: Correct but premature STEMI is decided by the ECG alone. Waiting for a troponin costs heart muscle.

questions.takeaway: Never wait for the troponin to treat ST elevation.
questions.strategy: When the ECG makes the diagnosis, a lab cannot overrule it.

questions.stem: A patient with chest pain has an SpO2 of 96% on room air. The student nurse asks whether to start oxygen. Which response is correct?

options.text: "Only if the patient asks for it first."
options.rationale: Near miss concept The decision is based on the saturation, not the request.

options.text: "Yes; MONA puts oxygen second."
options.rationale: Near miss concept MONA is a list, not an order, and oxygen is only for low saturation.

options.text: "No; give it if SpO2 is below 90%."
options.rationale: Oxygen is given only if SpO2 is below 90%. Extra oxygen at a normal saturation can narrow the coronary vessels.

options.text: "Yes; all chest pain gets oxygen."
options.rationale: Absolute language Extra oxygen at a normal saturation can narrow the coronary vessels.

questions.takeaway: No oxygen at a normal saturation.
questions.strategy: Reject any absolute rule. Check the threshold.

questions.stem: An older adult with diabetes has had new fatigue and nausea while resting for the last hour. There is no chest pain. Heart rate is 104/min, SpO2 is 95% and the skin is cool and damp. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Start oxygen at 4 L by nasal cannula and recheck the saturation.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Oxygen is only given when SpO2 is below 90%.

options.text: Give an antiemetic and reassess in 30 minutes.
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Treating the nausea delays recognizing a possible MI.

options.text: Stay, call for help, get a 12 lead ECG in 10 minutes.
options.rationale: Older adults and patients with diabetes often have atypical or silent MI. New symptoms at rest with tachycardia and cool damp skin call for an ECG within 10 minutes and the chest pain protocol.

options.text: Check the glucose, since this suggests hypoglycemia.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Glucose may be checked, but new symptoms at rest with tachycardia and diaphoresis in this patient are treated as ACS first.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult with diabetes, fatigue and nausea can be the MI.
questions.strategy: When the classic sign is missing, treat the most dangerous explanation first.

questions.stem: A patient took one nitroglycerin tablet for chest pain 5 minutes ago and the pain is worse. Which action is correct?

options.text: Drive to the nearest emergency department.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Driving with possible ACS is always wrong.

options.text: Call 911 now.
options.rationale: If chest pain is not better or is worse 5 minutes after the first dose, the patient calls 911, then takes a second dose while waiting.

options.text: Lie down and wait 30 minutes.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Waiting allows muscle to die.

options.text: Take two more tablets and then call 911 if the pain continues.
options.rationale: Correct but premature The call comes after the first dose fails, not after all three.

questions.takeaway: Call 911 after the first dose fails.
questions.strategy: Choose the earliest point help is called.

questions.stem: A patient's blood pressure was 128/78 mm Hg before the first sublingual nitroglycerin. Five minutes later the pressure is 96/60 mm Hg and the pain is 5 of 10. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Hold the next dose and notify the provider.
options.rationale: Nitroglycerin is held for a systolic below 100 mm Hg or a drop of 25 mm Hg from the last reading. The next dose depends on the pressure just taken.

options.text: Wait 15 minutes and give the second dose.
options.rationale: Near miss concept The hold parameter is the blood pressure, not timing.

options.text: Give the second dose because the pain persists.
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Pain persists, but the systolic is below 100 and fell by 32 points.

options.text: Give the second dose with the patient lying flat.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Positioning does not make a hypotensive patient safe for more nitroglycerin.

questions.takeaway: Hold nitro for systolic below 100 or a 25 point drop.
questions.strategy: Check both hold criteria before giving the next dose.

questions.stem: A patient reports crushing substernal pressure radiating to the left arm that started 40 minutes ago at rest and has not improved after one sublingual nitroglycerin. The patient is diaphoretic. Blood pressure is 142/88 mm Hg, SpO2 is 95% and the ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF. Complete the bow tie.

options.text: Start oxygen at 6 L by face mask
Give aspirin 325 mg chewed as prescribed
Wait for the troponin result before treatment
Give a fluid bolus for the diaphoresis
Prepare the patient for PCI
Stable angina
ST elevation myocardial infarction
Unstable angina
Pericarditis
Daily weight
ECG changes and cardiac rhythm
Blood pressure before each nitroglycerin dose
Blood glucose before meals
Lipid panel

questions.takeaway: Pain at rest that is not relieved by nitroglycerin with ST elevation in contiguous leads is a STEMI. Aspirin is given early and the artery is opened with PCI. Oxygen is not needed at 95%. Rhythm is watched because dysrhythmias are the leading cause of early death, and blood pressure is checked before each nitroglycerin dose. STEMI: aspirin, open the artery, watch the rhythm.
questions.strategy: The ECG makes the diagnosis; pick actions that restore flow, not ones that wait.

questions.stem: A patient who had a coronary stent placed 6 hours ago reports new chest pain. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Reassure the patient that discomfort is expected after a stent.
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Reassurance without assessment can miss a closed stent.

options.text: Help the patient walk to relieve the pain.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Activity increases demand on the heart.

options.text: Give acetaminophen for procedural soreness.
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Chest pain after a stent is acute closure until proven otherwise.

options.text: Obtain a 12 lead ECG and notify the provider now.
options.rationale: Chest pain after a stent is acute closure until proven otherwise. The nurse gets a 12 lead ECG and notifies the provider now.

questions.takeaway: Chest pain after a stent means closure until proven otherwise.
questions.strategy: Treat new pain after a procedure as a complication first.

questions.stem: A patient has had chest pressure when climbing stairs for 6 months that goes away with rest. Today the same pressure started while watching television. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: It is anxiety because the patient was resting.
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Pressure at rest in a patient with known angina is ACS until proven otherwise.

options.text: It is stable angina because the pressure feels the same as usual.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Stable angina comes with effort. Pain at rest means the artery has changed.

options.text: The pattern has changed, which suggests unstable angina, an acute coronary syndrome.
options.rationale: Stable angina comes with effort and is relieved by rest or nitroglycerin. Unstable angina is new, worsening or at rest. The key word is pattern: the same pressure starting at rest means the plaque has changed.

options.text: It is expected for a patient who has had angina for months.
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A familiar pain in a new setting is a change, not the expected course.

questions.takeaway: A change in the pattern is the warning.
questions.strategy: Compare today with the patient's own baseline pattern.

questions.stem: A patient with a new coronary stent is taking aspirin and clopidogrel and asks to stop the clopidogrel because of easy bruising. Which response is best?

options.text: "Switch to ibuprofen for the pain and stop the clopidogrel."
options.rationale: Near miss concept NSAIDs raise MI, stroke and heart failure risk and add bleeding risk.

options.text: "You can stop it for a few days until the bruising goes away."
options.rationale: Absolute language Stopping without the cardiologist can cause stent thrombosis.

options.text: "Bruising is expected with it, so you can simply ignore it."
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Bruising is expected in part but still needs to be reported, and stopping is not the patient's call.

options.text: "Do not stop it; that risks a stent clot. Call your cardiologist."
options.rationale: Dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and a P2Y12 inhibitor continues up to 12 months after a stent. It is never stopped without the cardiologist because the stent can clot.

questions.takeaway: Never stop clopidogrel without the cardiologist.
questions.strategy: When a drug protects a device, stopping it is the danger.

questions.stem: A patient is 3 hours after coronary artery bypass surgery. Chest tube drainage was 180 mL in the last hour. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Lower the head of the bed to reduce drainage.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Positioning does not stop bleeding.

options.text: Milk the tubing and recheck in 2 hours.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Drainage over 150 mL an hour is bleeding and needs reporting now.

options.text: Report the drainage to the provider as bleeding.
options.rationale: After CABG, chest tube drainage over 150 mL an hour is bleeding. Heavy drainage that suddenly stops with low BP, JVD and muffled heart sounds suggests tamponade.

options.text: Document it as expected after surgery.
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Some drainage is expected, but over 150 mL an hour is not.

questions.takeaway: Over 150 mL an hour from the chest tube is bleeding.
questions.strategy: Compare the amount with the threshold.

questions.stem: Two days after a myocardial infarction, a patient has a temperature of 38.2 °C. Other vital signs are stable and the lungs are clear. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: The patient is having a reaction to the aspirin.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fever is not an aspirin reaction.

options.text: The patient has an infection and needs blood cultures drawn now.
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism A temperature up to 38.9 °C for a few days after MI is inflammation, not infection, when nothing else points to an infection.

options.text: The patient is developing cardiogenic shock.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Shock would show low blood pressure, low urine and cold clammy skin.

options.text: Mild fever for a few days after an MI is expected.
options.rationale: A temperature up to 38.9 °C for a few days after an MI comes from inflammation in dead muscle, not infection.

questions.takeaway: Low grade fever after MI is inflammation.
questions.strategy: Recognize which abnormal finding is expected in context.

questions.stem: A patient becomes jaundiced with dark urine, and laboratory results show a rising unconjugated bilirubin and a falling hemoglobin. What is happening?

options.text: Slow bleeding into the gastrointestinal tract is lowering the counts
options.rationale: Near miss concept Blood loss drops the hemoglobin without the jaundice.

options.text: The liver has failed and can no longer conjugate or clear bilirubin
options.rationale: Near miss concept Liver failure can raise bilirubin and does not drop the hemoglobin this way.

options.text: The bone marrow has stopped producing enough new red blood cells
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would not raise bilirubin, since nothing is breaking down.

options.text: Red cells are breaking down faster than the marrow replaces them
options.rationale: Hemolysis dumps heme into the circulation. The liver cannot conjugate it fast enough, so unconjugated bilirubin rises and the patient yellows, while the breakdown products darken the urine. A reticulocyte count would be high, because the marrow is working hard to keep up, which is what separates destruction from a production failure.

questions.takeaway: Jaundice plus dark urine plus falling hemoglobin is destruction, not loss.
questions.strategy: The reticulocyte count is the question that separates these: high means destruction or loss, low means the marrow quit.

questions.stem: A patient with anemia has a very low reticulocyte count. What does this indicate?

options.text: A destruction problem, with cells lost faster than they are made
options.rationale: Near miss concept Destruction drives the count up, not down.

options.text: A recovering anemia, with the marrow now resting after a response
options.rationale: Near miss concept A rising reticulocyte count signals recovery; a low one signals the opposite.

options.text: Acute bleeding, with the marrow not yet signaled to respond
options.rationale: Near miss concept Bleeding raises the reticulocyte count as the marrow compensates.

options.text: A production problem, with the marrow not making new red cells
options.rationale: Reticulocytes are immature red cells, so the count tells you whether the marrow is responding. Low means the factory is down: marrow suppression, chemotherapy, missing erythropoietin, or missing building blocks. High means the marrow is working hard, which points to bleeding or hemolysis. It is the single most useful test for sorting anemias.

questions.takeaway: Low retics means the marrow quit. High retics means something is destroying or losing cells.
questions.strategy: This one value splits every anemia into two categories, which is why it is ordered.

questions.stem: Match each pattern to what it most suggests.

rows.text: Neutrophils below 1,000
Elevated eosinophils
Elevated lymphocytes
Elevated neutrophils

questions.takeaway: The differential tells you what the immune system is fighting. Neutrophils rise against bacteria, lymphocytes against viruses, eosinophils in allergy and parasitic disease. A neutrophil count under 1,000 is neutropenia, where infection becomes the deadliest risk and may arrive without a fever, especially in an older adult. A total white count can be normal while the differential is screaming. Read the parts.
questions.strategy: Ask which cell line moved, then ask what that cell line fights.

questions.stem: Select all of the findings that suggest a bleeding problem in a patient with thrombocytopenia.

options.text: Black tarry stool
options.rationale: Platelet problems bleed into skin and mucosa, which is why petechiae, gum bleeding and unexplained bruising cluster together, and why a black tarry stool means he is bleeding somewhere you cannot see. Last week's normal panel describes a patient who no longer exists, and brisk capillary refill is a normal finding.

options.text: Bleeding gums when brushing
options.rationale: Platelet problems bleed into skin and mucosa, which is why petechiae, gum bleeding and unexplained bruising cluster together, and why a black tarry stool means he is bleeding somewhere you cannot see. Last week's normal panel describes a patient who no longer exists, and brisk capillary refill is a normal finding.

options.text: A hemoglobin of 14.2 with a normal platelet count on last week's panel
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Last week does not describe today, which is why the count is repeated.

options.text: Petechiae over the lower legs
options.rationale: Platelet problems bleed into skin and mucosa, which is why petechiae, gum bleeding and unexplained bruising cluster together, and why a black tarry stool means he is bleeding somewhere you cannot see. Last week's normal panel describes a patient who no longer exists, and brisk capillary refill is a normal finding.

options.text: Brisk capillary refill in all extremities
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit A normal perfusion finding.

options.text: New bruising without remembered injury
options.rationale: Platelet problems bleed into skin and mucosa, which is why petechiae, gum bleeding and unexplained bruising cluster together, and why a black tarry stool means he is bleeding somewhere you cannot see. Last week's normal panel describes a patient who no longer exists, and brisk capillary refill is a normal finding.

questions.takeaway: Petechiae and mucosal bleeding point at platelets. Deep joint and muscle bleeding points at factors.
questions.strategy: One wrong option is an outdated value and the other is normal.

questions.stem: Select all of the nursing responsibilities during a red cell transfusion.

options.text: Stay with the patient and monitor closely during the first 15 minutes
options.rationale: The first fifteen minutes is when a hemolytic reaction declares itself, which is why you do not leave the room, and the slow start is deliberate. Blood runs with normal saline only; dextrose causes hemolysis and calcium containing solutions clot the line. Nothing is ever added to a blood product.

options.text: Obtain baseline vital signs immediately before starting
options.rationale: The first fifteen minutes is when a hemolytic reaction declares itself, which is why you do not leave the room, and the slow start is deliberate. Blood runs with normal saline only; dextrose causes hemolysis and calcium containing solutions clot the line. Nothing is ever added to a blood product.

options.text: Complete the infusion within the maximum time allowed by policy
options.rationale: The first fifteen minutes is when a hemolytic reaction declares itself, which is why you do not leave the room, and the slow start is deliberate. Blood runs with normal saline only; dextrose causes hemolysis and calcium containing solutions clot the line. Nothing is ever added to a blood product.

options.text: Prime and infuse the unit with dextrose 5 percent in water
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dextrose hemolyzes red cells; saline only.

options.text: Add the ordered premedication directly to the blood bag
options.rationale: Absolute language Nothing is added to a blood product.

options.text: Verify the unit against the order and the patient with a second qualified person
options.rationale: The first fifteen minutes is when a hemolytic reaction declares itself, which is why you do not leave the room, and the slow start is deliberate. Blood runs with normal saline only; dextrose causes hemolysis and calcium containing solutions clot the line. Nothing is ever added to a blood product.

questions.takeaway: Normal saline only, and stay for the first fifteen minutes. That is when it goes wrong.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options put the wrong substance into the blood or the line.

questions.stem: Select all of the measures for a patient with an absolute neutrophil count of 350.

options.text: Meticulous hand hygiene by everyone entering the room
options.rationale: Most of what infects a neutropenic patient is his own flora, so hand hygiene and food handling matter more than the mask on the door. A rectal temperature breaks mucosa and seeds bacteria directly into the bloodstream, which is why rectal anything is avoided here. Standing water in flowers and soil in potted plants carry Pseudomonas and Aspergillus.

options.text: Take the temperature rectally for accuracy
options.rationale: Near miss concept Breaks mucosa and introduces bacteria; use another route.

options.text: Avoid raw and undercooked foods and unwashed produce per facility policy
options.rationale: Most of what infects a neutropenic patient is his own flora, so hand hygiene and food handling matter more than the mask on the door. A rectal temperature breaks mucosa and seeds bacteria directly into the bloodstream, which is why rectal anything is avoided here. Standing water in flowers and soil in potted plants carry Pseudomonas and Aspergillus.

options.text: Report any temperature at or above the facility threshold immediately
options.rationale: Most of what infects a neutropenic patient is his own flora, so hand hygiene and food handling matter more than the mask on the door. A rectal temperature breaks mucosa and seeds bacteria directly into the bloodstream, which is why rectal anything is avoided here. Standing water in flowers and soil in potted plants carry Pseudomonas and Aspergillus.

options.text: Screen visitors for any infectious symptoms and exclude those who are ill
options.rationale: Most of what infects a neutropenic patient is his own flora, so hand hygiene and food handling matter more than the mask on the door. A rectal temperature breaks mucosa and seeds bacteria directly into the bloodstream, which is why rectal anything is avoided here. Standing water in flowers and soil in potted plants carry Pseudomonas and Aspergillus.

options.text: Allow fresh flowers and potted plants to brighten the room
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Standing water and soil carry Pseudomonas and Aspergillus.

questions.takeaway: Nothing rectal in a neutropenic patient. Not a thermometer, not a suppository.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options introduce organisms, one through broken mucosa and one from the environment.

questions.stem: A patient's platelet count is 28,000. Select all of the precautions the nurse should implement.

options.text: Encourage vigorous nose blowing to clear congestion
options.rationale: Near miss concept A direct cause of nosebleeds at this platelet count.

options.text: Use a soft toothbrush and avoid flossing
options.rationale: Below about 50,000 you start protecting mucosa and skin, and below 20,000 spontaneous bleeding becomes a real risk. Every precaution is about not breaking a surface: gums, skin, rectal mucosa, puncture sites. Aspirin inhibits the platelets he has left, and forceful nose blowing starts the epistaxis you are trying to prevent.

options.text: Use an electric razor rather than a blade
options.rationale: Below about 50,000 you start protecting mucosa and skin, and below 20,000 spontaneous bleeding becomes a real risk. Every precaution is about not breaking a surface: gums, skin, rectal mucosa, puncture sites. Aspirin inhibits the platelets he has left, and forceful nose blowing starts the epistaxis you are trying to prevent.

options.text: Avoid rectal temperatures and suppositories
options.rationale: Below about 50,000 you start protecting mucosa and skin, and below 20,000 spontaneous bleeding becomes a real risk. Every precaution is about not breaking a surface: gums, skin, rectal mucosa, puncture sites. Aspirin inhibits the platelets he has left, and forceful nose blowing starts the epistaxis you are trying to prevent.

options.text: Encourage aspirin for any headache that develops
options.rationale: Near miss concept Antiplatelet effect on top of a low count.

options.text: Apply prolonged pressure after any needle stick
