options.rationale: Below about 50,000 you start protecting mucosa and skin, and below 20,000 spontaneous bleeding becomes a real risk. Every precaution is about not breaking a surface: gums, skin, rectal mucosa, puncture sites. Aspirin inhibits the platelets he has left, and forceful nose blowing starts the epistaxis you are trying to prevent.

questions.takeaway: Aspirin in thrombocytopenia disables the few platelets the patient still has.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options would cause the bleeding the rest of the list prevents.

questions.topic: sorting the anemias with one value
questions.stem: Four patients have a hemoglobin of 9.2. Which laboratory value would most efficiently separate a production problem from a loss or destruction problem?
questions.objective: sorting the anemias with one value

options.text: The mean corpuscular volume
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sorts micro from macrocytic, which subdivides production problems rather than separating the two categories.

options.text: The reticulocyte count
options.rationale: Reticulocytes are immature red cells, so the count tells you whether the marrow is responding. High means it is working hard, which points to bleeding or hemolysis. Low means the factory is down: marrow suppression, missing erythropoietin or missing building blocks. Cell size and ferritin narrow the production causes, and bilirubin only helps if hemolysis is the answer, so all three come after the first split.

options.text: The ferritin
options.rationale: Near miss concept Excellent for iron deficiency specifically, which is one production cause among several.

options.text: The total bilirubin
options.rationale: Near miss concept Rises in hemolysis and is normal in blood loss, so it answers only part of the question.

questions.takeaway: One value splits every anemia in half. Order it first and the rest of the workup narrows.
questions.strategy: The question asks which is most efficient, not which is useful. Look for the one that sorts into two groups.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic kidney disease has a hemoglobin of 8.6 g/dL. What explains the anemia?

options.text: The kidneys make too little erythropoietin to drive red cell production
options.rationale: Erythropoietin is made in the kidney and tells the marrow to build red cells. When kidney tissue is lost, that signal fades and production falls, which is a production problem rather than a loss or destruction problem. That is also why treatment is an erythropoiesis stimulating agent plus iron rather than transfusion alone.

options.text: The kidneys are destroying red blood cells as the blood is filtered
options.rationale: Near miss concept Destruction happens in the spleen and the circulation, not by filtration.

options.text: Reduced kidney function blocks iron absorption from the gut entirely
options.rationale: Near miss concept Iron absorption is a gut and hepcidin story; the kidney contributes the hormone.

options.text: The kidneys are losing large numbers of red blood cells in the urine
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hematuria occurs in some kidney disease and is not the mechanism of this anemia.

questions.takeaway: The kidney is an endocrine organ. Losing it costs you red cells.
questions.strategy: Sort anemias into production, loss and destruction. The kidney belongs to production.

questions.stem: A patient reports fatigue and a craving for ice. Laboratory results show a low hemoglobin with small, pale red cells and a low ferritin. What does this indicate?

options.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency
options.rationale: Near miss concept Macrocytic, with numbness, tingling and glossitis.

options.text: Anemia of chronic kidney disease
options.rationale: Near miss concept Usually normocytic, from an erythropoietin shortage rather than empty iron stores.

options.text: Iron deficiency anemia
options.rationale: Small and pale is microcytic hypochromic, which is the iron picture, and a low ferritin confirms the stores are empty. Pica, the craving for ice or clay or starch, is a classic and easily missed clue. B12 makes the cells large rather than small and brings neurologic signs. The next question is always where the iron went, which usually means looking for blood loss.

options.text: Hemolytic anemia
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would bring jaundice, dark urine and a high reticulocyte count.

questions.takeaway: Microcytic and hypochromic is iron. Macrocytic with neuropathy is B12.
questions.strategy: Cell size splits these: small for iron, large for B12 and folate.

questions.stem: A patient with anemia reports numbness and tingling in both feet, and the nurse notes a smooth, beefy red tongue. Which deficiency does this suggest?

options.text: Vitamin K
options.rationale: Near miss concept A clotting problem, not an anemia.

options.text: Vitamin B12
options.rationale: Neurologic symptoms are what separate B12 from every other anemia. B12 is needed for myelin, so deficiency brings numbness, tingling and gait problems, with glossitis in the mouth. Iron and folate deficiency make a person tired and pale without the neuropathy. Absorption requires intrinsic factor, which is why gastric surgery and pernicious anemia cause it.

options.text: Folate
options.rationale: Near miss concept Also macrocytic, and it spares the nerves, which is the classic discriminator from B12.

options.text: Iron
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fatigue, pallor and pica, and no neurologic findings.

questions.takeaway: Anemia plus neuropathy is B12 until proven otherwise.
questions.strategy: Three anemias look alike until you ask about the feet.

questions.topic: the neutropenic patient who looks well
questions.stem: A patient on chemotherapy has an absolute neutrophil count of 320. He is afebrile and feels fine. Select all of the appropriate nursing measures.
questions.objective: the neutropenic patient who looks well

options.text: Reassure the patient that being afebrile means he is not infected
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Infection can precede the fever, and the local signs are gone, so afebrile proves nothing.

options.text: Encourage fresh salads and uncooked fruit for nutrition
options.rationale: Near miss concept Raw produce is restricted on many neutropenic protocols.

options.text: Perform thorough oral assessment and gentle oral care several times daily
options.rationale: Without neutrophils he cannot make pus, erythema or induration, so an infection will not show you where it is. What it can still do is produce a fever, and often that is the only sign it gives, which is why any single temperature at the threshold in a neutropenic patient is an emergency rather than something to recheck. Sometimes even the fever is absent and all you get is new confusion, malaise or a falling pressure. Rectal instrumentation breaks a mucosal barrier and seeds the bloodstream. The mouth is the most common portal. Raw produce carries organisms and is restricted on many protocols.

options.text: Perform meticulous hand hygiene and limit the number of people entering
options.rationale: Without neutrophils he cannot make pus, erythema or induration, so an infection will not show you where it is. What it can still do is produce a fever, and often that is the only sign it gives, which is why any single temperature at the threshold in a neutropenic patient is an emergency rather than something to recheck. Sometimes even the fever is absent and all you get is new confusion, malaise or a falling pressure. Rectal instrumentation breaks a mucosal barrier and seeds the bloodstream. The mouth is the most common portal. Raw produce carries organisms and is restricted on many protocols.

options.text: Assess frequently for subtle changes such as new confusion, hypotension or malaise
options.rationale: Without neutrophils he cannot make pus, erythema or induration, so an infection will not show you where it is. What it can still do is produce a fever, and often that is the only sign it gives, which is why any single temperature at the threshold in a neutropenic patient is an emergency rather than something to recheck. Sometimes even the fever is absent and all you get is new confusion, malaise or a falling pressure. Rectal instrumentation breaks a mucosal barrier and seeds the bloodstream. The mouth is the most common portal. Raw produce carries organisms and is restricted on many protocols.

options.text: Avoid rectal temperatures, suppositories and enemas
options.rationale: Without neutrophils he cannot make pus, erythema or induration, so an infection will not show you where it is. What it can still do is produce a fever, and often that is the only sign it gives, which is why any single temperature at the threshold in a neutropenic patient is an emergency rather than something to recheck. Sometimes even the fever is absent and all you get is new confusion, malaise or a falling pressure. Rectal instrumentation breaks a mucosal barrier and seeds the bloodstream. The mouth is the most common portal. Raw produce carries organisms and is restricted on many protocols.

questions.takeaway: No neutrophils means no pus and no localizing redness, so the fever may be the only sign you get. Treat it as an emergency.
questions.strategy: One wrong option reads an absent sign as safety; the other adds an exposure he cannot clear.

questions.stem: A patient with cirrhosis has a platelet count of 62,000 and an international normalized ratio of 2.1. He has not received any anticoagulant. What explains both findings?

options.text: Vitamin K deficiency from poor intake is the sole cause of both
options.rationale: Near miss concept Contributes to the coagulopathy and explains neither the platelets nor the full picture.

options.text: Heparin induced thrombocytopenia from exposure during this stay
options.rationale: Near miss concept He has had no heparin, and it would not raise the international normalized ratio.

options.text: The liver cannot make clotting factors; the spleen holds platelets
options.rationale: Two separate mechanisms in one organ system. Clotting factors are synthesized in the liver, so a failing liver lengthens the prothrombin time and raises the international normalized ratio without any anticoagulant. Portal hypertension enlarges the spleen, and an enlarged spleen traps platelets. Both are expected in advanced cirrhosis and together they make him a serious bleeding risk.

options.text: Disseminated intravascular coagulation is consuming both of them
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would consume fibrinogen and raise D dimer, with clinical bleeding and clotting together.

questions.takeaway: The liver makes the factors and portal hypertension traps the platelets. Both at once.
questions.strategy: No heparin in the stem rules out one option on its face, which is the detail to look for.

questions.stem: A patient receiving chemotherapy has a white blood cell count of 1,200 with a low neutrophil fraction. He is afebrile and feels well. What is the nursing priority?

options.text: Implement neutropenic precautions and monitor for infection even without fever
options.rationale: Neutrophils are what generate a fever, so a neutropenic patient can be septic and afebrile. That makes absence of fever meaningless and makes subtle changes, a new confusion, a drop in pressure, a vague malaise, the signs you actually act on. Fresh produce is restricted on many neutropenic protocols, not encouraged.

options.text: Place the patient on bleeding precautions
options.rationale: Near miss concept That follows the platelet count, which the stem does not give.

options.text: Encourage fresh fruit and vegetables to support recovery
options.rationale: Near miss concept Raw produce carries organisms and is restricted on many neutropenic protocols.

options.text: Reassure the patient that being afebrile means there is no infection
options.rationale: Near miss concept Uses the one sign this patient cannot mount as evidence of safety.

questions.takeaway: No neutrophils, no fever. Waiting for a temperature is waiting for nothing.
questions.strategy: The afebrile detail is placed there to reassure you. It should do the opposite.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic anemia from kidney disease has a hemoglobin of 7.4. He is ambulating without dyspnea, has no chest pain, and his heart rate is 78. What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Transfusion of two units today, since the hemoglobin is below 8
options.rationale: Near miss concept Treats a threshold, and two units is rarely the starting point even when transfusion is indicated.

options.text: Transfusion of one unit now, then reassessment of the hemoglobin
options.rationale: Near miss concept Correct practice when transfusion is indicated; he is asymptomatic and adapted.

options.text: No transfusion; expect erythropoiesis stimulating therapy and iron
options.rationale: A patient with chronic anemia has adapted over months, and he is asymptomatic at a number that would distress someone who dropped there in a day. Restrictive transfusion practice is the standard because transfusion carries real risks and, in kidney disease, repeated transfusion complicates future transplantation. Treat the cause, which is the missing erythropoietin, and transfuse for symptoms.

options.text: Transfusion only once the hemoglobin falls below 6 on a recheck
options.rationale: Near miss concept Another fixed threshold, in the other direction; symptoms decide.

questions.takeaway: Chronic anemia is tolerated far better than acute. Transfuse for symptoms, not for a threshold.
questions.strategy: A single numeric trigger is almost always the wrong answer in transfusion decisions.

questions.stem: A patient with a hemoglobin of 6.8 g/dL is short of breath at rest and has chest pain. What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Observation with a repeat count in the morning
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Watches a patient with demand ischemia overnight.

options.text: Transfusion of packed red blood cells
options.rationale: Symptoms decide, not the number alone. A patient with angina and dyspnea at rest is not delivering enough oxygen to the heart muscle right now, and iron or erythropoietin take weeks to build cells. One unit raises the hemoglobin by roughly 1 g/dL. The cause still gets worked up afterward.

options.text: Oral iron supplementation and dietary teaching
options.rationale: Correct but premature Weeks to work, in a patient with chest pain now.

options.text: An erythropoiesis stimulating agent
options.rationale: Correct but premature Also weeks, and it needs iron available to work with.

questions.takeaway: Transfuse for symptoms, not for a number.
questions.strategy: Two options are correct treatments on a timescale this patient does not have.

questions.stem: A patient on heparin for five days has a platelet count that has fallen from 210,000 to 48,000. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Hold the heparin and notify the provider immediately
options.rationale: A platelet drop of more than half after about five days of heparin is heparin induced thrombocytopenia. The counterintuitive part is that the danger is clotting, not bleeding: the antibodies activate the remaining platelets. Giving platelets adds fuel. The heparin stops and a non heparin anticoagulant takes over.

options.text: Recheck the platelet count in the morning to confirm the trend
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting The trend is already clear, and the delay is spent clotting.

options.text: Continue the heparin and institute bleeding precautions
options.rationale: Near miss concept Precautions are reasonable and the heparin is the cause.

options.text: Administer the ordered platelet transfusion
options.rationale: Near miss concept Feeds the clotting process in a patient whose problem is activation, not deficiency.

questions.takeaway: Low platelets on heparin means stop the heparin. The risk is thrombosis, not hemorrhage.
questions.strategy: The instinct to transfuse a low platelet count is exactly what this condition punishes.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a 78 year old patient at a clinic visit. Which statement by the patient requires follow up?

options.text: My hair has been thinning slowly on my legs for years
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Slow, even hair loss on the legs is a normal aging change.

options.text: My skin gets drier in the winter
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Dry skin is common in older adults and is not a reliable sign of a blood problem.

options.text: I bruise more easily now that I am older
options.rationale: New or easier bruising is a bleeding tendency to evaluate, not an aging change. Compare with the patient's baseline and assess for a platelet or clotting problem.

options.text: I have had the same energy level as last year
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Energy that matches the patient's own baseline is reassuring, not a finding to follow up.

questions.takeaway: Unexplained or easier bruising in an older adult is evaluated, not explained away by age. Slow leg hair loss and dry skin are expected.
questions.strategy: Find the statement that describes a change in bruising, bleeding, energy or infections; the patient's own explanation of aging does not make it normal.

questions.stem: A patient receiving chemotherapy has a platelet count of 22 K/µL this morning. The nurse reviews the note below. Select all of the findings that require follow up. Note: “0800. Alert and oriented. Pinpoint red spots scattered on both lower legs. Gums bleed when brushing teeth. Temperature 36.9 °C. Heart rate 84/min. Reports a new headache since last night, 7 of 10. Pink tinged urine in the urinal. Skin warm and dry. Ate 75% of breakfast.”

options.text: Alert and oriented
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Normal mental status is reassuring. A change such as confusion would need follow up because it can signal bleeding in the brain.

options.text: Pinpoint red spots scattered on both lower legs
options.rationale: These are petechiae, tiny bleeds in the smallest vessels. They are a classic sign that platelets are too low to plug small vessel injuries. Gum bleeding is mucous membrane bleeding from thrombocytopenia. It needs follow up and bleeding precautions. A new, severe headache in a patient with very low platelets can signal bleeding inside the skull. It is the most urgent finding in the note and is reported right away. Pink urine suggests hematuria, which is bleeding from the urinary tract caused by low platelets.

options.text: Gums bleed when brushing teeth
options.rationale: These are petechiae, tiny bleeds in the smallest vessels. They are a classic sign that platelets are too low to plug small vessel injuries. Gum bleeding is mucous membrane bleeding from thrombocytopenia. It needs follow up and bleeding precautions. A new, severe headache in a patient with very low platelets can signal bleeding inside the skull. It is the most urgent finding in the note and is reported right away. Pink urine suggests hematuria, which is bleeding from the urinary tract caused by low platelets.

options.text: Temperature 36.9 °C
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem This temperature is normal and does not need follow up right now.

options.text: Heart rate 84/min
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A heart rate of 84/min is within normal limits. Tachycardia would suggest blood loss or anemia.

options.text: Reports a new headache since last night, 7 of 10
options.rationale: These are petechiae, tiny bleeds in the smallest vessels. They are a classic sign that platelets are too low to plug small vessel injuries. Gum bleeding is mucous membrane bleeding from thrombocytopenia. It needs follow up and bleeding precautions. A new, severe headache in a patient with very low platelets can signal bleeding inside the skull. It is the most urgent finding in the note and is reported right away. Pink urine suggests hematuria, which is bleeding from the urinary tract caused by low platelets.

options.text: Pink tinged urine in the urinal
options.rationale: These are petechiae, tiny bleeds in the smallest vessels. They are a classic sign that platelets are too low to plug small vessel injuries. Gum bleeding is mucous membrane bleeding from thrombocytopenia. It needs follow up and bleeding precautions. A new, severe headache in a patient with very low platelets can signal bleeding inside the skull. It is the most urgent finding in the note and is reported right away. Pink urine suggests hematuria, which is bleeding from the urinary tract caused by low platelets.

options.text: Skin warm and dry
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Warm, dry skin is a normal finding.

options.text: Ate 75% of breakfast
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Good intake is reassuring and is not a sign of bleeding.

questions.takeaway: Low platelets show first as bleeding in small vessels and mucous membranes: petechiae, gum bleeding and hematuria. A new headache can mean bleeding in the brain and is reported right away.
questions.strategy: With a low platelet count, scan the note for any sign of bleeding in any system: skin, mouth, urine, stool and the brain.

questions.topic: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes
questions.stem: The nurse receives morning results for four patients. Which patient does the nurse assess first?
questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

options.text: Taking warfarin, INR 2.6, no bleeding noted
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem An INR of 2.6 is within the usual warfarin goal of 2 to 3, and there is no bleeding. This result is therapeutic and expected.

options.text: Neutrophils low after chemotherapy, temperature 38.4 °C
options.rationale: Neutropenia carries the highest infection risk, and a fever here can mean a fast moving infection the body cannot fight. This is the unstable patient and is seen first.

options.text: Heparin infusion, aPTT twice the control value
options.rationale: Near miss concept An aPTT about 1.5 to 2.5 times the control value is the usual therapeutic range for unfractionated heparin. This result is on target.

options.text: Enoxaparin daily, no aPTT ordered this week
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Enoxaparin usually needs no routine clotting test, and the aPTT does not measure its effect. No aPTT is expected, not a problem.

questions.takeaway: Neutropenia carries the highest infection risk, so a fever in a neutropenic patient is urgent. Therapeutic INR and aPTT values are expected findings.
questions.strategy: Sort each patient as expected or unexpected. Three results are on target for their drug; only one shows a new problem in a high risk patient.

questions.topic: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes
questions.stem: The nurse teaches a patient going home on enoxaparin injections. Which patient statements indicate understanding? Select all that apply.
questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

options.text: I will need an INR blood test every week
options.rationale: Absolute language INR monitors warfarin. Enoxaparin usually needs no routine clotting test, and INR and aPTT do not measure its effect.

options.text: I will report black, tarry stools right away
options.rationale: Black, tarry stool is melena, a sign of GI bleeding. Bleeding is the main risk of any anticoagulant. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen can cause GI bleeding and add to anticoagulant bleeding risk. Fish oil can increase bleeding, so supplements are part of the medication review. Enoxaparin can lower platelets, so bleeding, platelet counts and kidney function are monitored.

options.text: I will cut out leafy green vegetables completely
options.rationale: Absolute language Vitamin K intake matters for warfarin, and even then the teaching is to keep it consistent, not to cut it out. Enoxaparin works through antithrombin, not vitamin K.

options.text: I will check with my provider before taking ibuprofen
options.rationale: Black, tarry stool is melena, a sign of GI bleeding. Bleeding is the main risk of any anticoagulant. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen can cause GI bleeding and add to anticoagulant bleeding risk. Fish oil can increase bleeding, so supplements are part of the medication review. Enoxaparin can lower platelets, so bleeding, platelet counts and kidney function are monitored.

options.text: I will tell my provider that I take fish oil
options.rationale: Black, tarry stool is melena, a sign of GI bleeding. Bleeding is the main risk of any anticoagulant. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen can cause GI bleeding and add to anticoagulant bleeding risk. Fish oil can increase bleeding, so supplements are part of the medication review. Enoxaparin can lower platelets, so bleeding, platelet counts and kidney function are monitored.

options.text: I will keep my appointments for platelet count checks
options.rationale: Black, tarry stool is melena, a sign of GI bleeding. Bleeding is the main risk of any anticoagulant. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen can cause GI bleeding and add to anticoagulant bleeding risk. Fish oil can increase bleeding, so supplements are part of the medication review. Enoxaparin can lower platelets, so bleeding, platelet counts and kidney function are monitored.

questions.takeaway: Enoxaparin usually needs no routine INR or aPTT; teaching focuses on bleeding signs, avoiding NSAIDs and supplements that add bleeding risk, and platelet checks.
questions.strategy: Sort each statement by which anticoagulant it belongs to. INR checks and vitamin K diet rules belong to warfarin, not enoxaparin.

questions.topic: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes
questions.stem: A patient with pancytopenia after chemotherapy is admitted. The nurse reviews the admission findings. The nurse is admitting a patient with pancytopenia after chemotherapy. For each finding, indicate the risk it most directly signals.
questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

rows.text: Hemoglobin 7.4 g/dL
Petechiae across the chest
Platelets 18 K/µL
Neutrophils 0.4 K/µL
Temperature 38.2 °C with chills
Short of breath walking to the bathroom

questions.takeaway: Low hemoglobin means less oxygen carrying protein, so tissues receive less oxygen. This is the anemia part of pancytopenia. Petechiae are pinpoint bleeds in tiny vessels and are a classic sign of thrombocytopenia. A very low platelet count means platelets cannot form the initial plug at vessel injuries, so bleeding risk is high. Neutropenia carries the highest infection vulnerability because neutrophils are the first responders to bacteria. A count this low means almost no first responders are available. Fever with chills in a patient with low WBCs signals infection, even if other signs of inflammation are muted. Dyspnea and activity intolerance are how anemia shows itself: the heart and lungs work harder to deliver oxygen with too few RBCs. Pancytopenia lowers all three cell lines, so assess for bleeding, infection and poor oxygen delivery at every encounter. Each finding points back to the cell line that is low.
questions.strategy: Link each finding to the cell that is missing: platelets mean bleeding, neutrophils mean infection, RBCs and hemoglobin mean oxygen delivery.

questions.topic: Understand nursing care before and after bone marrow tests
questions.stem: Three hours after an iliac crest aspiration, a patient's platelets are 62 K/µL. A quarter size spot on the dressing is larger than 1 hour ago. What does the nurse do first?
questions.objective: Understand nursing care before and after bone marrow tests

options.text: Give an aspirin free analgesic
options.rationale: Correct but premature Pain control matters, but the growing spot is active bleeding, which comes first.

options.text: Mark the spot and recheck in 1 hour
options.rationale: Near miss concept Marking helps track drainage, but waiting an hour lets active bleeding continue in a patient with low platelets.

options.text: Change the dressing and assess the site
options.rationale: Near miss concept Removing the dressing disturbs the clot forming at the site and delays pressure.

options.text: Apply firm pressure to the site
options.rationale: Bleeding is the priority after a bone marrow procedure. A growing spot with low platelets is active bleeding, so pressure comes first, then the provider is notified.

questions.takeaway: After a bone marrow aspiration, bleeding is the priority. A growing spot on the dressing means active bleeding: apply firm pressure first.
questions.strategy: Spot the active problem (the spot is growing) and choose the action that stops it now.

questions.topic: Understand nursing care before and after bone marrow tests
questions.stem: A patient is scheduled for a bone marrow aspiration at the posterior iliac crest with sedation this afternoon. Which actions does the nurse include before the procedure? Select all that apply.
questions.objective: Understand nursing care before and after bone marrow tests

options.text: Apply firm pressure to the iliac crest
options.rationale: Correct but premature Pressure is applied after the needle is removed, to control bleeding. It is not a preparation step.

options.text: Position the patient prone or side lying as ordered
options.rationale: Prone or side lying exposes the posterior iliac crest, the usual site. Fasting is needed for local anesthetic alone, but when sedation is planned the patient is kept NPO as ordered. Bleeding risks and anticoagulants are reviewed before the procedure; the provider decides whether to hold them.

options.text: Keep the patient NPO as ordered because sedation will be used
options.rationale: Prone or side lying exposes the posterior iliac crest, the usual site. Fasting is needed for local anesthetic alone, but when sedation is planned the patient is kept NPO as ordered. Bleeding risks and anticoagulants are reviewed before the procedure; the provider decides whether to hold them.

options.text: Ask the provider whether warfarin is to be held
options.rationale: Prone or side lying exposes the posterior iliac crest, the usual site. Fasting is needed for local anesthetic alone, but when sedation is planned the patient is kept NPO as ordered. Bleeding risks and anticoagulants are reviewed before the procedure; the provider decides whether to hold them.

options.text: Withhold all fluids for 24 hours beforehand
options.rationale: Absolute language NPO time follows the sedation order; a 24 hour fluid restriction is not standard and risks dehydration.

options.text: Give aspirin for comfort before the procedure
options.rationale: Near miss concept Aspirin blocks platelets and raises bleeding risk; it is avoided around the procedure.

questions.takeaway: Before a bone marrow aspiration with sedation: position prone or side lying, keep NPO as ordered, and review anticoagulants with the provider. Pressure comes after; aspirin is avoided.
questions.strategy: Sort each option by timing and safety: preparation steps before, site pressure after, and nothing that adds bleeding risk.

questions.topic: Identify environmental exposures affecting blood health
questions.stem: A patient with new anemia gives this history. Which detail is most important for the nurse to follow up?
questions.objective: Identify environmental exposures affecting blood health

options.text: Eats red meat about once a week
options.rationale: Near miss concept Diet matters for blood health, but eating some red meat weekly is not a strong cause of new anemia and is not an exposure risk.

options.text: Takes a daily multivitamin with iron
options.rationale: Near miss concept A multivitamin with iron supports RBC production. It does not explain the anemia and is not a hazard.

options.text: Cooks on a gas stove with a working CO alarm
options.rationale: Near miss concept Carbon monoxide impairs hemoglobin function but does not lower the hemoglobin count, and a working alarm lowers the risk. This does not explain anemia.

options.text: Has been stripping paint in a 1920s home
options.rationale: Disturbing older paint during renovation is a common source of lead exposure. Lead interferes with heme production and can cause anemia, so the nurse follows up and anticipates a blood lead test.

questions.takeaway: Ask about home, work and hobby exposures in every hematologic history. Old paint disturbed during renovation is a classic lead source, and lead blocks heme production.
questions.strategy: Match the problem to the exposure that causes it. Anemia means less hemoglobin is being made, so look for the exposure that blocks heme production.

questions.topic: Recognize carbon monoxide poisoning and nursing priorities
questions.stem: A patient found in a closed garage with a running generator is receiving 100% oxygen by nonrebreather. Which finding most indicates the need for escalation and possible hyperbaric oxygen?
questions.objective: Recognize carbon monoxide poisoning and nursing priorities

options.text: Headache rated 7 of 10
options.rationale: Near miss concept Headache is the most common symptom of carbon monoxide poisoning; by itself it does not mark severe poisoning.

options.text: Nausea and one episode of vomiting
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nausea and vomiting are common symptoms and do not on their own signal a severe exposure.

options.text: SpO2 of 99% on the nonrebreather
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Pulse oximetry can read falsely normal in carbon monoxide poisoning, so this number neither reassures nor signals severity.

options.text: New confusion that is getting worse
options.rationale: Worsening neurologic status, such as new confusion or loss of consciousness, signals severe poisoning and is escalated promptly; severe cases may need hyperbaric oxygen.

questions.takeaway: In carbon monoxide poisoning, neurologic changes such as new or worsening confusion or loss of consciousness mark severe poisoning and are escalated promptly. A normal SpO2 means nothing here.
questions.strategy: Separate common symptoms from signs of severity: the brain is the organ that shows a dangerous oxygen shortage.

questions.topic: Recognize carbon monoxide poisoning and nursing priorities
questions.stem: Three people from one household arrive at the emergency department in winter. They spent the night heating a closed room with a kerosene heater. The patient the nurse is assessing reports a throbbing headache, nausea and dizziness, and the other two have the same headache. Heart rate is 112/min. SpO2 is 98% on room air. Complete the bow tie.
questions.objective: Recognize carbon monoxide poisoning and nursing priorities

options.text: Give an antiemetic and encourage oral fluids
Apply 100% oxygen by nonrebreather mask
Give oxygen at 2 L by nasal cannula
Notify the provider and expect a carboxyhemoglobin level
Titrate oxygen down to an SpO2 of 94%
Viral gastroenteritis
Carbon monoxide poisoning
Migraine headache
Influenza
Blood lead level
Pulse oximetry trend
Carboxyhemoglobin level
Hemoglobin level
Neurologic status and level of consciousness

questions.takeaway: 100% oxygen speeds removal of carbon monoxide from hemoglobin and is given right away, regardless of the SpO2 value. Prompt reporting is a priority, and a carboxyhemoglobin level confirms the diagnosis. Severe cases may need hyperbaric oxygen. Headache, nausea and dizziness in several people from one home heated by a fuel burning heater is the classic pattern. The SpO2 is falsely normal. This level confirms carbon monoxide poisoning and shows whether treatment is working as it falls. The brain is very sensitive to low oxygen. Confusion, seizures or loss of consciousness signal severe poisoning. Several people from one home with headache, nausea and dizziness near a fuel burning heater means carbon monoxide until proven otherwise. Give 100% oxygen, report promptly, and follow the carboxyhemoglobin level and neuro status, not the SpO2.
questions.strategy: Start with the condition: the shared symptoms and the heater make the pattern. Then pick actions and parameters that do not depend on the oximeter.

questions.topic: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes
questions.stem: Fifteen minutes into a unit of packed red blood cells, a patient reports chills and low back pain. Temperature rose from 36.9 °C to 38.3 °C. What does the nurse do first?
questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

options.text: Slow the transfusion and recheck vital signs in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Near miss concept Slowing still delivers incompatible cells. Chills, back pain and a fever early in a transfusion suggest a hemolytic reaction, so the transfusion is stopped, not slowed.

options.text: Give acetaminophen and continue the transfusion as ordered
options.rationale: Near miss concept Treating the fever hides the reaction while more incompatible blood is given.

options.text: Stop the transfusion and keep the IV line open
options.rationale: Stopping limits how much incompatible blood enters. Keeping the line open with 0.9% sodium chloride (new tubing) preserves access for treatment; then the provider and blood bank are notified.

options.text: Send a blood sample for a Coombs test before stopping
options.rationale: Correct but premature A Coombs test helps confirm a hemolytic reaction, but testing never comes before stopping the infusion.

questions.takeaway: Signs of a transfusion reaction mean stop the transfusion first, keep the line open with 0.9% sodium chloride, then notify the provider and blood bank. Typing, antibody screen and crossmatch exist to prevent this reaction.
questions.strategy: Every option except one keeps the blood running or delays stopping it. In a suspected reaction, the first action removes the cause.

questions.topic: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes
questions.stem: On heparin day 6, a patient's platelets are 98 K/µL, down from 260 K/µL on admission. The activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) is in the ordered range. What does the nurse do?
questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

options.text: Continue the infusion because the aPTT is therapeutic
options.rationale: Near miss concept A therapeutic aPTT shows the dose is right, but it says nothing about platelets. The drop is a separate safety problem.

options.text: Report the platelet drop to the provider promptly
options.rationale: Heparin can lower the platelet count, which is why platelets are monitored during therapy. A fall of more than half from baseline is reported promptly so the provider can decide whether to stop heparin.

options.text: Increase the infusion rate to prevent new clots
options.rationale: Near miss concept Raising the dose ignores the platelet drop and adds bleeding risk.

options.text: Recheck the platelet count again in 1 week
options.rationale: Near miss concept Waiting a week lets a dangerous drop continue.

questions.takeaway: During heparin therapy, the nurse watches the platelet count as well as the aPTT. A large drop from baseline is reported promptly, even when the aPTT is therapeutic.
questions.strategy: Two labs are given. Decide which one is the problem: the aPTT is in range, the platelets have fallen by more than half.

questions.topic: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes
questions.stem: A patient with neutropenia after chemotherapy is going home. Which teaching points does the nurse include? Select all that apply.
questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

options.text: Wash hands often and before eating
options.rationale: Hand hygiene is the most important protection when neutrophils, the first responders to bacteria, are low. Fever may be the only sign of infection when neutrophils are low, and it needs prompt care. Limiting exposure lowers the chance of catching an infection the body cannot fight well. Undercooked foods can carry bacteria that a neutropenic patient cannot fight off.

options.text: Check temperature daily and report 38 °C or higher right away
options.rationale: Hand hygiene is the most important protection when neutrophils, the first responders to bacteria, are low. Fever may be the only sign of infection when neutrophils are low, and it needs prompt care. Limiting exposure lowers the chance of catching an infection the body cannot fight well. Undercooked foods can carry bacteria that a neutropenic patient cannot fight off.

options.text: Avoid people who are sick, and crowds when possible
options.rationale: Hand hygiene is the most important protection when neutrophils, the first responders to bacteria, are low. Fever may be the only sign of infection when neutrophils are low, and it needs prompt care. Limiting exposure lowers the chance of catching an infection the body cannot fight well. Undercooked foods can carry bacteria that a neutropenic patient cannot fight off.

options.text: Use a soft toothbrush and an electric razor
options.rationale: Near miss concept These protect against bleeding from low platelets, a different cytopenia. Nothing here says platelets are low.

options.text: Take temperatures rectally for the most accurate result
options.rationale: Near miss concept Rectal temperatures can injure the mucosa and introduce bacteria; they are avoided in neutropenia.

options.text: Avoid raw or undercooked meat and eggs
options.rationale: Hand hygiene is the most important protection when neutrophils, the first responders to bacteria, are low. Fever may be the only sign of infection when neutrophils are low, and it needs prompt care. Limiting exposure lowers the chance of catching an infection the body cannot fight well. Undercooked foods can carry bacteria that a neutropenic patient cannot fight off.

questions.takeaway: Neutropenia carries the highest infection risk: teach hand hygiene, avoiding sick people, safe food handling, and to report a fever right away.
questions.strategy: Match each teaching point to the problem this patient has. Infection prevention fits neutropenia; bleeding precautions fit a low platelet count.

questions.topic: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes
questions.stem: After starting a daily spinach and kale smoothie, a patient on the same warfarin dose has an international normalized ratio (INR) of 1.5, down from 2.6. How does the nurse interpret this?
questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

options.text: New vitamin K intake is reducing warfarin's effect
options.rationale: Warfarin works by reducing the vitamin K dependent clotting factors. A sudden rise in vitamin K from leafy greens lets the liver make more factors, so the INR falls below goal.

options.text: The patient needs to stop eating leafy greens
options.rationale: Near miss concept Leafy greens do not have to be removed; the teaching is to keep vitamin K intake consistent.

options.text: The INR is in the expected range for warfarin
options.rationale: Near miss concept An INR of 1.5 is below the usual goal of 2 to 3, so the patient is less protected from clots.

options.text: The smoothie is raising the risk of bleeding
options.rationale: Near miss concept More vitamin K pushes toward clotting, not bleeding. A falling INR means less anticoagulant effect.

questions.takeaway: A sudden increase in vitamin K lowers warfarin's effect and the INR. Teach consistent vitamin K intake, not avoidance, and report the change to the provider.
questions.strategy: Link the new habit to how warfarin works: more vitamin K means more clotting factors, which means a lower INR.

questions.topic: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes
questions.stem: A patient taking warfarin reports black, tarry stools for 2 days and feels lightheaded when standing. The international normalized ratio (INR) is 4.8. Which action does the nurse take first?
questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

options.text: Teach the patient to avoid foods high in vitamin K
options.rationale: Near miss concept Vitamin K foods do not cause a high INR, and teaching does not address active bleeding.

options.text: Hold the warfarin dose and notify the provider
options.rationale: Melena with lightheadedness and an INR above goal is active GI bleeding from too much anticoagulant effect. The dose is held and the provider notified so reversal and a hemoglobin can be ordered.

options.text: Give the scheduled warfarin dose and recheck the INR tomorrow
options.rationale: Near miss concept Giving more anticoagulant to a bleeding patient worsens the bleed.

options.text: Collect a stool sample for occult blood testing
options.rationale: Near miss concept The stool is already black and tarry, which is visible blood. Testing for hidden blood delays action.

questions.takeaway: Melena plus an INR above goal on warfarin means active bleeding: hold the dose and notify the provider. Teaching and further testing come later.
questions.strategy: Find the active problem first. Black stools and lightheadedness show the patient is bleeding now, so the action must stop more anticoagulant and get help.

questions.stem: An 83 year old patient is newly confused 2 days after hip surgery. Temperature is 37.7 °C, crackles are present, and white blood cells are 8,400/mm3. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Report the findings as a possible infection
options.rationale: New confusion with crackles and a temperature rise suggests pneumonia. In older adults the WBC count may not rise with infection, so a normal count does not rule it out.

options.text: Document the confusion as expected after surgery in older adults
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem New confusion is a change from baseline, often the first sign of infection in an older adult, and is not assumed to be normal.

options.text: Reassure the family that the normal WBC rules out infection
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem This is the trap: aging blunts the WBC response, so the count can be normal with infection.

options.text: Recheck the temperature in 4 hours before reporting
options.rationale: Near miss concept Waiting delays care when several cues already point to infection.

questions.takeaway: In older adults the WBC count may not rise with infection. New confusion, a temperature rise and focal lung findings are reported even with a normal WBC.
questions.strategy: Weigh the cluster of cues against the one normal lab: the WBC is the unreliable piece in an older adult.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the admission note for a patient with fatigue. Select all of the findings that point to vitamin B12 deficiency anemia. Note: “Age 58. Reports increasing fatigue over 3 months. Has followed a strict vegan diet for 12 years and takes no supplements. Tongue is smooth and beefy red. Reports tingling and numbness in both feet. Skin is warm and dry. Hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL. Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) is elevated. Blood pressure 124/78.”

options.text: Has followed a strict vegan diet for 12 years and takes no supplements
options.rationale: Vitamin B12 comes from animal foods; a long vegan diet without supplements is the cause. A smooth, beefy red tongue is a classic sign of pernicious or B12 deficiency anemia. B12 deficiency damages nerves, and the damage can become permanent if untreated. B12 deficiency makes large (macrocytic) red cells, so the MCV is high. Iron deficiency would lower it.

options.text: Tongue is smooth and beefy red
options.rationale: Vitamin B12 comes from animal foods; a long vegan diet without supplements is the cause. A smooth, beefy red tongue is a classic sign of pernicious or B12 deficiency anemia. B12 deficiency damages nerves, and the damage can become permanent if untreated. B12 deficiency makes large (macrocytic) red cells, so the MCV is high. Iron deficiency would lower it.

options.text: Reports tingling and numbness in both feet
options.rationale: Vitamin B12 comes from animal foods; a long vegan diet without supplements is the cause. A smooth, beefy red tongue is a classic sign of pernicious or B12 deficiency anemia. B12 deficiency damages nerves, and the damage can become permanent if untreated. B12 deficiency makes large (macrocytic) red cells, so the MCV is high. Iron deficiency would lower it.

options.text: Skin is warm and dry
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Dry skin is common and not specific to B12 deficiency.

options.text: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) is elevated
options.rationale: Vitamin B12 comes from animal foods; a long vegan diet without supplements is the cause. A smooth, beefy red tongue is a classic sign of pernicious or B12 deficiency anemia. B12 deficiency damages nerves, and the damage can become permanent if untreated. B12 deficiency makes large (macrocytic) red cells, so the MCV is high. Iron deficiency would lower it.

options.text: Blood pressure 124/78
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A normal blood pressure does not point to any type of anemia.

questions.takeaway: B12 deficiency anemia shows as fatigue with a smooth beefy red tongue, tingling from nerve damage and a high MCV. A vegan diet without supplements is a common cause.
questions.strategy: Look for the three things that set B12 apart from other anemias: the diet, the nerve signs and the large cells.

questions.topic: Describe major blood components and their functions
questions.stem: The nurse reviews discharge teaching with a patient who had a splenectomy after a car crash. Which patient statement requires further teaching?
questions.objective: Describe major blood components and their functions

options.text: I will call my provider right away if I get a fever
options.rationale: Near miss concept Teaching: after splenectomy, infection can progress quickly, so a fever is reported right away.

options.text: I will stay up to date on my vaccines
options.rationale: Near miss concept Teaching: vaccines lower the higher infection risk that follows splenectomy.

options.text: I will tell new providers that I have no spleen
options.rationale: Near miss concept Teaching: providers need to know so they can treat infections early.

options.text: I can wait out a fever if I feel well
options.rationale: This needs correction. The spleen filters blood and helps fight infection; without it, infection and sepsis can develop fast, so every fever is reported.

questions.takeaway: After splenectomy, infection and sepsis risk rises because the spleen filters blood and helps with immune defense. Teach to report any fever right away and keep vaccines current.
questions.strategy: This is a negative question: find the statement that would put the patient at risk.

questions.stem: Three weeks after a Johnson & Johnson COVID vaccine, a patient calls the clinic. Which reported findings require immediate follow up? Select all that apply.

options.text: Severe headache that started yesterday
options.rationale: A new severe headache can signal a clot in the brain, a feature of vaccine induced thrombotic thrombocytopenia (VITT). Leg pain and swelling suggest a deep vein clot, one half of the VITT picture. Unexplained bruising points to low platelets, the other half of VITT. New shortness of breath can signal a pulmonary embolism from a vaccine related clot.

options.text: Sore arm at the injection site
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Arm soreness is an expected local effect in the first days after a vaccine, not a sign of clotting or low platelets.

options.text: Swelling and pain in one calf
options.rationale: A new severe headache can signal a clot in the brain, a feature of vaccine induced thrombotic thrombocytopenia (VITT). Leg pain and swelling suggest a deep vein clot, one half of the VITT picture. Unexplained bruising points to low platelets, the other half of VITT. New shortness of breath can signal a pulmonary embolism from a vaccine related clot.

options.text: New bruises without any injury
options.rationale: A new severe headache can signal a clot in the brain, a feature of vaccine induced thrombotic thrombocytopenia (VITT). Leg pain and swelling suggest a deep vein clot, one half of the VITT picture. Unexplained bruising points to low platelets, the other half of VITT. New shortness of breath can signal a pulmonary embolism from a vaccine related clot.

options.text: Mild fatigue the day after the shot
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Short lived fatigue right after vaccination is expected. The window that matters for VITT is 4 to 42 days later.

options.text: Shortness of breath when walking
options.rationale: A new severe headache can signal a clot in the brain, a feature of vaccine induced thrombotic thrombocytopenia (VITT). Leg pain and swelling suggest a deep vein clot, one half of the VITT picture. Unexplained bruising points to low platelets, the other half of VITT. New shortness of breath can signal a pulmonary embolism from a vaccine related clot.

questions.takeaway: VITT is clotting plus low platelets 4 to 42 days after an adenovirus vector COVID vaccine. Report severe headache, leg swelling, shortness of breath and unexplained bruising or bleeding right away.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding by timing and meaning: expected effects come in the first days; clot signs and bleeding signs weeks later are reported.

questions.topic: Identify environmental exposures affecting blood health
questions.stem: The occupational health nurse is reviewing the note for a refinery worker with fatigue. Select all of the findings that require follow up. Note: “Works 12 years at a refinery cleaning fuel storage tanks. Reports fatigue for 2 months. Smokes half a pack of cigarettes daily. Bruises appear on the arms without injury. Has had 3 sinus infections since spring. Wears hearing protection at work. Blood pressure 122/76 mm Hg. Hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL. Platelets 88 K/µL.”
questions.objective: Identify environmental exposures affecting blood health

options.text: Works 12 years at a refinery cleaning fuel storage tanks
options.rationale: Long exposure to gasoline vapors at a refinery is a benzene exposure, which disrupts blood cell production in the marrow. Cigarette smoke is another benzene source, adding to the work exposure. Unexplained bruising points to low platelets, which fits marrow disruption. Frequent infections suggest low white cells, another cell line the marrow is failing to make. A low platelet count confirms that the bruising has a cause and adds to the picture of marrow suppression.

options.text: Smokes half a pack of cigarettes daily
options.rationale: Long exposure to gasoline vapors at a refinery is a benzene exposure, which disrupts blood cell production in the marrow. Cigarette smoke is another benzene source, adding to the work exposure. Unexplained bruising points to low platelets, which fits marrow disruption. Frequent infections suggest low white cells, another cell line the marrow is failing to make. A low platelet count confirms that the bruising has a cause and adds to the picture of marrow suppression.

options.text: Bruises appear on the arms without injury
options.rationale: Long exposure to gasoline vapors at a refinery is a benzene exposure, which disrupts blood cell production in the marrow. Cigarette smoke is another benzene source, adding to the work exposure. Unexplained bruising points to low platelets, which fits marrow disruption. Frequent infections suggest low white cells, another cell line the marrow is failing to make. A low platelet count confirms that the bruising has a cause and adds to the picture of marrow suppression.

options.text: Has had 3 sinus infections since spring
options.rationale: Long exposure to gasoline vapors at a refinery is a benzene exposure, which disrupts blood cell production in the marrow. Cigarette smoke is another benzene source, adding to the work exposure. Unexplained bruising points to low platelets, which fits marrow disruption. Frequent infections suggest low white cells, another cell line the marrow is failing to make. A low platelet count confirms that the bruising has a cause and adds to the picture of marrow suppression.

options.text: Wears hearing protection at work
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hearing protection addresses noise, not a blood related exposure.

options.text: Blood pressure 122/76 mm Hg
options.rationale: Near miss concept This blood pressure does not point to a hematologic problem.

options.text: Platelets 88 K/µL
options.rationale: Long exposure to gasoline vapors at a refinery is a benzene exposure, which disrupts blood cell production in the marrow. Cigarette smoke is another benzene source, adding to the work exposure. Unexplained bruising points to low platelets, which fits marrow disruption. Frequent infections suggest low white cells, another cell line the marrow is failing to make. A low platelet count confirms that the bruising has a cause and adds to the picture of marrow suppression.

questions.takeaway: Benzene from gasoline, industrial emissions and cigarette smoke disrupts the marrow. Low counts in more than one cell line in an exposed worker are followed up, along with the exposures themselves.
questions.strategy: Highlight both the exposures and the findings that show the marrow is affected; leave out details unrelated to blood.

questions.topic: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes
questions.stem: A patient with type O positive blood is ordered one unit of red blood cells. At the bedside check, the unit is labeled A positive. What does the nurse do?
questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

options.text: Hang the unit slowly and stay for 15 minutes
options.rationale: Near miss concept Staying the first 15 minutes is correct for a compatible unit, but this unit is incompatible. Slow infusion still risks a hemolytic reaction.

options.text: Ask the patient whether they have had transfusions before
options.rationale: Near miss concept A transfusion history matters for antibodies, but it does not change the fact that this unit does not match.

options.text: Return the unit to the blood bank unused
options.rationale: An O patient has antibodies against A cells. A mismatched unit is never given; it goes back to the blood bank so the right unit can be issued.

options.text: Give it because both are Rh positive
options.rationale: Near miss concept Rh matching alone is not enough. ABO must also be compatible, and an O patient cannot receive A cells.

questions.takeaway: ABO/Rh typing, antibody screen and crossmatch exist to prevent a transfusion reaction. If the unit does not match at the bedside check, it is not given.
questions.strategy: Check both parts of the type: Rh matches, but ABO does not, and either mismatch stops the transfusion.

questions.stem: A patient with suspected leukemia has left upper abdominal fullness, petechiae on both legs and a platelet count of 34 K/µL. The nurse is observing a nursing student assess a patient with suspected leukemia. For each student action, indicate whether it is appropriate or requires the nurse to intervene.

rows.text: Palpates deeply under the left ribs to feel the spleen
Palpates lymph nodes gently and notes size
Asks about bleeding after brushing teeth
Applies brief pressure, then moves on after a blood draw
Uses a firm, tight blood pressure cuff on the same arm repeatedly
Inspects the skin and gums for bleeding

questions.takeaway: An enlarged spleen ruptures easily. The nurse does not palpate it when a hematologic problem is suspected; the provider assesses it. Gentle lymph node palpation is part of the hematologic assessment; document size, tenderness and whether the node moves. Gum bleeding is a platelet related finding worth asking about. With a known or suspected bleeding problem, pressure is held until the bleeding stops, which can take several minutes. Repeated, prolonged cuff pressure can cause bruising and petechiae with a low platelet count; handle the patient gently. Inspection for petechiae, bruising and gum bleeding is a key part of assessing a patient with low platelets. With a suspected hematologic problem, examine gently, do not palpate the spleen, and hold pressure on puncture sites until bleeding stops.
questions.strategy: For each action ask: could it cause bleeding or rupture in a patient with low platelets and an enlarged spleen?

questions.topic: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes
questions.stem: The nurse teaches a patient scheduled for a bone scan with an IV radioactive tracer. Which statements indicate understanding? Select all that apply.
questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

options.text: “I will need to lie still for about an hour during the scan.”
options.rationale: The scan itself takes about an hour of lying still on the table, so the teaching was understood. Extra fluids help flush the tracer out through the urine. Small amounts of tracer can set off airport radiation detectors for several days, so the patient may carry a note.

options.text: “I should keep away from my family for a week afterward.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept The tracer dose is small and short lived. No isolation from family is needed after a bone scan.

options.text: “I will drink extra water after the scan.”
options.rationale: The scan itself takes about an hour of lying still on the table, so the teaching was understood. Extra fluids help flush the tracer out through the urine. Small amounts of tracer can set off airport radiation detectors for several days, so the patient may carry a note.

options.text: “The tracer will be given to me as a pill.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept The tracer is usually injected IV, then the scan is done after it collects in bone.

options.text: “Airport screening may detect the tracer for a few days.”
options.rationale: The scan itself takes about an hour of lying still on the table, so the teaching was understood. Extra fluids help flush the tracer out through the urine. Small amounts of tracer can set off airport radiation detectors for several days, so the patient may carry a note.

questions.takeaway: A bone scan uses a small IV dose of radioactive tracer: lie still about an hour, drink water afterward, and expect that airport screening may detect it for several days. No isolation is needed.
questions.strategy: Judge each statement as true or false about a diagnostic tracer, which is a small dose that leaves through the urine.

questions.topic: Describe major blood components and their functions
questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a patient with advanced liver cirrhosis. Which findings does the nurse expect because of the liver's role in blood health? Select all that apply.
questions.objective: Describe major blood components and their functions

options.text: Platelet count above normal
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Platelets are often low in cirrhosis, because an enlarged spleen traps them. A high count is not expected.

options.text: Easy bruising on the arms
options.rationale: The liver makes most clotting factors. With fewer factors, small bumps bruise easily. The INR rises when the liver cannot make enough clotting factors, even without warfarin. Low clotting factors cause oozing from small mucosal injuries like brushing.

options.text: Shortened time for blood to clot
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fewer clotting factors make clotting slower, not faster.

options.text: Prolonged international normalized ratio
options.rationale: The liver makes most clotting factors. With fewer factors, small bumps bruise easily. The INR rises when the liver cannot make enough clotting factors, even without warfarin. Low clotting factors cause oozing from small mucosal injuries like brushing.

options.text: Gums that bleed when brushing teeth
options.rationale: The liver makes most clotting factors. With fewer factors, small bumps bruise easily. The INR rises when the liver cannot make enough clotting factors, even without warfarin. Low clotting factors cause oozing from small mucosal injuries like brushing.

questions.takeaway: The liver makes many plasma proteins and clotting factors. In liver failure, expect bruising, mucosal bleeding and a prolonged INR.
questions.strategy: Start from what the liver makes: clotting factors. Every correct finding is a result of having too few of them.

questions.topic: Explain clot formation and breakdown mechanisms
questions.stem: A patient with a new leg clot started on heparin asks, “Will this dissolve my clot?” Which response by the nurse is accurate?
questions.objective: Explain clot formation and breakdown mechanisms

options.text: “Heparin keeps the clot from growing while your body breaks it down.”
options.rationale: Heparin is an anticoagulant: it stops new fibrin from forming. The body's own fibrinolytic system, through plasmin, dissolves the existing clot over time.

options.text: “Yes, heparin dissolves the clot within the first few hours.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Heparin does not break down fibrin. Dissolving a clot quickly takes a fibrinolytic drug such as alteplase.

options.text: “Heparin thins the blood so the clot passes through your veins.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Heparin does not thin the blood or move the clot. A clot that travels is an embolism, which is a danger, not a goal.

options.text: “No, the clot will stay the same size for the rest of your life.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept The body's fibrinolytic system breaks clots down over weeks, so the clot usually shrinks.

questions.takeaway: Anticoagulants such as heparin stop new clot formation; they do not dissolve an existing clot. Fibrinolysis, through plasmin, breaks the clot down.
questions.strategy: Separate the two halves of hemostasis: formation and breakdown. Heparin acts on formation only, so any option claiming it dissolves or moves the clot is wrong.

questions.stem: A patient with severe anemia has hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL. Which finding requires immediate follow up?

options.text: Pale inner eyelids and nail beds
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Pallor is expected with this hemoglobin. It confirms the anemia but is not a new danger.

options.text: Chest pressure while walking to the bathroom
options.rationale: Chest pressure on exertion means the heart is not getting enough oxygen. Low hemoglobin can cause myocardial ischemia, so this needs immediate follow up.

options.text: Fatigue after showering in the morning
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Fatigue is expected with low oxygen carrying capacity. It is planned for, not escalated.

options.text: Cool hands and feeling cold in the room
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Feeling cold is a common, expected finding with anemia.

questions.takeaway: With severe anemia, pallor, fatigue and cold intolerance are expected; chest pain or pressure means the heart is short of oxygen and is escalated right away.
questions.strategy: Every option fits anemia, so ask which one threatens an organ. Chest pressure signals the heart is starved of oxygen.

questions.topic: Identify environmental exposures affecting blood health
questions.stem: A patient has new anemia with a low white blood cell count. Which history findings suggest an environmental exposure that can harm blood health? Select all that apply.
questions.objective: Identify environmental exposures affecting blood health

options.text: Drinks filtered tap water at home
options.rationale: Near miss concept Filtered water is not a known source of a blood harming exposure.

options.text: Sanded old paint while restoring a 1940s house
options.rationale: Old paint often contains lead, which blocks heme production and can cause anemia. Gasoline contains benzene, which damages the bone marrow and can lower blood cell counts. Cigarette smoke contains benzene, a marrow toxin.

options.text: Uses a fitness tracker every day
options.rationale: Absolute language A fitness tracker is not an exposure that affects the blood.

options.text: Works at a refinery handling gasoline products
options.rationale: Old paint often contains lead, which blocks heme production and can cause anemia. Gasoline contains benzene, which damages the bone marrow and can lower blood cell counts. Cigarette smoke contains benzene, a marrow toxin.

options.text: Smokes one pack of cigarettes a day
options.rationale: Old paint often contains lead, which blocks heme production and can cause anemia. Gasoline contains benzene, which damages the bone marrow and can lower blood cell counts. Cigarette smoke contains benzene, a marrow toxin.

questions.takeaway: Ask about home, work and hobby exposures: lead from old paint impairs hemoglobin production, and benzene from gasoline, industry and cigarette smoke harms the marrow.
questions.strategy: Match each history detail to a known blood toxin: lead or benzene. Anything that is not a source of either is not the answer.

questions.topic: Understand nursing care before and after bone marrow tests
questions.stem: Two hours after a posterior iliac crest bone marrow biopsy, a patient with platelets of 54 K/µL rates site pain 5 of 10 and asks for ibuprofen. A 2 cm spot on the dressing is unchanged from the last check. Blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg and heart rate 84/min. Which action is most appropriate?
questions.objective: Understand nursing care before and after bone marrow tests

options.text: Give the prescribed ibuprofen, since the bleeding is controlled
options.rationale: Near miss concept Ibuprofen is an NSAID that impairs platelet function. With platelets already low, it raises the risk of new bleeding at the site even if the spot is stable now.

options.text: Remove the dressing to look directly at the puncture site
options.rationale: Near miss concept Removing the pressure dressing this early can restart bleeding. An unchanged spot is assessed through the dressing.

options.text: Give the prescribed acetaminophen and apply an ice pack
options.rationale: Acetaminophen relieves pain without affecting platelets, and ice reduces bleeding and swelling at the site. The stable spot and normal vital signs show no active bleeding.

options.text: Notify the provider about the drainage on the dressing
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A small spot that has not grown, with normal vital signs, is expected after a biopsy. Calling about it delays the pain relief the patient needs now.

questions.takeaway: After a bone marrow biopsy in a patient with low platelets, avoid NSAIDs and aspirin, keep the pressure dressing on, use ice and a non platelet drug for pain, and watch for a growing stain.
questions.strategy: Two cues decide it: the low platelet count rules out the NSAID, and the unchanged spot with normal vital signs means there is nothing new to report.

questions.topic: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes
questions.stem: A patient is on day 6 of subcutaneous enoxaparin after a hip replacement. Which result does the nurse report to the provider?
questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

options.text: Activated partial thromboplastin time 31 seconds
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Enoxaparin is not monitored with the aPTT, so a normal aPTT is expected and says nothing about the drug's effect.

options.text: Hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, down from 12.1 g/dL
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A drop of 0.3 g/dL after hip surgery is small and expected from postoperative blood loss and fluids. It does not suggest new bleeding.

options.text: International normalized ratio 1.0
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem The INR measures warfarin effect. Enoxaparin does not change it, so a normal INR is expected.

options.text: Platelets 105 K/µL, down from 240 K/µL
options.rationale: A platelet count that falls by more than half 5 to 10 days into heparin or enoxaparin suggests heparin induced thrombocytopenia, which needs prompt report.

questions.takeaway: INR and aPTT do not measure enoxaparin. What is monitored is bleeding, kidney function and the platelet count; a fall of more than half 5 to 10 days in is reported.
questions.strategy: Ask which test actually tracks enoxaparin safety. The two clotting times are normal because the drug does not affect them; the platelet trend is the danger signal.

questions.topic: Recognize carbon monoxide poisoning and nursing priorities
questions.stem: A patient rescued from a house fire has a headache and is slow to answer questions. Pulse oximetry reads 99% on room air. Which action should the nurse take first?
questions.objective: Recognize carbon monoxide poisoning and nursing priorities

options.text: Apply 100% oxygen by nonrebreather mask
options.rationale: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin, and the pulse oximeter reads carboxyhemoglobin as oxygenated, so 99% is falsely reassuring. Headache and confusion after smoke exposure call for high flow oxygen right away.

options.text: Draw an arterial blood gas with carboxyhemoglobin
options.rationale: Near miss concept A carboxyhemoglobin level confirms the poisoning, but it is drawn after oxygen is started. Waiting for the result delays treatment.

options.text: Recheck the oxygen saturation on another finger
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Rechecking at another site gives the same falsely normal value. The problem is the device, not the finger.

options.text: Give acetaminophen for the headache as prescribed
options.rationale: Near miss concept The headache comes from poor oxygen delivery to the brain. Treating the symptom leaves the cause untreated.

questions.takeaway: In suspected carbon monoxide poisoning, a normal pulse oximetry value is not reassuring. Start 100% oxygen by nonrebreather first, then confirm with a carboxyhemoglobin level.
questions.strategy: Weigh the cue against the number: smoke exposure plus headache and confusion outranks a 99% value the device cannot get right.

questions.topic: Identify environmental exposures affecting blood health
questions.stem: The occupational health nurse reviews six workers with new blood or oxygen related complaints. For each worker, indicate the environmental exposure the nurse most suspects.
questions.objective: Identify environmental exposures affecting blood health

rows.text: Forklift driver in a closed propane warehouse with headaches that ease on weekends
Painter scraping old paint off a 1930s bridge with fatigue and anemia
Refinery worker with bruising, frequent infections and low counts of all blood cells
Home renovator sanding window frames in an older house, with abdominal pain and anemia
Mechanic who runs engines in a closed garage, now with headache and nausea
Gas station attendant with fatigue and a falling platelet count over a year

questions.takeaway: Fuel burning engines indoors produce carbon monoxide. Symptoms that improve away from the site point to an exposure at work. Old paint is a major lead source. Lead blocks heme production, which causes anemia. Benzene damages the bone marrow itself, so every cell line can fall: bleeding, infection and anemia. Sanding releases lead dust. Abdominal pain with anemia is a classic lead picture. Running engines in a closed space builds up carbon monoxide, which binds hemoglobin and starves tissues of oxygen. Gasoline vapor contains benzene, a marrow toxin. A slow fall in counts fits long term exposure. Lead comes from old paint, dust and soil and causes anemia by blocking heme production. Benzene from gasoline and industry harms the marrow, lowering all counts. Carbon monoxide from burning fuel in closed spaces binds hemoglobin.
questions.strategy: Match the source first, then confirm with the blood effect: anemia alone fits lead, all cell lines low fits benzene, headache that clears away from the site fits carbon monoxide.

questions.topic: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes
questions.stem: A patient on a continuous heparin infusion has an activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) of 118 seconds; the target range is 60 to 80 seconds. The patient has new oozing at an old IV site and the gums bleed with brushing. Blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg and heart rate 88/min. Which action should the nurse take first?
questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

options.text: Stop the heparin infusion
options.rationale: The aPTT is far above the target and new bleeding has started. Stopping the drug removes the cause, and heparin's short half life means its effect begins to fade within hours.

options.text: Give protamine sulfate as the heparin antidote
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Protamine reverses heparin, but it needs a provider order and is usually saved for serious bleeding. Stopping the infusion comes first and may be enough.

options.text: Recheck the aPTT in 1 hour to confirm the result
options.rationale: Near miss concept Confirming the value while the drug keeps running lets the bleeding worsen. The bleeding already confirms the result.

options.text: Apply firm pressure to the oozing IV site
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pressure helps the site, but the infusion is still delivering the drug that causes bleeding everywhere. Treat the cause first.

questions.takeaway: An aPTT far above target with new bleeding means stop the heparin first, then notify the provider, who may order protamine. Pressure and rechecks come after.
questions.strategy: Every option is reasonable, so ask which one stops the harm at its source. The vital signs are normal, so this is not yet a resuscitation; removing the drug is.

questions.stem: A patient with iron deficiency anemia started oral ferrous sulfate 2 weeks ago. Hemoglobin is 7.6 g/dL. At a clinic visit, the patient reports four concerns. Which finding requires immediate follow up?

options.text: Heart rate 118/min at rest and dizziness when standing
options.rationale: A fast resting heart rate with dizziness on standing shows the body can no longer compensate for the low hemoglobin. This patient may need a transfusion and an evaluation for ongoing blood loss.

options.text: Stools that have turned dark green to black
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Oral iron commonly darkens stools. Without a tarry texture, lightheadedness or a falling hemoglobin, this is expected.

options.text: A strong craving to chew ice throughout the day
options.rationale: Near miss concept Craving ice, called pica, is a typical sign of iron deficiency. It confirms the diagnosis but is not dangerous.

options.text: Tiredness after climbing one flight of stairs
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Fatigue with exertion is expected at this hemoglobin. It is planned for with rest periods, not escalated.

questions.takeaway: In anemia, pallor, fatigue, pica and dark stools on oral iron are expected. A fast resting heart rate with orthostatic dizziness means compensation is failing and needs follow up now.
questions.strategy: Three options are classic findings of iron deficiency or its treatment. The decision is which one shows the body is decompensating; a trap is the dark stool, which is expected on iron.

questions.topic: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes
questions.stem: A patient receiving chemotherapy has a temperature of 37.6 °C. White blood cells are 2,000/mm3 with 20% neutrophils and 5% bands. The patient asks whether visitors can come. Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes
