questions.takeaway: Maladaptive coping provides short-term relief and is harmful or ineffective over time: avoidance, substance use, disordered eating, excessive sleeping, withdrawal, aggression.
questions.strategy: One distractor uses the support system rather than retreating from it.

questions.stem: 1530: Patient is 34, admitted following a house fire two days ago in which her partner died. Sitting upright, staring at the door. Has not slept since admission. Startles when the door opens. Says she cannot stop seeing it. Has not eaten. States she does not see the point of any of this and that everyone would manage without her. Declines to contact her sister. Vital signs stable. No injuries requiring treatment. Chart notes she has a supportive sister two hours away. Select all of the findings that require immediate nursing action.

options.text: States she does not see the point of any of this and that everyone would manage without her
options.rationale: A statement suggesting suicidal ideation. Stay with the patient, complete screening per policy, ensure immediate safety, and notify the team. This is the finding that outranks everything else here. Two days without sleep worsens every other finding and is itself a safety issue. An immediate need. Identifying pain, food, rest, privacy and support is part of acute crisis care. Hypervigilance and intrusive images. Trauma responses are not overreactions and they need recognizing. options.rationale: Near miss concept A reassuring finding, and it is what tells you the problem is not physiological.

options.text: No injuries requiring treatment

questions.takeaway: In acute crisis: ensure safety first, screen for self-harm when it is mentioned or suspected, then identify immediate needs of pain, food, rest, privacy, information and support.
questions.strategy: One finding outranks all the others and it is easy to read past because it is phrased indirectly. Everyone would manage without her is not a throwaway line.

questions.stem: A patient in the emergency department after an assault says she does not want to talk about it and asks whether she can keep her coat on. Which response reflects trauma-informed care?

options.text: Tell her she can keep the coat on and ask what would make her more comfortable
options.rationale: Choice and safety are two of the elements. Offering options wherever possible restores control to someone who has just had it taken.

options.text: Encourage her to talk, since expressing what happened will help
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Overrides her stated preference. Listening without minimizing does not mean requiring disclosure.

options.text: Arrange for a family member to stay with her to provide support
options.rationale: Near miss concept Well intentioned, and it decides for her who should be present.

options.text: Explain that the coat must be removed for the examination
options.rationale: Near miss concept May be true eventually, and stated as an instruction it removes the choice she has just asked for.

questions.takeaway: Trauma-informed care: safety, trust, choice, collaboration, empowerment, respect.
questions.strategy: Three distractors decide something on her behalf. Ask which option returns a decision to her.

options.text: Whether the patient is currently safe
options.rationale: Named first, and safety is prioritized before anything else. Named, and appraisal determines the impact more than the event does. Named, and it covers support, finances and problem-solving skills. Named, and it changes both the risk and the plan. Named, and it covers sleep, eating and activity.

options.text: Adherence to healthy practices
options.rationale: Named first, and safety is prioritized before anything else. Named, and appraisal determines the impact more than the event does. Named, and it covers support, finances and problem-solving skills. Named, and it changes both the risk and the plan. Named, and it covers sleep, eating and activity.

options.text: Which defense mechanism the patient is using
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Defense mechanisms are useful to recognize and are not among the named assessment questions. They operate unconsciously and labelling them is not the assessment.

questions.takeaway: Assessment questions: patient safety, perception of the stressor, available coping resources, maladaptive coping used, and adherence to healthy practices.
questions.strategy: One distractor names a real concept from the chapter that is not one of the five assessment questions.

questions.stem: A nurse on an oncology unit reports feeling emotionally drained and numb, irritable with colleagues, and less affected by patients' distress than she used to be. She has made no errors. Which does this describe?

options.text: A situational crisis provoked by an external event
options.rationale: Near miss concept No single external event is described. This is cumulative.

options.text: Compassion fatigue from repeated exposure to others' suffering
options.rationale: Emotional and physical exhaustion from repeated exposure. Irritability, numbness, decreased empathy and reduced job satisfaction.

options.text: Second victim syndrome following an adverse patient event
options.rationale: Near miss concept Second victim syndrome follows involvement in a specific adverse event, error or injury. The stem states she has made no errors.

options.text: The alarm stage of the General Adaptation Syndrome
options.rationale: Near miss concept Alarm is the acute sympathetic response to an immediate threat.

questions.takeaway: Compassion fatigue: irritability, trouble sleeping, emotional numbness, decreased empathy, feeling overwhelmed or detached, reduced job satisfaction.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is second victim syndrome, and the stem rules it out by stating she has made no errors.

questions.stem: A nurse involved in a medication error that harmed a patient reports guilt, shame and loss of confidence in her practice. Which support is most appropriate?

options.text: Reassure her that errors happen to everyone
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic False reassurance. It minimizes what she is carrying and closes the conversation.

options.text: Recommend she take time away from clinical practice
options.rationale: Near miss concept May be appropriate and it is a decision, not a support. Offered first it can read as removal.

options.text: Recognize this as second victim syndrome and connect her with peer support
options.rationale: Emotional and psychological trauma after involvement in an adverse event. Naming it is what allows support to be offered rather than endured privately.

options.text: Advise her to focus on the system factors rather than her own role
options.rationale: Near miss concept System analysis is necessary and it does not address what she is feeling.

questions.takeaway: Second victim syndrome: guilt, shame, anxiety, fear and decreased confidence after involvement in an unexpected adverse event, error or injury.
questions.strategy: Two distractors redirect her away from the feeling. Ask what she has actually described.

questions.stem: A nurse plans care for a patient experiencing severe stress after a serious diagnosis. Which is the first priority in the plan?

options.text: Realistic, patient-centered outcomes
options.rationale: Near miss concept Named second. Outcomes matter once safety is established.

options.text: Including the patient in defining what better coping looks like
options.rationale: Near miss concept Named, and it follows safety rather than preceding it.

options.text: Collaborating with the health care team and support system
options.rationale: Near miss concept Named, and it is part of the plan rather than its first priority.

options.text: Safety
options.rationale: Prioritize safety first. Everything else in the plan depends on the patient being safe while it happens.

questions.takeaway: Planning for stress management: prioritize safety first, then realistic patient-centered outcomes, include the patient in defining better coping, collaborate, and set time frames that match the setting.
questions.strategy: All four appear on her planning slide. The question asks which comes first.

questions.stem: A nurse implements health promotion interventions for a patient with high stress. Which are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Teaching deep breathing and progressive muscle relaxation
options.rationale: Named relaxation techniques, alongside guided imagery. Named, and it lets the patient recognize the pattern rather than only the episode. Named, and it extends support beyond the admission. Environmental modification, named directly. Named alongside environmental modification.

options.text: Educating about stress triggers and self-management strategies
options.rationale: Named relaxation techniques, alongside guided imagery. Named, and it lets the patient recognize the pattern rather than only the episode. Named, and it extends support beyond the admission. Environmental modification, named directly. Named alongside environmental modification.

options.rationale: Named relaxation techniques, alongside guided imagery. Named, and it lets the patient recognize the pattern rather than only the episode. Named, and it extends support beyond the admission. Environmental modification, named directly. Named alongside environmental modification.

options.rationale: Named relaxation techniques, alongside guided imagery. Named, and it lets the patient recognize the pattern rather than only the episode. Named, and it extends support beyond the admission. Environmental modification, named directly. Named alongside environmental modification.

options.text: Scheduling rest breaks
options.rationale: Named relaxation techniques, alongside guided imagery. Named, and it lets the patient recognize the pattern rather than only the episode. Named, and it extends support beyond the admission. Environmental modification, named directly. Named alongside environmental modification.

options.text: Advising the patient to avoid thinking about the stressor
options.rationale: Near miss concept Avoidance is named as maladaptive coping. It provides short-term relief and does not help over time.

questions.takeaway: Health promotion interventions: relaxation techniques, education on triggers and self-management, referral, and environmental modification. Tailor them to the patient.
questions.strategy: One distractor recommends the first item on the maladaptive coping list.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old living alone tells the nurse she has stopped going out since her husband died, cannot get to the shops, and is worried about money. Which additional assessments does her age make important?

options.text: Depression, loneliness, safety and suicidal thoughts
options.rationale: Named specifically for older adults, and each of her stated concerns raises the likelihood of all four.

options.text: Cognitive function and memory
options.rationale: Near miss concept Relevant generally and not what her slide names for stress and coping in older adults.

options.text: Medication adherence and polypharmacy
options.rationale: Near miss concept Important in older adults generally and not what this chapter names for stress and coping.

options.text: Nutritional intake and weight
options.rationale: Near miss concept Worth assessing given she cannot reach the shops, and it is not among the four named.

questions.takeaway: In older adults, assess depression, loneliness, safety and suicidal thoughts when indicated. Daily stressors include health changes, transportation, finances, loss and home maintenance.
questions.strategy: Three distractors are genuinely important in older adults. The question asks what this chapter names for stress and coping.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old is admitted for observation after a collapse at work. Tests show no physical cause. She tells the nurse she has been working double shifts for seven months since her divorce, sleeps about four hours a night, has lost 9 kg, and has had three chest infections this year. She says she is coping and does not want to worry anyone. She has stopped seeing the friends she used to see weekly. Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem this represents, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Assess her safety, her perception of the stressor, and what support is available
Explore with her what reconnecting with her support system could look like
Reassure her that many people go through difficult periods after a divorce
Recommend she reduce her shifts and take time off work
Exhaustion stage with maladaptive coping and depleted resources
Alarm stage with sympathetic activation
An adventitious crisis following a catastrophic event
An expected adjustment reaction following divorce
Whether she reports her stress feels more manageable
Sleep, appetite and concentration at follow-up
Whether she can name three relaxation techniques
Whether her employer reduces her shift allocation

questions.takeaway: Seven months of sustained stress with fatigue, poor sleep, weight loss, frequent infection and social withdrawal. That is depletion, not adaptation. The named assessment questions, and safety comes first. Withdrawal plus exhaustion plus I do not want to worry anyone warrants direct enquiry. Support systems are one of the factors determining coping, and she has withdrawn from one she had. Asking the patient directly is the first evaluation step named on her slide. The symptoms that defined the exhaustion, reassessed. Named among the evaluation measures. Exhaustion presents physically: fatigue, poor sleep, impaired concentration and frequent illness. I am coping is what people say while depleted.
questions.strategy: Two condition distractors describe short-term responses. The timeframe of seven months and the three infections are what rule them out.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses a 44-year-old eight weeks after a workplace injury ended her employment. For each finding, indicate which nursing diagnosis it most directly supports.

rows.text: Pulse 104, respirations 22, unable to sit still, rechecking the clock before her disability hearing
Drinking most evenings since the injury, saying it is the only thing that stops the thoughts
States there is no point preparing for the hearing because the outcome has already been decided by other people
Has stopped returning the calls of the two friends who used to visit every week
Reports her chest tightens and her hands shake whenever an unknown number rings

questions.takeaway: Anxiety names the physiologic and felt experience of apprehension, which is what a pulse of 104 with restlessness and a somatic response to a ringing phone describes. Ineffective coping names a strategy that relieves in the short term and costs more later, which is what the evening drinking is. Powerlessness names the belief that one's own action cannot change the outcome, which is different from not wanting to act. Social isolation names the withdrawal from existing supports. All four are nursing diagnoses because each names her response, not a disease. Powerlessness and ineffective coping both look like giving up. Powerlessness is about whether she believes acting would matter; ineffective coping is about what she does instead.
questions.strategy: Two rows are anxiety, so you cannot pair one row to each column. Separate the belief from the behavior: "the outcome is already decided" is a belief about control, and drinking is a behavior that buys relief.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old has cared for her husband through eight months of advancing dementia with no respite. At a clinic visit her blood pressure is 152/94, up from a baseline of 118/74. She has lost 15 pounds, has had three respiratory infections since the spring, and says she cannot remember the last time she slept through a night. She adds quietly that some mornings she hopes she simply will not wake up. Complete the bow tie.

options.text: Ask her directly about thoughts of harming herself and remain with her while help is arranged
Notify the provider and follow the practice's safety protocol
Teach relaxation breathing and provide a caregiver support pamphlet
Reassure her that caregiver exhaustion is common and will ease once he is settled
Arrange respite care for her husband before she leaves today
Exhaustion stage of the general adaptation syndrome
Resistance stage of the general adaptation syndrome
Alarm stage of the general adaptation syndrome
Compassion fatigue
Her statements about safety and her willingness to accept help
Sleep, appetite, concentration and anxiety on reassessment
The stage of her husband's dementia
Her blood pressure at a routine visit in three months

questions.takeaway: Eight months is far past the alarm stage, and she is no longer maintaining function, which is what resistance means: her pressure, her weight, her sleep and her immune defenses have all given way together, and three infections in one season is what chronic stress does to immunity. Compassion fatigue is the term for a health care provider, not a family caregiver. Planning for stress management prioritizes safety first, so her remark is assessed directly rather than noted and moved past; asking plainly does not plant the idea, and leaving her alone to arrange services does. Evaluation of stress interventions reassesses sleep, appetite, concentration, anxiety and safety, which is why those are what you measure. Safety first is not a slogan about equipment. When a stressed patient says something about not wanting to wake up, that sentence is the assessment priority and everything else waits.
questions.strategy: Two distractors are genuinely good caregiver interventions, which is what makes them dangerous here: respite care and relaxation teaching both address the right problem at the wrong moment. Prioritize safety, then return to them.

questions.stem: Select all of the measures that make a bed to chair transfer safe.

options.text: Place the chair on the patient's stronger side
options.rationale: Brakes, bed height, footwear, and the chair positioned so the patient pivots toward the side that works. The two wrong options cause the two classic injuries: lifting under the axillae can dislocate a shoulder or damage the brachial plexus, and a patient holding your neck can pull you both down and injure your cervical spine. Use a gait belt instead.

options.text: Apply nonslip footwear
options.rationale: Brakes, bed height, footwear, and the chair positioned so the patient pivots toward the side that works. The two wrong options cause the two classic injuries: lifting under the axillae can dislocate a shoulder or damage the brachial plexus, and a patient holding your neck can pull you both down and injure your cervical spine. Use a gait belt instead.

options.text: Lock the bed and the wheelchair brakes
options.rationale: Brakes, bed height, footwear, and the chair positioned so the patient pivots toward the side that works. The two wrong options cause the two classic injuries: lifting under the axillae can dislocate a shoulder or damage the brachial plexus, and a patient holding your neck can pull you both down and injure your cervical spine. Use a gait belt instead.

options.text: Lower the bed so the patient's feet reach the floor
options.rationale: Brakes, bed height, footwear, and the chair positioned so the patient pivots toward the side that works. The two wrong options cause the two classic injuries: lifting under the axillae can dislocate a shoulder or damage the brachial plexus, and a patient holding your neck can pull you both down and injure your cervical spine. Use a gait belt instead.

options.text: Lift the patient under the axillae
options.rationale: Near miss concept Risks shoulder dislocation and brachial plexus injury.

options.text: Have the patient hold around the nurse's neck
options.rationale: Near miss concept Puts your cervical spine at risk and gives you no control.

questions.takeaway: Never lift under the arms and never let them hold your neck. Use a gait belt.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options are habits that injure the patient or the nurse.

questions.stem: Select all of the things the nurse should reassess immediately after repositioning a patient.

options.text: The patient's most recent laboratory results
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Relevant to the plan and unaffected by turning him.

options.text: The patient's dietary preferences
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Nothing about a turn changes them.

options.text: Pressure areas and skin
options.rationale: A turn can kink a catheter, pull a line, trap an arm under a hip or put a heel on a rail. Reassessment after the move takes thirty seconds and catches all of it. The two wrong options are real nursing concerns and have nothing to do with what just changed.

options.text: Body alignment
options.rationale: A turn can kink a catheter, pull a line, trap an arm under a hip or put a heel on a rail. Reassessment after the move takes thirty seconds and catches all of it. The two wrong options are real nursing concerns and have nothing to do with what just changed.

options.text: Tubes, lines and drains
options.rationale: A turn can kink a catheter, pull a line, trap an arm under a hip or put a heel on a rail. Reassessment after the move takes thirty seconds and catches all of it. The two wrong options are real nursing concerns and have nothing to do with what just changed.

options.text: Comfort and ability to breathe easily
options.rationale: A turn can kink a catheter, pull a line, trap an arm under a hip or put a heel on a rail. Reassessment after the move takes thirty seconds and catches all of it. The two wrong options are real nursing concerns and have nothing to do with what just changed.

questions.takeaway: What changed in the last minute is what you check. Lines move when patients do.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options are unrelated to the act of repositioning.

questions.stem: Select all of the measures that reduce cardiovascular complications of immobility.

options.text: Gradual position changes from lying to sitting to standing
options.rationale: The cardiovascular problems are orthostatic hypotension and venous stasis leading to clots. Staged position changes give the baroreceptors time. Leg exercises and compression devices move blood out of the calves. Dependent sitting pools it, and massaging a calf that may already contain a clot can send it to the lungs.

options.text: Adequate hydration where not contraindicated
options.rationale: The cardiovascular problems are orthostatic hypotension and venous stasis leading to clots. Staged position changes give the baroreceptors time. Leg exercises and compression devices move blood out of the calves. Dependent sitting pools it, and massaging a calf that may already contain a clot can send it to the lungs.

options.text: Ankle pumps and other leg exercises
options.rationale: The cardiovascular problems are orthostatic hypotension and venous stasis leading to clots. Staged position changes give the baroreceptors time. Leg exercises and compression devices move blood out of the calves. Dependent sitting pools it, and massaging a calf that may already contain a clot can send it to the lungs.

options.text: Massaging the calves to improve venous return
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dangerous. A clot you do not know about dislodges.

options.text: Prolonged sitting with the legs dependent
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pools blood in the legs, which is the problem you are preventing.

options.text: Sequential compression devices
options.rationale: The cardiovascular problems are orthostatic hypotension and venous stasis leading to clots. Staged position changes give the baroreceptors time. Leg exercises and compression devices move blood out of the calves. Dependent sitting pools it, and massaging a calf that may already contain a clot can send it to the lungs.

questions.takeaway: Never massage a calf to improve circulation. That is how an undiagnosed clot becomes an embolism.
questions.strategy: One wrong option causes the stasis and the other can kill the patient.

questions.stem: Select all of the complications a nurse should anticipate in a patient on prolonged bedrest.

options.text: Constipation from decreased gastrointestinal motility
options.rationale: Immobility touches nearly every system. Lungs do not expand and secretions pool. Blood pools and the baroreceptor response dulls. Protein breaks down faster than it is built. The gut slows. Bone demineralizes rather than strengthening, and appetite usually falls rather than rises.

options.text: Negative nitrogen balance and loss of lean muscle
options.rationale: Immobility touches nearly every system. Lungs do not expand and secretions pool. Blood pools and the baroreceptor response dulls. Protein breaks down faster than it is built. The gut slows. Bone demineralizes rather than strengthening, and appetite usually falls rather than rises.

options.text: Increased bone density from reduced mechanical stress
options.rationale: Near miss concept Backwards. Bone needs weight bearing, and without it calcium leaves.

options.text: Increased appetite from the lowered metabolic demand
options.rationale: Near miss concept Appetite typically drops, which compounds the protein loss.

options.text: Atelectasis from decreased lung expansion and retained secretions
options.rationale: Immobility touches nearly every system. Lungs do not expand and secretions pool. Blood pools and the baroreceptor response dulls. Protein breaks down faster than it is built. The gut slows. Bone demineralizes rather than strengthening, and appetite usually falls rather than rises.

options.text: Orthostatic hypotension and venous stasis
options.rationale: Immobility touches nearly every system. Lungs do not expand and secretions pool. Blood pools and the baroreceptor response dulls. Protein breaks down faster than it is built. The gut slows. Bone demineralizes rather than strengthening, and appetite usually falls rather than rises.

questions.takeaway: Immobility is not rest. It is a slow injury to seven systems.
questions.strategy: The two wrong options both describe the body getting stronger from doing nothing. It never does.

questions.stem: Match each complication to the system it affects.

rows.text: Atelectasis from retained secretions
Renal calculi from urinary stasis and calcium
Depression and loss of self concept
Orthostatic hypotension on standing

questions.takeaway: Immobility touches metabolic, respiratory, cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, urinary, integumentary and psychosocial systems. The urinary one surprises students: lying flat means urine pools in the renal pelvis instead of draining, and the calcium leaving the bones has to go somewhere, so stones form. Bone demineralization and urinary stasis combine into stones. That is why the two appear together.
questions.strategy: For any immobility question, walk the seven systems rather than reaching for the obvious one.

questions.stem: Select all of the metabolic changes that occur with prolonged immobility.

options.text: Decreased appetite
options.rationale: Metabolic demand falls, so the body stops building and starts breaking down. Protein catabolism outpaces intake, which is negative nitrogen balance, and it shows up as lost muscle and as wounds that will not heal. Calcium leaves unloaded bone. Appetite typically drops, which makes the protein problem worse.

options.text: Altered calcium metabolism as bone demineralizes
options.rationale: Metabolic demand falls, so the body stops building and starts breaking down. Protein catabolism outpaces intake, which is negative nitrogen balance, and it shows up as lost muscle and as wounds that will not heal. Calcium leaves unloaded bone. Appetite typically drops, which makes the protein problem worse.

options.text: An increase in basal metabolic rate
options.rationale: Near miss concept Demand falls with inactivity, so the rate goes down.

options.text: Loss of lean muscle mass
options.rationale: Metabolic demand falls, so the body stops building and starts breaking down. Protein catabolism outpaces intake, which is negative nitrogen balance, and it shows up as lost muscle and as wounds that will not heal. Calcium leaves unloaded bone. Appetite typically drops, which makes the protein problem worse.

options.text: Negative nitrogen balance from protein breakdown exceeding intake
options.rationale: Metabolic demand falls, so the body stops building and starts breaking down. Protein catabolism outpaces intake, which is negative nitrogen balance, and it shows up as lost muscle and as wounds that will not heal. Calcium leaves unloaded bone. Appetite typically drops, which makes the protein problem worse.

options.text: Improved glucose tolerance
options.rationale: Near miss concept Immobility worsens insulin resistance.

questions.takeaway: Negative nitrogen balance is why an immobile patient does not heal, even on a good diet.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options describe metabolism improving with inactivity. It does the opposite.

questions.stem: Select all of the enzyme levels that rise with muscle injury or disease.

options.text: Serum albumin
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data A protein, not an enzyme, and it reflects nutrition and oncotic pressure.

options.text: Lactate dehydrogenase
options.rationale: Damaged muscle leaks its enzymes into the blood. CK-MM is the skeletal muscle isoenzyme, distinct from CK-MB which points to the heart. LDH, AST and aldolase are nonspecific and rise with muscle damage too. Albumin and the platelet count are not enzymes and answer different questions.

options.text: Aspartate aminotransferase
options.rationale: Damaged muscle leaks its enzymes into the blood. CK-MM is the skeletal muscle isoenzyme, distinct from CK-MB which points to the heart. LDH, AST and aldolase are nonspecific and rise with muscle damage too. Albumin and the platelet count are not enzymes and answer different questions.

options.text: Aldolase
options.rationale: Damaged muscle leaks its enzymes into the blood. CK-MM is the skeletal muscle isoenzyme, distinct from CK-MB which points to the heart. LDH, AST and aldolase are nonspecific and rise with muscle damage too. Albumin and the platelet count are not enzymes and answer different questions.

options.text: Creatine kinase MM
options.rationale: Damaged muscle leaks its enzymes into the blood. CK-MM is the skeletal muscle isoenzyme, distinct from CK-MB which points to the heart. LDH, AST and aldolase are nonspecific and rise with muscle damage too. Albumin and the platelet count are not enzymes and answer different questions.

options.text: Platelet count
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data A cell count, unrelated to muscle breakdown.

questions.takeaway: CK-MM is muscle, CK-MB is heart. The suffix is the organ.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options are standard labs that answer different questions.

questions.stem: Select all of the findings a nurse should report immediately.

options.text: New numbness or tingling below an injury
options.rationale: The red flags are all neurovascular and all distal. A cool pale limb, lost pulses, new paresthesia, lost movement and swelling that is outrunning the clock mean the circulation or the nerve is being compressed, and the window to save the limb is hours. Fading bruising is normal healing.

options.text: Rapidly increasing swelling
options.rationale: The red flags are all neurovascular and all distal. A cool pale limb, lost pulses, new paresthesia, lost movement and swelling that is outrunning the clock mean the circulation or the nerve is being compressed, and the window to save the limb is hours. Fading bruising is normal healing.

options.text: Mild soreness that improves with repositioning
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Improving with a position change is reassuring.

options.text: Absent or diminished pulses distal to the site
options.rationale: The red flags are all neurovascular and all distal. A cool pale limb, lost pulses, new paresthesia, lost movement and swelling that is outrunning the clock mean the circulation or the nerve is being compressed, and the window to save the limb is hours. Fading bruising is normal healing.

options.text: Bruising that is fading from purple to yellow
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem That is the normal sequence of a resolving bruise.

options.text: Sudden loss of movement in the extremity
options.rationale: The red flags are all neurovascular and all distal. A cool pale limb, lost pulses, new paresthesia, lost movement and swelling that is outrunning the clock mean the circulation or the nerve is being compressed, and the window to save the limb is hours. Fading bruising is normal healing.

questions.takeaway: Every red flag here is something that is getting worse quickly, measured below the injury.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options describe things improving on schedule.

questions.stem: A patient with severe acute respiratory distress syndrome is placed prone. What is the rationale?

options.text: It reduces the risk of pressure injury over the sacrum
options.rationale: Near miss concept It unloads the sacrum and loads the face, chest and knees instead.

options.text: It improves oxygenation by changing ventilation and perfusion
options.rationale: Face down, the dependent posterior lung units that were compressed open up and ventilation distributes more evenly against the blood flow already going there. It is a guideline recommended intervention in moderate to severe ARDS, used alongside lung protective low tidal volume ventilation rather than instead of it. The pressure risk shifts to the face, chest and knees, which then need their own plan.

options.text: It makes airway suctioning easier for the nursing staff
options.rationale: Near miss concept It makes airway access harder, which is part of the risk.

options.text: It is more comfortable for a patient who is deeply sedated
options.rationale: Near miss concept Comfort is not the indication.

questions.takeaway: Prone is a gas exchange intervention. It creates a new set of pressure points, it does not remove them.
questions.strategy: Two of the wrong options treat a treatment for the lungs as if it were about the skin or convenience.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a patient with a dense hemiplegia after a stroke. What is the most important nursing measure to prevent contractures?

options.text: Keep the affected limbs elevated on pillows all day
options.rationale: Near miss concept Positioning helps alignment and does not move the joint through its range.

options.text: Apply heat to the affected joints before each repositioning to reduce any stiffness
options.rationale: Near miss concept May ease stiffness and is not what prevents the shortening.

options.text: Do passive range of motion to the affected limbs several times daily
options.rationale: A contracture is permanent shortening of muscle and tendon, and it forms because the joint never goes through its range. The patient cannot move that side, so you move it for him. Elevation and heat are comfort measures, and exercising the good side does nothing for the joints that are stiffening.

options.text: Encourage active range of motion on the unaffected side
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Good for the side that is already moving.

questions.takeaway: If the patient cannot move the joint, someone has to. Otherwise the joint closes.
questions.strategy: Two options work on the limb that is not at risk, or on comfort rather than range.

questions.stem: A patient has a long leg cast that immobilizes the knee and is on bedrest. Which exercise can he do to maintain strength in that leg?

options.text: Quadriceps setting, tightening the muscle without joint motion
options.rationale: Isometric contraction tightens the muscle with no joint movement, which is exactly what you need around an immobilized or painful joint. It maintains static strength and joint stability. Everything else listed requires the knee to move, which the cast prevents.

options.text: Active assistive range of motion at the casted knee joint
options.rationale: Near miss concept Still moves the joint.

options.text: Isotonic straight leg lifts against gravity several times daily
options.rationale: Near miss concept Isotonic requires joint movement, which the cast prevents.

options.text: Resistance band work through full knee extension and flexion
options.rationale: Near miss concept Full extension through a cast is not possible.

questions.takeaway: Isometric is the one you can do inside a cast.
questions.strategy: Three options all move a joint that is immobilized.

questions.stem: A nurse positions a patient in supported Fowler position. What does the support need to accomplish?

options.text: Maximize chest expansion by extending the neck backward
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hyperextension compromises the airway.

options.text: Allow hip and knee flexion while keeping the spinal curves
options.rationale: Alignment means supporting the spine's natural curves, not flattening them. Hips and knees flex slightly so the patient does not slide down the bed, which is what creates shear at the sacrum. A hyperextended neck compromises the airway rather than opening the chest.

options.text: Keep the spine completely straight from the neck to the pelvis
options.rationale: Near miss concept Flattens the lumbar curve, which causes pain and poor mechanics.

options.text: Keep both legs fully extended to prevent hip contractures
options.rationale: Near miss concept Full extension in Fowler position makes the patient slide and shear.

questions.takeaway: Support the curves the spine already has. Straight is not the same as aligned.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options straighten something that is supposed to be curved or flexed.

questions.topic: types of exercise and range of motion
questions.stem: A nurse supports a patient's arm while the patient moves it through the available range himself. How should this be documented?
questions.objective: types of exercise and range of motion

options.text: Passive range of motion
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is you doing all of it for a patient who cannot move the joint.

options.text: Active range of motion
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is the patient with no help at all.

options.text: Isometric exercise
options.rationale: Near miss concept No joint movement occurs in isometric work, and here the arm is moving.

options.text: Active assistive range of motion
options.rationale: Range of motion is sorted by who generates the movement. Active is the patient alone, passive is you moving a limb the patient cannot move, and active assistive is both, with the patient doing what he can and you making up the difference. Isometric is different again: the muscle contracts and the joint does not move at all, which is what you use around a painful or immobilized joint.

questions.takeaway: Ask who is generating the movement. That is the whole distinction.
questions.strategy: Three options are range of motion and one is an exercise type, which is the first sort to make.

questions.stem: A patient can lift her arm off the bed and hold it against gravity, but it drops when the nurse applies light resistance. What strength grade is this?

options.rationale: Near miss concept Full strength, which the resistance test just ruled out.

The scale turns on gravity and resistance. Grade 2 moves only with gravity eliminated, grade 3 moves against gravity but not against resistance, grade 4 holds against some resistance, and grade 5 is full strength. She clears gravity and fails resistance, so she is a 3.
Near miss concept Grade 4 holds against some resistance, and hers gave way.
Near miss concept Grade 2 cannot lift against gravity at all and only slides sideways.

questions.takeaway: Three is the gravity line. Below it the limb cannot lift itself.
questions.strategy: Decide first whether the limb beat gravity. That splits the scale in half before you think about resistance.

questions.stem: An older adult with kyphosis is being assessed for fall risk. How does the kyphosis contribute?

options.text: It shifts the center of gravity forward
options.rationale: Aging brings osteoporosis, stiffer cartilage, less ROM, muscle atrophy, and slower movement. Kyphosis shifts the center of gravity forward, which raises fall risk.

options.text: It lowers the center of gravity and widens the base
options.rationale: Near miss concept Kyphosis shifts the center of gravity forward, not lower; a forward shift makes balance harder.

options.text: It reduces muscle mass in the legs
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Muscle atrophy is a separate change of aging; kyphosis acts through posture.

options.text: It causes orthostatic hypotension on standing
options.rationale: Near miss concept Orthostatic hypotension is a cardiovascular change, not a result of spinal curvature.

questions.takeaway: Kyphosis pitches the body forward.
questions.strategy: Pick the option that explains the mechanism for this specific change, not another change of aging.

questions.stem: Which mobility task can the nurse delegate to assistive personnel?

options.text: Performing the Bedside Mobility Assessment Tool before a first time up
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Setting the BMAT level stays with the nurse; delegating it is outside the UAP's role.

options.text: Evaluating a patient's activity tolerance after ambulation
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Interpreting the vital sign response and recovery is a nursing assessment.

options.text: Performing the neurovascular check on a newly casted leg
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope The neurovascular check stays with the nurse.

options.text: Walking a stable patient whom the nurse has already assessed
options.rationale: A UAP can reposition and walk a stable patient you have assessed. The BMAT level, activity tolerance, and the neurovascular check stay with you.

questions.takeaway: UAP moves the patient; you judge the patient.
questions.strategy: Any option that asks for assessment or evaluation stays with the RN.

questions.stem: A nurse performs the Bedside Mobility Assessment Tool. The patient sits at the edge of the bed unassisted for more than 2 minutes, reaches across midline and shakes the nurse's hand, and can straighten each knee and point the toes. He cannot lift his buttocks off the bed for a count of 5. What level is he?

options.text: Level 1, total assist
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is failing sit and shake, and he sat unassisted and shook your hand.

options.text: Level 3, moderate assist
options.rationale: BMAT is a ladder and the patient is assigned the level of the test he FAILS. He passed sit and shake and passed stretch and point, then could not lift his buttocks for a count of 5, so he fails the stand test and is Level 3, moderate assist. He has some lower extremity strength and not enough to progress safely toward walking.

options.text: Level 2, maximum assist
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is failing stretch and point, and he extended both legs and pointed his toes.

options.text: Level 4, minimum or standby assist
options.rationale: Near miss concept Requires advancing a step, which he never reached.

questions.takeaway: The level is the test he failed, not the last one he passed.
questions.strategy: Walk the ladder up until something fails. That failure names the level.

questions.stem: A patient's heart rate rises from 78 to 128 during ambulation and is still 118 five minutes after he sits down. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: Poor activity tolerance, since the heart rate did not recover
options.rationale: A rise with exertion is expected. The measure of tolerance is recovery: how fast the rate, respirations and oxygenation come back toward baseline once the activity stops. Five minutes later at 118 says the demand exceeded what his heart could supply. The answer is to grade the activity down, not to stop it.

options.text: A normal exertional response for a deconditioned patient
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem The rise is expected; the failure to recover is not.

options.text: Evidence that the patient should be placed on strict bedrest
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would worsen the deconditioning that caused this.

options.text: An expected finding that requires no change to the plan
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Ignores the recovery failure.

questions.takeaway: Tolerance is about recovery, not about the peak.
questions.strategy: The bedrest option is wrong even when tolerance is poor, because immobility makes it worse.

questions.stem: A patient returns from knee arthroscopy. What is the nursing priority?

options.text: Neurovascular checks of the operative leg, documented each time
options.rationale: Anything done to a limb puts the circulation and the nerves below it at risk, and neurovascular assessment is the priority monitoring after arthroscopy. Teach the patient to report what you are watching for: swelling, severe pain, signs of thrombophlebitis and signs of infection.

options.text: Applying heat to the knee to reduce postoperative stiffness
options.rationale: Near miss concept Heat increases swelling in the acute postoperative period.

options.text: Keeping the knee fully extended for the first 24 hours
options.rationale: Near miss concept Positioning is per the surgeon, and immobilizing in extension is not routine.

options.text: Full weight bearing as soon as the patient is fully awake
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Weight bearing status is ordered, not assumed.

questions.takeaway: After anything done to a limb, the assessment is always distal.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options prescribe an activity or a position the surgeon has not ordered.

questions.stem: A patient who has been on bedrest for five days is being gotten up for the first time. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Stand him straight up from lying flat with two staff members assisting on each side
options.rationale: Near miss concept Staff catch him when he faints. They do not prevent the drop.

options.text: Apply compression devices and then walk him right away
options.rationale: Near miss concept Compression helps venous return and does not replace the staged change.

options.text: Have him stand quickly, since a short transition prevents dizziness
options.rationale: Near miss concept Exactly backwards; speed is what causes it.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed, then dangle at the edge before standing
options.rationale: Five days down dulls the baroreceptor response, so blood pools when he sits up and his pressure drops before his body corrects it. Staged position changes with a pause at each stage give the reflex time to catch up. Dangling is not a courtesy; it is the assessment.

questions.takeaway: Change position in stages and let each one settle.
questions.strategy: Any option that shortens the transition misunderstands why the dizziness happens.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a patient who has been on bedrest for two weeks. Which finding indicates a developing complication that requires intervention?

options.text: The patient's foot rests in plantar flexion and resists dorsiflexion
options.rationale: That is foot drop, a plantar flexion contracture, and it becomes permanent if the tendon shortens. The fix is prevention: neutral alignment, supportive devices and range of motion. Once the foot will not come back to neutral, walking is in jeopardy even after the rest of the recovery goes well.

options.text: The patient's calves are symmetric and nontender
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data A normal finding, and worth noting given the clot risk.

options.text: The patient needs a rest break partway through range of motion exercises
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Reduced activity tolerance is expected after two weeks down.

options.text: The patient reports stiffness that eases after a few minutes of movement
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Deconditioning stiffness that loosens with motion.

questions.takeaway: A contracture is the one immobility complication you cannot undo with time.
questions.strategy: Three of these are expected in a deconditioned patient. One is a joint being lost.

questions.stem: A patient has had a total hip replacement with a posterior approach. Which position should the nurse prevent?

options.text: Hip flexion beyond 90 degrees with adduction and internal rotation
options.rationale: That combination is how a posterior hip dislocates, and it is also what happens every time someone sits on a low toilet, bends to pick something off the floor, or crosses their legs. The precautions follow directly: no flexion past 90, no adduction past midline, no internal rotation, an abduction wedge, a raised toilet seat and a high chair.

options.text: Supine with the operative leg in neutral alignment
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Also correct and desirable.

options.text: Hip abduction with a wedge pillow between the legs
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit That is the protective position you want.

options.text: Sitting in a high chair with the knees below the hips
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Exactly the seating you arrange, to keep flexion under 90.

questions.takeaway: Flexion past 90 with adduction and internal rotation is the dislocating position. Everything you teach follows from it.
questions.strategy: Three options are the positions you are deliberately maintaining.

questions.stem: A patient is scheduled for a bone scan. What should the nurse include in teaching?

options.text: Expect to be in an enclosed tube and hold completely still
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is magnetic resonance imaging, which also needs metal screening.

options.text: Report any allergy to iodine or shellfish before the scan
options.rationale: Near miss concept That belongs to iodinated contrast studies, not to a radioisotope scan.

options.text: Drink extra fluids afterward to help excrete the isotope
options.rationale: A bone scan uses a radioactive isotope that concentrates where bone activity is increased, so it picks up occult fractures, infection, tumor and unexplained bone pain. The teaching point is fluids afterward to clear it. Iodine allergy screening belongs to contrast studies such as a contrast computed tomography scan, and the enclosed tube is magnetic resonance imaging.

options.text: Remain nothing by mouth for 8 hours before the scan
options.rationale: Near miss concept Not required for a bone scan.

questions.takeaway: Extra fluids after a bone scan. That is the teaching point they test.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options belong to other studies, which is what the item is sorting.

questions.stem: A patient has been on bedrest for four days. Select all of the nursing measures that address the complications of immobility.

options.text: Cough, deep breathe and use the incentive spirometer hourly while awake
options.rationale: Each correct option targets a different system: skin, circulation and muscle, lungs, and the protein balance behind all of it. The catheter is the trap, because it does make toileting easier and it adds an infection risk and removes a reason to get up. And a continuous 45 degrees creates shear at the sacrum, which is why 30 or less is the target when the condition allows.

options.text: Ankle pumps, quadriceps setting and progressive activity as tolerated
options.rationale: Each correct option targets a different system: skin, circulation and muscle, lungs, and the protein balance behind all of it. The catheter is the trap, because it does make toileting easier and it adds an infection risk and removes a reason to get up. And a continuous 45 degrees creates shear at the sacrum, which is why 30 or less is the target when the condition allows.

options.text: Ensure adequate protein and fluid intake
options.rationale: Each correct option targets a different system: skin, circulation and muscle, lungs, and the protein balance behind all of it. The catheter is the trap, because it does make toileting easier and it adds an infection risk and removes a reason to get up. And a continuous 45 degrees creates shear at the sacrum, which is why 30 or less is the target when the condition allows.

options.text: Reposition on a schedule and offload the heels
options.rationale: Each correct option targets a different system: skin, circulation and muscle, lungs, and the protein balance behind all of it. The catheter is the trap, because it does make toileting easier and it adds an infection risk and removes a reason to get up. And a continuous 45 degrees creates shear at the sacrum, which is why 30 or less is the target when the condition allows.

options.text: Keep the head of the bed at 45 degrees continuously for lung expansion
options.rationale: Near miss concept Continuous 45 degrees shears the sacrum; 30 or less when the condition allows.

options.text: Insert a urinary catheter to reduce the effort of toileting
options.rationale: Near miss concept Convenience is not an indication; it adds infection risk and reduces mobility.

questions.takeaway: A catheter inserted for convenience is a device that will cause its own complication.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options make the nursing easier at the patient's expense.

questions.stem: A patient with hypertension and heart disease has a leg cast and is being taught quadriceps setting. What should the nurse keep in mind?

options.text: Isometric exercise raises blood pressure; use caution and monitor
options.rationale: Isometric exercise is the pick for a cast or painful joint, but it raises blood pressure. The slide calls it safe for casts and sore joints; in hypertension or heart disease you use it with caution.

options.text: Isometric exercise is not allowed for a joint immobilized in a cast
options.rationale: Near miss concept The opposite: isometric exercise is the choice for a cast, because the muscle tightens while the joint stays still.

options.text: Isometric exercise lowers blood pressure by relaxing the muscle
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sustained contraction raises blood pressure; that is why heart disease calls for caution.

options.text: Isometric exercise builds no strength, so it is safe for anyone
options.rationale: Near miss concept Building no strength describes passive ROM, not isometric exercise.

questions.takeaway: Isometric fits the cast; caution with the heart.
questions.strategy: Two facts are true at once here. The answer keeps the indication and adds the exception.

questions.stem: A patient has been on bed rest for 7 days. Select all of the findings that suggest a complication of immobility.

options.text: Crackles, a low grade fever, and a falling SpO₂
options.rationale: Immobility hits every system at once, so a new finding in an immobile patient is an immobility complication until proven otherwise. Crackles, low grade fever, and falling SpO₂ suggest atelectasis or pneumonia. A warm, swollen calf suggests a clot from venous stasis. Nonblanchable redness over the sacrum is a pressure injury. Slow GI motility causes constipation.

options.text: A warm, swollen calf on one side
options.rationale: Immobility hits every system at once, so a new finding in an immobile patient is an immobility complication until proven otherwise. Crackles, low grade fever, and falling SpO₂ suggest atelectasis or pneumonia. A warm, swollen calf suggests a clot from venous stasis. Nonblanchable redness over the sacrum is a pressure injury. Slow GI motility causes constipation.

options.text: Nonblanchable redness over the sacrum
options.rationale: Immobility hits every system at once, so a new finding in an immobile patient is an immobility complication until proven otherwise. Crackles, low grade fever, and falling SpO₂ suggest atelectasis or pneumonia. A warm, swollen calf suggests a clot from venous stasis. Nonblanchable redness over the sacrum is a pressure injury. Slow GI motility causes constipation.

options.text: A modest rise in heart rate with repositioning that settles within a few minutes
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A modest heart rate rise that settles quickly is good activity tolerance.

options.text: No bowel movement for 4 days
options.rationale: Immobility hits every system at once, so a new finding in an immobile patient is an immobility complication until proven otherwise. Crackles, low grade fever, and falling SpO₂ suggest atelectasis or pneumonia. A warm, swollen calf suggests a clot from venous stasis. Nonblanchable redness over the sacrum is a pressure injury. Slow GI motility causes constipation.

options.text: Strength graded 5 of 5 and equal on both sides
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Full strength equal on both sides is the normal comparison, not a complication.

questions.takeaway: Match each finding to its system.
questions.strategy: Walk through the systems: respiratory, cardiovascular, skin, GI. The two wrong options are normal findings dressed up as concerns.

questions.stem: An assistive personnel reports, "The patient walked all the way to the door and back. Activity tolerance is great." What does the nurse need to judge the patient's activity tolerance?

options.text: Heart rate, SpO2 and symptoms during activity, and recovery time
options.rationale: Activity tolerance is the heart rate, respiratory rate, SpO₂, dyspnea, fatigue, pain, dizziness, and how fast the patient recovers. A modest heart rate rise that settles within a few minutes is good tolerance.

options.text: The exact number of feet the patient walked to the door and back
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Distance says nothing on its own; the body's response decides tolerance.

options.text: Whether the patient says he wants to walk again later today
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Motivation matters for the plan, but it is not a measure of tolerance.

options.text: The patient's mobility assessment level recorded on admission
options.rationale: Near miss concept BMAT sets the level of help, not how the body handles the activity.

questions.takeaway: Distance is not tolerance.
questions.strategy: Pick the physiologic data. Anything that measures the task rather than the body is the trap.

questions.stem: A patient feels a pop at the back of the ankle while running. The calf muscle still tightens when the patient tries to move, but the pull no longer reaches the heel bone. The patient cannot point the foot. Which structure is most likely torn?

options.text: A ligament, which joins one bone to another bone
options.rationale: Near miss concept A ligament holds bone to bone and steadies a joint. The break here is between a muscle and a bone, so the link that failed is not bone to bone.

options.text: A tendon, which joins a muscle to a bone
options.rationale: Movement needs a chain: the muscle contracts, a tendon carries that pull to the bone, and the bone moves at a joint. A tendon is the cord that joins muscle to bone. Ask: where did the chain break? Here the muscle still contracts and the heel bone does not move, so the break sits between them, in the tendon. A ligament is the band that joins bone to bone; it fails with a twisted joint, not with a muscle that pulls on nothing. Cartilage is the smooth layer that cushions bone ends and reduces friction; damage there causes joint pain, not loss of pull. Skeletal muscle makes voluntary movement, and this one still contracts.

options.text: Cartilage, which cushions the bone ends in a joint
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cartilage lines the joint and cuts friction. A cartilage injury makes a joint painful or stiff. It does not stop a working muscle from pulling on a bone.

options.text: Skeletal muscle, which contracts to make movement
options.rationale: Near miss concept The stem says the calf muscle still tightens. A torn muscle could not contract well, so the muscle itself is working.

questions.takeaway: Tendons join muscle to bone; ligaments join bone to bone.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out a muscle tear is that the calf still tightens. Find where the chain from muscle to bone broke.

questions.stem: With the eyes closed, a patient cannot tell whether the nurse has moved the big toe up or down. Strength in both legs is 5 of 5, and range of motion is full in every joint. Which function is impaired, and what risk does it create?

options.text: Muscle strength, causing a risk for contractures
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Muscle strength is the force a muscle can produce. It is graded 5 of 5 here, which is full strength, so strength is not the problem.

options.text: Joint range of motion, causing a risk for stiffness
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Range of motion is how far a joint can move. The stem says it is full in every joint, so the joint is not limited.

options.text: Proprioception, causing a risk for poor balance and falls
options.rationale: Proprioception is the sense of where a body part is without looking at it. The nervous system uses it to keep posture and balance. The test that decides it: can the patient name the position of a joint with the eyes closed? This patient cannot, so proprioception is impaired. A patient who cannot feel where the feet are cannot correct a shift in balance, so the fall risk rises even with full strength. Muscle strength is graded 0 to 5, and 5 of 5 is full, so that option fails. Range of motion is the arc a joint moves through, and it is full. Activity tolerance is the heart, lung and symptom response to exercise, and nothing in the stem tests it.

options.text: Activity tolerance, causing a risk for dyspnea on exertion
options.rationale: Near miss concept Activity tolerance is how the heart and lungs respond to exertion. Knowing where the toe is has nothing to do with heart rate or breathing.

questions.takeaway: Normal strength does not mean safe balance. Balance also needs proprioception.
questions.strategy: The details that rule out the near misses are 5 of 5 strength and full range of motion. With those normal, the only function left is position sense.

questions.stem: A patient lying on the back can move one leg sideways across the sheet. When asked to lift that heel off the bed, the patient cannot raise it at all. What muscle strength grade should the nurse record for that leg?

options.text: 2, movement with gravity eliminated
options.rationale: Strength grades run 0 to 5. Grade 0 is no contraction. Grade 1 is a trace contraction you can feel or see with no movement. Grade 2 is movement when gravity is taken out, such as sliding along the bed. Grade 3 is movement against gravity, such as lifting the limb up. Grade 4 adds some resistance, and grade 5 is full strength. The deciding question: does the limb move, and if so, can it lift against gravity? This leg moves sideways across the sheet, which takes gravity out of the work, and cannot lift. That is grade 2.

options.text: 3, movement against gravity
options.rationale: Near miss concept Grade 3 means the limb lifts against gravity. This heel cannot leave the bed, so the patient has not reached grade 3.

options.text: 1, a trace contraction only
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Grade 1 is a flicker of contraction with no movement. This leg moves across the sheet, which is more than a trace.

options.text: 0, no contraction at all
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Grade 0 means no contraction at all. A leg that moves sideways is clearly contracting.

questions.takeaway: Sliding along the bed is grade 2; lifting off the bed is grade 3.
questions.strategy: The detail that separates 2 from 3 is that the heel cannot leave the bed. Ask whether gravity was part of the movement.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses the musculoskeletal system of a patient who is 69 years old. Select all of the findings that fit expected aging.

options.text: Bone density in the osteopenia range on a bone density scan
options.rationale: Expected aging changes are slow, gradual and usually even on both sides. The test for each finding: is it gradual and symmetric, or new and one sided? Bone loss to the range of osteopenia or osteoporosis is a known aging change. Range of motion decreases as joint cartilage becomes less elastic, so mild loss in both shoulders fits. Muscle tissue atrophies, which means it shrinks, so equal thigh wasting fits. Movement slows, and slow but smooth movement fits. New weakness in one arm since this morning is sudden loss of movement, a red flag that needs reporting. Cartilage becoming more elastic is the opposite of what happens.

options.text: Slightly reduced range of motion in both shoulders
options.rationale: Expected aging changes are slow, gradual and usually even on both sides. The test for each finding: is it gradual and symmetric, or new and one sided? Bone loss to the range of osteopenia or osteoporosis is a known aging change. Range of motion decreases as joint cartilage becomes less elastic, so mild loss in both shoulders fits. Muscle tissue atrophies, which means it shrinks, so equal thigh wasting fits. Movement slows, and slow but smooth movement fits. New weakness in one arm since this morning is sudden loss of movement, a red flag that needs reporting. Cartilage becoming more elastic is the opposite of what happens.

options.text: Mild thigh muscle wasting that is equal on both sides
options.rationale: Expected aging changes are slow, gradual and usually even on both sides. The test for each finding: is it gradual and symmetric, or new and one sided? Bone loss to the range of osteopenia or osteoporosis is a known aging change. Range of motion decreases as joint cartilage becomes less elastic, so mild loss in both shoulders fits. Muscle tissue atrophies, which means it shrinks, so equal thigh wasting fits. Movement slows, and slow but smooth movement fits. New weakness in one arm since this morning is sudden loss of movement, a red flag that needs reporting. Cartilage becoming more elastic is the opposite of what happens.

options.text: Movements that are slower but smooth and coordinated
options.rationale: Expected aging changes are slow, gradual and usually even on both sides. The test for each finding: is it gradual and symmetric, or new and one sided? Bone loss to the range of osteopenia or osteoporosis is a known aging change. Range of motion decreases as joint cartilage becomes less elastic, so mild loss in both shoulders fits. Muscle tissue atrophies, which means it shrinks, so equal thigh wasting fits. Movement slows, and slow but smooth movement fits. New weakness in one arm since this morning is sudden loss of movement, a red flag that needs reporting. Cartilage becoming more elastic is the opposite of what happens.

options.text: New weakness in the right arm that began this morning
options.rationale: Near miss concept Aging changes come on slowly and on both sides. Weakness in one arm that began this morning is sudden and one sided, which is a red flag to report, not aging.

options.text: Joint cartilage that is more elastic than in midlife
options.rationale: Near miss concept Aging makes joint cartilage less elastic and less able to absorb load. This option reverses the direction of the change.

questions.takeaway: Aging is slow and symmetric. Sudden or one sided change is never just aging.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out the arm weakness is that it began this morning on one side. Sort each finding by speed and symmetry.

questions.stem: A nurse uses the Bedside Mobility Assessment Tool before a patient gets out of bed for the first time. Place the functional tests in the order the nurse performs them.

options.text: Stand: lift the buttocks off the bed and hold for a count of 5
Sit and shake: sit at the bed edge, reach across midline and shake hands
Walk: march in place, then step one foot forward and back
Stretch and point: straighten each knee, then flex the ankle and point the toes

questions.takeaway: The Bedside Mobility Assessment Tool is a four level nursing check that finds how much help a patient needs and which handling equipment is safe. Each test asks more of the body than the one before, and the nurse stops at the first one the patient fails. First, sit and shake tests trunk strength and seated balance; the patient sits unassisted for more than 2 minutes, reaches across midline and shakes hands. Second, stretch and point tests leg strength and stability while still seated. Third, stand tests whether the legs can lift and hold the body; the patient hovers the buttocks off the bed for a count of 5. Fourth, walk tests standing balance and gait; the patient marches in place and steps forward and back. Testing standing before seated balance would put a patient on the feet who might not be able to sit upright. Sit, then legs while seated, then stand, then step. Stop at the first failure.
questions.strategy: Order by risk: each test needs the one before it to be safe. A patient who cannot sit steady should never be asked to stand.

questions.topic: isotonic, isometric and range of motion exercise
questions.stem: For each activity, select the type of exercise it is.
questions.objective: isotonic, isometric and range of motion exercise

rows.text: Walking the length of the hallway
Tightening the buttock muscles and holding without moving the hips
Pressing the palms together hard while the arms stay still
Lifting a light weight by bending and straightening the elbow
The nurse moving a sedated patient's wrist through its full arc

questions.takeaway: Isotonic exercise means the muscle contracts while the joint moves; it builds dynamic strength and functional movement. Isometric exercise means the muscle contracts while the joint stays still; it builds static strength and joint stability and is safe around a painful or healing joint. Range of motion exercise moves a joint through its arc to keep it flexible. The test for each row: does the joint move, and is the goal strength or flexibility? Walking moves the hips, knees and ankles under muscle power, so it is isotonic. Tightening the buttocks without moving the hips is isometric. Pressing the palms together with still arms is isometric. Bending and straightening the elbow against a weight moves the joint under load, so it is isotonic. A nurse moving a sedated patient's wrist is passive range of motion; the patient's muscle is not working, and the goal is flexibility. Joint moves with muscle work: isotonic. Muscle works, joint still: isometric. Joint moved to keep it flexible: range of motion.
questions.strategy: The detail that separates the elbow row from range of motion is the weight. Load means strength work, so it is isotonic.

questions.stem: For each clinical question, select the imaging study best suited to answer it.

rows.text: Suspected torn ligament in the knee
Suspected injury to a spinal disc and nearby soft tissue
Measuring bone mineral density to screen for osteoporosis
Shattered pelvis that needs detailed bone images to plan surgery
Checking the alignment of a wrist fracture after it was set

questions.takeaway: Each study answers a different question. An X ray shows fractures, dislocations, alignment and degenerative bone change; it is the first look at bone. A CT scan gives more detailed images of bone and is useful for complex fractures. An MRI is best for soft tissue such as muscles, ligaments, tendons, cartilage, spinal structures and bone marrow. A DEXA scan measures bone mineral density and is used to assess osteoporosis. The deciding question for each row: is the target soft tissue, bone detail, simple bone position, or bone density? A knee ligament is soft tissue, so MRI. A spinal disc is a spinal structure, so MRI. Bone density is the DEXA scan's job. A shattered pelvis is a complex fracture needing detail, so CT. Checking a set wrist's alignment is a simple bone question, so X ray. Soft tissue: MRI. Bone detail: CT. Bone position: X ray. Bone density: DEXA.
questions.strategy: The detail that moves the pelvis from X ray to CT is the word shattered. A complex fracture needs more detail than a plain film gives.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence: In the supine position, the patient lies on the [[1]] with the arms at the sides or abducted less than [[2]]. In the prone position, the patient lies on the [[3]] with the head turned to the left or right. A patient lying on the right side is in the [[4]] position.

options.text: back
stomach
right side
left side
90 degrees
45 degrees
120 degrees
180 degrees
stomach
back
right side
left side
right lateral recumbent
left lateral recumbent
prone
supported Fowler

questions.takeaway: [1] back: Supine means lying face up on the back. [2] 90 degrees: Abducted means moved out away from the body; in supine the arms rest at the sides or out to less than 90 degrees, not raised to shoulder height or above. [3] stomach: Prone means lying face down, with the head turned to one side so the airway stays clear. [4] right lateral recumbent: Lateral means side and recumbent means lying down, and the named side is the side the patient lies on. Left lateral recumbent is the opposite side. Prone is face down. Supported Fowler is sitting up with the head of the bed raised. Supine is face up, prone is face down, and lateral recumbent is named for the side the patient lies on.
questions.strategy: Supine and prone are the pair that gets swapped. Remember that a patient lying supine could hold soup in a bowl on the chest.

questions.stem: The spouse of an unconscious patient watches the nurse perform passive range of motion and says, "These exercises will help build up the strength to walk again." How should the nurse respond?

options.text: “Yes, doing them several times a day will rebuild his leg muscles.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Passive ROM builds no strength; the patient's own muscles are not contracting.

options.text: “They are ordered by the provider, so we do them every single shift.”
options.rationale: Institution as rationale An order is not the reason, and the reply leaves the misunderstanding in place.

options.text: “They keep the joints flexible and prevent contractures, not build strength.”
options.rationale: Passive ROM is for a patient who is unconscious or paralyzed: you move the joint so it stays flexible and does not contract. Strength comes only from the patient's own contraction, as in isometric, active assistive, or active exercise.

options.text: “You will need to ask physical therapy about what these are for.”
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Explaining the purpose of a nursing intervention is within the nurse's role.

questions.takeaway: Passive ROM keeps the joint, not the muscle.
questions.strategy: Correct the misunderstanding gently and accurately; affirming a false belief is never therapeutic.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to transfer a patient from bed to chair for the first time after three days of bedrest. What should she do first?

options.text: Have two staff members lift him straight into the chair
options.rationale: Near miss concept A manual lift of unknown weight bearing capacity risks both of you.

options.text: Sit him at the bed edge and check balance and symptoms first
options.rationale: That is the BMAT logic: establish what he can do before you choose the equipment. Sit and shake tells you about trunk strength and seated balance, and whether he becomes dizzy. If he cannot hold that, he is a total assist and the lift is correct; if he can, forcing a lift costs him the function he still has. Assessment selects the equipment, not the other way round.

options.text: Get a mechanical lift, since he has been on bedrest for days
options.rationale: Correct but premature Equipment chosen before the assessment that would justify it.

options.text: Check his most recent hemoglobin before any activity at all
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Useful context and not what tells you whether he can sit up.

questions.takeaway: Assess first, then pick the equipment. The level determines the lift.
questions.strategy: Reaching for the lift first is safe for your back and may take away function he has.

questions.stem: Six hours after a long leg cast is applied, a patient reports pain that is worse than before and a tingling in the toes. The toes are cool and capillary refill is 4 seconds. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Apply warm blankets to the foot to improve its circulation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Warms the skin without opening the vessel, and delays the call.

options.text: Elevate the limb above the heart and reassess in an hour
options.rationale: Near miss concept Wrong twice. Elevating above heart level drops arterial perfusion pressure further, and an hour is a long time for tissue with no blood supply. Keep the limb at heart level.

options.text: Notify the provider now; this is neurovascular compromise
options.rationale: Neurovascular assessment is color, temperature, capillary refill, pulses, sensation, movement and pain, compared side to side. Pain out of proportion plus paresthesia plus a cool limb with sluggish refill is compromise, and it is time dependent. Medicating the pain hides the only symptom that was telling you.

options.text: Give the ordered analgesic and reassess the pain in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Near miss concept Masks the finding that would have told you it was getting worse.

questions.takeaway: Pain out of proportion is the earliest sign, and it is the one people treat instead of report.
questions.strategy: Any option that treats the symptom buys the limb nothing but time it does not have.

questions.stem: A patient ambulating in the hallway on day 3 after knee surgery suddenly becomes short of breath, reports sharp chest pain worse on inspiration, and his heart rate rises to 124. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Obtain a 12 lead ECG in the hallway before moving him
options.rationale: Correct but premature Useful and it is not the first action, and he needs oxygen and help now.

options.text: Walk him back to bed and then assess his pain level
options.rationale: Near miss concept Walking him back is continued exertion; get him seated where he is.

options.text: Slow the pace and finish walking to the end of the hallway
options.rationale: Near miss concept Continues the activity during an acute event.

options.text: Stop, sit him down, apply oxygen and call for urgent help
options.rationale: Sudden dyspnea with pleuritic chest pain and tachycardia in a postoperative orthopedic patient is pulmonary embolism until proven otherwise, and this is the population it happens in. Stop, get him off his feet safely, oxygen on, call. Walking him back to the room, even slowly, keeps a patient with a possible embolism exerting himself.

questions.takeaway: Sudden dyspnea plus pleuritic pain in a postoperative patient is an embolism until ruled out.
questions.strategy: Every option that keeps him moving, including back to the room, is an option that keeps him exerting.
