questions.stem: A patient with a stroke passed the RN's bedside swallow screen this morning and ate breakfast with no coughing. The patient needs help cutting food and bringing it to the mouth. Assistive personnel ask who should feed supper. What should the nurse say?
questions.objective: delegating feeding after a swallow screen

options.text: You can feed supper and report any coughing to me
options.rationale: Delegation means handing a task to another member of the team while the RN keeps responsibility. Feeding a stroke patient is safe to delegate only after the RN has assessed swallowing safety. Ask: has the RN confirmed a safe swallow? Yes, the screen was passed and breakfast went without coughing. So assistive personnel can feed supper and report coughing back to the RN. Saying only the RN may feed ever turns an assess first rule into a ban. A speech therapy consult may be useful but is not a condition for feeding after a passed screen. Keeping the patient NPO is the rule before a screen, not after one has been passed.

options.text: Only the RN may feed a stroke patient on any day
options.rationale: Absolute language The rule is to assess first, not that only the RN may ever feed.

options.text: Ask speech therapy to see the patient before anyone feeds
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question A consult can help, but it is not required once the screen is passed.

options.text: Keep the patient NPO until a second screen is done
options.rationale: Near miss concept NPO applies before a screen; this patient already passed one.

questions.takeaway: RN screens the swallow first. After a passed screen, feeding can be delegated with clear reporting.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out NPO is that the RN screen was passed this morning.

questions.stem: At 0400 the nurse reviews four findings on a patient admitted yesterday with an ischemic stroke. Which finding needs action first?

options.text: Right arm weakness, unchanged since admission
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data The presenting deficit, unchanged, is not a new problem.

options.text: Sleeping, but wakes fully to a normal voice and is oriented
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Waking fully and oriented shows intact level of consciousness.

options.text: Incontinent of urine and lying on wet sheets
options.rationale: Correct but premature Perineal care is needed, but oxygenation comes first.

options.text: SpO₂ 88% on room air while asleep
options.rationale: Secondary injury is further brain damage after the stroke itself, and hypoxia (low oxygen) and hypotension cause it because the injured brain is already short on perfusion. Ask: which finding takes oxygen away from the brain now? An SpO₂ of 88% on room air does, so it comes first under airway and oxygenation. Right arm weakness unchanged since admission is the baseline deficit, not a change. A patient who wakes fully to a normal voice and is oriented has a stable level of consciousness. Wet sheets need perineal care to protect the skin, but that is a good action at the wrong moment while the brain is low on oxygen.

questions.takeaway: Prevent secondary injury: avoid hypoxia and hypotension. Airway and oxygen before hygiene.
questions.strategy: Rank by airway first. The detail that rules out the incontinence is that it threatens skin, while the SpO₂ threatens the brain.

questions.stem: A patient admitted 4 hours ago with a stroke has a facial droop and a weak voice. No swallow screen has been done. A visitor gave the patient a glass of water because the patient said they were thirsty. The patient is now coughing, the voice sounds wet, and SpO₂ has fallen from 96% to 91%. Complete the bow tie.

options.text: Stop all oral intake and keep the patient NPO
Give small sips to see whether the cough settles
Sit the patient upright and support oxygenation per protocol
Offer thickened water so the patient is less thirsty
Ask assistive personnel to feed the next meal slowly
Aspiration
Extension of the stroke
Hypoglycemia
Anxiety about being thirsty
SpO₂ trend
Pupil size and reaction
Daily weight
Temperature and breathing for signs of pneumonia
Bedside glucose

questions.takeaway: Aspiration is fluid or food going into the airway instead of the esophagus. Ask: did the problem start right after something went into the mouth? Yes: coughing, a wet voice and a falling SpO₂ began after water, in a patient with facial droop who had no swallow screen. That is aspiration. An extension of the stroke would show new neurologic deficits, not a cough after drinking. Hypoglycemia causes confusion and weakness, not a wet voice. Anxiety does not drop the SpO₂ after a drink. Actions: stop all oral intake and keep the patient NPO, because no food, fluids or medications are given until a swallow screen is passed. Sit the patient upright and support oxygenation, because protecting the airway comes first. More sips, thickened water or delegated feeding all put more fluid at the airway before any screen. Parameters: the SpO₂ trend shows whether oxygenation is recovering, and temperature and breathing show whether aspiration pneumonia is developing. Pupils track pressure, weight tracks fluid, and glucose does not answer this problem. Thirsty does not mean give water. NPO until the swallow screen, and watch for aspiration pneumonia.
questions.strategy: Link the symptom to its trigger. The detail that rules out stroke extension is that the cough and wet voice began right after the water.

questions.stem: Select all of the instructions the nurse should give after cataract surgery.

options.text: Sleep on the operative side to keep pressure on the eye
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pressure on the operative eye is exactly what you are avoiding.

options.text: Expect best vision within 24 hours of surgery
options.rationale: Near miss concept Vision improves early and keeps improving for 4 to 6 weeks.

options.text: Avoid bending at the waist and lifting more than 10 pounds
options.rationale: Everything after cataract surgery is about not raising intraocular pressure: no bending, no heavy lifting, no straining. Sudden pain or vision loss suggests hemorrhage or increased pressure and is reported immediately. Best vision takes 4 to 6 weeks, not a day.

options.text: Avoid straining during bowel movements
options.rationale: Everything after cataract surgery is about not raising intraocular pressure: no bending, no heavy lifting, no straining. Sudden pain or vision loss suggests hemorrhage or increased pressure and is reported immediately. Best vision takes 4 to 6 weeks, not a day.

options.text: Report sudden eye pain or sudden loss of vision right away
options.rationale: Everything after cataract surgery is about not raising intraocular pressure: no bending, no heavy lifting, no straining. Sudden pain or vision loss suggests hemorrhage or increased pressure and is reported immediately. Best vision takes 4 to 6 weeks, not a day.

options.text: Wear the dark glasses provided when outdoors
options.rationale: Everything after cataract surgery is about not raising intraocular pressure: no bending, no heavy lifting, no straining. Sudden pain or vision loss suggests hemorrhage or increased pressure and is reported immediately. Best vision takes 4 to 6 weeks, not a day.

questions.takeaway: Anything that would make you grunt raises eye pressure.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options invent a timeline and a position the surgery does not call for.

questions.stem: A nurse is instilling glaucoma drops. Which technique is correct?

options.text: Drop into the lower conjunctival sac, then press the inner corner
options.rationale: The conjunctival sac holds the drop without touching the sensitive cornea. Punctal occlusion, pressing the inner corner, keeps the drug from draining into the nasolacrimal duct and being absorbed systemically, which matters because glaucoma beta blockers can slow the heart and cause bronchospasm. Wait about five minutes between different drops.

options.text: Place the drop directly onto the cornea so it absorbs faster
options.rationale: Near miss concept Painful and it triggers a blink that ejects the drop.

options.text: Instill both prescribed drops back to back without any wait
options.rationale: Near miss concept The second washes out the first.

options.text: Have the patient blink rapidly afterward to spread the drop
options.rationale: Near miss concept Blinking pumps the drop into the duct and out of the eye.

questions.takeaway: Punctal occlusion is what keeps an eye drop from becoming a systemic drug.
questions.strategy: Two options push the drop out of the eye faster than it can be absorbed.

questions.stem: Select all of the discharge instructions after cataract extraction with lens implantation.

options.text: Report sudden pain, decreasing vision or a curtain across the vision immediately
options.rationale: Everything here protects against raised intraocular pressure and against her own hands. Bending, straining and lifting raise pressure inside the eye, the shield stops her rubbing it in her sleep, and pain with decreasing vision is the call that cannot wait. Bleeding is not expected and rubbing is exactly what the shield exists to prevent.

options.text: Do not bend at the waist or lift more than the weight you were told
options.rationale: Everything here protects against raised intraocular pressure and against her own hands. Bending, straining and lifting raise pressure inside the eye, the shield stops her rubbing it in her sleep, and pain with decreasing vision is the call that cannot wait. Bleeding is not expected and rubbing is exactly what the shield exists to prevent.

options.text: Expect some bleeding from the eye for the first several days
options.rationale: Near miss concept Not expected; it is reported.

options.text: Rub the eye gently if it itches to relieve the sensation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Rubbing risks dehiscence and infection, which is why she wears a shield.

options.text: Instill the prescribed drops without touching the dropper to the eye
options.rationale: Everything here protects against raised intraocular pressure and against her own hands. Bending, straining and lifting raise pressure inside the eye, the shield stops her rubbing it in her sleep, and pain with decreasing vision is the call that cannot wait. Bleeding is not expected and rubbing is exactly what the shield exists to prevent.

options.text: Wear the eye shield as directed, including while sleeping
options.rationale: Everything here protects against raised intraocular pressure and against her own hands. Bending, straining and lifting raise pressure inside the eye, the shield stops her rubbing it in her sleep, and pain with decreasing vision is the call that cannot wait. Bleeding is not expected and rubbing is exactly what the shield exists to prevent.

questions.takeaway: Pain plus decreasing vision after eye surgery is never something to watch overnight.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options normalize something that should be reported or prevented.

questions.stem: Select all of the correct steps for instilling eye drops.

options.text: Give a second prescribed drop immediately after the first
options.rationale: Near miss concept Wait about five minutes or the first drop is washed away.

options.text: Apply gentle pressure to the inner corner after instillation if the drug is systemically absorbed
options.rationale: The drop goes into the lower sac, never on the cornea, which is exquisitely sensitive and will make her blink the dose straight out. Punctal occlusion at the inner corner keeps a drug like timolol from draining into the nose and reaching the circulation, which is how eye drops cause bradycardia. Two different drops are separated by about five minutes so the first is not washed away.

options.text: Have the patient look up and pull down the lower lid to form a pocket
options.rationale: The drop goes into the lower sac, never on the cornea, which is exquisitely sensitive and will make her blink the dose straight out. Punctal occlusion at the inner corner keeps a drug like timolol from draining into the nose and reaching the circulation, which is how eye drops cause bradycardia. Two different drops are separated by about five minutes so the first is not washed away.

options.text: Place the drop directly on the cornea so it spreads evenly
options.rationale: Near miss concept The cornea is too sensitive; the blink reflex ejects the drop.

options.text: Drop the medication into the conjunctival sac without touching the eye
options.rationale: The drop goes into the lower sac, never on the cornea, which is exquisitely sensitive and will make her blink the dose straight out. Punctal occlusion at the inner corner keeps a drug like timolol from draining into the nose and reaching the circulation, which is how eye drops cause bradycardia. Two different drops are separated by about five minutes so the first is not washed away.

options.text: Perform hand hygiene before and after
options.rationale: The drop goes into the lower sac, never on the cornea, which is exquisitely sensitive and will make her blink the dose straight out. Punctal occlusion at the inner corner keeps a drug like timolol from draining into the nose and reaching the circulation, which is how eye drops cause bradycardia. Two different drops are separated by about five minutes so the first is not washed away.

questions.takeaway: Occlude the inner corner with beta blocker drops. That is how an eye drop slows a heart.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options waste the dose, one by provoking a blink and one by washing it out.

questions.stem: Which statement about assessing an older adult's eyes is accurate?

options.text: A yellowed sclera in an older adult reliably signals liver disease
options.rationale: Near miss concept The exact assumption the first option warns against.

options.text: Older pupils dilate more readily, which improves night vision
options.rationale: Near miss concept Backwards; less dilation is why night driving becomes hard.

options.text: The sclera is unreliable for judging jaundice in older adults
options.rationale: The aging sclera and the aging lens both yellow, so scleral color is an unreliable sign of jaundice and the eye is a poor hydration check. The pupil also dilates less, which is why dark adaptation is poor and older adults need more light, and blues, greens and violets become harder to tell apart.

options.text: Color discrimination improves with age as the lens thickens
options.rationale: Near miss concept A thickening yellow lens filters out blues, greens and violets.

questions.takeaway: The aging eye yellows on its own. Judge jaundice somewhere else.
questions.strategy: Two options describe the aging eye getting better at something. It does not.

questions.stem: Select all of the findings consistent with acute angle closure glaucoma.

options.text: Blurred vision with halos around lights
options.rationale: Angle closure is an emergency because the pressure rises in hours and takes the optic nerve with it. The pain, the fixed mid dilated pupil, the halos and the hazy cornea all come from that sudden rise. Painless peripheral loss over years is open angle glaucoma, which is the opposite presentation, and bilateral itching with clear discharge is allergic conjunctivitis.

options.text: Sudden severe eye pain with a headache
options.rationale: Angle closure is an emergency because the pressure rises in hours and takes the optic nerve with it. The pain, the fixed mid dilated pupil, the halos and the hazy cornea all come from that sudden rise. Painless peripheral loss over years is open angle glaucoma, which is the opposite presentation, and bilateral itching with clear discharge is allergic conjunctivitis.

options.text: A fixed, moderately dilated pupil
options.rationale: Angle closure is an emergency because the pressure rises in hours and takes the optic nerve with it. The pain, the fixed mid dilated pupil, the halos and the hazy cornea all come from that sudden rise. Painless peripheral loss over years is open angle glaucoma, which is the opposite presentation, and bilateral itching with clear discharge is allergic conjunctivitis.

options.text: A gradual painless loss of peripheral vision over years
options.rationale: Near miss concept Open angle glaucoma, which is why it goes undetected.

options.text: A red eye with a hazy or cloudy cornea
options.rationale: Angle closure is an emergency because the pressure rises in hours and takes the optic nerve with it. The pain, the fixed mid dilated pupil, the halos and the hazy cornea all come from that sudden rise. Painless peripheral loss over years is open angle glaucoma, which is the opposite presentation, and bilateral itching with clear discharge is allergic conjunctivitis.

options.text: Clear drainage from the eye with itching in both eyes
options.rationale: Near miss concept Allergic conjunctivitis.

questions.takeaway: Painful and sudden is angle closure. Painless and slow is open angle. The treatment urgency is completely different.
questions.strategy: One wrong option is the other kind of glaucoma; the other is a benign condition.

questions.stem: Match each description to the refractive error.

rows.text: Uneven corneal curvature distorts the image at all distances
The image focuses in front of the retina and distance vision is blurred
The lens loses elasticity with age, starting in the forties
The image focuses behind the retina and near vision is blurred

questions.takeaway: Myopia is nearsighted and corrected with a concave lens; hyperopia is farsighted and corrected with a convex lens. Presbyopia is the aging lens losing the ability to accommodate, which is why reading glasses appear in the forties even in people who never needed correction. Myopia and presbyopia both blur, and only one of them is about age.
questions.strategy: Ask where the image lands relative to the retina. In front is myopia, behind is hyperopia.

questions.stem: Select all of the postoperative instructions after scleral buckling surgery.

options.text: Maintain the head position the surgeon specifies
options.rationale: If gas or oil is holding the retina in place, position is the treatment and it is not negotiable. Everything that raises intraocular pressure is out. Reading moves the eyes constantly, which is why close work is restricted early. Pain with nausea suggests rising pressure and is reported, not endured.

options.text: Expect vision to be fully restored within 48 hours
options.rationale: Near miss concept Recovery takes weeks and may be incomplete depending on the detachment.

options.text: Avoid bending, straining and heavy lifting
options.rationale: If gas or oil is holding the retina in place, position is the treatment and it is not negotiable. Everything that raises intraocular pressure is out. Reading moves the eyes constantly, which is why close work is restricted early. Pain with nausea suggests rising pressure and is reported, not endured.

options.text: Resume driving as soon as the eye patch is removed
options.rationale: Correct but premature Depth perception and acuity take far longer, and head position may still be required.

options.text: Report sudden pain, pain with nausea, or sudden vision change immediately
options.rationale: If gas or oil is holding the retina in place, position is the treatment and it is not negotiable. Everything that raises intraocular pressure is out. Reading moves the eyes constantly, which is why close work is restricted early. Pain with nausea suggests rising pressure and is reported, not endured.

options.text: Avoid reading and close work during the first week
options.rationale: If gas or oil is holding the retina in place, position is the treatment and it is not negotiable. Everything that raises intraocular pressure is out. Reading moves the eyes constantly, which is why close work is restricted early. Pain with nausea suggests rising pressure and is reported, not endured.

questions.takeaway: Position is the treatment. The bubble only works where the surgeon aims it.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options promise a recovery faster than this surgery allows.

questions.stem: A patient reports a sudden shower of floaters and flashes of light in one eye, with no pain. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: Normal vitreous changes that need no follow up
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Posterior vitreous detachment is common with aging and can tear the retina, so it is evaluated rather than dismissed.

options.text: Open angle glaucoma, which is painless in early stages
options.rationale: Near miss concept Painless, and it takes peripheral vision slowly, without flashes.

options.text: Cataract progression, which develops painlessly
options.rationale: Near miss concept Painless and gradual over months, with blurring rather than flashes.

options.text: Retinal detachment, which is an emergency
options.rationale: Flashes, floaters and a curtain across the field, sudden and painless, is the classic triad. The flashes are the retina being tugged. Painlessness is the reason patients wait, and waiting is what costs the vision. Preoperative care restricts head movement and may include an eye patch to reduce eye movement.

questions.takeaway: Painless does not mean benign. Sudden is the word that matters.
questions.strategy: Two of the distractors are also painless, which is exactly why this item works.

questions.stem: A patient's tonometry reading is 28 mm Hg. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: Low, suggesting a wound leak after recent eye surgery
options.rationale: Near miss concept Low would be below 10.

options.text: Elevated above 21 mm Hg; needs evaluation for glaucoma
options.rationale: Normal runs about 10 to 21 mm Hg, and open angle glaucoma typically sits in the 22 to 32 range. A single elevated pressure is ocular hypertension; glaucoma is diagnosed on optic nerve damage and visual field loss, not on a number alone. That is why the next step is evaluation rather than a diagnosis. Angle closure pressures are usually above 30 and come with pain, a red eye and a hazy cornea, none of which this patient has.

options.text: Within the normal range of 10 to 21 mm Hg for adults
options.rationale: Near miss concept 28 is above that range.

options.text: Diagnostic by itself of acute angle closure glaucoma
options.rationale: Near miss concept Angle closure is a clinical picture, not a pressure threshold.

questions.takeaway: Pressure raises the suspicion. Nerve damage makes the diagnosis.
questions.strategy: The number alone cannot diagnose angle closure, which is the distractor.

questions.stem: A patient with a corneal abrasion is prescribed antibiotic drops hourly for the first 24 hours. He asks why an eye scratch needs such aggressive treatment. What should the nurse say?

options.text: The frequency prevents the abrasion from scarring rather than preventing infection
options.rationale: Near miss concept Scarring is a consequence of infection, not the reason for the schedule.

options.text: Hourly dosing is routine for all eye medications
options.rationale: Near miss concept It is not routine; it is specific to this risk.

options.text: The drops are mainly for comfort and the schedule can be relaxed if the eye feels better
options.rationale: Near miss concept Invites him to stop when the pain settles, which is when the infection is still there.

options.text: The cornea has no blood supply of its own, so an infection there is an emergency
options.rationale: The cornea is avascular, which is what keeps it clear and also means the immune system cannot reach an infection there the way it reaches everywhere else. That is why corneal infection is treated as an emergency and why the drops run hourly at first. No contact lenses until it is fully healed, and separate bottles if both eyes are infected.

questions.takeaway: No blood supply means no immune response. The drops are the defense.
questions.strategy: The answer is a mechanism, so an option that explains the schedule by routine or comfort is not it.

questions.stem: A patient has a bacterial infection in both eyes and is prescribed antibiotic drops. What should the nurse teach?

options.text: Stop the drops as soon as the redness has resolved, even if doses remain
options.rationale: Near miss concept The classic antibiotic error; symptoms resolve before the organism does.

options.text: Use a separate bottle for each eye; keep the tip off the eye
options.rationale: One bottle moving between two infected eyes carries organisms back and forth and reinfects whichever one was improving. A tip that touches the eye contaminates the bottle. Finish the full course, because stopping at symptom relief is how the resistant organism survives, and no contact lenses until it is fully healed.

options.text: Wear contact lenses between doses to protect the eye
options.rationale: Near miss concept Lenses are out until healing is complete.

options.text: Use one bottle for both eyes so dosing stays consistent
options.rationale: Near miss concept Moves organisms between eyes.

questions.takeaway: Separate bottles, untouched tips, full course.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options shorten the treatment or reintroduce the organism.

questions.stem: A patient's corrected visual acuity in the better eye is 20/200. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: This is within normal limits with correction
options.rationale: Near miss concept Normal is 20/20; this is ten times worse.

options.text: This indicates the patient needs a stronger prescription
options.rationale: Near miss concept This is corrected acuity, so glasses have already been accounted for.

options.text: This means the patient can see at 200 feet what a normal eye sees at 20
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reverses the fraction and describes better than normal vision.

options.text: This meets the criterion for legal blindness
options.rationale: Snellen notation gives the test distance over the distance a normal eye could read that line. 20/200 means she sees at 20 feet what a normal eye sees at 200, so it is far worse than normal, not better. Legal blindness is 20/200 or worse in the better eye with correction, which is what unlocks services and accommodations.

questions.takeaway: The bottom number is how far away a normal eye could be and still read it. Bigger is worse.
questions.strategy: One distractor reverses the fraction, which is the most common misreading.

questions.stem: A patient has a small piece of grit on the surface of the eye, with tearing and photophobia. What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Fluorescein examination and irrigation with sterile saline
options.rationale: A surface foreign body is different from a penetrating one. Fluorescein stains any corneal defect green so it can be seen, and irrigation flushes loose material out. Nothing is grasped with forceps at the bedside, and MRI is contraindicated whenever metal might be involved.

options.text: Immediate patching of both eyes without examination
options.rationale: Correct but premature Patches an eye nobody has looked at.

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging to locate the particle
options.rationale: Near miss concept Contraindicated with possible metal, and unnecessary for surface grit.

options.text: Removal with forceps at the bedside
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Instrument removal belongs to the eye provider.

questions.takeaway: Surface gets irrigated. Penetrating gets left alone.
questions.strategy: Two options treat a surface particle like a penetrating injury or like surgery.

questions.stem: A patient reports that colors look washed out, night driving has become difficult because of glare from headlights, and she has had two new glasses prescriptions in a year that did not help. What does this suggest?

options.text: Corneal abrasion
options.rationale: Near miss concept Acutely painful with a foreign body sensation.

options.text: Retinal detachment
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sudden flashes, floaters and a curtain, over hours to days.

options.text: Acute angle closure glaucoma
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sudden, painful, with a red eye and halos, not a year of gradual change.

options.text: Cataract
options.rationale: The lens is clouding, so light scatters and color washes out. The two failed prescriptions are the giveaway: patients blame their glasses first because the change is gradual and painless. Surgery is the only treatment and is done when the patient's daily activities are affected, not at a particular acuity number.

questions.takeaway: New glasses that do not help is a cataract story, not a refraction story.
questions.strategy: The other three are painful, sudden, or both. This is neither.

questions.stem: A patient with cataracts in both eyes asks when surgery should be done. Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: Surgery is done as soon as a cataract is seen, before it hardens
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cataracts progress gradually and are managed until function suffers.

options.text: Surgery is done once vision drops to the legal blindness level
options.rationale: Near miss concept The trigger is function, not an acuity threshold.

options.text: Surgery is done only after eye drops fail to clear the lens
options.rationale: Near miss concept No drop clears a cataract; surgery is the only treatment.

options.text: Surgery is done when the cataract interferes with daily life
options.rationale: A cataract is gradual and painless, so there is no rush. Until surgery the patient is managed with bright, glare free light and fall prevention. Surgery is the only treatment and is done when the cataract affects activities of daily living, not at a particular acuity number.

questions.takeaway: Cataract surgery is timed by daily function, not by a number on the chart.
questions.strategy: Gradual conditions are managed, not rushed. Options that set a deadline or promise a drop misread a cataract.

questions.stem: Place the structures in the order that light passes through them to form an image.

options.text: Lens
Retina
Cornea
Vitreous humor
Aqueous humor

questions.takeaway: Light enters through the cornea, the clear front window, which does most of the bending. It then crosses the aqueous humor, the fluid in the front chamber. The lens fine tunes the focus. The light then passes through the vitreous humor, the gel that fills the back of the eye, and lands on the retina, where rods and cones turn it into nerve signals. Every structure before the retina is refractive media: each one bends light toward the retina, so a clouded or misshapen part anywhere along the path blurs the image. Cornea, aqueous, lens, vitreous, retina: front to back, every clear part bends light.
questions.strategy: Students swap the two humors. Aqueous is in front of the lens and vitreous is behind it, which is why raised aqueous pressure is the glaucoma problem and vitreous changes are the detachment problem.

questions.stem: For each task, identify which retinal cells do most of the work.

rows.text: Finding the way down a dark hallway at night
Telling a red tablet from a white one
Noticing a car coming up from the side
Reading small print straight ahead
Seeing movement at the edge of the field in dim light

questions.takeaway: Rods are spread through the outer retina and work in low light and for peripheral vision, so they handle the dark hallway, the car at the side, and movement at the edge in dim light. Cones are packed in the center of the retina and handle color and sharp central vision, so they sort the red tablet from the white one and read fine print. This is why losing peripheral vision, as in glaucoma, harms navigation and night safety, while central damage harms reading and color tasks. Rods for dim light and the edges; cones for color and the center.
questions.strategy: Ask two questions per row: is the light low, and is the target off to the side? Yes to either points to rods. The detail that decides the last row is dim light at the edge, which is rods on both counts.

questions.stem: During a PERRLA check, the nurse shines a penlight into the patient's right eye only. Both pupils constrict equally and briskly. What does the constriction of the left pupil show?

options.text: A direct response in the right eye
options.rationale: Near miss concept The direct response is the right pupil, the one the light entered. The question asks about the left pupil.

options.text: A consensual response in the left eye
options.rationale: PERRLA stands for pupils equal, round, reactive to light and accommodation. The direct response is constriction of the pupil that receives the light. The consensual response is constriction of the other pupil at the same time, because the light signal is shared between both sides of the brain. Here the left eye got no light and still constricted, so that is the consensual response. Accommodation is a separate test with a near and far target. An equal and brisk response in both eyes is normal, so nothing needs escalation.

options.text: A normal response to accommodation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Accommodation is tested by moving a target near and far, not by shining a light.

options.text: An abnormal finding needing escalation
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Equal, brisk constriction in the unlit eye is exactly what should happen.

questions.takeaway: The lit eye shows the direct response; the other eye shows the consensual response.
questions.strategy: The detail that decides it is that the light went into the right eye only. Any change in the left pupil therefore has to be the consensual response.

questions.stem: A patient has had slowly worsening, painless blurred vision in one eye for several years. Which examination finding fits a mature cataract?

options.text: A fixed, moderately dilated pupil in a red eye
options.rationale: Near miss concept A fixed, dilated pupil in a red eye belongs to acute angle closure glaucoma, which is sudden and painful, not gradual.

options.text: A bluish white pupil with no red reflex
options.rationale: A cataract is a clouding of the lens. As it matures, the lens becomes so opaque that the red reflex, the red glow from the retina seen through the ophthalmoscope, disappears, and the pupil looks bluish white. The other options are the signature findings of other eye problems: a fixed pupil in a red eye is angle closure glaucoma, green staining is a damaged cornea, and a shadow in the field is a detached retina. The painless, gradual history fits only the cataract.

options.text: Green staining of the cornea after fluorescein
options.rationale: Near miss concept Green fluorescein staining marks a corneal abrasion or ulcer, a surface injury that is painful.

options.text: A dark shadow across one part of the field of vision
options.rationale: Near miss concept A shadow over part of the field is retinal detachment, which comes on suddenly.

questions.takeaway: Mature cataract: painless and gradual, no red reflex, bluish white pupil.
questions.strategy: Match the time course first. The detail that rules out the near misses is painless and gradual over years; angle closure, abrasion and detachment are all sudden.

questions.stem: Classify each presentation by the type of glaucoma.

rows.text: Gradual loss of peripheral vision found at a routine visit, IOP 26 mm Hg
Sudden severe eye pain, red eye and corneal edema, IOP 38 mm Hg
Raised IOP after months of corticosteroid eye drops
New blood vessels from diabetes blocking aqueous drainage
No symptoms at all, IOP 24 mm Hg, early optic nerve changes

questions.takeaway: Open angle glaucoma is the most common type. Drainage slows gradually, pressure rises slowly into the low twenties or low thirties, and peripheral vision is lost without symptoms, which is why it is called the silent thief of sight. Both the routine visit finding and the symptom free patient with early nerve changes fit. Angle closure glaucoma is sudden: the iris shifts and blocks drainage, pressure jumps above 30 mm Hg, and the eye is painful, red and edematous. It is an emergency. Secondary glaucoma has an identifiable outside cause, such as steroid use, trauma, or new vessels from diabetes that block drainage. Gradual and silent is open angle; sudden and painful is angle closure; a named cause makes it secondary.
questions.strategy: Look for a cause before you look at the pressure. The detail that moves the steroid and diabetes rows into secondary is that something outside the drainage angle started the problem.

questions.stem: A patient can read a book easily but cannot read road signs until close to them. Testing shows the image focuses in front of the retina. Which correction fits?

options.text: A convex lens, because the image falls in front of the retina
options.rationale: Near miss concept It names the right problem but the wrong lens. A convex lens adds focusing power, which would pull the image even further forward.

options.text: Reading glasses, because close work is what looks blurred
options.rationale: Near miss concept Near vision is fine in this patient. The blur is at a distance.

options.text: A convex lens, because the lens has lost its elasticity
options.rationale: Near miss concept Loss of lens elasticity is presbyopia, which blurs near vision. This patient reads easily.

options.text: A concave lens, because the image falls in front of the retina
options.rationale: Myopia, or nearsightedness, means the eye focuses the image in front of the retina, so near objects are clear and distant ones blur. A concave lens spreads light out slightly and pushes the focus back onto the retina. Hyperopia is the opposite: the image falls behind the retina and a convex lens corrects it. Presbyopia is age related loss of lens elasticity that blurs near vision. Reading glasses treat near blur, which this patient does not have.

questions.takeaway: Myopia: in front of the retina, concave lens. Hyperopia: behind the retina, convex lens.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out presbyopia and reading glasses is that the patient reads a book easily. Distance blur with clear near vision is myopia.

questions.stem: After a patient reports new floaters, the provider finds a small retinal tear. The retina is still attached. Which treatment should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Laser photocoagulation or cryopexy to seal the tear
options.rationale: A retinal tear is a break in the retina that has not yet pulled away from the layer beneath it. Laser photocoagulation or cryopexy creates a scar that seals the edges, so fluid cannot get under the retina and lift it off. Once the retina has fully separated, it needs scleral buckling, a band that indents the sclera, with oil or gas to hold the retina in place. Phacoemulsification is cataract surgery, and iridotomy treats angle closure glaucoma.

options.text: Scleral buckling with gas to hold the retina in place
options.rationale: Correct but premature Scleral buckling is the surgery for a full detachment. This retina is still attached, so the goal is to seal the tear before it detaches.

options.text: Phacoemulsification with a lens implant
options.rationale: Near miss concept Phacoemulsification removes a cataract. It does nothing for the retina.

options.text: Laser peripheral iridotomy to open drainage
options.rationale: Near miss concept Iridotomy is the emergency treatment for angle closure glaucoma, a drainage problem.

questions.takeaway: Seal a tear with laser or cold; buckle a detachment.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out scleral buckling is the phrase the retina is still attached. The stage decides the treatment.

questions.stem: Four patients call the clinic. Which should be seen most urgently?

options.text: Sudden painless flashes, floaters and a shadow over one eye
options.rationale: Retinal detachment, and the window to reattach a retina before the photoreceptors die is short. The painlessness is why patients wait and why this item works. Conjunctivitis is uncomfortable and not sight threatening, gradual near blurring is presbyopia or cataract, and a surface foreign body needs attention today rather than this hour.

options.text: A red, itchy, watery eye with crusting of the lids on waking
options.rationale: Near miss concept Conjunctivitis: contagious, uncomfortable, not sight threatening.

options.text: A gritty foreign body feeling and tearing after doing yard work
options.rationale: Near miss concept Needs evaluation today, and it is not minutes to hours.

options.text: Reading vision that has gradually blurred over six months
options.rationale: Near miss concept Gradual change over months is a refraction or lens problem.

questions.takeaway: Painless does not mean benign. Sudden and painless with a shadow is the eye emergency people sit on.
questions.strategy: Rank by threat to sight and by how fast tissue dies, not by how uncomfortable the patient is.

questions.stem: A patient newly diagnosed with open angle glaucoma says, "I will use the drops until my vision comes back." How should the nurse respond?

options.text: “Once your eye pressure is normal, you can stop the drops.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept The pressure is normal because of the drops.

options.text: “New glasses will correct the vision that has been lost.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Glaucoma loss is nerve loss, and glasses correct refraction.

options.text: “The drops prevent more loss; lost vision will not return.”
options.rationale: Glaucoma kills optic nerve fibers, starting peripherally, and dead nerve does not regenerate. The entire goal is preventing further damage, which is why adherence matters so much in a disease that causes no symptoms early. Teach punctal occlusion so less drug is absorbed systemically.

options.text: “Vision usually returns within months of starting the drops.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Promises something the disease does not allow.

questions.takeaway: You are protecting the vision that is left. There is nothing to win back.
questions.strategy: A patient who expects improvement stops the drops when it does not come.

questions.stem: A patient arrives with a metal fragment protruding from his eye. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Leave it in place, stabilize it, and prepare for eye evaluation
options.rationale: Never remove a protruding object from an eye: it may be the only thing holding the contents in, and pulling it can prolapse them. Only the eye care provider assesses and removes it. MRI is contraindicated when a metal fragment is suspected, because the magnet can move it. X ray or CT is used instead, with intravenous antibiotics and a tetanus booster before surgery.

options.text: Arrange an MRI to find out how deep the fragment has gone
options.rationale: Near miss concept Contraindicated with suspected metal; the magnet can drag the fragment through the eye.

options.text: Remove it only if it slides out easily, then patch both eyes
options.rationale: Near miss concept Easily is not a criterion. It stays in.

options.text: Remove the fragment and irrigate the eye with sterile saline
options.rationale: Near miss concept Irrigation is for a surface foreign body, not a penetrating one.

questions.takeaway: Nothing comes out of an eye at the bedside, and no metal fragment goes near a magnet.
questions.strategy: Two of these options remove the object. Both are wrong for the same reason.

questions.topic: assessing the eye in an emergency
questions.stem: A patient has a chemical splash in one eye. What should the nurse do first?
questions.objective: assessing the eye in an emergency

options.text: Identify the exact chemical before starting any irrigation
options.rationale: Correct but premature Identification guides later care; irrigation is the same at the start.

options.text: Patch the eye loosely and arrange an urgent ophthalmology review today
options.rationale: Near miss concept Traps the chemical against the cornea.

options.text: Irrigate with water or saline now for at least 15 minutes
options.rationale: Every second of contact is more corneal damage, especially with an alkali, which keeps penetrating. Irrigation starts before anything else, including the acuity check and the identification of the agent, both of which happen while the eye is being flushed or after. Patching holds the chemical against the cornea.

options.text: Check visual acuity in both eyes before any intervention
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting A baseline matters and it can be obtained after flushing begins.

questions.takeaway: Irrigate first. Identify the chemical while the water is running.
questions.strategy: Every wrong option delays irrigation for something that can be done during or after it.

questions.stem: A patient arrives with sudden severe eye pain, blurred vision, a red eye and a hazy cornea. She reports seeing halos around lights and is nauseated. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Darken the room and administer an analgesic for the pain
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Treats the pain and leaves the pressure crushing the nerve.

options.text: Treat this as an emergency and escalate immediately
options.rationale: Sudden pain with a red eye, corneal edema and nausea is angle closure glaucoma. The iris has shifted and blocked drainage, pressure is climbing fast, and the optic nerve is being damaged while you decide. Pressure comes down first with drops and systemic acetazolamide; laser peripheral iridotomy is the definitive fix once the cornea clears. Open angle glaucoma is the silent one; this is the one that hurts.

options.text: Instill the patient's usual glaucoma drops and reassess in an hour
options.rationale: Near miss concept Maintenance drops do not reverse an acute angle closure.

options.text: Apply a cool compress and schedule an urgent clinic appointment
options.rationale: Correct but premature Urgent is not the same as now, and vision is being lost by the hour.

questions.takeaway: Painful red eye with halos and nausea is an emergency, not an eye appointment.
questions.strategy: The nausea is the detail students skip. It comes from the pressure, not the stomach.

questions.stem: A patient 8 hours after cataract surgery reports sudden severe eye pain and says his vision has become much worse since the afternoon. He is nauseated. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Administer the ordered analgesic and antiemetic and reassess
options.rationale: Near miss concept Masks the two findings that define the emergency.

options.text: Have him lie on the operative side and rest
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pressure on the operative eye is specifically avoided.

options.text: Escalate immediately, because this suggests raised intraocular pressure or hemorrhage
options.rationale: Mild scratchiness and itching are expected after cataract surgery. Sudden severe pain with worsening vision is not, and with nausea it points to acutely raised intraocular pressure or bleeding into the eye. These are the exact symptoms patients are told to report immediately, and treating the pain removes the signal and the urgency.

options.text: Apply a cool compress and reassure him that discomfort is expected
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Mild discomfort is expected; this is not mild.

questions.takeaway: The discharge teaching says report sudden pain or vision loss. This is that patient.
questions.strategy: The analgesic option is the trap, because it treats what the patient complained of.

questions.stem: A patient with asthma and bradycardia is prescribed a topical beta blocker for glaucoma. Select all of the appropriate nursing actions.

options.text: Reassure the patient that eye drops have no systemic effects
options.rationale: Near miss concept False, and in this patient the systemic effect is the main hazard.

options.text: Teach him to hold the dropper against the eye to steady his hand
options.rationale: Near miss concept Contaminates the bottle and can injure the cornea.

options.text: Teach that one drop per eye is the dose, and more does not help
options.rationale: Eye drops drain into the nasolacrimal duct and are absorbed systemically, and a topical beta blocker can cause bronchospasm and bradycardia, which matters a great deal in this patient. Punctal occlusion for about a minute reduces it. The conjunctival sac holds one drop, so a second just overflows. Touching the dropper to the eye contaminates the bottle.

options.text: Assess heart rate and respiratory status and report the asthma history
options.rationale: Eye drops drain into the nasolacrimal duct and are absorbed systemically, and a topical beta blocker can cause bronchospasm and bradycardia, which matters a great deal in this patient. Punctal occlusion for about a minute reduces it. The conjunctival sac holds one drop, so a second just overflows. Touching the dropper to the eye contaminates the bottle.

options.text: Teach punctal occlusion to reduce systemic absorption
options.rationale: Eye drops drain into the nasolacrimal duct and are absorbed systemically, and a topical beta blocker can cause bronchospasm and bradycardia, which matters a great deal in this patient. Punctal occlusion for about a minute reduces it. The conjunctival sac holds one drop, so a second just overflows. Touching the dropper to the eye contaminates the bottle.

options.text: Space different eye medications about five minutes apart
options.rationale: Eye drops drain into the nasolacrimal duct and are absorbed systemically, and a topical beta blocker can cause bronchospasm and bradycardia, which matters a great deal in this patient. Punctal occlusion for about a minute reduces it. The conjunctival sac holds one drop, so a second just overflows. Touching the dropper to the eye contaminates the bottle.

questions.takeaway: An eye drop is a systemic drug. In asthma and bradycardia, a topical beta blocker is a real problem.
questions.strategy: The reassurance option is the dangerous one, because it is what most patients already believe.

questions.stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes for 12 years says his vision is fine so he does not need an eye examination. What is the most important point for the nurse to make?

options.text: Retinopathy damages vision silently; a yearly dilated exam is needed
options.rationale: Retinopathy destroys the retina from the periphery and around the macula long before the patient notices anything, and by the time vision changes the damage is often advanced and irreversible. Treatment exists and works when it is started early, which is the entire argument for screening someone who feels fine. Glucose control slows progression; it does not reverse damage already done.

options.text: He needs an eye exam only if his A1C rises above 8 percent
options.rationale: Near miss concept Screening is not triggered by a laboratory value.

options.text: Reading glasses will correct any vision changes that develop
options.rationale: Near miss concept Retinal damage is not a refractive problem.

options.text: Diabetic vision changes reverse once glucose is well controlled
options.rationale: Near miss concept Control slows progression; established retinal damage does not reverse.

questions.takeaway: Good vision is not evidence of a healthy retina. That is the whole point of screening.
questions.strategy: Any option that waits for a symptom or a lab threshold has misunderstood what screening is for.

questions.stem: A patient is waiting for surgery after the provider confirms a retinal detachment. Which nursing action is most appropriate while the patient waits?

options.text: Restrict head movement and activity and keep the patient at rest
options.rationale: Retinal detachment is a sudden, painless emergency. Once it is reported, the nursing measure while the patient waits for repair is to restrict head movement and activity so the detachment does not extend. The usual bed rest precautions give way to protecting the retina.

options.text: Encourage reading to keep the patient calm until surgery
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Calming, and reading moves the eyes constantly, which is what you are trying to limit.

options.text: Have the patient walk in the hall to prevent complications of bed rest
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sound general advice for a hospitalized patient, and activity is exactly what this patient restricts.

options.text: Apply warm compresses to the affected eye
options.rationale: Near miss concept Has no role in a detached retina.

questions.takeaway: Retinal detachment: notify now, then keep the head and the patient still.
questions.strategy: The wrong options are reasonable for almost any other inpatient. Ask what each one does to the eye.

questions.stem: A patient who wears soft contact lenses slept in them for three nights. The patient now has a painful, red right eye, tearing and blurred vision. The cornea looks hazy, and fluorescein shows a green stained area. The pupils are equal and reactive, and the IOP is 16 mm Hg. Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters to monitor.

options.text: Remove the lenses and keep them out until the cornea heals
Give the antibiotic drops on the ordered schedule
Prepare the patient for laser peripheral iridotomy
Restrict head movement and patch the eye before surgery
Corneal infection
Acute angle closure glaucoma
Retinal detachment
Mature cataract
Clearing of the corneal haze
Pain and visual acuity
Intraocular pressure
Presence of the red reflex

questions.takeaway: Condition: a corneal infection or ulcer. Contact lens overwear, a hazy cornea and green fluorescein staining all point to damage of the cornea. The cornea has no blood supply of its own, so an infection there can scar it and threaten sight quickly, which makes it an emergency. Angle closure glaucoma is ruled out by the normal IOP and reactive pupils. Retinal detachment is painless and does not stain. A cataract is painless and gradual. Actions: the lenses come out and stay out until the cornea fully heals, because the lens traps organisms against the injury. Broad spectrum antibiotic drops are given on the ordered schedule, often hourly for the first 24 hours, and the full course is finished. Iridotomy treats angle closure, and head restriction with patching is preparation for retinal surgery. Parameters: clearing of the corneal haze shows the infection is resolving, and pain with visual acuity shows whether sight is being protected. IOP is not the problem here, and the red reflex is used to judge the lens. Contact lens overuse plus a hazy, stained cornea is a corneal emergency: lenses out, antibiotics on time.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out angle closure glaucoma is the IOP of 16 mm Hg with reactive pupils. A red, painful eye alone does not decide it; the stain and the pressure do.

questions.topic: imaging after a penetrating eye injury
questions.stem: A patient was grinding steel without eye protection and felt something strike the left eye. Vision in that eye is reduced and a small wound is visible on the cornea. The nurse reviews the admission orders. Which order should the nurse question?
questions.objective: imaging after a penetrating eye injury

options.text: Intravenous antibiotics before surgery
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question IV antibiotics before surgery are expected after a penetrating injury to prevent infection inside the eye.

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the orbits
options.rationale: A penetrating injury means an object has broken through the surface of the eye. When the object may be metal, MRI is contraindicated: the magnet can move the fragment inside the eye and cause more damage. X ray or CT is used instead. IV antibiotics and a tetanus booster are standard before surgery. The nurse questions the MRI before the patient goes to the scanner.

options.text: A tetanus booster
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question A tetanus booster is expected for a penetrating wound from a dirty metal source.

options.text: Computed tomography of the orbits
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question CT is the preferred imaging when a metal fragment may be in the eye, because it does not use a magnetic field.

questions.takeaway: Metal in the eye: CT or X ray, never MRI.
questions.strategy: The detail that makes the MRI dangerous is grinding steel. A metal source turns a routine imaging order into an injury risk.

questions.stem: Select all of the self management measures for a patient with Meniere disease.

options.text: Follow a low sodium diet
options.rationale: The disease is too much endolymph, so sodium restriction and diuretics reduce the volume. Caffeine, stress and fatigue are triggers. Safety drives the rest, because a drop attack arrives without warning. Vestibular rehabilitation exercises are done between attacks, not during one, when they would simply worsen the vertigo and the vomiting.

options.text: Increase fluid intake sharply to dilute the inner ear fluid
options.rationale: Near miss concept The problem is too much endolymph; loading fluid does not dilute it.

options.text: Do not drive or climb ladders during an attack
options.rationale: The disease is too much endolymph, so sodium restriction and diuretics reduce the volume. Caffeine, stress and fatigue are triggers. Safety drives the rest, because a drop attack arrives without warning. Vestibular rehabilitation exercises are done between attacks, not during one, when they would simply worsen the vertigo and the vomiting.

options.text: Avoid caffeine, excessive stress and fatigue
options.rationale: The disease is too much endolymph, so sodium restriction and diuretics reduce the volume. Caffeine, stress and fatigue are triggers. Safety drives the rest, because a drop attack arrives without warning. Vestibular rehabilitation exercises are done between attacks, not during one, when they would simply worsen the vertigo and the vomiting.

options.text: Perform rapid head turning exercises during an acute attack
options.rationale: Near miss concept Vestibular rehabilitation happens between attacks.

options.text: Sit or lie down immediately when an attack begins
options.rationale: The disease is too much endolymph, so sodium restriction and diuretics reduce the volume. Caffeine, stress and fatigue are triggers. Safety drives the rest, because a drop attack arrives without warning. Vestibular rehabilitation exercises are done between attacks, not during one, when they would simply worsen the vertigo and the vomiting.

questions.takeaway: Low sodium for the fluid, and safety for the attack you cannot predict.
questions.strategy: One wrong option treats a fluid excess with more fluid, the other does rehabilitation at the worst possible moment.

questions.stem: Which statement about age related changes in the ear is accurate?

options.text: The tympanic membrane becomes more elastic and mobile with age
options.rationale: Near miss concept It loses elasticity and may look dull or retracted.

options.text: High pitches go first, and drier earwax impacts more easily
options.rationale: Presbycusis takes the high frequencies first, which is why consonants blur and people seem to mumble while vowels still come through. The cerumen gets drier and impacts, which is a conductive loss layered on top and is the most common correctable cause. The tympanic membrane loses elasticity rather than gaining it.

options.text: Cerumen production stops entirely in most older adults
options.rationale: Near miss concept It continues and becomes drier, which is why impaction increases.

options.text: Every older adult develops significant, disabling hearing loss
options.rationale: Absolute language Prevalence rises with age and it is not universal; assess individually.

questions.takeaway: Consonants go first. That is why speech sounds mumbled before anything sounds quiet.
questions.strategy: The absolute option is wrong for the usual reason: assess each patient.

questions.stem: A nurse places a vibrating tuning fork on the center of a patient's forehead. The patient hears it louder in the left ear. What does this suggest?

options.text: A sensorineural hearing loss in the left ear
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sound moves away from a sensorineural loss, not toward it.

options.text: Normal hearing in both ears with equal conduction
options.rationale: Near miss concept Normal Weber is equal in both ears, with no lateralization.

options.text: A conductive hearing loss in the right ear only
options.rationale: Near miss concept A right conductive loss would lateralize to the right.

options.text: Left conductive loss or right sensorineural loss
options.rationale: The Weber test checks whether sound is heard equally in both ears. Sound lateralizes toward a conductive loss, because the blocked ear is not competing with room noise, and away from a sensorineural loss, because that ear cannot process it. Louder on the left means conductive on the left or sensorineural on the right. Rinne, comparing air to bone conduction, sorts out which.

questions.takeaway: Weber lateralizes TOWARD a conductive loss and AWAY from a sensorineural one.
questions.strategy: Weber alone cannot name the ear. It gives you two possibilities and Rinne resolves them.

questions.stem: Select all of the measures for a patient with Meniere disease and acute vertigo.

options.text: A quiet room with dim lighting during an attack
options.rationale: An acute attack is a fall waiting to happen, so safety comes first and stimulation comes down. Slow head movement is the single most useful instruction she can follow. Ambulating during an attack is dangerous, and the dietary measure in Meniere disease is sodium restriction, not fluid restriction, which is a detail worth keeping straight.

options.text: Side rails up and the bed kept in the low position
options.rationale: An acute attack is a fall waiting to happen, so safety comes first and stimulation comes down. Slow head movement is the single most useful instruction she can follow. Ambulating during an attack is dangerous, and the dietary measure in Meniere disease is sodium restriction, not fluid restriction, which is a detail worth keeping straight.

options.text: Restrict all fluids to lower the inner ear pressure
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sodium is the restriction; fluid restriction is not the treatment.

options.text: Assist with all walking; keep the call light in reach
options.rationale: An acute attack is a fall waiting to happen, so safety comes first and stimulation comes down. Slow head movement is the single most useful instruction she can follow. Ambulating during an attack is dangerous, and the dietary measure in Meniere disease is sodium restriction, not fluid restriction, which is a detail worth keeping straight.

options.text: Encourage walking during an attack to help her adapt
options.rationale: Near miss concept Vestibular rehabilitation happens between attacks, not during one.

options.text: Move the head slowly and avoid sudden position changes
options.rationale: An acute attack is a fall waiting to happen, so safety comes first and stimulation comes down. Slow head movement is the single most useful instruction she can follow. Ambulating during an attack is dangerous, and the dietary measure in Meniere disease is sodium restriction, not fluid restriction, which is a detail worth keeping straight.

questions.takeaway: Sodium is restricted in Meniere disease, not fluid. Those get swapped constantly.
questions.strategy: One wrong option mobilizes her mid attack and the other restricts the wrong thing.

questions.stem: A patient is going home after tympanoplasty. Which instruction is most important?

options.text: Do not blow your nose, and sneeze with your mouth open
options.rationale: Blowing the nose drives pressure up the eustachian tube and straight against the repair. Sneezing with the mouth open vents it instead. No water in the ear, no straining, and no air travel until cleared. Hearing improves over about four to six weeks, not by discharge.

options.text: Expect your hearing to be normal by the time you leave
options.rationale: Near miss concept Improvement takes weeks, and swelling and packing blunt it at first.

options.text: You may resume swimming one week after the surgery
options.rationale: Near miss concept Water exposure is restricted far longer.

options.text: Irrigate the ear canal daily to keep it clean and clear
options.rationale: Near miss concept Water near a fresh tympanic repair risks infection and graft failure.

questions.takeaway: Anything that pressurizes the middle ear threatens the graft.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options put water or pressure where the repair is.

questions.stem: A patient's Weber test lateralizes to the right ear. The Rinne test on the right shows bone conduction heard longer than air conduction. What does this indicate?

options.text: Normal hearing in both ears
options.rationale: Near miss concept Normal is no lateralization on Weber and air longer than bone on Rinne.

options.text: A sensorineural hearing loss in the left ear
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is the other Weber possibility, and the right Rinne result rules it out.

options.text: A sensorineural hearing loss in the right ear
options.rationale: Near miss concept Weber would lateralize away from a sensorineural ear, and Rinne would show air longer than bone.

options.text: A conductive hearing loss in the right ear
options.rationale: Weber lateralizing right means either a conductive loss on the right or a sensorineural loss on the left. Rinne resolves it: normally air conduction is heard longer than bone, and when bone beats air in that ear, sound is being blocked on its way in. Both tests together point to a right conductive loss, which is often correctable.

questions.takeaway: Weber gives you two possibilities. Rinne tells you which. Bone longer than air is conductive.
questions.strategy: Work Weber first for the two candidates, then let Rinne pick.

questions.stem: Classify each cause of hearing loss.

rows.text: Fluid behind the tympanic membrane from otitis media
Presbycusis from cochlear nerve degeneration
Gentamicin given for five days
Cerumen impaction in the ear canal

questions.takeaway: Conductive loss is anything blocking sound on its way in: wax, fluid, a perforation, otosclerosis. It is often correctable. Sensorineural loss is damage to the inner ear or cranial nerve VIII from aging, noise, ototoxic drugs or tumors, and it is usually permanent. Mixed loss is both. Blocked on the way in is conductive and often fixable. Damaged at the end of the line is sensorineural and usually not.
questions.strategy: Trace the sound: canal, eardrum and ossicles are conduction; cochlea and nerve are sensorineural.

questions.stem: Select all of the measures that protect a patient's hearing.

options.text: Do not insert cotton swabs or any object into the ear canal
options.rationale: Noise induced loss is permanent and entirely preventable, which is why protection and volume matter more than anything else here. Swabs push wax against the drum and perforate it. Tinnitus on aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, high dose salicylates or cisplatin is the early warning, and reporting it is what preserves the hearing. Routine irrigation and routine drops are both unnecessary and can cause harm.

options.text: Keep personal listening device volume at a moderate level
options.rationale: Noise induced loss is permanent and entirely preventable, which is why protection and volume matter more than anything else here. Swabs push wax against the drum and perforate it. Tinnitus on aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, high dose salicylates or cisplatin is the early warning, and reporting it is what preserves the hearing. Routine irrigation and routine drops are both unnecessary and can cause harm.

options.text: Report tinnitus or new hearing change in a patient on an ototoxic drug
options.rationale: Noise induced loss is permanent and entirely preventable, which is why protection and volume matter more than anything else here. Swabs push wax against the drum and perforate it. Tinnitus on aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, high dose salicylates or cisplatin is the early warning, and reporting it is what preserves the hearing. Routine irrigation and routine drops are both unnecessary and can cause harm.

options.text: Use over the counter ear drops routinely to prevent infection
options.rationale: Near miss concept No preventive role, and drops are contraindicated with a perforated drum.

options.text: Irrigate the ears monthly to remove wax that could muffle sound
options.rationale: Near miss concept Wax is protective; irrigation is done for impaction, not routinely, and never with a perforated drum.

options.text: Use hearing protection around loud equipment and at concerts
options.rationale: Noise induced loss is permanent and entirely preventable, which is why protection and volume matter more than anything else here. Swabs push wax against the drum and perforate it. Tinnitus on aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, high dose salicylates or cisplatin is the early warning, and reporting it is what preserves the hearing. Routine irrigation and routine drops are both unnecessary and can cause harm.

questions.takeaway: Tinnitus on an ototoxic drug is the warning. Report it before the hearing goes.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options turn an as needed intervention into a routine one.

questions.stem: A patient has cerumen impaction. Which finding means the nurse should not irrigate the ear?

options.text: A suspected perforation of the tympanic membrane
options.rationale: Irrigating past a perforation pushes water and whatever is in the canal into the middle ear, which spreads infection. Do not irrigate with a suspected perforation or active otitis media, and do not irrigate vegetable matter, which swells with water. A live insect is killed with mineral oil or lidocaine first, because irrigating something still moving drives it deeper and worsens the pain.

options.text: A sensation of fullness in the ear
options.rationale: Near miss concept An indication, not a contraindication.

options.text: Hearing loss that developed gradually over a month
options.rationale: Near miss concept Consistent with impaction and a reason to treat it.

options.text: Itching in the ear canal
options.rationale: Near miss concept Another symptom of impaction.

questions.takeaway: No irrigation through a hole, into an infection, or onto something that swells.
questions.strategy: Three of these are the reasons you would irrigate. One is the reason you would not.

questions.topic: communicating with a hard of hearing patient
questions.stem: Select all of the measures that improve communication with a patient who has a hearing impairment.
questions.objective: communicating with a hard of hearing patient

options.text: Reduce background noise before you start
options.rationale: Age related loss takes the high frequencies first, so lowering your pitch helps and raising it, which is what shouting does, makes you harder to understand. Exaggerated mouth movements distort the shapes a lip reader depends on. Rephrasing works because a different word may carry frequencies he can still hear.

options.text: Shout toward the better ear
options.rationale: Near miss concept Raises pitch into the range already lost and distorts the sound.

options.text: Face the patient at eye level with your mouth visible
options.rationale: Age related loss takes the high frequencies first, so lowering your pitch helps and raising it, which is what shouting does, makes you harder to understand. Exaggerated mouth movements distort the shapes a lip reader depends on. Rephrasing works because a different word may carry frequencies he can still hear.

options.text: Rephrase rather than repeat when you are not understood
options.rationale: Age related loss takes the high frequencies first, so lowering your pitch helps and raising it, which is what shouting does, makes you harder to understand. Exaggerated mouth movements distort the shapes a lip reader depends on. Rephrasing works because a different word may carry frequencies he can still hear.

options.text: Exaggerate your mouth movements so speech can be read more easily
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Distorts the lip shapes a reader relies on.

options.text: Speak at a normal rate in a slightly lowered pitch
options.rationale: Age related loss takes the high frequencies first, so lowering your pitch helps and raising it, which is what shouting does, makes you harder to understand. Exaggerated mouth movements distort the shapes a lip reader depends on. Rephrasing works because a different word may carry frequencies he can still hear.

questions.takeaway: Lower your pitch rather than raising your volume. Shouting raises pitch and makes it worse.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options are well meant and both make the speech less intelligible.

questions.stem: Which observation most suggests an undiagnosed hearing loss?

options.text: He reads the written discharge instructions slowly
options.rationale: Near miss concept Points to literacy or vision, not hearing.

options.text: He turns his head to one side and leans in to listen
options.rationale: The behavioral cues are head tilting, leaning in, frequent what, answers that do not match the question, shouting, and withdrawing from group conversation. Turning one ear toward the speaker says he has a better ear and is using it. Asking about one unfamiliar word is comprehension, not hearing.

options.text: He prefers the television at a moderate volume
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Moderate volume argues against loss, if anything.

options.text: He asks the nurse to repeat a complex medical term during the teaching session
options.rationale: Near miss concept Vocabulary, not audibility.

questions.takeaway: Watch the head. A patient who aims one ear at you is telling you something.
questions.strategy: Three options are normal behavior that could happen to anyone.

questions.stem: Select all of the instructions for a patient with a new behind the ear hearing aid.

options.text: Wash the aid in warm soapy water weekly
options.rationale: Near miss concept Water ruins the aid; clean it dry.

options.text: Expect whistling and ignore it, since it means the aid is working
options.rationale: Near miss concept Feedback means a poor seal, excess volume or wax.

options.text: Turn the aid off and open the battery door when it is not in use
options.rationale: The body of the aid is electronics and is wiped dry only, never submerged. On a behind the ear aid the earmold and tubing detach and may be washed in warm soapy water and dried completely, but the aid itself never goes near water, heat or spray. Opening the battery door saves the battery and prevents corrosion. Whistling is feedback from a poor seal, a volume set too high or wax in the opening, and it is a fixable problem rather than a sign of function, which is why so many aids end up in a drawer.

options.text: Clean the ear mold with a dry cloth and check the opening for wax
options.rationale: The body of the aid is electronics and is wiped dry only, never submerged. On a behind the ear aid the earmold and tubing detach and may be washed in warm soapy water and dried completely, but the aid itself never goes near water, heat or spray. Opening the battery door saves the battery and prevents corrosion. Whistling is feedback from a poor seal, a volume set too high or wax in the opening, and it is a fixable problem rather than a sign of function, which is why so many aids end up in a drawer.

options.text: Keep the aid away from heat, hair spray and water
options.rationale: The body of the aid is electronics and is wiped dry only, never submerged. On a behind the ear aid the earmold and tubing detach and may be washed in warm soapy water and dried completely, but the aid itself never goes near water, heat or spray. Opening the battery door saves the battery and prevents corrosion. Whistling is feedback from a poor seal, a volume set too high or wax in the opening, and it is a fixable problem rather than a sign of function, which is why so many aids end up in a drawer.

options.text: Start with low volume and increase gradually as you adjust
options.rationale: The body of the aid is electronics and is wiped dry only, never submerged. On a behind the ear aid the earmold and tubing detach and may be washed in warm soapy water and dried completely, but the aid itself never goes near water, heat or spray. Opening the battery door saves the battery and prevents corrosion. Whistling is feedback from a poor seal, a volume set too high or wax in the opening, and it is a fixable problem rather than a sign of function, which is why so many aids end up in a drawer.

questions.takeaway: Whistling means a bad fit or wax. It is the reason people stop wearing the aid.
questions.strategy: One wrong option soaks electronics and the other normalizes a fixable malfunction.

questions.stem: Which patient should the nurse monitor most closely for drug related hearing loss?

options.text: A patient taking an antihistamine for seasonal allergies
options.rationale: Near miss concept Not on the ototoxic list.

options.text: A patient taking acetaminophen for headache
options.rationale: Near miss concept Aspirin and NSAIDs are ototoxic; acetaminophen is not on the list.

options.text: A patient receiving gentamicin together with furosemide
options.rationale: The ototoxic drugs are gentamicin and other aminoglycosides, furosemide, NSAIDs, aspirin, quinine and chemotherapy. Two of them together, an aminoglycoside with a loop diuretic, raise the risk beyond either one alone, so that patient is monitored most closely for tinnitus, hearing loss and dizziness.

options.text: A patient taking a proton pump inhibitor for reflux
options.rationale: Near miss concept Not on the ototoxic list.

questions.takeaway: Aminoglycoside plus loop diuretic is the combination that doubles the worry.
questions.strategy: One option holds two drugs from the list. The others hold none.

questions.stem: A patient reports episodes of the room spinning, with nausea, ringing in one ear and a sense of fullness, lasting hours. Select all of the appropriate nursing actions.

options.text: Institute fall precautions and assist with all ambulation during episodes
options.rationale: The triad of vertigo, tinnitus and hearing loss with aural fullness, lasting hours, is Meniere disease. Safety dominates because a Tumarkin drop attack comes without warning. Low sodium and diuretics reduce the endolymph. During an attack you keep things still and quiet. Vestibular rehabilitation happens between attacks, and the hearing loss is progressive rather than temporary.

options.text: Encourage ambulation during attacks to help the vestibular system adapt
options.rationale: Near miss concept Rehabilitation is done between attacks; during one it causes falls and vomiting.

options.text: Keep the room quiet with minimal head movement during an attack
options.rationale: The triad of vertigo, tinnitus and hearing loss with aural fullness, lasting hours, is Meniere disease. Safety dominates because a Tumarkin drop attack comes without warning.
