Low sodium and diuretics reduce the endolymph. During an attack you keep things still and quiet. Vestibular rehabilitation happens between attacks, and the hearing loss is progressive rather than temporary.

options.text: Teach that the hearing loss from this condition is always temporary
options.rationale: Absolute language It fluctuates early and becomes permanent and progressive.

options.text: Teach a low sodium diet and avoidance of caffeine and nicotine
options.rationale: The triad of vertigo, tinnitus and hearing loss with aural fullness, lasting hours, is Meniere disease. Safety dominates because a Tumarkin drop attack comes without warning. Low sodium and diuretics reduce the endolymph. During an attack you keep things still and quiet. Vestibular rehabilitation happens between attacks, and the hearing loss is progressive rather than temporary.

options.text: Advise against driving, swimming alone and climbing during active disease
options.rationale: The triad of vertigo, tinnitus and hearing loss with aural fullness, lasting hours, is Meniere disease. Safety dominates because a Tumarkin drop attack comes without warning. Low sodium and diuretics reduce the endolymph. During an attack you keep things still and quiet. Vestibular rehabilitation happens between attacks, and the hearing loss is progressive rather than temporary.

questions.takeaway: Meniere hearing loss is progressive. Do not promise it comes back.
questions.strategy: One wrong option does rehabilitation at the worst moment; the other gives false reassurance about the hearing.

questions.stem: A patient is one day post stapedectomy. Which nursing action is the priority?

options.text: Schedule air travel teaching for the week after surgery
options.rationale: Near miss concept Air travel is avoided, not scheduled.

options.text: Encourage the patient to blow the nose gently to equalize pressure
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nose blowing is contraindicated; it raises middle ear pressure against the repair.

options.text: Assist with ambulation, because vertigo is common after this surgery
options.rationale: The stapes sits next to the vestibular apparatus, so disturbing it makes the room spin. Ambulation is assisted. Teaching is the opposite of the distractors here: no nose blowing, no straining, no air travel. Hearing takes about 4 to 6 weeks to improve, so testing it at discharge measures nothing. Watch for facial nerve damage, since cranial nerve VII runs close to the field.

options.text: Confirm hearing improvement before discharge
options.rationale: Correct but premature Improvement takes 4 to 6 weeks.

questions.takeaway: Vertigo after ear surgery is expected, and it is a fall risk on day one.
questions.strategy: Two of the wrong options are things this patient is specifically told not to do.

questions.stem: A child with acute otitis media has been crying with ear pain for hours. The parent reports the pain suddenly stopped and there is drainage from the ear. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: The analgesic has taken effect and the drainage is cerumen
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cerumen does not appear suddenly with pain relief.

options.text: The tympanic membrane has likely perforated, which relieves the pressure and the pain
options.rationale: The otoscopic progression runs retracted, then red with dilated vessels, then bulging, then perforation. The pain comes from pressure, so when the eardrum gives way the pressure drops and the pain stops. Sudden relief with drainage is the tell. Untreated, this leads to ossicle necrosis and permanent conductive loss.

options.text: The child has developed external otitis in addition to the middle ear infection
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would add pain rather than take it away.

options.text: The infection has resolved and no further care is needed
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reads relief as cure, which is exactly the error this item tests.

questions.takeaway: Pain that vanishes with drainage is not recovery. Something tore.
questions.strategy: Sudden relief is the trap. It reads as improvement and it is a complication.

questions.stem: A patient with profound hearing loss is admitted. Which action most directly protects his safety?

options.text: Set up how he will be alerted and call for help; tell the team
options.rationale: A patient who cannot hear will not hear a fire alarm, an overhead page, a code announcement or someone calling from the doorway, and he cannot use a call system that answers by intercom. Working out the alerting and calling method and recording it so every shift uses it is the safety intervention. A sign tells staff about the deficit without solving any of that.

options.text: Ask a family member to stay at the bedside at all times
options.rationale: Near miss concept Shifts a hospital responsibility onto the family.

options.text: Place a sign on the door saying the patient is hearing impaired so all staff know
options.rationale: Near miss concept Informs staff and arranges nothing, and it broadcasts his condition.

options.text: Speak loudly and slowly every time anyone enters the room
options.rationale: Near miss concept Shouting raises pitch into the lost range and does not solve alerting.

questions.takeaway: Ask how he will know there is an emergency. Nobody thinks of that until it is one.
questions.strategy: Shouting and a door sign both address communication convenience rather than safety.

questions.stem: A patient with Meniere disease is admitted during an acute attack. What is the nursing priority?

options.text: Hearing conservation with an immediate audiogram
options.rationale: Correct but premature Testing during an acute attack, with a patient who cannot sit still.

options.text: Fluid replacement for the vomiting and dehydration
options.rationale: Near miss concept Appropriate and secondary to not falling.

options.text: Safety, since vertigo and drop attacks cause falls
options.rationale: The triad is episodic vertigo, tinnitus and hearing loss, with nausea, vomiting and nystagmus alongside it. A Tumarkin crisis is a sudden drop attack with no warning at all, which is why safety outranks the rest: no ladders, no driving during attacks, fall precautions in the hospital. Management is a low sodium diet, diuretics to reduce endolymph, antiemetics and avoiding caffeine, stress and fatigue.

options.text: Pain control for the headache that accompanies it
options.rationale: Near miss concept Comfort, below safety.

questions.takeaway: The vertigo is miserable. The drop attack is what breaks a hip.
questions.strategy: The other three are real problems, and none of them can happen in the next ten seconds without warning.

questions.stem: A patient reports ear pain that worsens sharply when the nurse moves the pinna. Which condition does this suggest?

options.text: Meniere disease
options.rationale: Near miss concept Vertigo, tinnitus and hearing loss, not canal pain.

options.text: Cerumen impaction
options.rationale: Near miss concept Causes fullness and hearing loss, usually without this kind of pain.

options.text: External otitis
options.rationale: Pain on moving the pinna or pressing the tragus is the bedside finding that separates external otitis from a middle ear problem: the inflamed tissue is right there in the canal where you are pushing. Otitis media hurts from pressure behind an intact eardrum and is not reproduced by moving the ear. Treatment is cleaning by the provider, topical antibiotic or steroid drops, and no water or earbuds for 7 to 10 days.

options.text: Otitis media
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pain comes from pressure behind the eardrum and does not change when you move the pinna.

questions.takeaway: If moving the ear hurts, the problem is in the part you just moved.
questions.strategy: One physical maneuver separates these two. That is why the stem gives it to you.

questions.stem: A patient has moderate hearing loss and is not wearing hearing aids. How should the nurse speak with him?

options.text: Stand in front of the window so he can see the nurse clearly
options.rationale: Near miss concept Backlighting hides your face rather than revealing it.

options.text: Raise the volume substantially and exaggerate mouth movements
options.rationale: Near miss concept Shouting raises pitch into the lost range, and exaggeration distorts lip reading.

options.text: Speak into his ear from behind so the sound is closer to him
options.rationale: Near miss concept Removes the face entirely.

options.text: Face him in good light and speak clearly at a lower pitch
options.rationale: High frequencies go first, so shouting raises the pitch into the range he has already lost and distorts the face he is reading. Lowering the pitch does the opposite. Standing in front of a window backlights you and turns your face into a silhouette. Move to the better ear if he has one, and write things down.

questions.takeaway: Do not shout. Lower the pitch and let him see your face.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options take away the visual information he is using to fill in what he cannot hear.

questions.stem: A patient's audiogram shows a 35 decibel hearing loss. What should the nurse expect functionally?

options.text: Inability to hear speech unless the speaker is directly beside him
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is a 71 to 90 decibel loss.

options.text: No functional difficulty, since this is within normal limits
options.rationale: Near miss concept 35 decibels is a real loss; it is just a subtle one.

options.text: Difficulty following conversation in a noisy environment
options.rationale: Normal conversational speech is about 60 decibels and a whisper is about 30. A loss in the 20 to 40 range makes speech hard to follow when there is competing noise, which is why these patients do fine one to one in a quiet room and struggle at a family dinner. A 71 to 90 decibel loss is what requires the speaker to be right beside them.

options.text: Complete deafness requiring a cochlear implant
options.rationale: Near miss concept Far beyond what this audiogram shows.

questions.takeaway: Mild loss shows up in noise first. That is why family notice it before the patient does.
questions.strategy: Two options jump to a severity this number does not support.

questions.stem: A patient with profound sensorineural hearing loss asks why a hearing aid has not helped. What should the nurse explain?

options.text: Sensorineural loss always responds to enough amplification
options.rationale: Absolute language It often does not, which is the whole reason implants exist.

options.text: An aid only amplifies sound; a damaged cochlea cannot process it
options.rationale: Amplification helps when sound is being blocked on the way in, which is conductive loss. If the cochlea is the broken part, a louder signal arrives at the same broken machinery. A cochlear implant stimulates the nerve directly, skipping the cochlea altogether.

options.text: Hearing aids take several months before they become effective
options.rationale: Near miss concept Adjustment takes time; the benefit is apparent well before months.

options.text: The hearing aid is probably the wrong style and needs refitting
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fit matters and does not change what amplification can do.

questions.takeaway: Aids help conduction problems more than nerve problems. Louder is not clearer.
questions.strategy: The absolute option is false and the refitting option sends the patient back for more of what did not work.

questions.topic: when an ear complaint is an emergency
questions.stem: A patient with poorly controlled diabetes has severe ear pain, foul drainage, and granulation tissue visible in the canal, with pain out of proportion to the examination. What should the nurse suspect?
questions.objective: when an ear complaint is an emergency

options.text: Cerumen impaction with secondary irritation of the canal
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would not produce foul drainage or granulation tissue.

options.text: Routine swimmer's ear that needs only topical drops
options.rationale: Near miss concept The population and the granulation tissue make this the dangerous variant.

options.text: Necrotizing otitis externa needing urgent evaluation
options.rationale: In a diabetic or immunocompromised patient, external otitis can invade bone and reach the skull base and cranial nerves, and it can be fatal. The red flags are pain out of proportion, foul drainage and granulation tissue in the canal. It needs systemic treatment and imaging, not drops, and it is one of the few ear complaints that is genuinely an emergency.

options.text: Acute otitis media with a perforated eardrum
options.rationale: Near miss concept Middle ear pain relieved by perforation, not pain out of proportion with canal granulation.

questions.takeaway: Severe ear pain in a diabetic patient is not swimmer's ear until someone has ruled this out.
questions.strategy: The diabetes in the stem is the whole reason this is not a routine complaint.

questions.topic: pinna position for a young child
questions.stem: A nurse is about to instill ear drops for a 2 year old with external otitis. How should the nurse straighten the ear canal?
questions.objective: pinna position for a young child

options.text: Pull the pinna up and back
options.rationale: Near miss concept Correct for adults and children over 3; this child is under 3.

options.text: Pull the pinna down and back
options.rationale: The canal is straightened before anything goes in, and the direction depends on age. Under 3, the canal runs differently, so the pinna is pulled down and back. Adults and children over 3 get up and back.

options.text: Pull the pinna straight forward
options.rationale: Near miss concept Does not straighten the canal at any age.

options.text: Leave the pinna alone and insert the dropper tip into the canal
options.rationale: Near miss concept Skips straightening the canal and risks injury and contamination.

questions.takeaway: Under 3, down and back. Over 3, up and back.
questions.strategy: Up and back is the answer you have practiced on adults, which is why it is the trap for a toddler.

questions.stem: An older adult has cerumen impaction with an intact tympanic membrane and no infection. Select all of the actions that are correct for removing the wax.

options.text: Instill a ceruminolytic first to soften the wax
options.rationale: Impaction is treated with a ceruminolytic and then irrigation. The solution is body temperature, because cold or hot fluid in the ear stimulates the vestibular system and causes vertigo. The stream is aimed at the canal wall, never at the eardrum, and an adult's pinna is pulled up and back to straighten the canal.

options.text: Warm the irrigating solution to body temperature
options.rationale: Impaction is treated with a ceruminolytic and then irrigation. The solution is body temperature, because cold or hot fluid in the ear stimulates the vestibular system and causes vertigo. The stream is aimed at the canal wall, never at the eardrum, and an adult's pinna is pulled up and back to straighten the canal.

options.text: Direct the stream toward the wall of the canal
options.rationale: Impaction is treated with a ceruminolytic and then irrigation. The solution is body temperature, because cold or hot fluid in the ear stimulates the vestibular system and causes vertigo. The stream is aimed at the canal wall, never at the eardrum, and an adult's pinna is pulled up and back to straighten the canal.

options.text: Use cold solution to reduce discomfort in the canal
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cold or hot fluid in the ear causes vertigo.

options.text: Aim the stream directly at the eardrum to dislodge the wax
options.rationale: Near miss concept The stream goes at the canal wall, never at the eardrum.

options.text: Pull the pinna up and back to straighten the canal
options.rationale: Impaction is treated with a ceruminolytic and then irrigation. The solution is body temperature, because cold or hot fluid in the ear stimulates the vestibular system and causes vertigo. The stream is aimed at the canal wall, never at the eardrum, and an adult's pinna is pulled up and back to straighten the canal.

questions.takeaway: Body temperature, canal wall, up and back for an adult.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options sound like they would work faster. One makes the patient dizzy and the other aims at the structure you are protecting.

questions.stem: A patient with external otitis is starting antibiotic ear drops. Which instruction should the nurse include?

options.text: Keep water out of the ear for 7 to 10 days
options.rationale: External otitis is an infection of the canal itself, which is why moving the pinna hurts. Treatment is drops plus keeping water out of the ear for 7 to 10 days so the canal can heal. Swimming and irrigation reintroduce the moisture that drives it.

options.text: Irrigate the ear daily with warm water to clear the drainage
options.rationale: Near miss concept Water is what the canal must be kept free of.

options.text: Swim as usual once the pain starts to ease
options.rationale: Correct but premature Pain relief comes before healing; the restriction runs 7 to 10 days.

options.text: Clean the canal with cotton swabs after each dose
options.rationale: Near miss concept Swabs injure the inflamed canal and push material deeper.

questions.takeaway: External otitis: drops and a dry ear for 7 to 10 days.
questions.strategy: Every wrong option puts water or an object back into the canal you are trying to let heal.

questions.stem: A patient is recovering from a stapedectomy for otosclerosis. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider right away?

options.text: Mild dizziness when getting out of bed
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Vertigo is expected after this surgery; it calls for assisted walking, not a report.

options.text: Hearing that is not yet improved on the first postoperative day
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Improvement takes weeks.

options.text: Drooping of the mouth on the operative side
options.rationale: Otosclerosis causes a slow conductive loss and is treated with stapedectomy. After surgery, vertigo is expected and handled by assisting with walking, and the patient avoids nose blowing and flying. Facial droop is the finding that gets reported, because the facial nerve, cranial nerve VII, runs close to the surgical field.

options.text: A feeling of fullness in the operative ear
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Expected early after middle ear surgery with packing and swelling.

questions.takeaway: After stapedectomy, dizziness gets an arm to lean on. Facial droop gets a phone call.
questions.strategy: Three options are expected after this surgery. Find the one that signals injury to a nearby structure.

questions.stem: Place the steps of normal hearing in order.

options.text: The cochlea turns vibration into nerve signals
Air carries sound into the ear canal
The auditory cortex interprets the sound
The ossicles pass the vibration along
Cranial nerve VIII carries the signal
The eardrum vibrates

questions.takeaway: Sound waves travel through the air in the ear canal and strike the eardrum, which vibrates. The three ossicles in the middle ear, the malleus, incus and stapes, carry that vibration to the inner ear. In the cochlea, the organ of Corti turns vibration into nerve signals. Cranial nerve VIII carries the signals to the auditory cortex, which makes sense of them. Everything up to the ossicles is conduction, so a blockage there causes conductive loss. Damage from the cochlea onward causes sensorineural loss. Canal, eardrum, ossicles, cochlea, nerve VIII, cortex. Before the cochlea is conductive; after is sensorineural.
questions.strategy: Students place the cochlea before the ossicles. Remember that the ossicles are in the middle ear and must deliver the vibration to the inner ear.

questions.stem: A patient with an inner ear disorder asks why the nurse placed the patient on fall precautions when the problem is in the ear. What should the nurse explain?

options.text: The eustachian tube controls balance by keeping pressure equal
options.rationale: Near miss concept The eustachian tube equalizes middle ear pressure. It is not a balance organ.

options.text: The ossicles send body position signals to the brain
options.rationale: Near miss concept The ossicles carry sound vibration to the cochlea. They play no part in position sense.

options.text: Hearing loss removes warning sounds, but balance is unaffected
options.rationale: Absolute language It is true that lost warning sounds raise risk, but saying balance is unaffected is wrong for an inner ear disorder.

options.text: The inner ear holds both the cochlea and the balance organs
options.rationale: The inner ear has two jobs. The cochlea, with the organ of Corti, handles hearing. The semicircular canals and vestibule handle balance. A disorder of the inner ear can therefore cause vertigo and unsteadiness as well as hearing loss, which raises fall risk. The eustachian tube and the ossicles are middle ear structures for pressure and sound conduction. Missing warning sounds adds risk, but the bigger reason here is direct damage to balance.

questions.takeaway: The inner ear does hearing and balance, so an inner ear problem is a fall risk.
questions.strategy: The detail that decides it is the word inner. Middle ear structures handle pressure and sound; only the inner ear holds the balance organs.

questions.stem: For each set of findings, identify the most likely condition.

rows.text: Pain when the tragus is pressed, with a swollen canal
Fever, low pitched tinnitus and a red, bulging eardrum
Fullness and itching, with dry wax filling the canal
Dizziness and muffled hearing with a red, retracted eardrum
Plugged feeling after a week of daily swimming, with pain when the pinna is moved

questions.takeaway: External otitis, or swimmer's ear, is inflammation of the skin of the ear canal. Moving the pinna or pressing the tragus stretches that inflamed skin, so it hurts, and the canal swells and feels plugged. Water exposure is a common trigger, so both the tragus row and the swimming row fit. Otitis media is infection of the middle ear behind the eardrum. Pressure builds, causing pain, fever, conductive hearing loss and low pitched tinnitus, and the eardrum moves from retracted to red to bulging. The dizziness row fits too: the problem is behind the eardrum, which looks red and retracted early on, and the hearing loss is conductive. Cerumen impaction causes fullness, itching and hearing loss with wax visible in the canal. Pain on moving the outer ear is external otitis; pressure pain with fever behind the eardrum is otitis media.
questions.strategy: The dizziness row is the trap: dizziness sounds like an inner ear problem, but a red, retracted eardrum places it in the middle ear, so it is otitis media.

questions.stem: A patient with constant ringing in both ears asks, "Which test will show the ringing so I know it is real?" How should the nurse respond?

options.text: An audiogram will measure how loud your ringing is
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Audiometry measures what the patient can hear. It does not detect the ringing the patient perceives.

options.text: No test shows the ringing; tests look for its causes
options.rationale: Tinnitus is the perception of ringing or noise with no outside sound. No diagnostic test confirms it directly. Testing such as audiometry, tuning fork tests and otoscopy is done to rule out causes like cerumen, otitis media, Meniere disease, noise damage or ototoxic drugs. The response also tells the patient the symptom is taken seriously without promising a test that does not exist.

options.text: A Weber test will confirm which ear the ringing is in
options.rationale: Near miss concept The Weber test helps tell conductive from sensorineural loss. It does not locate tinnitus.

options.text: An otoscope will show the inflamed nerve causing it
options.rationale: Near miss concept An otoscope shows the canal and eardrum. Nerve tissue cannot be seen with it.

questions.takeaway: Tinnitus is diagnosed by what the patient reports; tests rule out causes.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option names a real ear test, which makes it sound right. The detail that decides it is what the patient asked for: a test that shows the ringing itself, and none does.

questions.stem: A patient with Meniere disease has had disabling vertigo despite a low sodium diet, diuretics and intratympanic injections. The surgeon recommends a labyrinthectomy. Which statement shows the patient understands the surgery?

options.text: "It should stop the vertigo and bring my hearing back."
options.rationale: Near miss concept The surgery destroys the inner ear on that side, so hearing does not return; it is lost.

options.text: "It is the first treatment, before I try changing my diet."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Surgery is the last resort. Diet, trigger avoidance and drug therapy come first, as this patient has already tried.

options.text: "It should stop the vertigo, but I will lose hearing on that side."
options.rationale: Labyrinthectomy removes the balance and hearing structures of the inner ear on the operative side. It stops the vertigo, but the trade is total hearing loss in that ear. That is why it is a last resort after lifestyle measures, diuretics, antiemetics and intratympanic gentamicin or steroids fail. Endolymphatic sac decompression is the other surgical option and aims to relieve fluid pressure without destroying hearing.

options.text: "It drains the extra fluid out of the sac in my inner ear."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Draining the endolymphatic sac describes endolymphatic sac decompression, a different procedure that keeps hearing.

questions.takeaway: Labyrinthectomy trades all hearing on that side for an end to vertigo.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out the first option is the name: the labyrinth is removed, so nothing is left to hear with. Watch for the decompression option, which describes a real but different surgery.

questions.topic: when not to irrigate the ear
questions.stem: Select all of the situations in which the nurse should not irrigate the ear canal.
questions.objective: when not to irrigate the ear

options.text: A suspected perforation of the eardrum
options.rationale: Irrigation flushes the canal with fluid. It is unsafe whenever fluid can push infection or cause swelling. A perforated eardrum lets fluid into the middle ear, and suspected otitis media can spread infection. Vegetable matter like a bean absorbs water and swells, wedging tighter. A live insect should be suffocated with oil first, never irrigated. Cerumen with an intact eardrum, especially after a ceruminolytic, is exactly when irrigation is used.

options.text: Suspected otitis media
options.rationale: Irrigation flushes the canal with fluid. It is unsafe whenever fluid can push infection or cause swelling. A perforated eardrum lets fluid into the middle ear, and suspected otitis media can spread infection. Vegetable matter like a bean absorbs water and swells, wedging tighter. A live insect should be suffocated with oil first, never irrigated. Cerumen with an intact eardrum, especially after a ceruminolytic, is exactly when irrigation is used.

options.text: A dried bean lodged in the canal
options.rationale: Irrigation flushes the canal with fluid. It is unsafe whenever fluid can push infection or cause swelling. A perforated eardrum lets fluid into the middle ear, and suspected otitis media can spread infection. Vegetable matter like a bean absorbs water and swells, wedging tighter. A live insect should be suffocated with oil first, never irrigated. Cerumen with an intact eardrum, especially after a ceruminolytic, is exactly when irrigation is used.

options.text: A live insect moving in the canal
options.rationale: Irrigation flushes the canal with fluid. It is unsafe whenever fluid can push infection or cause swelling. A perforated eardrum lets fluid into the middle ear, and suspected otitis media can spread infection. Vegetable matter like a bean absorbs water and swells, wedging tighter. A live insect should be suffocated with oil first, never irrigated. Cerumen with an intact eardrum, especially after a ceruminolytic, is exactly when irrigation is used.

options.text: Hard cerumen after two days of softening drops, eardrum intact
options.rationale: Near miss concept Softening the wax first and then irrigating with an intact eardrum is the standard method, so irrigation is safe here.

options.text: Fullness from cerumen in an older adult, eardrum intact
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cerumen impaction is common and often correctable in older adults. With an intact eardrum, irrigation is appropriate.

questions.takeaway: Do not irrigate through a hole, into an infection, onto vegetable matter, or at a live insect.
questions.strategy: Ask of each option: is the eardrum intact, is there infection, and will the object swell or move? The detail that clears the two cerumen options is the phrase eardrum intact.

questions.stem: A patient taking high dose aspirin for arthritis reports a new constant ringing in both ears. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Suggest more fluids so the medication is flushed out faster
options.rationale: Near miss concept Does not change salicylate levels meaningfully and delays the report.

options.text: Report it; ringing can be a reversible drug effect if caught
options.rationale: Tinnitus is often the first warning of an ototoxic effect, and aspirin is on that list along with NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, loop diuretics and quinine. Caught early, salicylate related tinnitus often reverses when the dose comes down. Left alone, the next thing lost is hearing, and that part does not come back.

options.text: Recommend a hearing aid to mask the constant ringing sound
options.rationale: Correct but premature Masking is a management strategy after the cause has been addressed.

options.text: Reassure the patient that tinnitus is a normal part of aging
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Aging contributes, and a new onset on aspirin points at the drug.

questions.takeaway: New ringing on a known ototoxic drug is a reason to call, not a symptom to live with.
questions.strategy: Any option that normalizes a new symptom in a patient on an ototoxic drug is wrong.

questions.topic: the patient who refuses hearing aids
questions.stem: An older adult has moderate hearing loss and refuses hearing aids, saying people should just speak up. His wife reports he has stopped going to church and family dinners. What should the nurse do?
questions.objective: the patient who refuses hearing aids

options.text: Explain that untreated hearing loss is tied to faster cognitive decline in older adults
options.rationale: Near miss concept True, and raising severity without raising motivation usually produces defensiveness.

options.text: Suggest he try an inexpensive amplifier from the pharmacy
options.rationale: Correct but premature May help and skips finding out what the actual objection is.

options.text: Accept his decision and teach the family communication tips
options.rationale: Correct but premature Worth doing eventually, and it abandons the conversation after one refusal.

options.text: Explore what aids mean to him; link loss to what he gave up
options.rationale: Refusal is usually about stigma, cost or a previous bad experience, and you cannot address any of those without knowing which it is. The lever is the withdrawal: he has already lost church and family dinners, and connecting the device to getting those back is far more persuasive than a warning about what might happen later. Facts about cognitive decline come after he has a reason to care.

questions.takeaway: Lead with what he has already lost, not with what might happen to him.
questions.strategy: The option that states the strongest fact is not the one that changes behavior.

questions.stem: A patient receiving intravenous gentamicin and furosemide reports new ringing in both ears and feels unsteady when standing. The next gentamicin dose is due now. Select all of the appropriate nursing actions.

options.text: Hold the gentamicin dose
options.rationale: Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside, and an aminoglycoside given with a loop diuretic such as furosemide raises the risk of ototoxicity. New tinnitus, hearing loss or dizziness is the warning. Assess hearing and balance, hold the dose, check the trough, notify the provider, and start fall precautions because the ear controls balance as well as hearing. Continuing the drug because tinnitus is common is the classic wrong answer: the damage is often permanent.

options.text: Check the gentamicin trough level
options.rationale: Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside, and an aminoglycoside given with a loop diuretic such as furosemide raises the risk of ototoxicity. New tinnitus, hearing loss or dizziness is the warning. Assess hearing and balance, hold the dose, check the trough, notify the provider, and start fall precautions because the ear controls balance as well as hearing. Continuing the drug because tinnitus is common is the classic wrong answer: the damage is often permanent.

options.text: Give the dose and recheck hearing at the end of the course
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Continues the drug causing the damage and defers the finding.

options.text: Assess hearing and balance
options.rationale: Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside, and an aminoglycoside given with a loop diuretic such as furosemide raises the risk of ototoxicity. New tinnitus, hearing loss or dizziness is the warning. Assess hearing and balance, hold the dose, check the trough, notify the provider, and start fall precautions because the ear controls balance as well as hearing. Continuing the drug because tinnitus is common is the classic wrong answer: the damage is often permanent.

options.text: Notify the provider
options.rationale: Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside, and an aminoglycoside given with a loop diuretic such as furosemide raises the risk of ototoxicity. New tinnitus, hearing loss or dizziness is the warning. Assess hearing and balance, hold the dose, check the trough, notify the provider, and start fall precautions because the ear controls balance as well as hearing. Continuing the drug because tinnitus is common is the classic wrong answer: the damage is often permanent.

options.text: Start fall precautions
options.rationale: Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside, and an aminoglycoside given with a loop diuretic such as furosemide raises the risk of ototoxicity. New tinnitus, hearing loss or dizziness is the warning. Assess hearing and balance, hold the dose, check the trough, notify the provider, and start fall precautions because the ear controls balance as well as hearing. Continuing the drug because tinnitus is common is the classic wrong answer: the damage is often permanent.

options.text: Reassure the patient that tinnitus is common with antibiotics and usually harmless
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic False reassurance; ototoxic damage is often permanent.

questions.takeaway: New tinnitus on gentamicin: hold, check the trough, notify, and protect from falls.
questions.strategy: The unsteadiness is the detail that adds fall precautions. Ear disorders affect balance, not just hearing.

questions.topic: acute otitis media in an adult
questions.stem: A patient has had a cold for five days and now has deep, throbbing pain in the right ear, muffled hearing and a low pitched ringing. Temperature is 38.6 °C. Moving the pinna and pressing the tragus cause no extra pain. Otoscopy by the provider shows a red, bulging eardrum with no drainage. Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters to monitor.
questions.objective: acute otitis media in an adult

options.text: Teach the patient to finish the full antibiotic course
Give the ordered analgesic and apply mild heat
Irrigate the ear canal to clear the fluid
Teach the patient to keep water out of the ear for 7 to 10 days
Acute otitis media
External otitis
Cerumen impaction
Meniere disease
Ear pain and temperature
Hearing compared with baseline
Pain when the tragus is pressed
Amount of cerumen in the canal

questions.takeaway: Condition: acute otitis media, infection of the middle ear. A red, bulging eardrum, fever, pressure pain, conductive hearing loss and low pitched tinnitus are its signs. External otitis is ruled out because moving the pinna and tragus does not hurt. Cerumen impaction would show wax, not a bulging eardrum, and Meniere disease causes episodic vertigo, not fever. Actions: teach the patient to finish the full antibiotic course, because stopping early allows chronic infection and permanent damage. Give analgesia and apply mild heat for comfort. Irrigation is unsafe when otitis media is suspected, because it can spread infection. Keeping water out for 7 to 10 days is teaching for external otitis. Parameters: ear pain and temperature show whether the infection is responding, and hearing should return toward baseline as fluid clears. Tragus pain judges external otitis, and the amount of cerumen judges impaction. Red, bulging eardrum with fever is otitis media: full antibiotic course, comfort, and never irrigate.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out external otitis is that moving the pinna and pressing the tragus cause no extra pain. A sudden end to the pain later would suggest perforation, not cure.

questions.stem: A patient with severe hearing loss in both ears lives alone and is going home. The patient takes out the hearing aids at bedtime and says, "I would never hear the smoke alarm at night." Which action best addresses this concern?

options.text: Arrange a flashing alert system for the smoke alarm and doorbell
options.rationale: Assistive devices for hearing loss turn sound into something the patient can see or feel. A flashing alert system links the smoke alarm and doorbell to a light, so the warning reaches the patient without hearing aids. Neighbor checks, louder ringers and future surgery all leave the nighttime gap open. The problem is a safety risk during sleep, so the fix has to work during sleep.

options.text: Ask a neighbor to check on the patient each morning
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic A morning check is caring, but it does nothing for an alarm that sounds at night.

options.text: Refer the patient for a cochlear implant evaluation
options.rationale: Correct but premature An implant may be an option later, but it needs evaluation and surgery. The alarm risk exists tonight.

options.text: Place the phone by the bed with the ringer on full volume
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data A louder ringer is still a sound. Without hearing aids at night, the patient will not hear it.

questions.takeaway: When a patient cannot hear an alarm, change the alarm to light, not volume.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out the louder ringer is that the hearing aids come out at bedtime. Any fix that still depends on sound fails at night.

questions.topic: assessing hearing loss in an older adult
questions.stem: A 97 year old reports that hearing in the left ear has become muffled over the last several weeks, with a feeling of fullness and itching. The family says, "It is just old age." The patient has no pain, fever or dizziness. What should the nurse do first?
questions.objective: assessing hearing loss in an older adult

options.text: Escalate urgently, because new hearing loss in one ear is an emergency
options.rationale: Most dramatic finding Sudden loss over hours to a day is urgent. This developed over weeks with fullness and itching, which points to a common, correctable cause.

options.text: Teach the family to face the patient and speak at a lower pitch
options.rationale: Correct but premature Communication tips help any hearing loss, but they skip finding out whether the loss can be fixed.

options.text: Look into the canal for cerumen before deciding the cause
options.rationale: Do not assume an older adult's hearing loss is from aging; assess each patient. Cerumen gets drier with age and impacts more easily, and it is the most common cause of ear canal blockage. Fullness, itching and gradual loss in one ear fit impaction, which is often correctable with softening drops and removal. The nurse assesses before acting: inspect the canal first. Communication strategies and a hearing aid come later if the loss remains. Urgent escalation fits a sudden loss, not one over several weeks.

options.text: Refer the patient to be fitted for a hearing aid in that ear
options.rationale: Correct but premature A hearing aid before checking the canal could treat a blockage that wax removal would solve.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult with new hearing loss, look for a fixable cause before accepting old age.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out escalation is several weeks with fullness and itching. The age is there to tempt you into agreeing with the family.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a patient three days after a skin graft. Which statement about sleep is most relevant to this patient's healing?

options.text: Rapid eye movement sleep supports tissue repair through memory consolidation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Splices the right phase to the wrong function.

options.text: Sleep requirements do not change during acute illness
options.rationale: Absolute language Illness raises the requirement.

options.text: Older adults require less than seven hours of sleep, so interruptions matter less
options.rationale: Near miss concept A common claim is under seven hours. The need is actually preserved at about seven to eight; what changes is continuity.

options.text: Non rapid eye movement sleep supports tissue repair through growth hormone release
options.rationale: Deep non rapid eye movement sleep is the physical repair phase, with growth hormone release, tissue repair and wound healing. Rapid eye movement sleep is the cognitive and emotional phase. If a stem is about a wound, it is about non rapid eye movement sleep.

questions.takeaway: Illness increases the need for sleep while making it harder to get, which is exactly why you assess it.
questions.strategy: Match the phase to the problem. Wound means NREM; memory or mood means REM.

questions.stem: A patient recovering from major surgery has been waking every two hours for vital signs. Which consequence should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Impaired tissue repair, because fragmented sleep reduces the deep NREM stages
options.rationale: NREM is the physical repair phase, when growth hormone is released and tissue healing happens, and the deep stages come in the longer uninterrupted blocks that two hourly checks destroy. REM is the cognitive and emotional phase. Clustering care so the patient gets uninterrupted blocks is a nursing intervention, not a courtesy.

options.text: Impaired emotional regulation only, because REM is the stage lost first
options.rationale: Near miss concept Names a real consequence and limits it with only.

options.text: Increased daytime energy from the shorter sleep cycles
options.rationale: Near miss concept Broken sleep costs energy. Nobody wakes rested from this.

options.text: No clinically significant effect, because total sleep time is preserved
options.rationale: Near miss concept Treats hours as interchangeable with quality.

questions.takeaway: NREM repairs the body. REM repairs the mind. Fragmentation costs you both.
questions.strategy: Total hours is the wrong metric. Continuity is the metric.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the sleep patterns of patients across different age groups. For each patient, indicate whether the reported sleep duration is expected or requires further assessment.

rows.text: A 2-month-old sleeping 15 to 16 hours a day
A 15-year-old sleeping 5 hours on school nights
A 34-year-old sleeping 8 hours
An 80-year-old sleeping about 6 hours with two brief awakenings
An 80-year-old who falls asleep during conversations and has fallen twice

questions.takeaway: A 2-month-old sleeping 15 to 16 hours a day: Neonates and infants sleep 15 to 16 hours a day, with a high proportion of REM. A 15-year-old sleeping 5 hours on school nights: Children and adolescents need 9 to 12 hours. Five is well short and affects mood, learning and safety. A 34-year-old sleeping 8 hours: Adults need 7 to 9 hours. An 80-year-old sleeping about 6 hours with two brief awakenings: Older adults sleep under 7 hours and their sleep is fragmented. This is the expected pattern rather than a problem. An 80-year-old who falls asleep during conversations and has fallen twice: Excessive daytime sleepiness significantly increases fall risk, and two falls makes it urgent rather than expected. Neonates 15 to 16 hours, children and adolescents 9 to 12, adults 7 to 9, older adults under 7 and fragmented.
questions.strategy: Two rows describe 80-year-olds and they fall on opposite sides. Fragmented nighttime sleep is expected; falling asleep in the daytime is not.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence: A nurse reviews sleep physiology with a student. The internal clock governing the 24-hour sleep-wake cycle is the [[1]]. The stage that supports memory consolidation and emotional processing is [[2]]. The chemicals promoting wakefulness and REM are [[3]]. The tool that measures daytime sleepiness specifically is the [[4]].

options.text: circadian rhythm
sleep latency
the sleep cycle
the hypothalamus
REM sleep
NREM sleep
sleep latency
a parasomnia
hypocretins, also called orexins
melatonin
L-tryptophan
prostaglandin
Epworth Sleepiness Scale
Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index
Holmes-Rahe Life Stress Inventory
Geriatric Depression Scale

questions.takeaway: [1] circadian rhythm: Governs the 24-hour sleep-wake cycle. [2] REM sleep: Supports memory consolidation and emotional processing. [3] hypocretins, also called orexins: Named on her slide for wakefulness and REM. [4] Epworth Sleepiness Scale: Measures daytime sleepiness. Circadian rhythm sets the 24-hour cycle. REM supports memory and emotion; NREM supports physical repair. Epworth measures daytime sleepiness; Pittsburgh measures overall quality.
questions.strategy: Three near-miss pairs: circadian against the sleep cycle, REM against NREM, and Epworth against Pittsburgh. Each turns on what is being measured or restored.

questions.stem: A nurse wants to improve sleep for patients on a busy medical unit. Which intervention addresses the most common modifiable cause of nighttime awakening in hospital?

options.text: Dim the lights during evening hours
options.rationale: Near miss concept Named and useful, supporting melatonin release. It does not stop anyone entering the room.

options.text: Close doors and lower alarm volumes
options.rationale: Near miss concept Named under noise control and it addresses a different disruption.

options.text: Position patients for comfort and airway safety
options.rationale: Near miss concept Named, and it addresses comfort rather than the number of awakenings.

options.text: Cluster nursing care to reduce the number of nighttime interruptions
options.rationale: Named first among hospital environment interventions, and interruptions are the cause nursing most directly controls.

questions.takeaway: Hospital sleep interventions: cluster care, dim lights in the evening, control noise, and position for comfort and airway safety.
questions.strategy: All four are on her slide. The question asks which addresses the most common modifiable cause.

questions.stem: A nurse takes a sleep history. Which source of information is primary?

options.text: The overnight nurse's observations of when he appeared asleep
options.rationale: Near miss concept Useful supporting data, and appearing asleep is not the same as sleeping. Only he knows what the night was like.

options.text: The number of hours recorded on the flow sheet
options.rationale: Near miss concept A count of observed time, which misses awakenings and quality entirely.

options.text: His partner's account of his sleep pattern
options.rationale: Near miss concept Valuable for witnessed events such as apnea or movement, and it is a supplementary source rather than the primary one.

options.text: The patient's own report of his sleep
options.rationale: Sleep is subjective and the patient is the primary source. Perceived quality matters as much as the hours.

questions.takeaway: Sleep is subjective. The patient is the primary source: bedtime routine, sleep latency, nighttime awakenings, wake time, and perceived quality.
questions.strategy: Three distractors are genuinely useful supporting sources. The question asks which is primary.

questions.stem: A nurse explains why rest is not the same as sleep. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Rest is a state of mental, physical and spiritual calm, and does not require inactivity
options.rationale: Her wording. Rest is not the absence of activity, and it is not a substitute for sleep.

options.text: Rest is any period during which the patient is not moving
options.rationale: Near miss concept Equates rest with inactivity, which her slide explicitly separates.

options.text: Rest is only achievable once a patient is free of pain
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pain makes rest harder and does not make it impossible.

options.text: Rest and sleep are interchangeable in meeting the body's needs
options.rationale: Near miss concept Both are basic needs and they are not the same. Sleep does things rest cannot.

questions.takeaway: Sleep and rest are as essential as nutrition and exercise. Rest is a state of mental, physical and spiritual calm rather than inactivity.
questions.strategy: One distractor collapses rest and sleep into the same thing. Her slide separates them deliberately.

questions.stem: A preceptor listens to a new graduate discuss sleep. Which statement requires correction?

options.text: "Older adults need less sleep, so fragmented sleep is not a concern."
options.rationale: Their pattern changes and their need does not. Around 30 to 40% report sleep problems, and treating fragmentation as expected means it goes unassessed.

options.text: "The patient is the primary source of information about his own sleep."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Accurate, because sleep is subjective.

options.text: "Non-drug strategies come first and sedatives are a last resort."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Accurate, and it is her stated order.

options.text: "Sleep deprivation raises fall risk through confusion and slowed reflexes."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Accurate, and it is why sleep is a safety issue.

questions.takeaway: Older adults sleep less and their sleep is fragmented. That is a change in pattern, not a reduced need, and problems still require assessment.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate her slides correctly. The fourth uses an expected pattern to dismiss a problem.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old takes his furosemide at 6 pm because that is when he remembers it with his evening meal. He wakes three or four times each night to void and struggles to fall back asleep. He is drowsy during the day and has stumbled twice on the way to the bathroom. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.text: Restrict his fluid intake after the early evening
options.rationale: Near miss concept Commonly suggested, and it risks dehydration in an older adult while the 6 pm dose keeps working. The fluid he passes at night is drug-driven.

options.text: Review his sleep hygiene and evening routine
options.rationale: Near miss concept The right approach when habits are the problem. No bedtime routine will outlast a diuretic taken at 6 pm.

options.text: Discuss moving the diuretic to the morning with the provider
options.rationale: A diuretic peaks two to six hours after the dose. At 6 pm that peak lands overnight; in the morning it is finished before bedtime. Changing the timing removes the cause.

options.text: Provide a bedside commode to shorten the walk
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reduces the immediate fall risk and is worth doing alongside the timing change, and on its own it accepts three or four awakenings as unchangeable.

questions.takeaway: Diuretic timing affects nocturia and nighttime awakenings. Medication reconciliation and timing review are part of the sleep assessment.
questions.strategy: Three options manage the consequences of the awakenings. Ask what is producing them, and check the time the drug is given.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old admitted for elective surgery is accompanied by his wife, who reports that he snores loudly and that she has watched him stop breathing for several seconds at a time most nights. He falls asleep during meetings and once while stopped in traffic, though he believes he sleeps enough. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Advise him to sleep alone so his wife is not disturbed
options.rationale: Near miss concept Solves her problem, not his, and it removes the only person who has witnessed the pauses.

options.text: Report the findings and discuss evaluation for obstructive sleep apnea
options.rationale: Snoring with witnessed pauses plus daytime sleepiness is the classic picture, and it matters now because anesthesia and opioids relax the airway further.

options.text: Teach sleep hygiene and reassess in one month
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hygiene does not open an obstructed airway, and a month's delay means his surgery happens first.

options.text: Reassure him that snoring is common and not concerning
options.rationale: Near miss concept Snoring alone is common. Snoring with witnessed apnea and falling asleep in traffic is not, and reassurance sends him to theatre with an unassessed airway.

questions.takeaway: Obstructive sleep apnea: loud snoring, witnessed pauses, and daytime sleepiness. Before surgery it is urgent, because anesthesia and opioids worsen airway collapse.
questions.strategy: The surgery in the stem is doing work. Ask what changes about the risk once he is anesthetized.

questions.stem: A patient recovering from abdominal surgery has slept poorly for three nights because of noise and frequent checks. Which consequence should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Slower wound healing and reduced pain tolerance
options.rationale: Growth hormone released during sleep drives tissue repair. Poor sleep impairs immune function, wound healing and pain tolerance.

options.text: Improved memory consolidation as the body compensates
options.rationale: Near miss concept REM supports memory consolidation, and losing sleep reduces it rather than triggering compensation.

options.text: No measurable effect, since the surgery itself drives recovery
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sleep plays a critical role in physical healing and clinical outcomes. It is not incidental to recovery.

options.text: A reduced requirement for analgesia over the next few days
options.rationale: Near miss concept The opposite. Reduced pain tolerance means he is likely to need more, not less.

questions.takeaway: Growth hormone released during sleep drives tissue repair and wound healing. Poor sleep impairs immunity, healing and pain tolerance.
questions.strategy: One distractor reverses the effect on analgesia. Ask what happens to a wound when growth hormone release is interrupted.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old with heart failure tells the nurse he wakes most nights with chest discomfort that eases when he sits up. Which does this most likely represent?

options.text: Nocturnal angina related to his cardiac disease
options.rationale: Named under cardiac disease. Lying flat increases venous return and cardiac workload, which is what brings it on and why sitting up relieves it.

options.text: Gastroesophageal reflux causing nocturnal symptoms
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reflux does wake people and is worse lying flat, which makes it a real possibility. Chest discomfort relieved specifically by sitting up in a patient with heart failure points to the heart.

options.text: A parasomnia occurring during the night
options.rationale: Near miss concept Parasomnias are abnormal behaviors during sleep, such as sleepwalking. Chest discomfort is not a behavior.

options.text: Obstructive sleep apnea causing the awakenings
options.rationale: Near miss concept Apnea wakes people through obstruction rather than pain, and his wife would describe snoring and pauses.

questions.takeaway: Cardiac disease disrupts sleep through nocturnal angina and heart failure-related apnea. Lying flat raises venous return.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is reflux, which is genuinely worse lying flat. His diagnosis and the relief on sitting up are what separate them.

questions.takeaway: Sleep hygiene: consistent times including weekends, avoid caffeine, alcohol and heavy meals near bedtime, limit screens and reserve the bed for sleep, daytime exercise not within 1 to 2 hours of bed, relaxation techniques.
questions.strategy: One distractor sounds restful and contradicts reserving the bed for sleep.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old in intensive care has been sleeping poorly and is becoming confused at night. Which evidence-based intervention should the nurse consider?

options.text: A benzodiazepine at bedtime to establish a sleep pattern
options.rationale: Near miss concept Benzodiazepines carry a risk of falls and confusion in older adults, and confusion is already present.

options.text: Moving him to a single room away from the nursing station
options.rationale: Near miss concept May reduce noise and it distances him from observation in a unit where he needs it, and it is not the intervention with the evidence behind it.

options.text: A sleep bundle including earplugs, eye masks and lavender aromatherapy
options.rationale: Sleep bundles have shown measurable benefit in intensive care, reducing delirium and improving perceived sleep quality.

options.text: Allowing him to sleep during the day to make up the deficit
options.rationale: Near miss concept Daytime sleep reduces the drive to sleep at night and worsens the circadian disruption.

questions.takeaway: Sleep bundles in intensive care use earplugs, eye masks and aromatherapy. They reduce delirium and improve perceived sleep quality.
questions.strategy: One distractor treats confusion with a drug that causes confusion. Ask what the evidence supports in this setting.

questions.stem: 0800: Patient is 71, admitted three days ago with a chest infection. Reports sleeping poorly since admission. Furosemide scheduled at 2000. Chest discomfort rated 6 of 10 overnight, no analgesia given since 2200. Overhead light switched on each time staff enter. Vital signs taken separately by three different staff members between 2300 and 0500. Drinks one cup of coffee at breakfast. Has a history of hypertension managed with medication. Slept well at home before admission. Room is shared with one other patient. Select all of the findings contributing to his poor sleep that nursing can modify.

options.text: Furosemide scheduled at 2000
options.rationale: Diuretic timing affects nocturia. The nurse cannot change the order alone and raising it with the provider is squarely nursing work. Pain is a named cause of disrupted sleep in older adults, and this is uncontrolled and within nursing control. Dimming lights during evening hours supports melatonin release. Using a task light is a nursing decision. Clustering care is the first named hospital intervention, and three separate entries is the clearest example of what it prevents.

options.rationale: Near miss concept Caffeine matters close to bedtime. One cup at breakfast is not what is waking him at 0300.

options.text: History of hypertension managed with medication
options.rationale: Near miss concept A stable condition, and nothing about it is contributing to the awakenings.

options.text: Slept well at home before admission
options.rationale: Near miss concept The finding that tells you this is situational rather than a chronic sleep disorder. Useful, and not a modifiable cause.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with insomnia asks for something to help her sleep. She has already tried a consistent bedtime and reducing evening caffeine. Which is the most appropriate first pharmacological option to discuss?

options.text: Trazodone as a safer alternative
options.rationale: Near miss concept Named as a safer alternative for older or depressed patients, and it sits behind melatonin rather than ahead of it.

options.text: Melatonin, which is generally safe, particularly in older adults with low endogenous levels
options.rationale: Named as generally safe and specifically useful in older adults whose own melatonin production has fallen.

options.text: A benzodiazepine for short-term use
options.rationale: Near miss concept Short-term use only, with risk of falls, confusion and respiratory depression in older adults. Not the first option.

options.text: Diphenhydramine, available without prescription
options.rationale: Near miss concept Anticholinergic, and it causes confusion and falls in older adults. Availability is not safety.

questions.takeaway: Non-drug strategies come first. Melatonin is generally safe, benzodiazepines are short-term only, and trazodone is a safer alternative for older or depressed patients.
questions.strategy: The stem tells you non-drug strategies have been tried, which is what makes this a pharmacological question at all. Rank the options by risk in an older adult.

questions.stem: A patient's family says they co-sleep with their toddler and asks whether the nurse disapproves. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Explain that co-sleeping is unsafe and should be discontinued
options.rationale: Near miss concept Delivers a verdict rather than a conversation, and it is likely to end the discussion of safety entirely.

options.text: Acknowledge the practice and discuss safety considerations without judgment
options.rationale: Her slide names respecting cultural sleep practices such as co-sleeping, and discussing safety without judgment.

options.text: Tell them the practice is entirely a family matter
options.rationale: Near miss concept Avoids the safety discussion the nurse is placed to have.

options.text: Refer them to the pediatrician for advice about sleeping arrangements
options.rationale: Near miss concept Passes on a conversation within nursing scope, and it implies the topic is too difficult to discuss.

questions.takeaway: Respect cultural sleep practices such as co-sleeping, and discuss safety without judgment.
questions.strategy: One distractor avoids the safety topic and one delivers it as a verdict. The instruction is to do both things at once.

questions.stem: A patient has been taking a benzodiazepine nightly for three weeks. His nurse stops it abruptly at discharge on the patient's request. Which does the nurse monitor for?

options.text: Increased REM sleep resolving his daytime drowsiness
options.rationale: Near miss concept REM does rebound, and the presentation is disrupted sleep rather than resolution of drowsiness.

options.text: Immediate improvement in sleep quality
options.rationale: Near miss concept Not what follows abrupt withdrawal after regular use.

options.text: Rebound insomnia, with sleep worse than before the drug was started
options.rationale: Named under the nursing role: monitor response, advocate for the lowest effective dose, and watch for rebound insomnia.

options.text: No change, since three weeks is too short for dependence
options.rationale: Near miss concept Three weeks of nightly use is enough for rebound to occur, which is why short-term use is specified.

questions.takeaway: Nursing role with sleep medications: monitor response, advocate for the lowest effective dose, and watch for rebound insomnia.
questions.strategy: One distractor treats three weeks as too brief to matter. Short-term use is specified precisely because this happens.

questions.topic: sleep as a basic human need
questions.stem: A hospitalized 82-year-old has slept four hours a night for three nights. Which safety concern should the nurse prioritize?
questions.objective: sleep as a basic human need

options.text: Delayed wound healing from reduced growth hormone
options.rationale: Near miss concept A genuine consequence of poor sleep and it is not the immediate safety concern.

options.text: Impaired immune function raising infection risk
options.rationale: Near miss concept Also genuine, and it develops over a longer period than the next few hours.

options.text: Reduced pain tolerance requiring more analgesia
options.rationale: Near miss concept Real, and it concerns comfort and management rather than immediate safety.

options.text: Increased fall risk from confusion and slowed reflexes
options.rationale: Sleep deprivation produces confusion, slowed reflexes and higher fall risk, and excessive daytime sleepiness raises it further in older adults.

questions.takeaway: Sleep deprivation causes confusion, slowed reflexes and higher fall risk. Sleep disturbances affect patient safety directly.
questions.strategy: Three distractors are genuine consequences of poor sleep. The question asks specifically about safety.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has slept in a chair for four nights because lying flat leaves him breathless. He asks the nurse to get him something to help him sleep. He is using his inhalers correctly, his oxygen saturation is 93% on room air, and his pain is 1 of 10. He says he is exhausted and cannot think straight. Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem this represents, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and support him with pillows so he can sleep in bed
Cluster overnight care and reduce light and noise during the night
Request an order for a sedative so he can settle
Reassure him that sleeping in a chair is adequate rest
Sleep disrupted by a positioning need arising from his respiratory disease
Insomnia requiring pharmacological management
Obstructive sleep apnea causing fragmented sleep
Uncontrolled pain preventing sleep
Whether he is able to sleep in bed rather than the chair
His own report of sleep quality the following morning
The number of hours recorded as asleep on the flow sheet
Whether his oxygen saturation remains above 92%

questions.takeaway: Respiratory disease disrupts sleep through positioning needs and breathlessness. The cause is mechanical and it is solvable. Positioning for comfort and airway safety is a named hospital intervention. A chair gives him neither proper rest nor proper positioning. The environmental interventions named first for the hospital setting, and four nights of poor sleep needs every lever pulled. Measures whether the positioning change solved the mechanical problem. Sleep is subjective, so the patient's perception is the measure. Compare it with his report from the previous nights. Respiratory disease disrupts sleep through positioning and breathlessness. Fix the position before reaching for a drug, and evaluate sleep by what the patient reports.
questions.strategy: He asks for a sedative, which is the pull. His pain and saturation are given to rule out the two obvious alternatives.

options.rationale: Near miss concept Crushing extended release drugs causes dose dumping.

options.rationale: Use liquids when available, pause the feeding, flush before, between and after with a 30 mL or larger syringe, crush each tablet separately, never mix drugs into the formula and never crush extended release or enteric coated drugs.

questions.strategy: Keep steps that protect the dose and the tube.

questions.stem: A patient has a jejunostomy tube. Which feeding method is appropriate?

options.text: Bolus feeding every 4 hours
options.rationale: Near miss concept The jejunum has no reservoir, so a bolus causes cramping, diarrhea and dumping.

options.text: Continuous feeding by pump
options.rationale: A J tube feeds into the jejunum, which has no reservoir. Feeding is continuous only.

options.text: Gravity bolus with each meal
options.rationale: Near miss concept A bolus is for the stomach only.

options.text: Oral feeding with thickened liquids
options.rationale: Near miss concept The tube is in place because oral feeding is not the plan.

questions.takeaway: J tube: continuous only.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the destination can hold a volume.

questions.stem: A family member suggests flushing a clogged feeding tube with cola. Which response is best?

options.text: "We will force water through with a small syringe instead."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Force and small syringes can rupture the tube.

options.text: "Cola is acidic and clumps formula; we use warm water."
options.rationale: No cola, cranberry or force. Warm water with gentle push pull is used, then enzyme declogging per policy.

options.text: "That is a good idea, because cola dissolves most clogs."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Acid clumps formula.

options.text: "We can use cranberry juice instead, since it is gentler."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cranberry is acidic too.

questions.takeaway: No cola, no cranberry, no force.
questions.strategy: Reject anything acidic or forceful.

questions.stem: Which medication should not be crushed and given through a feeding tube?

options.text: Metoprolol succinate ER
options.rationale: Extended release (ER, XR, SR) and enteric coated (EC) drugs are never crushed because the dose dumps at once.

options.text: Acetaminophen liquid
options.rationale: Near miss concept Liquids are preferred.

options.text: Plain lisinopril tablet
options.rationale: Near miss concept A plain tablet can be crushed after checking with the pharmacist.

options.text: Plain furosemide tablet
options.rationale: Near miss concept A plain tablet can be crushed.

questions.takeaway: Never crush ER, XR, SR or EC.
questions.strategy: Look for the letters after the drug name.

questions.stem: For each situation, indicate the most appropriate feeding tube.

rows.text: Feeding after a total gastrectomy
Permanent dysphagia after a stroke
Short term feeding for 2 weeks after a head injury
Long term feeding for head and neck cancer

questions.takeaway: NG tubes are short term (under about 4 weeks). A PEG is long term into the stomach. A J tube is used when the stomach is bypassed or failing, as after gastrectomy or with gastroparesis. Short term through the nose; long term through the abdomen; no stomach, go to the jejunum.
questions.strategy: Decide length of need first, then whether the stomach can be used.

questions.stem: Why are feeding tubes fitted with ENFit connectors?

options.text: They allow formula to run in at a faster rate.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Speed is not the purpose.

options.text: They make the tube much less likely to clog.
options.rationale: Near miss concept ENFit is a misconnection safety feature.

options.text: They cannot connect to IV lines, preventing misconnection.
options.rationale: Formula in a vein is often fatal. ENFit connectors cannot connect to Luer IV lines. The nurse traces every line at connection and at hand off.

questions.takeaway: Trace every line.
questions.strategy: Choose the safety feature that prevents a fatal error.

questions.stem: A feeding tube will not flush. Place the nurse's actions in order.

questions.takeaway: The simple cause is checked first, then warm water with gentle push pull and soaking, then an enzyme declogger or a new tube. Check the simple cause first.
questions.strategy: Least invasive and simplest first.

questions.stem: A patient receiving tube feedings develops diarrhea. Select all possible causes the nurse should check.

options.text: Keeping the head of bed at 30 to 45 degrees
options.rationale: Near miss concept Head of bed position prevents aspiration; it does not cause diarrhea.

options.text: Antibiotics
options.rationale: Medications come first: sorbitol in liquid drugs and antibiotics are common causes. Then C. difficile testing, rate, concentration and hang time. The trap is blaming the formula before checking the medication list.

options.text: Liquid medications that contain sorbitol
options.rationale: Medications come first: sorbitol in liquid drugs and antibiotics are common causes. Then C. difficile testing, rate, concentration and hang time. The trap is blaming the formula before checking the medication list.

options.rationale: Near miss concept Mouth care does not cause diarrhea.

options.rationale: Medications come first: sorbitol in liquid drugs and antibiotics are common causes. Then C. difficile testing, rate, concentration and hang time. The trap is blaming the formula before checking the medication list.

options.text: C. difficile infection
options.rationale: Medications come first: sorbitol in liquid drugs and antibiotics are common causes. Then C. difficile testing, rate, concentration and hang time. The trap is blaming the formula before checking the medication list.
