options.rationale: Medications come first: sorbitol in liquid drugs and antibiotics are common causes. Then C. difficile testing, rate, concentration and hang time. The trap is blaming the formula before checking the medication list.

questions.takeaway: Check the medication list before blaming the formula.
questions.strategy: Keep anything that changes what reaches the bowel or adds an organism.

questions.stem: Which patient is the best candidate for enteral tube feeding?

options.text: A patient with a complete small bowel obstruction
options.rationale: Near miss concept Enteral feeding needs a working gut.

options.text: A stroke patient who coughs with sips of water
options.rationale: Enteral feeding is for a patient whose gut works but who cannot eat safely or enough, such as dysphagia after stroke (a wet voice or coughing with sips), coma, head and neck cancer or a ventilator.

options.text: A patient who simply prefers liquid meals
options.rationale: Near miss concept Preference is not an indication for a tube.

options.text: A surgical patient who is not hungry but swallows safely
options.rationale: Near miss concept Poor appetite in a safe swallower is managed with oral options first.

questions.takeaway: If the gut works, use it.
questions.strategy: Look for an unsafe swallow with a working gut.

questions.stem: Why is mouth care important for a patient receiving tube feedings?

options.text: Mouth care helps keep the tube secured in place.
options.rationale: Near miss concept It does not secure the tube.

options.text: Mouth care improves the taste of the formula.
options.rationale: Near miss concept The formula does not pass through the mouth.

options.text: Oral bacteria are what get aspirated into the lungs.
options.rationale: A patient who is not eating still aspirates oral secretions. Mouth care reduces the bacteria that cause aspiration pneumonia.

options.text: Mouth care is mainly done for patient comfort.
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Comfort matters, but the safety reason is preventing pneumonia.

questions.takeaway: Oral bacteria are what get aspirated.
questions.strategy: Choose the reason tied to preventing harm.

questions.stem: Why does the nurse use a 30 mL or larger syringe to flush a feeding tube?

options.text: Smaller syringes are not sterile for enteral use.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sterility is not the issue.

options.text: A larger syringe gives the medication faster.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Speed is not the reason.

options.text: A small syringe makes more pressure and can rupture it.
options.rationale: Smaller syringes generate higher pressure, which can rupture the tube. A 30 mL or larger syringe is used.

options.text: The larger syringe holds the entire medication dose at once.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Volume is not the reason.

questions.takeaway: Small syringe, high pressure.
questions.strategy: Choose the option that names the physical risk.

questions.stem: A continuous feeding runs at 65 mL/hr from 0700 to 2300 with a 1 hour hold. The tube is flushed with 30 mL every 4 hours. How much formula did the patient receive?

options.text: 975 mL
options.rationale: Hours run: 16 minus 1 = 15. Formula: 65 × 15 = 975 mL. The 120 mL of flushes are water and recorded separately, for a total intake of 1,095 mL.
Near miss concept This forgets to subtract the 1 hour hold.
Near miss concept This adds the water flushes to the formula.
Near miss concept This assumes 24 hours of running.

questions.takeaway: Subtract the hold; record flushes separately.
questions.strategy: Do the two steps: hours, then rate times hours.

questions.stem: A patient receives continuous NG feeding. Select all actions that help prevent aspiration.

options.text: Lower the head of bed flat at night for sleep
options.rationale: Near miss concept The head of bed stays up with a continuous feeding.

options.text: Watch for coughing or a wet voice
options.rationale: The head of bed is 30 to 45 degrees during and 1 hour after a bolus and always with continuous feeding. The pump is paused before lying flat. Mouth care matters because oral bacteria are what get aspirated.

options.text: Pause the pump before lowering the bed for a bath
options.rationale: The head of bed is 30 to 45 degrees during and 1 hour after a bolus and always with continuous feeding. The pump is paused before lying flat. Mouth care matters because oral bacteria are what get aspirated.

options.text: Increase the rate when the residual is large
options.rationale: Near miss concept A large residual means slow or hold and notify.

options.text: Provide regular mouth care
options.rationale: The head of bed is 30 to 45 degrees during and 1 hour after a bolus and always with continuous feeding. The pump is paused before lying flat. Mouth care matters because oral bacteria are what get aspirated.

options.text: Keep the head of bed at 30 to 45 degrees
options.rationale: The head of bed is 30 to 45 degrees during and 1 hour after a bolus and always with continuous feeding. The pump is paused before lying flat. Mouth care matters because oral bacteria are what get aspirated.

questions.takeaway: Head of bed up; pause before flat.
questions.strategy: Keep actions that keep formula out of the airway.

questions.stem: A nurse is about to give a bolus feeding through an existing NG tube. Which action confirms placement?

options.text: Place the tube end in water and look for bubbles.
options.rationale: Near miss concept This is not a reliable check.

options.text: Ask the patient to hum and listen for the voice.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Humming does not confirm placement.

options.text: Check the external mark and the aspirate pH.
options.rationale: Before every feeding or drug, the nurse confirms the external mark and tests the aspirate pH. Gastric fluid is about 5 or below. A new tube needs an x ray before first use.

options.text: Inject air and listen over the stomach for a whoosh.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Air sounds the same over a tube coiled in the esophagus or in a bronchus.

questions.takeaway: Air and listening is not reliable.
questions.strategy: Reject the classic method that has been shown unreliable.

questions.stem: A severely malnourished patient started tube feedings 2 days ago and now has weakness and an irregular pulse. Which labs should the nurse check?

options.text: Glucose and hemoglobin A1c
options.rationale: Near miss concept These do not explain refeeding syndrome.

options.text: Albumin and prealbumin
options.rationale: Near miss concept These reflect nutrition over time, not an acute shift.

options.text: Sodium and chloride
options.rationale: Near miss concept The dangerous drops are in phosphorus, potassium and magnesium.

options.text: Phosphorus, potassium and magnesium
options.rationale: In refeeding syndrome, food brings insulin, which drives phosphorus, potassium and magnesium into cells. Low levels cause weakness, arrhythmias, heart or lung failure and seizures. Feeding starts low and goes slow, with these three checked daily at first.

questions.takeaway: Refeeding: phosphorus, potassium, magnesium.
questions.strategy: Link insulin to the electrolytes it moves into cells.

questions.stem: A patient receiving a continuous NG feeding begins coughing and vomiting. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Notify the provider and document
Suction the mouth and airway as needed
Assess breathing, SpO2, lung sounds and placement
Stop the feeding
Position the patient on the side or upright

questions.takeaway: Stop the formula first so no more enters the airway, then position, suction, assess and notify. The dropped step is stopping the feeding.
questions.strategy: Stop the source of harm before anything else.

questions.stem: A patient on a continuous NG feeding coughs and vomits, and the SpO2 falls from 96% to 90%. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Call the provider.
options.rationale: Correct but premature The provider is notified after the feeding is stopped and the airway protected.

options.text: Check tube placement with the pH test.
options.rationale: Correct but premature Placement is assessed after the feeding is stopped.

options.text: Check the SpO2 again with a different probe.
options.rationale: Correct but premature Rechecking delays stopping formula from entering the airway.

options.text: Stop the feeding.
options.rationale: The cues point to aspiration. Stopping the feeding comes first, then positioning, suctioning, assessing and notifying.

questions.takeaway: Stop the formula before reaching for the probe or the phone.
questions.strategy: When something harmful is flowing, stop it first.

questions.stem: An open system feeding bag was filled with formula 5 hours ago and still has formula in it. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Add fresh formula on top of what remains.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Topping off mixes old formula with new.

options.text: Discard what remains and refill with fresh.
options.rationale: Open bag formula hangs 4 hours at most. A closed system hangs 24 hours once spiked, and opened cans are labeled and discarded at 24 hours.

options.text: Refrigerate the bag and restart it later.
options.rationale: Near miss concept The bag has already exceeded hang time.

options.text: Continue the feeding until the bag is empty.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Open system formula hangs for 4 hours at most.

questions.takeaway: Open system: 4 hours.
questions.strategy: Compare the time with the hang limit.

questions.stem: A patient with a PEG tube has a tube that suddenly will not rotate or move. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Push harder to rotate the tube.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Force could injure tissue.

options.text: Continue feedings as usual.
options.rationale: Near miss concept A tube that will not move needs a provider check.

options.text: Notify the provider.
options.rationale: A PEG gets daily site care, with checks for redness and drainage. A tube that suddenly will not rotate or move needs a provider check.

options.text: Remove the tube.
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Removing a PEG is not a nursing action.

questions.takeaway: A PEG that will not move needs a provider check.
questions.strategy: Report a sudden change in the device.

questions.stem: The aspirate from an NG tube has a pH of 7.2, and the mark at the nostril is 6 cm farther out than recorded. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Do not use the tube and notify the provider.
options.rationale: Gastric fluid is acidic, about 5 or below. A higher pH suggests intestine or lung, and a moved mark suggests displacement. The tube is not used, the provider is notified and an x ray is expected.

options.text: Push the tube back to the recorded mark and give the feeding.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reinserting without confirmation is unsafe; an x ray is expected.

options.text: Give the feeding because the patient is not coughing.
options.rationale: Near miss concept The moved mark and high pH suggest the tube is not in the stomach.

options.text: Retest the pH after giving the feeding.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Checks happen before use.

questions.takeaway: A moved mark means do not use the tube.
questions.strategy: When a safety check fails, stop.

questions.stem: A medication is due through a small bore nasogastric tube. The external mark is 6 cm farther out than documented. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Give the medication, then report the change
options.rationale: Near miss concept Using a tube that may have moved risks putting the drug into the esophagus or lungs.

options.text: Push the tube back to the original mark
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pushing a small bore tube back can place it in the airway. Placement must be verified, not guessed.

options.text: Inject air and listen over the stomach
options.rationale: Near miss concept Air bolus auscultation is not reliable for checking placement.

options.text: Hold the medication and verify placement
options.rationale: A changed external length suggests the tube moved. When placement is uncertain, nothing goes down the tube until it is verified.

questions.takeaway: If the external length changes or placement is uncertain, hold tube use and verify placement before giving anything.
questions.strategy: The changed mark is the cue. Any option that uses or moves the tube before verifying is unsafe.

questions.stem: Thirty minutes after a bolus feeding, a patient asks to lie flat for a nap. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: “You can lie flat now since the feeding is done.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Formula is still in the stomach; lying flat soon after a feeding raises aspiration risk.

options.text: “I will keep the head of the bed up while you rest.”
options.rationale: The patient stays upright for a period after intermittent feedings. The patient can nap with the head of the bed raised.

options.text: “You can lie on your left side instead of flat.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Side lying does not replace head elevation after a feeding.

options.text: “You need to sit in the chair for the next 4 hours.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept The patient can rest in bed with the head raised; 4 hours in a chair is not required.

questions.takeaway: Keep the patient upright after intermittent feedings to prevent reflux and aspiration.
questions.strategy: Meet the patient's wish to rest while keeping the safeguard: head elevation.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the note of a patient receiving continuous nasogastric feeding at 55 mL/hr. Select all of the findings that require follow up. Note: “Head of bed at 15 degrees. External tube mark at 62 cm, documented baseline 62 cm. Coughing after each sip of water. Bowel sounds active in all 4 quadrants. Abdomen distended and firm compared with this morning. Formula container labeled with date, time and initials. Respiratory rate 26/min, up from 18/min.”

options.text: Head of bed at 15 degrees
options.rationale: The head of the bed must be at 30 to 45 degrees during feeding. Coughing with liquids suggests unsafe swallowing and aspiration risk. New distention signals feeding intolerance. A rising respiratory rate compared with baseline can be an early sign of aspiration.

options.text: External tube mark at 62 cm, documented baseline 62 cm
options.rationale: Near miss concept The external length matches the baseline.

options.text: Coughing after each sip of water
options.rationale: The head of the bed must be at 30 to 45 degrees during feeding. Coughing with liquids suggests unsafe swallowing and aspiration risk. New distention signals feeding intolerance. A rising respiratory rate compared with baseline can be an early sign of aspiration.

options.text: Bowel sounds active in all 4 quadrants
options.rationale: Absolute language Active bowel sounds are expected.

options.text: Abdomen distended and firm compared with this morning
options.rationale: The head of the bed must be at 30 to 45 degrees during feeding. Coughing with liquids suggests unsafe swallowing and aspiration risk. New distention signals feeding intolerance. A rising respiratory rate compared with baseline can be an early sign of aspiration.

options.text: Formula container labeled with date, time and initials
options.rationale: Near miss concept Labeling is correct practice.

options.text: Respiratory rate 26/min, up from 18/min
options.rationale: The head of the bed must be at 30 to 45 degrees during feeding. Coughing with liquids suggests unsafe swallowing and aspiration risk. New distention signals feeding intolerance. A rising respiratory rate compared with baseline can be an early sign of aspiration.

questions.takeaway: During feeding, act on a low head of bed, signs of intolerance (distention) and signs of aspiration (coughing, rising respiratory rate). Compare with the baseline.
questions.strategy: Compare each finding with its baseline or standard: the bed angle, the abdomen and the breathing all changed.

questions.stem: Before an intermittent feeding, the nurse aspirates clear fluid with a pH of 7 from a nasogastric tube in a patient taking no acid suppressants. Which action is appropriate?

options.text: Give the feeding since fluid was aspirated
options.rationale: Near miss concept Getting fluid back does not prove gastric placement; the pH does not fit the stomach.

options.text: Flush with 30 mL of water and recheck the pH
options.rationale: Near miss concept Putting water down a tube of uncertain placement is unsafe.

options.text: Hold the feeding and follow policy to verify placement
options.rationale: A pH above 5 without an acid suppressant suggests the tube may not be in the stomach. Hold use and verify.

options.text: Advance the tube 5 cm and give the feeding
options.rationale: Near miss concept Moving the tube blindly does not confirm placement.

questions.takeaway: Gastric aspirate is usually pH 5 or less. An unexpected pH with no acid suppressant means hold the tube and verify placement.
questions.strategy: Rule out the explanation first: no acid suppressant, so the high pH is unexplained.

questions.topic: Give formula, flushes and medications safely
questions.stem: The nurse is giving three medications through a gastrostomy tube during continuous feeding. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
questions.objective: Give formula, flushes and medications safely

options.text: Mix all three medications in one cup
options.rationale: Absolute language Mixing can cause interactions and clog the tube; each is given separately.

options.text: Flush with 30 mL of water before the first medication
options.rationale: The flush clears formula from the tube. Flushing between doses prevents interactions in the tube. Flushes count in total intake.

options.text: Crush the extended release tablet
options.rationale: Near miss concept Extended release forms cannot be crushed; confirm each drug is right for the tube.

options.text: Flush with water between each medication
options.rationale: The flush clears formula from the tube. Flushing between doses prevents interactions in the tube. Flushes count in total intake.

options.text: Add the flush volumes to the intake record
options.rationale: The flush clears formula from the tube. Flushing between doses prevents interactions in the tube. Flushes count in total intake.

questions.takeaway: Give tube medications one at a time, confirm each is right for the tube, flush before, between and after, and record the flushes as intake.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option either combines drugs or damages a form that should not be crushed.

questions.topic: Identify patients who need enteral nutrition
questions.stem: An older adult living alone has unintentionally lost 5 kg in 2 months and has a slow healing wound. Which action is the nursing priority?
questions.objective: Identify patients who need enteral nutrition

options.text: Teach the patient to eat three large meals a day
options.rationale: Correct but premature Teaching before assessing the cause skips the first step, and large meals may not be realistic.

options.text: Request an order for a feeding tube
options.rationale: Correct but premature A tube may never be needed; assessment comes first.

options.text: Encourage the patient to rest more to heal the wound
options.rationale: Near miss concept Rest does not address the nutrition deficit behind the poor healing.

options.text: Assess intake and nutritional risk and report the findings
options.rationale: Weight loss and poor healing are signs of undernutrition. The priority is to identify the deficit early so feeding can be planned and monitored.

questions.takeaway: The nursing priority in undernutrition is to identify deficits early and monitor the response to feeding.
questions.strategy: Recognize the pattern (weight loss, poor healing, low interest in food), then choose assessment before intervention.

questions.topic: Give formula, flushes and medications safely
questions.stem: The nurse finds a feeding set connector that will not fit the patient's ENFit feeding tube port. A Luer IV adapter is in the drawer. Which action should the nurse take?
questions.objective: Give formula, flushes and medications safely

options.text: Use the adapter to connect the set
options.rationale: Near miss concept Adapting connectors defeats the safety design and risks connecting enteral and IV systems.

options.text: Get an ENFit compatible feeding set
options.rationale: ENFit connectors fit only enteral devices to prevent wrong route errors, so the nurse gets matching equipment.

options.text: Tape the connector to the port securely
options.rationale: Near miss concept Taping does not make an incompatible connection safe.

options.text: Give the feeding by syringe through the IV adapter
options.rationale: Near miss concept This still uses an IV style connection on an enteral tube.

questions.takeaway: Never force or adapt connections between enteral and IV equipment; use ENFit compatible supplies.
questions.strategy: Any workaround that joins mismatched connectors creates a wrong route risk.

questions.topic: Compare types of feeding tubes and routes
questions.stem: A patient will need tube feeding for several months after head and neck cancer surgery. Which tube does the nurse anticipate?
questions.objective: Compare types of feeding tubes and routes

options.text: Nasogastric tube
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nasal tubes are for short feeding periods; months of use risk nasal injury and dislodgement.

options.text: Nasojejunal tube
options.rationale: Near miss concept This is also a short term nasal route.

options.text: Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube
options.rationale: Long term feeding needs an enterostomal tube such as a PEG.

options.text: Large bore Salem sump tube
options.rationale: Near miss concept A Salem sump is for decompression and lavage, not long term feeding.

questions.takeaway: Nasal tubes are for short periods; gastrostomy, PEG or jejunostomy tubes are for long term feeding.
questions.strategy: Duration decides the route: months means enterostomal.

questions.topic: Give formula, flushes and medications safely
questions.stem: A patient receiving continuous feeding at 60 mL/hr also receives 30 mL water flushes every 4 hours. What is the total enteral intake for an 8 hour shift?
questions.objective: Give formula, flushes and medications safely

options.text: 480 mL
options.rationale: Near miss concept This counts the formula only (60 × 8) and leaves out the two flushes.

options.text: 510 mL
options.rationale: Near miss concept This counts only one flush; every 4 hours in an 8 hour shift is two.

options.text: 600 mL
options.rationale: Near miss concept This counts four flushes, the number for a full 16 hours.

options.text: 540 mL
options.rationale: Formula 60 mL/hr × 8 hr = 480 mL, plus two flushes of 30 mL = 60 mL, for 540 mL.

questions.takeaway: Total enteral intake = formula volume plus every water flush.
questions.strategy: Two steps: formula by rate times hours, then add each flush in the shift.

questions.stem: A patient who receives cyclic feedings overnight asks why the feeding stops in the morning. Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: “It runs during set hours so you are free during the day.”
options.rationale: Cyclic feeding runs by pump over a set period, often overnight, which leaves daytime free for activity and eating if allowed.

options.text: “Feedings have to stop when you are awake.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Many patients receive continuous feeding while awake; cyclic is chosen, not required.

options.text: “The formula is only safe to give at night while you sleep.”
options.rationale: Absolute language Formula is safe at any time; timing is a choice.

options.text: “It stops because the bag must be changed daily.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Bag changes do not explain the schedule.

questions.takeaway: Cyclic feeding runs by pump over a set period, such as overnight.
questions.strategy: Name the method from the schedule, then pick its purpose.

questions.stem: After bowel surgery, a patient has absent bowel sounds and abdominal distention, and total parenteral nutrition is ordered. The family asks why tube feeding is not used. Which response is best?

options.text: “Tube feeding costs more money than nutrition given through the vein.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cost is not the reason; parenteral nutrition is usually more costly and has more risks.

options.text: “IV nutrition is always better after any surgery.”
options.rationale: Absolute language When the gut works, enteral feeding is preferred; “always” is wrong.

options.text: “A feeding tube cannot be placed after surgery.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Tubes can be placed after surgery; the problem is the bowel, not the tube.

options.text: “The bowel is not working yet, so nutrition goes by vein.”
options.rationale: Enteral feeding needs a working GI tract. With an ileus, nutrition is given parenterally until bowel function returns.

questions.takeaway: Enteral nutrition needs a working GI tract; parenteral nutrition is used when the GI tract cannot be used, and the patient moves to enteral feeding when it recovers.
questions.strategy: Absent bowel sounds and distention tell you the gut cannot take formula.

questions.topic: Identify patients who need enteral nutrition
questions.stem: The nurse reviews four newly admitted patients. Which patients does the nurse anticipate will need enteral nutrition? Select all that apply.
questions.objective: Identify patients who need enteral nutrition

options.text: A patient eating 90% of each meal after knee surgery
options.rationale: Near miss concept This patient meets needs by mouth.

options.text: A patient with a stroke who failed the swallow screen
options.rationale: Unsafe swallowing with a working gut is a key reason for tube feeding. Progressive loss of swallowing with a working gut calls for enteral feeding, often long term.

options.text: A patient with a complete small bowel obstruction
options.rationale: Near miss concept An obstructed gut cannot be used; this patient needs parenteral nutrition.

options.text: A patient with advanced amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) who chokes on liquids
options.rationale: Unsafe swallowing with a working gut is a key reason for tube feeding. Progressive loss of swallowing with a working gut calls for enteral feeding, often long term.

options.text: A patient with mild nausea after anesthesia who is eating small meals
options.rationale: Near miss concept Short lived nausea with some intake is managed with antiemetics and diet, not a tube.

questions.takeaway: Enteral nutrition fits a working gut with intake that is unsafe or not enough by mouth.
questions.strategy: Check both conditions for each patient: a working gut, and oral intake that is unsafe or inadequate.

questions.topic: Identify patients who need enteral nutrition
questions.stem: A patient with advanced dementia can no longer swallow safely. The patient's advance directive declines artificial nutrition, and a family member asks for a feeding tube. Which action is best?
questions.objective: Identify patients who need enteral nutrition

options.text: Share the directive with the provider and family
options.rationale: The nurse advocates for the patient's documented wishes, brings the directive to the team and family, and supports a care discussion.

options.text: Insert the tube because the family requested it
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting The patient's documented wishes take priority over a family member's request.

options.text: Tell the family the tube is not allowed by law
options.rationale: Near miss concept This is inaccurate and closes the discussion instead of supporting the family.

options.text: Start parenteral nutrition instead of a tube
options.rationale: Near miss concept Parenteral nutrition is also artificial nutrition that the directive declines.

questions.takeaway: The decision to start enteral nutrition includes the patient's treatment goals and preferences, including an advance directive. The nurse advocates for those wishes.
questions.strategy: The patient's own documented choice guides care; the nurse's role is advocacy and communication.

questions.topic: Compare types of feeding tubes and routes
questions.stem: A provider orders a nasogastric tube to low intermittent suction for a bowel obstruction. Which tube does the nurse gather?
questions.objective: Compare types of feeding tubes and routes

options.text: A 10 Fr single lumen Dobhoff tube
options.rationale: Near miss concept Small bore tubes are for feeding and medications and collapse under suction.

options.text: An 8 Fr feeding tube with a weighted tip
options.rationale: Near miss concept This is a small bore feeding tube, not a decompression tube.

options.text: A 16 Fr double lumen Salem sump tube
options.rationale: Decompression needs a large bore tube; the second lumen, the air vent, protects the stomach lining during suction.

options.text: A percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube
options.rationale: Near miss concept A PEG is a long term feeding tube placed by a procedure, not a bedside decompression tube.

questions.takeaway: Large bore double lumen tubes (14 to 18 Fr, Salem sump) are for decompression, lavage and medications; small bore tubes are for feeding and medications only.
questions.strategy: The word suction in the order calls for a large bore tube.

questions.stem: A small bore feeding tube was just inserted at the bedside. The x ray is not done yet, and the provider asks to start feeding now. Which action is correct?

options.text: Start the feeding at a slow rate until the x ray
options.rationale: Near miss concept Even a slow rate puts formula into the lungs if the tube is misplaced.

options.text: Hold the feeding until the x ray confirms placement
options.rationale: A blindly inserted tube is not used for formula, water or medications until an x ray confirms placement. The nurse explains this to the provider.

options.text: Inject air and listen, then start the feeding
options.rationale: Near miss concept Air bolus auscultation is not reliable and does not replace an x ray.

options.text: Give only water flushes until the x ray
options.rationale: Absolute language Water in a misplaced tube can also be aspirated.

questions.takeaway: Get an x ray before using any blindly inserted tube; nothing goes in until placement is confirmed.
questions.strategy: The rule covers formula, water and medications alike, whatever the rate or who asks.

questions.stem: A patient taking famotidine has aspirate with a pH of 6 from a nasogastric feeding tube. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Conclude the tube is in the lung and pull it out
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A pH of 6 is common with acid suppressants and does not prove lung placement.

options.text: Conclude the tube is in the stomach and feed
options.rationale: Near miss concept pH alone never proves placement.

options.text: Hold the famotidine so the pH can be retested
options.rationale: Near miss concept The nurse does not stop a prescribed medication to change a test result.

options.text: Compare the external tube length with the baseline
options.rationale: Acid suppressants can raise gastric pH, so pH alone neither proves nor disproves placement. The nurse adds other checks per policy, and holds the tube if any doubt remains.

questions.takeaway: Acid suppressants raise gastric pH. Use pH with other checks such as the external length, follow policy, and hold the tube if placement is uncertain.
questions.strategy: When one check is skewed, add another check rather than jumping to a conclusion.

questions.stem: A patient receiving continuous nasogastric feeding at 60 mL/hr suddenly coughs and becomes short of breath. Oxygen saturation drops from 96% to 88%, and suctioned secretions look like the formula. Complete the bow tie.

options.text: Flush the tube with 30 mL of water
Increase the rate to finish the feeding
Stop the feeding
Lay the patient flat on the right side
Raise the head of the bed and suction the airway
Dumping syndrome
Feeding tube clog
Fluid overload from flushes
Aspiration of tube feeding
Capillary blood glucose
Oxygen saturation
Stool frequency
Bowel sounds
Lung sounds

questions.takeaway: Stopping the feeding prevents more formula from entering the airway. Upright positioning and suctioning clear the airway and ease breathing. Sudden coughing, shortness of breath, falling saturation and formula in secretions point to aspiration. Shows whether gas exchange is improving after the airway is cleared. New crackles or wheezes show aspiration and possible pneumonia. Suspected aspiration during tube feeding: stop the feeding, position upright, suction, give oxygen as ordered, notify the provider, and monitor saturation and lung sounds.
questions.strategy: The formula in the secretions names the condition; airway actions come first.

questions.stem: A feeding is ordered to advance 10 mL/hr every 8 hours to 60 mL/hr as tolerated. At 40 mL/hr, the patient vomits and is newly distended. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Advance to 50 mL/hr as scheduled
options.rationale: Near miss concept Vomiting and distention show the patient is not tolerating the current rate.

options.text: Switch to a bolus feeding to rest the stomach
options.rationale: Near miss concept A bolus delivers a large volume quickly and worsens intolerance, and method changes need an order.

options.text: Hold the advance and notify the provider
options.rationale: “As tolerated” means advancing only when the patient tolerates the feeding. Vomiting and distention are intolerance and an aspiration risk.

options.text: Advance the rate but lower the head of the bed
options.rationale: Near miss concept Lowering the head of the bed increases aspiration risk.

questions.takeaway: Advance a continuous rate only as ordered and as tolerated; signs of intolerance (vomiting, distention) mean hold the advance and report.
questions.strategy: The words “as tolerated” make tolerance the condition for each step.

questions.topic: Give formula, flushes and medications safely
questions.stem: The nurse observes a nursing student caring for a patient receiving tube feedings. For each action, indicate whether it is appropriate or requires the nurse to intervene.
questions.objective: Give formula, flushes and medications safely

rows.text: Lets an open formula container keep hanging past its time limit
Flushes 30 mL of water before and after the medication
Adds a crushed tablet to the formula bag
Uses a Luer IV adapter because the ENFit syringe is missing
Labels the new formula bag with date, time and initials
Performs hand hygiene before handling the feeding set

questions.takeaway: Formula past its hang time can grow bacteria and is discarded. Flushes keep the tube open and deliver the full dose. Medications are never added to formula; they are given separately with flushes. Adapting connectors defeats wrong route protection. Labeling lets staff track hang time. Hand hygiene and minimal handling prevent contamination. Safe formula handling: hand hygiene, minimal handling, labeling, hang time limits, ENFit connectors, medications given separately with flushes.
questions.strategy: Test each action against infection prevention, wrong route prevention and medication safety.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient on continuous tube feeding. Which task can be delegated to the nursing assistant?

options.text: Keep the head of the bed raised and report coughing
options.rationale: Maintaining position and reporting observations is within the nursing assistant's role; the nurse interprets the findings.

options.text: Check tube placement before a medication
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Placement checks require nursing assessment and judgment.

options.text: Give the scheduled medication through the tube
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Medication administration is not delegated to a nursing assistant.

options.text: Advance the feeding rate by 10 mL/hr per the order
options.rationale: Near miss concept Adjusting a feeding requires assessment of tolerance.

questions.takeaway: Delegate routine positioning, comfort care and reporting to the nursing assistant; keep placement checks, medications and feeding changes with the nurse.
questions.strategy: Delegate tasks with a set procedure and no judgment; keep anything that needs assessment.

questions.topic: Give formula, flushes and medications safely
questions.stem: A small bore feeding tube will not flush, and the pump alarms for occlusion. The tubing is not kinked or clamped. Which action is appropriate?
questions.objective: Give formula, flushes and medications safely

options.text: Push water forcefully with a 10 mL syringe
options.rationale: Near miss concept Small syringes create high pressure that can rupture the tube.

options.text: Gently push and pull warm water with a 60 mL syringe
options.rationale: Warm water with a large syringe and a gentle push and pull motion is the first measure for a clog, per policy.

options.text: Instill a cola drink into the tube to dissolve the clog
options.rationale: Near miss concept Acidic drinks can make formula clump and are not recommended.

options.text: Reinsert the guidewire to clear the tube
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reinserting the stylet can perforate the tube and the GI tract.

questions.takeaway: For a clogged tube, check for kinks and clamps, then gently flush warm water with a 60 mL syringe; never force, never use small syringes or the stylet. Prevent clogs with routine flushes.
questions.strategy: Reject anything forceful or invasive; choose the gentle first step.

questions.topic: Give formula, flushes and medications safely
questions.stem: A patient receiving continuous tube feeding has had five liquid stools today. Which actions does the nurse take? Select all that apply.
questions.objective: Give formula, flushes and medications safely

options.text: Stop tube feeding permanently
options.rationale: Absolute language Diarrhea is evaluated and managed; the feeding is not simply stopped for good.

options.text: Check how long the formula has been hanging
options.rationale: Contaminated formula past its hang time can cause diarrhea. Medications are a common cause of diarrhea in tube fed patients. Frequent liquid stools in a hospitalized patient may be infection and are reported.

options.text: Review medications such as antibiotics and sorbitol elixirs
options.rationale: Contaminated formula past its hang time can cause diarrhea. Medications are a common cause of diarrhea in tube fed patients. Frequent liquid stools in a hospitalized patient may be infection and are reported.

options.text: Increase the rate to replace lost fluid
options.rationale: Near miss concept A faster rate can worsen diarrhea, and rate changes need an order.

options.text: Report the stools and check for C. difficile per order
options.rationale: Contaminated formula past its hang time can cause diarrhea. Medications are a common cause of diarrhea in tube fed patients. Frequent liquid stools in a hospitalized patient may be infection and are reported.

questions.takeaway: Diarrhea on tube feeding: look for contaminated formula, medication causes and infection, track intake and output, and report.
questions.strategy: Look for causes first; avoid changes that worsen the diarrhea or need an order.

questions.stem: Before starting a patient's first intermittent tube feeding, the nurse completes an assessment. Which finding requires the nurse to hold the feeding and notify the provider?

options.text: Bowel sounds present in all four quadrants
options.rationale: Absolute language Active bowel sounds support feeding.

options.text: Weight 2 kg below the usual weight
options.rationale: Near miss concept Weight loss is a reason for feeding, not a reason to hold it.

options.text: A soft stool this morning
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A normal stool supports feeding.

options.text: A firm, distended abdomen with new vomiting
options.rationale: Distention with vomiting suggests the gut cannot handle formula and raises aspiration risk.

questions.takeaway: Before feeding, assess the abdomen, nausea and vomiting, bowel pattern, swallowing, consciousness, airway and breathing; hold and report signs of intolerance.
questions.strategy: Find the finding that makes feeding unsafe right now.

questions.topic: Compare types of feeding tubes and routes
questions.stem: A patient with gastroparesis and two recent aspiration pneumonias will need tube feeding for at least 6 months. Complete the sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.objective: Compare types of feeding tubes and routes
questions.sentence: The nurse anticipates a [[1]] because the feeding is long term, and feeding into the [[2]] may lower aspiration risk, although aspiration precautions [[3]].

options.text: nasogastric tube
large bore Salem sump tube
nasoduodenal tube
gastrostomy tube with a jejunal extension
large intestine
esophagus
small intestine
stomach
are no longer needed
apply only at night
are replaced by suction
still apply

questions.takeaway: Long term feeding needs an enterostomal tube; a jejunal extension bypasses the slow stomach. Formula past the stomach is less likely to reflux. Small intestine feeding lowers but does not eliminate aspiration risk. Route choice depends on duration, anatomy and gastric emptying; small intestine feeding may lower aspiration risk but precautions still apply.
questions.strategy: Use the duration to pick the tube type and the slow stomach to pick the site.

questions.topic: Identify patients who need enteral nutrition
questions.stem: Two weeks after starting enteral feeding for undernutrition, which finding best shows the patient is responding?
questions.objective: Identify patients who need enteral nutrition

options.text: Weight up 1 kg and the wound edges closing
options.rationale: Gradual weight gain with wound healing shows the feeding is meeting needs.

options.text: Weight up 2 kg since yesterday
options.rationale: Near miss concept A sudden overnight gain reflects fluid, not nutrition.

options.text: Eats 25% of a meal tray each day
options.rationale: Near miss concept Low oral intake does not show the feeding is working.

options.text: Sleeps most of the day and no longer reports any hunger
options.rationale: Absolute language Sleeping more can mean fatigue or weakness, not improvement in nutrition.

questions.takeaway: Monitor the response to feeding: gradual weight gain, better wound healing and more strength and energy show it is working; sudden weight gain is fluid.
questions.strategy: Pick the outcome that reverses the signs of undernutrition, at a believable pace.

questions.topic: Compare types of feeding tubes and routes
questions.stem: On day 4 after percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) placement, which finding at the insertion site does the nurse report?
questions.objective: Compare types of feeding tubes and routes

options.text: A small amount of clear drainage on the dressing
options.rationale: Near miss concept Small amounts of clear drainage are common in the first days.

options.text: Mild tenderness when the dressing is changed
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Mild tenderness is expected as the site heals.

options.text: Spreading redness with thick yellow drainage
options.rationale: Spreading redness and purulent drainage suggest a site infection that needs treatment.

options.text: The external bumper resting lightly against the skin
options.rationale: Near miss concept A bumper resting lightly without pressure is the correct fit.

questions.takeaway: PEG site care: keep it clean and dry, check daily for redness, drainage, leakage and bumper fit; report spreading redness, purulent drainage or formula leaking around the tube.
questions.strategy: Separate expected healing from infection: spreading and purulent are the cues.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a patient about fecal occult blood testing. Which instruction is correct?

options.text: A single negative result rules out colorectal cancer
options.rationale: Absolute language Bleeding is intermittent, which is why screening repeats.

options.text: The test detects parasites as well as blood
options.rationale: Near miss concept Ova and parasite testing is a separate study.

options.text: Collect the sample during a menstrual period for a more sensitive result
options.rationale: Near miss concept Menstrual blood contaminates the sample and causes false positives.

options.text: Follow the dietary and medication restrictions the specific test requires before collecting
options.rationale: Older guaiac tests react to things that are not human blood, so red meat, some raw vegetables and certain drugs can produce false positives, and vitamin C can produce a false negative. The immunochemical test is specific to human hemoglobin and needs fewer restrictions. Screening is repeated on a schedule because a single sample can miss intermittent bleeding.

questions.takeaway: Know which test you are using. The restrictions differ, and so does what a result means.
questions.strategy: A negative screening test never rules out a cancer, which rules out one option on principle.

questions.stem: Select all of the correct techniques for an abdominal assessment.

options.text: Have the patient empty the bladder first
options.rationale: The abdomen is the one region where auscultation comes before percussion and palpation, because pressing on the bowel changes the sounds you are trying to hear. Painful areas go last for the same reason the guarding would contaminate everything else. A pulsating mass is a possible aneurysm, and deep palpation over one can rupture it, which is where you take your hands off and escalate.

options.text: Palpate first so you can locate the problem before listening
options.rationale: Near miss concept Palpation alters bowel sounds, so auscultation comes first.

options.text: Position the patient supine with knees slightly flexed
options.rationale: The abdomen is the one region where auscultation comes before percussion and palpation, because pressing on the bowel changes the sounds you are trying to hear. Painful areas go last for the same reason the guarding would contaminate everything else. A pulsating mass is a possible aneurysm, and deep palpation over one can rupture it, which is where you take your hands off and escalate.

options.text: Palpate deeply over a pulsating mass to characterize it
options.rationale: Near miss concept A possible aneurysm; stop and escalate instead.

options.text: Inspect, then auscultate, then percuss, then palpate
options.rationale: The abdomen is the one region where auscultation comes before percussion and palpation, because pressing on the bowel changes the sounds you are trying to hear. Painful areas go last for the same reason the guarding would contaminate everything else. A pulsating mass is a possible aneurysm, and deep palpation over one can rupture it, which is where you take your hands off and escalate.

options.text: Palpate any tender or reported painful area last
options.rationale: The abdomen is the one region where auscultation comes before percussion and palpation, because pressing on the bowel changes the sounds you are trying to hear. Painful areas go last for the same reason the guarding would contaminate everything else. A pulsating mass is a possible aneurysm, and deep palpation over one can rupture it, which is where you take your hands off and escalate.

questions.takeaway: Abdomen is the exception: listen before you touch. Pressing changes the sounds.
questions.strategy: One wrong option reverses the sequence; the other is the finding that stops the exam.

questions.topic: pre and post procedure teaching for colonoscopy
questions.stem: Select all of the correct teaching points for a patient scheduled for colonoscopy.
questions.objective: pre and post procedure teaching for colonoscopy

options.text: Eat a large meal the evening before to prevent hunger
options.rationale: Near miss concept Defeats the bowel preparation.

options.text: Drive yourself home if you feel alert after the sedation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sedation impairs judgment longer than it impairs wakefulness.

options.text: Complete the bowel preparation exactly as prescribed
options.rationale: An incomplete prep means the study has to be repeated. Mild cramping and gas are expected; severe pain or significant bleeding suggest perforation or hemorrhage.

Mild cramping and gas are expected; severe pain or significant bleeding suggest perforation or hemorrhage.

options.text: Arrange for someone to drive you home
options.rationale: An incomplete prep means the study has to be repeated. Sedation means no driving for the rest of the day no matter how alert the patient feels, because judgment and reaction time recover later than wakefulness does. Mild cramping and gas are expected; severe pain or significant bleeding suggest perforation or hemorrhage.

options.text: Report severe abdominal pain or significant bleeding afterward
options.rationale: An incomplete prep means the study has to be repeated. Sedation means no driving for the rest of the day no matter how alert the patient feels, because judgment and reaction time recover later than wakefulness does. Mild cramping and gas are expected; severe pain or significant bleeding suggest perforation or hemorrhage.

questions.takeaway: Feeling alert after sedation is not the same as being safe to drive.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options undo something the preparation or the sedation requires.

questions.stem: Match each finding to what it indicates.

rows.text: Clay colored stool with dark urine
Bright red blood per rectum
Greasy foul stool that floats, normal in color
Black tarry stool

questions.takeaway: Color is the diagnosis. Black means blood that has been digested on the way through, so it entered high. Bright red has not been digested, so it entered low. Clay colored means no bile is reaching the stool, and the bilirubin that cannot get out that way comes through the urine instead, which is why the urine is dark. Greasy and floating with normal color is fat that was never digested, usually from missing pancreatic lipase. Clay colored stool and dark urine together is the pair that names biliary obstruction.
questions.strategy: Ask what is missing or added, and where in the tract that would have happened.

questions.stem: A nurse is about to assess a patient's abdomen. Which sequence is correct?

options.text: Inspect, palpate, percuss, auscultate
options.rationale: Near miss concept The general sequence applied to the one region that reverses it.

options.text: Inspect, percuss, palpate, auscultate
options.rationale: Near miss concept Percussion also stimulates the bowel, so the sounds are still altered.

options.text: Auscultate, percuss, inspect, palpate
options.rationale: Near miss concept Right instinct about listening early, and inspection still comes first.

options.text: Inspect, auscultate, percuss, palpate
options.rationale: The abdomen is the exception to the usual order. Palpating or percussing first changes bowel motility, so the sounds you hear afterward are sounds you caused. Listen with the diaphragm, start in the right lower quadrant, and save palpation for last. Light palpation is about half an inch for tenderness and masses; deep palpation goes further for organ size.

questions.takeaway: Everywhere else it is IPPA. The abdomen is IAPP.
questions.strategy: Inspection is never displaced from first, which eliminates one option immediately.

questions.stem: Select all of the measures for a patient receiving enteral feeding through a nasogastric tube.

options.text: Flush the tube with water before and after feedings and medications
options.rationale: Head elevation is the single most effective thing you do against aspiration, and verification before every use is what stops a feeding going into a lung. The air insufflation method was taught for decades and has been abandoned because it cannot distinguish stomach from lung. Medications are given separately and flushed between, since combining them clogs the tube and causes interactions.

options.text: Assess for abdominal distension, nausea and tolerance
options.rationale: Head elevation is the single most effective thing you do against aspiration, and verification before every use is what stops a feeding going into a lung. The air insufflation method was taught for decades and has been abandoned because it cannot distinguish stomach from lung. Medications are given separately and flushed between, since combining them clogs the tube and causes interactions.

options.text: Confirm placement by auscultating over the abdomen while injecting air
options.rationale: Near miss concept Unreliable and no longer recommended; it cannot rule out the airway.

options.text: Crush and combine all medications together for a single administration
options.rationale: Near miss concept Give separately with flushes; some forms are never crushed.

options.text: Keep the head of the bed elevated at least 30 degrees during and after feeding
options.rationale: Head elevation is the single most effective thing you do against aspiration, and verification before every use is what stops a feeding going into a lung. The air insufflation method was taught for decades and has been abandoned because it cannot distinguish stomach from lung. Medications are given separately and flushed between, since combining them clogs the tube and causes interactions.

options.text: Verify tube placement before each feeding or medication per policy
options.rationale: Head elevation is the single most effective thing you do against aspiration, and verification before every use is what stops a feeding going into a lung. The air insufflation method was taught for decades and has been abandoned because it cannot distinguish stomach from lung. Medications are given separately and flushed between, since combining them clogs the tube and causes interactions.

questions.takeaway: The air bolus whoosh is not placement verification. It was taught for years and it is wrong.
questions.strategy: One wrong option is an abandoned technique; the other clogs the tube.

questions.stem: Select all of the laboratory values that help evaluate liver function.

options.text: Aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase
options.rationale: Transaminases rise when hepatocytes are injured. Bilirubin rises when the liver cannot conjugate or excrete it. Ammonia rises when the liver cannot convert it to urea, which is why it tracks with encephalopathy. Prothrombin time lengthens because clotting factors are made in the liver, which makes it a function test rather than a damage test. Amylase is pancreas.

options.text: Serum amylase
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pancreatic, paired with lipase.

options.text: Prothrombin time
options.rationale: Transaminases rise when hepatocytes are injured. Bilirubin rises when the liver cannot conjugate or excrete it. Ammonia rises when the liver cannot convert it to urea, which is why it tracks with encephalopathy. Prothrombin time lengthens because clotting factors are made in the liver, which makes it a function test rather than a damage test. Amylase is pancreas.

options.text: Total and direct bilirubin
options.rationale: Transaminases rise when hepatocytes are injured. Bilirubin rises when the liver cannot conjugate or excrete it. Ammonia rises when the liver cannot convert it to urea, which is why it tracks with encephalopathy. Prothrombin time lengthens because clotting factors are made in the liver, which makes it a function test rather than a damage test. Amylase is pancreas.

options.text: Serum ammonia
options.rationale: Transaminases rise when hepatocytes are injured. Bilirubin rises when the liver cannot conjugate or excrete it. Ammonia rises when the liver cannot convert it to urea, which is why it tracks with encephalopathy. Prothrombin time lengthens because clotting factors are made in the liver, which makes it a function test rather than a damage test. Amylase is pancreas.

options.text: Blood urea nitrogen
options.rationale: Near miss concept A kidney value. Order it to assess renal function, not hepatic.

questions.takeaway: Prothrombin time is a liver function test. That one catches people out.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options belong to other organs, pancreas and kidney.

questions.stem: Select all of the expected age related gastrointestinal changes.

options.text: Increased gastric acid production that speeds protein digestion
options.rationale: Near miss concept Acid production falls with mucosal atrophy, which is part of why B12 absorption suffers.

options.text: Faster drug clearance by the liver, so higher doses are needed
options.rationale: Near miss concept Exactly backwards, and acting on it causes toxicity.

options.text: Gastric mucosal atrophy that reduces iron and B12 absorption
options.rationale: The aging gut slows and absorbs less. The clinically dangerous one is the liver: less mass and less enzyme activity means standard doses behave like larger ones, so toxicity builds over days. That is the same mechanism behind polypharmacy problems in older adults.

options.text: Reduced liver mass and enzyme activity that slows drug metabolism
options.rationale: The aging gut slows and absorbs less. The clinically dangerous one is the liver: less mass and less enzyme activity means standard doses behave like larger ones, so toxicity builds over days. That is the same mechanism behind polypharmacy problems in older adults.

options.text: Slower peristalsis and a dulled urge to defecate
options.rationale: The aging gut slows and absorbs less. The clinically dangerous one is the liver: less mass and less enzyme activity means standard doses behave like larger ones, so toxicity builds over days. That is the same mechanism behind polypharmacy problems in older adults.

options.text: Less pancreatic lipase, which can lead to steatorrhea
options.rationale: The aging gut slows and absorbs less. The clinically dangerous one is the liver: less mass and less enzyme activity means standard doses behave like larger ones, so toxicity builds over days. That is the same mechanism behind polypharmacy problems in older adults.

questions.takeaway: The aging liver is why a normal dose becomes a high dose by day three.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options describe an aging system working faster. It does not.

questions.stem: A nurse is palpating a patient's abdomen. What is assessed with light palpation?

options.text: Tenderness, guarding and superficial masses at about half an inch
options.rationale: Light palpation goes about half to one inch and tells you where it hurts and whether the muscles are guarding. Deep palpation goes further for organ size and shape. You palpate the tender area last, so the guarding it produces does not contaminate the rest of the exam. Sounds and bruits are auscultation, which happens before any touching.

options.text: Organ size and deep masses, pressing in more than an inch deep
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is deep palpation, which follows light.

options.text: A bruit over the aorta, felt as a vibration under the hand
options.rationale: Near miss concept Also auscultation, with the bell or diaphragm.

options.text: Bowel sound activity in all four quadrants of the abdomen
options.rationale: Near miss concept Auscultation, and it comes before palpation in the abdomen.

questions.takeaway: Light first, tender area last. Otherwise the guarding you cause ruins the rest.
questions.strategy: Two options are auscultation findings in a question about palpation.

questions.stem: A patient taking ibuprofen daily for arthritis reports new epigastric burning and has a hemoglobin that has fallen from 13.1 to 10.4. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Iron deficiency from inadequate dietary intake
options.rationale: Near miss concept Diet does not drop a hemoglobin this fast in an adult.

options.text: Gastroesophageal reflux that will respond to diet changes
options.rationale: Near miss concept Explains the burning and not the hemoglobin.

options.text: Peptic ulcer disease with gastrointestinal bleeding
options.rationale: Nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs strip the gastric mucosa of its protection, and regular use is a leading cause of ulcer and bleeding. Epigastric burning plus a dropping hemoglobin is blood loss until proven otherwise. Ask about melena, check a stool for occult blood and watch for dizziness or syncope.

options.text: Expected variation in the hemoglobin between draws
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Normalizes a change of nearly 3 grams.

questions.takeaway: Daily nonsteroidals plus a falling hemoglobin is a bleed, not a diet problem.
questions.strategy: A 2.7 gram drop is not variation, and the stem gives you the drug that explains it.

questions.stem: Six hours after an endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography a patient reports severe epigastric pain radiating to the back. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Post procedure pancreatitis
options.rationale: Pancreatitis is the complication this procedure is known for, because the scope enters the pancreatic duct. Severe epigastric pain boring through to the back after an ERCP is that until proven otherwise, and it gets reported immediately along with amylase and lipase. Watch also for bleeding and for sedation related respiratory depression.

options.text: Constipation from the bowel preparation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Bowel prep belongs to colonoscopy, and the pain pattern does not fit.

options.text: A reaction to the sedation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sedation reactions are respiratory and hemodynamic, not this pain pattern.

options.text: Expected soreness from the scope
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Throat discomfort is expected; severe epigastric pain radiating to the back is not.

questions.takeaway: ERCP plus severe back radiating pain equals pancreatitis.
questions.strategy: Scope soreness is in the throat and mild. This pain is in the wrong place and the wrong intensity to normalize.

questions.stem: Four hours after a colonoscopy a patient reports severe abdominal pain, has a distended rigid abdomen, a heart rate of 118 and a blood pressure of 94/58. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Bowel perforation, a surgical emergency
options.rationale: Cramping and gas after a colonoscopy are expected and get better. Severe pain with a rigid distended abdomen, tachycardia and hypotension four hours later is perforation with peritonitis developing, and it needs surgery. The vital signs are what separate it: retained air does not drop a blood pressure.

options.text: A vasovagal response to the procedure
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would bring bradycardia rather than a rate of 118, and no rigidity.

options.text: Cramping from retained insufflated air
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Expected, and it does not produce rigidity, tachycardia or hypotension.

options.text: Dehydration caused by the bowel prep
options.rationale: Near miss concept Can cause tachycardia and hypotension and not a rigid abdomen with severe pain.

questions.takeaway: Expected post colonoscopy discomfort improves. Pain with rigidity and unstable vitals is a hole.
questions.strategy: The expected finding option is credible right up until you read the blood pressure.

questions.stem: A patient with cirrhosis has ascites, asterixis, an ammonia of 92, and is increasingly confused. Select all of the appropriate nursing actions.

options.text: Monitor for gastrointestinal bleeding, which can precipitate encephalopathy
options.rationale: Hepatic encephalopathy is ammonia the liver cannot convert to urea, and the nursing work is tracking the trend, keeping him safe and watching for the triggers, of which gastrointestinal bleeding is the big one because digested blood is a protein load delivered straight into the gut. Lactulose traps ammonia there. A sedative in a patient with a liver that cannot metabolize it deepens the encephalopathy. The protein option fails on its premise rather than on protein: dietary protein will not raise his albumin, and protein is no longer restricted in encephalopathy, since restriction drives muscle loss without shortening the episode.

options.text: Institute fall and injury precautions
options.rationale: Hepatic encephalopathy is ammonia the liver cannot convert to urea, and the nursing work is tracking the trend, keeping him safe and watching for the triggers, of which gastrointestinal bleeding is the big one because digested blood is a protein load delivered straight into the gut. Lactulose traps ammonia there. A sedative in a patient with a liver that cannot metabolize it deepens the encephalopathy. The protein option fails on its premise rather than on protein: dietary protein will not raise his albumin, and protein is no longer restricted in encephalopathy, since restriction drives muscle loss without shortening the episode.

options.text: Administer a sedative to settle the confusion
options.rationale: Near miss concept A failing liver cannot clear it, and sedation deepens encephalopathy.

options.text: Encourage a high protein diet to correct the low albumin
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dietary protein does not correct cirrhotic hypoalbuminemia, and protein is not restricted here; the protein load that matters is a bleed.

options.text: Assess orientation and asterixis each shift and document the trend
options.rationale: Hepatic encephalopathy is ammonia the liver cannot convert to urea, and the nursing work is tracking the trend, keeping him safe and watching for the triggers, of which gastrointestinal bleeding is the big one because digested blood is a protein load delivered straight into the gut. Lactulose traps ammonia there. A sedative in a patient with a liver that cannot metabolize it deepens the encephalopathy. The protein option fails on its premise rather than on protein: dietary protein will not raise his albumin, and protein is no longer restricted in encephalopathy, since restriction drives muscle loss without shortening the episode.

options.text: Anticipate lactulose to reduce ammonia production and absorption
options.rationale: Hepatic encephalopathy is ammonia the liver cannot convert to urea, and the nursing work is tracking the trend, keeping him safe and watching for the triggers, of which gastrointestinal bleeding is the big one because digested blood is a protein load delivered straight into the gut. Lactulose traps ammonia there. A sedative in a patient with a liver that cannot metabolize it deepens the encephalopathy. The protein option fails on its premise rather than on protein: dietary protein will not raise his albumin, and protein is no longer restricted in encephalopathy, since restriction drives muscle loss without shortening the episode.

questions.takeaway: A gastrointestinal bleed in cirrhosis is a protein meal. It is the classic precipitant.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options are reasonable in another patient and dangerous in this one.

questions.stem: On examination a patient's abdominal muscles tense involuntarily and stay rigid, and he reports pain when the nurse releases pressure. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: Peritoneal inflammation, which requires urgent evaluation
options.rationale: Voluntary guarding relaxes if you distract the patient or have him bend his knees. Involuntary rigidity does not, because the peritoneum is inflamed and the muscle over it is splinting reflexively. Rebound tenderness points the same way. Together they are an acute abdomen until someone proves otherwise.

options.text: Expected tenderness after abdominal surgery
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Incisional tenderness is expected; rigidity with rebound is not.

options.text: Normal voluntary guarding from anxiety about the examination
options.rationale: Near miss concept Voluntary guarding relaxes with distraction; this does not.

options.text: Constipation with stool in the colon
options.rationale: Near miss concept Produces fullness and discomfort, not rigidity with rebound.

questions.takeaway: Guarding that relaxes is anxiety. Guarding that will not is peritoneum.
questions.strategy: The word involuntary in the stem is doing all the work.

questions.stem: A patient reports black, tarry stools for two days. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: Steatorrhea from fat malabsorption
options.rationale: Near miss concept Greasy, foul and floating, from pancreatic insufficiency rather than bleeding.

options.text: Biliary obstruction preventing bile from reaching the stool
options.rationale: Near miss concept Makes stool clay colored or acholic, the opposite of dark.

options.text: Bleeding in the lower gastrointestinal tract or rectum
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is bright red blood, because it has not been digested.

options.text: Bleeding in the upper gastrointestinal tract
options.rationale: Black and tarry is melena, and the color comes from blood that has been digested on its way through, which means it entered high: stomach or duodenum. Bright red blood is hematochezia and comes from low down. Acholic stool from biliary obstruction is clay colored, not black, and steatorrhea is greasy and floats.

questions.takeaway: Black means digested, which means it came from upstream.
questions.strategy: Four stool descriptions, four different problems. The color is the whole question.

questions.stem: A patient reports greasy, foul smelling stools that float and are normal brown in color. What does this suggest?

options.text: Infectious diarrhea
options.rationale: Near miss concept Watery and acute, usually with fever or cramping.

options.text: Fat malabsorption, as from reduced pancreatic lipase
options.rationale: Undigested fat makes stool greasy, foul and buoyant. The usual cause is not enough lipase, which happens in pancreatic insufficiency and as a normal aging change as pancreatic lipase declines. Biliary obstruction also causes fat malabsorption, and its signature stool is clay colored or acholic rather than greasy.

options.text: Upper gastrointestinal bleeding
options.rationale: Near miss concept Produces black tarry melena.

options.text: Biliary obstruction with no bile reaching the stool
options.rationale: Near miss concept Close, and its stool is clay colored; this one is described as greasy.

questions.takeaway: Floating and greasy is fat. Black is blood. Clay colored is bile that never arrived.
questions.strategy: Three stool descriptions, three mechanisms. The adjective is the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A patient returns from an upper endoscopy. What is the priority nursing action before offering fluids?

options.text: Confirm that vital signs are at baseline
options.rationale: Near miss concept Monitored closely after sedation, and not the aspiration safeguard.

options.text: Confirm that the sore throat has resolved
options.rationale: Near miss concept A sore throat is expected for a day or so and is unrelated to the reflex.

options.text: Confirm that the gag reflex has returned
options.rationale: The throat was anesthetized so the scope could pass, and a patient who cannot gag cannot protect the airway. Nothing by mouth until the reflex is back, usually 30 to 60 minutes. Vital signs and orientation matter, and they are not what stands between this patient and aspiration.

options.text: Confirm that the patient is fully oriented
options.rationale: Near miss concept Important after sedation and it does not tell you the throat works.

questions.takeaway: No gag, no fluids. That is the whole rule.
questions.strategy: Three correct assessments, one of which is the one that prevents aspiration.

questions.stem: A patient has severe upper abdominal pain radiating to the back. Which lab is most specific for acute pancreatitis?

options.text: ALT
options.rationale: Near miss concept ALT reflects liver cell damage.

options.text: Ammonia
options.rationale: Near miss concept Ammonia reflects liver detox.

options.text: Lipase
options.rationale: Amylase and lipase both rise in acute pancreatitis. Lipase is more specific and stays raised longer.

options.text: Amylase
options.rationale: Near miss concept Amylase also rises but lipase is more specific and stays up longer.

questions.takeaway: Lipase is the more specific pancreas test.
questions.strategy: Pick the lab that belongs to the pancreas and is most specific.

questions.stem: A patient will collect a guaiac fecal occult blood test. Which instruction is correct?

options.text: No food or drug limits are needed before the test.
options.rationale: Near miss concept That applies to the FIT, not the gFOBT.

options.text: Avoid NSAIDs 7 days; red meat and high vitamin C 3 days.
options.rationale: The gFOBT can give a false positive with NSAIDs, red meat or high dose vitamin C. The FIT has no food or drug limits. Any positive stool test needs a colonoscopy.

options.text: Stay NPO for 8 hours before each of the three stool collections.
options.rationale: Near miss concept NPO is not needed for a stool test.

options.text: Drink only clear liquids on the day before the test.
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is colonoscopy prep.

questions.takeaway: gFOBT: no NSAIDs, red meat or vitamin C.
questions.strategy: Separate the gFOBT from the FIT, which has no limits.

questions.stem: A patient with cirrhosis is newly confused. Which lab result best explains this?

options.text: Total bilirubin of 0.8 mg/dL
options.rationale: Near miss concept This bilirubin is unremarkable.

options.text: Amylase of 90 units/L
options.rationale: Near miss concept Amylase reflects the pancreas.

options.text: Ammonia of 145 mcg/dL
options.rationale: A failing liver cannot convert ammonia to urea, so ammonia builds up and causes confusion (hepatic encephalopathy). Lactulose pulls it out in the stool, with a goal of 2 to 3 soft stools a day.

options.text: Albumin of 3.8 g/dL
options.rationale: Near miss concept This albumin is acceptable and does not cause confusion.

questions.takeaway: High ammonia causes confusion.
questions.strategy: Match the lab to the organ job that is failing.

questions.stem: For each stool description, indicate what it most likely means.

rows.text: Black, sticky, tarry stool
Bright red blood with the stool
Bulky, greasy, foul smelling stool that floats
Pale, clay colored stool with dark urine

questions.takeaway: Melena is an upper GI bleed digested on the way down. Hematochezia is a lower GI bleed. Acholic stool means no bile (blocked duct or liver disease). Steatorrhea means fat malabsorption from pancreatic disease or low lipase. The longer the trip, the darker the blood.
questions.strategy: Match the color or texture to what is missing or added.

questions.stem: Why should a patient who recently had a myocardial infarction avoid straining at stool?

options.text: Straining raises the blood glucose level.
options.rationale: Near miss concept It does not.

options.text: Straining leads to painful hemorrhoids that bleed easily.
options.rationale: Near miss concept True in general but not the cardiac concern.

options.text: Valsalva slows the heart and can cause dysrhythmias.
options.rationale: Bearing down stimulates the vagus nerve and slows the heart, which is a risk after an MI or heart surgery.

options.text: Straining sets off episodes of diarrhea.
options.rationale: Near miss concept It does not.

questions.takeaway: Valsalva slows the heart.
questions.strategy: Link the action to the organ that is vulnerable.

questions.stem: A patient is preparing for a colonoscopy. Select all liquids that are acceptable the day before.

options.text: Grape juice
options.rationale: Near miss concept Purple liquids can look like blood during the exam.

options.text: Water
options.rationale: Clear liquids the day before, with no red, orange or purple. The prep continues until stool is clear liquid, and the patient needs a driver home even once alert.

options.text: Orange soda
options.rationale: Near miss concept Orange liquids are avoided.

options.text: Clear broth
options.rationale: Clear liquids the day before, with no red, orange or purple. The prep continues until stool is clear liquid, and the patient needs a driver home even once alert.

options.text: Apple juice
options.rationale: Clear liquids the day before, with no red, orange or purple. The prep continues until stool is clear liquid, and the patient needs a driver home even once alert.

options.text: Lemon gelatin
options.rationale: Clear liquids the day before, with no red, orange or purple. The prep continues until stool is clear liquid, and the patient needs a driver home even once alert.

options.text: Red gelatin
options.rationale: Near miss concept Red liquids are avoided.

questions.takeaway: No red, orange or purple before colonoscopy.
questions.strategy: Eliminate any color that could look like blood.

questions.stem: Place the steps of the nurse's abdominal assessment in the correct order.

options.text: Auscultate bowel sounds
Inspect the abdomen
Have the patient empty the bladder
Percuss the abdomen
Palpate the abdomen, tender area last

questions.takeaway: The bladder is emptied first. The order is inspect, auscultate, percuss, palpate, because touch stirs the bowel and changes the sounds. The tender area is examined last. Inspect, auscultate, percuss, palpate.
questions.strategy: The abdomen is the one exam where listening comes before touching.

questions.stem: Why does the nurse auscultate the abdomen before palpating it?

options.text: The provider requires that order on every exam.
options.rationale: Institution as rationale The order has a physiological reason.

options.text: Palpation is painful, so it is saved for last.
options.rationale: Near miss concept The tender area is examined last, but that is not why auscultation comes first.

options.text: Auscultation is the fastest part of the exam.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Speed is not the reason.

options.text: Touching the abdomen changes the bowel sounds.
options.rationale: Touch stirs the bowel and changes the sounds, so the nurse listens before percussing or palpating.

questions.takeaway: Touch changes the sounds.
questions.strategy: Choose the option that gives a mechanism.

questions.stem: A patient who takes iron supplements has dark stool. Which finding suggests bleeding rather than an iron effect?

options.text: The stool is formed.
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Formed stool does not separate iron from bleeding.

options.text: The stool is tarry.
options.rationale: Iron and bismuth turn stool black but not tarry or sticky. Black, sticky, tarry stool is melena from an upper GI bleed.

options.text: The stool is dark green.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Iron can darken stool to green or black without being sticky or tarry.

options.text: The stool is darker.
