options.rationale: Near miss concept Iron darkens stool too.

questions.takeaway: Iron makes stool black, not tarry.
questions.strategy: Look for the texture that only digested blood produces.

questions.stem: Where should the nurse begin auscultating bowel sounds?

options.text: The right lower quadrant
options.rationale: Bowel sounds are auscultated with the diaphragm, starting in the RLQ. Normal is irregular gurgles, 5 to 30 per minute.

options.text: The umbilicus
options.rationale: Near miss concept The nurse starts in the RLQ.

options.text: The most tender area
options.rationale: Near miss concept The tender area is examined last.

options.text: The left upper quadrant
options.rationale: Near miss concept Auscultation starts in the RLQ, where the ileocecal valve area is usually active.

questions.takeaway: Start bowel sounds in the RLQ.
questions.strategy: Recall the starting point.

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate the condition it most suggests.

rows.text: Cramping pain in waves with high pitched bowel sounds
Vomiting of fecal material
No bowel sounds and distention 2 days after surgery on opioids
Rigid, board like abdomen with fever and the patient lying still

questions.takeaway: Mechanical obstruction is a physical block with colicky pain and high pitched sounds that later become absent. Paralytic ileus is a bowel that stopped moving after surgery or opioids. Peritonitis is an inflamed peritoneum with a rigid abdomen, fever and sepsis risk. Block, stopped or inflamed.
questions.strategy: Ask whether something is blocking, the bowel has stopped or the lining is inflamed.

questions.stem: Select all expected age related changes in the GI system.

options.text: Increased lipase production
options.rationale: Near miss concept Lipase decreases with age.

options.text: Slower peristalsis
options.rationale: Every aging change is a decrease except bacterial growth: less acid (less iron and B12 absorbed), slower peristalsis (constipation), less lipase (steatorrhea) and slower drug metabolism (toxicity at normal doses).

options.text: Less stomach acid
options.rationale: Every aging change is a decrease except bacterial growth: less acid (less iron and B12 absorbed), slower peristalsis (constipation), less lipase (steatorrhea) and slower drug metabolism (toxicity at normal doses).

options.text: Slower drug metabolism by the liver
options.rationale: Every aging change is a decrease except bacterial growth: less acid (less iron and B12 absorbed), slower peristalsis (constipation), less lipase (steatorrhea) and slower drug metabolism (toxicity at normal doses).

options.text: Enhanced peristalsis
options.rationale: Near miss concept Peristalsis slows with age.

options.text: Less lipase from the pancreas
options.rationale: Every aging change is a decrease except bacterial growth: less acid (less iron and B12 absorbed), slower peristalsis (constipation), less lipase (steatorrhea) and slower drug metabolism (toxicity at normal doses).

questions.takeaway: Every GI aging change is a decrease except bacterial growth.
questions.strategy: Eliminate anything that says increased or enhanced.

questions.stem: How often is a stool DNA test repeated when results are normal?

options.text: Every 3 years
options.rationale: FIT and gFOBT are yearly, the stool DNA test every 3 years, and colonoscopy every 10 years from age 45.

options.text: Every 10 years
options.rationale: Near miss concept Every 10 years is for colonoscopy.

options.text: Every year
options.rationale: Near miss concept Yearly is for the FIT and gFOBT.

options.text: Every 5 years
options.rationale: Near miss concept The stool DNA test is every 3 years.

questions.takeaway: Stool DNA every 3 years.
questions.strategy: Match each test to its interval.

questions.stem: An 81 year old patient has fatigue and pallor. Which age related GI change best explains this?

options.text: Less acid reduces iron and B12 absorption.
options.rationale: Atrophy of the gastric mucosa means less acid, so less iron and B12 are absorbed, causing anemia with fatigue and pallor.

options.text: Slower peristalsis causes constipation.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Constipation does not explain anemia.

options.text: Slower liver metabolism raises circulating drug levels.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Drug toxicity is a different problem.

options.text: Less pancreatic lipase causes fatty stools.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fat malabsorption does not explain fatigue and pallor.

questions.takeaway: Less acid means less iron and B12.
questions.strategy: Trace the symptom back to the change that would cause it.

questions.stem: A patient taking lactulose for a high ammonia level has 2 soft stools a day. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: The patient needs an antidiarrheal.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Stopping the stools would let ammonia build up.

options.text: The patient has diarrhea and the dose should be held.
options.rationale: Near miss concept 2 to 3 soft stools a day is the goal.

options.text: The dose is too low.
options.rationale: Near miss concept The goal has been met.

options.text: The drug is working as intended.
options.rationale: Lactulose pulls ammonia out in the stool. The goal is 2 to 3 soft stools a day.

questions.takeaway: Lactulose goal: 2 to 3 soft stools a day.
questions.strategy: Recognize when a drug effect is the goal.

questions.stem: A patient with liver disease has a prolonged PT. What should the nurse monitor for?

options.text: Confusion from ammonia
options.rationale: Near miss concept That relates to ammonia, not PT.

options.text: Bleeding
options.rationale: The liver makes clotting factors. In liver disease the PT is prolonged, so the nurse watches for bleeding.

options.text: High blood glucose
options.rationale: Near miss concept PT does not relate to glucose.

options.text: Clots in the legs
options.rationale: Near miss concept A prolonged PT means slower clotting, not more clotting.

questions.takeaway: The liver makes clotting factors.
questions.strategy: Link the lab to the liver job it reflects.

questions.stem: A patient returns from an esophagogastroduodenoscopy. Select all correct nursing actions.

options.text: Keep the patient NPO until the gag reflex returns
options.rationale: After EGD the patient is NPO until the gag reflex returns (30 to 60 minutes), with no test sips. Breathing is watched, rails are up and a sore throat is expected. Pain, fever or bleeding suggest perforation.

options.text: Report pain, fever or bleeding
options.rationale: After EGD the patient is NPO until the gag reflex returns (30 to 60 minutes), with no test sips. Breathing is watched, rails are up and a sore throat is expected. Pain, fever or bleeding suggest perforation.

options.text: Give a test sip of water to check swallowing
options.rationale: Near miss concept No test sips. The gag reflex is checked first.

options.text: Report a mild sore throat as a complication
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A sore throat is expected.

options.text: Monitor breathing
options.rationale: After EGD the patient is NPO until the gag reflex returns (30 to 60 minutes), with no test sips. Breathing is watched, rails are up and a sore throat is expected. Pain, fever or bleeding suggest perforation.

options.text: Keep the side rails up
options.rationale: After EGD the patient is NPO until the gag reflex returns (30 to 60 minutes), with no test sips. Breathing is watched, rails are up and a sore throat is expected. Pain, fever or bleeding suggest perforation.

questions.takeaway: After EGD: NPO until the gag reflex returns.
questions.strategy: Protect the airway first after a scope through the mouth.

questions.stem: Four hours after a colonoscopy with polyp removal, a patient has worsening abdominal pain, a rigid abdomen and a temperature of 38.4 °C. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Expected cramping from the air used during the procedure
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Cramping and gas are expected, but worsening pain with rigidity and fever are not.

options.text: A reaction to the bowel prep
options.rationale: Near miss concept Prep does not cause a rigid abdomen with fever.

options.text: Bowel perforation
options.rationale: After colonoscopy, cramping, gas and a small amount of blood after polyp removal are expected. Worsening pain, a rigid abdomen and fever suggest perforation.

options.text: Constipation from sedation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Constipation does not cause a rigid abdomen with fever.

questions.takeaway: Rigid abdomen with fever after a scope means perforation.
questions.strategy: Separate expected discomfort from signs of a complication.

questions.stem: A patient reports black stools. Select all questions the nurse should ask.

options.text: Does anyone in your family have diabetes?
options.rationale: Near miss concept This does not relate to bleeding.

options.text: Do you take aspirin or ibuprofen?
options.rationale: For black or bloody stool, the nurse asks about aspirin, NSAIDs, anticoagulants and alcohol, which cause ulcers and bleeding, and about iron or bismuth, which blacken stool without making it tarry.

options.text: Do you take a blood thinner?
options.rationale: For black or bloody stool, the nurse asks about aspirin, NSAIDs, anticoagulants and alcohol, which cause ulcers and bleeding, and about iron or bismuth, which blacken stool without making it tarry.

options.text: Do you take iron or bismuth?
options.rationale: For black or bloody stool, the nurse asks about aspirin, NSAIDs, anticoagulants and alcohol, which cause ulcers and bleeding, and about iron or bismuth, which blacken stool without making it tarry.

options.text: How often do you exercise?
options.rationale: Near miss concept Exercise does not explain black stools.

options.text: How much alcohol do you drink?
options.rationale: For black or bloody stool, the nurse asks about aspirin, NSAIDs, anticoagulants and alcohol, which cause ulcers and bleeding, and about iron or bismuth, which blacken stool without making it tarry.

questions.takeaway: Tie the history question to the complaint.
questions.strategy: Keep questions that could explain the complaint in the stem.

questions.stem: A patient starts scheduled oxycodone after surgery. Which order should the nurse expect?

options.text: An antidiarrheal
options.rationale: Near miss concept Opioids cause constipation, not diarrhea.

options.text: A fluid restriction
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fluids help prevent constipation.

options.text: A daily stool softener or laxative
options.rationale: Opioids slow the bowel, so a daily softener or laxative starts with the opioid, not only once constipated.

options.text: A laxative only after 3 days with no stool
options.rationale: Correct but premature Opioids always constipate, so prevention starts with the opioid.

questions.takeaway: Opioids: start the bowel regimen with the first dose.
questions.strategy: Prevention beats treatment when the side effect is certain.

questions.stem: A patient is 2 days after abdominal surgery. Which finding best shows that bowel function has returned?

options.text: The patient is hungry.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hunger does not confirm peristalsis.

options.text: The abdomen is soft.
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data A soft abdomen does not show motility.

options.text: The patient reports passing flatus.
options.rationale: After abdominal surgery, the best sign the bowel works is passing flatus, not bowel sounds.

options.text: Bowel sounds are heard in all four quadrants.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sounds can be heard before the bowel moves contents forward.

questions.takeaway: Ask about flatus, not just bowel sounds.
questions.strategy: Choose the finding that shows contents moving through.

questions.stem: A patient with a new jejunostomy tube is receiving continuous feeding. He develops cramping, abdominal distention and large volume watery diarrhea. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Stop the feeding and keep the patient nothing by mouth for 24 hours
options.rationale: Near miss concept Overcorrects and costs him a day of nutrition he needs.

options.text: Assess the rate, concentration and temperature of the feeding and the tube position
options.rationale: Diarrhea on tube feeding usually comes from the delivery rather than the patient: too fast, too concentrated, too cold, or a tube that has migrated. Dumping syndrome happens when a hyperosmolar load hits the jejunum quickly. Check those before changing formulas or treating the symptom, because the fix is often a rate adjustment. Also consider medications and C. difficile.

options.text: Request a change to a fiber free formula
options.rationale: Correct but premature A formula change may help later and the rate is the first variable.

options.text: Administer the ordered antidiarrheal
options.rationale: Near miss concept Treats a symptom whose mechanical cause has not been looked for, and masks possible C. difficile.

questions.takeaway: Diarrhea on tube feeds is usually the rate or the concentration, not the formula.
questions.strategy: Treating the diarrhea without checking the delivery means the next shift has the same problem.

questions.stem: A patient with a new colostomy avoids looking at the stoma and declines to participate in care. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Teach the family the care instead so the patient is not burdened
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Removes his independence under the appearance of help.

options.text: Acknowledge the difficulty and keep offering care at her own pace
options.rationale: Body image disruption is an expected part of ostomy adjustment, and avoidance early on is not refusal. Pressure produces compliance in the room and avoidance at home. Keep offering, keep doing the care in front of him, and let the participation come. Teaching the family instead quietly confirms that he cannot manage it.

options.text: Document noncompliance with the ostomy teaching plan for the team
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Turns an adjustment reaction into a character judgment.

options.text: Insist she watch the next change, since discharge is approaching
options.rationale: Near miss concept Real time pressure, and coercion does not build competence.

questions.takeaway: Avoidance is grief, not noncompliance. Keep offering without pushing.
questions.strategy: Two options take the skill away from him permanently.

questions.stem: A patient reports pain that began periumbilically and has moved to the right lower quadrant over six hours. He lies very still with his knees drawn up, the abdomen is rigid, and he has rebound tenderness. Temperature is 38.3. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Apply a heating pad to the right lower quadrant for comfort
options.rationale: Near miss concept Heat can accelerate rupture of an inflamed appendix.

options.text: Encourage walking in the hallway to help the pain settle
options.rationale: Near miss concept He is still for a reason; movement worsens peritoneal pain.

options.text: Keep him nothing by mouth, get vital signs, and escalate now
options.rationale: Migrating pain, rigidity, rebound tenderness, fever and a patient who will not move is a peritoneal picture, most likely appendicitis with possible perforation. Nothing by mouth because he is heading to surgery, and escalate now. Analgesia is not withheld, which is worth knowing because it was taught for years: giving it does not mask the surgical findings or delay the diagnosis. Heat increases blood flow and can speed rupture, and a laxative in a possible obstruction or appendicitis can perforate the bowel.

options.text: Give the ordered laxative, since this may be constipation
options.rationale: Near miss concept A laxative in a possible appendicitis or obstruction can perforate the bowel.

questions.takeaway: A patient who lies perfectly still has peritoneal pain. One who cannot keep still has colic.
questions.strategy: The two comfort options here are the two that can perforate him.

questions.stem: While inspecting a patient's abdomen the nurse notices a visible pulsation above the umbilicus. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Auscultate for a bruit and then palpate deeply to assess the borders
options.rationale: Near miss concept The auscultation is fine and the deep palpation is what can rupture it.

options.text: Document the finding as normal aortic pulsation in a thin patient
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Visible aortic pulsation can be normal in a thin person, and that call is not made at the bedside before imaging.

options.text: Do not palpate the area and notify the provider
options.rationale: A pulsating midline abdominal mass may be an abdominal aortic aneurysm, and pressing on it can rupture it. You inspect, you may auscultate for a bruit, and you keep your hands off. This is one of the few findings where the correct nursing action is to stop examining.

options.text: Palpate gently to determine the size of the mass
options.rationale: Near miss concept Gentle is not a safe amount of pressure on an aneurysm.

questions.takeaway: Some findings end the exam. This is one of them.
questions.strategy: Two of the wrong options palpate. The depth does not matter.

questions.stem: A patient two days after abdominal surgery has a distended, firm abdomen, absent bowel sounds and increasing pain. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Document the findings as expected after abdominal surgery
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Hypoactive would be expected; this combination is not.

options.text: Notify the provider, because this pattern suggests ileus or peritonitis
options.rationale: Hypoactive sounds are expected after abdominal surgery. Absent sounds with distention, rigidity and worsening pain are a different picture and point to ileus or peritoneal inflammation. You listen long enough to call them absent, and then you escalate rather than treating it as slow return of function.

options.text: Encourage ambulation and a warm beverage to stimulate peristalsis
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reasonable for a sluggish gut, and dangerous if this is peritonitis.

options.text: Administer the ordered stool softener and reassess in the morning
options.rationale: Correct but premature Treats an acute abdomen as constipation.

questions.takeaway: Hypoactive after surgery is expected. Absent plus rigid plus worsening is not.
questions.strategy: The stem deliberately includes the postoperative context so you will normalize it.

questions.stem: An older adult on opioids after hip surgery has had no formed stool for 5 days and now has liquid stool leaking. Loperamide is ordered. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Hold the loperamide and check for impaction.
options.rationale: Liquid stool oozing with no formed stool is impaction until proven otherwise. Hold the antidiarrheal, do a gentle digital check and report. During removal, watch the pulse because it can be vagal.

options.text: Give the loperamide to control the diarrhea.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Liquid seeping around an impaction is not diarrhea, and an antidiarrheal makes it worse.

options.text: Increase the opioid dose for better comfort.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Opioids worsen constipation.

options.text: Start contact precautions for C. difficile.
options.rationale: Near miss concept The history points to impaction, not an antibiotic related infection.

questions.takeaway: Liquid oozing with no formed stool is impaction.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the stool pattern fits diarrhea or seepage around a blockage.

questions.stem: Before a colonoscopy, a patient asks the nurse what the risks of perforation are. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give a brochure on the risks and have the patient sign.
options.rationale: Near miss concept A brochure does not replace the provider's explanation.

options.text: Have the patient sign now and ask the provider afterward.
options.rationale: Near miss concept A patient who does not understand cannot give informed consent.

options.text: Explain the risks of perforation to the patient herself.
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Explaining risks is the provider's role.

options.text: Have the provider answer before the consent is signed.
options.rationale: The provider explains the procedure, risks, benefits and alternatives. The nurse witnesses the signature and confirms it was voluntary. If the patient has questions, the nurse notifies the provider and does not explain in the provider's place.

questions.takeaway: The step people drop: questions go back to the provider.
questions.strategy: Reject any option where the nurse explains risks.

questions.stem: A patient with a ruptured appendix lies very still with the knees bent. The abdomen is rigid and the heart rate is 118/min. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Notify the provider now and keep the patient NPO.
options.rationale: Peritonitis is an emergency with sepsis risk: notify now, NPO, IV fluids and antibiotics, and often surgery.

options.text: Apply a heating pad to the abdomen for comfort.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Heat is not used for a possible surgical emergency.

options.text: Give the ordered laxative to relieve the pressure.
options.rationale: Near miss concept A laxative could worsen the problem.

options.text: Encourage the patient to walk to relieve the gas.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Walking helps ileus, not peritonitis.

questions.takeaway: A rigid abdomen means notify now.
questions.strategy: Recognize the emergency, then choose escalation.

questions.stem: An older adult has had diarrhea for 2 days. Which finding is most concerning?

options.text: Two loose stools today
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data The number alone does not show the effect.

options.text: New confusion
options.rationale: Diarrhea threatens fluid volume. In older adults, new confusion may be the sign of dehydration or electrolyte loss, especially low potassium.

options.text: Thirst
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Thirst is expected with fluid loss and is an early cue.

options.text: Mild abdominal cramping
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Cramping is expected with diarrhea.

questions.takeaway: In older adults, confusion may be the sign of fluid loss.
questions.strategy: Choose the finding that shows the brain is affected.

questions.stem: While inspecting the abdomen, the nurse sees a pulsating mass in the midline and hears a bruit. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Palpate the mass gently to measure its size.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pressure could rupture an aneurysm.

options.text: Document the finding and continue the exam.
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting A possible aneurysm needs reporting now.

options.text: Percuss over the area to check for dullness.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Percussion adds pressure.

options.text: Avoid palpating it and notify the provider.
options.rationale: A pulsating midline mass or aortic bruit suggests an aneurysm. No palpation and no percussion; the patient rests and the provider is notified now.

questions.takeaway: A pulsating mass is never palpated.
questions.strategy: Reject any action that puts pressure on a possible aneurysm.

questions.stem: A patient received IV midazolam 15 minutes ago and has not signed the consent for an EGD. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Have a family member sign for the patient.
options.rationale: Near miss concept A patient with capacity before sedation was the one who needed to consent.

options.text: Witness the signature if the patient can hold the pen.
options.rationale: Near miss concept The patient must not be sedated.

options.text: Have the patient sign now because the procedure is about to start.
options.rationale: Near miss concept A signature after IV sedation is invalid.

options.text: Do not obtain the signature and notify the provider.
options.rationale: Consent requires capacity. A signature after an opioid or IV sedation is invalid. A medical interpreter is used when needed, never family.

questions.takeaway: A signature after sedation is invalid.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the patient has capacity at the moment of signing.

questions.stem: Select all urine findings that the nurse should report.

options.text: Mucus threads in the urine from an ileal conduit
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem The ileum keeps making mucus, so threads are expected.

options.text: Bright red urine
options.rationale: Cloudy, foul urine suggests infection. Red or tea colored urine suggests blood (bright red low in the tract, dark red or cola from the kidney). Output below 30 mL an hour is reported.

options.text: Output of 22 mL/hr for 2 hours
options.rationale: Cloudy, foul urine suggests infection. Red or tea colored urine suggests blood (bright red low in the tract, dark red or cola from the kidney). Output below 30 mL an hour is reported.

options.text: Pale yellow urine with an output of 1,600 mL in 24 hours
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit This is normal output and color.

options.text: Tea colored urine
options.rationale: Cloudy, foul urine suggests infection. Red or tea colored urine suggests blood (bright red low in the tract, dark red or cola from the kidney). Output below 30 mL an hour is reported.

options.text: Cloudy, foul smelling urine
options.rationale: Cloudy, foul urine suggests infection. Red or tea colored urine suggests blood (bright red low in the tract, dark red or cola from the kidney). Output below 30 mL an hour is reported.

questions.takeaway: Color, clarity and amount all carry meaning.
questions.strategy: Keep findings that point to infection, bleeding or low perfusion.

questions.stem: For each patient, indicate the type of incontinence.

rows.text: Has a sudden overwhelming need to void and leaks on the way
Has constant dribbling and a palpable bladder
Feels a normal urge but cannot get to the bathroom in time with a walker
Leaks a small amount when coughing or lifting

questions.takeaway: Stress: leaks with pressure from coughing or lifting. Urge: a sudden strong urge and a large leak. Overflow: constant dribbling from a bladder that never empties. Functional: a normal urge with barriers to the toilet. A sudden overwhelming urge is urge; a normal urge with a slow walker is functional.
questions.strategy: Find the trigger word in each row.

questions.stem: Which action is most effective at preventing catheter associated urinary tract infection?

options.text: Irrigating the catheter with saline every shift
options.rationale: Near miss concept Irrigation opens the system.

options.text: Reviewing the need daily and removing it early
options.rationale: Time in place is the strongest predictor of CAUTI. The step people drop is removal.

options.text: Changing the catheter every 3 days on schedule
options.rationale: Near miss concept Routine changes do not prevent infection.

options.text: Giving antibiotics while the catheter is in place
options.rationale: Near miss concept Prophylactic antibiotics drive resistance and are not part of the bundle.

questions.takeaway: The step people drop is removal.
questions.strategy: Choose the action that shortens exposure.

questions.stem: Select all valid reasons for an indwelling urinary catheter.

options.text: Measuring output in a patient who can use a urinal
options.rationale: Near miss concept Output can be measured without a catheter.

options.text: Incontinence in a patient who can use a bedside commode
options.rationale: Near miss concept Incontinence alone is not a valid reason.

options.text: Healing a stage 4 sacral wound in an incontinent patient
options.rationale: Valid indications include acute retention or obstruction, exact hourly output in critical illness, certain surgeries, healing a stage 4 sacral or perineal wound in an incontinent patient and comfort at the end of life. Incontinence alone and convenience are not valid.

options.text: Acute urinary retention
options.rationale: Valid indications include acute retention or obstruction, exact hourly output in critical illness, certain surgeries, healing a stage 4 sacral or perineal wound in an incontinent patient and comfort at the end of life. Incontinence alone and convenience are not valid.

options.text: Exact hourly output in a critically ill patient
options.rationale: Valid indications include acute retention or obstruction, exact hourly output in critical illness, certain surgeries, healing a stage 4 sacral or perineal wound in an incontinent patient and comfort at the end of life. Incontinence alone and convenience are not valid.

options.text: Comfort at the end of life
options.rationale: Valid indications include acute retention or obstruction, exact hourly output in critical illness, certain surgeries, healing a stage 4 sacral or perineal wound in an incontinent patient and comfort at the end of life. Incontinence alone and convenience are not valid.

questions.takeaway: Every day a catheter stays in raises CAUTI risk.
questions.strategy: Ask whether a less invasive option would work.

questions.stem: For each statement, indicate whether it applies to an ileal conduit or a continent reservoir.

rows.text: A small flat stoma is covered by a small dressing
Urine flows all the time into an external pouch
The pouch is emptied when one third to half full
The patient catheterizes the stoma 4 to 6 times a day

questions.takeaway: An ileal conduit is incontinent: urine flows constantly into an external pouch. A continent reservoir is an internal pouch with a one way valve that the patient catheterizes 4 to 6 times a day. Conduit flows all the time; reservoir is emptied by catheter.
questions.strategy: Ask whether urine leaves on its own or the patient empties it.

questions.stem: For each factor, indicate the elimination problem it most likely causes.

rows.text: Furosemide
Benign prostatic hyperplasia
A call light out of reach for a patient who uses a walker
Caffeine
Diphenhydramine
Morphine after surgery

questions.takeaway: More urine coming in (fluids, diuretics, alcohol, caffeine) causes frequency. A blocked outlet (BPH, stricture) or a weak squeeze (opioids, anesthesia, anticholinergics) causes retention. Barriers to the toilet cause functional incontinence. Sort by mechanism: more urine, blocked outlet, weak squeeze or barrier.
questions.strategy: For each factor, ask what it does to the bladder.

questions.stem: Place the steps for collecting a clean catch urine specimen in order.

options.text: Start the stream into the toilet
Catch 90 to 120 mL midstream without stopping the flow
Teach the patient and provide a sterile cup
Label the cup in front of the patient and send it within 20 minutes
Cleanse the area

questions.takeaway: The patient is taught and given a sterile cup, cleanses, starts the stream in the toilet to flush surface bacteria, catches 90 to 120 mL midstream and the specimen is labeled in front of the patient and sent within 20 minutes or refrigerated. Start in the toilet to flush surface bacteria.
questions.strategy: The step people drop is starting in the toilet.

questions.stem: A patient with an indwelling catheter has a urine culture that grows bacteria. The patient has no fever, no flank pain and no change in mental status. What does the nurse expect?

options.text: A broad spectrum antibiotic immediately
options.rationale: Near miss concept Asymptomatic bacteriuria in a catheterized patient is not treated.

options.text: No antibiotic treatment, because this is colonization without symptoms.
options.rationale: Bacteria in the urine of a catheterized patient without symptoms is colonization and is not treated. Symptoms such as fever, flank pain, new confusion or a falling blood pressure are treated.

options.text: Removal of the catheter and a new one inserted
options.rationale: Near miss concept A new catheter does not treat colonization and adds risk.

options.text: Contact precautions
options.rationale: Near miss concept Colonization of the urine does not require contact precautions.

questions.takeaway: Treat symptoms, not a culture alone.
questions.strategy: Check whether the patient has any symptoms before treating a lab result.

questions.stem: A patient voids 40 mL every 30 minutes and is always damp. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Retention with overflow
options.rationale: Small frequent voids with constant dribbling suggest retention with overflow. The nurse scans before calling it incontinence.

options.text: Urge incontinence episodes
options.rationale: Near miss concept It looks like urge, but small frequent leaks with constant dampness suggest a bladder that never empties.

options.text: Normal frequent voiding
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Small frequent voids with constant dampness are not normal.

options.text: Stress incontinence episodes
options.rationale: Near miss concept Stress leaks happen with coughing or lifting, and the patient is dry at night.

questions.takeaway: Scan before you call it incontinence.
questions.strategy: When the amounts are small and constant, think of a full bladder spilling over.

questions.stem: A patient has continuous bladder irrigation. Over 8 hours, 3,000 mL of irrigant was instilled and the drainage bag held 3,850 mL. What is the true urine output?

options.rationale: Near miss concept The drainage includes the irrigant, which must be subtracted.
Near miss concept Adding the irrigant counts it twice.

options.text: 850 mL
options.rationale: During bladder irrigation, true urine output = total drainage minus the irrigant instilled: 3,850 minus 3,000 = 850 mL.
Near miss concept That is the irrigant, not the urine.

questions.takeaway: Subtract the irrigant.
questions.strategy: Remove what you put in before measuring what came out.

questions.stem: A nurse needs a urine culture from a patient with an indwelling catheter. Select all correct actions.

options.text: Unclamp the tubing after collecting the sample
options.rationale: Clamp below the port for about 15 minutes and never longer than 30, scrub the port and let it dry, aspirate with a sterile needleless syringe into a sterile cup and unclamp afterward. Never from the bag and never open the system.

options.text: Clamp the tubing below the sampling port for about 15 minutes
options.rationale: Clamp below the port for about 15 minutes and never longer than 30, scrub the port and let it dry, aspirate with a sterile needleless syringe into a sterile cup and unclamp afterward. Never from the bag and never open the system.

options.text: Scrub the port with antiseptic and let it dry
options.rationale: Clamp below the port for about 15 minutes and never longer than 30, scrub the port and let it dry, aspirate with a sterile needleless syringe into a sterile cup and unclamp afterward. Never from the bag and never open the system.

options.text: Pour urine from the drainage bag into a sterile cup
options.rationale: Near miss concept Urine in the bag is stale and growing bacteria.

options.text: Disconnect the catheter from the tubing to collect from the end
options.rationale: Near miss concept Opening the closed system raises the risk of infection.

options.text: Aspirate with a sterile needleless syringe
options.rationale: Clamp below the port for about 15 minutes and never longer than 30, scrub the port and let it dry, aspirate with a sterile needleless syringe into a sterile cup and unclamp afterward. Never from the bag and never open the system.

questions.takeaway: Unclamp after: the step people drop.
questions.strategy: Drop anything that opens the system or uses stale urine.

questions.stem: A patient drank 240 mL of juice, ate 120 mL of gelatin and had 200 mL of ice chips. What is the intake for this period?

options.text: 360 mL
options.rationale: Near miss concept Gelatin is liquid at room temperature and counts as intake.

options.text: 560 mL
options.rationale: Near miss concept Ice chips count as about half their volume, not the full amount.

options.text: 240 mL
options.rationale: Near miss concept Gelatin and ice chips are both recorded.

options.text: 460 mL
options.rationale: Intake includes everything liquid at room temperature, including gelatin. Ice chips count as about half their volume: 240 + 120 + 100 = 460 mL.

questions.takeaway: Ice chips count as half.
questions.strategy: List each item, apply the rule, then add.

questions.stem: A patient voids 250 mL. A bladder scan 10 minutes later shows 380 mL. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: The patient needs more oral fluids to flush the bladder.
options.rationale: Near miss concept More fluid adds to a bladder that is not emptying.

options.text: The bladder is not emptying fully; report the finding.
options.rationale: A postvoid residual is scanned within about 15 minutes of voiding. Below 100 mL is expected; a large residual means incomplete emptying.

options.text: The bladder emptied normally, with an expected residual.
options.rationale: Near miss concept A residual below 100 mL is expected. 380 mL is large.

options.text: The scan should be repeated tomorrow to confirm it.
options.rationale: Correct but premature A large residual needs reporting now.

questions.takeaway: A residual over 100 mL means incomplete emptying.
questions.strategy: Compare the residual with the threshold.

questions.stem: A 24 hour urine collection starts at 0700. The patient voids at 0700. What should the nurse do with that urine?

options.text: Refrigerate it until the end time.
options.rationale: Near miss concept It is discarded, not saved.

options.text: Send it as a separate sample.
options.rationale: Near miss concept It is not part of the collection.

options.text: Save it as the first sample.
options.rationale: Near miss concept That urine was made before the collection period.

options.text: Discard it and start the timing.
options.rationale: At the start time the patient voids and that urine is discarded; the clock starts then. Every void after is saved, and the last void at the end time is kept. A missed void means the test starts over.

questions.takeaway: Discard the first, keep the last.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the urine was made during the collection period.

questions.stem: A patient with stress incontinence asks what will help. Which instruction is best?

options.text: Limit fluids to 1 L a day to reduce leaking.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Limiting fluids concentrates the urine and irritates the bladder.

options.text: Use an indwelling catheter for continence.
options.rationale: Near miss concept A catheter adds CAUTI risk and does not treat the cause.

options.text: Do pelvic floor exercises daily for months.
options.rationale: Stress incontinence comes from a weak pelvic floor or sphincter. Kegel exercises and weight loss are the treatment.

options.text: Take oxybutynin to calm the bladder muscle.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Oxybutynin is for urge incontinence. No drug fixes stress incontinence.

questions.takeaway: Stress incontinence: Kegels.
questions.strategy: Match the fix to the cause.

questions.stem: A patient's urine is dark amber and the specific gravity is 1.034. What does this suggest?

options.text: A fluid deficit
options.rationale: Concentrated urine with a specific gravity above 1.030 points to a fluid deficit. The nurse assesses hydration and encourages fluids unless restricted.

options.text: A urinary tract infection
options.rationale: Near miss concept Infection is suggested by cloudy, foul urine, not concentration.

options.text: Normal kidney function
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A specific gravity above 1.030 shows concentrated urine.

options.text: Fluid overload
options.rationale: Near miss concept Overload produces dilute urine with a low specific gravity.

questions.takeaway: Dark, concentrated urine means dry.
questions.strategy: Think about what the kidneys do with water when the body is short.

questions.stem: A patient has not voided in 8 hours after surgery and has lower abdominal discomfort. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Push oral fluids and recheck
options.rationale: Near miss concept More urine into a bladder that will not empty worsens the problem.

options.text: Palpate and scan the bladder
options.rationale: For a patient who has not voided in 6 to 8 hours after surgery, the nurse palpates and scans. The scan avoids a catheter the patient may not need, which prevents a CAUTI.

options.text: Notify the provider right away
options.rationale: Correct but premature The nurse assesses before calling.

options.text: Insert a straight catheter now
options.rationale: Correct but premature A catheter is invasive. Data come first.

questions.takeaway: Scan before you catheterize.
questions.strategy: Reject invasive steps before assessment.

questions.stem: A patient 6 hours after abdominal surgery has hourly urine outputs of 60, 45, 28 and 22 mL. The heart rate is 114/min and the blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Document the outputs and recheck in an hour.
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting A falling output with a rising heart rate and low pressure is a circulation problem that needs action now.

options.text: Encourage oral fluids and recheck in 2 hours.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Oral fluids will not correct possible bleeding and delay reporting.

options.text: Insert a new catheter because the current one may be blocked.
options.rationale: Correct but premature Tubing is checked first, but the vital signs point to low perfusion, not a blocked catheter.

options.text: Assess for bleeding and notify the provider now.
options.rationale: Output below 30 mL an hour for 2 hours means low kidney perfusion. With tachycardia and a falling pressure after surgery, bleeding is the concern. The nurse checks the tubing, assesses and reports with SBAR.

questions.takeaway: A falling line is the finding.
questions.strategy: Read the trend and the vital signs together.

questions.stem: A patient with a new ileal conduit has a stoma that is dark purple. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Apply a tighter wafer.
options.rationale: Near miss concept A tight wafer could further reduce blood flow.

options.text: Clean it with soap and water.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cleaning does not address poor blood flow.

options.text: Document it as expected after surgery.
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting A healthy stoma is red and moist.

options.text: Report it to the provider immediately.
options.rationale: A healthy stoma is red and moist. A pale, dusky or black stoma means poor blood flow and is reported immediately.

questions.takeaway: Red and moist is healthy; dusky is an emergency.
questions.strategy: Ask what the color says about blood flow.

questions.stem: A patient's indwelling catheter has drained nothing in 2 hours. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Check the tubing for kinks or clots and the bag position.
options.rationale: A catheter with no drainage may be kinked, clotted or have the bag above the bladder. The tubing is checked first, then the patient is assessed.

options.text: Notify the provider that the patient has become anuric.
options.rationale: Correct but premature A kink or clot is a common, fixable cause that should be ruled out first.

options.text: Remove the catheter and insert a new one right away to restore drainage.
options.rationale: Correct but premature The tubing is checked before any invasive step.

options.text: Give a fluid bolus to increase the urine output.
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope A bolus needs an order and may not be the problem.

questions.takeaway: Check the tubing first, then the patient.
questions.strategy: Rule out the simple equipment problem before calling it a body problem.

questions.stem: A patient with benign prostatic hyperplasia started oxybutynin for urgency and now leaks all the time. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Increase the oxybutynin dose to control the urgency.
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope An anticholinergic weakens the bladder squeeze and can worsen retention.

options.text: Teach Kegel exercises to strengthen the pelvic floor muscles.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Kegels treat stress incontinence, not retention.

options.text: Scan the bladder for retention and report the finding.
options.rationale: Oxybutynin is an anticholinergic. In a patient with BPH it can cause retention with overflow. The nurse scans and reports.

options.text: Apply absorbent briefs and change them as needed.
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Briefs contain the leak but miss the retention.

questions.takeaway: Constant leaking on an anticholinergic can be overflow.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the new drug could stop the bladder from emptying.

questions.stem: A patient with dementia often wets the bed but voids normally when taken to the toilet. Select all appropriate interventions.

options.text: Oxybutynin
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nothing is wrong with the bladder, and anticholinergics cause confusion in older adults.

options.text: Scheduled toileting every 2 to 3 hours
options.rationale: Functional incontinence is an access problem. The fix removes barriers and schedules toileting every 2 to 3 hours, which keeps the patient independent.

options.text: A bedside commode
options.rationale: Functional incontinence is an access problem. The fix removes barriers and schedules toileting every 2 to 3 hours, which keeps the patient independent.

options.text: An indwelling catheter
options.rationale: Near miss concept A catheter adds CAUTI risk and incontinence alone is not an indication.

options.text: Clothing that is easy to remove
options.rationale: Functional incontinence is an access problem. The fix removes barriers and schedules toileting every 2 to 3 hours, which keeps the patient independent.

options.text: The call light within reach
options.rationale: Functional incontinence is an access problem. The fix removes barriers and schedules toileting every 2 to 3 hours, which keeps the patient independent.

questions.takeaway: Fix the cause: a toileting schedule comes before briefs or a catheter.
questions.strategy: Keep interventions that get the patient to the toilet.

questions.stem: A patient has not voided in 8 hours after surgery and reports lower abdominal discomfort. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Perform a bladder scan
Assess the time of the last void and the intake
Help the patient void with privacy and a normal position
Rescan, then insert a straight catheter by order or protocol if needed
Palpate above the symphysis pubis

questions.takeaway: The nurse gathers data, palpates, scans before any catheter, helps the patient void with privacy, running water and a normal position, then rescans and catheterizes only by order or protocol. Scan before any catheter.
questions.strategy: Least invasive first, and data before invasive steps.

questions.stem: An 84 year old patient tells the nurse, "I leak a little urine sometimes, but that is normal at my age." Which response is best?

options.text: "Leaking is not a normal part of aging; let us find the cause."
options.rationale: Aging brings a smaller bladder, nocturia and weaker sphincters, but incontinence is never normal. The nurse looks for the cause.

options.text: "You can wear briefs so the leaking does not bother you."
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Briefs contain the problem without finding the cause.

options.text: "Yes, it is common at your age, so there is nothing to worry about."
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Incontinence is never a normal part of aging.

options.text: "Drink less fluid during the day so that you leak less often."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Concentrated urine irritates the bladder and feeds bacteria.

questions.takeaway: Incontinence is never a normal part of aging.
questions.strategy: Reject any answer that reassures it is expected at that age.

questions.stem: A nurse observes assistive personnel caring for a patient with an indwelling catheter. Select all actions that need intervention.

options.text: Securing the catheter to the thigh
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Securing prevents tugging and trauma.

options.text: Hanging the bag on the bed frame below the bladder
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit This is the correct position.

options.text: Clamping the catheter while the patient walks
options.rationale: The bag hangs below the bladder and off the floor on the bed frame, the system stays closed and unclamped, and the catheter is secured. Clamping, raising the bag and placing it on the floor are classic errors.

options.text: Raising the bag above the bladder to move the patient
options.rationale: The bag hangs below the bladder and off the floor on the bed frame, the system stays closed and unclamped, and the catheter is secured. Clamping, raising the bag and placing it on the floor are classic errors.

options.text: Laying the bag on the floor to prevent kinks
options.rationale: The bag hangs below the bladder and off the floor on the bed frame, the system stays closed and unclamped, and the catheter is secured. Clamping, raising the bag and placing it on the floor are classic errors.

options.text: Cleansing the perineum from the meatus outward with soap and water
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit This is correct daily perineal care.

questions.takeaway: Below the bladder, off the floor, never clamped.
questions.strategy: For each action, ask whether urine could flow back or the system could be contaminated.

questions.stem: Select all of the measures that reduce sensory deprivation for a patient on prolonged bed rest in a private room.

options.text: Encourage family visits, familiar objects and preferred music or radio
options.rationale: The first fix is always the device she already owns, because a patient without her glasses is sensory deprived for no reason at all. Light, a clock, orientation and meaningful contact give her input she can organize. A permanently dim quiet room is deprivation, and a television left running is overload that becomes noise rather than stimulation.

options.text: Keep the room quiet and dim at all times so she can rest
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Comfortable sounding and the definition of a deprived environment.

options.text: Orient her to day, time and plan at each interaction
options.rationale: The first fix is always the device she already owns, because a patient without her glasses is sensory deprived for no reason at all. Light, a clock, orientation and meaningful contact give her input she can organize. A permanently dim quiet room is deprivation, and a television left running is overload that becomes noise rather than stimulation.

options.text: Make sure glasses and hearing aids are in place and working
options.rationale: The first fix is always the device she already owns, because a patient without her glasses is sensory deprived for no reason at all. Light, a clock, orientation and meaningful contact give her input she can organize. A permanently dim quiet room is deprivation, and a television left running is overload that becomes noise rather than stimulation.

options.text: Leave the television on continuously for stimulation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Continuous unselected noise is overload, not meaningful input.

options.text: Open the blinds and keep a clock and calendar in view
options.rationale: The first fix is always the device she already owns, because a patient without her glasses is sensory deprived for no reason at all. Light, a clock, orientation and meaningful contact give her input she can organize. A permanently dim quiet room is deprivation, and a television left running is overload that becomes noise rather than stimulation.

questions.takeaway: Check the glasses and hearing aids first. That is the deprivation you can fix in a minute.
questions.strategy: One wrong option deprives her further and the other overloads her, which is the same error at both ends.

questions.stem: Select all of the factors that can impair a hospitalized patient's sensory function.

options.text: Opioids and psychotropic medications
options.rationale: Drugs blunt perception, isolation removes meaningful stimuli, chronic disease damages the receptors themselves, and relentless noise produces overload. The last two options are protective: assistive devices restore reception, and meaningful stimuli are the specific antidote to deprivation.

options.text: Diabetes and hypertension
options.rationale: Drugs blunt perception, isolation removes meaningful stimuli, chronic disease damages the receptors themselves, and relentless noise produces overload. The last two options are protective: assistive devices restore reception, and meaningful stimuli are the specific antidote to deprivation.

options.text: Absence of visitors and social interaction
options.rationale: Drugs blunt perception, isolation removes meaningful stimuli, chronic disease damages the receptors themselves, and relentless noise produces overload. The last two options are protective: assistive devices restore reception, and meaningful stimuli are the specific antidote to deprivation.

options.text: Having eyeglasses and hearing aids available at the bedside
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Protective. The common failure is that they are locked in a drawer.

options.text: A clock, a window and family photographs in the room
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Meaningful stimuli, which prevent deprivation rather than cause it.

options.text: Continuous environmental noise and frequent monitoring
options.rationale: Drugs blunt perception, isolation removes meaningful stimuli, chronic disease damages the receptors themselves, and relentless noise produces overload. The last two options are protective: assistive devices restore reception, and meaningful stimuli are the specific antidote to deprivation.

questions.takeaway: Both too little and too much input cause the same confusion. Check which one you have.
questions.strategy: Two options are interventions you would add, not problems you would find.

questions.stem: A nurse enters the room of a patient who is blind. Which approach is correct?

options.text: Touch the patient's arm first so that he knows someone has entered the room
options.rationale: Near miss concept Being touched by an unannounced stranger is startling. Speak first, then touch.

options.text: Keep explanations brief, since room descriptions may overwhelm him
options.rationale: Near miss concept Detail is what replaces the view.

options.text: Speak more loudly, since the patient relies mainly on his hearing
options.rationale: Near miss concept A common and insulting reflex. His hearing is fine.

options.text: Speak normally, say who you are, and describe what you will do
options.rationale: Blindness is not deafness, so the volume stays the same. Announce yourself, because a patient who cannot see does not know who walked in. Describe in detail, including the room and where things are, and allow touch to fill in what words cannot.

questions.takeaway: Say your name on the way in and narrate what your hands are doing.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options treat vision loss as if it were a hearing or cognitive problem.

questions.stem: Which medication class should prompt the nurse to monitor for hearing changes?

options.text: Proton pump inhibitors
options.rationale: Near miss concept Not on the ototoxic list.

options.text: Aminoglycoside antibiotics
options.rationale: The ototoxic list worth memorizing: aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, high dose aspirin and other NSAIDs, quinine based drugs, and several chemotherapy agents. The damage is to the inner ear or cranial nerve VIII, which makes it sensorineural and often permanent, so the point of monitoring is to catch it before it is fixed.

options.text: Antihistamines
options.rationale: Near miss concept They can cause sedation and dizziness, not cochlear damage.

options.text: Beta lactam antibiotics
options.rationale: Near miss concept Penicillins and cephalosporins are not ototoxic; the aminoglycosides are the antibiotic class that is.

questions.takeaway: Ototoxic damage is usually permanent. Monitoring exists to stop the drug, not to reverse it.
questions.strategy: Tinnitus is often the first warning, which is why a new ringing on one of these drugs gets reported rather than noted.

questions.stem: Select all of the home modifications the nurse should recommend for a patient with low vision.

options.text: Paint stair edges a bright contrasting color
options.rationale: Low vision is managed with contrast, consistency and clear paths. Glare is as disabling as dimness, which is why warm incandescent light beats fluorescent. The aging eye needs more light and sharper contrast, and it adapts to darkness slowly.

options.text: Use warm incandescent lighting and reduce glare
options.rationale: Low vision is managed with contrast, consistency and clear paths. Glare is as disabling as dimness, which is why warm incandescent light beats fluorescent. The aging eye needs more light and sharper contrast, and it adapts to darkness slowly.

options.text: Rearrange furniture periodically to keep the patient engaged
options.rationale: Near miss concept Removes the mental map the patient navigates by.

options.text: Keep objects in consistent, predictable locations
options.rationale: Low vision is managed with contrast, consistency and clear paths. Glare is as disabling as dimness, which is why warm incandescent light beats fluorescent. The aging eye needs more light and sharper contrast, and it adapts to darkness slowly.

options.text: Remove throw rugs and keep pathways clear
options.rationale: Low vision is managed with contrast, consistency and clear paths. Glare is as disabling as dimness, which is why warm incandescent light beats fluorescent. The aging eye needs more light and sharper contrast, and it adapts to darkness slowly.

options.text: Switch to bright fluorescent lighting throughout the house
options.rationale: Near miss concept More light, and the glare it throws cancels the benefit.

questions.takeaway: Contrast and consistency. A room they know by heart is a room they can cross safely.
questions.strategy: The two wrong options both change something the patient relies on staying the same.

questions.stem: Classify each breakdown by where in the sensory process it occurs.

rows.text: A patient understands the fire alarm and cannot move to leave
Diabetic neuropathy stops the foot from registering a pebble in the shoe
Cerumen blocks the ear canal so sound never reaches the eardrum
A sedated patient hears the alarm but cannot make sense of it

questions.takeaway: Reception is the receptor picking up the stimulus. Perception is the brain making sense of it, which depends on the cortex and on level of consciousness. Reaction is the response. Knowing which step broke tells you what to fix: clear the canal, treat the sedation, or change the environment. Three steps, three different interventions. Find the broken one before you act.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the signal arrived, whether it was understood, and whether the patient could act on it.

questions.stem: A patient after a stroke cannot produce speech reliably. Which communication strategy is most appropriate?

options.text: Direct the questions to the family member sitting at the bedside instead
options.rationale: Near miss concept Excludes the patient from decisions about himself.

options.text: Speak loudly and slowly, since comprehension is impaired
options.rationale: Near miss concept In expressive aphasia comprehension is relatively preserved, so volume is irrelevant. Speaking slowly and simply helps; speaking loudly does not.

options.text: Finish his sentences so the conversation keeps moving
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Efficient and it tells him he is a delay.

options.text: Use yes or no questions, a picture board, and extra time
options.rationale: Closed questions let him answer with what he still has, and a board gives him a route around the words. Time is the kindest thing you can offer, because finishing his sentences tells him he is too slow to be worth waiting for. Volume does not help a language problem, and talking to the family instead removes him from his own care.

questions.takeaway: Give him time and a route around the words. Do not finish his sentences.
questions.strategy: Two options take the conversation away from the patient.

questions.stem: A patient has been in a single room on contact precautions for six days with no visitors. He is bored, flat in affect and increasingly disoriented to day and time. What is happening?

options.text: Sensory deprivation, from insufficient meaningful stimulation
options.rationale: Isolation, bedrest and restricted environments strip out the stimuli that keep a person oriented. The effects run cognitive (confusion, poor problem solving, disorientation), affective (boredom, anxiety, depression, emotional lability) and perceptual. The fix is meaningful stimulation: a clock, family photos, music, conversation, a window.

options.text: Sensory overload, from the constant noise of the unit
options.rationale: Near miss concept Overload looks similar and belongs to the ICU, the ER and constant monitoring, not a silent isolation room.

options.text: Expected adjustment to an unfamiliar environment
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Six days of worsening disorientation is not adjustment.

options.text: Sensory deficit, from an unrecognized hearing loss
options.rationale: Near miss concept A deficit is a loss of reception or perception itself, and nothing here points to one.

questions.takeaway: A quiet isolation room is not restful. It is a slow cognitive injury.
questions.strategy: Deprivation and overload both end in confusion and restlessness. The setting tells you which one you have.

questions.stem: An older adult with peripheral neuropathy, cataracts and vestibular dysfunction is being discharged home. Which teaching point addresses the greatest risk?

options.text: Taking vitamin B supplements to support nerve health at home
options.rationale: Near miss concept Relevant only in a specific deficiency and it changes nothing about tonight.

options.text: Night lights to the bathroom and a light switch reachable from bed
options.rationale: She has lost three of the systems that keep a person upright: position sense from the feet, vision, and the vestibular apparatus. In daylight, vision compensates for the other two. At night she has none of them, and the bathroom trip is where older adults fall. Lighting the route restores the one system that can compensate at the moment she needs it most.

options.text: Using a cane only when leaving the house for errands or visits
options.rationale: Near miss concept Most falls happen at home, which is where she is not using it.

options.text: Doing seated balance exercises twice a week with a family member
options.rationale: Near miss concept Genuinely useful over months, and not the greatest immediate risk.

questions.takeaway: When proprioception and balance are gone, vision is the backup. At night she has no backup.
questions.strategy: Balance exercises and a cane both help; neither helps at 0300 in the dark.

questions.topic: sensory deficit and safety at home
questions.stem: A nurse is assessing an older adult with peripheral neuropathy from diabetes. Which teaching point is most important?
questions.objective: sensory deficit and safety at home

options.text: Wear supportive, well fitting shoes whenever leaving the house
options.rationale: Near miss concept Partly right and the injuries usually happen barefoot indoors.

options.text: Report any numbness to the provider at the next scheduled visit
options.rationale: Correct but premature The numbness is established; the risk now is the injury he will not feel.

options.text: Keep the feet elevated on a stool whenever sitting for long
options.rationale: Near miss concept Addresses edema, not protective sensation.

options.text: Inspect the feet daily and test bath water with a thermometer
options.rationale: Loss of protective sensation means the patient will not feel a burn, a blister or a stone in the shoe. Vision substitutes for the missing sensation, which is why daily inspection is the intervention, and a body part that still has sensation substitutes for the testing. Scald burns in neuropathic feet are common and preventable.

questions.takeaway: When sensation is gone, the eyes have to do its job.
questions.strategy: Shoes outdoors only leaves the home injuries, which is where most of them happen.

questions.stem: A patient has been on contact precautions in a private room for five days. Select all of the nursing measures that address sensory deprivation.

options.text: Stay to talk for a few minutes rather than only entering for tasks
options.rationale: Deprivation is a shortage of meaningful stimulation, so the answer is meaning, not volume. Orientation cues, human contact, and a light cycle that tells the body what time it is. Clustering care so thoroughly that the patient sees one person per shift makes it worse, and a television running all day is noise rather than interaction.

options.text: Open the blinds during the day and dim lights at night
options.rationale: Deprivation is a shortage of meaningful stimulation, so the answer is meaning, not volume. Orientation cues, human contact, and a light cycle that tells the body what time it is. Clustering care so thoroughly that the patient sees one person per shift makes it worse, and a television running all day is noise rather than interaction.

options.text: Make sure a clock and a calendar are visible
options.rationale: Deprivation is a shortage of meaningful stimulation, so the answer is meaning, not volume. Orientation cues, human contact, and a light cycle that tells the body what time it is. Clustering care so thoroughly that the patient sees one person per shift makes it worse, and a television running all day is noise rather than interaction.

options.text: Keep the television on continuously for background noise
options.rationale: Near miss concept Adds noise without adding meaning or interaction.

options.text: Encourage family to visit or call on a schedule
options.rationale: Deprivation is a shortage of meaningful stimulation, so the answer is meaning, not volume. Orientation cues, human contact, and a light cycle that tells the body what time it is. Clustering care so thoroughly that the patient sees one person per shift makes it worse, and a television running all day is noise rather than interaction.

options.text: Cluster all care into one visit per shift to reduce interruptions
options.rationale: Near miss concept The right intervention for sensory overload, applied to its opposite.

questions.takeaway: Meaningful is the operative word. A television is stimulation with nothing in it.
questions.strategy: Clustering care is correct for overload and wrong for deprivation, which is why you have to know which one you are treating.

questions.stem: A 52 year old with no vision complaints asks how often she needs eye examinations. What should the nurse tell her?

options.text: Regular comprehensive exams, more often with age or diabetes
options.rationale: For an asymptomatic adult with no risk factors the American Academy of Ophthalmology suggests every 2 to 4 years from 40 to 54, every 1 to 3 years from 55 to 64, and every 1 to 2 years after 65. The diseases that take vision are silent early. Open angle glaucoma destroys peripheral vision for years before anyone notices, and diabetic retinopathy does the same. Screening frequency rises with age, and waiting for symptoms means waiting until something is already lost.

options.text: Only when she notices a change in how well she sees
options.rationale: Near miss concept Glaucoma and retinopathy are asymptomatic until late.

options.text: Every five years until she reaches the age of 65
options.rationale: Near miss concept Longer than any recommended interval for an adult over 40.

options.text: Only once she begins to need glasses for reading
options.rationale: Near miss concept Presbyopia is unrelated to the diseases screening is looking for.

questions.takeaway: Waiting for a symptom means waiting until vision is already gone.
questions.strategy: Any option that makes screening contingent on symptoms misses the point of screening.

questions.stem: A patient who works at a computer all day reports tired, dry, aching eyes. What should the nurse teach?

options.text: Raise the screen brightness by 20 percent to reduce strain
options.rationale: Near miss concept Not part of the rule, and extra brightness often adds glare.

options.text: Every 20 minutes, look 20 feet away for 20 seconds
options.rationale: Digital eyestrain comes from holding one focal distance and blinking less. Looking 20 feet away relaxes the ciliary muscle that has been holding the lens, and the pause restores the blink. Closing the eyes rests them without changing the focal distance, which is why it helps less.

options.text: Every 20 minutes, close both eyes for 20 seconds
options.rationale: Near miss concept Helps the dryness and does nothing for the sustained near focus.

options.text: Take a 20 minute screen break once every 2 hours
options.rationale: Near miss concept Right idea at the wrong interval; the strain builds within minutes.

questions.takeaway: The distance is the point. It is not a rest break, it is a focus change.
questions.strategy: Two options give the eyes a rest without ever changing what they are focused on.

questions.stem: An 84 year old has macular degeneration and moderate presbycusis. Select all of the measures that support safe, effective communication and care.

options.text: Face her directly in good light and speak clearly at a lower pitch
options.rationale: Two deficits together mean neither channel can carry the whole message, so you use both and verify each. The difference between the two written options is the word primarily. Large high contrast print that you watch her read is a legitimate reinforcement of what you said out loud; making print the main channel fails, because macular degeneration takes central vision and that is reading vision. Shouting raises the pitch into the range presbycusis has already taken and distorts the face she is reading.

options.text: Confirm she has her glasses and hearing aids in place before teaching
options.rationale: Two deficits together mean neither channel can carry the whole message, so you use both and verify each. The difference between the two written options is the word primarily. Large high contrast print that you watch her read is a legitimate reinforcement of what you said out loud; making print the main channel fails, because macular degeneration takes central vision and that is reading vision. Shouting raises the pitch into the range presbycusis has already taken and distorts the face she is reading.

options.text: Provide written material in large high contrast print and verify she can read it
options.rationale: Two deficits together mean neither channel can carry the whole message, so you use both and verify each. The difference between the two written options is the word primarily. Large high contrast print that you watch her read is a legitimate reinforcement of what you said out loud; making print the main channel fails, because macular degeneration takes central vision and that is reading vision. Shouting raises the pitch into the range presbycusis has already taken and distorts the face she is reading.

options.text: Rely primarily on written instructions, since her hearing is impaired
options.rationale: Near miss concept Print is a reinforcement, not a substitute; central vision is the vision she has lost.

options.text: Describe the room layout and keep objects in consistent locations
options.rationale: Two deficits together mean neither channel can carry the whole message, so you use both and verify each. The difference between the two written options is the word primarily. Large high contrast print that you watch her read is a legitimate reinforcement of what you said out loud; making print the main channel fails, because macular degeneration takes central vision and that is reading vision. Shouting raises the pitch into the range presbycusis has already taken and distorts the face she is reading.

options.text: Speak louder to compensate for both deficits
options.rationale: Near miss concept Raises pitch into the lost frequencies and distorts lip reading.

questions.takeaway: Print reinforces the spoken teaching. It cannot replace it when central vision is gone.
questions.strategy: Two options here look alike. The one that fails is the one that makes print the primary channel.

questions.stem: Classify each situation by the type of sensory alteration it describes.

rows.text: Cataracts blur the image before it reaches the retina
Strict bed rest in a bare room with no window, clock or visitors
Alarms, overhead pages and hourly checks in a hallway bed in the emergency department
Constant chronic pain that leaves no attention for anything else
Presbycusis that muffles high pitched voices

questions.takeaway: Sensory deficit means the sense organ or pathway itself has lost function, so less is received or perceived. Cataracts and presbycusis both damage the equipment: the lens clouds, the cochlear nerve degenerates. Sensory deprivation means the senses may work but there is too little meaningful stimulation. Bed rest in a bare room with no window, clock or visitors is the classic setting. Sensory overload means more stimulation than the brain can filter. A loud, busy emergency department bed and constant chronic pain both flood the brain, so it cannot respond to anything meaningfully. Ask one question of each row: is the equipment broken (deficit), is there too little input (deprivation), or too much input (overload)? Deficit is broken equipment. Deprivation is too little input. Overload is too much input.
questions.strategy: Chronic pain is the row that fools students: it is internal, but it is still excess stimulation, so it is overload. The detail that rules out deficit for the bed rest row is that nothing about the senses is damaged.

questions.stem: A patient with new hearing loss has stopped going to a weekly card group. The patient says, "I can't follow the talk at the table, so I just stay home now." In a quiet room with the nurse, the patient speaks clearly and answers every question correctly. Which nursing diagnosis fits best?

options.text: Impaired verbal communication
options.rationale: Near miss concept Impaired verbal communication means trouble sending or receiving messages in the moment. This patient communicates well one to one; the problem is the withdrawal from groups.

options.text: Risk for injury
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Risk for injury fits sensory loss in general, but nothing in this stem describes a hazard. The cue is a lost social activity.

options.text: Impaired socialization
options.rationale: Impaired socialization means a person takes part in social interaction less than needed or wanted. The test question is: has the person pulled back from relationships or activities? Here the patient stopped a valued group because conversation in noise is hard. Impaired verbal communication would need a breakdown in the actual exchange, and the stem shows the opposite in a quiet room. Risk for injury and impaired mobility are both common with sensory loss, but neither is supported by a single cue in this stem.

options.text: Impaired mobility
options.rationale: Near miss concept Impaired mobility means physical difficulty moving. The patient can go to the group and chooses not to.

questions.takeaway: When sensory loss makes a patient stop doing social things, the diagnosis is impaired socialization.
questions.strategy: The detail that rules out impaired verbal communication is that the patient speaks clearly and answers correctly one to one. The problem lives in the withdrawal, not the conversation.

questions.topic: age as a factor in sensory function
questions.stem: A nurse is planning fall prevention teaching for adults of different ages. Which statement about age and sensory function is accurate?
questions.objective: age as a factor in sensory function

options.text: Vision and hearing change from the forties; proprioception after sixty
options.rationale: Normal aging changes vision and hearing from the forties onward, which is why reading glasses appear in that decade. Proprioception, the sense of where the body is in space, changes later, after sixty. That later change matters for fall risk because the person can no longer rely on body position sense to correct a stumble. The option about retirement age is too late. The proprioception first option reverses the order. The vision stays stable option ignores normal lens changes.

options.text: Sensory changes do not begin until after retirement age in healthy adults
options.rationale: Absolute language Visual and hearing changes start decades before retirement, so waiting until then misses them.

options.text: Proprioception declines first, in the forties, before vision or hearing
options.rationale: Near miss concept It reverses the timeline. Position sense is the later change, after sixty.

options.text: Hearing declines with age, but vision stays stable unless disease develops
options.rationale: Near miss concept Vision changes with normal aging too, starting in the forties with presbyopia.

questions.takeaway: Eyes and ears change from the forties; position sense changes after sixty.
questions.strategy: Pin each sense to its decade. The detail that rules out the proprioception first option is the order: position sense changes last, not first.

questions.stem: A patient in the intensive care unit for five days is pulling at his lines, has a reversed sleep pattern, and is disoriented to day and place. Temperature 37.1, saturation 96 percent, glucose 104, sodium 138. What should the nurse address first?

options.text: Accept this as an expected consequence of critical illness
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Common does not mean acceptable; it is largely preventable.

options.text: Request an antipsychotic to control the agitated behavior
options.rationale: Correct but premature Chemical restraint for a problem the environment is causing.

options.text: Cut stimuli, protect sleep, restore orientation, look for causes
options.rationale: This is hyperactive delirium. The normal values rule out the fast reversible precipitants, hypoxia, hypoglycemia, sodium and fever, but they do not rule out delirium itself, which is what pulling at lines with a reversed sleep cycle on day five is. What is left driving it is the environment: constant noise, light and interruption, which is sensory overload layered on sleep deprivation.
