That is why the non pharmacologic bundle outranks a drug or a mitt. Reduce input, cluster care to protect blocks of sleep, restore a clock and daylight, and keep looking for other causes while you do it.

options.text: Apply soft mitts so that he cannot pull out his lines
options.rationale: Correct but premature A restraint before the alternative has been tried.

questions.takeaway: Normal labs do not rule out delirium. They rule out the precipitants you can fix in a minute.
questions.strategy: The stem hands you four normal values so you will conclude nothing is wrong. Delirium is the diagnosis; the labs only tell you what is not causing it.

questions.stem: A patient in the intensive care unit is restless, has racing thoughts and keeps picking at his dressings and lines. Vital signs are stable and oxygen saturation is 97 percent. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Apply soft mitts to protect the lines while the restlessness continues
options.rationale: Correct but premature A restraint applied before the alternative has been tried.

options.text: Request an order for a sedative to settle him
options.rationale: Correct but premature Chemical restraint for an environmental problem.

options.text: Cluster care, reduce noise and alarms, and schedule uninterrupted rest periods
options.rationale: Picking at tubes and dressings is a classic behavioral sign of sensory overload, and the vital signs here rule out the hypoxia you would check first. The intervention is to turn the input down: combine activities, silence what does not need to sound, institute quiet time.

options.text: Increase the frequency of reorientation to every 15 minutes
options.rationale: Near miss concept Adds stimulation to a brain already receiving too much.

questions.takeaway: When the brain cannot filter any more input, the answer is less input.
questions.strategy: Reaching for restraint or sedation before you have reduced the stimulus is treating the symptom you created.

questions.stem: An older adult admitted overnight seems confused during the morning assessment. Her hearing aids are in the bedside drawer. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Speak more loudly and simplify the questions
options.rationale: Near miss concept Compensates for the deficit instead of correcting it, and shouting distorts.

options.text: Put the hearing aids in and reassess
options.rationale: A patient who cannot hear the questions looks confused. Devices come out at night and nobody puts them back, and the chart then says confused. Restoring reception costs thirty seconds and prevents a cascade of workups, labels and sometimes restraints.

options.text: Request a cognitive screening evaluation
options.rationale: Correct but premature Screens a patient who cannot hear the screening questions.

options.text: Document new onset confusion and notify the provider
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Charts a finding produced by a missing device.

questions.takeaway: Before you call it confusion, give her the glasses and the hearing aids.
questions.strategy: Three options proceed with an assessment the patient cannot participate in.

questions.topic: communication when the patient cannot speak
questions.stem: A patient is intubated, awake and alert, and becoming visibly distressed when staff cannot understand him. What should the nurse do?
questions.objective: communication when the patient cannot speak

options.text: Set up a letter board or yes and no signals and share what works
options.rationale: He is alert and has things to say, and losing the ability to communicate is one of the most distressing parts of intubation, consistently reported afterward. A board, an agreed signal and a note in the record so every shift uses the same method gives him back some control. Sedating a man because we cannot understand him solves our problem with his distress.

options.text: Request sedation from the provider to reduce his distress
options.rationale: Near miss concept Treats our difficulty by removing his awareness.

options.text: Ask closed questions only and move on quickly to limit frustration
options.rationale: Near miss concept Closed questions help; leaving quickly means he never finishes.

options.text: Reassure him that the tube will come out soon and he can talk then
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic False reassurance, and it leaves him unable to say anything in the meantime.

questions.takeaway: Write down what works, so he does not have to reestablish it with every nurse.
questions.strategy: Sedation for a communication failure is the subtlest form of chemical restraint.

questions.stem: An 80 year old who reads the newspaper daily tells the nurse that over the past two days a gray curtain has moved across part of her vision in one eye. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Document it as an expected age related visual change
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Presbyopia and poor dark adaptation come on over years, not two days.

options.text: Schedule a routine eye examination within the next month
options.rationale: Correct but premature A month from now the retina is not salvageable.

options.text: Treat this as an emergency and notify the provider immediately
options.rationale: Sudden is never age related. A curtain across the visual field, with or without flashes and floaters, is retinal detachment until proven otherwise, and the window to reattach it is short. Her baseline matters: a woman who reads the paper every day has just lost function she had on Friday.

options.text: Reassure her and recheck her vision at the next visit
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Reassurance offered in place of the referral that saves the eye.

questions.takeaway: Gradual change gets a referral. Sudden change gets a phone call.
questions.strategy: Three options all treat a two day change as if it were a two year change.

questions.stem: A patient with longstanding bilateral hearing loss suddenly cannot hear at all in the right ear, with the loss developing over about a day. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Document the change and report it at the next provider round
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting The treatment window is measured in days and starts now.

options.text: Reassure the patient that hearing loss commonly progresses with age
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Progression is gradual; one day is not progression.

options.text: Check for cerumen impaction and arrange irrigation
options.rationale: Correct but premature Worth checking and not instead of escalating a sudden sensorineural loss.

options.text: Escalate urgently, because sudden sensorineural hearing loss is time sensitive
options.rationale: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is an emergency, and treatment started early has a far better chance of recovering hearing than treatment started a week later. The patient's existing gradual loss is a distraction: sudden is never explained by the chronic condition. Checking the canal is reasonable and does not come at the cost of the escalation.

questions.takeaway: Sudden is never age related and never explained by the chronic version of the same problem.
questions.strategy: Chronic deficits make new ones easy to miss, which is exactly why this is tested.

questions.stem: A patient who speaks only Mandarin is admitted for surgery tomorrow. An adult daughter who speaks English well is at the bedside and offers to translate the consent discussion and the preoperative teaching. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Accept the daughter's offer, since she knows the patient best and is already present
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Convenient and warm, and family members filter, soften or omit what they translate.

options.text: Ask a bilingual housekeeper who speaks Mandarin to translate during the break
options.rationale: Near miss concept Speaks the language and is not a qualified interpreter.

options.text: Arrange a qualified medical interpreter for the consent discussion and the teaching
options.rationale: A language barrier is a sensory and communication deficit the nurse corrects the same way as any other: with the right tool. For consent and teaching that tool is a qualified interpreter, not family. A relative may change the message, leave out frightening details, or answer for the patient, and the patient may not ask what matters in front of family. Being bilingual is not the same as being trained to interpret medical content.

options.text: Give the teaching in English with pictures and have the daughter explain anything unclear later
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pictures support teaching; they do not replace a language the patient understands, and it still routes the content through family.

questions.takeaway: Language barrier: qualified interpreter, not family, every time it matters.
questions.strategy: Two options use someone who speaks the language. Only one of them is qualified to interpret.

questions.topic: new confusion: rule out physiologic causes first
questions.stem: An 82 year old admitted two days ago for pneumonia was oriented and chatting this morning. At 1500 the patient is restless, disoriented to place and pulling at the oxygen cannula. Glasses and hearing aids are in place. What should the nurse do first?
questions.objective: new confusion: rule out physiologic causes first

options.text: Check oxygen saturation, blood glucose and vital signs
options.rationale: New confusion is a symptom to explain. In a patient with pneumonia who is pulling at the oxygen, hypoxia is the first thing to rule out, followed by glucose and vital signs. The sensory causes come after those, and the devices are already in, so the stem has removed the easiest sensory fix. Reorientation is a good intervention for deprivation, and doing it first would comfort a patient whose oxygen level may be falling.

options.text: Reorient the patient and add a clock and calendar to the room
options.rationale: Correct but premature A sensory measure for a cause not yet established; hypoxia has to be ruled out first.

options.text: Document the change as expected confusion in an older adult in a new environment
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A sudden change in a patient who was oriented this morning is never assumed to be aging.

options.text: Request an order for a sedative so the cannula stays in
options.rationale: Correct but premature Sedation hides the cause and can worsen hypoxia; it is never the first answer to new confusion.

questions.takeaway: New confusion: oxygen, glucose and vital signs before any sensory explanation.
questions.strategy: The stem tells you the glasses and hearing aids are in. That is the cue to look for a physiologic cause rather than a sensory one.

questions.stem: A patient builds furniture in a home workshop several hours a day using table saws and sanders. The patient wears contact lenses and has had no eye or hearing exams in years. Select all of the teaching the nurse should include.

options.text: Wear safety glasses or goggles whenever the saws or sanders are running
options.rationale: Occupational safety means protecting the eyes and ears from the hazards of the job. Saws throw chips, so the eyes need protection, and power tools are loud, so the ears need protection; prolonged noise is a major preventable cause of hearing loss. Proper contact lens care is a preventive behavior because poor lens habits are a route to corneal injury and infection. Regular screening is how the nurse's role of detection works. Earbud music feels like it blocks noise, but it adds sound on top of the saw. Waiting for symptoms defeats the point of screening.

options.text: Wear ear protection while operating the power tools
options.rationale: Occupational safety means protecting the eyes and ears from the hazards of the job. Saws throw chips, so the eyes need protection, and power tools are loud, so the ears need protection; prolonged noise is a major preventable cause of hearing loss. Proper contact lens care is a preventive behavior because poor lens habits are a route to corneal injury and infection. Regular screening is how the nurse's role of detection works. Earbud music feels like it blocks noise, but it adds sound on top of the saw. Waiting for symptoms defeats the point of screening.

options.text: Play music through earbuds to mask the noise of the saw
options.rationale: Near miss concept Masking noise with earbud music adds more sound energy to the ear. It is another noise exposure, not protection.

options.text: Follow the contact lens care routine exactly as taught
options.rationale: Occupational safety means protecting the eyes and ears from the hazards of the job. Saws throw chips, so the eyes need protection, and power tools are loud, so the ears need protection; prolonged noise is a major preventable cause of hearing loss. Proper contact lens care is a preventive behavior because poor lens habits are a route to corneal injury and infection. Regular screening is how the nurse's role of detection works. Earbud music feels like it blocks noise, but it adds sound on top of the saw. Waiting for symptoms defeats the point of screening.

options.text: Wait until hearing seems worse before booking a hearing test
options.rationale: Correct but premature Waiting for a change means detection comes after damage. Screening exists to find loss before the patient notices it.

options.text: Keep regular eye and hearing screening appointments
options.rationale: Occupational safety means protecting the eyes and ears from the hazards of the job. Saws throw chips, so the eyes need protection, and power tools are loud, so the ears need protection; prolonged noise is a major preventable cause of hearing loss. Proper contact lens care is a preventive behavior because poor lens habits are a route to corneal injury and infection. Regular screening is how the nurse's role of detection works. Earbud music feels like it blocks noise, but it adds sound on top of the saw. Waiting for symptoms defeats the point of screening.

questions.takeaway: Protect, maintain and screen: eye and ear protection, lens care, and exams before symptoms.
questions.strategy: Each keyed option matches one hazard in the stem: flying chips, noise, contact lenses, no recent exams. The detail that rules out the earbud option is that it adds sound instead of blocking it.

questions.topic: acute care for a patient with known deficits
questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.objective: acute care for a patient with known deficits
questions.sentence: A patient with low vision and moderate hearing loss is admitted from the emergency department to a shared room at 0200. On arrival, the nurse first finds out [[1]], because later changes cannot be judged without it. The nurse then [[2]]. To limit overload during the night, the nurse [[3]]. To prevent injury, the nurse [[4]].

options.text: which deficits the patient already had at home
the patient's usual bedtime routine
whether the patient feels anxious about the room
when family plans to visit
orients the patient to the room, bathroom and call bell and keeps items in fixed places
rearranges the bedside table each shift to fit the care being given
waits until morning to orient the patient so sleep is not lost
places a sign on the door that lists the patient's deficits
clusters care so the patient gets unbroken periods of rest
performs a full check every 15 minutes overnight
leaves the television on low for company
keeps the overhead light on so the patient can see
keeps the call bell in reach and positions the bed and chair safely
applies a vest restraint for the first night
closes the door to keep out hallway noise
asks the roommate to call for help if needed

questions.takeaway: [1] Baseline: the acute care plan starts with knowing whether a deficit already exists. Without the baseline, a new change cannot be told apart from an old one. Bedtime habits and anxiety matter, but they do not let the nurse judge later findings. [2] Orientation: a complete orientation to the room, bathroom and call bell, with objects kept in the same places, lets the patient move safely by memory. Rearranging items each shift undoes the orientation. Waiting until morning leaves the patient unoriented on the first night, when falls are most likely. [3] Controlling stimuli: clustering care and protecting rest reduces overload. Full checks every 15 minutes and a constant television add stimulation in a setting that already has too much. [4] Safety: the call bell in reach and safe bed and chair positioning prevent injury while the patient adapts. A restraint is never the first step, and a closed door reduces how often staff see the patient. Know the baseline, orient completely, cut the noise, and keep the call bell in reach.
questions.strategy: The trap in each blank is a kind act at the wrong moment, such as letting the patient sleep before orientation. The detail that rules out waiting until morning in blank 2 is the 0200 arrival: the first night in a strange room is when an unoriented patient falls.

questions.stem: A patient with new vision loss in both eyes from diabetes lives alone in a two story house. This week the patient missed a step twice on the stairs and caught the handrail each time. The patient now avoids going out and says, "I'm scared of what's happening to me." Which nursing diagnosis is the priority?

options.text: Fear related to loss of vision
options.rationale: Most dramatic finding The fear is real and stated, but it does not threaten physical safety today. It comes after the fall risk is addressed.

options.text: Impaired socialization
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Avoiding going out is a real change, but loneliness is not the immediate threat. Two near falls on the stairs are.

options.text: Impaired verbal communication
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nothing in the stem shows a breakdown in speech or understanding. The patient states feelings clearly.

options.text: Risk for falls
options.rationale: Risk for falls means a raised chance of a fall that could cause harm. The test question is: is there a physical hazard plus a pattern of near misses? Here there are stairs, new loss of vision in both eyes, living alone, and two missed steps this week. Safety comes before psychosocial needs on a priority question. Fear and impaired socialization are both supported by the stem and belong on the care plan, but they come next. Impaired verbal communication has no supporting cue.

questions.takeaway: When a sensory loss has already produced near falls, safety outranks the feelings about the loss.
questions.strategy: The detail that tips it is the two missed steps this week, with nobody else at home. Fear is the emotional pull, but stairs plus near misses is the physical threat.

questions.stem: Complete the statement about calcium balance.
questions.sentence: A serum calcium of 6.8 mg/dL will produce [[1]], and the nurse should assess for [[2]]. Parathyroid hormone acts to [[3]] the serum calcium level.

options.text: increased neuromuscular excitability
decreased neuromuscular excitability
no change in neuromuscular excitability
tetany, tingling and a positive Chvostek sign
bone pain and kidney stones
muscle weakness, constipation and lethargy
raise
lower
stabilize without changing

questions.takeaway: Calcium stabilizes the nerve membrane, so a low level makes nerves fire more easily. Low calcium excites, producing tetany, twitching, tingling, seizures and positive Trousseau and Chvostek signs. High calcium sedates. Parathyroid hormone raises calcium when it falls; calcitonin lowers it. The effect runs opposite to the number. Low excites, high sedates.
questions.strategy: Do not reason from the word low to the word decreased. Reason from what calcium does to the membrane.

questions.stem: Which aspect of blood glucose monitoring may the nurse delegate to assistive personnel?

options.text: Deciding whether a result requires a change in the patient's scheduled insulin dose
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Interpretation and a high alert medication decision.

options.text: Teaching the patient how to use the glucose meter at home
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Initial teaching belongs to the nurse.

options.text: Obtaining and running the sample on a stable patient, reporting set values
options.rationale: The task of obtaining a glucose can be delegated to trained assistive personnel on a stable patient, as long as you give them the numbers that must be reported immediately. Interpreting the value, adjusting the dose, teaching and assessing symptoms are all nursing judgment.

options.text: Judging whether the patient's sweating and shakiness mean hypoglycemia
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Assessment, and in this case an urgent one.

questions.takeaway: You can delegate the stick. You cannot delegate what the number means.
questions.strategy: The phrase with clear parameters is doing real work. Delegation without them is unsafe.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing insulin. Select all of the actions that are correct.

options.text: Write the dose as 12 units rather than 12 U
options.rationale: Insulin is a high alert medication. The letter U reads as a zero in handwriting, the double check is required, meal timing is part of the dose, and absorption varies by site. You do not aspirate a subcutaneous injection, and long acting insulins are never mixed.

options.text: Verify that the meal tray is on the unit before giving rapid acting insulin
options.rationale: Insulin is a high alert medication. The letter U reads as a zero in handwriting, the double check is required, meal timing is part of the dose, and absorption varies by site. You do not aspirate a subcutaneous injection, and long acting insulins are never mixed.

options.text: Rotate the injection site, knowing that the abdomen absorbs faster than the thigh
options.rationale: Insulin is a high alert medication. The letter U reads as a zero in handwriting, the double check is required, meal timing is part of the dose, and absorption varies by site. You do not aspirate a subcutaneous injection, and long acting insulins are never mixed.

options.text: Mix insulin glargine with regular insulin in the same syringe to reduce the number of injections
options.rationale: Near miss concept NPH may be mixed with rapid or regular. Glargine, detemir and degludec never are.

options.text: Aspirate before injecting to confirm the needle is not in a vessel
options.rationale: Near miss concept Carried over from intramuscular technique. Not done subcutaneously.

options.text: Complete an independent double check with a second nurse before administration
options.rationale: Insulin is a high alert medication. The letter U reads as a zero in handwriting, the double check is required, meal timing is part of the dose, and absorption varies by site. You do not aspirate a subcutaneous injection, and long acting insulins are never mixed.

questions.takeaway: Rapid acting insulin without a meal is a timing error with the same consequence as a dosing error.
questions.strategy: Two of these are things nurses actually do with other injections. Neither applies to insulin.

questions.stem: Select all of the foot care instructions for a patient with diabetes and neuropathy.

options.text: Soak the feet daily to soften calluses
options.rationale: Near miss concept Macerates the skin and raises infection risk; specifically taught against.

options.text: Check bath water temperature with a thermometer or the elbow
options.rationale: He cannot feel injury, so vision replaces sensation and an intact body part replaces the thermometer in his feet. Shoes indoors matter because most injuries happen at home. Soaking macerates the skin and raises infection risk, and a heating pad on a foot that cannot feel heat is how a third degree burn happens without a sound.

options.text: Cut nails straight across and report any break in the skin promptly
options.rationale: He cannot feel injury, so vision replaces sensation and an intact body part replaces the thermometer in his feet. Shoes indoors matter because most injuries happen at home. Soaking macerates the skin and raises infection risk, and a heating pad on a foot that cannot feel heat is how a third degree burn happens without a sound.

options.text: Inspect the feet daily, using a mirror for the soles if needed
options.rationale: He cannot feel injury, so vision replaces sensation and an intact body part replaces the thermometer in his feet. Shoes indoors matter because most injuries happen at home. Soaking macerates the skin and raises infection risk, and a heating pad on a foot that cannot feel heat is how a third degree burn happens without a sound.

options.text: Use a heating pad on the feet for comfort at night
options.rationale: Near miss concept He will not feel a burn until the damage is done.

options.text: Wear well fitting shoes and never go barefoot, including indoors
options.rationale: He cannot feel injury, so vision replaces sensation and an intact body part replaces the thermometer in his feet. Shoes indoors matter because most injuries happen at home. Soaking macerates the skin and raises infection risk, and a heating pad on a foot that cannot feel heat is how a third degree burn happens without a sound.

questions.takeaway: Never soak, never a heating pad, never barefoot. Those three prevent most of these ulcers.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options are comfort measures that burn or breach skin he cannot feel.

questions.stem: Classify each finding by the condition it fits best.

rows.text: Onset over hours in a patient who has never been diagnosed
Kussmaul respirations with a fruity odor on the breath
Dehydration requiring aggressive intravenous fluid replacement
Glucose over 600 with profound dehydration and a normal pH

questions.takeaway: Ketones are what separate them. In DKA there is no insulin at all, so fat is broken down, ketones accumulate, the pH falls and the lungs blow off carbon dioxide, which is the Kussmaul breathing and the fruity breath. In HHS there is enough insulin to prevent ketosis but not enough to control glucose, so the pH is normal and the problem is osmotic water loss over days to weeks. Both are profoundly dry, and fluid comes first in both. DKA is hours and acidotic. HHS is days to weeks and hyperosmolar. Fluids first in both.
questions.strategy: Check the pH. It sorts these two faster than the glucose does, because the glucose is high in both.

questions.stem: Select all of the statements about diabetes classification that are accurate.

options.text: Type 1 results from autoimmune destruction of the beta cells and always requires insulin
options.rationale: Type is about mechanism, not about age or body habitus. Type 1 is autoimmune beta cell destruction, so there is no endogenous insulin and exogenous insulin is required for life, at any age of onset. Type 2 is resistance plus relative deficiency, occurs at any weight, and often progresses to needing insulin.

options.text: Type 1 is diagnosed by the presence of obesity and a family history
options.rationale: Near miss concept Describes risk factors for type 2 and attaches them to type 1.

options.text: Type 2 can be ruled out in a patient of normal weight
options.rationale: Absolute language Weight is a risk factor, not a diagnostic criterion.

options.text: Type 2 involves insulin resistance with a relative insulin deficiency
options.rationale: Type is about mechanism, not about age or body habitus. Type 1 is autoimmune beta cell destruction, so there is no endogenous insulin and exogenous insulin is required for life, at any age of onset. Type 2 is resistance plus relative deficiency, occurs at any weight, and often progresses to needing insulin.

options.text: A patient with type 2 may require insulin
options.rationale: Type is about mechanism, not about age or body habitus. Type 1 is autoimmune beta cell destruction, so there is no endogenous insulin and exogenous insulin is required for life, at any age of onset. Type 2 is resistance plus relative deficiency, occurs at any weight, and often progresses to needing insulin.

options.text: Type 1 can present at any age, not only in childhood
options.rationale: Type is about mechanism, not about age or body habitus. Type 1 is autoimmune beta cell destruction, so there is no endogenous insulin and exogenous insulin is required for life, at any age of onset. Type 2 is resistance plus relative deficiency, occurs at any weight, and often progresses to needing insulin.

questions.takeaway: Age and weight are clues, never criteria.
questions.strategy: Any option that uses weight or age to rule a type in or out is wrong on principle.

questions.stem: Select all of the findings consistent with hypothyroidism.

options.text: Fatigue and cold intolerance
options.rationale: Thyroid hormone sets the metabolic rate, so too little slows everything: the heart, the gut, the temperature and the energy. Too much speeds all of it, which is the last two options. You can derive every sign from that one idea rather than memorizing two lists, which is also how you keep them straight under pressure.

options.text: Unintentional weight loss with increased appetite
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hyperthyroid. Metabolism outruns intake.

options.text: Weight gain despite reduced appetite
options.rationale: Thyroid hormone sets the metabolic rate, so too little slows everything: the heart, the gut, the temperature and the energy. Too much speeds all of it, which is the last two options. You can derive every sign from that one idea rather than memorizing two lists, which is also how you keep them straight under pressure.

options.text: Heat intolerance and diaphoresis
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hyperthyroid. Too much hormone raises heat production.

options.text: Constipation
options.rationale: Thyroid hormone sets the metabolic rate, so too little slows everything: the heart, the gut, the temperature and the energy. Too much speeds all of it, which is the last two options. You can derive every sign from that one idea rather than memorizing two lists, which is also how you keep them straight under pressure.

options.text: Bradycardia
options.rationale: Thyroid hormone sets the metabolic rate, so too little slows everything: the heart, the gut, the temperature and the energy. Too much speeds all of it, which is the last two options. You can derive every sign from that one idea rather than memorizing two lists, which is also how you keep them straight under pressure.

questions.takeaway: Hypothyroid is everything slowing down. Derive the signs from the metabolic rate.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options are hyperthyroid, and they are the mirror image of the correct ones.

questions.stem: Select all of the findings that are components of metabolic syndrome.

options.text: Central obesity with increased waist circumference
options.rationale: Metabolic syndrome is a cluster, and the cluster is what predicts type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease better than any single piece. Central obesity, insulin resistance, the dyslipidemia pattern and hypertension. Creatinine is a kidney value and a family history of type 1 is an autoimmune story, not this one.

options.text: Fasting hyperglycemia or insulin resistance
options.rationale: Metabolic syndrome is a cluster, and the cluster is what predicts type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease better than any single piece. Central obesity, insulin resistance, the dyslipidemia pattern and hypertension. Creatinine is a kidney value and a family history of type 1 is an autoimmune story, not this one.

options.text: A family history of type 1 diabetes
options.rationale: Near miss concept Type 1 is autoimmune beta cell destruction; this cluster predicts type 2.

options.text: Elevated triglycerides with low high density lipoprotein
options.rationale: Metabolic syndrome is a cluster, and the cluster is what predicts type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease better than any single piece. Central obesity, insulin resistance, the dyslipidemia pattern and hypertension. Creatinine is a kidney value and a family history of type 1 is an autoimmune story, not this one.

options.text: Elevated serum creatinine
options.rationale: Near miss concept Kidney function, which can be affected downstream and is not a component.

options.text: Hypertension
options.rationale: Metabolic syndrome is a cluster, and the cluster is what predicts type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease better than any single piece. Central obesity, insulin resistance, the dyslipidemia pattern and hypertension. Creatinine is a kidney value and a family history of type 1 is an autoimmune story, not this one.

questions.takeaway: Four components that travel together. One of them alone is not the syndrome.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options are real risk information that belongs to a different problem.

questions.stem: Select all of the accurate statements about insulin handling.

options.text: Clumping or frosting in the vial is acceptable if the insulin is still in date
options.rationale: Near miss concept Both indicate degraded insulin; discard it.

options.text: Unopened vials are refrigerated until the expiration date
options.rationale: Cold insulin stings, which is why an in use vial can sit at room temperature for a specified period. Shaking a suspension creates bubbles and inconsistent dosing, so you roll it. Rotating within one area, usually the abdomen, keeps absorption consistent, because absorption differs between the abdomen, arm and thigh. Frozen, clumped or frosted insulin is discarded.

options.text: Rotate injection sites within one anatomic area rather than across the body
options.rationale: Cold insulin stings, which is why an in use vial can sit at room temperature for a specified period. Shaking a suspension creates bubbles and inconsistent dosing, so you roll it. Rotating within one area, usually the abdomen, keeps absorption consistent, because absorption differs between the abdomen, arm and thigh. Frozen, clumped or frosted insulin is discarded.

options.text: Cloudy insulin suspensions are gently rolled rather than shaken
options.rationale: Cold insulin stings, which is why an in use vial can sit at room temperature for a specified period. Shaking a suspension creates bubbles and inconsistent dosing, so you roll it. Rotating within one area, usually the abdomen, keeps absorption consistent, because absorption differs between the abdomen, arm and thigh. Frozen, clumped or frosted insulin is discarded.

options.text: Insulin may be given through a frozen and thawed vial if it looks clear
options.rationale: Near miss concept Freezing destroys insulin regardless of appearance.

options.text: An opened vial in use may be kept at room temperature for the period the manufacturer specifies
options.rationale: Cold insulin stings, which is why an in use vial can sit at room temperature for a specified period. Shaking a suspension creates bubbles and inconsistent dosing, so you roll it. Rotating within one area, usually the abdomen, keeps absorption consistent, because absorption differs between the abdomen, arm and thigh. Frozen, clumped or frosted insulin is discarded.

questions.takeaway: Rotate within an area, not between them. Absorption speed changes with the site.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options use an insulin that has been damaged, which costs the patient the dose without their knowing.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of hyperthyroidism is admitted after a motor vehicle crash. Over four hours the temperature rises from 99.8 F to 103.4 F and the heart rate from 112 to 148. The patient is agitated. What is the nurse's priority interpretation?

options.text: This is anxiety related to the crash and the patient needs reorientation and reassurance
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Names the behavior and ignores the physiology.

options.text: This is a thyroid storm and requires immediate escalation
options.rationale: A rising heart rate together with a rising temperature in a patient with known hyperthyroidism, triggered by a physiologic stressor such as trauma, is thyroid storm. It is a life threatening emergency. The priority nursing concerns are cardiovascular status, temperature control, reduced stimulation and rest.

options.text: This is an expected stress response to trauma and warrants continued monitoring
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A real phenomenon used to explain away a crisis.

options.text: This is an infection developing at an injury site and cultures should be obtained
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fever plus tachycardia does fit sepsis, which is why this is tempting. The known thyroid history and the four hour trajectory fit storm better.

questions.takeaway: Watch the two numbers move together. Rising rate with rising temperature in hyperthyroidism is the tell.
questions.strategy: A stem that gives you a known endocrine diagnosis plus a new stressor is usually asking about the crisis state of that gland.

questions.stem: Two patients are admitted with severe hyperglycemia. Patient A has a pH of 7.21 with moderate serum ketones and became ill over the past 10 hours. Patient B has a pH of 7.36, negative ketones, a serum osmolality of 352 and has been declining over about a week. Which statement about patient B is correct?

options.text: Patient B is at least as likely to die and needs aggressive fluid replacement
options.rationale: Patient B has hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state. There is enough endogenous insulin to suppress ketone formation but not enough to control glucose, so there is no acidosis and the patient is nonetheless profoundly dehydrated with a high mortality. It develops over days to weeks, typically in older patients with type 2 diabetes, and fluid comes before insulin.

options.text: Patient B should start an insulin infusion before any fluid replacement is given
options.rationale: Near miss concept Inverts the order. Giving insulin first drives glucose and water into cells and worsens the vascular collapse.

options.text: Patient B is more stable, since the lack of acidosis shows a milder process
options.rationale: Near miss concept The exact reasoning error the item is built on.

options.text: Patient B most likely has type 1 diabetes, given how high the glucose has risen
options.rationale: Near miss concept The slow onset and absent ketones point to type 2.

questions.takeaway: Students under rank hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state because there is no acidosis. That is the trap.
questions.strategy: No acidosis does not mean less danger. Ask what the fluid deficit is.

questions.topic: the patient with several endocrine problems
questions.stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes is started on prednisone for a flare of an autoimmune condition. What should the nurse anticipate?
questions.objective: the patient with several endocrine problems

options.text: Rising glucose levels that may need a stronger diabetes regimen
options.rationale: Corticosteroids raise glucose by increasing hepatic production and opposing insulin at the tissues, which is exactly what cortisol is for. Any patient with diabetes started on steroids needs closer monitoring and usually more treatment, and the glucose falls again when the steroid is tapered, so the regimen has to come back down with it.

options.text: Falling glucose levels that will require a lower insulin dose
options.rationale: Near miss concept Backwards; that is what happens when the steroid is stopped.

options.text: A higher risk of ketoacidosis rather than of hyperglycemia
options.rationale: Near miss concept A type 2 patient with some insulin is far more likely to run high or go toward HHS than into ketoacidosis.

options.text: No change, since prednisone does not alter glucose metabolism
options.rationale: Near miss concept Glucose elevation is one of its most predictable effects.

questions.takeaway: Steroids raise glucose. The dose goes up when they start and down when they stop.
questions.strategy: If you know cortisol maintains glucose, you can derive this rather than memorizing it.

questions.stem: A patient with a glucose of 468 mg/dL reports urinating constantly, unquenchable thirst and being hungry all the time. Which explains all three symptoms?

options.text: High glucose directly stimulates the hypothalamic thirst and hunger centers
options.rationale: Near miss concept Names the right centers and the wrong pathway.

options.text: Glucose spills into urine pulling water, while cells cannot use blood glucose
options.rationale: Once glucose exceeds the renal threshold it spills into the urine and drags water with it: that is osmotic diuresis, and it produces the polyuria. The fluid loss produces the polydipsia. The polyphagia comes from cells that are starving in the middle of a bloodstream full of fuel they cannot get into. One mechanism, three Ps.

options.text: Insulin deficiency makes the kidneys retain sodium, and the retained sodium is what drives thirst
options.rationale: Near miss concept Backwards. The kidney is dumping water and sodium, not holding them.

options.text: Dehydration from a fever raises urine output and stimulates the appetite
options.rationale: Near miss concept No fever in the stem, and dehydration reduces urine output.

questions.takeaway: The cells starve while the blood is full. That sentence explains all three Ps.
questions.strategy: When a stem gives you three symptoms, look for the one mechanism that produces all of them.

questions.stem: A patient with long standing adrenal insufficiency stops taking her replacement corticosteroid. Which set of findings should the nurse expect?

options.text: Hypertension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia and hyperglycemia
options.rationale: Near miss concept Mixes the deficient and excess pictures.

options.text: Hypotension, hypernatremia, hypokalemia and hypoglycemia
options.rationale: Near miss concept Gets the pressure and glucose right and inverts the electrolytes.

options.text: Hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia and hypoglycemia
options.rationale: The adrenals handle salt, stress and pressure. Aldosterone holds sodium and water and excretes potassium, so losing it drops the sodium, the volume and the pressure while potassium climbs. Cortisol maintains glucose, so losing it drops the glucose. Reason from the two hormones and all four values fall out of it; the excess state, Cushing, is the mirror image.

options.text: Hypertension, hypernatremia, hypokalemia and hyperglycemia
options.rationale: Near miss concept The mirror image, which is cortisol and aldosterone excess.

questions.takeaway: Aldosterone sets sodium, potassium and pressure. Cortisol sets glucose and the stress response.
questions.strategy: An option set of four lab directions is a mechanism question. Derive it from the hormone instead of memorizing the set.

questions.topic: insulin peaks and timing of risk
questions.stem: A patient receives regular insulin at 0730 with breakfast. At which time is the nurse most alert for hypoglycemia?
questions.objective: insulin peaks and timing of risk

options.text: Between 2200 and 0200
options.rationale: Near miss concept Long past this dose; overnight risk comes from intermediate or long acting insulin.

options.text: Between 0930 and 1130
options.rationale: Regular insulin onsets in about 30 minutes, peaks at about 2 to 3 hours and lasts 3 to 6, so the risk window after a 0730 dose is roughly mid to late morning, which is also when the breakfast carbohydrate has been used up. Rapid acting insulin peaks in about 1 hour, and NPH peaks at roughly 4 to 12, which is why an NPH patient is at risk in the afternoon and overnight.

options.text: Between 1400 and 1600
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is the NPH window, not regular insulin given at 0730.

options.text: Between 0745 and 0815
options.rationale: Near miss concept Barely past onset; the insulin has not peaked.

questions.takeaway: Hypoglycemia happens at the peak, not at the dose. Know the peak of what you gave.
questions.strategy: Map the peak against the next meal. The gap between them is the risk.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to give NPH and regular insulin in the same syringe. Which action is correct?

options.text: Inject air into NPH, then into regular, then draw up the regular first
options.rationale: Air into the cloudy vial first, air into the clear, then draw clear before cloudy. The reason is contamination: if NPH gets into the regular vial it changes how that insulin acts, and regular is the one you may need to act predictably. Long acting insulins, glargine, detemir and degludec, are never mixed with anything.

options.text: Mix glargine with the regular insulin instead, since both are clear
options.rationale: Near miss concept Clear does not mean mixable. Glargine is never mixed.

options.text: Use two separate syringes, because no two insulins can ever be mixed
options.rationale: Absolute language Rapid and regular can both be mixed with NPH.

options.text: Draw up the NPH first, then the regular, so no cloudy insulin is wasted
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reverses the order and contaminates the regular vial with NPH.

questions.takeaway: Clear before cloudy, and air into cloudy first.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options break the one absolute rule: long acting insulin is never mixed.

questions.stem: A patient's A1C is 6.1 percent. How should the nurse interpret this result?

options.text: It is within the normal range and requires no further discussion
options.rationale: Near miss concept Normal stops at 5.7.

options.text: It is diagnostic of diabetes and requires a confirmatory test
options.rationale: Near miss concept Diagnosis begins at 6.5.

options.text: It indicates adequate control in a patient with established diabetes
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question True if he already had diabetes. The stem does not say he does.

options.text: It indicates prediabetes and the patient should receive lifestyle counseling
options.rationale: Normal is under 5.7 percent, prediabetes is 5.7 to 6.4 percent, and 6.5 percent or higher is diagnostic with confirmation. The common treatment goal in established diabetes is under 7 percent, which is why the same number means different things depending on whether the patient already carries the diagnosis.

questions.takeaway: The A1C reflects roughly three months of glucose, so a single good day does not move it and a single bad day does not either.
questions.strategy: Know the three cut points cold. Two of the wrong options here are correct interpretations of the number in a different patient.

questions.stem: A patient is to receive rapid acting insulin before breakfast. When should the nurse give it?

options.text: At the same time every morning, whenever the breakfast tray arrives
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome Rapid acting insulin is timed to the meal, not the clock; giving it with no food coming risks hypoglycemia.

options.text: Thirty to sixty minutes before the meal arrives, to allow enough time for its onset
options.rationale: Near miss concept The window for regular, short acting insulin.

options.text: Right after the patient finishes eating, once intake is known
options.rationale: Near miss concept Giving it after the meal is done for some patients with unreliable intake by order, but the routine timing is within 15 minutes of eating.

options.text: Within about 15 minutes of the meal, with the tray confirmed on its way
options.rationale: Rapid acting insulin starts working in roughly 15 minutes, so giving it without food in front of the patient sets up hypoglycemia. The rule is to know where the tray is before you give the dose. Regular insulin, which is short acting, is the one given about 30 minutes before a meal.

questions.takeaway: Match the dose to the food, not to the clock.
questions.strategy: Insulin timing items are testing onset. Pair the onset with when food will actually arrive.

questions.stem: Which statement by a patient with diabetic peripheral neuropathy indicates that teaching has been effective?

options.text: “I will trim my toenails in a curve to match the shape of each toe.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Straight across is correct.

options.text: “I will go barefoot inside the house so the skin on my feet can breathe and stay dry all day.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Most injuries happen at home.

options.text: “I will soak my feet in warm water every evening to keep the skin soft.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sounds like good skin care and is a burn waiting to happen.

options.text: “I will check the soles of my feet daily with a mirror, since I may not feel injuries.”
options.rationale: The correct answer states the mechanism, which is that neuropathy removes the warning. Soaking is contraindicated because reduced sensation means the patient cannot judge water temperature. Going barefoot removes protection, waiting for pain assumes a warning system that no longer works, and curved nail trimming promotes ingrown nails.

options.text: “I will check my feet carefully whenever they start to hurt or feel sore.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Relies on the exact sensation the disease has destroyed.

questions.takeaway: The option that explains WHY is usually the one that shows understanding.
questions.strategy: On an indicates understanding item, look for the answer that contains a mechanism rather than a rule.

questions.stem: An 18 year old with type 1 diabetes is admitted with a glucose of 528 mg/dL, deep rapid respirations, a fruity odor to the breath and a serum pH of 7.19. Complete the bow tie.

options.text: Prepare for a continuous IV insulin infusion
Administer subcutaneous rapid acting insulin and recheck in two hours
Encourage oral fluids to correct the dehydration
Place the patient in high Fowler position and apply a nonrebreather
Establish IV access and begin isotonic fluid per protocol
Respiratory alkalosis from anxiety
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
Sepsis with lactic acidosis
Diabetic ketoacidosis
Serum potassium
Daily weight
Deep tendon reflexes
Serum pH and anion gap
Serum calcium

questions.takeaway: Ketones with acidosis in type 1 diabetes is ketoacidosis. Management is intravenous fluid first and then a continuous insulin infusion, because subcutaneous dosing is unreliable in a dehydrated patient and the acidosis needs a controlled correction. Potassium is monitored because treatment drives it into the cells and the level can fall fast even when it starts high. Kussmaul respirations are compensation for the acidosis, not a respiratory problem. Do not treat them as one.
questions.strategy: In a bow tie, the two actions are almost always the two that change physiology, not the two that make the patient comfortable.

questions.stem: A patient with type 1 diabetes calls because she has vomited twice, cannot keep food down, and her glucose is 240. She asks whether to skip her insulin. What should the nurse tell her?

options.text: Skip the insulin until she can eat again, to avoid a low blood sugar
options.rationale: Near miss concept The intuitive answer and the one that causes ketoacidosis.

options.text: Come to the emergency department before taking any of her insulin today
options.rationale: Correct but premature She may need to be seen, and she should not travel having withheld insulin.

options.text: Take half her usual dose now and recheck her glucose in the morning
options.rationale: Near miss concept Arbitrary reduction with no monitoring, and morning is too long.

options.text: Keep taking insulin, check glucose and ketones every 4 hours, sip carbohydrate fluids
options.rationale: Illness raises counterregulatory hormones, so insulin requirements go up even when intake goes down, and a type 1 patient who stops insulin is on the road to ketoacidosis within hours. Sick day rules: never stop the insulin, check glucose and ketones every four hours, take fluids with carbohydrate, and call if ketones are moderate or large or vomiting continues.

questions.takeaway: Illness raises the insulin requirement. Stopping it is how type 1 patients end up in DKA.
questions.strategy: Skipping insulin because the patient is not eating is the single most dangerous piece of intuition in diabetes care.

questions.stem: A patient with diabetes becomes diaphoretic, confused and tachycardic at 0300. Select all of the nursing actions that are appropriate.

options.text: If unable to check promptly, treat as hypoglycemia
options.rationale: The brain runs on glucose and tolerates a shortage for minutes, so when you cannot measure quickly you treat. Fifteen grams of rapid carbohydrate, recheck at 15 minutes, repeat if still low, then a protein and carbohydrate snack once it is corrected. Starting with milk and a sandwich is too slow for the acute correction, and waiting for the laboratory is how a confused patient becomes a seizing one.

options.text: Withhold treatment until the glucose result confirms hypoglycemia
options.rationale: Near miss concept Delays treatment of a brain that is already symptomatic.

options.text: Give the patient a glass of milk and a sandwich as the initial treatment
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is the follow up snack after correction, not the rapid treatment.

options.text: Recheck the glucose 15 minutes after treatment
options.rationale: The brain runs on glucose and tolerates a shortage for minutes, so when you cannot measure quickly you treat. Fifteen grams of rapid carbohydrate, recheck at 15 minutes, repeat if still low, then a protein and carbohydrate snack once it is corrected. Starting with milk and a sandwich is too slow for the acute correction, and waiting for the laboratory is how a confused patient becomes a seizing one.

options.text: Give 15 grams of a rapid acting carbohydrate if the patient can swallow safely
options.rationale: The brain runs on glucose and tolerates a shortage for minutes, so when you cannot measure quickly you treat. Fifteen grams of rapid carbohydrate, recheck at 15 minutes, repeat if still low, then a protein and carbohydrate snack once it is corrected. Starting with milk and a sandwich is too slow for the acute correction, and waiting for the laboratory is how a confused patient becomes a seizing one.

options.text: Check the capillary glucose immediately
options.rationale: The brain runs on glucose and tolerates a shortage for minutes, so when you cannot measure quickly you treat. Fifteen grams of rapid carbohydrate, recheck at 15 minutes, repeat if still low, then a protein and carbohydrate snack once it is corrected. Starting with milk and a sandwich is too slow for the acute correction, and waiting for the laboratory is how a confused patient becomes a seizing one.

questions.takeaway: Fifteen grams, fifteen minutes. When in doubt, treat; glucose is cheap and brain is not.
questions.strategy: Nocturnal hypoglycemia presents as confusion and sweating, and gets charted as a bad dream more often than anyone would like.

questions.stem: A patient with a pituitary tumor has a urine output of 4,800 mL in 12 hours with a urine specific gravity of 1.002 and reports intense thirst. Which order should the nurse question?

options.text: Record strict intake and output
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem You want this. He is losing liters and you need the number.

options.text: Monitor serum sodium every 6 hours
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Exactly what you want, since the risk is hypernatremia.

options.text: Restrict oral fluids to 1,200 mL per day
options.rationale: This is diabetes insipidus: a large volume of very dilute urine with intense thirst. Thirst is the compensation keeping the patient from severe hypernatremia and hypovolemia. Restricting fluids removes the only defense the patient has. The other three orders are all appropriate monitoring.

options.text: Weigh the patient daily on the same scale
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A kilogram is a liter. This is how you catch the loss early.

questions.takeaway: Never restrict fluids in diabetes insipidus. Monitor the sodium instead.
questions.strategy: When one order would remove a compensation the patient is depending on, that is the order to question.

questions.stem: A patient with untreated hypothyroidism is found lethargic with a temperature of 34.4 degrees Celsius, a heart rate of 48 and a blood pressure of 86/50. What is the priority nursing concern?

options.text: Rewarming the patient rapidly with external heat
options.rationale: Near miss concept Addresses the temperature and drops the pressure further.

options.text: Preventing injury from the altered level of consciousness
options.rationale: Near miss concept Real, and below airway and breathing.

options.text: Obtaining a thyroid stimulating hormone level before any intervention
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting A laboratory value before an airway.

options.text: Airway and breathing, because respiratory depression accompanies this state
options.rationale: This is myxedema coma: hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension and a falling level of consciousness, with hypoventilation and carbon dioxide retention alongside it. Airway and breathing come first. Rapid external rewarming causes vasodilation and worsens the hypotension. Thyroid storm is the mirror image: fever, tachycardia, agitation.

questions.takeaway: Myxedema coma slows everything down. Thyroid storm speeds everything up.
questions.strategy: Both thyroid emergencies are ABC problems. Pick the airway option before the one that treats the most visible number.

questions.stem: A 74 year old with type 2 diabetes is found confused and combative at 0300. The nursing assistant reports that he was oriented at 2300. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Notify the provider of an acute change in mental status
options.rationale: Correct but premature You will call, with a number in hand.

options.text: Perform a neurologic assessment and compare it to the admission baseline
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Correct action, slower, and it will not find the cause.

options.text: Reorient the patient and institute fall precautions
options.rationale: Correct but premature Treats the behavior and ignores the cause.

options.text: Review the medication record for a recently administered insulin dose
options.rationale: Correct but premature Useful context that does not treat a brain starving right now.

options.text: Check a bedside blood glucose
options.rationale: The brain runs almost exclusively on glucose, so any acute change in mental status in a patient with diabetes is a glucose check until proven otherwise. It takes seconds, it is reversible, and hypoglycemia is routinely mistaken for delirium, intoxication or dementia. Everything else listed is appropriate and comes after.

questions.takeaway: Always check a glucose when mental status changes. It is the single most repeatable rule in this content.
questions.strategy: When every option is a reasonable nursing action, choose the one that is fastest, reversible and most lethal if missed.

chapters.title: Assessment of the Renal and Urinary System

questions.stem: A patient with reduced kidney function is scheduled for a contrast computed tomography scan. Which measure best protects the kidneys?

options.text: Encouraging a high protein meal before the study
options.rationale: Near miss concept Protein load increases renal work and does not protect.

options.text: Intravenous hydration before and after the study, per protocol
options.rationale: Contrast injures the kidney partly through reduced medullary blood flow and direct tubular toxicity, and volume expansion is the one measure that reliably reduces it. Nephrotoxic drugs are held where possible. Diuresing a patient after contrast dries them out at exactly the wrong moment.

options.text: Withholding all fluids for 8 hours before the study
options.rationale: Near miss concept Confuses contrast protocol with surgical nothing by mouth, and leaves the kidney dry for the insult.

options.text: Administering a diuretic immediately after the contrast
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reduces volume when volume is what is protective.

questions.takeaway: Hydration before and after. Everything else is secondary.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options actively dehydrate the patient around the insult.

questions.stem: Select all of the findings consistent with fluid overload in a patient with kidney disease.

options.text: Dry mucous membranes and poor skin turgor
options.rationale: Near miss concept Deficit findings, not excess.

options.text: Urine specific gravity of 1.035
options.rationale: Near miss concept Concentrated urine, which fits a volume deficit.

options.text: Rapid weight gain over two days
options.rationale: The kidney cannot excrete the water, so the volume shows up in the weight, the lungs, the neck veins and the pressure. Weight is the most reliable of the four because it moves first and cannot be argued with. The last two options are deficit findings and belong to the opposite problem.

options.text: Crackles in the lung bases
options.rationale: The kidney cannot excrete the water, so the volume shows up in the weight, the lungs, the neck veins and the pressure. Weight is the most reliable of the four because it moves first and cannot be argued with. The last two options are deficit findings and belong to the opposite problem.

options.text: New or worsening hypertension
options.rationale: The kidney cannot excrete the water, so the volume shows up in the weight, the lungs, the neck veins and the pressure. Weight is the most reliable of the four because it moves first and cannot be argued with. The last two options are deficit findings and belong to the opposite problem.

options.text: Jugular venous distention
options.rationale: The kidney cannot excrete the water, so the volume shows up in the weight, the lungs, the neck veins and the pressure. Weight is the most reliable of the four because it moves first and cannot be argued with. The last two options are deficit findings and belong to the opposite problem.

questions.takeaway: A kilogram is a liter. Weight catches overload before the lungs do.
questions.strategy: Two options describe a dry patient, which is the wrong direction.

questions.stem: Match each urine finding to what it suggests.

rows.text: Positive nitrites and leukocyte esterase
Red blood cell casts
White blood cell casts
Muddy brown granular casts

questions.takeaway: Casts form in the tubules and carry whatever was there, so they tell you where the problem is. Red cell casts mean blood is crossing the glomerulus. White cell casts mean inflammation up in the kidney rather than down in the bladder. Muddy brown casts are sloughed tubular cells, which is the fingerprint of acute tubular necrosis. A cast means the kidney. Cells without casts can come from anywhere downstream.
questions.strategy: Ask what is inside the cast, then ask what structure that cell had to pass through.

questions.stem: Select all of the measures that reduce catheter associated urinary tract infection.

options.text: Secure the catheter to prevent traction and movement
options.rationale: The single most effective measure is taking it out. Every extra day raises the risk. Keep the bag below the bladder so urine does not run back, keep the system closed, and secure the catheter so it is not sawing at the urethra. Routine irrigation and breaking the system both introduce organisms.

options.text: Maintain a closed drainage system
options.rationale: The single most effective measure is taking it out. Every extra day raises the risk. Keep the bag below the bladder so urine does not run back, keep the system closed, and secure the catheter so it is not sawing at the urethra. Routine irrigation and breaking the system both introduce organisms.

options.text: Disconnect the tubing to empty the bag more easily
options.rationale: Near miss concept Every disconnection is a chance for organisms to enter.

options.text: Review daily whether the catheter is still necessary
options.rationale: The single most effective measure is taking it out. Every extra day raises the risk. Keep the bag below the bladder so urine does not run back, keep the system closed, and secure the catheter so it is not sawing at the urethra. Routine irrigation and breaking the system both introduce organisms.

options.text: Keep the drainage bag below the level of the bladder
options.rationale: The single most effective measure is taking it out. Every extra day raises the risk. Keep the bag below the bladder so urine does not run back, keep the system closed, and secure the catheter so it is not sawing at the urethra. Routine irrigation and breaking the system both introduce organisms.

options.text: Irrigate the catheter routinely to keep it patent
options.rationale: Near miss concept Routine irrigation is not indicated and breaks the closed system.

questions.takeaway: The best catheter care is removing the catheter.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options open or disturb a system whose whole protection is being closed.

questions.stem: Select all of the causes of acute kidney injury that are prerenal.

options.text: Heart failure with a low cardiac output
options.rationale: Prerenal means not enough blood is reaching a structurally normal kidney, whether the volume is gone, the vessels are dilated, or the pump has failed. It is the reversible category if you catch it. Obstruction is postrenal and a catheter fixes it. Nephrotoxic tubular damage is intrinsic, and fluid alone will not reverse it.

options.text: Severe dehydration from vomiting and diarrhea
options.rationale: Prerenal means not enough blood is reaching a structurally normal kidney, whether the volume is gone, the vessels are dilated, or the pump has failed. It is the reversible category if you catch it. Obstruction is postrenal and a catheter fixes it. Nephrotoxic tubular damage is intrinsic, and fluid alone will not reverse it.

options.text: Sepsis with distributive shock
options.rationale: Prerenal means not enough blood is reaching a structurally normal kidney, whether the volume is gone, the vessels are dilated, or the pump has failed. It is the reversible category if you catch it. Obstruction is postrenal and a catheter fixes it. Nephrotoxic tubular damage is intrinsic, and fluid alone will not reverse it.

options.text: Acute tubular necrosis from an aminoglycoside
options.rationale: Near miss concept Intrinsic. The tubules themselves are damaged.

options.text: Hemorrhage with a blood pressure of 78/44
options.rationale: Prerenal means not enough blood is reaching a structurally normal kidney, whether the volume is gone, the vessels are dilated, or the pump has failed. It is the reversible category if you catch it. Obstruction is postrenal and a catheter fixes it. Nephrotoxic tubular damage is intrinsic, and fluid alone will not reverse it.

options.text: Benign prostatic hyperplasia with urinary retention
options.rationale: Near miss concept Postrenal. The kidney is fine and the exit is blocked.

questions.takeaway: Prerenal is a perfusion problem. Left long enough it becomes intrinsic and stops reversing.
questions.strategy: Sort by where the problem sits relative to the nephron: before it, in it, or after it.

questions.stem: Select all of the history findings that raise this patient's risk for acute kidney injury.

options.text: A computed tomography scan with contrast yesterday
options.rationale: Contrast, nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs, aminoglycosides and any period of poor perfusion are the classic kidney insults, and they add up. Nonsteroidals are the one patients do not think to mention because they bought them at the grocery store. Acetaminophen at ordinary doses is a liver question, not a kidney one.

options.text: A daily multivitamin
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Not nephrotoxic at ordinary doses.

options.text: An episode of hypotension during surgery
options.rationale: Contrast, nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs, aminoglycosides and any period of poor perfusion are the classic kidney insults, and they add up. Nonsteroidals are the one patients do not think to mention because they bought them at the grocery store. Acetaminophen at ordinary doses is a liver question, not a kidney one.

options.text: Gentamicin started four days ago
options.rationale: Contrast, nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs, aminoglycosides and any period of poor perfusion are the classic kidney insults, and they add up. Nonsteroidals are the one patients do not think to mention because they bought them at the grocery store. Acetaminophen at ordinary doses is a liver question, not a kidney one.

options.text: Ibuprofen three times daily for two weeks
options.rationale: Contrast, nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs, aminoglycosides and any period of poor perfusion are the classic kidney insults, and they add up. Nonsteroidals are the one patients do not think to mention because they bought them at the grocery store. Acetaminophen at ordinary doses is a liver question, not a kidney one.

options.text: Acetaminophen 650 mg twice in the last day
options.rationale: Near miss concept The hepatotoxic one, and at this dose it is neither.

questions.takeaway: Ask about the over the counter drugs. That is where the nephrotoxin usually is.
questions.strategy: Four of these options are drugs and only two of them hurt kidneys. Sort by organ, not by whether it is a medication.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic kidney disease stage 3 is being discharged. Which teaching point best protects his remaining kidney function?

options.text: Take a daily multivitamin with extra potassium added
options.rationale: Near miss concept Potassium is restricted, not supplemented, as function declines.

options.text: Avoid all protein in the diet to rest the kidneys
options.rationale: Absolute language Protein is moderated with guidance; eliminating it causes malnutrition.

options.text: Avoid over the counter NSAIDs and tell every provider
options.rationale: Nonsteroidals are the most common avoidable nephrotoxin and patients do not think of them as medication, because they come off a grocery shelf. Telling every provider matters for contrast studies and for dose adjustment. Fluid restriction is not standard at stage 3 and can cause prerenal injury, extra potassium is dangerous, and protein is moderated rather than eliminated.

options.text: Restrict fluids to 1 liter per day starting today
options.rationale: Near miss concept Not standard at stage 3, and dehydration causes prerenal injury.

questions.takeaway: The ibuprofen in his cupboard is the biggest modifiable threat to his kidneys.
questions.strategy: Three options prescribe a restriction that is either wrong for this stage or actively harmful.

questions.stem: A patient reports severe colicky pain in the left flank that radiates to the groin, and is unable to lie still. What does this most suggest?

options.text: Acute urinary retention
options.rationale: Near miss concept Suprapubic fullness and pressure, not flank pain.

options.text: Pyelonephritis
options.rationale: Near miss concept Steady flank pain with fever and chills, not colicky waves.

options.text: Renal calculi
options.rationale: A stone moving down the ureter produces waves of pain that radiate along the path of the ureter toward the groin, and patients cannot find a position that helps, which is the detail that separates it from peritoneal pain where people lie very still. Pyelonephritis gives steady flank pain with fever. Retention gives suprapubic pressure.

options.text: Bladder infection
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dysuria, frequency and suprapubic discomfort.

questions.takeaway: Colicky, radiating to the groin, and unable to stay still is a stone.
questions.strategy: The location of the pain tells you the structure: flank is kidney, suprapubic is bladder, radiating to the groin is ureter.

questions.stem: A dehydrated patient has a urine specific gravity of 1.035. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: The finding suggests the patient has been overhydrated
options.rationale: Near miss concept Overhydration dilutes the urine and drops the specific gravity.

options.text: The kidneys have lost the ability to concentrate urine
options.rationale: Near miss concept That would be a specific gravity stuck near 1.010 despite dehydration.

options.text: The finding points to glomerular damage in the kidneys
options.rationale: Near miss concept Glomerular damage shows up as protein and red cell casts, not high specific gravity.

options.text: The kidneys are concentrating urine to conserve water
options.rationale: A high specific gravity in a dry patient is good news: the kidney is holding water the way it should. The worrying number in dehydration is a low or fixed specific gravity near 1.010, which means the kidney has stopped concentrating and the problem is now the kidney rather than the volume.

questions.takeaway: High and dry is working kidneys. Dilute and dry is kidney failure.
questions.strategy: Read the lab against the patient's volume status, never on its own.

questions.stem: A patient with advanced chronic kidney disease develops confusion, nausea, pruritus and a pericardial friction rub. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: A medication side effect requiring dose adjustment
options.rationale: Near miss concept No drug in the stem, and the constellation is classic uremia.

options.text: An expected progression that will respond to a phosphate binder
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Normalizes a set of findings that mean the patient needs dialysis now.

options.text: Uremic complications, which are an indication for urgent dialysis
options.rationale: When the kidney stops clearing waste, it accumulates and poisons other organs: the brain gives you encephalopathy, the skin itches, the gut rejects food, and the pericardium inflames. Uremic pericarditis is the U in AEIOU and it is a dialysis indication, not a wait and see.

options.text: Anxiety related to the chronic illness
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Explains away confusion in a patient who is encephalopathic.

questions.takeaway: A friction rub in kidney failure is uremic pericarditis. That is a dialysis call.
questions.strategy: The option that normalizes this as expected progression is the trap.

questions.stem: A patient reports flank pain and has a temperature of 38.9 degrees Celsius. The nurse percusses the costovertebral angle and the patient winces sharply. What does this suggest?

options.text: Musculoskeletal back strain
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Explains the pain and ignores the temperature.

options.text: Renal calculi, which typically produce colicky pain without fever
options.rationale: Near miss concept Right about stones and it does not account for the fever.

options.text: Pyelonephritis, which requires cultures and prompt antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: Costovertebral angle tenderness with fever and flank pain is upper urinary tract infection until proven otherwise, and it can go to sepsis quickly. Stones give colicky pain that radiates to the groin, usually without fever unless infection is layered on top. Percuss once and move on; you do not keep testing an inflamed kidney.

options.text: Bladder distention from urinary retention
options.rationale: Near miss concept Produces suprapubic pain and fullness, not CVA tenderness.

questions.takeaway: Flank pain plus fever plus CVA tenderness is a kidney infection, not a back problem.
questions.strategy: The fever is the discriminator. Take it out and two other answers become plausible.

questions.stem: An older man reports that he has been unable to void for 8 hours and has lower abdominal pain. The nurse palpates a firm, distended suprapubic area. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Bladder scan and prepare to catheterize per protocol
options.rationale: This is acute urinary retention, which is painful and backs pressure up toward the kidneys. Confirm the volume with the scanner, then decompress. Benign prostatic hyperplasia is the usual cause in an older man, and comfort measures do not open an obstructed outlet.

options.text: Encourage fluids and ambulation to stimulate voiding
options.rationale: Near miss concept Adds volume above an obstruction.

options.text: Apply a warm compress to the abdomen and reassess in 2 hours
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Comfort for a mechanical problem, plus a two hour delay.

options.text: Document the finding and report it at the change of shift
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Charts an acute problem and hands it off.

questions.takeaway: A distended painful bladder gets decompressed, not encouraged.
questions.strategy: Three options treat this as reluctance to void rather than inability.

questions.stem: An 84 year old nursing home resident with a chronic indwelling catheter has a urinalysis showing bacteria and white cells. She is afebrile, at her baseline mentally, and has no symptoms. What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: No antibiotics, because asymptomatic bacteriuria is not treated
options.rationale: Every long term catheter is colonized, so bacteria and white cells in that urine are expected and mean nothing on their own. Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria produces resistance and C. difficile without benefit. What would change the picture is a symptom: fever, flank pain, new confusion, hypotension. Pregnancy and some urologic procedures are the exceptions where it is treated.

options.text: Catheter removal and replacement before the culture result
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reviewing the need for the catheter is right; swapping it for a positive urinalysis alone is not.

options.text: More fluids and a repeat urinalysis in 48 hours to confirm
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Repeating a test that will be positive again changes nothing.

options.text: Antibiotic treatment, because bacteria in urine mean infection
options.rationale: Near miss concept Bacteriuria without symptoms is colonization, not infection.

questions.takeaway: A colonized catheter plus a positive urinalysis is not an infection. A symptom makes it one.
questions.strategy: The urinalysis is abnormal and the patient is not, which is exactly the trap.

questions.stem: A patient with acute kidney injury has a potassium of 6.4 mEq/L and reports palpitations and muscle weakness. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Encourage fluid intake to dilute the potassium
options.rationale: Near miss concept Does not meaningfully lower serum potassium, and this patient may not be able to excrete the fluid.

options.text: Administer the ordered sodium polystyrene sulfonate
options.rationale: Correct but premature Appropriate, and it works over hours; you need to know the rhythm first.

options.text: Restrict dietary potassium and recheck in the morning
options.rationale: Correct but premature Prevention offered for an acute arrhythmia risk.

options.text: Place the patient on a cardiac monitor
