options.rationale: Potassium kills through the heart, so the first move is to see the rhythm. The monitor tells you whether you have time: peaked T waves and a widening QRS change the plan from binders to calcium right now. Assessment before intervention holds even when the intervention is obviously indicated.

questions.takeaway: The number tells you there is a problem. The monitor tells you how fast.
questions.strategy: Three of these treat the potassium. Only one tells you how much time you have to do it.

questions.stem: A postoperative patient's urine output has been 20 mL per hour for three hours. The bladder scan shows 40 mL. Blood pressure is 88/52 and heart rate is 112. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: An expected postoperative finding requiring no action
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Some output reduction is expected after surgery; this plus hypotension is not.

options.text: Prerenal, from inadequate perfusion
options.rationale: The empty bladder rules out obstruction, and the hypotension with tachycardia points straight at perfusion. Prerenal is the reversible one if you catch it: restore the volume and the urine comes back. Leave it long enough and the ischemia kills tubules and it becomes intrinsic, which does not reverse with fluid.

options.text: Intrinsic, from acute tubular necrosis already established
options.rationale: Correct but premature Possible later; right now the hypotension is the correctable cause.

options.text: Postrenal, from an obstruction below the bladder
options.rationale: Near miss concept The scan shows 40 mL, so nothing is backing up.

questions.takeaway: Prerenal is reversible. It becomes intrinsic if you wait.
questions.strategy: The bladder scan in the stem exists to eliminate one of the three categories for you.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure needs accurate hourly urine output measurement during diuresis. He is alert, continent and able to use a urinal. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Measure output with a urinal; avoid a catheter without a real need
options.rationale: An alert continent patient who can use a urinal does not need a catheter, and accurate measurement is not an indication on its own, because every catheter day raises infection risk and removes a reason to get up. Measured voids plus daily weights give you what you need. Weight is the most reliable fluid indicator and it complements intake and output rather than replacing it.

options.text: Weigh the patient daily instead and stop measuring the output
options.rationale: Near miss concept Weight is the best single indicator and does not replace output during active diuresis.

options.text: Insert a catheter only at night and remove it each morning to limit infection risk
options.rationale: Near miss concept Repeated insertions multiply the infection risk.

options.text: Insert an indwelling catheter to make hourly measurement accurate
options.rationale: Near miss concept Convenience and precision are not indications in a continent patient.

questions.takeaway: Accurate measurement is not a catheter indication when the patient can void.
questions.strategy: The convenience option is the one that causes the next infection.

questions.stem: A patient who was voiding normally has produced 15 mL of urine in the last 4 hours. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Increase the intravenous fluid rate
options.rationale: Correct but premature Right for a prerenal cause and harmful if the problem is downstream.

options.text: Notify the provider that the patient is in acute kidney injury
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Names a diagnosis before ruling out the mechanical cause.

options.text: Draw a serum creatinine
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Confirms injury hours later and changes nothing in the next ten minutes.

options.text: Perform a bladder scan
options.rationale: Sudden oliguria has three possible homes: perfusion, the kidney tissue itself, or obstruction. Obstruction is the one you can find and fix at the bedside in two minutes, and a full bladder answers the question immediately. Giving fluid to an obstructed patient makes it worse, and a creatinine takes hours to tell you something the scanner tells you now.

questions.takeaway: Scan the bladder before you blame the kidney.
questions.strategy: Two of the wrong options treat a cause you have not established yet.

questions.stem: A patient 12 hours after surgery has produced 60 mL of urine in 6 hours. Blood pressure 104/62, heart rate 92, bladder scan 35 mL, creatinine risen from 0.8 to 1.3. She received ketorolac twice and had 90 minutes of intraoperative hypotension. What is the most likely mechanism?

options.text: Chronic kidney disease that the surgery has unmasked
options.rationale: Near miss concept Her baseline creatinine was 0.8, which argues against established chronic disease.

options.text: Prerenal hypoperfusion combined with nephrotoxic injury
options.rationale: Two insults, same patient. Ninety minutes of intraoperative hypotension is a prerenal ischemic hit, and ketorolac is a nonsteroidal that reduces the prostaglandin mediated dilation the kidney uses to protect its own perfusion, so it makes the ischemia worse. The empty bladder rules out obstruction. Real acute kidney injury usually has more than one cause.

options.text: Normal postoperative oliguria needing no intervention
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Some reduction is expected; 10 mL per hour with a rising creatinine is not.

options.text: Postrenal obstruction from a blocked urinary catheter
options.rationale: Near miss concept The scan shows 35 mL, so nothing is backing up.

questions.takeaway: A nonsteroidal during a hypotensive period is a double hit. Neither alone might have done it.
questions.strategy: When a stem lists two exposures, the answer is usually both rather than one.

questions.stem: A patient with stage 5 chronic kidney disease has potassium 6.3 unresponsive to medical therapy, pH 7.19, pulmonary edema despite diuretics, and new confusion with a pericardial friction rub. Select all of the statements that are accurate.

options.text: Further diuretic doses are unlikely to help, because the kidneys cannot respond
options.rationale: He has four of the five AEIOU indications: acidosis, refractory electrolytes, refractory overload and uremic complications in the form of pericarditis and encephalopathy. At this point the medical measures have run out, because every one of them needs functioning kidneys. Oral bicarbonate and dietary restriction are chronic management offered during an emergency.

options.text: The confusion may be uremic encephalopathy
options.rationale: He has four of the five AEIOU indications: acidosis, refractory electrolytes, refractory overload and uremic complications in the form of pericarditis and encephalopathy. At this point the medical measures have run out, because every one of them needs functioning kidneys. Oral bicarbonate and dietary restriction are chronic management offered during an emergency.

options.text: The potassium can be managed with dietary restriction at this point
options.rationale: Correct but premature Diet is prevention; this is 6.3 and already refractory.

options.text: The acidosis should be corrected first with oral bicarbonate
options.rationale: Correct but premature Far too slow at pH 7.19, and it adds a sodium and volume load.

options.text: The friction rub reflects uremic pericarditis
options.rationale: He has four of the five AEIOU indications: acidosis, refractory electrolytes, refractory overload and uremic complications in the form of pericarditis and encephalopathy. At this point the medical measures have run out, because every one of them needs functioning kidneys. Oral bicarbonate and dietary restriction are chronic management offered during an emergency.

options.text: He meets several indications for urgent dialysis
options.rationale: He has four of the five AEIOU indications: acidosis, refractory electrolytes, refractory overload and uremic complications in the form of pericarditis and encephalopathy. At this point the medical measures have run out, because every one of them needs functioning kidneys. Oral bicarbonate and dietary restriction are chronic management offered during an emergency.

questions.takeaway: AEIOU. When several appear at once, the answer is dialysis rather than another drug.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options are correct chronic interventions applied to an acute emergency.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic kidney disease has a potassium of 7.1 mEq/L that has not responded to medical therapy, a pH of 7.18 and pulmonary edema. What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Urgent dialysis
options.rationale: The indications are remembered as AEIOU: acidosis, electrolytes that will not come down, ingestions, overload that will not respond, and uremic complications such as pericarditis or encephalopathy. This patient has three of the five. Diuretics need functioning kidneys, which is the thing that has failed.

options.text: A higher dose of the loop diuretic
options.rationale: Near miss concept Requires a kidney that can respond.

options.text: An increase in the oral phosphate binder
options.rationale: Near miss concept Addresses phosphate, which is not what is threatening him.

options.text: Fluid restriction and a repeat set of labs in the morning
options.rationale: Correct but premature A patient in pulmonary edema at pH 7.18 does not have until morning.

questions.takeaway: AEIOU. When two or three show up at once, the treatment is dialysis, not another drug.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option is a reasonable chronic kidney disease intervention offered in an acute emergency.

questions.stem: A patient is scheduled for a CT scan with contrast. Select all findings the nurse should report before the scan.

options.text: A previous reaction to contrast
options.rationale: Before contrast, the nurse asks about a prior reaction (the strongest predictor), checks creatinine (report 1.5 or higher), holds metformin as ordered and identifies nephrotoxins such as NSAIDs.

options.text: Creatinine of 1.8 mg/dL
options.rationale: Before contrast, the nurse asks about a prior reaction (the strongest predictor), checks creatinine (report 1.5 or higher), holds metformin as ordered and identifies nephrotoxins such as NSAIDs.

options.text: Takes ibuprofen daily for arthritis
options.rationale: Before contrast, the nurse asks about a prior reaction (the strongest predictor), checks creatinine (report 1.5 or higher), holds metformin as ordered and identifies nephrotoxins such as NSAIDs.

options.text: Blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit This is normal.

options.text: Had a light breakfast 6 hours ago
options.rationale: Near miss concept NPO is per protocol and this is not a contraindication by itself.

options.text: Takes metformin daily
options.rationale: Before contrast, the nurse asks about a prior reaction (the strongest predictor), checks creatinine (report 1.5 or higher), holds metformin as ordered and identifies nephrotoxins such as NSAIDs.

questions.takeaway: A prior contrast reaction is the highest risk.
questions.strategy: Keep anything that raises the risk of kidney injury or a reaction.

questions.stem: What is the earliest sign of acute kidney injury?

options.text: A falling hourly urine output
options.rationale: Output below 0.5 mL/kg/hr for 6 hours or more, or below 30 mL an hour, is the earliest sign. The nurse checks the catheter, assesses volume status and reports.

options.text: New confusion and nausea
options.rationale: Correct but premature Uremic symptoms come later as wastes build.

options.text: Dependent edema and crackles
options.rationale: Correct but premature Overload develops as water is retained over time.

options.text: A rising serum potassium level
options.rationale: Correct but premature Potassium rises as filtration falls, after output drops.

questions.takeaway: Output falls first.
questions.strategy: Ask which finding the kidney shows before the blood chemistry changes.

questions.stem: Select all drugs or agents that can injure the kidney.

options.text: Acetaminophen at usual doses
options.rationale: Near miss concept Acetaminophen is the safer analgesic for the kidney.

options.text: Ibuprofen
options.rationale: NSAIDs, iodinated contrast and aminoglycosides such as gentamicin are nephrotoxins. Gentamicin needs peak and trough levels and creatinine checks.

options.text: Normal saline
options.rationale: Near miss concept Saline is used to protect the kidney before contrast.

options.text: Naproxen
options.rationale: NSAIDs, iodinated contrast and aminoglycosides such as gentamicin are nephrotoxins. Gentamicin needs peak and trough levels and creatinine checks.

options.text: Gentamicin
options.rationale: NSAIDs, iodinated contrast and aminoglycosides such as gentamicin are nephrotoxins. Gentamicin needs peak and trough levels and creatinine checks.

options.text: Iodinated contrast
options.rationale: NSAIDs, iodinated contrast and aminoglycosides such as gentamicin are nephrotoxins. Gentamicin needs peak and trough levels and creatinine checks.

questions.takeaway: NSAIDs, contrast and aminoglycosides injure the kidney.
questions.strategy: Recall the three nephrotoxin groups.

questions.stem: Why is metformin held before and after iodinated contrast?

options.text: Metformin blurs the contrast images on the scan.
options.rationale: Near miss concept It does not affect imaging.

options.text: Metformin triggers an allergic reaction to the iodinated contrast.
options.rationale: Near miss concept The concern is kidney injury and lactic acidosis, not allergy.

options.text: If contrast hurts the kidneys, metformin causes lactic acidosis.
options.rationale: Contrast can injure the kidneys, and metformin plus kidney injury can cause lactic acidosis. Metformin is held at least 24 hours before as ordered and restarted only after kidney function is rechecked, at least 48 hours later.

options.text: Metformin raises blood glucose during the scan itself.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Metformin lowers glucose.

questions.takeaway: Restart metformin only after kidney function is rechecked.
questions.strategy: Link the drug to the organ the procedure threatens.

questions.stem: Before a CT with contrast, a patient says, "I am allergic to shellfish." Which action is correct?

options.text: Ignore it, because a shellfish allergy is unrelated to contrast reactions.
options.rationale: Near miss concept All allergies are reported, and the nurse asks about prior contrast reactions.

options.text: Cancel the scan, since shellfish allergy means contrast allergy.
options.rationale: Absolute language A shellfish allergy alone is not a contraindication.

options.text: Report it and ask whether there was a past contrast reaction.
options.rationale: All allergies are asked about and reported. A previous contrast reaction is the strongest predictor of another one; a shellfish allergy alone is not a contraindication.

options.text: Give an antihistamine before the scan without an order.
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Premedication needs an order.

questions.takeaway: Report every allergy; a prior contrast reaction is the real red flag.
questions.strategy: Report the allergy, then ask the question that really predicts risk.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches a patient with a urinary tract infection. Select all correct instructions.

options.text: Drink 2 to 3 L of fluid a day unless restricted
options.rationale: Teaching includes finishing the antibiotic, drinking 2 to 3 L a day, voiding every 3 to 4 hours and before and after intercourse, wiping front to back, avoiding douches and bubble baths, limiting caffeine and alcohol and reporting fever, chills or flank pain.

options.text: Report fever, chills or flank pain
options.rationale: Teaching includes finishing the antibiotic, drinking 2 to 3 L a day, voiding every 3 to 4 hours and before and after intercourse, wiping front to back, avoiding douches and bubble baths, limiting caffeine and alcohol and reporting fever, chills or flank pain.

options.text: Take every dose of the antibiotic even after the burning stops
options.rationale: Teaching includes finishing the antibiotic, drinking 2 to 3 L a day, voiding every 3 to 4 hours and before and after intercourse, wiping front to back, avoiding douches and bubble baths, limiting caffeine and alcohol and reporting fever, chills or flank pain.

options.text: Wipe from front to back
options.rationale: Teaching includes finishing the antibiotic, drinking 2 to 3 L a day, voiding every 3 to 4 hours and before and after intercourse, wiping front to back, avoiding douches and bubble baths, limiting caffeine and alcohol and reporting fever, chills or flank pain.

options.text: Use a bubble bath to soothe the area
options.rationale: Near miss concept Bubble baths irritate the urethra.

options.text: Use cranberry juice instead of the antibiotic
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cranberry never treats an infection.

options.text: Void every 3 to 4 hours
options.rationale: Teaching includes finishing the antibiotic, drinking 2 to 3 L a day, voiding every 3 to 4 hours and before and after intercourse, wiping front to back, avoiding douches and bubble baths, limiting caffeine and alcohol and reporting fever, chills or flank pain.

questions.takeaway: Finish the course; flow flushes bacteria out.
questions.strategy: Keep instructions that remove bacteria or catch a worsening infection.

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate the condition it most suggests.

rows.text: WBC casts in the urine
Cola colored urine and puffy eyes 2 weeks after strep throat
Fever, chills and costovertebral angle tenderness
Red blood cell casts, protein and a positive ASO titer
Burning, urgency and suprapubic pain with no fever

questions.takeaway: Cystitis is a bladder infection with local symptoms and usually no high fever. Pyelonephritis is a kidney infection with fever, chills, flank pain and WBC casts. Glomerulonephritis is immune inflammation of the glomeruli after strep, with cola urine, edema, hypertension, RBC casts and protein. Fever and flank pain move the patient up the tract; strep plus cola urine is glomerulonephritis.
questions.strategy: Sort by location and cause: bladder infection, kidney infection or immune kidney inflammation.

questions.stem: Which meal shows understanding of a low sodium diet?

options.text: Grilled chicken, a baked potato, green beans and fruit
options.rationale: About three quarters of sodium comes from processed and restaurant food. Fresh foods are chosen. "Low sodium" on a label means 140 mg or less per serving.

options.text: Canned vegetable soup with saltine crackers on the side
options.rationale: Near miss concept Canned soup is high in sodium.

options.text: A turkey deli sandwich with pickles and a cup of milk
options.rationale: Near miss concept Deli meat and pickles are high in sodium.

options.text: A frozen low fat dinner with a dinner roll and butter
options.rationale: Near miss concept Low fat does not mean low sodium.

questions.takeaway: Can, package or deli counter means sodium.
questions.strategy: Pick the meal made from fresh, unprocessed food.

questions.stem: During a contrast injection, which findings require the nurse to stop the injection and treat it as a reaction? Select all that apply.

options.text: A metallic taste
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A metallic taste is expected.

options.text: Wheezing
options.rationale: A warm flush and a metallic taste are expected. Hives, wheezing or throat tightness are a reaction: stop, call for help and treat as anaphylaxis.

options.text: A warm flush
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A warm flush is an expected sensation with contrast.

options.text: Hives
options.rationale: A warm flush and a metallic taste are expected. Hives, wheezing or throat tightness are a reaction: stop, call for help and treat as anaphylaxis.

options.text: Throat tightness
options.rationale: A warm flush and a metallic taste are expected. Hives, wheezing or throat tightness are a reaction: stop, call for help and treat as anaphylaxis.

questions.takeaway: Warm flush and metallic taste are expected.
questions.strategy: Separate expected sensations from signs of an allergic reaction.

questions.stem: For each cause of acute kidney injury, indicate where the problem starts.

rows.text: Ibuprofen taken daily
Benign prostatic hyperplasia
A blocked urinary catheter
Hemorrhage after surgery
Iodinated contrast
Septic shock

questions.takeaway: Before the kidney is low perfusion (dehydration, hemorrhage, shock, sepsis, heart failure). In the kidney is direct injury (nephrotoxins, untreated low perfusion, glomerulonephritis). After the kidney is obstruction (BPH, stones, a blocked catheter). Before, in or after: perfusion, injury or obstruction.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the problem is blood getting in, the kidney itself or urine getting out.

questions.stem: A patient with rising creatinine takes ibuprofen daily for arthritis. Which analgesic is safer for the kidneys?

options.text: Ketorolac
options.rationale: Near miss concept Ketorolac is an NSAID.

options.text: Naproxen
options.rationale: Near miss concept Naproxen is also an NSAID and a nephrotoxin.

options.text: Higher dose ibuprofen taken less often
options.rationale: Near miss concept The drug is still nephrotoxic.

options.text: Acetaminophen
options.rationale: NSAIDs constrict the vessels into the glomerulus, worst in older or dehydrated patients or with an ACE inhibitor plus a diuretic. Acetaminophen is the safer analgesic for the kidney.

questions.takeaway: Over the counter does not mean safe for the kidney.
questions.strategy: Eliminate every NSAID first.

questions.stem: An older adult has a creatinine of 1.1 mg/dL. A year ago it was 0.6 mg/dL. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: Creatinine is not a useful test in older adults at all.
options.rationale: Absolute language It is useful when trended against the patient's baseline.

options.text: It looks normal but may hide real loss, given less muscle.
options.rationale: Creatinine comes from muscle. Older adults have less muscle, so a normal looking creatinine can hide real loss. Trend it.

options.text: The value is falsely high from too much muscle mass.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Older adults usually have less muscle, not more.

options.text: The kidney function is normal for an older adult.
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data A normal looking creatinine can hide loss in a patient with less muscle.

questions.takeaway: Trend creatinine; a normal value can hide loss in older adults.
questions.strategy: Compare with the patient's own baseline.

questions.stem: A patient with acute kidney injury has a potassium of 6.1 mEq/L. Select all appropriate nursing actions.

options.text: Teach the patient to avoid salt substitutes
options.rationale: The kidney is the main route out for potassium. A high level causes peaked T waves and dysrhythmias, so the nurse monitors, holds potassium sources and reports.

options.text: Place the patient on a cardiac monitor
options.rationale: The kidney is the main route out for potassium. A high level causes peaked T waves and dysrhythmias, so the nurse monitors, holds potassium sources and reports.

options.text: Encourage bananas and oranges
options.rationale: Near miss concept These are high in potassium.

options.text: Report the potassium level
options.rationale: The kidney is the main route out for potassium. A high level causes peaked T waves and dysrhythmias, so the nurse monitors, holds potassium sources and reports.

options.text: Give the scheduled potassium chloride
options.rationale: Near miss concept Giving potassium would raise it further.

options.text: Hold potassium supplements
options.rationale: The kidney is the main route out for potassium. A high level causes peaked T waves and dysrhythmias, so the nurse monitors, holds potassium sources and reports.

questions.takeaway: High potassium is a cardiac problem.
questions.strategy: Remove every source of potassium and watch the heart.

questions.stem: A patient with acute glomerulonephritis had a urine output of 400 mL yesterday. What is today's fluid allowance?

options.text: 900 mL
options.rationale: Fluid allowance = previous 24 hour output + 500 mL. 400 + 500 = 900 mL.
Near miss concept That is a normal daily output, not the formula.

options.text: 400 mL
options.rationale: Near miss concept The allowance adds 500 mL to the previous output to cover insensible loss.
Near miss concept This would worsen fluid overload.

questions.takeaway: Output plus 500.
questions.strategy: Apply the formula before reading the options.

questions.stem: A patient's creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 1.8 mg/dL in 2 days. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: The patient is dehydrated, so IV fluids alone will fix it.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dehydration can raise BUN, but a doubled creatinine shows real loss of filtration.

options.text: About half of filtration has been lost; report the rise.
options.rationale: Creatinine is not reabsorbed, so it tracks filtration. A doubled creatinine means about half the filtration is gone. A rise of 1.5 times baseline is reported.

options.text: The patient ate too much protein over the past two days.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Protein raises BUN, not creatinine.

options.text: Kidney function is still within the normal reference range.
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data A doubled creatinine is a major loss even when the value looks modest.

questions.takeaway: A doubled creatinine means half the filtration is gone.
questions.strategy: Compare with the baseline, not with the normal range.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of catheter trauma reports a weak stream, straining and frequent UTIs. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Normal age related urinary changes
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A weak stream with straining and recurrent infection is a finding to investigate.

options.text: A urethral stricture with stasis
options.rationale: A stricture is scar tissue after an STI, catheter trauma or instrumentation. It causes a weak stream, straining and incomplete emptying, and stasis brings recurrent infection.

options.text: Acute glomerulonephritis
options.rationale: Near miss concept Glomerulonephritis does not cause a weak stream.

options.text: Stress urinary incontinence
options.rationale: Near miss concept Stress incontinence causes leaks with coughing, not a weak stream.

questions.takeaway: Stasis brings recurrent infection.
questions.strategy: Link the history of trauma to the scar.

questions.stem: A patient has had four urinary tract infections this year. What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: A permanent indwelling catheter to drain the bladder
options.rationale: Near miss concept A catheter raises infection risk.

options.text: Long term cranberry juice as the primary treatment
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cranberry never treats an infection.

options.text: A workup, often cystoscopy once the urine is sterile
options.rationale: More than three UTIs a year needs a workup, often cystoscopy, to look for a cause such as a stricture causing stasis.

options.text: No further action, because UTIs are common in adults
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem More than three a year needs a workup.

questions.takeaway: More than three UTIs a year means look for a cause.
questions.strategy: Recurrent problems point to an underlying cause.

questions.stem: A patient had strep throat 2 weeks ago. Select all findings that suggest acute glomerulonephritis.

options.text: Burning and urgency with no other findings
options.rationale: Near miss concept That suggests cystitis.

options.text: Swelling around the eyes
options.rationale: Glomerulonephritis is immune inflammation of the glomeruli 1 to 3 weeks after strep throat or impetigo. It causes cola or tea colored urine, protein (foamy urine), periorbital and facial edema, hypertension, low output and weight gain.

options.text: Blood pressure 162/98 mm Hg
options.rationale: Glomerulonephritis is immune inflammation of the glomeruli 1 to 3 weeks after strep throat or impetigo. It causes cola or tea colored urine, protein (foamy urine), periorbital and facial edema, hypertension, low output and weight gain.

options.text: Low urine output
options.rationale: Glomerulonephritis is immune inflammation of the glomeruli 1 to 3 weeks after strep throat or impetigo. It causes cola or tea colored urine, protein (foamy urine), periorbital and facial edema, hypertension, low output and weight gain.

options.text: Cola colored urine
options.rationale: Glomerulonephritis is immune inflammation of the glomeruli 1 to 3 weeks after strep throat or impetigo. It causes cola or tea colored urine, protein (foamy urine), periorbital and facial edema, hypertension, low output and weight gain.

options.text: Fever with flank pain and WBC casts
options.rationale: Near miss concept That suggests pyelonephritis, a kidney infection.

options.text: Foamy urine
options.rationale: Glomerulonephritis is immune inflammation of the glomeruli 1 to 3 weeks after strep throat or impetigo. It causes cola or tea colored urine, protein (foamy urine), periorbital and facial edema, hypertension, low output and weight gain.

questions.takeaway: Glomerulonephritis is immune, not an infection of the kidney.
questions.strategy: Keep findings of blood, protein and fluid retention; drop signs of infection.

questions.stem: A patient has a BUN of 38 mg/dL and a creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL. Which explanation is most likely?

options.text: Liver failure reducing urea production
options.rationale: Near miss concept Liver failure lowers BUN.

options.text: Dehydration, GI bleeding or high protein
options.rationale: BUN rises with dehydration, GI bleeding and high protein intake even with a normal creatinine. Creatinine is the best marker of kidney function.

options.text: A laboratory error in the BUN result
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data A high BUN with normal creatinine has common, real causes.

options.text: Acute kidney injury affecting filtration
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism A high BUN alone is not kidney injury when the creatinine is normal.

questions.takeaway: A high BUN alone is not kidney injury.
questions.strategy: Trust creatinine for filtration.

questions.stem: A patient taking phenazopyridine says, "The burning stopped, so I can stop my antibiotic." Which response is best?

options.text: "Stop the phenazopyridine instead and keep the antibiotic."
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question This does not correct the plan to stop the antibiotic.

options.text: "That is fine, as long as the burning does not come back."
options.rationale: Absolute language Stopping early lets surviving bacteria return and resistance grow.

options.text: "The orange urine shows that the infection has cleared."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Orange urine is a harmless drug effect.

options.text: "That pill only numbs; the antibiotic still clears the infection."
options.rationale: Phenazopyridine is a urinary analgesic that masks pain but treats nothing. It turns urine bright orange. The antibiotic is finished.

questions.takeaway: Phenazopyridine masks the pain, not the infection.
questions.strategy: Choose the response that corrects the dangerous plan.

questions.stem: An older adult with pyelonephritis becomes newly confused. The blood pressure has fallen from 132/80 to 98/60 mm Hg and the heart rate is 112/min. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: A side effect of the antibiotic
options.rationale: Near miss concept The cluster points to sepsis, not a drug effect.

options.text: Dehydration from fever
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fluid loss may contribute, but infection with organ dysfunction is sepsis.

options.text: Expected confusion from a UTI
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Confusion can be the only sign of a UTI in older adults, but with a falling pressure and rising heart rate it signals sepsis.

options.text: Urosepsis
options.rationale: In pyelonephritis, falling blood pressure, rising heart rate and confusion signal urosepsis, which is reported first.

questions.takeaway: New confusion with falling BP in a kidney infection is urosepsis.
questions.strategy: When infection plus organ changes appear, think sepsis.

questions.stem: A patient being treated for cystitis develops a temperature of 38.6 °C and right flank pain on day 2. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Encourage the patient to finish the antibiotic course and recheck in 3 days.
options.rationale: Correct but premature Fever and flank pain suggest the infection has moved to the kidney.

options.text: Increase cranberry juice intake.
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cranberry may help prevent UTIs but never treats them.

options.text: Give acetaminophen and document the fever.
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Treating the fever does not address a kidney infection.

options.text: Report the findings to the provider now.
options.rationale: Fever and flank pain move the patient up the tract to pyelonephritis, which often needs IV antibiotics. It is reported now.

questions.takeaway: Fever and flank pain move the patient up the tract.
questions.strategy: A new systemic sign means the infection has changed. Report it.

questions.stem: A patient started phenazopyridine this morning and says, "My urine is bright orange. Am I bleeding?" Which response is best?

options.text: "Orange urine is expected; it can stain clothes and contacts."
options.rationale: Phenazopyridine turns urine bright orange. It is expected and stains clothing and contact lenses.

options.text: "Collect a urine sample so we can test it for blood."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Orange urine is expected with this drug.

options.text: "Drink less fluid today until the color clears up."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fluids help flush the infection.

options.text: "Stop the medicine now and call your provider today."
options.rationale: Near miss concept There is no reason to stop.

questions.takeaway: Orange urine on phenazopyridine is expected.
questions.strategy: Recognize an expected drug effect before treating it as a problem.
